en: Aparārka [869]: The third [section] in the Yājñavalkyasmṛti with its commentary.
The Chapter on Expiation;
therein, the Section on Impurity. (1)

In the preceding two chapters, the duties (*dharma*) of the social classes (*varṇas*) and of the two stages of life (*āśramas*), namely the student (*brahmacārin*) and the householder (*gṛhastha*), have been declared. Now, this new chapter is commenced for the purpose of determining both that cause by which the householder lacks eligibility regarding his own specific duties, and those duties to which he remains eligible when that [cause] exists. This being the case, the entire body of matters to be discussed hereafter attains the status of being the subject matter of a single chapter. To illustrate: in the section on impurity (*āśauca*), there is a three-night period of ineligibility caused by the birth or death of a *sapiṇḍa* relative; [conversely, there is eligibility for the mass of ritual acts such as the cremation of the corpse of a deceased *sapiṇḍa*]. Similarly, when one has fallen into distress and must subsist by the conduct of others, there is eligibility for the occupations prescribed for lower castes, such as weaponry or agriculture; likewise, while living, there is ineligibility for one's own usual means of livelihood, such as receiving gifts (*pratigraha*). Furthermore, for one who intends to combine all the stages of life, there is ineligibility for the householder’s state at the end of twenty-five years of domestic life, and instead, there is eligibility for the state of a forest-dweller (*vanastha*). Thus, having spent the third part of one’s life in the forest-dwelling stage, one should not remain a forest-dweller, but rather become a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*). Upon falling from one’s caste (*pātitya*), there is ineligibility for the rites of the twice-born; and as a corollary to that, even though there is no ineligibility for performing rites during minor offenses (*upapātaka*), it is precisely penance (*prāyaścitta*) that is ordained—thus the entirety of this chapter constitutes its subject matter. Although both loss of caste and penance apply equally to members of all stages of life, nevertheless, since these conditions also affect the householder, it is appropriate to discuss them here in this very chapter by way of incidental connection (*prasaṅga*).
One should bury a child less than two years old and should not offer water for it thereafter;
another who has died should be followed by his kinsmen as far as the cremation ground.

He should be cremated with a worldly fire by those reciting the Yama-sūkta and the Gāthās, provided he has entered [the order], in accordance with the procedure for one who maintained the sacred fires, as if he were still alive.

There are these four statements: regarding one who has died with less than two years having elapsed, a father or a close relative should bury him; having dug the earth and placed him therein, they should fill it up. In this matter, there is a specific rule from Manu: "Relatives should place a deceased child under two years of age outside, having adorned him, in pure ground, except for the collection of bones. [870]

The plural number in the word *bāndhavāḥ* (relatives) is not intended to be restrictive; the meaning is "outside the village. Having adorned the deceased with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, they should place him on pure, uncontaminated ground. This means that, except for the collection of bones (*asthisaṃcaya*), they should not perform the rite of bone-collection. It does not mean that they should place him on any ground where the collection of bones has not been performed, for that is already established by the requirement that the ground be "pure. Yama says:
"One should bury a deceased child less than two years old in the earth, smeared with clarified butter, while singing the verses of Yama and recollecting the *Yamasūkta*."
Manu says:
One should carry out a deceased Śūdra through the southern gate of the city;
but the twice-born [castes] should be carried out through the western, northern, or eastern gates, according to their respective order.
The word "to be carried out" (*nirharaṇīyāḥ*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. This refers to the sequence of castes in reverse order. Thus, the *Ādipurāṇa* states:
"A Brāhmaṇa should be led from the house by his kinsmen facing east;
a Kṣatriya facing north, and likewise a Vaiśya facing west."
"A Śūdra should be carried out facing south by his own kinsmen.

In the absence of kinsmen, others may carry him out. Regarding this, there is a specific rule from Manu: "While one's own [kinsmen] are present, one must not have a deceased Brāhmaṇa carried away by a Śūdra."
"For that oblation, defiled by the touch of a Śūdra, would not lead to heaven. [This refers to] among one's own twice-born [relatives]. Hārīta says:
"One should not perform the water-libation for a deceased person facing toward a village, nor should one do so thereafter."

Immediately after the burial, one should not perform the water libation; however, one must certainly perform a bath for the sake of purification. Furthermore, the prohibition of the water libation is intended to demonstrate the prohibition of all funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*). Thus says Manu regarding those who have not reached two years of age: "No consecration by fire should be performed for him, nor should the water rite be performed; having abandoned him like a piece of wood in the forest, one should simply leave him for three days."

Because of the statement "like a piece of wood," when all post-mortem rites (*aurdhvadaihika*) have been completed, the burial of a child less than two years old who has not undergone the tonsure ceremony (*acūḍaka*), as well as the prohibition of water-libations, are optional. For Laugākṣi says:
"One should perform the water-libation silently and the funeral rite (*saṃskāra*) also silently;
for all those who have undergone the tonsure ceremony, both may be performed at one's own will even in other cases. [871]

The meaning is: "except in the case of those whose *cūḍā* ceremony has not been performed. And thus, the rule "one should bury a child less than two years old" should be understood as referring specifically to those for whom the *cūḍā* has not been performed. For indeed, the *cūḍā-karman* may take place even in the first year. Furthermore, for one whose *cūḍā* has not been performed, there is an option regarding the consecration by fire (*agnisaṃskāra*), but this applies only after the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*). As Manu says: "The relatives need not perform the water-libation rite for a child under three years of age;
however, they may do so once the teeth have appeared, or when the naming has been performed."

One should perform the water-libation and the cremation rites because they are invariably required. Regarding the phrase "until the cemetery": another [child] who has died at less than two full years of age should be followed by his kinsmen and *sapiṇḍas* as far as the ground of the cemetery for the funeral rites. Then, while reciting the sixteen-verse hymn addressed to Yama seen by Yama himself, beginning with "pareyivāṃsam," which is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and dedicated to Yama, and the three verses addressed to Yama beginning with "yo 'sya kauṣṭhya jagataḥ," he should be cremated using common, unrefined fire. If one who has been initiated (*upanīta*) dies, then he should be cremated in such a way that the funeral rites—specifically those belonging to one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*)—are performed effectively so that their purpose is not lost. There is an omission of the sacrificial vessels, cups, and so forth, whose purposes have been superseded, but there is the performance of other ritual items such as the oblations (*homa*). Thus says Yama.
If a Śūdra brings fire, grass, wood, and sacrificial oblations for someone,
that person shall always remain in the state of a ghost, and he too is defiled by unrighteousness.
The meaning is that he is a Śūdra. Prajāpati [says]: "The bathing of the deceased should be performed by the son or others, followed by honoring with garments and such;
one must never burn the body naked, and nothing at all should be abandoned."

The meaning is that bathing and worship must be performed. One should discard any garment that is renowned in the world as being [consecrated] to a deity, as well as those belonging to outcastes (caṇḍāla) and others. Hārīta states:
"For the removal of the corpse and other rites for a deceased kinsman (sapiṇḍa) are prescribed;
there would be fault for one who is not a sapiṇḍa, except in the case of performing the funeral rites for one who has no protector."
Except for the five stars of Dhaniṣṭhā, one should place the five jewels in its mouth;
the performer should offer three oblations, saying, "Carry the omentum! (vaha vapām).
O Jātavedas, carry this omentum to the ancestors where you know them to be established in the distance;
let streams of fat flow from the sacrificial vessel, and may these blessings be fulfilled according to our desires.
Carry food, O Jātavedas, to the ancestors where you know them to be placed in the distance;
let streams of food flow toward them, and may these blessings be fulfilled according to our desires.
Carry this flesh, O Jātavedas, to the ancestors where you know them to be stationed in the distance;
let streams of flesh flow toward them, and may these blessings come true according to our desires.
Then one should perform the removal and cremate him according to the prescribed rule;
as for the other [the child], one should simply bury him or consign him to the water.
Likewise, excluding the three pādas and the nakṣatra, one should place a piece of gold in the mouth and then fashion three human figures made of flour.
One should perform the oblation facing [the deity], with the mantra "Then, O Fire, carry the omentum";
and having placed safflower along with cotton into the very mouth [of the fire].
Having brought him out, one should perform the funeral rites with the sacred fire, or otherwise, one should discard another [fire] upon the ground.
Another Smṛti states:
"Gold, diamond, sapphire, ruby,
together with pearl— these are declared by the all-seeing sages to be the five jewels."
Or, in the absence of gems,
a wise person should employ gold there according to his ability, whether it be one *karṣa* or even half a *karṣa*.
But wherever fragments of gold are not found,
one should bring clarified butter (ājya) to those places, according to the illustration of the mantra "tajo 'si."
The locus of action:
Punarvasu, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Kṛttikā, Uttaraphālgunī,
Pūrvabhādrapadā, and Viśākhā— this is to be known as Tripuṣkara.
And from the *Sārāvalī*:
"If an odd-footed lunar mansion (*dhiṣṇya*) and the lunar day (*tithi*) Bhadrā coincide with any day whatsoever of Saturn, the Sun, Jupiter, or Mars..."
This yoga, known as Tripuṣkara, has been proclaimed by the sages;
it yields a threefold fruit whether [the object] is acquired, lost, stolen, or even deceased.
The second, seventh, sixth, twelfth, tenth, eighth,
and ninth lunar days correspond respectively to Jupiter, Mercury, Venus, Saturn, Mars, and the Moon.
Whatever is lost, stolen, gained, or whatever other cause there may be—all that is said to possess the three qualities (guṇas); therefore, this is called Tripuṣkara.

Viṣṇu: "One should not have a deceased twice-born man carried out by a Śūdra, nor a Śūdra by a twice-born man. Sons should carry out their father and mother, but a Śūdra should not carry out even a twice-born father. Kātyāyana: "If the householder becomes weak after the evening oblation has been offered, the morning oblation should take place at that very time, whether he lives until tomorrow or not."
Having bathed the weak person and clothed him in clean garments,
one should place him on the ground covered with *barhis* grass, with his head toward the south.
Having bathed him who is anointed with ghee and wears a clean cloth as a sacred thread,
his entire body sprinkled with sandalwood paste and adorned with flowers;
Having thrown pieces of gold into its seven principal apertures and then having covered it, his sons and other relatives should carry it out.
Taking food in an unbaked clay vessel, one person should follow behind the deceased who is preceded by the fire;
he should discard half of that food on the ground along the way.
Having reached the cremation ground, he should sit facing south;
slowly placing his left knee on the ground, he should offer [the water] with sesame seeds, just as in the rite of offering rice-balls (piṇḍa).
Taking half of that food, one person should follow the deceased; another should discard that other half on the ground along the path. *Ādahana* means the cremation ground. Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya says:
One who maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should be cremated according to rule with the three fires;
one who did not maintain the sacred fires with a single [fire]; and any other person with a common worldly fire.

The meaning is "with one fire from the household. And the worldly fire (*laukika-agni*) is to be taken when the two kindling-sticks (*araṇī*) are absent; but when they are present, it must be the fire produced by friction alone. Regarding the case of using the worldly fire, Devala states the specific rule:

"The fire of a *caṇḍāla*, the fire of impurity (*amedhya*), the fire of a woman who has recently given birth, the fire of an outcast (*patita*), and the fire of a funeral pyre—these are never fit for being taken up by the learned (*śiṣṭa*). (3.1, 2)
When the corpse has been brought and placed [on the pyre], he prescribes the subsequent rites:
"On the seventh or even the tenth day, the kinsmen, facing the direction of the ancestors, approach the water with the mantra, 'May the sin burn away from us' (RV X.97.16). (3.3)

Relatives—both those who share the funeral cake (sapinda) and those for whom water is offered (samānodaka)—should, for seven or ten days, bathe and approach the water with their faces turned toward the direction of the ancestors, that is, facing south, in order to offer water to the deceased. Having gone there, they should bathe and offer water with the Gāyatrī verse beginning with *apa naḥ śośucad agham*, which was seen by Kutsa and is addressed either to Agni or to the Waters. (3.3)
He states an extension of this rule to those who are not kinsmen:

"In the same way, the water-rite is performed for deceased maternal grandfathers, teachers, friends, married daughters, sisters' sons, fathers-in-law, and officiating priests; [the offering] is according to one's desire. (3.4)

The water-rite (*udakakriyā*) for deceased maternal grandfathers and others should be performed by their daughters' sons and other descendants in the manner previously described; for friends and the like, one may offer *kāmodaka* (water out of affection). This means that if one desires to give water, one should do so. A "married daughter" (*prattā*) refers to a daughter who has undergone the marriage ceremony. Pāraskara states: "Water may be offered out of affection to the officiating priest, the father-in-law, a friend, a maternal uncle, and a sister's son. (3.4)
He states the ritual procedure for the offering of water:
"Restraining their speech, they should pour water once, [addressing the deceased] by name and lineage.

Relatives and others should, day after day, pour water once—meaning a single time—for as many [deceased ancestors] as have been specified, restraining their speech while using both the name and the lineage. Kātyāyana says:
Then, all those who have touched the corpse, having gone to water without hesitation,
shall bathe with their clothes on, sip water, and offer water for him on dry ground.
And at the end of the name of each lineage, saying "I satisfy," he should place kuśa grass with its tips pointing south, along with sesame seeds, separately for each.

Viṣṇu: "Having carried out the deceased and performed the cremation rites, the relatives should approach the funeral pyre in a counter-clockwise direction and immerse themselves in water while still wearing their clothes. Having offered the water libation for the deceased, they should offer a single rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) upon *kuśa* grass. Vasiṣṭha: "They should perform the water rite with the left hand uppermost; being an odd number, they should face the south. Baijavāpa: "Having gone to the edge of the water and wiped themselves once, they scratch the water with the little finger of the left hand, saying, 'May the least sin be removed. Upon that [spot], they should offer a single handful of water to the deceased, saying, 'Svadhā to such-and-such a person. Hārīta: "Having departed, performed the cremation, and gone to the water to bathe, they pour out a handful of water, saying, 'May he be satisfied. The phrase "having departed" means having departed from the village. Paiṭhīnasi: "Meditating on the deceased in his mind and facing the south, he should pour out three handfuls of water. Regarding the impurity caused by death, he should cease [the ritual] on the eleventh day. Pracetā: [The same as Paiṭhīnasi.]
Day by day, one should offer full handfuls for the sake of the deceased;
the increase [of the offerings] should be continued until the funeral cake (piṇḍa) is completed.

Gautama states: "The water-rites are performed on the first, third, seventh, and ninth days. Pracetas says: "The relatives of the deceased, descending into the water in order of seniority, should approach the water; at the water's edge, having placed their sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and garments over the right shoulder (*aprasavya*), facing south for a Brāhmaṇa, north for a Kṣatriya, and east for a Vaiśya, they should offer water and the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to the deceased for as long as the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts. From the Ādi Purāṇa: "At the beginning, however, having washed the garment, they should then [perform the rites] while covered by that very [garment]."
However, one must perform a bath with one's clothes on, which removes all impurities.
Then, on a stone surface, water with sesame seeds (tilodaka) should be offered by all;
ten handfuls (añjali) should be given to each individual Brahmin.
Twelve [handfuls] should be given for a Kṣatriya, fifteen for a Vaiśya,
and thirty should be given for a Śūdra who has gone to the land of the deceased.
Having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder with their garments in some cases,
the Brahmins, facing south, should offer three handfuls of water.

Then, by means of the flow from the left thumb, either upon the ground or in some other place, one should recite this while saying: "May this deceased person of such-and-such lineage be satisfied by this."

In this context, the offering of ten or more handfuls (*añjali*) of water to the Brahmins and others constitutes one ritual act, whereas the offering of three handfuls is a separate ritual act. Alternatively, the handful of water may be offered to him every day or in its entirety. In this case, the mantra is: "May this deceased person (*preta*), belonging to such-and-such a lineage (*gotra*), be satisfied. Śaṅkha states: "The kinsmen of the deceased, descending into the water in order of seniority, should pray for water with the words *'apa naḥ'*, and they should pour out water once, facing the right. The Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas do exactly the same. Having placed their garment and sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) in their joined palms (*añjali*), and having said, 'O [Name], this is the water,' they should emerge from there, discard the clothes touched by the deceased, and put on other garments. It should be understood that the prescription regarding the names and the number of handfuls is intended to provide a greater benefit to the deceased. In the *Rāmāyaṇa*, Rāma speaks the formula for the offering of water.
O tiger among men, may this pure, divine,
and inexhaustible water, given by me, attend upon you in all the worlds.
Likewise, Bharata, together with his friends, all the citizens, his ministers, and his family priest, offered libations to his father.
"He gratified the king with water according to the prescribed ritual. Thus [it is said]. Another Smṛti states:
"Having bathed with one's clothes on, having touched fire, and having consumed clarified butter, [one should offer oblations] separately on odd-numbered days."
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītin), facing south, they [should recite] the names and lineages.
They should offer water for the deceased in the water at midday until the period of impurity ends.
Regarding this, he states an exception: "Students of sacred knowledge (brahmacārins) and those who have fallen from their status (patitas) shall not perform the water-libation. (3.5)

Even though they are *sapiṇḍas* or *sodakas*, celibate students (*brahmacārins*) shall not offer water to the deceased; likewise, those who are outcasts (*patitas*), whose characteristics will be described later. Regarding this, Manu states a specific rule:
"One who has been initiated for a vow shall not offer water until the completion of that vow;
but when it is completed, having offered water, he shall remain impure for three nights."
"Bound by a vow" refers to the student (*brahmacārī*); the meaning is "until the completion of his vow," that is, until his formal return home (*samāvartana*). || 3.5 ||

Now he states an exception regarding the status of certain individuals as recipients of water offerings and as objects of the rite of impurity: Heretics, thieves, those who kill their husbands, those who have sexual relations at will, those who drink liquor, and women who commit suicide are not entitled to the period of impurity nor to the offering of water. (3.6)

Those who have resorted to heretics such as the Baudhas and entered their initiation; thieves, meaning robbers; and women who are murderers of their husbands, promiscuous, or wanton—by the word "and so forth" (ādi), those who kill their own embryos or Brahmins and others of that sort are included; as well as those who drink liquor and those who commit suicide, which are well known. Those who have resorted to heretics and the rest do not become eligible for the impurity—which will be described as removable after three nights and so on—nor for the offering of water, because they are not [proper] relatives. The meaning is that when these persons have died, the sapindas should not perform the rites of impurity and so forth upon the death of these [others], nor should these [persons] perform them upon the death of a sapinda. Thus says Vriddha-Manu:

Eunuchs and the like, thieves, those who have violated their vows, those who perform forbidden acts, those who harm the fetus or their master, and women who drink liquor shall not offer water libations.

The mention of those who drink *surā* is repeated for the purpose of prohibiting the offering of water to them, since they have already fallen from their status (*pātitya*) and are thus barred from receiving such offerings. Even in the case of specific modes of death, water should not be offered. As Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya says: "Those killed by lightning, a cow, a king, a Brahmin, water, a horned animal, a fanged beast, fire, or those who die in vain, as well as the great eunuch and one who has taken a vow—these are not worthy of the water offering."

One devoid of the *liṅga* is a great eunuch; one who observes vows is a great ascetic (*mahāvratin*) and so forth, or a heretic (*pāṣaṇḍin*). Yama says: "Death for those of evil deeds comes from a *caṇḍāla*, from water, from a serpent, from a Brāhmaṇa, from lightning, and also from fanged beasts."
Whatever water and offerings of rice balls are given to the departed spirits, none of that remains; it perishes in mid-air.
For those slain by the rod of Brahman, one should perform no impurity-rite, nor offer water, nor shed tears, nor perform cremation or other such rites, nor carry the funeral bier.

The "brahmadaṇḍa" is the curse of a Brahmin. A "kaṭa" is a bier for a corpse. Āpastamba says: "If one here should cause his own death by means of fire, water, or other such means, for him no period of impurity is prescribed, nor is the performance of water-libations required."
Manu says:
"The water-rite should be withheld for those born of mixed unions, for those who persist in wandering asceticism,
and for those who commit suicide."

Because it is undertaken by one's own volition (*svayaṃ-grahaṇāt*), it is understood that one has proceeded out of passion (*rāgataḥ*) and not according to scriptural injunction (*vidhitaḥ*). For this very reason, Gautama states: "If [they die] by means of fasting, starvation, weapons, fire, poison, water, hanging, or departure [to the forest], [this applies] to those who so desire. By the specific inclusion of the term "those who desire," it follows that there is no fault in the case of those who have died through negligence or even according to scriptural injunction. And likewise, Aṅgiras says:

"Now, if someone should die through negligence by means of fire, water, or the like, their period of impurity (*aśauca*) must be prescribed and the water-libation rites (*udaka-kriyā*) must be performed."
Negligence (*pramāda*) is a lack of attentiveness. Furthermore, there exists an injunction regarding expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and so forth; likewise, the *Ādipurāṇa* states:
"If a man is afflicted by incurable and great diseases, he may enter a blazing fire or likewise practice fasting."
Or one should go with devotion to a fathomless mass of water, or likewise to a precipice from which one leaps,
or even to the Great Path, or to the Snowy Mountain.
Or the high-minded one, when the time for the destruction of his body has arrived, effects the abandonment of the body at the branch of the banyan tree at Prayāga.
He shall attain the highest worlds and shall never be a self-killer;
through the destruction of great sins, he enjoys divine pleasures in heaven.
The eligibility for these, however, belongs to all living beings—
both men and women, and at all times, across all social classes.
If such a corpse should occur among those who are otherwise living,
their period of impurity shall last for three days, as it would in the case of death caused by lightning or fire.
He who dies in Vārāṇasī after having rejected medical treatment,
staying amidst wood and stone while standing in the midst of the waters of the Ganges;
Hara, standing at the root of his ear, facing one whose mind is directed toward liberation, utters the *praṇava*, the saving mantra; it is never otherwise for anyone, anywhere.
Likewise: To the eastern half of Vṛddhatīrtha, but to the west of the Gaṅgā,
is the meritorious Agnitīrtha, situated below Vṛddhatīrtha.
That place where the flames of Indra’s thunderbolt and other such [fires] are seen is not easily found by mortals, and they do not find it.
Or if some person, a bull among men, should obtain favor, he attains liberation by means of his own body; this I tell you as the truth.
Whether he be old, or a child, or even a man in the prime of youth,
whoever should cast off his body there must do so with his whole soul and without fear.
Having pierced through the solar orb, he too shall go to liberation;
this sacred ford is indestructible, for Hari is eternally present there.
If even an atom of sin is committed in the absence of Viśoka,
one shall surely cross over it— even if it be as vast as Mount Meru— by virtue of the presence of the sacred field’s greatness.
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid evil in that regard.
Likewise:
Hereafter I shall declare what the destination becomes for men through the abandonment of the body at Vṛddhatīrtha, situated to the south.
Having reached the Gate of Heaven, clothed in clean garments,
and having gone to the stone marked with the deer, he [should enter] by that very Gate of Heaven.
Then, having reached the celestial stone, that best of men of meritorious deeds,
having renounced his life and resorted to fortitude, there prays for a boon.
First, one should bow to the God and likewise to the Tīrtha worshipped by the gods:
"Oṃ, salutations to you who are named Viśvarūpa, the sorrowless one, the source of the universe!"
Salutations to you, the path to liberation, the supreme, the Supreme Self;
salutations to Viṣṇu, who has a golden navel and the head of a horse.
May the holy ford Ajatuṅga protect me from destruction;
and may Viṣṇu protect me from sorrow, just as that holy ford is free from ailment.
This is my request: let this boon be granted—let [the story] be heard.
Terrified by this, I am fainting on the great road of the path of the fathers, struck by a thousand blows of the staff;
I offer up that body, which was colored by the threefold passion and destroyed, out of fear of death.
Just as Puṇya is a great sacred ford, and just as Mount Naubandhana is a mountain,
by that truth may there be for me liberation from the body, which is imperishable.
"Having thus recollected this supreme mantra and abandoned the body in a body of water,
by virtue of the recollection of that mantra as well as of the tying of the boat, he pierces the solar orb and merges into the Supreme Brahman. Thus it is said.
[Vṛddhatīrtha and other such sites are to be known as being at the foot of Mount Nau-badha in the land of Kaśmīra.
Likewise: subsisting on alms, abstaining from food, eating sparingly, and free from longing.
By ceasing all dualities, a person should not dwell there.
Stainless, free from passion, a Brahmin, devoid of evil, and resembling the sky;
he attains fame in this world and eternal heaven after death.
Likewise,
the Great Departure (Mahāprasthāna) journey must be undertaken upon the snow;
relying upon courage and fortitude, it bestows heaven immediately.
As long as Purandara has not been born in the world due to the gravity of his task,
who indeed would venture to cast off their body amidst the frost?
But when he, consumed by the cold, becomes unconscious and releases his life-breaths,
he shall behold the blazing fire with its flames turning to the right.
The body of Viṣṇu as Saṃkarṣaṇa is a consuming fire like a fierce conflagration.
Vivasvān [said]: "For one who is detached from all the senses and incapable of their own functions..."
The prescribed atonement is falling into fire or walking along the great highway.
Even for a Brāhmaṇa who is incapable of acquiring merit, who is stained by sin, and who is the perpetrator of such acts, the relinquishing of life at a sacred ford (tīrtha) is permitted.
The gods desire life for the sake of dharma among the twice-born;
however, for one who lives unrighteously, the abandonment of the body at a sacred ford is prescribed.
The Brahmagarbha states: "He who, afflicted by a great disease, is unable to perform [the rites],
does not incur fault in the hereafter if he performs the fire-rite, the water-rite, or the Great Pilgrimage."
Vṛddhagārgya states:
For householders whose physical faculties have been impaired by diseases, the following are prescribed:
setting out on the Great Journey (mahāprasthāna) or entering into fire or water.

One should not desire to live in vain, even by means of leaping from a precipice; "bhṛgu" refers to a mountain slope. Vasiṣṭha says: "Through leaping from a precipice one gains a kingdom, and through fasting unto death, the vault of heaven."
Vyāsa says:
O King of kings, seven thousand [merits] are obtained in water and fourteen in fire; for one who fasts to death, however, the measure of the fruit is not known.
Jamadagni says:
One should cast the *vaitāna* fires into water and the *āvasathya* fire at a crossroads;
however, one should burn the sacrificial vessels in the fire if the sacrificer has died an untimely death.
Another Smṛti states:
"For those who have abandoned their own bodies and likewise for those who are outcasts, no funeral rite exists;
yet even for them, it is beneficial to place [their remains] in the waters of the Gaṅgā. (3.6)
Having described the offering of water with its accompanying recitations, he states the subsequent rite:
"When they have finished the water-offering and emerged, standing upon soft grass, they should address those who have bathed with ancient legends concerning their ancestors. (3.7)

When those sons and others related to the deceased have bathed, offered the water libations, and have emerged from the sacred bathing place (tīrtha), the other elders and virtuous men should console them—making them free from grief—by means of ancient histories and accounts of past events as they stand upon a soft, grassy plot covered with green turf. Paiṭhīnasi states: "Having emerged [from the water] with the mantra *āpo asmān*, they should put on other garments; having worshipped the sun with the mantra *tac cakṣur*, they [should proceed] with the children at their head. The ellipsis to be supplied is that they should stand upon the grassy plot (*śādvale*). Kātyāyana [also says]: *...[text fragment]*... [The remainder of the passage regarding Kātyāyana’s rules follows].
When they have thus properly performed the water-libations while standing on a grassy spot, and have bathed and sipped water again, those who are free from deceit should address them as follows.
Do not grieve over anything impermanent, for such is the nature of all living beings;
practice the Dharma with diligence, for it alone shall accompany you.
He spoke just as they had declared:
"He who seeks a core in human existence—which is as pithless as the trunk of a plantain tree and resembles a bubble on the water—is utterly deluded. (3.8)
If this body, composed of the five elements, has returned to the state of the five elements, what cause for lamentation is there over that which arose from one's own past actions? (3.9)
The earth, the vehicle-bearer, shall go to destruction, as will the ocean and the deities;
how then shall the world of mortals, which resembles foam, not go to destruction? (3.10)
This has been explained by the very words [of the verse]. In the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa:
"For those for whom union is desired, how can separation be unpleasant? For union is indeed born already seized by separation."
But why indeed are you so deluded? You are yourself an object of pity;
why do you grieve for others, when those who grieve for you will themselves go to that same destination as objects of pity?
Having emerged from the unseen, he has again gone to the unseen;
having gone there, he does not know its end—why, then, do you grieve?
There is no absolute cohabitation for anyone with anything,
even with one's own body, let alone with other ordinary people.
In the *Mahābhārata*, in the *Śalyaparvan*, after Duryodhana had been slain, this is the lamentation of Dhṛtarāṣṭra regarding Vāsudeva.
Then, O Great King, the blessed Lord Mādhava, the chariot-warrior, set forth and,
having reached Hastināpura, the valiant one entered it.
Having entered the city, making it resound with the noise of his chariot, the hero,
being recognized by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, descended from his excellent chariot.
With an undaunted soul, he approached the residence of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
where he saw that best of sages who had already arrived there before him.
Having pressed the feet of Vyāsa and also those of the king, Janārdana,
the composed Keśava, greeted Gāndhārī as well.
Then, as soon as Mādhava, the most excellent of men, took hold of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s hand, he wept aloud.
Having shed tears born of grief for a moment,
he washed his eyes with water and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) according to the rules.
The subduer of enemies spoke these humble words to Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall."
Unions end in separation, for life ends in death. (3.8, 9, 10)
He states the fault in weeping:

"Since the deceased, being powerless, must consume the phlegm and tears shed by his kinsmen, therefore one should certainly not weep; rather, the funeral rites should be performed with diligence. (3.11)
This verse, too, has been explained by its very recitation. 3.11
Regarding the subsequent rite, he says:
Having thus made their formal agreement, they should go home with the children at their head;
having bitten neem leaves, they should remain restrained at the door of the house. (3.12)
Having sipped water, they should then touch fire, water, cow dung, and white mustard seeds;
then, having touched them, they should enter while placing their feet slowly upon a stone.

Having heard the collection of Itihāsa passages recited by the Sādhyas, they should return home preceded by children. At its door, having chewed neem leaves with their teeth and discarded them, being self-restrained, they should sip water (ācamana) and thereafter touch fire, water, [cow dung], and white mustard seeds; then, placing a foot upon a stone, they should enter slowly. Śaṅkha says: "Having touched young durvā grass, fire, and a bull, and having offered a funeral ball (piṇḍa) for the deceased at the door of the house, they should enter afterwards. Paiṭhīnasi [says the same].
Having gone home, they should stand at the door; then, having touched clarified butter, fire, water, and cow dung, they should enter the house and lie down upon mats.
For those who touch a corpse, even the rites such as entering [the village] and so forth [are permitted];
for those who desire it, purification occurs at that very moment, while for others it comes through bathing and self-restraint.

The entry into the house has been described; that which will be stated hereafter—namely, "for three nights or ten nights"—should be understood as the rite prescribed for those who are not *sapiṇḍas*. However, for those who touch a corpse not out of personal desire but by virtue of the rule, purification occurs immediately following bathing and breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). Those who perform the decoration, the removal, and the cremation of a corpse are "touchers of the corpse. Manu states that for those who touch a corpse without [following the specific] rule, purification occurs after ten nights.
Those who touch a corpse are purified in one day and night, or even in three nights;
however, those who offer water for the deceased are purified after three days.

The phrase "by one day and one night" is intended as an illustration for a full day and night (*ahorātra*). Likewise, "by three [periods] of three nights each" refers to nine nights. Thus, this ten-night period is prescribed for the purification of those who touch the corpse of a Kṣatriya or others—that is, those who touch the corpse of someone other than a Brāhmaṇa. In this regard, purification from touching the corpse of a Brāhmaṇa occurs after ten nights, whereas for those who touch the corpse of a Kṣatriya or others, it occurs after a different duration of time. As it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"If a man, having purchased [the right to cremate] from one of a different caste, should cremate [the body], his impurity shall always be equal to that of the deceased's own caste."

But when the engagement does not proceed from greed for payment, then this [penalty] does not apply; rather, it is due to bathing. As Manu says: "A Brahmin who carries out a deceased twice-born man as if he were a kinsman is purified after three nights, as are the maternal relatives who are his mother's kin."
And this should be understood to apply when the resident of that house has not eaten their food; as he himself says:
"If, however, one eats their food, one is purified in ten days;
but if one does not eat their food and does not dwell in that house, one is purified in a single day."

The mention of "ten days" is intended as an illustration for the period of impurity (*āśauca*) applicable to all castes. Regarding this, Parāśara states that there is no fault whatsoever for one who touches a corpse for the sake of dharma:
"Those twice-born who carry a deceased Brāhmaṇa who is without a protector obtain, step by step, the fruit of a sacrifice."
For them, there is no impurity whatsoever, nor any sin in an impure act;
by immersing themselves in water, their immediate purification is ordained.
Likewise: "A Brahmin is not defiled by the funeral rites involving contact with the deceased;
both the carrier of the body and the giver of the fire become pure immediately after bathing."

As for that which was stated by Hārīta: "Those who have touched a corpse shall not enter a village until the appearance of the stars, or, if it is at night, until the appearance of the sun"—this should be understood as applying to those who, out of affection, have touched a corpse (whether they were the primary mourners or not), or who eat the funeral rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) of the deceased, or who consume their food, or who reside in their house. (3.14)

It has been stated that a religious student (*brahmacārin*) shall not perform water-libations, this being intended to show the prohibition of all funeral rites for the deceased, such as the carrying out of the body and so forth. He now states an exception to that rule in a specific case:
"Even after carrying out his teacher, his father, or his maternal grandfather, the observer of the vow remains an observer of the vow;
he shall not eat food from a mat, nor shall he dwell together with them. (3.15)

Even while performing the cremation and other rites for his teacher (ācārya) and others, a religious student (brahmacārī) remains one who observes his vows; he does not become vow-less. On the other hand, by carrying out [the funeral] for others, he becomes vow-less—meaning, in effect, that he is no longer entitled to the vows consisting of celibacy and that his initiatory rite (upanayana-saṃskāra) has been destroyed. Such a religious student, even while carrying out the cremation of his teacher and others, must not eat food from a mat (kaṭa), nor food associated with impurity (aśauca). Furthermore, he must not dwell together with them during such periods of impurity. However, Manu states that there is no fault in carrying out the cremation of one's mother or of a teacher—even one who is merely formal (aupacārika).
Even after carrying out the funeral rites for his own teacher, sub-teacher, father, mother, or guru who has passed away, one who is under a vow is not deprived of that vow.

Vasiṣṭha: "For a religious student (*brahmacārin*), there is no suspension of his vow (*vratāvṛtti*) due to the funeral rites of anyone other than his mother or father. Suspension of the vow means re-initiation (*punarupanayana*). The *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Having cremated his own teacher (*ācārya*), sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), preceptor (*guru*), father, or mother, one who remains under a vow may eat there [at that place]."
Having done so, one does not fall [to that state]; therefore, one should not eat the food of the pretas there.
One should take food elsewhere and should not dwell together with them.
Having remained impure for one day, he becomes pure on the second day. Likewise:
"A Brāhmaṇa shall not cremate a Śūdra, whether he be a friend or anyone else."
Having burned [the body] out of delusion, one should then bathe, touch fire, and consume clarified butter.
One devoted to fasting is purified after three nights;
for all others, purification occurs after a day and night, even from following a corpse.
The procedure for touching a corpse, as prescribed, is ordained for all social classes.

He states the specific rule for the relatives: "Eating food that has been purchased or obtained [by begging], they should sleep separately on the ground; for three days, food should be offered to the deceased according to the procedure of the Piṇḍayajña. (3.16)

[885] Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”—“Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? They are the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. These, bhikkhus, are the five aggregates subject to clinging. [885]

Those relatives, having entered the house, shall eat food that is purchased or obtained unasked for a period of three nights; likewise, they shall sleep separately on the ground. Furthermore, a *piṇḍa* (funeral cake) must be offered to the deceased by the son or others using the procedure of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, but without the recitation of mantras. This rule regarding eating purchased food and so forth is prescribed for those who are unable to observe the three-night fast; as Vasiṣṭha says: "Having gone to the house, they should remain for three days without eating on a bed of grass (*aghaprastara*), or they may subsist on what is purchased or produced. An *aghaprastara* is a mat used for the sleeping and other needs of those in a state of impurity. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi.
There should be a fast for one day, or they may eat whatever is obtained;
having gone to the forest on the fourth day, the collection of bones takes place in the forenoon.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
They should subsist on food that is purchased or obtained as alms and remain well-composed;
they should not eat meat, nor should they go to women.
Manu says:
They should subsist on alkaline salt and food, and they should immerse themselves for three days;
they should not eat meat, and they should sleep separately on the ground.

Gautama states: "All [the mourners] shall sit together, sleeping on the ground, observing celibacy, and abstaining from meat until the *pradāna* (the offering). Water-libations (*udakakarma*) are performed on the first, third, seventh, and ninth days; on the ninth day, there is the discarding of clothes. However, for those of the lowest class (*antyānām*), this occurs at the end. The *pradāna* refers to the *śrāddha* rites performed on the eleventh day and subsequent days. The "discarding of clothes" means handing them over to a washerman for washing. The "end" (*antya*) refers to the final day of the period of impurity (*āśauca*). In that context, for those of the lowest class, there is the discarding of clothes that are utterly unfit for use—or alternatively, for those of the lowest class, i.e., the Śūdras. Some also read the text as: "But at the end, for those of the lowest class. —Bṛhaspati.
On the first, third, fifth, and seventh days, as well as on the ninth, there is the discarding of garments; likewise, at the final [day], there is the discarding of nails and hair.

The phrase "one must bathe" is to be understood as the remainder [of the rule] even for the seventh day. However, on the ninth and tenth days, the discarding of clothes and the clipping of nails and so forth are combined with the bathing. The *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
"Having bathed, they perform the water-libation (*udakatarpaṇa*) for the deceased for three nights;
thereafter, on the fourth day, they perform the sacrifice to the deities of the cremation ground."
For Śaṅkara and the other deities residing there are worshipped by those who have bathed,
put on well-washed garments, and approached the vicinity of the cremation ground.
With materials prescribed for one's own caste, gathered according to one's ability,
in earthen vessels and in pleasing sacrificial pots (carus).
The flesh-eating deities (kravyādadevatāḥ) are to be worshipped with well-cooked foods and edibles, milk-rice (pāyasa), drinks, as well as fruits and roots grown in the forest.
Some should offer the respectful water (arghya), while others should offer beautiful flowers;
incense, lamps, and garlands should likewise be offered by some with haste.
There, the vessels filled [with offerings] should be placed all around the cremation fire;
indeed, all those that have been prepared by others should be offered by some.
All those who are free from egoism should say, "Announce [this]," and always recite: "Homage to the gods whose mouths are like carrion-eaters."
Whatever eternal deities may reside in this cremation ground,
may they accept from me this imperishable eight-limbed bali offering.
May they grant this deceased being auspicious and eternal worlds;
may these excellent ones bestow upon us long life, health, and happiness.
Having thus prepared all the offerings and sprinkled them with milk, those who are restrained in speech and composed in mind should perform the dismissal of the deities.
Then, having taken a branch from a sacrificial tree while remaining silent,
a kinsman of the same lineage, wearing his garment over the right shoulder in the prescribed order, should proceed.
One should take the bones of the deceased, especially those originating from the principal limbs;
having bathed them thoroughly with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and wrapped them in a linen cloth.
Having placed it in a new earthen vessel that is well-covered and auspicious,
one should deposit it somewhere in a pure forest or at the foot of a tree.
Having slowly brought it from that place, someone— a virtuous son, a daughter's son, or a uterine brother— might at some time cast it into the waters of the Ganges.
Having taken the bones and that ash, one should carry them away and cast them into water;
thereafter, the ground should be swept clean with cow-dung and water.
And worship with flowers, incense, and so forth, as well as with offerings, should be performed in sequence as before.
Furthermore, for the purpose of covering the ground, there should be a tree or a pond.
Or a funeral mound (eḍūka) should be constructed there by all their kinsmen;
thereafter, they must perform a ritual bath with their clothes on according to the prescribed rule.
Likewise: in some cases on the third day for a Brahmin, on the fourth for a Kṣatriya,
on the fifth for one of the Vaiśya caste, and on the tenth day for a Śūdra.
[887] However, the collection of bones is performed for one who has died due to the gravity of the fault;
this same procedure is also applied to the castes while they are still living when [the fault] has occurred.
For Brāhmaṇas it is on the fourth day, for kings (Kṣatriyas) on the fifth day,
for those of the Vaiśya caste on the ninth, and for Śūdras after the tenth.
Men should perform the śrāddha rite according to the requirements of place and time; those who are eligible for the sapinda-rite, kinsmen of the same caste, and others who are hungry [should be fed].
The poor, the helpless, the blind, and the wretched may eat even food there;
however, on the second day after the purification has been performed on the third day, the collection of the bones must be carried out.
Likewise:
Even those who sometimes carry the bones of their parents and ancestors to the Ganges—
because they are overcome by compassion even for a mere corpse— their sacred bathing places (tīrthas) indeed yield fruit.
Likewise:
having bathed and then sprinkled [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), having combined it with gold, clarified butter, and sesame seeds,
and then having placed it within a hollowed-out lump of clay, one should gaze toward the direction inhabited by the hosts of pretas.
Having entered the water while reciting "Homage be to the Dharma," he should cast [the offering] into it, saying, "May this be for my deceased ancestor.
Then, having risen and gazed at the radiant sun, he should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brahmin.
When this has been done, for one dwelling in the city of the departed, there shall be a journey to heaven equal to that of Mahendra.
Likewise:
"Excluding the mother's family and the father's family, that lowest of men who takes the bones of one born of another family becomes pure by performing the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
Marīci says:
Having bathed and being pure in mind, one should prepare the *caru* oblation in the north-eastern direction and offer the *piṇḍa* for the deceased outside, devoid of *darbha* grass and mantras.

Pracetās states: "One should offer the rice-ball on the ground for those who have not undergone consecration rites, and on *kuśa* grass for those who have been consecrated. This is from the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*.
Whether he belongs to a different lineage or the same lineage, whether she be a woman or a man, whoever offers [the first ball] on the first day must complete it through the tenth day.
Śunaḥpuccha said:
With fruits, roots, milk, vegetables, and molasses,
one should offer a ball of food mixed with ghee upon the Darbha grass to the south.
It should be offered at the doorway or in the temples of the deities;
likewise, one should silently offer a libation, flowers, a lamp, and incense.
One should offer either rice, or roasted flour (saktu), or even vegetables;
whatever substance is used on the first day, that same substance shall be used for the ten-day period.

Śaṅkha: "They should offer a garland, a rice-ball (piṇḍa), water, and an anointing upon the ground. [888] Pāraskara: "For a Brāhmaṇa, ten rice-balls are prescribed; for a Kṣatriya, twelve are recorded;
for a Vaiśya, fifteen are declared; and for a Śūdra, thirty are proclaimed."
Regarding those who are incapable of the aforementioned number, he himself states another number:
"To the deceased of all castes, one should offer exactly ten rice-balls;
when the Śrāddha rite has arrived, however, only one rice-ball is prescribed."

According to the opinion of Yājñavalkya, these rice-balls (piṇḍas) are to be offered for exactly three nights; however, according to other opinions, one rice-ball should be offered every day for as long as the period of impurity (āśauca) lasts. Thus says Viṣṇu: "For as long as the impurity lasts, they should offer water and one rice-ball for the deceased. Vṛddha-Pracetas states:
"Having taken new vessels, as well as a mirror and sacrificial porridge (caru), one should then go for the sake of water, taking a person along."
Having carefully taken up a staff that wards off all evils,
he should then enter the house where the food of the deceased is always kept.
Taking a handful of that [grain], it should be used for the rite of the rice-balls;
having washed it thoroughly twice, one should then prepare the sacrificial porridge (caru).
Then, taking him while he is still shedding tears, one should place him upon the darbha grass;
the darbha blades should have their tips pointing toward the south, and he himself should face the south.
It should be offered at the doorway or sometimes in a temple;
having lifted up that entire funeral ball (piṇḍa), one should present it by name and lineage.
Restraining his speech and remaining pure, he should stand near the funeral cake;
then, once the steam has ceased, he should cast it into a river.
Day by day, one should offer full handfuls for the sake of the deceased;
the increase should continue in this manner until the funeral cake (piṇḍa) is completed.
Śātātapa says:
Even when there is a reduction in the period of impurity, one should offer exactly ten rice-balls (piṇḍas);
or else, one may properly offer a single rice-ball at the śrāddha according to the prescribed rule.
Pāraskara says: "On the first day, three funeral cakes (piṇḍas) should be offered by those who are composed;
on the second day, one should offer four, as well as the collection of the bones."
On the third day, however, one should give three [garments] and likewise wash the clothes and other items;
thereafter, the Ekoddiṣṭa Śrāddha rite must be performed.
Dakṣa says:
On the first day one should offer that single pinda; on the second, four; and on the third, five. This is remembered as the rule for the pindas. [889]
Marīci: On the first day, the third, the seventh, and likewise the ninth, one should eat together with the kinsmen; this is difficult to obtain for the deceased.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "One should perform the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) for the deceased for twelve days;
for that is declared to be his provision for the journey, since it brings him great satisfaction."
Because a deceased person is led to the city of the hungry ghosts within twelve days,
and for those twelve days he beholds his home, sons, and wife.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
"By the funeral cake (piṇḍa) offered on the first day, the head is produced;
the eyes, ears, and nose are produced on the second day."
On the third day, the two arms, the chest, and likewise the neck are produced;
on the fourth day, the region of the navel, the anus, and the genitals are produced.
The thighs should be known as the fifth [stage], and one should point out the vital points (marmas) in the sixth;
in the seventh, however, all the vessels (śirās) are produced—of this there is no doubt.
Then, at the eighth *piṇḍa*, all the body hairs [are formed];
immediately thereafter, at the ninth, there is the perfection of virility; and at the tenth, the destruction of hunger.
Then, at the end of the period of impurity, the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍas) is properly completed;
thereafter, the Śrāddha feast should be offered—this is the rule for all social classes.

This being the case, it is understood that even when purification has been achieved through the impurity resulting from the *saṃnipāta* (conjunction of births or deaths), the rites such as the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) must still be performed individually for each person, such as the son and others, on separate days. However, their state of untouchability (*aspṛśyatva*) and the fact that their food is unfit to be eaten (*abhojyānnatva*) certainly persist, because those two conditions arise from distinct causes. As Manu says: "The touchability of the social classes [is restored] in three, four, five, and six days respectively;
a Brahmin becomes one whose food may be eaten after ten days, while the rest [become so] after two, three, and six additional days."

This being the case, his constant acts of giving and so forth are not prohibited as being "dry" (ineffective), because there is a traditional rule (smṛti) stating that such acts cease during impurity. And thus says Viṣṇu: "During impurity, the performance of fire-offerings, giving, receiving, and Vedic study are suspended. Nor does he himself undergo impurity, since he is already exempted from it by the rules regarding impurity resulting from a fatal accident (saṃnipāta). || 3.16 ||
Furthermore: Water and milk should be placed in the air for one day.

Having set water in an earthen vessel and milk in another earthen vessel on behalf of the deceased (preta), they should be placed in the air—on a swing or similar support elsewhere than on the ground. "For one day" means on the first day. Pāraskara states: "The mantra for the water is: 'O deceased one, bathe here'; the mantra for the milk is: 'Drink this. The Matsya Purāṇa [states]:
Then, for twelve days, milk should be offered into the fire;
this is to pacify all burning sensations and to prevent the first stage of exhaustion.

He states an exception to the impurity (āśauca) that is about to be described, in a specific case: "The sacrificial rites of the three fires, the domestic rites of the sacred fire, and the rituals enjoined by the Vedas must be performed. (3.17)

The *tretā* is the sacrificial fire; those rites connected with it are the *vaitānya*. These are both those [rites] and the meditations (*upāsanā*), thus they are called *vaitānopāsanāḥ*. Due to the rule of masculine gender (*puṃvadbhāva*), the feminine suffix is elided in the word *vaitāna*. And as for the meditations: having performed the evening twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*) and having offered oblations into those fires, one should perform the meditations.

Thus they are prescribed by the Smṛtis. Here, the worship of the fires (*agnyupāsanā*) is enjoined for the sake of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), and not as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the oblation (*homa*), because there is no evidence for such a claim. Nor should it be argued that the suffix *-ktvā* enjoin[s] it as a subordinate part of the oblation, and that this is the evidence for its being a subordinate part; for if that were so, the syntactical connection would have to be "having offered the oblation (*hutvā*), one should worship (*upāsya*)," yet there is no such connection between two words ending in the suffix *-ktvā*, since both are equally subordinate to the verb (*ākhyāta*). For what purpose, then, is this statement? We say: it is for the purpose of establishing the sequence (*paurvāparya*). And when the sentence is intended to prescribe a sequence, this meaning is established: "Having performed the twilight worship (*saṃdhyām upāsya*), one should offer the oblation (*juhuyāt*); having offered the oblation (*hutvā*), one should perform the worship (*upāsīta*)," and so forth. At present, it is not possible for the hearing of the suffix *-ktvā* to establish a relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), because that would contradict the determination that the sentence is concerned with sequence. Nor should it be argued that if the sentence is concerned with sequence, it is untenable for it to be concerned with the injunction of worship; for here the injunction of worship is not explicit (*śrauta*), but rather implied (*ārtha*). Indeed, a sequence regarding an object cannot be enjoined unless that object has been enjoined. Since there is no other injunction for it, the injunction for worship is inferred right here. Once it is established that worship serves the human goal, then—in order to effect that—a result such as the destruction of sin or the attainment of *apūrva* (unseen merit) must be postulated. The plural number in "worships" (*upāsanāḥ*) refers to individual instances. The "rites" (*kriyāḥ*) are those rites enjoined by the Śruti, namely the Agnihotra and others; the word "and" (*ca*) is used to carry over the qualification of being "pertaining to the sacrificial fires" (*vaitānika*). Therefore, only those rites pertaining to the sacrificial fires are intended here. To qualify them specifically, it is said they are "enjoined by the Śruti. A qualification is meaningful when there is the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Since the fact that the aforementioned rites are enjoined by the Śruti does not deviate from the truth, the word "Śruti" is added as a qualification of the meaning to avoid the defect of over-extension; thus, "directness" (*pratyakṣatva*) is supplied. By this, the following is established: those rites pertaining to the sacrificial fires which are worship of the fires, and those rites pertaining to the sacrificial fires which are directly enjoined by the Śruti. Rites such as the Brahmayajña and others are indeed to be avoided during impurity (*āśauca*), for they do not pertain to the sacrificial fires. Likewise, even among those rites pertaining to the sacrificial fires, those not directly enjoined by the Śruti—such as... [text ends].
"In the absence of these, a twice-born man should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice"—
such are the rules prescribed by the Smṛtis.

On this point, some explain as follows: *vaitānāḥ* means those rites pertaining to the *vitāna* (the sacrificial shed); likewise, *aupāsanāḥ* means those rites pertaining to the domestic fire (*aupāsana*). Thus, they claim the compound *vaitānopāsanāḥ* refers to the ritual acts belonging to both the *vaitāna* and *aupāsana* categories. This explanation is untenable; for in that case, the word would have to be *vaitānyaupāsanyāḥ*, and not *vaitānopāsanāḥ*. In the previous explanation, however, this is a *karmadhāraya* compound. Therein, by applying the rule for masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*), the grammatical correctness of the term *vaitānopāsanāḥ* is established. Furthermore, the word *upāsanā* does not end in the suffix *aṇ*, which would cause it to take the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. Moreover, their interpretation—having adopted the reading *śruticodanāt* and explaining it as referring to the reason—is also incorrect. For they believe that because the Śruti prescribes these acts as mandatory through such injunctions as "One should perform the *Agnihotra* as long as one lives" and "One should sacrifice with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* as long as one lives," the Smṛti cannot ordain their suspension even during a period of impurity (*āśauca*). This argument is inconclusive; for although the Śruti prescribes them, even mandatory acts like the *Agnihotra* prescribed by Śruti are indeed suspended by Smṛti during the state of impurity due to the risk of falling from caste (*pātitya*). Therefore, the explanation of the phrase as a statement of reason is incorrect. Furthermore, the word *vaitāna* should not be explained as referring to the Veda itself on the grounds that its usage is not observed there. Consequently, the former explanation alone is superior. —Manu.
One should not prolong the days of impurity, nor should one interrupt the rites performed in the sacred fires;
and while performing those rites, even a kinsman does not become impure.

One should not increase the days of impurity with the thought, "I shall remain at ease by being free from ritual duties. The meaning is that one must not exceed the number of days prescribed by the scriptures. Regarding the fires: those obligatory rites performed in the *śrauta* fires, such as the *agnihotra*, one should not obstruct—that is, one should not abandon them. The meaning is that one should perform them even while in a state of impurity. To the objection that since one who is impure lacks the qualification (*adhikāra*) for rituals, it would indeed be proper to obstruct them, he says: "And that rite [is not so]. Even though there is no qualification when impurity exists, one should understand that by the force of the specific scriptural injunction regarding particular rites, impurity itself does not exist [in that context]. Here, because of the *ātmanepada* ending in the word "kurvāṇaḥ" (performing), it is understood that the qualified person performing that rite—even if he is a close relative (*sanābhya*) and thus near to someone for whom a birth or death has occurred—does not become impure, but rather remains pure. Therefore, for close relatives, there is indeed impurity regarding the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*). Thus says Vyāghrapāt.
During a period of ritual impurity (sūtaka), one should abandon Smārta rites except for those performed by Rāhu (eclipses);
however, regarding Śrauta rites, one attains purity by bathing at that very time.

The meaning is that, except during the *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) of Rāhu [an eclipse], there is *sūtaka*, which is to say, impurity (*āśauca*). However, Pāraskara specifies: "The obligatory rites are suspended, with the exception of the *vaitāna* (sacrificial fire) rites; some say this also applies to the *śālāgni* (domestic fire). Others should perform these. The *śālāgni* is the domestic fire; if the rites related to it are to be performed, then they should be done by others than the *sapiṇḍas*. The meaning is that one should have them performed by others. One should perform the sacrifice and the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) oneself alone, because since those two consist of the renunciation of one's own property, they cannot be performed by others. Thus says Jābāla.
In the case of birth, death, or a canopy ceremony, there is no abandonment of ritual duties;
the oblation must indeed be performed in the domestic fire alone by those born of other lineages.
Bṛhaspati says:

In the event of birth-impurity or death-impurity, or when unable to eat at a śrāddha, or due to causes such as being on a journey, one should cause [the sacrifice] to be offered; one must not let it lapse.
Jātūkarṇya says:
When a birth-impurity has arisen, so that the Smārta rites may be performed,
one should have the Piṇḍayajña, the Caru-offering, and the Homa performed by someone not of the same lineage (asagotra).
Saṃvarta says:
In that case, however, the fire-oblation should be performed with dry food or fruit;
and one should not perform the ritual for the five great sacrifices during the periods of death and birth.
Dry food consists of rice, barley, and the like; however, he himself states that the Vaiśvadeva oblation is not to be performed [during this period]:
"A Brahmin shall remain for ten days excluded from the Vaiśvadeva," as it was stated by Manu.
In both cases, for ten days the food of the family is not eaten;
giving, receiving, burnt offerings, and Vedic study are suspended.
Thus, that [statement] refers to the subject of *smārta* (traditionally prescribed) oblations. From the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"The worship of the *saṃdhyā* at all times is required for a king, except in cases of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), ritual pollution (*āśauca*), confusion, illness, or fear."

Paiṭhīnasi: "During a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka), one should cast an añjali of water with the Sāvitrī mantra, perform a circumambulation, and pay obeisance while meditating upon the Sun. Pulastya:
"One should perform the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), the iṣṭi sacrifice, the caru offering, and the fire-oblation (homa) throughout one's life.
One should not abandon them even during a period of impurity; by abandoning them, a twice-born man goes to a lower state."
During both birth-impurity and death-impurity, a twice-born man should not abandon the twilight rituals;
he should mentally recite the mantras, with the exception of breath control (prāṇāyāma).

This being the case, it should be understood that when there is impurity, the prohibitions regarding the *saṃdhyā* refer specifically to the *saṃdhyā* characterized by the recitation of mantras. However, the offering of the *añjali* (the cupped hands) may be performed with the *Sāvitrī* as it is being recited. || 3.17 ||

Thus has been described the collection of rites, such as burial and so forth, which serve as the cause for the removal of impurity; now he states the specific period of time capable of bringing about that removal:
"Impurity on account of a death (śāva) is prescribed for either three nights or ten nights.
In the case of a child less than two years old, however, the birth-impurity (sūtaka) belongs to both [parents], but in fact it belongs to the mother alone. (3.18)

Impurity caused by a corpse (*śava*)—that is, impurity resulting from a death—is prescribed by Manu and others as lasting three nights for those related by water (*samānodaka*), and ten nights for those who share the funeral cake (*sapiṇḍa*). However, when a child less than two years old has died, the impurity belongs to both parents alone. Impurity caused by birth (*sūtaka*)—that is, impurity resulting from a delivery—belongs to the mother alone; the meaning is that it pertains only to the woman who has given birth. Regarding this, Manu says: "Those who touch a corpse are purified in one day, one night, and three sets of three days [respectively];
but those who offer water are purified after three days. (MDh 5.103)
Those who offer water are the *samānodaka*s (water-relation kinsmen). Their definition is stated by that same [author]:
"The status of being a *sapiṇḍa* ceases with the seventh person;
however, the status of being a *samānodaka* persists as long as there is no knowledge of [the deceased's] birth or name."

And by this very implication, as long as the knowledge persists that "the birth of our own and their [ancestors'] continuums is designated in this way," so long does their status as *samānodaka* (distant kinsmen) endure. The ten-day period of impurity (*daśarātrāśauca*) pertains to the *sapiṇḍas*. Manu himself has stated this:
"Impurity on account of death (*śāva-āśauca*) for ten days is prescribed for the *sapiṇḍas*.
Regarding that [period of ten days], he [Manu] himself has also stated three alternative views.

The gathering of the bones may take place on the third day or even on the first day; the phrase "the gathering of the bones from the dwelling" is an indication of the fourth day, because it is prescribed for that fourth day. And so says Saṃvarta:
"On the fourth day after death, the gathering of the bones should be performed by the twice-born."

Although Āśvalāyana (ĀśG 4.5.1) prescribes the collection of the bones (*saṃcayana*) at another time—stating that "it should be done after the tenth day in the dark fortnight"—nevertheless, because there is a rule for it on the fourth day, the collection is indicated as occurring precisely on the fourth day. This is because a period of less than ten nights is intended here. For this very reason, Dakṣa says:
"Immediate purification, as well as one day, three days, and likewise four days..."

Thus he spoke. This being the case, regarding that period of impurity (āśauca), there are four alternatives: ten days, four days, three days, and one day. Their systematic application is prescribed in another Smṛti. Regarding this, Parāśara says: "A Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with both the sacred fires and the Vedas becomes pure after one day; one who possesses only the Vedas after three days; but one devoid of qualities [becomes pure] after ten days."
Dakṣa, however, stated ten periods:
"Immediate purity, then one day, three days, four days,
as well as six, ten, twelve days, a fortnight, and likewise a month."
Likewise, there is another [impurity] ending at death; however, regarding the ten periods of birth-impurity (sūtaka), I shall explain them in their proper order and in their entirety.

He understands the Veda together with its limbs, along with the ritual manuals and secret doctrines, both in letter and in spirit; being a performer of rites, he does not become impure through birth-impurity.

The meaning is that one is immediately pure. Bṛhaspati says: "Where the private recitation of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*) is performed, as well as the fire-oblation (*homa*) at both times, and the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice is constantly offered, there no impurity (*aśauca*) exists."
Parāśara says:
Where the Vedic study is performed, where the Mahābhārata is recited,
and where the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is constantly offered, there no impurity is found.
Bṛhaspati says: A Brahmin who is endowed with the sacred fires and the Vedas is purified in one day;
if he is deficient in these, or even more deficient, he is purified in three or four days respectively.

One who possesses only the Veda is inferior to one who is endowed with both the Veda and the sacred fires (*agni*). However, he who, despite having studied the Veda, does not maintain it, is even more inferior. Alternatively, one who lacks the *śrauta* fires is inferior; one who maintains the *smārta* fires and studies only the Veda is more inferior still; and so too is one who lacks both *śrauta* and *smārta* fires, even if he has mastered the complete Veda. Bṛhaspati states: "A Brahmin endowed with the Veda and the sacred fires is purified in just three nights;
but one devoid of the fires is purified in five, while a Brahmin who is firm [in his duties] is purified in ten days."
A preeminent twice-born man living by means of gleanings and alms,
even if his essence consists solely of the Gāyatrī, shall be immediately purified if he performs the three twilight devotions.
[895] One who does not follow the conduct of a dog (i.e., one who is not a servant) shall observe impurity for six days.
Dakṣa says:
"That twice-born man who eats without having bathed, without having offered oblations, and without having given gifts..."
For such a Brahmin, there shall always be impurity (sūtaka).
[This applies] especially to one who is diseased, miserly, perpetually burdened by debt,
devoid of religious rites, foolish, and particularly one who is dominated by his wife.
For one whose mind is attached to vices, who is perpetually dependent on others,
and who is devoid of faith and renunciation, his impurity (sūtaka) shall last until the end of his ashes.
There shall never be impurity (sūtaka) [in that state], for as long as one lives, it is indeed impurity;
thus, by virtue of such a specific quality, it is designated as "impurity."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"If a woman who has previously belonged to another should become one's wife,
for that man there shall always be impurity in his body at all times regarding all ritual activities."
For him, giving, receiving, and bathing—all that shall be in vain.
Śātātapa says:
A Brahmin who has fallen away from his birth-rites and duties, who neglects the twilight prayers,
and who is a Brahmin in name only, becomes pure after ten days.

And here, the term *sūtaka* refers to impurity (*āśauca*) in general. Restrictions regarding impurity—such as those concerning giving, receiving gifts, and so forth—are prescribed for times of distress (*āpatti*), not universally for all ritual acts. As Gautama says: "And for a Brāhmaṇa, it is so that his private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) may not cease. The meaning of this is: when full impurity is observed for one who has many *sapiṇḍas* and is of dull intellect, his private Vedic study would cease. And the mention of the non-cessation of Vedic study is illustrative; for if there were full impurity in every case, then for those whose livelihood is restricted to living on grain in granaries or jars and the like, their very survival would become impossible due to the cessation of receiving gifts. Therefore, for them, the prescriptions of immediate purity (*sadyaḥśauca*) or one-day purity (*ekāha*) and so forth, as far as possible, apply specifically to the matter of receiving gifts. In other matters, however, even they must observe full impurity. When a child under two years dies, or in the case of a miscarriage, the impurity characterized by untouchability belongs to both parents alone; however, the impurity characterized by disqualification from religious duties belongs to everyone. As Vasiṣṭha says: "When a child under two years dies, or in the case of a miscarriage, the impurity for the *sapiṇḍas* lasts three nights. As for what was stated by him [Gautama]: "Immediate purity, according to Gautama," that refers to the impurity of untouchability. The phrase "the *sūtaka* belongs to the mother alone" is for the sake of an illustration: just as in the case of childbirth (*sūtaka*) there is untouchability for the mother alone, so too upon the death of a child under two, it belongs to the parents alone. Thus, at birth and death, there exists for the *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas* an impurity characterized by disqualification from specific rites and characterized by untouchability. (3.18)
Regarding that birth, he states a specific distinction concerning untouchability:
"But for the parents, there is *sūtaka* (birth-impurity); for the mother, it is certain because of the appearance of that blood.
On that day, one is not defiled, because of the cause of birth for the ancestors. (3.19)

*Sūtaka*—the impurity arising from childbirth, characterized by untouchability—pertains to the mother and father, but not to other *sapiṇḍa* relatives. In that regard, if the father does not engage in contact with the woman who has given birth, characterized by physical touch, then the untouchability of the mother alone—which is caused by the appearance of menstrual blood—is certain and immutable for ten nights. As Vasiṣṭha says:
"There is no impurity for the man in childbirth if he does not enter into contact;
in that case, it is the [menstrual] blood that is impure, and that does not exist in the man."

The meaning is that the day on which a son is born is not defiled; on that day, the father does not become impure. Here, the reason given is "because of the birth of the ancestors.
