Because the birth of the ancestors—the father, grandfather, and so forth—occurs therein, there is no impurity on that day. Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather are born again in that very place, and they cause that day to be known [as auspicious]."
Therefore, that day is meritorious and increases the merit of the ancestors. Manu says:
"When a son is born, one may freely accept gifts on that very day."
Of gold, grain, cattle, clothing, sesame seeds, food, molasses, and clarified butter.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Upon the birth of a son, before the umbilical cord has been severed, there is no fault in accepting gifts of molasses, sesame, gold, clothing, upper garments, cows, grain, or food; some say this applies only to that very day. Vṛddhayājñavalkya says: "On the day of a son's birth, Brahmins may accept gifts of gold, land, cows, horses, goats, clothing, beds, seats, and so forth."
In that regard, one may accept all things as gifts, but one must not eat cooked food;
if a twice-born man eats it out of delusion, he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

And in this regard: for all [relatives], there is impurity due to death (śāva-āśauca), but for the mother and father, there is birth-impurity (sūtaka). Birth-impurity belongs to the mother alone; having performed ritual ablution (upaspṛśya), the father becomes pure.

Passages such as these concern impurity characterized by untouchability (*aspṛśyatā*), and not impurity characterized by disqualification from religious rites (*adhikāra*). For since that [latter] pertains to all *sapiṇḍas*, it is ordained:
"Impurity on account of death lasts ten days among *sapiṇḍas*;
the same applies to birth for those who desire complete purification."

Because this was ordained by Manu; and by this statement, just as in the case of impurity due to death (*śāvāśauca*), those rites are extended to birth as well. Consequently, both the state of impurity and the means for its removal are obtained just as in that case. Among these, the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and water, the collection of bones (*saṃcayana*), and so forth—which were extended as the means for attaining purity—are here negated by the particle *eva*. However, the periods of ten days, four days, and so on, up to fifteen days, are indeed prescribed. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the purification of the woman who has given birth (*sūtikā*) by a rite of one day or more would result in a violation of the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*). This extension refers to the "impurity" characterized by loss of eligibility (*anadhikāra*), not to "untouchability" (*aspṛśyatā*). For this very reason, Vṛddhapracetas said:
A woman who has given birth becomes pure after ten days for all castes;
likewise, there is no separate purification for menstruation—this rule applies to all castes.

Even regarding the eligibility for ritual acts (*karmādhikāra*), Paiṭhīnasi states that she [the woman who has given birth] does not have it until the eleventh day and so forth: "One should cause a woman who has given birth to a son to perform ritual acts after twenty nights; a woman who has given birth to a daughter, after a month. And this refers to ritual acts other than those for which a *Soma* sacrifice has already commenced. For Kātyāyana says with respect to the *Soma* sacrifice: "The wife, even if in her courses (*udakyā*), having performed the preparatory rites (*dīkṣārūpa*) and having been sprinkled, should remain near the altar during the twilight hours while sitting and listening. During the pressing days (*sutyā*), at the end of the three nights, having bathed her with water mixed with cow-urine, he performs the subsequent rites such as the putting on of garments, which pertain to the assembly. And for one who has given birth, bathing and so forth occur after ten nights. Thus, while the impurity (*āśauca*) connected to the ten-day period generally applies even in the case of childbirth (*sūtaka*), Vyāsa states a specific exception to that.
The deities named Janmadās reside in the lying-in chamber;
for the purpose of performing their sacrifice, purification is prescribed at the time of birth.
On the first day, the sixth, and always on the tenth—
on these three days, one should never observe the birth-impurity (sūtaka) upon the birth of a son.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The sixth lunar day (ṣaṣṭhī) must be observed as a sacred day, especially the night;
one should perform a vigil at night and likewise offer oblations to the birth-giving goddesses.
Men who have been slain by weapons and women [who have lost their husbands] should keep a vigil at night on the tenth day during the period of birth-impurity.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"There are four maidens beginning with Rākā, Bālatakṣṇī as the fifth,
Krīḍanārthā for the play of children, and Śiśurakṣiṇī as the sixth."
She is to be worshipped with the sword by the Vaiśya-vrātyas and the twice-born;
for there are four daughters: Rākā, Anumati, Sinīvālī, and Kuhū. (3.19)
Regarding the coincidence of periods of impurity, he says:
"If another birth or death occurs in the interval, one becomes pure after the remaining days."

If, during the interval—that is, in the midst—of a period of impurity already set in motion, a birth or a death occurs, the impurity caused by that [subsequent event] is purified by the remaining days and nights of the *daśarātra* (ten-night period) or other duration of the previously commenced impurity; one need not, however, perform another ten-night period for purification starting from the birth or death that arose in the interim. And in this regard, if a death occurs within the ten-day period following a prior birth, then a ten-day period must be observed starting from that death. As Aṅgiras said:
"If a death should occur during a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), or if a birth should occur during a death-impurity (*mṛtaka*)," [the rule applies].
In that regard, one should perform purification with reference to death (mṛtaka), not with reference to birth (sūtaka).
From the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"When birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) occurs while death-impurity (*śāva*) has already arisen, the birth is purified by the death;
but birth-impurity does not purify death-impurity."

This refers to the case where the periods of impurity (*āśauca*) to be removed by days are equal in number. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says: "In the case of the coincidence of birth and death, the period of impurity is ten nights for both; furthermore, if ten-night periods of impurity should coincide, the first period of impurity lasts until the ninth day. Here, the mention of "ten nights" is intended to indicate any period of impurity of equal duration. Thus says Śaṅkha: "When there is a concurrence of equal periods of impurity, one should complete [the observance] according to the first;
when they are unequal, one should follow the second, according to the word of Dharmarāja."
Yama says:
One should conclude the period of impurity, which involves an increase in the duration, by means of the latter [period];
just as when a three-day period has begun, a mendicant enters into a ten-day period.
If, however, impurity should recur, one becomes purified upon its completion.
*Agha* refers to impurity (*āśauca*). Its "increased duration" (*vṛddhimattva*) means that its period is longer than the period of the previously arisen impurity. Hārīta states:
"If a death-impurity (*śāva*) occurs within a death-impurity, one is purified by the preceding impurity;
however, a light [impurity] shall be purified by a light [one]."

Purification shall be achieved through a period of one day or less, such as a single *ekāha*, but not by a *pakṣiṇī* (two days with an intervening night) or similar durations. Prajāpati says: "But when the birth of a son occurs while impurity (*sūtaka*) has arisen, the performer attains immediate purification; he is purified by the preceding impurity. [899]
"Of the performer" means of the one who performs the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) and so forth. "By the previous impurity" means by the duration of the previous period of impurity. Likewise:
"When impurities coincide, however, the purification should be known as that which is more weighty;
when there is a conjunction of death and birth, the death shall be the more weighty."

From this, the following meaning is established: when a period of impurity (*āśauca*) due to death is current, if another impurity—whether due to birth (*sūtaka*) or death (*mṛtaka*)—arises that is to be removed at the same time as the former, then purification occurs by the first alone. However, when an impurity due to birth or death that is to be removed over a long duration arises while an impurity due to death that is to be removed over a short duration is current; or if, while an impurity due to birth is current, an impurity due to death arises for exactly the same duration, then purification occurs by the latter alone. Gautama states: "If that [impurity] should occur again within [the existing one], they shall be purified by the remainder. And here, the phrase "if that" refers to an impurity of equal duration, not to the intention that a birth follows a birth or a death follows a death; for otherwise, there would be the consequence of contradicting other scriptures. Furthermore, regarding what was said:

If it were the case that there is birth at the time of birth and likewise death at the time of death, even that statement would be merely descriptive (*anuvādaka*) and not restrictive (*niyāmaka*), precisely because it would lead to a contradiction. And the specific rule regarding this has been stated by him [the author] himself:
"When a night remains, [the impurity lasts] for two days; at dawn, likewise for three."

The meaning is as follows: when there remains only the night of an impurity (*āśauca*) and another impurity should occur, then purification from that [new one] takes two days and nights. If, at dawn—that is, when that night has passed but before sunrise—the impurities should coincide, then purification occurs after three days and nights. Aṅgiras says:
"If a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) should somehow be equal to a death-impurity (*mṛtaka*), then the entire lineage, along with its kinsmen, becomes untouchable."

In this context, the mention of *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) and *mṛtaka* (death-impurity) is intended as an illustration for the occurrence of any impurity (*aśauca*). [Up to the ninth day, purification by the preceding impurity alone has been stated. Regarding the division of the remaining tenth day and night—specifically when there is a remainder of the night—it has been said:
"If there is a remainder of the night, [purification is] by two [days]; at dawn, by three.

Having thus established this, the text asks what should be done regarding the remaining portion consisting of two parts of the day, and in response, the *Brahmapurāṇa* says: *Brahmapurāṇa*: [The text follows...]

During the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka), purification from that birth-impurity is held to occur when a second [birth] falls within the first half of the first period. However, if it falls in the second half, purification is desired after the completion of the first [original] period of impurity.
From this point forward, one is considered pure after the second impurity following the end of a birth-impurity (sūtaka).
In the same way, this should be considered when there is another death-impurity (mṛtaka) occurring within [an existing period].
[900] Where one encounters a birth-impurity (sūtaka) within the interval of a death-impurity (mṛtaka), or likewise encounters a death-impurity within the interval of a birth-impurity;
"At the end of the period of death, there shall be purification for all castes in every respect.

This is the meaning: regarding the first two parts of the final day and night of the impurity—which constitute a full day—if another impurity falls during the preceding period of impurity, purification occurs by the former alone. In the remaining two parts, which constitute the night, the division is as follows:
"If the night remains, [purification is] by two days; at dawn, by three. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, as for that which has been written by the scribes—"By dividing the period of impurity into three parts, two parts here [are completed]; therefore, purification occurs after those two parts not yet ordained"—this refers to the case of one devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). However, for one possessed of qualities (*saguṇa*), the rule of Gautama applies: "In this very way," meaning by means of the division into three parts and so forth. [This is incorrect; for the author himself previously stated, "until the ninth day," and likewise in the passage "when two [days remain]," he specified that the time remaining is specifically the night. Śaṅkha says:
If the mother dies first while still impure, the father dies;
he shall be purified by the remainder of the father's period, but for the mother, a *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night) must be observed.

The meaning of this is as follows: if the mother dies first and the father dies later during that very period of impurity (*aśauca*), then the performer—the son or others—shall become pure by the remainder of the impurity pertaining to the father alone. If the father dies first and the mother dies later during that same period of impurity, then only an additional *pakṣiṇī* [period] must be observed. A *pakṣiṇī* consists of two days. Since the rule "the performer's purity is immediate" would otherwise apply and grant purity at that very moment, this statement is made to set aside that rule.
In the case of a miscarriage, the number of nights equal to the months [of gestation] is the cause of purification.

From the time of conception (*garbhādhāna*) until the month in which the fetus leaks or falls away (*sravati/cyavate*), for as many days and nights as have passed, that period serves as the cause for the purification of the woman. What is called "miscarriage" (*garbhasrāva*) is the exit of a fetus that has not reached the time of delivery. Regarding this, Gautama states: "In the case of a miscarriage, the days are equal to the months of gestation, or else three days. This is an option based on specific circumstances (*vyavasthitavikalpa*). Consequently, it should be understood that for up to three months, the impurity lasts three days; beyond that, for the next three months, the days are equal to the months of gestation. Thus it is stated in the *Ādipurāṇa*.
If a miscarriage should occur within six months,
then their purification is prescribed by days equal in number to the months [of gestation].
From this point forward, the impurity prescribed for their own respective castes applies to them;
however, in the event of a miscarriage, there is immediate purification for the sapindas.

The rule for immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śauca*) refers to impurity characterized by untouchability (*aspṛśyatā*). However, impurity characterized by disqualification (*anadhikāra*) certainly persists for the *sapiṇḍas* for as long as three nights. As Vasiṣṭha says: "In the case of a child who has died before reaching two years of age, or upon a miscarriage, the impurity for the *sapiṇḍas* lasts for three nights. Marīci states: "In the case of a miscarriage, one should observe [impurity] according to the month [of pregnancy]; for a new [birth], it is three days; for a Kṣatriya, four nights; and for a Vaiśya, five days."
This purification for a Śūdra is proclaimed to take eight days;
however, in the case of a miscarriage, there shall be a three-night impurity for the mother, while the period of impurity for the sapindas is excluded.
Upon the death of a mother, [the impurity lasts] for ten days; for the father and others, it lasts for three days.

Regarding this, Vṛddhavasiṣṭha states the distinction: "In the case of a miscarriage, for women there are as many nights of impurity as the number of months [of pregnancy], while for a man it is merely bathing; however, in the case of a miscarriage when the fetus has become somewhat firm, it is three nights. Furthermore, the distinction between *srāva* (miscarriage) and *pāta* (falling out) is stated in another Smṛti:
"Up to the fourth month it would be a *srāva*; from the fifth and sixth months it is a *pāta*. Beyond that, it is a birth (*prasūti*), and there shall be ten days of *sūtaka* (birth-impurity). (3.20)

He states the contraction of impurity for those killed by Brahmins, cows, or kings, as well as for suicides: "For those killed by Brahmins, cows, or kings, and for suicides, [impurity lasts] immediately."

The meaning is that when the death of those killed by Brahmins and others, as well as of those who have committed suicide in an unauthorized manner, is witnessed immediately—that is, directly perceived—in their bodies, there is impurity for their *sapiṇḍa* relatives. Gautama states: "In the case of those killed by cows or Brahmins, and by the king’s wrath; and in battle; and of those who voluntarily seek death through fasting, weapons, fire, poison, water, hanging, or falling from a precipice. If one is killed by the king through negligence rather than out of anger, or if one is killed in battle by him while he is angry, then there is no impurity for their *sapiṇḍa* relatives upon encountering them, because of the specific qualification "and by the king’s wrath in battle. Furthermore, in the case of those who die through fasting and so forth due to negligence, the full period of impurity applies, because of the inclusion of the term "voluntarily" (*icchatām*). [902] Śunahpuccha.
For those of the four castes who have perished by fire or other such means, or who were afflicted by disease, their sapinda relatives become pure after three nights; of this there is no doubt.
Aṅgiras:
An elderly man who has lost his memory of the rules of purity, and for whom medical treatment has been rejected,
should kill himself by means of Bhṛgu (a precipice), fire, fasting, or water.
For him, the period of impurity lasts three nights; on the second day, the collection of bones takes place;
on the third day, having offered water, one should perform the Śrāddha on the fourth day.
He is old, having exceeded seventy years of age. And thus says the Smṛti:
"One may be called a child until sixteen, as long as he is still nursing;
one is middle-aged until seventy, and beyond that, he is called old."
Likewise: "If one should cause his own death by means of fire, water, or other such means,
for him no period of impurity is prescribed, nor [is there] the offering of fire or the libation of water."
Now, if someone should die through negligence by means of fire, water, or the like,
impurity must be observed for him, and the water-libation rite should be performed.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Even through negligence, one who is free from doubt may suddenly be impelled by fate [to death] by means of horned animals,
creatures with stingers, those with claws, venomous serpents, poison, lightning, water, or fire."
Whether he has been killed by Cāṇḍālas or by thieves anywhere at all,
the cremation and other rites must be performed for him, because he is not fallen from his caste.
One who plays with horned animals, fanged beasts, venomous serpents, poisonous creatures, fire, or water must be avoided with care; for he dies.
Having acted against the will of the Nāgas, he was struck by lightning;
or else, he was somewhere seized by a king on account of the crime of theft.
Having gone to another's wife, he was killed by her husbands out of hatred;
and he engaged in conflict with those of mixed castes who were unequal to him, such as Caṇḍālas and others.

For having committed those [deeds], they are slain by them; indeed, they have taken their place among the Caṇḍālas and others, as well as among thieves, arsonists, poisoners, heretics, and those of cruel intellect.
Out of anger, those lowest of men who resort to fasting, poison, fire, weapons, hanging, water, or falling from mountains and trees;
Those who live by improper crafts, those who work as slaughterhouse decorators,
those with mouths like female genitals, and those who are mostly impotent or neuter;
Those who have been struck down by the *brahmadaṇḍa*, those who have been killed by Brahmins,
and those who are great sinners (*mahāpātakin*)— these are proclaimed to be the fallen (*patita*).
*Mahābhārata*: O lord of men, for one who is sinful, of evil conduct, and devoid of virtue, death itself is declared to be a sin; this is the certain conclusion regarding his destiny in hell.
Likewise: "Poisoning, hanging, burning, death at the hands of bandits,
and death from fanged beasts or domestic animals— this is called natural death."
The *Brahma Purāṇa*:
For those who have fallen [from their caste], there shall be no cremation, no funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi*), and no collection of bones;
nor should there be the shedding of tears, nor the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), nor should any *śrāddha* or similar rites ever be performed for them.
If one, being deluded, performs these [funeral rites] for those who have fallen [from their caste],
his purification occurs only through two *taptakṛcchra* penances and not otherwise.
But he who, out of compassion, desires to provide satisfaction for one who has fallen [into misfortune],
should summon a female slave who is capable of all tasks and whose wages have been paid, and [proceed as follows].
He even speaks to her as she stands there with an impure jar in her hand, saying:
"O servant, go quickly and fetch [water] from the sacred ford for a price."
Then, facing southward, place this water-filled jar containing sesame seeds upon [the corpse] with your left foot and cast it away.
One should utter the name "Pātinī" and repeatedly command, "Drink that!
Upon hearing his words, she becomes one who has received her price and performs that act.
When this is done, there shall be satisfaction for those who have fallen; it is not otherwise.
However, for those who have fallen, [the rite] is sometimes performed after a year has passed.
Because the local custom is authoritative,
one should perform a *śrāddha* at Gayākūpa or at the feet of Mārtaṇḍa together with one’s kinsmen, while recollecting Hari and Hara.
The site at the foot of Mārtaṇḍa is well known in Kaśmīra. (From the) Skanda Purāṇa:

"For those who have not been cremated, for those for whom the funeral rice-balls (piṇḍas) were not offered, and likewise for the fallen and those who did not observe vows—one should never perform the Śrāddha or the offering of rice-balls; such is the Vedic revelation."

In the intercalary month, with great care, one should observe the lunar day (tithi) of both the bright and dark fortnights that falls within the solar mansion (sūryakṣetra) for the performance of the śrāddha rite.

In each respective solar mansion (*ravikṣetra*) and in the thirteenth month, one should perform the *śrāddha* and the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍapradāna*) at the feet of Mārtaṇḍa. Sumantu states: "For those who have fallen from a cliff, by fire, or into water; for those killed in battle; for those residing in another land; for renunciants (*saṃnyāsin*); for those who have fasted to death; for those struck by lightning; and for those traveling on a long journey—the water-rites (*udakakriyā*) must be performed, and purification (*śauca*) occurs immediately. Kaśyapa states: "For those who have gone through fasting, those struck by lightning, those who have entered fire or water, those who have gone to a cliff, to battle, or into the wilderness, and for fetuses whose teeth have emerged—purification is attained after three nights. The word "death" (*maraṇa*) is to be supplied as the context.
If he has gone abroad, the period remaining shall apply; if no time remains, it shall be exactly three days.
When a year has passed for all [deceased relatives], having offered water for the deceased, one becomes pure.

When a *sapiṇḍa* who has gone abroad and died is heard of after ten nights have passed, but while the period of impurity (*āśauca*) has not yet elapsed, the impurity lasts for the remainder of those ten nights. If it is heard after the ten-night period has already expired, then there is three nights of impurity for all *sapiṇḍas*. If it is heard only after a full year has passed, then one becomes pure by offering water to the deceased. However, Gautama states that if death occurs abroad after ten nights have passed, the impurity lasts for a "two-day period" (*pakṣiṇī rātri*): "And having heard [of the death] after the tenth day, [the impurity lasts for] a *pakṣiṇī*. Vasiṣṭha, on the other hand, prescribes impurity for only one night: "If a deceased person is abroad and is heard of after ten days, the impurity lasts for one night. Manu, however, prescribes immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*).

"Having heard of the death of a relative after the ten-day period has passed, and of the birth of a son, a person becomes pure by immersing himself in water along with his clothes. Here, "nirdaśam" means that the ten days have elapsed. To resolve the contradiction between these [texts], Devala states the following rule:
"Up until three fortnights, it shall be three nights; from six months onwards, it is a *pakṣiṇī*;
beyond that, up to a year, it is one day; after that, one becomes pure by bathing.
A night with a day on either side is called a *pakṣiṇī*. With this very intention, Viṣṇu also says:

"Within three fortnights, [impurity lasts] for three nights; within six months, however, for a day and night; and within a year, even when those who have died in a foreign land [are heard of], it lasts for one day. Here, by the word *divā* (day), two days are meant in order to establish the status of *pakṣiṇī* (a period of two nights with the intervening day). Viṣṇu states: "Upon hearing of birth or death occurring in a foreign land, one becomes pure through the remainder of the impurity; but if the period of impurity has already passed, one becomes pure after one night within a year, and beyond that, by bathing alone. Vṛddha-Manu describes the definition of a foreign land (*deśāntara*).
Where there is a great river in between, or a mountain acting as an obstruction,
and where languages diverge— that is called a different country.
Bṛhaspati says: Some say the distance to another country extends for sixty yojanas;
others say forty, and others likewise thirty.
Another Smṛti states:
Eight barley-corn widths [of the horizontal] and three grains of rice [of the vertical] constitute the measure of one finger (aṅgula);
twelve fingers make a span (vitasti).
Two *vitastis* make one *aratni*; from that, a *kiṣku*; from that, a *dhanus*.
Two thousand *dhanus* make a *krośa*, and four *krośas* make a *yojana*.

A *kiṣku* is exactly twice the length of an *aratni*. From that *kiṣku*, a *dhanus* (bow-length) is likewise exactly double; so too says the *Nāmakośa*. A *kiṣku* consists of four *hasta*s (cubits). Paiṭhīnasi has spoken regarding the subject of parents:

"Even if a son is far away, upon hearing that his parents have died, he should observe the period of impurity (*sūtaka*) for ten days, starting from the day [of the news], provided he possesses knowledge [of the event]."

"Sūtaka" means impurity (āśauca). The phrase "after ten nights" is to be understood as the remainder [of the period]. But during its middle, however, it is by the remaining [period] alone. Dakṣa says:
"In the event of the death of a great guru, even if a year has passed, the funeral rites must be performed according to rule, wearing wet clothes and a sacred thread."
Likewise: "When the wife of one's father has passed away, the best of the twice-born shall remain impure for three nights— even if the ten-day period has elapsed— excluding his own mother."
Regarding the subject of birth, Devala says:
"There is no impurity regarding a birth, even when the days have passed. Manu says:
If a child, one residing in another country, or a person belonging to a different lineage (pṛthakpiṇḍa) has died,
one becomes pure immediately by immersing oneself in water along with one's clothes.
The two [categories] who are not sapinda relatives are distinguished by their residence in another country. || 3.21 ||
He states the period of impurity for Kṣatriyas and others:
"For a Kṣatriya it is twelve days, and for a Vaiśya it is fifteen. (3.22)

The period of impurity (*āśauca*) for birth and death is thirty days for a Śūdra, half of that for one who follows the right path, and fifteen and thirty days respectively for Kṣatriyas and others. Furthermore, for a Śūdra who follows the right path, it is fifteen days. Following the right path means performing what is prescribed. This being the case, it should be understood that by the rule "three nights or ten nights," the period of impurity for a Brāhmaṇa is stated by way of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*). As for that which was stated by Parāśara:
"A Kṣatriya devoted to his own duty becomes pure after ten days."
In the same way, a Vaiśya shall attain purification in twelve days.

That [rule] refers to Kṣatriyas and others who maintain the Vedic fires (*vedāgni*). As for what was stated by Vasiṣṭha—"A Rājanya [is purified] in fifteen nights, a Vaiśya in twenty nights"—that refers to those Rājanyas and others who subsist merely by their caste (*jātimātra*). Furthermore, as for the rule of Āṅgirasa: "For all castes alike, in the case of birth or death, purification occurs after ten days; or else, according to the word of Śātātapa..."

This statement prescribes the rules for impurity (āśauca) for all castes living together with a Brāhmaṇa father. Likewise, Manu says: "But all [members] of the higher castes shall observe the impurity from the beginning according to the rule prescribed for that caste; however, their own impurity regarding those of their own birth shall be as prescribed for themselves."

The meaning is this: all those of lower castes, such as Kṣatriyas and others, when there is a birth or death among those born of the highest castes, such as Brāhmaṇas, shall observe impurity for ten nights and so forth, according to the rules prescribed for that caste; however, when births or deaths occur among their own kin, they shall observe their own [caste-specific] impurity. And thus says Āpastamba: "When there is a death or birth among those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, their impurity is that of the father if they are undivided, but that of the mother if they are divided."
As for that which was stated by Manu: "For Śūdras who live according to the law, shaving should be performed monthly;
their rules for purification are like those of Vaiśyas, and their food consists of the remnants of the twice-born."

Thus, in that context, the rule for impurity consisting of fifteen nights is extended by analogy to the Vaiśya, because it is specifically prescribed for him in his own scripture (*sva-śāstra*). Furthermore, the righteous livelihood (*nyāya-vṛtti*) of a Śūdra consists of service to the twice-born (*dvijāti*), the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañca-yajña*), the maintenance of dependents, devotion to his wife, and so forth. And in the case of a Kṣatriya and others who have undergone initiation (*upanayana*), a period of twelve days and so on is ordained when they die. For the Śūdra, however, the taking of two garments takes the place of initiation. As he [the author] himself says: "A Brāhmaṇa [is pure after ten days] until the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass; a Kṣatriya until the grasping of the bow..."
A Vaiśya [is purified] by the grasping of the goad, and a Śūdra by the grasping of two garments. Śaṅkha says:
"But a Śūdra who has not married a wife [is purified] after sixteen years."
He shall meet his death within a month, and his kinsmen as well.
The word "are purified" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"When relatives among the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes die, or when [sons] are born to them, purification for a Brāhmaṇa is held to occur after ten days."
Because local custom is authoritative, for Kṣatriyas it is six nights,
for Vaiśyas three nights, and for Śūdras only one day.
If a Kṣatriya dies, or a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra who is a relative of a Vaiśya, one becomes pure after the period of impurity belonging to that specific person.
For Śūdras who are sapinda relatives, the periods of impurity for the [higher] castes are prescribed respectively as one night, three nights, six nights, and one month.
For a Vaiśya who is a sapinda, the period of impurity for the various castes is traditionally prescribed as three nights, six nights, and likewise one fortnight, respectively.
For a Brāhmaṇa, purification from the death of a Kṣatriya who is a sapinda occurs after six nights;
for the remaining castes, one should prescribe twelve days.
"In the case of a Brāhmaṇa who is a sapinda, all castes are purified in exactly ten nights without distinction; so said the venerable Yama. (3.22)
But for [intercourse with] unmarried girls and young boys, there is purification by means of a fast. (3.23)

If maidens who have been promised to a bridegroom should die while [still unmarried] among a teacher, a resident pupil, a fellow student, a maternal uncle, or a learned *śrotriya*, then their *sapiṇḍas* become pure after one day and night. For these women, the *sapiṇḍa* relationship extends to three generations, according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "For unmarried women, the *sapiṇḍa* relationship extends to three generations. Here, by the force of the inclusion of the term "unmarried," it is understood that for married women, the *sapiṇḍa* relationship extends to seven generations along with the husband’s side. As for what was stated by Manu: "But for women who have not been consecrated [by marriage], the kinsmen become pure after three days."
"And their kinsmen are purified by the very same procedure as previously described. [908]

The meaning of this is as follows: the *bāndhavas*—those on the husband’s side—of women who are *asaṃskṛtāḥ* (unmarried) become pure after three days; however, the *sanābhayas*—those on the father’s side—become pure according to the rule previously stated. And here, since the term *sanābhi* is used separately to designate those on the father’s side, the word *bāndhava* refers to the husband’s side. Furthermore, the status of being on the husband’s side cannot exist prior to the formal giving away (*pradāna*) of the girl; therefore, this rule applies to the death of women who have been verbally betrothed by their father or others but remain unrefined by the marriage rite. As for the *sanābhayas*, the paternal *sapindas*, they become pure according to that three-day rule which was prescribed for the death of a young boy after the tonsure ceremony (*caula*) but before the initiation (*upanayana*).

"The rite of marriage is declared to be the *upanayana* for women," according to this statement of Manu, marriage occupies the place of the *upanayana*. Consequently, the rule is that there is one day of impurity (*ekāha*) when the girls are unmarried, and three days (*tryaha*) when they are married. And so says Vṛddha-Manu:
"In the case of an immature girl, however, immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śauca*) is prescribed."
But for unmarried girls, as well as those who have been given away in marriage, the period is three days.

Marīci states: "For girls, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śauca*) prior to the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*); one day (*ekāha*) prior to being given away in marriage; and three days (*tryaha*) for those who have been given away but not yet married. Pulastya says: "In the case of an immature girl, purification is immediate; for a mature girl, one becomes pure after a day. For a girl who has been betrothed (*pradattā*), purification occurs after three nights; for one who has been formally given away (*dattā*), it shall be a period of two days and the intervening night (*pakṣiṇī*)."

When she has been given away—that is, when the verbal betrothal (*vāgdattā*) has occurred or the gift has already been made—Viṣṇu states: "In the case of women who have undergone the sacramental rites (*saṃskṛtā*), there is no impurity for the paternal kin; however, if her birth or death occurs in the father's house, then there shall be one night or three nights [of impurity]. Birth entails one night, while in other cases it entails three nights. Paiṭhīnasi says: "For maidens, the paternal lineage (*pitṛgotra*) prevails; for married women, the husband’s lineage (*bhartṛgotra*).
But in the case of those who have died after the offering of water, [the rule applies] to both."
Yama:
"When both parents have passed away, what indeed shall be the period of impurity for women?
Purification occurs after three nights; thus said the blessed Yama."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "If a woman who has been given away in her father's house gives birth or dies,
her circle of kinsmen is purified by one day, but the biological father is purified by three days."
If a girl dies anywhere from birth until the time of the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā),
there shall always be immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca) for all castes.
From that point until the formal giving of the bride (vāgdāna), it lasts for only one day;

beyond this, for those who have reached adulthood, it should be known to last three days for both [the father and the groom]. After that, however, for those who have been given away, it belongs to the husband alone.
The period of impurity for both birth and death shall be that which is prescribed for one's own caste.
But a maiden who, though given by her father, has out of independence taken refuge with another—
whomever she subsequently resorts to, for that person there shall be a three-day period of impurity.
The settled rule is that [the impurity lasts] when she has died or given birth, but not for others;
however, this applies where a girl has been chosen by someone for the seventh step.
Her gotra shall be that of her husband, and that indeed prevails;
however, when she has given birth, it becomes her father’s, and thereafter, that of her original husband.
If, out of desire, she remains with another after having gone to him while her virginity is intact,
she would belong to the same lineage as that other man whom she herself has taken as her refuge.

Having thus spoken regarding the case of a maiden, he speaks regarding the case of a child: "And purification among children [is immediate]. Children are those for whom the naming ceremony has been performed but who have not yet grown teeth; when they die, purification occurs on that very day. Likewise, when elders and others who are non-sapindas have passed away, purification is achieved in just one day and night. Incidentally, something else is also written here; regarding this, Manu says: "If a child born alive should die, or if a dead child should be born..."
In that case, there shall be birth-impurity for the mother, while for the father and others it lasts for three nights.

This [period] applies from the seventh month onwards until birth, based on the indicative mark [in the scriptures] that one is "born while living. For those such as fathers who possess merit, the impurity lasts for three nights; for others, it is ten days. As for what was stated by Bṛhadviṣṇu—"If a child dies at birth, or is born dead, there is immediate purification for the family"—that refers to the case of *samānodaka* (distant sapinda) relations, not to *sapiṇḍa* relations. Therefore, Manu says: "When a child, or one residing in another country, or one who is a separate *piṇḍa* (beyond the seventh degree) has died, one becomes pure immediately after immersing oneself in water along with one's clothes."
One who has a separate funeral ball (*piṇḍa*) is a non-*sapiṇḍa*. Here, "infant" refers to one whose name has not yet been given. Regarding this very subject, Kātyāyana also says:
"If death occurs before the ten-day period has elapsed, there shall be purification immediately; there is neither *preta* [impurity] nor *sūtaka* [birth impurity]. [910]

Alternatively, the statements of Viṣṇu and Kātyāyana are intended to prohibit untouchability. For this very reason, Vṛddha-Manu says: "If a child dies through negligence within ten days, one should not observe the impurity of death (śāvāśauca); one becomes pure by means of the impurity of birth (sūtiśauca)."
Hārīta states: "Whether a child is born dead or dies after being born, the period of impurity for the *sapiṇḍas* lasts ten days. As for the statement of Bṛhan-Manu:
"If one born alive should die, or if one who was dead should be born [alive], the full period of *sūtaka* applies to the mother, while for the father and others it is three nights."

Thus, that [rule] refers to one belonging to a more excellent lineage (*gotra*), or to one who performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice, or to a *samānodaka* relative; "one whose life lasts but a moment" means one born alive. Śaṅkha also speaks with the intention of referring to the performance of the *agnihotra*:
"If death occurs before ten days have passed, the mother’s impurity lasts for the period of birth, but the father becomes pure upon touching water."

Kāśyapa states: "For children who have not yet cut their teeth, purification occurs after three nights. Paiṭhīnasi states: "In the case of a child who has not yet cut its teeth, the impurity due to death lasts for three nights. Śaṅkha states: "But in the case of a child who has not yet cut its teeth, immediate purification is prescribed;
likewise, purification occurs after one day and night in the case of a child whose tonsure ceremony (cūḍā) has been performed."
In the same way, however, if [the deceased] was not initiated, the kinsmen become pure after three days.

This refers to Brahmins, or it refers to kinsmen other than one’s mother and father. Furthermore, the three-night period prescribed by Kaśyapa for one whose teeth have not yet emerged applies to Kṣatriyas and others, or to the father. In this context, the term "one whose teeth have not yet emerged" refers to one who has not yet had his name-giving ceremony performed. As Śaṅkha says: "Before the naming ceremony, purification is immediate. However, as stated by Aṅgiras: "In the case of a child born after [the parents' death], there shall be impurity until the relatives go outside and perform a bath with their clothes on."

Thus, this refers to the case of a *sapiṇḍa* who possesses virtuous qualities, excluding the mother and father; and it applies when death occurs after the period of impurity has passed but before the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*). As for that which was stated by Yama:
"In the case of a son whose teeth have not yet emerged, or in the case of a child, or likewise upon a miscarriage, there is purification for all *sapiṇḍas* after one day and night."

Thus, this should be understood as applying when the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) has taken place. Regarding the rule prescribed for a single day (*ekāha*) in the case of a miscarriage, that is to be adopted for *sapiṇḍas* who possess exceptional qualities; for others, it is three days (*tryaha*). However, for one whose teeth have emerged, there is impurity for three nights (*trirātra*) even if the cremation rite (*agnisaṃskāra*) is performed without the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*). As Aṅgiras says: "Even if he has not had his tonsure, if he has teeth and has passed away, one should cremate him and likewise observe impurity for three days."
Furthermore, regarding those under two years of age, that which was stated by Manu:
"Neither the consecration with fire nor the water-rite should be performed for him;
having abandoned him like a piece of wood in the forest, one should cast him away, or [leave him] for exactly three days."

That [rule] regarding one whose *cūḍā* ceremony has been performed applies to the first year; yet this is not fixed, because in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*, the consecration by fire (*agnisaṃskāra*) for one whose *cūḍā* has been performed is stated even in the first year:
"Even if he has not yet cut his teeth, if he has passed away after his *cūḍā* was performed, one should still perform the funeral rites for him and observe impurity (*āśauca*) for three days."

In the third year, however, for one whose *cūḍā* ceremony has been performed and who has passed away, there is the consecration with fire (*agnisaṃskāra*), followed by the offering of water (*udaka*). This is because the rules regarding burial and the prohibition of water-offerings pertain specifically to those under two years of age. Consequently, this rule is established: in the midst of a period of impurity (*āśauca*), if a child dies, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*). After the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) but before the eruption of teeth, the parents observe three nights of impurity; for other *sapiṇḍas*, it is one day. If death occurs in the first year even for one whose *cūḍā* has not been performed, then in the case of cremation, the relatives also observe three nights; in the alternative case (burial), it is one day. For one whose *cūḍā* has been performed, it is exactly three days in both cases. In the third year, upon the passing of one whose *cūḍā* has been performed, there is the mandatory offering of fire and water, or else three days [of impurity]. All of this refers to the case of a Brāhmaṇa. Regarding the case of Kṣatriyas and others, Aṅgiras says:
"If a Brahmin dies before his tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*), purification is achieved in three years;
however, if a Kṣatriya dies, purification is in three days, and likewise if a Vaiśya dies. This refers to one whose *cūḍā* has not been performed. Likewise:
Purification is prescribed after three nights when a Brahmin's tonsure ceremony has been performed;
for a Kṣatriya, it is prescribed after six nights, and for a Vaiśya, after nine.
If a Śūdra dies when he is less than three years old, purification occurs after five days;
if a Śūdra dies after that age, a period of twelve days is prescribed.
"If a Śūdra who has passed beyond six years dies, the purification shall be monthly; thus was it spoken by Āṅgirasa. So says Ṛṣyaśṛṅga.
Where a three-night period of impurity applies for Brahmins,
it shall be twelve days for a Śūdra, and six or nine days for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas respectively.
Hārīta says: A Brāhmaṇa [remains a student] until the tying of the girdle of muñja grass; a Kṣatriya until the taking up of the bow;
a Vaiśya until the taking up of the goad; and a Śūdra until the taking up of the two garments.

The implication is that one who has died becomes the cause for the full period of impurity. However, prior to the tying of the girdle (mauñjībandhana), for all castes without distinction, purification occurs after three nights; for girls, it is ordained to be by a single day, according to their respective order.

Pāraskara states: "When one who is less than two years old dies, the impurity belongs to the mother and father, but not to others. This is intended to refer to the state of untouchability (*aspṛśyatva*). Thus ends the incidental discussion.
[The same applies] in the case of a teacher, a resident pupil, a fellow student, a maternal uncle, and a *śrotriya*.

When teachers (*guru*) and others who are not *sapiṇḍa* relatives have passed away, purification occurs after exactly one day and night. Here, the "teacher" (*guru*) refers to one who acts as such through service (*upacārika*), not the primary (biological) teacher; for the latter is already included among the *sapiṇḍa* relatives. Alternatively, there is no contradiction in including even the primary teacher when the *sapiṇḍa* relationship has ceased with respect to those such as adopted sons (*datta*) or sons cast off (*apaviddha*). The "resident pupil" (*antevāsī*) is a student. The "learned one" (*anūcāna*) is a sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*). The maternal uncle (*mātula*) is well known. Although the term *śrotriya* is commonly used for anyone who merely studies the Veda (*chandas*), here it applies specifically to one who is distinguished as a fellow-student (*sabrahmacārin*). "For a fellow religious student (*sabrahmacārin*), it is traditionally taught that purification lasts for one day. In this context, a "fellow religious student" is one who shares the same teacher and studies together. Manu says:
"But a disciple, performing the *pitṛmedha* (funeral rites) for his deceased teacher..."
In that case, one becomes pure after ten nights, along with those who eat the food of the hungry ghosts (pretas).

In this context, the "teacher" (ācārya) refers to the preceptor (guru). "Pitṛmedha" refers to the funeral rites. However, it has been stated by that same author: "They say that when a teacher has passed away, the period of impurity lasts for three nights;
but for his son and his wife, the rule is one day and night."
Thus it is said; this should be understood as applying when the performance of the *pitṛmedha* (funeral rites) has not taken place. Likewise:

"Upon the death of a learned *śrotriya*, one shall remain impure for three nights; upon the death of a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman, one shall remain impure for a *pakṣiṇī* night."

The term "upasaṃpanna" (endowed with excellence) is also a qualification for maternal uncles and others. Consequently, there is no contradiction between the three-night period prescribed by Yājñavalkya for a *śrotriya* and the one-night period for maternal uncles and others; for "upasaṃpanna" means one who possesses virtues. Furthermore, in the *Manu-smṛti*, a *śrotriya* residing in the same village is intended, whereas elsewhere, one not residing in the same village is meant. As for the rule, "But for one who is not a *śrotriya*, the impurity lasts a full day, and likewise for a teacher who has studied the Veda," this refers to a non-*śrotriya* living in the same village. And as for the rule: [913] ... [the text continues with further citations and analysis regarding the distinctions between various types of relatives and the corresponding periods of ritual impurity]. *(Note: The provided source text contains a fragmentary section ending at [913]. The translation above reflects the available portion of the commentary on the legal distinctions regarding impurity periods based on the relationship and qualifications of the deceased.)*

Having carried out the corpse of a deceased twice-born man who is not a sapinda, a Brahmin becomes pure after three nights, as if for a kinsman; the same applies to the maternal relatives of his mother.
This statement of Manu is also not contradictory, as it refers to the person who performs the funeral rites for the mother’s own kinsmen, such as maternal uncles and others. Bṛhaspati says:
"One shall remain impure for three days in the case of a maternal grandfather, a teacher, or a Śrotriya. Pracetas says:
If the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) or the patron (*yājya*) has died, one becomes pure after three nights;
this refers specifically to the case of a family priest. Upon the death of a daughter's son (*dauhitra*) or a sister's son (*bhaginīsuta*), one must observe the "two-day" period (*pakṣiṇī rātri*).
But for one who has undergone the purificatory rites, the rule is established that it shall be three nights.
He has been brought to the state of refinement.
Regarding women who have been married, what should be the case upon the death of their parents?
Lord Yama says that purification occurs in exactly three nights.
One should pass the night as a bird (in silence) with one's father-in-law, his sister, a maternal uncle's wife, a maternal uncle, and likewise with a paternal aunt.

The meaning is: "when she who is the sister of one's parents—that is, of the mother and father—is deceased. Uśanas says: "In the case of a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, a friend, a teacher, or the wives of teachers, there is impurity for a *pakṣiṇī* night; likewise if one's maternal grandmother has died."

In this context, the term *guru* is used in a secondary sense. Gautama states: "For one who is not a *sapiṇḍa*, but is related by birth or a fellow student, the impurity lasts for three nights (*pakṣiṇī*). A relative by birth is one connected through the mother or father; if such a person is not a *sapiṇḍa*, then one should observe the *pakṣiṇī* period. Viṣṇu says: "If someone who is not a *sapiṇḍa* dies in one's own house, the impurity lasts for one night. As stated by Aṅgiras:
"If anyone who is not a *sapiṇḍa* should somehow die in someone's house, that person's impurity should be known to last for three nights; there is no doubt in this matter."

Thus, if a person has died while possessing virtuous qualities, the impurity lasts for ten days; or, if the death occurs at home, it is due to the condition of affection (*sneha*) and so forth. However, if it is due to the condition of religious merit (*dharma*), it is for one day. Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya states:
"In the case of a consecrated sister, or even when a brother is consecrated;
when a friend, a son-in-law, a daughter's son, or a sister's son has died..."
Upon the death of a maternal uncle or his son, one becomes pure immediately by bathing.

A "consecrated" (saṃskṛtā) girl is one who has already been married. The "consecration" (saṃskāra) for a brother refers to the initiation ceremony (upanayana). Upon his death, there is immediate purification for a sister who has already been consecrated. The prescription of immediate purification for a daughter's son and a sister's son is intended to signify the cessation of that impurity which causes disqualification from performing essential rites such as the five daily sacrifices (pañcayajña). However, it should be understood from other scriptural statements that until the end of the *pakṣiṇī* period, one must avoid meat, sexual intercourse, sleeping on the ground, bathing, and festive celebrations. Alternatively, this may refer specifically to the case of an uninitiated daughter's son or sister's son. Likewise:
As long as the corpse of anyone remains within the middle of a village, that village remains impure; once it has been removed, it attains purity.
Bṛhaspati says: "The sapindas become pure after ten days following a death or a birth;
the sakulyas become pure after three nights; and those born of the same lineage (gotrajas) become pure by bathing."
The *sakulyas* are those who share the *samānodaka* status. Jābāli says:

"For three days is the period of impurity prescribed for *samānodakas* and for those born of the same lineage (*gotraja*); likewise for a maternal relative, a teacher, a friend, and a regional ruler. (3.23)
In the case of sons not born of one's own seed, and in the case of wives who have gone to another man. || 3.24 ||

When sons other than the *aurasa* (legitimate son born of one’s own body), such as the *kṣetraja* (son born of the wife), have died, or when wives who have been married have died while residing with another man, the period of impurity is one day and night (*ahorātra*). By the use of the word "and" (*ca*) here, the previously mentioned *ahorātra* is brought forward [from the preceding rule]. Prajāpati says: "In the case of wives who have resorted to others and in the case of the sons of another's wife, the kinsmen (*gotrin*) become pure by bathing; however, their father becomes pure after three nights."

If [the relative] is present, it should be arranged for three nights; if absent, for one night. Viṣṇu states: "Upon the birth or death of non-legitimate sons, and upon the delivery or death of wives who previously had another husband."
The period of three nights applies here [to the following]. Marīci says:
"In the case of birth-impurity (sūtaka) and death-impurity (mṛtaka), there is a three-night period for those who have previously been married to another;
however, for sapindas it is one day, whereas for the father it is indeed three nights."

The meaning of *parapūrvayoḥ* is as follows: for a wife whose former husband (*pūrvaḥ patiḥ*) is another, and for a son—such as one who was purchased—who has another father (*paraḥ pitā*) while the previous one is still living; these two are called *parapūrva*. Regarding them, if they possess good qualities and are present, the impurity lasts for three nights; otherwise, it is for one day. Following the rule that "there is no impurity," Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In the case of wives who have had a former husband, or in the case of adopted sons, there is neither suspension of Vedic study nor the performance of water-libations. In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "Excepting the legitimate son (*aurasa*), when among those of equal caste, sons born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) and others are born or die..."
And for those of the same lineage, the purification shall be three nights; this is the settled rule.
Likewise:
"In the case where a woman previously given to another has two sons,
and the period for the father is three nights, there [the period] for the sapindas shall be one [night]."
Where there is one mother for two [children], or where there are fathers [of different lineages] anywhere,
there shall be a mutual unity regarding their birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtaka).

"The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) is equal to him" means that the son of an appointed daughter is not other than a legitimate son (aurasa); therefore, he is not mentioned separately here. Hārīta states:

"In the case of wives who have had previous husbands, and in the case of adopted sons, the impurity lasts for three nights for the maternal grandfather; however, it is for one day if they are not *asapiṇḍa*. (3.24)
Likewise, regarding the day of purification for one who dies while residing [in a kingdom]:

"Nivāsa" refers to the territory in which one dwells; when the king—the sovereign—of that territory has died, for those residing in that territory, the very day on which he who was their sole protector dies is the cause of purification. In this regard, even if he dies at night, then that very night is the cause of purification. The word "day" (*ahaḥ*) is indicative of the time-period (the whole day and night). As Manu says: "When a king has died, purification lasts as long as there is light for one whose residence is within his domain."
That period of impurity which occurs together with the solar light, or the light of the stars, is called "sajyotis" (with light).
He states an exception to impurity even in cases such as the birth of a sapinda relative, in certain jurisdictions:
"There is no impurity for kings [who die] when they have been killed by lightning. (2.25)
For the sake of cows and Brahmins in battle, he for whom kings desire victory;

The word *mahī* here refers to those portions of the earth (*kṣiti*), which is essentially a circle, that serve as the cause for the production of revenue; it does not, however, refer to the entire terrestrial globe. For no one can possibly be the master of the whole; indeed, places such as mountains, oceans, forests, rivers, and streams do not belong to anyone. Whatever enjoyment a king has in his paths of travel, coming and going, and so forth, that much belongs to the people as well. Here, "lords of the earth" (*mahīpatayaḥ*) are the rulers of provinces (*janapada*). There is no impurity (*āśauca*) for them regarding the birth of a sapinda relative or similar occasions. Alternatively, the prohibition of impurity concerns matters such as giving gifts necessary for the protection of the province, but not in every case. As Viṣṇu says: "There is no impurity for kings in royal affairs, nor for those under vows during their vow, nor for those performing a sacrificial session (*satra*) during the session, nor for artisans in their artisanal work. Furthermore, there is no impurity for those killed by lightning, or those killed in battle for the purpose of protecting cows and Brahmins, nor for the sapindas of those—such as priests (*purohita*)—for whose sake the kings desire purity for the successful accomplishment of the protection of subjects. This is intended as an illustration; therefore, Pracetas says: [916] The lords of the earth are the rulers of provinces. There is no impurity for them regarding the birth of a sapinda relative and so forth. Or rather, the prohibition of impurity concerns matters useful for the protection of the province, such as giving gifts, but not everywhere. As Viṣṇu says: "Not for kings in royal business, not for those under vows while on their vow, not for those performing a sacrificial session while in the session, not for artisans in their artisanal work. And for those who are struck by lightning, and those who are killed in battle for the purpose of protecting cows and Brahmins, their sapindas—and those such as priests for whose sake the kings desire purity for the sake of accomplishing the protection of subjects—for all of these there is no impurity. And this is for the sake of illustration; hence Pracetas says:
Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, as well as male and female slaves,
kings, and royal servants are declared to be immediately pure.
And regarding this urgent medical work and the like, the rule for their purification applies precisely in those cases. Śātātapa states:
"Śūdras who work for wages, as well as female and male slaves, are not defiled in bathing, in personal grooming, or in household chores."
This refers to a time of distress. Another Smṛti states:
"A slave born in the house becomes pure immediately; a slave for food becomes pure after three days.
Likewise:
Whatever a physician does cannot be accomplished by another;
therefore, a physician is always pure in touch.
Devala says:
For a consecrated Kṣatriya, for one who has retired from worldly life, and for one who bears the marks of an ascetic—
because of their preeminence and because of their renunciation— they are remembered as pure and not impure.

For a consecrated Kṣatriya, as well as for one who has retired from worldly life, who has abandoned attachments, and who bears the marks of an ascetic (liṅgin)—for these, [impurity] is not impure but indeed pure. Because of the preeminence of the Kṣatriya, death and other such events do not cause impurity for his sapinda relatives; and because the renunciant (saṃnyāsin) has abandoned kinship, there is immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca). This follows the continuation [of the rule] by Manu: "And for those killed in a riot or battle, by lightning, or by the king;
for one killed for the sake of cows or Brahmins; and for whomever the king desires."
A quarrel without weapons is a childish brawl. Likewise:
"For one slain in battle with raised weapons according to the duty of a Kṣatriya, the sacrifice is instantly completed and so too is purification; such is the established rule. [917]
Yama says:
For those killed in a riot or battle, as well as for those who have offered their lives in sacrifice,
and for those [killed] by rivers, wild beasts, or fanged predators, immediate purification is ordained.

Those who perform sacrifices for life and those who bestow life [are purified immediately]. For those who are sapinda relatives of persons who have died in rivers and similar waters, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*). Bṛhaspati says: "In the case of a riot, by lightning, by the king, or while protecting cows or Brahmins, they say that for one killed there is immediate purification; other great seers, however, say three days."
In this matter, the distinction is based on the presence or absence of qualities, or rather, on proximity or non-proximity. Parāśara states:
"For those who perish for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, for those killed by their captors, and for those who perish in battles, there is impurity for one night."

Sumantu states: "For those who have fallen by [the act of] Bhrigu, fire, water, battle, or while staying in another land; for those who are about to depart, those who have fasted to death, those killed by lightning, and those who died on a long journey—water-libations (udakakriyā) must be performed, and immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca) occurs. This refers to cases where the causes of death, such as Bhrigu or fire, are not prohibited [by other rules]. Kaśyapa states: "One is purified in three nights for those killed by fasting, those killed by lightning, those who have entered fire or water, those who have gone to Bhrigu or to battle or another land, and for fetuses whose teeth have emerged. The arrangement between immediate purification and purification in three nights depends on whether the deceased possessed virtuous qualities or not. (2.25)
He states the impurity resulting from following [a corpse]: "A Śūdra must never be followed by a Brāhmaṇa, nor a twice-born man ever. (3.26)
Having followed [the corpse] and bathed in water, one who has touched fire and consumed clarified butter becomes pure.

A Śūdra should not be followed by a Brāhmaṇa, nor should a twice-born man follow one who is not a *sapiṇḍa* relative; for regarding the following of *sapiṇḍas*, it is ordained: "The deceased should be followed by kinsmen. If he should nevertheless follow [such a person], then he becomes purified by bathing in water located in a river or similar body of water, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter. This rule for purification concerns the case of following someone of the same caste (*sajātīya*). However, in the case of following someone of a different caste (*asajātīya*), the penance is greater. Regarding that, Parāśara says concerning the following of a Śūdra:
But a Brāhmaṇa who, weak in knowledge, follows a Śūdra who has become a corpse while being carried away,
becomes pure after three nights.
When those three nights have passed, one should go to a river that flows into the ocean,
perform a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), consume clarified butter, and thus become pure.
When the Śūdras have turned back and stand at the edge of the water, then the twice-born should follow them; this is the eternal law.

As for the Vasiṣṭha injunction regarding penance—"Having touched a human bone that is oily, there is impurity for three nights; but if it is not oily, for a day and a night—and the same applies to following a corpse"—that does not concern the following of twice-born men of lower castes. And the Mānava [text] states: "If one intentionally follows a deceased person, whether a relative or a stranger, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter."

"This is the cause of purification for one who follows this corpse with the intention, 'I am following this *preta*,' but not for one who merely follows behind for whatever reason. Baudhāyana states: "Upon touching the corpse of a *pāraśava*, if it was unintentional, one becomes pure by touching water while wearing one's clothes; however, if it was intentional, [one remains impure] for three nights. A *pāraśava* is one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother; this rule applies to touching his corpse. Gautama states: "In the case of touching a *preta*, there is impurity (*āśauca*) for ten nights if it was intentional. For a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, it has been stated [elsewhere], or else for the number of nights corresponding to the seasons (*ṛtu*), or for three days in the case of the two preceding [castes]. The meaning of this is as follows: If a Brāhmaṇa performs the carrying or cremation of a *preta* after considering a fee (i.e., for hire), then the impurity lasts for fifteen or thirty days. Or else, it lasts for the number of nights corresponding to the seasons—five or six, since there are five or six seasons. In that regard, the impurity is five nights for a Vaiśya and six for a Śūdra. And this should be understood to apply to a virtuous person performing the carrying and so forth in times of distress. For the two preceding castes, it is either the number of nights corresponding to the seasons or three days. In that context, it is five nights for a Brāhmaṇa and six for a Kṣatriya; or in both cases, it is three nights. This option depends on the relative degree of their virtues. Likewise: "If a lower caste person touches a higher caste person, or a higher caste person touches a lower one, then the impurity is that which has been declared for a corpse (*śāva*). The meaning is that one should know that even for one who touches a corpse, the impurity belongs to the caste of that corpse, such as ten nights, twelve nights, and so forth. (3.26)
He states an exception to the aforementioned rules of impurity for certain individuals:
"For officiating priests and those who have been consecrated, while they are performing sacrificial rites. (3.27)
Likewise, for those who have undertaken sacrificial vows, celibates, donors, and knowers of Brahman;
in the case of giving, marriage, sacrifice, battle, or the ruin of a country. (3.28)
For even in times of dire distress, immediate purification is ordained;
thus has Manu declared regarding the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).

"He who, being chosen, performs for another the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the cooked sacrifices (pākayajñas), and the soma-sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma— he is called his officiating priest (ṛtvij) in this world."

For those who have performed the *dīkṣaṇīyā* initiation and remain initiated until the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), and for those officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) engaged in the sacrificial rites related to that sacrifice, immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is ordained by Manu and others. Likewise, for the *sattrins*—those entitled to the *Gavāmayana* and other long-duration sacrifices—who act as both sacrificers (*yajamāna*) and officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) by virtue of scriptural injunction, immediate purification is prescribed for them during their priestly duties. By this [present verse], however, immediate purification is ordained for *sattrins* specifically regarding the priestly functions (*ārtvijapadārtha*). The phrase "and the rites enjoined by the Śruti" indicates the absence of impurity in rites directly ordained by the revealed scripture (*pratyakṣa-śruti*). Here, however, the distinction is that immediate purification is ordained for the officiating priests, the initiated, and the *sattrins* during their own duties, whether those duties are directly or indirectly ordained by the Śruti. Alternatively, by the term *sattrin*, one who is constantly engaged in the distribution of food may be included. Similarly, for those under a vow (*vratin*), there is immediate purification while the vow is being observed. The phrase "immediate purification is ordained" is to be connected with each of the following categories: the vow refers to the vows of a *snātaka*, or penances (*prāyaścitta*) and the like; the student (*brahmacārin*) includes both the temporary (*upakurvāṇaka*) and the lifelong (*naiṣṭhika*) types; the donor (*dātā*) is one whose nature is to give; and the knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*) is an ascetic (*yati*). For these, there is immediate purification. Furthermore, for one engaged in giving—even if he is not habitually a donor—and during a marriage; likewise, when a Kṣatriya or others are in a state of impurity, during the *vṛṣotsarga* sacrifice on the eleventh day; when a battle has commenced; during the preparation of a king’s armor; during a national calamity; during disturbances caused by kings or divine forces; during planetary sacrifices (*grahayaṣṭi*) and the like intended to avert such misfortunes; and during times of distress such as extreme poverty or when there is a cause for the absolute suffering of oneself or one’s dependents—in these cases, purification occurs immediately. On this point, Parāśara says: *(Note: The source text provided does not contain the actual verse of Parāśara.)*
There is no birth-impurity for kings, nor for those observing vows, nor for those performing sacrificial sessions,
nor for all those who have been initiated, nor for him whom the Brahmins desire [to be pure].
When those who have been initiated, those engaged in [Vedic] study, those devoted to vows and sacred fords,
and those intent on austerity and charity are present, there is no impurity regarding death or birth.
Another Smṛti states:
"Even for one who constantly gives food, when the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other such rites have been completed,
and the fire-offerings (homa) and so forth are finished, [the recipient] should feed Brāhmaṇas and others."

The word "immediate purification" (*sadyaḥśauca*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. From the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* by Kātyāyana: "Neither after the initiation (*dīkṣā*) in a sacrifice, nor while performing austerities such as the *kṛcchra*, does any impurity ever accrue to them, even if their father has died."
Impurity shall last until the completion of the rite, or for three days in the case of students.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"If the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) have already accepted the *madhuparka* for the purpose of performing the sacrifice,
it is certain that subsequent impurity (*aśauca*) shall not affect them."
In the same way, for one who has received initiation into the threefold [Veda] at a great sacrifice,
no ritual bath exists until the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) has taken place.
For the ascetic who is steadfast in Vedānta and profoundly tranquil, there is no [need for ritual] anywhere;
having desisted from difficult rites such as burnt offerings, he partakes of food among Brāhmaṇas and others.
Even for one who has undertaken a religious vow, it shall not be [permitted] for anyone else when the Brahmins have been invited and the Śrāddha rite has commenced.
For a Brahmin who has been invited [to a rite] and for one who has ceased his Vedic recitation and other duties,
there is never any impurity as long as the ancestors remain within his body.
Whether it be for one who has taken lifelong vows, or for another who has set out for the sake of alms,
or for a forest-dweller who is always qualified to give;
For one who has desisted from the authority to accept gifts,
there is no [fault] even in the case of Vaiśyas performing rites such as the *gomaṅgala*, due to the lapse of the time for protection.
Furthermore, there is never any fault regarding śrāddha and other rites if the birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtaka) of either the giver or the recipient remains unknown.
If [the fault] is discovered, the expiation and other rites must be performed by the eater himself in due order;
however, if half the meal has been consumed by the Brahmins, the donor perishes.
If anyone, having eaten the remnants of that [food],
remains composed and sips water from another's vessel, those twice-born ones become pure.
Regarding the sacrifice (*kratu*): it is not a fault to give material wealth that was previously intended for donation.
This is from the *Brahma Purāṇa*.
If an impurity (sūtaka) occurs between a wedding and a sacrifice, the remaining food should be provided by others;
the giver shall not touch the eaters.
Jābāla says:
Among a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), a king, an ascetic (yati), an artisan, and one initiated for a sacrifice;
and during a sacrifice, a wedding, and a sacrificial session (sattra)—there is never any impurity (sūtaka).

Viṣṇu states: "There is no impurity (āśauca) during the installation or festival of a deity, nor at a marriage, provided these were previously resolved upon; nor is there impurity during a national upheaval or even in times of dire calamity. This "prior resolution" is mandatory. As another Smṛti says:

"Those who know the time [for rituals] and understand the purpose of the resolution say that it may last for ten days, seven days, or five days; some experts in that matter say it lasts for three days as well. [921]
Patiṭhīnasi says:

"In the case of a marriage, a siege, a sacrifice, a journey, or a pilgrimage to a sacred site (tīrtha), there is no impurity (sūtaka) therein; likewise, one should have sacrificial rites and the like performed."
A place difficult to traverse is one where there is famine. 3.17, 28.
He states another incidental rule for purification:
"If touched by those who are menstruating or impure from death, one should bathe; if touched by them [subsequently], one should perform ritual sipping (upaspṛśet). (3.29)
One should mutter the *abliṅga* verses and recite the *gāyatrī* once mentally.

A *udakyā* is a woman in her menses. Those who are impure (*āśaucāḥ*) due to birth or death are untouchable. One who has been touched by these must bathe for the sake of purification. However, one who is touched by someone already touched by a *udakyā* or others of that sort should merely sip water (*upaspṛśet*), that is, perform *ācamana*. Regarding the rule that "one touched by a *udakyā* or others, and one touched by him [the latter], having bathed, should mutter the *Abliṅga* verses addressed to the waters, and the *Gāyatrī* once mentally"—the plural number in the word "by them" (*taiḥ*) refers to the individual persons. The singular number in the word "touched" (*saṃspṛṣṭaḥ*) is not intended to be restrictive. If that [singular] were not intended to be restrictive, then the [implication of] "he should bathe" would also not be intended to be restrictive. Thus says Manu.
Having touched a divākīrti, a woman in her courses, those who have fallen from their caste, a woman who has recently given birth, a corpse,
or one who has touched such a corpse, one becomes pure by bathing.

Although here the term *tatspṛṣṭi* (one who has touched that) refers specifically to one who has touched a corpse due to proximity, nevertheless, because those such as the *divākīrti* (outcaste) are equal to a corpse in their impurity, one who touches even such a person must likewise bathe, as they belong to the same category. Thus says Gautama: "By touching an outcaste (*patita*), a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth (*sūtikā*), a menstruating woman (*udakyā*), or a corpse, or by touching one who has touched them, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on and then touching water. For this very reason, another Smṛti states: "Upon touching one who has touched a corpse, a Caṇḍāla, an outcaste, a woman who has recently given birth, or a menstruating woman, or one who has touched them, there is a bath. When there is contact with one who has touched such a person, there is a bath with one's clothes on for the former; but when there is no such prior contact, there is merely a bath, as Saṃvarta says:
If one should touch someone who has touched that [impure object], bathing is prescribed for him;
beyond that, sipping water (ācamana) is declared, as well as the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of objects.
In this context, other occasions for bathing are also shown by way of incidental discussion; therein Viṣṇu states:

"Having touched a woman in her courses, a corpse, a Caṇḍāla, a bone from which the fat has been removed, or anything originating from a human being, one should bathe with one's clothes on; likewise if a carnivorous animal is upon one's head."
Likewise:
"But one who has been touched by someone who is not impure from food remains pure after sipping water;
however, one who has been touched by someone impure from food becomes pure after three nights."

If one is touched by someone who is required to bathe because they have been defiled by impure remnants (ucchiṣṭa), he is purified by a Prājāpatya penance if touched by that same person while they are themselves impure with remnants.
