Parāśara says: After a bad dream, sexual intercourse, vomiting, evacuation, or the act of shaving; and upon touching a funeral pyre, a sacrificial post, or the fire of a cremation ground, one should perform a bath.
Bṛhaspati says:
Immediate bathing is prescribed for sexual intercourse and for exposure to the smoke from a funeral pyre;
however, when one approaches [his wife] outside the fertile period, the purification is the same as that for voiding urine or excrement.
Another Smṛti states:
Having engaged in sexual intercourse on the eighth day, the fourteenth day, during the day, or on a festival day (parvan),
one should bathe with one's clothes on and purify oneself with the Vāruṇī verses.
Manu says: One who has vomited or been purged should bathe and then consume clarified butter;
one who has eaten food should simply sip water, while bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse.

The distinction is that this applies during the proper season (*ṛtu*). Yama states: "When food is undigested, when the sun has risen [before the morning meal], when one has vomited, likewise when the sun has set, upon a bad dream, or contact with a wicked person—only bathing is prescribed."

Sleep that extends from sunrise until sunset constitutes both the rising and the setting of sleep. Cyavana states: "Having touched a dog, an outcaste (śvapāka), the smoke from a funeral pyre, one who subsists on the property of the gods, a village priest, a seller of *soma*, a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), a funeral mound (*citi*), wood from a funeral pyre, liquor, a liquor vessel, a human bone with fat, one who has touched a corpse, a woman in her courses, a great sinner (*mahāpātakin*), or a corpse—one should immerse oneself in water with one's clothes on, emerge, touch fire, and mutter the *Gāyatrī* mantra one hundred and eight times. Having consumed clarified butter and bathed again, one should sip water three times. This applies to intentional contact; likewise, Bṛhaspati says:
Having intentionally touched an outcaste, a woman who has recently given birth, or a corpse belonging to the lowest castes,
one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter.
Having intentionally touched one who touches a corpse, a divākīrti, a funeral pyre, a sacrificial post, or a woman in her menses, a Brahmin becomes pure by performing a ritual bath.

And likewise, that [is done] with one's clothes on. Kaśyapa states: "Upon spitting at sunrise or sunset, upon the twitching of an eye, upon being reviled in the ear, upon ascending a funeral pyre, and upon touching a sacrificial post, one should bathe with one's clothes on and then mutter 'Punar mā' (*punar mā*). One should offer seven oblations of clarified butter with the *mahāvyāhṛtis*. [923] Another Smṛti text says: "Having touched a *devalaka*, a Brahmin who is devoted to the worship of the gods for three years for the sake of wealth, shall enter the water with his clothes on."
This man named Devalaka is censured in matters concerning offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya),
according to the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"A man who touches domestic dogs, cocks, and pigs [is likewise censured]."
Having bathed with one's clothes on and including the head, one becomes pure at that very moment.
Having touched Buddhists, Pāśupatas, Lokāyatas, nihilists, or twice-born men who follow forbidden occupations, one should enter the water with one's clothes on.
Another Smṛti states:
"Upon seeing naked Pāśupatas, Buddhists, Kālāmukhas, Kaulas, or those who wander in all directions, one should look at the sun; upon touching them, one should perform a bath."
Aṅgiras:
If a Brāhmaṇa indeed steps upon the shadow of a dog-cooker (śvapāka), he should perform a bath there; by consuming clarified butter (ghṛta), he becomes purified.

In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "One who knows the Dharma [should avoid] those whose food is unfit to be eaten, a woman in childbirth, a eunuch, a cat, an outcaste, a dog, a cock, those who have fallen from their status, those pierced by arrows, a Caṇḍāla, and those who carry corpses."
A woman in her courses and a village pig become pure by bathing after physical contact;
likewise, two men defiled by the impurity of childbirth also become pure in that same manner.
Furthermore: "A man who neglects his daily obligatory rites day by day,
and likewise neglects his fortnightly rites, becomes untouchable."
One who has been cast out by his kinsmen is considered "outcasted. Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya states:
"Having touched a Caṇḍāla, a Pukkasa, a Mleccha, a Bhilla, a Pārasika, and so forth, as well as those who have committed the great sins (mahāpātakin), one should bathe along with one's clothes."
Vyāsa says: Having touched the impurity of a vulture, a monkey, a cat, a donkey, a camel, as well as dogs, or pigs, one should indeed bathe with one's clothes on.
Āpastamba states: "If the body should become defiled by the contact of a crow or a crane, or if it should be smeared with impure matter,
and if that [impurity] should enter the ears or the mouth, purification occurs for one whose smearing has been removed through a complete bath."
Parāśara:
Having touched a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa), a funeral pyre (cit), a sacrificial post (yūpa), a Caṇḍāla, or a seller of Soma,
a Brāhmaṇa shall enter the water with his clothes on.

A tree growing on a cremation ground is a *caitya*. Devala says: [One should avoid] an outcaste, one who has fallen from his caste, one who is mutilated, one who is insane, a corpse-bearer, a woman who has recently given birth, a woman about to give birth, and a woman overwhelmed by her menstrual flow.
Having bathed with his clothes on and including his head, he becomes pure at that very moment;
the word "having touched" is understood as the remainder of the sentence.
If one who is himself impure should touch these [impure persons] who are already impure, [he too must bathe].
One is purified by the fast, or again by the kṛcchra penance.
A man who has become impure by touching something impure, or even a third person who has touched that which was touched,
becomes pure by washing his hands and feet with water and performing the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Likewise: "If one should touch the human bone, fat, excrement, menstrual blood, urine, semen, marrow, or even the blood of another,"
Having bathed, wiped away the bodily excretions and so forth, and sipped water (ācamana), he becomes pure;
by touching those very same [limbs] of his own and performing a thorough wiping, he shall be purified.
Saṃvarta: Having touched a dog, a boar, a donkey, a camel, a wolf, a jackal, a monkey, a crow, a cock, or a vulture, one should perform a bath.
Likewise:
"If a twice-born man touches the leavings of a Śūdra, or even a Śūdra who is himself in a state of impurity from leavings,
or if he embraces one who is pure but has been defiled by such contact, he should perform a bath along with his clothes."
A twice-born man, having touched indigo, products of indigo, or even a human bone, as well as the shadow of a Caṇḍāla or an outcast, should perform a bath.

Paiṭhīnasi states: "Upon touching a crow or an owl, one must bathe with one's clothes on. Upon voiding urine or feces without water, one must bathe with one's clothes on and perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with the Mahāvyāhṛtis. Upon touching a dog, a donkey, a camel, or a *caṇḍāla*, one must bathe with one's clothes on. The phrase "voiding urine or feces without water" means delaying the performance of purification rites. In the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "Having touched a woman in her courses, a woman who has recently given birth, a dog, an outcaste (*antyāvasāyin*), naked ascetics, or corpse-bearers, impurity (*aśauca*) is prescribed."
Having bathed with his clothes on, a man shall become pure by means of twelve applications of clay.
In the *Kālikāpurāṇa*:
"Having touched the remains of Rudra's offerings (*nirmālya*), one becomes pure by bathing along with one's clothes."
Another Smṛti states: "Indeed, [the initiation is forbidden] regarding the words of a guru, in the Aghora mantra, in one's own personal mantra, in the Dakṣiṇa and Uttara [mantras],
as well as in a mobile liṅga, in a tūra, in a painted cloth, or in one made of gold."
And likewise, one should not offer faded flowers to those made of crystal, nor to Bāṇa, nor to the Self-born (Svayambhū).
Or on a golden head, or one made of ruby. The mantra:
Having touched a human bone that still has fat or marrow, a Brahmin becomes pure by bathing;
however, if it is free of fat or marrow, he becomes pure simply by sipping water (ācamana) and then touching a cow and looking at the sun. [925]

In the cases of touching a cow, looking at the sun, or eating sugarcane, there is a combination [of rules] through the act of sipping water (*ācamana*). This refers to instances of unintentional contact; however, regarding intentional contact, the rule of Vasiṣṭha applies: "Having touched a moist human bone, one must observe impurity for three nights; but if it is dry, for a day and night. Viṣṇu states: "Having touched the carcass of a five-toed animal—excluding those that are edible—as well as its bone, one should bathe and wear washed clothes. These are instances requiring bathing with one's clothes on (*sacailasnāna*). Now, regarding various types of baths, Yama says: "When food is undigested, when the sun has risen, after vomiting, after shaving, and after sexual intercourse..."
It is declared that one should bathe after a bad dream or upon contact with a wicked person.
Devala says: Having touched the human bone, fat, feces, menstrual blood, urine, semen, marrow, or blood of another, one should perform a bath.

Viṣṇu: "If one is defiled below the navel or on the arms by bodily impurities, or by spirituous liquors or wines, one becomes pure by washing that limb with earth and water and sipping water (ācamana). If defiled elsewhere, one becomes pure by washing that limb with earth and water and bathing; however, if defiled in the sense organs, or if defiled by the lips, one must fast, bathe, and [consume] the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). *Prabāhu* refers to the portion of the arms from the elbows to the tips of the hands. This rule concerns objects that are extremely impure (*amedhya*). Aṅgiras: "If an impure substance should ever enter the sense organs..."
Even in the mouth, bathing is prescribed there for that which has reached the point of contact.
Śaṅkha says:
A man who is touched above the navel by the mud or water of a street, or likewise by saliva and the like, becomes pure immediately by bathing.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says:
If the region of the mouth is touched by drops of wine, feces, or urine,
it is purified by smearing with clay and cow dung and then by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Viṣṇu: One who has been touched by the water of a Caṇḍāla becomes pure after bathing;
however, one who has been touched by [the person] while he is impure from eating (ucchiṣṭa) becomes pure after three nights.
Āpastamba: If a Caṇḍāla or similar person should climb onto the same branch [of the tree] as a Brāhmaṇa residing there, the Brāhmaṇa becomes pure by means of bathing.
Devala says: Human bone, a corpse, feces, semen, urine, menstrual blood,
fat, phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, sweat, and wine are called impure substances.
Menstrual blood is the female seed. Dūṣikā is the impurity of the eyes. [926] Mādhūka, aikṣava, ṭāṅka, kaula, khārjūra, pānasa, mārdvīka, kāramārdīka, maireya, and nālikera-ja [are types of wine].
For these intoxicants are indeed impure for a Brāhmaṇa;
however, a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya do not incur sin by touching them.

*Mādhūka* is liquor derived from *madhūka* flowers. *Aikṣava* is a specific variety of sugarcane product. *Ṭāṅka* is a specific type of liquor made from the fruit of the *ṭaṅka*. *Kaula* is that made from jujube (*badara*). *Mārdvīka* is that made from grapes (*drākṣā*). *Kāramārdīka* is that made from the *karamarda* fruit. The others are well known. Bṛhaspati says:

"If any part of the body above the navel—excluding the hands—is defiled, one becomes pure by bathing; but for parts below the navel, one is purified by washing and performing the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*)."
Manu says: One who has vomited or been purged should bathe and then perform the consumption of clarified butter;
one who has eaten food should merely sip water, while bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse.

Having eaten food and then vomited, one should indeed rinse with water. Āpastamba states: "Or else, having washed away the residue and rinsed with water, there is sprinkling of the limbs; [this is the purification] for sexual intercourse and the emission of urine or semen. Likewise:

"Upon touching something that should not be touched, upon vomiting, upon the falling of tears, and after shaving or sexual intercourse, a mandatory bath must be performed, excluding [rites dedicated to] the gods and ancestors."
The meaning is that [the rite] is devoid of the libations to the gods (devatārpaṇa), according to the *Vāgbhaṭasmṛtisaṃgraha*.

One should perform a bath after weeping prior to the collection of the bones; for a Brahmin, this is prescribed within the ten-day period, while after that period, only sipping water (*ācamana*) is enjoined.
Yama says:
When the occasion for bathing due to illness has arisen, one who is not ill should bathe ten times;
having bathed repeatedly, he should touch that sick person, and then that sick person shall become pure.
The afflicted one is the sick person. Parāśara says: When the sun has set, if contact with a Caṇḍāla, a corpse, or the like should somehow occur, how is purification prescribed?
Having bathed at Jātavedas, Suvarṇa, and likewise Somamārga,
and having beheld them with the permission of Brāhmaṇas, one becomes purified.
A *kuṇapa* is a corpse. Śātātapa says: "O Blessed One, if one should touch something untouchable at night after the sun has set, by what means would purification occur? Tell me that with certainty."
If water has been collected before the sun has set, purification is achieved by using that water in its entirety; however, one must avoid water that has been touched by a corpse.
— Devala.
One should perform a bath at night with water collected during the day for a specific reason,
having cast gold [into the water] and having placed a fire nearby.
Now, summarizing the causes of purification mentioned in various ways, he says:
Time, fire, ritual action, earth, wind, mind, knowledge, austerity, and water. (3.30)
Repentance, fasting, and all these are causes of purification.

Time and all the others have each been stated in various places as causes for purification (*śuddhi*) and non-defilement (*aduṣṭatā*). Time, for instance, in such passages as "three nights and ten nights"; fire, in "purification of the ground by sweeping or burning"; ritual action such as recitation (*japa*), in "one should recite mantras containing the word *ap* (water)"; earth, in "water, ashes, earth, or water"; wind, in "by the wind and the sun"; the mind, in another scripture, "one should perform what is purified by the mind"; spiritual knowledge (*jñāna*), in "knowledge is the purifier of the intellect"; austerity (*tapas*), in "the elemental self [is purified] by learning and austerity"; water, in "water for the body"; remorse (*paścāttāpa*), in "by confession and remorse"; and fasting (*nirāhāra*), the absence of food, in "they should remain without eating for three days. (3.30)
Furthermore:
"The gift of those who perform improper acts is like the current of a river; it brings purification. (3.31)
For one to be purified, there is clay and water; for the twice-born, renunciation; for those who know the Vedas, austerity; for the wise, forbearance; and for the body, water. (3.32)

Recitation is said to be the purification for those whose sins are concealed; truth is the purification of the mind; austerity and knowledge are the purification of the elemental self (bhūtātman); wisdom is the purification of the intellect (buddhi); and the supreme purification of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is held to arise from the knowledge of the Lord. 3.33.

The gift to those who perform forbidden acts is a cause of impurity; so too is the current of a river filled with impurities, and being filled with fast-flowing water. Prior to each of these, the term "purifier" (*śuddhikṛt*) is understood to be applied individually. For that which is to be purified and is joined with impurities, earth and water are the purifiers. Renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), or the life of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*), is for the twice-born. Austerity (*tapas*)—such as the *kṛcchra* penances—is for those who know the Vedas and have studied them. For the learned, those who know the meaning of the Vedas, forbearance (*kṣānti*)—the endurance of offenses committed by others—is the purifier. Truth (*satya*)—the desire to speak of things exactly as they were perceived—is for the mind, the internal organ. The self surrounded by the elements (*bhūta*), that is, the subtle elements, is the "self of the elements" (*bhūtātman*); for him, both austerity—consisting of obligatory and occasional rites according to one's caste and stage of life—and knowledge (*vidyā*), which is the meditation on Brahman, are said to be purifiers. Furthermore, the purification of the elemental self is the destruction of the unseen merit and demerit (*apūrva*) resulting from optional and forbidden actions. For the intellect (*buddhi*), which is characterized by resolve, knowledge is the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self as they truly exist. For the "field" (*kṣetra*), which appears distinct from the Lord due to the difference of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the supreme purification approved by Manu and others is the realization of the Lord, namely: "I am indeed the Lord. Bṛhaspati says:
The destruction of sin occurs here through the study of sacred texts, through remorse, through fire-offerings,
through austerity, through meditation, through dwelling in sacred places, and through giving.
Not hearing slander of others, not looking upon the wives of others—this is the purification of the ears and eyes; while purity of the tongue consists in the absence of backbiting.
Abstaining from killing living beings, refraining from theft, purity of hands and feet,
and avoiding contact with the wives of others— this is prescribed as bodily purity.
Vasiṣṭha says: Time, fire, contentment of mind, water, scrubbing with earth, and ignorance [of the act]—these six are held to be the means of purification for living beings. (3.31, 32, 33)

Thus ends the section on Impurity (*āśaucaprakaraṇa*) in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, who was born in the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the noble Vidyādhara clan. 1.
Now begins the section on duties in times of distress (*āpaddharma*) in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* with its commentary.
(2) The immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) in times of distress has been stated.
"In even a dire calamity, immediate purification is prescribed," and so forth. In connection with that, he states the specific modes of livelihood in times of distress:
"In times of distress, a twice-born man may live by the occupation of a Kṣatriya or even that of a Vaiśya."
Having crossed over that [obstacle] and purified oneself, one should then place [the burden] upon the path.

When there is a failure to obtain wealth through the means prescribed for one's own caste (*svavarṇa*) as well as those common to all castes (*sarvavarṇasādhāraṇa*), that constitutes a state of distress (*āpad*). In such a situation, a twice-born man (*dvija*), specifically a Brāhmaṇa, may live by the work of a Kṣatriya—that is, by the occupation of a Kṣatriya, such as the conquest of enemies and so forth. In the absence of even that, he may live by the occupation of a Vaiśya, such as agriculture and so forth. Having crossed over that distress, provided that his dependents and himself can be maintained even by a deficient Brāhmaṇical occupation (*brāhmī vṛtti*), he should then purify himself through penances (*prāyaścitta*) and settle himself back upon the path—that is, establish himself in the occupation prescribed for his own caste. Alternatively, whatever has been acquired by the occupation of a lower caste should be "set aside on the path" (*pathi nyaset*); in this latter case, the word "wealth" (*dravyam*) is to be supplied after "acquired. The authority for this is as follows: [929] *Yājñavalkyasmṛti*, 3.40–41: *yātrāmātraprasiddhyarthaṃ svaiḥ karmabhir agarhitaiḥ / akleśena śarīrasya kurvīta dhanasañcayam // ṛtāmṛtābhyāṃ jīvettu mṛtena pramṛtena vā / satyānṛtābhyām api vā na śvavṛttyā kadācana // ṛtamuñchaśilaṃ jñeyam amṛtaṃ syādayācitam / mṛtaṃ tu yācitaṃ bhaikṣaṃ pramṛtaṃ karṣaṇaṃ smṛtam // satyānṛtaṃ tu vāṇijyaṃ tena caivāpi jīvyate / sevā śvavṛttir ākhyātā tasmāt tāṃ parivarjayet //* One should accumulate wealth without hardship to the body, using one’s own irreproachable occupations, merely for the sake of maintaining one’s livelihood. One should live by the *ṛta* and *amṛta*, or by the *mṛta* and *pramṛta*, or even by the *satyānṛta*; but never by the "dog’s livelihood" (*śvavṛtti*). *Ṛta* is to be known as gathering grain with a winnowing basket or a sickle; *amṛta* is what is obtained unasked; *mṛta* is alms obtained by begging; *pramṛta* is declared to be agriculture; *satyānṛta* is trade, and one may live by that as well; service is called the "dog’s livelihood," therefore one should avoid it.
When Brahmins acquire wealth through a censurable action,
they become pure by relinquishing it, as well as by recitation and austerity.
Thus says the verse of Manu. Regarding this, Nārada states the means of acquiring wealth common to all social classes (*varṇa*):
"They know that common property is of three kinds and the remainder is of nine kinds:
[wealth] inherited in due order, a gift out of affection, and what is acquired together with one's wife."
For all social classes without distinction, there are three kinds of wealth;
however, one should know that the Brahmin possesses a specific wealth characterized by three features.
That which is obtained through acceptance of gifts, from a patron for whom one sacrifices, and likewise from a pupil—
these three are said to be the specific types of wealth for a Kṣatriya as well.

The *kāra* obtained from war and the *daṇḍa* arising from legal proceedings; *kāra* is that which originates from the collection of taxes. Furthermore, the specific [revenue] of a Vaiśya should be known as having three characteristics.
The Śūdra [should live] by agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade; however, he may also support himself through service to those [other classes].
This is the righteous means of acquiring wealth for all social classes;
by the opposite course it would be unrighteous, unless there is a grave emergency.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "For him, his own duty alone is better, even if performed only slightly; he should not resort to an inferior one. For a Brāhmaṇa who resorts to an inferior way of life falls into inferior states; therefore, he should accept from all that which accords with the conduct of the praiseworthy, but he should not seek personal satisfaction from that. He may perform the officiating at sacrifices for the three other castes, and having obtained his livelihood from them in accordance with dharma, he should apply it toward religious duties. Gautama, continuing the section on the Brāhmaṇa’s rules for times of distress (*āpadkalpa*), says: "Officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts—for all [castes], each preceding one is more important than the next. In its absence, the occupation of a Kṣatriya; in its absence, the occupation of a Vaiśya. The meaning is that officiating at sacrifices and so forth are to be performed by a Brāhmaṇa for all castes. Vasiṣṭha says: "Or, at will, they may themselves produce sesame seeds through cultivation and sell them; however, officiating at sacrifices for those for whom it is forbidden, or the acceptance of gifts, is never permitted. Furthermore, they cite this: * *Note: The text provided ends mid-sentence regarding Vasiṣṭha's citation.*
The best of the twice-born blaze like fires through their asceticism and oblations;
yet they are extinguished by the acceptance of gifts, just as fires are quenched by water.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In times of distress, the rule is that for one who has parents and many dependents, the livelihood of the next [lower] order is permissible. Among Brāhmaṇas endowed with the three qualities, one should announce one's weakness regarding livelihood. Whatever they may say, that is the law. His next livelihood is the pursuit of the Kṣatriya way; if he still cannot subsist by the three Brāhmaṇa occupations—namely, officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts—he may subsist upon a Vaiśya. This means he may follow the occupation of a Vaiśya. "Endowed with the three qualities" means being accomplished in sacrifice, study, and charity. Even when the Vaiśya livelihood is unavailable, a Brāhmaṇa must not resort to the livelihood of a Śūdra. And so says Nārada:
In times of distress, the immediate livelihood is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa;
likewise, the livelihood of a Vaiśya is declared, but never that which is lower.

The livelihood of a Śūdra is the lowest. A Brāhmaṇa should never, under any circumstances, perform the work of a Vārṣala (Śūdra), nor should a Vārṣala perform the work of a Brāhmaṇa; for those two [actions] lead to their downfall.
Neither superior nor inferior karma exists for those two;
for, having abandoned middling karma, they are indeed common to all.

The duties of the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya belong to the middle [caste]. Even a Kṣatriya, in times of distress, may follow the occupation of a Vaiśya, which is the next lower; and a Vaiśya may follow the occupation of a Śūdra, which is likewise the next lower. As Vasiṣṭha says: "Those who cannot subsist by their own duty should adopt the next lower occupation, even if it be inferior, but never one that is higher. Their own duty (*svadharma*) extends up to gleaning ears of grain (*śiloñcha*). In its impossibility, they may live by the occupation of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya. "In times of distress, one may accept gifts from virtuous men, but one must not cause a mixture of castes (*saṃkara*). One may, at will, effect a mixture of castes for the sake of securing the fruit of the field. Here, "field" refers to a wife, and its "fruit" is offspring. The permission for such a mixture applies only to cases where it follows the order of the castes (*varṇānulomya*); it does not intend the reverse order (*pratiloma*). (3.34)
He states the prohibition against a Brāhmaṇa living by the occupation of a Vaiśya who sells certain specific commodities:
fruits, stones, linen, Soma, humans, cakes, climbing plants, sesame seeds, cooked rice, liquids, alkali, curd, milk, ghee, and water. (3.35)
Weapons, liquor, beeswax, honey, lac, and the sacrificial grass;
earth, leather, flowers, a woolen blanket, hair, buttermilk, poison, and the ground. (3.36)
Silk, indigo, salt, meat, one-hoofed animals, lead, vegetables, half-ripe fruits, medicinal herbs, oil-cakes, livestock, and perfumes—likewise these [should not be accepted]. (3.37)
Even while living by the livelihood of a Vaiśya, one should never sell [these].

A Brāhmaṇa living by the occupation of a Vaiśya should never sell fruits and the like—*phalam* meaning betel nuts and so forth; *upalaḥ* meaning stone; *kṣaumam* meaning cloth made of *atasī* (flax); *somaḥ* meaning a specific creeper; *apūpāḥ* meaning cakes; *vīrudhaḥ* meaning plants shorter than shrubs, a specific type of stationary being; *rasāḥ* meaning sugarcane juice and the like; *śastram* meaning swords and the like; *āsavaḥ* meaning liquor; *madhūcchiṣṭam* meaning beeswax; *madhu* meaning honey; *lākṣā* meaning lac; *barhiṣaḥ* meaning *kuśa* grass; *mṛd* meaning clay; *kutapaḥ* meaning a specific kind of woolen blanket; *keśaḥ* meaning yak-tail hair and the like; *takram* meaning buttermilk; *kṣitiḥ* meaning land, fields, and so forth; *kauśeyam* meaning silk; *nīlī* meaning a specific dyeing substance; *ekaśaphāḥ* meaning one-hoofed animals such as horses; *sīsakaḥ* meaning lead; *ārdram* meaning fresh ginger; *oṣadhayaḥ* meaning grains such as rice and barley; *piṇyākam* meaning a cake of sesame from which the oil has been extracted; *paśavaḥ* meaning cattle and the like; *gandhāḥ* meaning sandalwood and the like; the rest is well known. Here, "animals" refers to those of the forest.
"Also all wild animals, fanged beasts, and birds"—from such a Smṛti of Manu. This prohibition applies specifically to the Brāhmaṇa. As Nārada says:
"In the occupation of a Vaiśya, milk and curd are not to be sold by a Brāhmaṇa."

Regarding the conduct of Brahmins here, Gautama states: "For one whose merchandise consists of perfumes, liquids, prepared food, sesame, oil-cakes, hemp, linen, and skins; dyed and white garments; milk and its products; roots, fruits, flowers, herbs, honey, meat, grass, water, and provisions for a journey; women, men, heifers, girls, and barren cows; and always varieties of rice and barley—some say also bulls, milch-cows, and oxen. A *vaśā* is a barren cow. A *vehad* is one that destroys the fetus. A *dhenur* is one that has recently calved. Vasiṣṭha says: "For those who subsist by the livelihood of a Vaiśya and live by trade, stone and salt are not to be sold; nor hemp, silk, linen, skins, and woven cloth that is dyed. Nor any kind of prepared food. Nor flowers, roots, fruits, perfumes, liquids, and water. Of herbs, the juice is *soma*. Poison, meat, and milk along with its products; iron, tin, lac, and lead; single-hoofed domestic animals and manes (horses); all wild animals, birds, and fanged beasts. Whether domestic or wild refers to those living in villages or forests, or according to technical definitions. As stated in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: [932]... (text continues).
The cow, the horse, the human being, goats and sheep, and both the donkey and the mule—
these seven domestic animals have been enumerated by the wise.
"Lions, boars, tigers, elephants, buffaloes, as well as bears and monkeys—these are proclaimed as the seven wild animals. Thus it is said.
However, those that fall between these two categories [of domestic and wild] are indeed not for sale, because they partake of both domestic and wild natures.
"The wild ox, the wolf, the hyena, the dog, the cock, the cātaka bird, and the sparrow—these seven are remembered as the intermediate [beings]. Thus it is said.

Āpastamba: "Trade is not prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa; if he should engage in commerce, he must exclude from his merchandise [the following]: humans, liquids, perfumes, food, hides, barren cows, *śleṣman* (phlegm), water, sprouts, fermenting agents (*kiṇva*), long pepper and black pepper, grain, meat, weapons, well-made [liquor], fermented spirits (*āsava*), sesame, and rice. He should especially not sell grain. Sprouted grain is *tokma*; *kiṇva* is the substance used for preparing *surā* liquor; "well-made" refers to merit (*dharma*). Chāgaleya: "One should not sell the Veda, nor indeed should one sell fire."
Whatever hell awaits men for the sale of the Dharma, that very same one arises here.
Therefore, selling [the Veda] is not permitted in the Vedas, nor likewise in the Agnihotra;
the same applies to teaching, studying, and receiving gifts preceded by a question.
Performing sacrifices for others, teaching for a fee, and debate constitute the sixfold sale of the Veda.
Yama says: But he who sells cows shall become a worm in a cow-pen for as many thousands of years as there are hairs upon the cows. (3.35, 36, 37)
Regarding the sale of sesame seeds, he states an exception:
"For the sake of dharma, sesame seeds may be sold for an amount of grain equal to them. (3.38)

Having taken grain, one may sell sesame seeds of equal measure for the sake of dharma; this should be understood as applying specifically when there is an urgent necessity for dharma. Regarding this, Manu says:
"A farmer, having personally undertaken cultivation, may at his pleasure sell pure sesame seeds that have not been kept for long, provided it is for the sake of dharma."
"Pure" means unmixed with other substances. Nārada says:
"If one is unable [to pay], for the sake of medicine or likewise for the purpose of a sacrifice, sesame seeds may necessarily be sold for an amount equal to grain."
Manu says: "If one performs any act other than eating, anointing, or giving with sesame seeds,
he becomes a worm and clings to the excrement of dogs along with his ancestors."
Likewise: "Flavors should be bartered for flavors, but salt must never be exchanged for flavors;
prepared food may be exchanged for unprepared food, sesame seeds for grain, and these are considered equivalent."

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should acquire goods with unaltered dry wood, *badara*, *iṅguda*, and *bilva* fruits, ropes, and cotton threads. Hārīta says: "If one cannot subsist through the practice of *pūrta* (charitable works), one may sell dry wood and grass, or guard cows. Vasiṣṭha states: "Liquids may be bartered for liquids, either equal or inferior [in quality]. But salt must never be exchanged for a liquid; likewise, sesame, rice, cooked food, knowledge, and persons are prescribed for exchange. Regarding the exchange of sesame and rice, Āpastamba says: "Their exchange is permitted with grain, as well as of persons for persons; and of liquids for liquids, and of knowledge for knowledge. One should deal in goods that have not been purchased. One should not dwell excessively on the sale of *muñja* grass, *bilva* fruits, grass, or wood; having obtained one's own means of livelihood, one should desist from the livelihood of others. The meaning of this is: one should sell goods produced on one's own land that have not been purchased, but not those that have been bought. Furthermore, one should not adopt the profession of a merchant as a permanent occupation; having attained one's own livelihood, one should cease from the livelihood of others. Baudhāyana says: "Grass and wood that have not been purchased may be sold. Moreover, they cite this:"

"One-tusked animals, stone free from salt, and this which is not for sale by a Brāhmaṇa—namely, thread that has been dyed: [this is the list]. "Free from salt" means it is not salty; "not dyed" (arañjanīkṛta) means it is colorless (nīrāga). —Nārada.
A Brāhmaṇa may sell dry wood and grass,
as well as fragrant substances, salt, and wool, with the exception of cotton and cotton-cloth.
[934] A split bamboo vessel that has fallen apart by itself, fruits of the jujube or the *iṅguda* tree,
and a rope made of cotton thread, provided that it remains unaltered.

*Ekārā* is a particular kind of grass. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In times of distress, a Brāhmaṇa desiring to live may, if necessary, adopt a livelihood that is one degree lower [than his own], yet he must not say, 'This is for sale, this is for sale. Once the price has been stated, he may accept it. Or he may tend cattle; while they are drinking, he must not drink; while they are standing, he must not sit down; nor should he drive them himself. He should gently strike their backs with a moist branch bearing leaves. He must not lead them across a dangerous path, a precipice, or through shallow water. He should set down children, the elderly, the sick, and the exhausted. He should provide medical aid according to his ability. This is the duty regarding cattle; otherwise, there is ruin. (3.38)
He states the specific sin incurred from the sale of specific substances:
"Lac, salt, and meat cause one to fall [from caste] when sold;
milk, curd, and liquor, however, cause one to become of a lower caste. (3.39)

Lac and other such items, when sold, constitute causes for the downfall of a Brāhmaṇa seller; "downfall" (patana) means the loss of eligibility for the duties of the twice-born. However, milk and similar substances cause one to become of a lower caste; the meaning is that they lead to the state of a Śūdra or a Vaiśya. On this point, there is a specific rule from Manu: "One falls immediately by selling meat, lac, and salt;
by selling milk, a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra in three days."
Likewise:
"By selling other goods that are forbidden for sale here out of desire,
a Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a Vaiśya within seven nights."

And these two statements refer to a Brāhmaṇa who has not performed penance. Because of the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa," this fault does not apply to a Kṣatriya selling salt and such items. Thus says Manu:
"A Kṣatriya, having fallen into distress, may live by all this [trade], but he should never at any time covet a higher mode of livelihood."
The livelihood of a Brāhmaṇa is superior. Likewise:
"A Vaiśya who cannot subsist by his own duty may live even by the livelihood of a Śūdra;
yet, being capable, he should avoid forbidden acts and desist from them. (3.39)

[935] In times of distress, even a Brahmin’s own livelihood is better, though it be deficient in merit, than another’s, even if it be excellent; thus he says: "One who has fallen into distress, while accepting and eating from whatever source available,"
The Brahmin shall not be smeared by sin, for he is equal to fire and the sun.

One who has fallen into calamity and is living in distress is not tainted or joined with sin (*enas*) even when receiving from a person of inferior caste, provided he eats and consumes [the food] in that manner; for by virtue of his purity, he is equal to fire or the sun. Here, the use of the two prefixes *sam* and *pra* is intended to include the acts of officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*), teaching (*adhyāpana*), and receiving gifts (*pratigraha*). By this, even Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas may be officiated for and taught; however, the acceptance of gifts is permitted even from a Śūdra. On this point, Manu says: "Better is one's own duty, though deficient, than the duty of another well-performed."
For one who lives by the dharma of another falls immediately from his caste.
A Brahmin who does not follow the occupation of a Vaiśya, yet remains on his own path and is suffering from being distressed by his own means of livelihood, should practice this dharma.
A Brahmin who has fallen into misfortune may accept [gifts] from anyone;
that a purifier should become defiled—this is not tenable according to the Dharma.
He who lives by whatever food he obtains, even when fallen into distress,
is not smeared by sin, just as the sky is not defiled by mud.
No fault accrues to Brahmins from teaching, officiating at sacrifices, or from accepting gifts— even those that are censured— for they are like fire and water.
Ajīgarta, being hungry, approached to kill his own son;
yet he was not tainted by sin, as he was merely acting to counteract his hunger.
Though distressed and desiring to eat dog-meat for the sake of preserving his life, Vāmadeva— who was discerning in matters of dharma and adharma— was not defiled by it.
Bhāradvāja, together with his son, accepted many cows from the high-souled Śuśrutīkṣṇa in the lonely forest in order to satisfy his hunger.
Afflicted by hunger, Viśvāmitra— who was discerning in matters of dharma and adharma— approached to eat the haunch of a dog, having taken it from the hand of a Caṇḍāla.
Between receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, and likewise teaching,
the acceptance of gifts is the lowest and is censured for a Brahmin after death.
Sacrificing for others and teaching are always performed by those whose souls have been refined;
however, the acceptance of gifts may be performed even from a Śūdra or one of the lowest birth.
Sin incurred through officiating at sacrifices or teaching is removed by recitation and burnt offerings;
however, that caused by accepting gifts is removed only by renunciation and austerity.

This being the case, the meaning of Gautama’s statement—"Among sacrificing for others, teaching, and receiving gifts, each preceding one is more serious than the following"—is as follows: with respect to all twice-born men, these activities such as sacrificing for others constitute a secondary alternative (*apatkalpa*) for the Brāhmaṇa; and among them, each preceding one is more serious and less blameworthy. As for the fact that Manu did not state that receiving gifts is more serious than sacrificing for others and so forth, that refers specifically to the acceptance of gifts from Śūdras. Alternatively, it should be understood that Gautama’s statement regarding the increasing gravity of the acts starting with sacrificing for others is based on their capacity to produce greater spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*), in accordance with the authority of Manu’s own words. (3.40)
He states another mode of livelihood in times of distress:
"Agriculture, craftsmanship, service for wages, learning, usury, a cart, a mountain, service to others, marshlands, a king, and begging—these are the means of subsistence in times of distress. (3.41)

Agriculture and the like serve as means of livelihood in times of distress. They are called "livelihoods" (*jīvanāni*) because one lives by them. Agriculture is well known. *Śilpa* refers to skill in the making of garments, ornaments, soups, songs, and houses. A cart is well known, and by it, the bringing of goods and such for its sake is indicated. A mountain (*giri*) is a hill; by that, the processing of timber and other products arising therefrom is meant. Service (*sevā*) is well known. A region with many trees and water is a marshy land (*anūpa*); by that, the subsistence on the bulbs, roots, and fruits found there is indicated. A king is well known, and by him, a livelihood based on rendering service to him is implied. Begging (*baikṣya*) is well known. Here, the mention of agriculture is for the sake of illustration; by it, cattle-rearing and trade are also included. And so says Manu:
Knowledge, craftsmanship, wages, service, cattle-rearing, trade, agriculture, mountain-mining, begging, and usury— these are the ten means of livelihood.

Although the practice of agriculture and other such means is already established by the rule, "In times of distress, a twice-born man may live by the occupation of a Kṣatriya or even of a Vaiśya," nevertheless, this specific statement is intended as a counter-exception for extreme emergencies regarding both self-performed agriculture and the sale of fruits and the like, which are otherwise prohibited. In that regard, the prohibition of agriculture is cited from the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]: "Let him not himself perform manual labor; let him not be addicted to trade; let him avoid giving false testimony and causing injury to living beings. (MDh 10.83) "Let him not, out of greed, engage in agriculture involving the use of iron and cattle; for agriculture is a source of suffering and is censured by those who know the sacred law. (MDh 10.84) "Trade causes the loss of dharma; tending cattle leads to the loss of dharma; service to a Śūdra brings about the loss of heaven; and agriculture results in the destruction of all three. (MDh 10.85) "Let him never, out of greed, sow seeds with his own hand, nor engage in the sale of various grains; for by selling these, he falls into sin. (MDh 10.90) "Let him avoid selling the following: cooked food, sesame seeds, salt, cows, curd, milk, honey, meat, roots, fruits, flowers, perfumes, liquids, indigo, and lac. (MDh 10.91) "Let him not sell white mustard, nor substances used for sacrificial offerings, nor medicinal herbs, nor fragrant grass, nor the juice of the Soma plant, nor water, nor weapons, nor forest trees. (MDh 10.92) "Let him not sell human beings, nor beasts of burden, nor animals with fangs or tusks, nor birds, nor any kind of creature that destroys life, nor woven cloth dyed red. (MDh 10.93) "Let him not sell a goat, a sheep, a camel, a donkey, a horse, a cow, or a buffalo, nor a young bull, nor a breeding cow, nor a draught ox. (MDh 10.94) "However, in times of distress, he may exchange, on equal terms, sesame seeds for unhusked grain, and cooked food for uncooked food, provided there is no surplus. (MDh 10.95) "Let him not, out of greed, give false testimony; let him not cut down green trees; let him not eat the food of a Śūdra, nor wear garments given by a Śūdra. (MDh 10.96) "Let him not carry arms for his own protection, nor travel with a Śūdra woman, nor dwell in a village where no Brahmins reside, nor ever associate with one who has been initiated for a sacrifice (*avakīrṇin*). (MDh 10.97) "Let him not step over a rope to which a calf is tied, nor enter a village or a house by a path other than the gate; let him not look at the sun when it rises or sets, nor while it is eclipsed. (MDh 10.98) "Let him not void urine or excrement facing the sun, nor while looking at a woman, nor in water, nor on ashes, nor on a plowed field, nor on a path, nor on a place covered with grass. (MDh 10.99) "Let him not injure plants even if they are meant for sacrificial purposes, nor cut grass with his nails, nor eat anything from which oil has been extracted, nor anything containing worms or insects. (MDh 10.100) "Let him not sleep alone in an empty house, nor wake up a sleeping superior, nor converse with a woman during her menses, nor with one who has not bathed after her courses. (MDh 10.101) "Let him not step on a threshold, nor on sandals, nor on refuse, nor on ashes, nor on cotton seeds, nor on potsherds, nor on hair, nor on bones. (MDh 10.102) "Let him not eat with his wife, nor look at her while she is eating, nor at a woman lying with a child, nor at one who is anointed, nor at one who is laughing loudly, nor at one who is naked. (MDh 10.103) "Let him not teach for a fee, nor officiate at the sacrifice of another for a fee, nor study while being paid, nor ever sell the knowledge of the Veda; let him not become the servant of a Śūdra. (MDh 10.104) "Let him not cut his nails or hair, nor bite off pieces with his teeth, nor scratch his body with his nails, nor crush clods of earth, nor tear grass with his nails. (MDh 10.105) "Let him not play with dice, nor engage in gambling, nor wear garlands, nor anoint himself with unguents, nor bathe in water intentionally, nor dance, nor sing. (MDh 10.106) "Let him not carry a single staff, nor a weapon, nor wear shoes or a turban, nor use an umbrella, nor ride in a carriage, nor travel in a boat by himself. (MDh 10.107) "Let him not climb a tree, nor a mountain, nor a rampart, nor look down into a well, nor a pit, nor into the interior of a house through a hole. (MDh 10.108) "Let him not intentionally step on shadows belonging to a deity, a Brahmin, or a cow, nor on urine, excrement, ash, bones, husks, or anything vomited. (MDh 10.109) "Let him not enter a temple, nor a cremation ground, nor a fort, nor a royal palace, nor a festival, nor an assembly, nor a place where people are drinking. (MDh 10.110) "Let him not stay in a place where there is much idle talk, nor where there is much singing, nor where there is dancing, nor where women are laughing, nor where there is a crowd of low-caste people. (MDh 10.111) "Let him not dwell in a city, nor in a forest, nor in a village, nor in a place where there is no livelihood, nor in a place where there is constant fear, nor in a place where there is no learning. (MDh 10.112) "Let him always follow the conduct prescribed for his stage of life (*āśrama*), remaining pure and self-controlled; for by following such conduct, a twice-born man attains the highest state. (MDh 10.113) Thus, the prohibition of agriculture is illustrated by the *Mānava*.

Even if he lives by the occupation of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa or even a Kṣatriya should carefully avoid agriculture, which consists mostly of violence and depends upon others. People consider agriculture to be a virtuous thing, yet that livelihood is censured by the righteous.
Just as wood with an iron tip destroys both the earth and those who dwell within it.

Furthermore, this prohibition concerns agriculture performed by oneself; for Gautama says in the *Āpaddharma* (duties in times of distress): “Agriculture, trade, and usury [are permitted] when performed by oneself. Regarding this, Hārīta states the rule for one who performs agriculture himself during extreme distress: “In times of distress, they say agriculture is permitted. If he practices agriculture, he should employ iron, fire, and water. He should avoid using children, the elderly, the emaciated, the afflicted, and so forth. He should drive the oxen slowly with a short goad. He should not strike them excessively with sticks, fists, clods of earth, elbows, knees, ropes, or verbal abuse. He should not drive them on festival days or at the junctions of time (*saṃdhivelā*). If an ox becomes distressed, he should release it rather than trample it; if it is exhausted, he should provide it with drink and food. He should protect it from worms, insects, spiders, gadflies, mosquitoes, flies, excessive wind, cold, sun, and excessive heat or rain by providing shelter, covering, scratching, smoke, fire, protection from wind, and bedding. For those that are weary, broken, or stuck, he should provide medicine, fodder, salt, oil, and the like, as required. He should perform sowing, salting, rubbing, fanning, and driving them about. He should offer oblations (*bali*) and sacrifices. Having bathed and adorned the oxen, he should feed the Brahmins. Having given a sixth part to the king for the sake of the merit of the cattle (*saurabheya*), he should satisfy the Brahmins with the fifth part. Thus they also cite:
This sacrificial post has been established here in the midst of the Bethīs by the Kārṣikas;
therefore, one should unweariedly give gifts of food, grain, wealth, and dakṣiṇā.
Having broken the earth, having cut down medicinal herbs, and having killed insects and ants, farmers purify themselves by means of the *khalayajña*; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, regarding the rule for oxen, he himself said:
"The plough of Dharma has eight oxen; that of those seeking a livelihood has six oxen;
that of the cruel has four oxen; and that of the slayers of Brahmins has two oxen."
Bṛhaspati says: Having given a sixth part to the king, a twentieth part to the deities,
and a thirtieth part to the Brahmins, one incurs no fault by practicing agriculture.
[938] A plough with eight oxen is declared by those learned in the scriptures to be righteous; one with six is considered middling; and one with four is said to be inferior.
Hārīta says: "The taming and riding of young elephants is not recommended, nor that of old or weak ones; such is the word of Prajāpati."
One should not cause a snuff treatment that impairs virility to be administered to draft animals, nor should one yoke to the pole an ox that is old or diseased. (3.41)
Having stated the means of livelihood for one who does not live by the aforementioned methods, he now describes another way of living:
"If a man remains hungry for three days, he may take grain from a non-Brāhmaṇa. Having received it, he must report it according to dharma when questioned. (3.42)

One who is hungry and has not eaten for three nights—having remained thus for three nights—should take or steal grain from a master other than a Brāhmaṇa. Having received and taken that grain, when questioned, "Why have you taken this grain belonging to us?", he should answer him truthfully according to dharma: "While remaining for three nights without eating, I have stolen this grain of yours for the sake of sustaining my life. Manu says:
likewise, by one who has not eaten six meals, the seventh meal [may be taken].
One may take from a person of low conduct according to the rule of not providing for the morrow.
Whether from a threshing floor, a field, a house, or wherever it may be found—
if he asks, one must tell that to him who asks.

This is the meaning: one who does not eat six meals may, at the conclusion of the seventh meal, take from a field or similar source an amount of grain sufficient for a single day—according to the rule of "not providing for tomorrow"—from a person of low caste or low occupation. Regarding this, Manu himself states the exception:

"The property of a Brāhmaṇa must never be taken by a Kṣatriya; however, he is entitled to take the property of robbers or of those who perform no religious rites, if he has no other means of livelihood" (3.42).
In this context, he states another rule for the king:
"Having ascertained his conduct, lineage, character, learning, study, austerity, and family, the king shall determine his righteous mode of livelihood. (3.43)

Having ascertained the conduct, behavior, family, lineage, character, disposition, learning, mastery of the meaning of the Vedas, study, renowned austerity, adherence to one’s own duty (*svadharma*), and the household—including the group of dependents—of that aforementioned fallen Brahmin, the king shall provide him with a righteous livelihood (*dharmyā vṛtti*) and sufficient wealth for his maintenance. Dakṣa says regarding the group of dependents:
"Father, mother, teacher, wife, offspring, the indigent, those who have sought refuge, guests, visitors, and the sacred fire—this is declared to be the group of dependents."
Relatives, kinsmen, the destitute, and those who have come for refuge—
even others— are declared to be the circle of dependents for one possessed of wealth.
It should be given to those who possess knowledge; otherwise, one would go to hell.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always support the group of dependents.
"The maintenance of those who are to be supported is praised as a means to attain heaven;
hell results from their oppression. Therefore, one should support them with diligence. (3.43)

Thus ends the second chapter, on the Duties in Times of Distress (*āpaddharma-prakaraṇa*), in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, who was born in the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the family of the glorious Vidyādharas.
Now begins the section on the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* with its commentary.

(3) Since it has been stated that one who has completed his student life (*brahmacarya*) is entitled to the householder stage (*gṛhasthāśrama*), the householder stage was described immediately after student life; however, as for the forest-dweller, he may become one either after being a householder or after being a student. Therefore, following the description of both of those, [the author] now speaks of the forest-dweller stage.

Having formally entrusted his wife to his sons, or otherwise accompanied by her, the forest-dweller, observing celibacy and maintaining both the sacred fire and the domestic hearth, shall depart for the forest. (3.44)

A *vānaprastha* is one who has formally resolved upon the stage of forest-dwelling (*vānaprasthāśrama*). Having entrusted his wife to his sons—that is, having placed her under their care for maintenance—or else accompanied and followed by her, he remains a celibate (*brahmacārī*), abstaining from sexual intercourse. If he should depart together with his wife, then he must go with the sacred fires (*sāgni*) and the domestic fire (*sopāsana*). Regarding the renunciation from the home for one accompanied by his wife, Chāgaleya says: "Having settled his wife among his sons, he should go to the forest according to the rule; a Brāhmaṇa who is without a wife, having consigned [the fires] within himself, should renounce from his home."

In this context, the word *samāropya* (having consigned) should be construed with the distant phrase *vanaṃ gacchet* (he should go to the forest). The word *agnīn* (the fires) is to be supplied as an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). Vasiṣṭha states that when a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) has gone to the forest alone, he must establish the sacred fire according to another rule: "Taking the fire according to the *Śrāvaṇaka* [tradition], one who has maintained the sacred fires, dwelling at the foot of a tree, for more than six months being without fire and without a fixed abode, should make offerings to the gods, ancestors, and men; he shall go to eternal heaven. *Śrāvaṇaka* refers to the *Vaikhānasa-śāstra*; having taken the fire according to the procedure prescribed therein, and making his abode at the root of a tree, he should tend the fire for six months. Then, having consigned the fires into himself (*ātmani samāropya*), being without fire and without a fixed abode, he should make offerings to the gods and others. One who follows such a practice and performs only ritual action (*kevala-karma*) goes to heaven; however, the man of knowledge (*jñānin*) attains eternity consisting of liberation (*mokṣa*). Thus says Yama.
Having lived for the second portion of his life at home, the twice-born man,
as a householder, should dwell in the forest during the third portion of his life.
Having procreated sons according to the Dharma, having performed sacrifices according to his ability,
and having seen the offspring of his offspring, a Brāhmaṇa should take refuge in the forest.

The mention of the *brāhmaṇa* is intended to indicate the twice-born (*dvija*) in general. Vasiṣṭha states that one may become a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) even immediately after the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*): "There are four stages of life (*āśrama*): the student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the wandering mendicant. Having studied one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas, and having completed his period of studentship, he may enter whichever of these he desires. Śaṅkha and Likhita state a specific rule for one proceeding from the householder’s stage to the stage of the forest-dweller: "Having procreated sons, performed their sacraments, taught them the Veda, provided for their livelihood, united them with wives, and entrusted the family responsibilities to a virtuous son, one who has adopted the signs of departure should follow the specific modes of subsistence in due order. Having gradually practiced the mode of subsistence of the *yāyāvara* [forest-dwellers], he should resort to the forest during the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight. Thus says Yama.
Taking with him the implements of sacrifice, the *agnihotra* fire, cows,
and his household utensils, the twice-born man may then go to the forest together with his wife.
He describes the specific materials, garments, and particular requirements for the performance of *śrauta* and *smārta* rites by the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*):
"Self-possessed, wearing a beard, matted hair, and body hair, he should satisfy the sacred fires, the ancestors, the gods, guests, and his dependents with food not produced by the plow. (4.45)

He should satisfy the sacrificial fire, the gods, the ancestors, guests, and his dependents with crops such as *śyāmāka* and *nīvāra*, which grow on land not tilled by the plow. "Satisfying the fire" means the performance of rites accomplished through the fire; "satisfying the gods and others" refers to the performance of rituals dedicated to deities such as the gods and ancestors; and "satisfying dependents" is well known. He should also maintain his beard and other such features. He should be self-possessed and have conquered his senses. Manu says:
"He should offer the *agnihotra* pertaining to the three sacred fires according to the rules, performing the *darśa* and *paurṇamāsa* sacrifices as far as his ability permits."
One should perform the Ṛkṣeṣṭi, the Āgrayaṇa, and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices;
likewise, one should perform them in succession during the northern course and the southern course of the sun.

The ṛkṣeṣṭis are sacrifices performed under the lunar mansions; they are to be offered during the northern course or the southern course of the sun. With pure forest foods fit for sages, gathered by himself in spring or autumn, he should separately prepare the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) and the cooked rice offerings (carus).
Having offered that forest-grown oblation, which is more pure than other sacrificial food, to the deities,
he should consume the remainder for himself, as well as salt prepared by his own hand.
Likewise: "With various kinds of pure food fit for sages, or with vegetables, roots, and fruits,
one should perform these very great sacrifices according to the prescribed rule."
From whatever food he may have, he should offer a bali-oblation and alms according to his ability;
he should honor those who have come to his hermitage with water, roots, fruits, and alms.
He should wear either a skin or a garment of bark; he should bathe in the evening as well as in the morning;
and he should always bear matted hair, as well as a beard, body hair, and nails.
Yama said: One should provide food grown without cultivation, roots, fruits, other varieties of rice,
and sacrificial food (haviṣya) during the five great sacrifices (mahāsattras).
For whichever deity the twice-born has seen the oblation prescribed, for that very deity he should duly prepare the appropriate sacrificial food separately.

He states the specific measure of the substances to be collected: "For the sake of a purpose, he may make a store for a day, a month, six [months], or likewise for a year; what has been stored should be discarded in the month of Āśvayuja. (3.46)

For the sake of a collection of grains intended for the purpose of a set of activities—whether their benefits are visible or invisible—that are to be accomplished in a single day, one should gather a store of grain. Alternatively, for the sake of limited activities to be performed within a month, six months, or a year, the acquisition of grain should be made accordingly. Whatever remains from that, one should discard in the month of Āśvayuja. Thus says Manu:
"One may be a daily-washer (sadyaḥprakṣālaka), or one who stores for a month;
or one who stores for six months, or even one who stores for a year."
One should avoid honey, meat, mushrooms growing from the ground,
bhūstṛṇa grass, śigruka, and the fruits of the śleṣmātaka tree.
In the month of Āśvayuja, one should discard the food of sages previously stored,
as well as worn-out garments, vegetables, roots, and fruits.
One should not eat what has been ploughed by a ploughshare, even if it has been abandoned by someone; nor should one eat roots and fruits grown within a village, even if one is distressed.
Laukāksi states that those produced in villages are:
rice, barley, wheat, both sesame and mustard, sugarcane, and millet; these are remembered as the village plants (grāmyā oṣadhayaḥ). 3.46.
Furthermore:
Self-controlled, bathing at the three sessions of the day, abstaining from accepting gifts, devoted to sacred study, habitually generous, and intent on the welfare of all beings. (3.47)

Self-controlled, with unrestrained effort, abstaining from falsehood and other such evils, bathing at the three junctions of the day, and desisting from accepting gifts—and by the use of the word "and," also from officiating at sacrifices and teaching—he should be devoted to the study of his own Veda, habituated to giving alms and the like, and intent on the welfare of living beings. (3.47)
Using his teeth as a mortar, eating only what is ripened by time, or grinding with a stone,
he should perform the rites and activities prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti using fruits and oils.

One who performs with his teeth the function of a mortar—that is, the act known as the removal of husks and grains—is a *dantolūkhalika*. Alternatively, he may observe a rule of eating only that which has ripened naturally over time and yields juice without the use of fire; or else, he may be a stone-pounder (*aśmakuṭṭaka*), meaning he should eat the food of sages after having pounded it with a stone. Furthermore, he should perform those rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti that require clarified butter (*ājya*) using oil produced from the fruits and roots of pure trees. This applies also to worldly activities such as eating and anointing the body. Thus says Manu:
He may eat food cooked by fire, or he may eat only what is ripened by time;
he may be one who grinds with stones, or likewise one who uses his teeth as a mortar.
Coarse water-born vegetables, flowers, roots, and fruits,
as well as other items produced from pure trees and oils derived from fruits.
He should pass his time with Cāndrāyaṇa fasts and always subsist on Kṛcchra penances; he may eat food once a fortnight, or once a month, or even once a day. (3.49)

One should pass the time by means of *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts such as those with the "ant's waist" (*pipīlikāmadhya*) or the "barley's waist" (*yavamadhya*), or one should always subsist by means of *kṛcchra* penances such as the *prājāpatya*. The word "time" (*kālam*) is to be supplied [from the previous verse]. Alternatively, one may eat food once every fortnight, month, or day; this is intended as an illustration, and therefore other modes of austerity are also to be adopted. Thus says Manu: "Having collected [food] according to his ability, he may eat at night or during the day; or he may eat at every fourth meal-time, or even at every eighth."
Choice depends upon one's capacity; and the position once accepted must be maintained until the completion of the stage of life. 3.49

Pure, he should sleep on the ground at night; during the day, he should spend his time standing on the tips of his toes, or by alternating between standing, sitting, and walking, or again by the practice of yoga. (3.50)

Pure and self-restrained, he should sleep on the ground itself, not on a bed or similar furniture. He should spend the day standing on his *prapadas*—the tips of his toes. He should pass the day by means of standing (the cessation of movement), sitting (seated posture), walking about (*vihāra*), and pacing (*caṅkramaṇa*). Alternatively, he should spend it through the practice of *yoga* endowed with the eight limbs, beginning with *yama* and *niyama*. Manu says: "He should roll about on the ground or stand on his *prapadas* during the day; or he may pass the time alternating between standing and sitting, approaching the waters at the ritual sessions (*savanas*)."
Living in the forest, a Brahmin should practice these and other initiations,
as well as various Upaniṣads and sacred scriptures for the sake of self-perfection.

Initiation is the resolve for austerity; its perfection is firm determination. These have been practiced by seers, brahmins, and householders alike for the sake of increasing knowledge and austerity, and for the purification of the body. (3.50)
In summer he should stand amidst five fires, in the rainy season sleep on the bare ground, and in winter wear wet clothes; or he should perform penance according to his capacity. (3.51)

[944] Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks!”—“Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four establishments of mindfulness. What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... He dwells contemplating mind in mind... He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. These, monks, are the four establishments of mindfulness. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this: “The body in the body, feelings in feelings, Mind in the mind, and phenomena in phenomena— One who dwells thus with clear comprehension, Armed with mindfulness, is called a sage. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, those monks rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words. [944] Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks!”—“Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four foundations of mindfulness. What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... He dwells contemplating mind in mind... He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. These, monks, are the four foundations of mindfulness. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this: “The body in the body, feelings in feelings, Mind in the mind, and phenomena in phenomena— One who dwells thus with clear comprehension, Armed with mindfulness, is called a sage. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, those monks rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.

Above the sun, in the four directions of the circle of the quarters, are the four fires. One should remain situated amidst these five fires during the summer. During the rainy season, one should sleep on the bare ground (*sthaṇḍila*); by the term "ground," a surface of earth that is not covered by a house, trees, or the like is meant. By the mention of "sleeping," it is indicated that one should remain there even at night. During the winter, however, one should wear wet clothes; by the word "clothes," rags, bark, and so forth are intended here. This is said with reference to a year consisting of three seasons: thus, the four months beginning with Caitra are summer; the same number of months beginning with Śrāvaṇa are the rainy season; and the same number of months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa are winter. Alternatively, in another manner, one should perform penance according to one's ability for the purpose of emaciating the body. As Śaṅkha says: "In due time, one should emaciate the body according to one's capacity through restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), mantras, fasting, and so forth; wearing garments of *kuśa* grass, rags, skins, or bark, with matted hair and a black antelope skin as an upper garment, intent upon sleeping in water, the five-fire penance (*pañcatapas*), and staying in the open air."—thus Manu.
He should perform ablutions at the three sessions of the day and offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
practicing most rigorous austerity, he should wither his own body.
Moreover:
He who pricks with thorns and he who anoints with sandalwood—toward both of them he is equal, neither angry nor pleased. (3.52)

One who causes suffering through the piercing with thorns and the like, and one who causes happiness through the anointing with sandalwood paste and the like—one should be equanimous and indifferent toward both, abandoning respectively anger and gratification. For one who correctly contemplates that "happiness and suffering are produced by these two, which are dependent upon the virtuous and non-virtuous actions performed by me," indifference toward those objects arises. (3.52)

Or, having internalized the sacred fires within himself, dwelling among trees and restricting his food, he should beg for alms solely for the sake of sustenance from the dwellings of forest-dwellers. (3.53)

Furthermore, he who, having undertaken the stage of life (*āśrama*), has tended the sacred fires for six months but is thereafter unable to continue tending them, should consign those fires to himself by causing them to mount into his own self; then, dwelling among trees and performing his domestic duties with the tree itself as his home, he shall subsist on restricted food. When, however, he is unable to sustain his bodily existence through such means, he may then practice begging for alms in the huts of forest-dwellers for the sake of maintaining his body. Manu says:
"But having duly internalized the sacrificial fires within himself..."
He should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling, a silent sage subsisting on roots and fruits.

(945) "Dwelling" (*niketa*) means a house; "sage" (*muni*) means one who observes silence. The rule regarding alms-gathering should be understood as applying when roots and fruits are unavailable. For this very reason, Manu himself stated immediately thereafter:
"One should practice alms-gathering for sustenance among Brahmin ascetics."
Or among other householders, or among the twice-born who dwell in the forest. || 3.53 ||
But when the maintenance of the body cannot be sustained by begging in the forest, he states what is to be done in that case:

"Or, having brought eight morsels from a village, he should eat while restraining his speech. This is explained by its very recitation (*nigadavyākhyātam*). Regarding the consumption of forest food, the number [of morsels] in villages is sixteen.

"An ascetic (muni) shall take eight morsels for alms, and a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) sixteen"—thus it is prescribed by such rules. However, there is no contradiction here, as this number eight refers specifically to morsels of village-grown food.
He speaks next with regard to one who is incapable of performing the entire regimen:
Subsisting on air, he should go toward the north-east until his body is withered away.

Until the dissolution of the body—that is, until its fall—he should go toward the north-easterly direction, the unconquered quarter, subsisting on air alone. Thus, it should be understood that for a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) who is unable to perform his own prescribed duties, there is no sin in the abandonment of the body; rather, there is spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*), because such an act is ordained. Manu says:
"Taking recourse to the unconquered quarter, he should walk straight forward until the fall of the body, disciplined, subsisting on water and air."

He is disciplined and concentrated. And this instruction regarding the Great Departure (*mahāprasthāna*) is intended as an illustration; by it, entering fire or water and so forth is also prescribed. Thus, another *Smṛti* states: "A forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) may set out on a long journey, enter fire or water, or throw himself from a precipice. Manu says:
"Having abandoned his body by one of these means, a Brahmin, freed from sorrow and fear, is glorified in the world of Brahmā."

By the phrase "these are their ascetic practices," such observances as "in summer, one should perform the five-fire penance" (*pañcatapas*) and others are referred to. The non-contradictory duties mentioned in the section on the student (*brahmacārin*) are to be practiced by householders, forest-dwellers, and renunciants as well. Thus says Gautama: "And this is not contradictory for those who follow the subsequent stages. This means that the collection of duties mentioned in the section on the student is to be understood as applicable to those who follow the subsequent stages, such as the householder and others, which will be described hereafter; the sense is that these are not in conflict with the duties prescribed for their own respective stages of life (*āśrama*). (3.54)

Thus ends the third section, on the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, who was born in the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the family of the glorious Vidyādharas.
Now, in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* with its commentary, the section on ascetics (*yatiprakaraṇa*). (4) Now he begins to expound the duties (*dharma*) of those who have renounced the world (*pravrjita*).

Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, at which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee, either from the forest or from the home, and having at its conclusion internalized those sacred fires within oneself; 3.55.

Having studied the Vedas, performed recitations, fathered sons, given food, maintained the sacred fires, and offered sacrifices according to his ability, one should then set one's mind on liberation; it should not be otherwise. (3.56)

Having studied the Vedas during the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*), having performed the daily and occasional prayers, meditations, and recitations such as the *sandhyopāsana*, and having produced offspring according to the rules during the householder stage (*gārhasthya*), one who gives food to gods, ancestors, men, and others, performs the necessary rites achievable through the *śrauta* and *smārta* fires, and performs sacrifices according to his capacity—by virtue of these and other such qualifications—one should perform the sacrifice dedicated to Prajāpati with the gift of all one's possessions (*sarvasvadakṣiṇā*). At the conclusion of that sacrifice, having internalized those sacrificial fires (*vaitānāgni*) within oneself, one should direct the mind—the internal organ—toward liberation, toward the means of liberation, which is the life of renunciation (*pārivrājya*). The meaning is that one should resolve upon renunciation. By the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) here, the Soma-sacrifice is intended; because that requires many materials, even though he is described as "possessing the fires," he is separately designated as a "performer of sacrifice. This rule for renunciation preceded by the householder stage should be understood as such. However, in the case of renunciation preceded by studentship alone, qualifications such as "having sons" and the performance of the sacrifice are excluded due to impossibility. Furthermore, renunciation exists immediately after studentship. Thus says the Jābāla Śruti: "Having completed studentship, one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller; having been a forest-dweller, one should go forth. Or otherwise, one may go forth directly from studentship, or from the home, or from the forest. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "After the forest-dwelling stage, for one who is peaceful and advanced in age, there is renunciation at will. Having internalized that very fire within himself, free from fear, greed, delusion, anger, grief, malice, pride, and envy, he should not worry about time, because the mind is unstable and faith is uncertain. Therefore, he should not wait for tomorrow and tomorrow. On that very day, he should renounce, casting off all undertakings and possessions."
On this point, Baudhāyana says:

Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). According to some, one who has completed his period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) may go forth directly from that state. Now, for those of the *śālīna* and *yāyāvara* classes who are childless, or for one whose wife is barren or deceased, they prescribe renunciation after seventy years, or after having established their offspring in their own duty (*svadharma*), or upon the cessation of ritual activity for a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). This is the eternal majesty of the Brahmin: "He does not increase by action, nor does he diminish. Having known his own goal through the Self alone, he is not smeared by evil action. Thus it leads to non-rebirth; "the eternal leads him to greatness"—this is "majesty" (*mahimā*). Having shaved off his hair, beard, and nails, and having bathed, he prepares himself.
