Taking a staff, a sling, a water-purifier, a water-pot, and a bowl—having gathered these—he should consume the threefold mixture of clarified butter, milk, and curds at the edge of a village or at the boundary of a village, or in a fire-sanctuary, and then fast, or consume only water. Saying: "Oṃ Bhūḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *tat savitur vareṇyam*"; "Oṃ Bhuvaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *bhargo devasya dhīmahī*"; "Oṃ Svaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*. Having thus entered the Sāvitrī quarter-verse by quarter, then half-verse by half, and finally with the whole verse, he leads himself from stage to stage by means of the Self, and becomes one with Brahman; so it is known. Moreover, they cite this:
Having gone from stage to stage of life, having offered oblations and conquered his senses,
and being exhausted by alms and offerings, he finally becomes a mendicant.

This very monk, for the sake of infinity, before the setting of the sun, having kindled the *gārhapatya* fire, having brought the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, having drawn out the blazing *āhavanīya* fire, having established it and kindled it, having melted clarified butter over the *gārhapatya*, having purified it, and having taken four portions in the *sruva*-ladle, he offers a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the kindled *āhavanīya* with "Oṃ Svāhā. This is known as the "Brahman's Fuel-Addition" (*brahmānvādhāna*). Then, after the evening *agnihotra* has been offered, having spread grass to the north of the *gārhapatya*, and having placed the vessels upon them in pairs with their openings facing downward, having spread *darbha* grass in the *brahmāyatana* to the south of the *āhavanīya* and having placed a black antelope skin over it, he remains awake that night. A Brahmin who, knowing this, fasts through the "Brahman-night," whether he dies while having consigned the fires into himself or otherwise, crosses over all evil; he crosses over even the murder of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). Then, rising during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, he performs the morning *agnihotra* at the proper time. Then, having strewn grass on the ground and having carried forward the water, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. That sacrifice concludes in the well-known manner. [He says: "O *āhavanīya* and *gārhapatya*, may you two be of one mind for us," and then consigns the fires into himself. With the verse, "That body of yours, O Agni, which is worthy of sacrifice," he smells each fire three times. Then, standing within the altar (*antarvedi*), having announced three times aloud—"Oṃ! Bhūr! Bhuvaḥ! Svaḥ! I have renounced"—and having spoken it once in a whisper, he speaks it three times aloud, for it is known that "the gods are based on the three truths. He pours out a full handful of water, saying, "Fearlessness to all beings from me. Moreover, they cite this:
"The sage who wanders about after granting fearlessness to all beings—
no fear from any beings whatsoever exists for him even in this world."

Restraining his speech, he goes forth. Taking up a staff, a sling, a water-strainer, a water-pot, and an alms-bowl—having gathered these—he goes to where there is water, bathes, sips water, and purifies himself with the *surabhimatī*, *ābliṅga*, *hiraṇyavarṇā*, and *pāvamānī* verses. Having gone into the water, he performs sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while reciting the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn. Emerging from the water, wringing out his garment, and putting on another clean garment, he sips water again. Taking the purifier with the words, "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he offers libations: "Oṃ bhūs, I satisfy; Oṃ bhuvas, I satisfy; Oṃ svas, I satisfy; Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, to Mahas, obeisance. Having offered the joined palms to the gods and the ancestors, he says: "Oṃ bhūḥ svadhā; Oṃ bhuvaḥ svadhā; Oṃ svaḥ svadhā; Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, to Mahas, obeisance. Then he worships the Sun with the two verses, "ud u tyaṃ" and "citram. "Oṃ" is Brahman; "Oṃ" is the Veda. He who shines is the light; he who shines is the deity; he who shines is that which is to be known. This very Self satisfies him; he offers obeisance to the Self; the Self is Brahman, the Self is the light. "Oṃ, I satisfy the Sāvitrī; Oṃ bhūs, I satisfy; Oṃ bhuvas, I satisfy; Oṃ svas, I satisfy; Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svas, I satisfy. He should repeat this a thousand times, or a hundred times, or an unlimited number of times. Taking the purifier with "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he holds it. From this point forward, he must not sip water that has not been drawn up, nor strained, nor purified. Nor from this point forward should he wear white garments. He may carry one staff or three staves. Now, these are the observances: non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, avoidance of sexual intercourse, and renunciation—these are the five secondary vows (*upavrata*). Furthermore: freedom from anger, service to the teacher, serenity, purity, and purity of food.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"Thus, remaining in the forest hermitage, having burnt away his sins through austerity,
the twice-born man should enter the fourth stage of life after renouncing according to the prescribed rule."
One should diligently give to the twice-born, to the gods, and to one's own ancestors;
having performed the śrāddha for the sages, for human beings, and likewise for oneself.
Having performed either the Vaiśvānara sacrifice or the Prājāpatya sacrifice,
and having established the fires within himself according to the mantras, he should then depart as a wandering mendicant.
From that time forward, one should abandon affection, greed, and the like toward sons and others;
and one should offer water upon the ground, granting fearlessness to all beings.
And the staff should be made of bamboo, pleasing to the sight, with its bark intact, having joints at equal intervals,
four finger-breadths in thickness, and wrapped with a cord made of black cow-hair.
One who knows the Dharma should take it in his right hand— provided it is bound with three knots and covered above with a water-strainer— using the mantra alone.
[950] A carrying-net (śikya) woven from those very materials— whether linen, kusha grass thread, or cotton thread— and fashioned in the shape of a lotus.
A wise man, by means of mantras, should take up the vessel characterized as a *śikyam* (sling-bag) joined with six sections and fist-sized compartments, as well as the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).
A seat made of wood is prescribed— either square, circular, or level—
and it was practiced by those sages for the sake of purification or for the purpose of sitting.
He may take a garment to cover his private parts, a patched cloak to ward off the cold, and even sandals; he should not make a collection of anything else.
These are declared to be the marks of that ascetic according to dharma; having embraced these and performed the renunciation of worldly ties, he went to an unsurpassed sacred ford.
Having bathed and sipped water according to the rules,
and having indeed gratified [the ancestors] with water purified by a cloth while reciting mantras, one should bow to the Sun.
Seated, facing east, and observing silence, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma);
having recited the Gāyatrī as much as possible, one should meditate upon the supreme state.
Having thus spent a third part of his life in the forests,
he should abandon all attachments and renounce them during the fourth part of his life.
Passing from one stage of life to the next, having performed the purificatory oblations and conquered his senses,
one who goes forth as a mendicant— exhausted by begging and making offerings— thrives after death.
Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation;
but he who pursues liberation without having discharged them falls downward.
Having studied the Vedas according to the rules, having procreated sons in accordance with dharma,
and having performed sacrifices to the best of one's ability, one should direct the mind toward liberation.
A twice-born man who, without having studied the Vedas, without having procreated sons,
and without having performed sacrifices, desires liberation, goes downward.

And this should be understood in the context of the view that renunciation (*pravrajyā*) is preceded by the householder stage (*gārhasthya*). However, for one who becomes detached while still in the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*), there is no taking of a wife, because that [stage] is motivated by passion for women. Furthermore, one who lacks a wife has no entitlement (*adhikāra*) to procreation or sacrifice; and for one who lacks such entitlement, there is no sin (*pratyavāya*) even in the non-performance [of these duties]. Consequently, for a student renouncing the world, the sole ground for eligibility for renunciation is the fact of having studied the Vedas, not the fulfillment of [the duties of] procreation and so forth. Nor should it be argued that, on the strength of scriptural statements such as "A Brāhmaṇa, indeed, when being born... [Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.3.10.5], one who is merely distinguished by birth alone has the entitlement to study, sacrifice, and the clearing of debts. This is because of incapacity. For one who has merely been born is not able to perform these; therefore, the meaning of the sentence is that a Brāhmaṇa and others, being entitled [only after reaching maturity], are born with three debts. Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever in renunciation being preceded by the mere stage of studentship. [Objection: But does this not contradict the rule, "One should renounce after seventy [years]"? [Reply: Not so. This time limit prescribed in the Smṛti is intended for one who, out of passion, has taken up the householder life and possesses weak dispassion (*vairāgya*); it prescribes that dispassion must be acquired [by then]. Otherwise, it would be difficult to avoid contradicting the Śruti which says, "On the very day one becomes detached, on that very day one should renounce. And thus says the Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa: [The text continues with the citation from the Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa.]
He whose tongue, genitals, stomach, and head are well-restrained—
such a Brahmin, remaining celibate and subsisting on alms, should renounce the world.
Having gone forth from the home, the sage, purified by his observances,
should wander as a mendicant, indifferent even when sensual pleasures are presented.
Attachment to the objects of passion and so forth, as well as children, wife, and the auspicious and inauspicious.
Likewise:
"He who has renounced this house, wife, children, and fields— which bring only suffering—
having first cultivated detachment and wisdom, is indeed without equal in this world."
In the Mahābhārata: "There are four kinds of mendicants: the Kuṭīcara, the Bahūdaka, the Haṃsa, and the Paramahaṃsa; each subsequent one among these is superior. (3.56)
To the question of what one should do after having gone forth, he says:
"Devoted to the welfare of all beings, tranquil, carrying the triple staff and the water-pot, delighting in solitude, one who has gone forth should resort to a village for the sake of alms. (3.57)

Having gone forth according to the prescribed manner, he is beneficial and non-injurious even toward beings who have done him harm; that is to say, his affection has ceased even toward those who have been helpful, such that he does not favor them. And thus says Gautama: "One who abstains from both injury and favor. He is a *tridaṇḍin*, meaning one who possesses three bamboo staffs. As for what was stated by Manu:
"The staff of speech, the staff of mind, and the staff of action—these are the three;
he whose actions are restrained by these staffs is called a *tridaṇḍin*."
"The staff of speech is silence; the staff of action is non-violence;
but for the staff of mind, breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is prescribed.

[952] In this passage, the word "staff" (daṇḍa) is used figuratively because it stands in grammatical apposition with speech and the other senses. However, it is not figurative here [in the current context] either, as there is no reason for it to be so. He should carry a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) and be one who maintains a water-pot for the sake of accomplishing purposes such as purification and ritual sipping (ācamana). He should delight in solitude and remain alone. And thus says Dakṣa:
A single monk is as described; two are known as a pair;
three are declared to be a village, while more than that acts like a city.
A forest-dweller should not establish a city, nor a village, nor likewise a household;
for by performing these three, an ascetic falls away from his own duty.
Among them, talk of kings and the like, as well as talk of alms, arises one toward another;
through close proximity, affection, backbiting, and envy will undoubtedly arise.
For the sake of gain and honor, there is exposition and the gathering of disciples;
these and many other such elaborations belong to those wretched ascetics.
Meditation, purity, alms-gathering, and constant habituation to solitude—these are the four duties of a monk; a fifth does not exist.

He should resort to or enter a village solely for the purpose of alms, not for the sake of residing there or other reasons; he should dwell elsewhere than that village. This is the rule for the Haṃsa and Paramahaṃsa. However, for the Kuṭīcara and Bahūdaka, residence even in a village is permitted; and thus says Prajāpati: "In this regard, there are four kinds of wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*): namely, the Kuṭīcara, the Bahūdaka, the Haṃsa, and the Paramahaṃsa. The one called Kuṭīcara is as follows: remaining in his own house, free from impurity, eating alms among those who maintain the sacred fires, having abandoned desire, anger, greed, delusion, and egoism—he who practices self-benefit is called a Kuṭīcara. The one called Bahūdaka is as follows: staying one night in a village and five nights in a town, eating food when it is obtained—he is called a Bahūdaka. Therein, the one called Haṃsa is as follows: dwelling in mountain caves, hermitages, temples, or groves, he should enter a village only for the purpose of alms—he is called a Haṃsa. Therein, the one called Paramahaṃsa is as follows: sleeping on riverbanks, forest regions, or grassy meadows, being unshakable, wearing rags, a loincloth, and ochre garments—he who gives up his life is called a Paramahaṃsa. *Asaṃkusuka* means one who does not accumulate and is skillful.
For the wise man regards [women] as an ornament, a burden, a stain, and likewise a smearing;
but the fool prizes them highly.
Even those gods, whose strength is superior, are overcome by sense objects;
what then can be said of humans, who are of little strength and prone to negligence?
Therefore, the wielding of the staff should be performed by one whose passions have been ripened;
another, however, is not capable of it, as he is carried away by the objects of the senses.
Many people live by the pretext of the triple staff;
for he who does not know Brahman should certainly not be a bearer of the triple staff.
The staff of speech, the staff of mind, and the staff of action—these three;
he for whom these three staves are restrained is called a *tridaṇḍin*.
One should never study, speak, or listen [to worldly matters].
One who is perfected through all these becomes a *yati*, and no other. By means of the girdle, the deerskin, and the staff, one is characterized as a *brahmacārī*.
The householder is characterized by the sacrificial post and the Vedas; the forest-dweller by his nails and hair;
and the ascetic by the triple staff—these are their respective characteristics.
He who does not possess these characteristics is not an ascetic, even if he performs penance.
Manu says: One should always wander alone for the sake of accomplishment, without a companion;
perceiving that success belongs to the solitary one, he neither abandons it nor is he abandoned by it.
He does not abandon his accomplishment; the meaning is that he is not deprived of it by her.

He should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling, resorting to a village only for the sake of food. Indifferent, free from accumulation, the sage should be endowed with the true state of being (*bhāva*).
A skull, the roots of trees, ragged clothing, solitude,
and equanimity toward all things— these are the characteristics of one who is liberated.
One should not rejoice in death, nor should one rejoice in life;
one should simply await the time, just as a hired laborer awaits his wages.
One should set down one's foot purified by vision; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak words purified by truth; and one should act with a mind that is purified.
The term of residence is for a limited time.
One should endure harsh words and should not despise anyone.
Nor, depending upon this body, should one harbor enmity toward anyone.
One should not become angry with one who is angry; when reviled, one should speak kindly;
and one should not utter speech scattered through the seven gates.
One should not utter speech defiled by desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, and egoism.
Delighting in the inner self, one should remain indifferent and free from longing;
seeking happiness, one should wander here with the self alone as one's companion.
With his hair, nails, and beard clipped, carrying a bowl and a staff,
he should wander constantly, self-restrained, never causing pain to any living beings.
For the sake of protecting living beings, whether by night or by day,
he should always walk upon the earth with careful observation, even when his body is exhausted.
He should generally wander during the eight months of summer and winter;
for the sake of compassion toward all living beings, he should dwell in one place during the rainy season.
One should withdraw the senses when they are being carried away by their objects, either by consuming little food or by staying and sitting in solitude.
Through the restraint of the senses, through the destruction of passion and hatred,
and through non-violence toward living beings, one becomes fit for immortality.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "For ascetics of restrained mind, there should be wandering for eight months;
they should, moreover, dwell in one place for the four months of the rainy season."
For those who have entered Avimukta, no dwelling place exists;
there, no body shall remain—this has been seen in the ancient scriptures.

Vasiṣṭha says: "A wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) should set forth after giving the gift of fearlessness to all beings. He is called a *parivrājaka* because he departs, having abandoned worlds, wealth, and sons; this is a derivative designation based on the fact that his departure (*vrajan*) has been fully cultivated. Having given the gift of fearlessness alone to all beings, both moving and stationary—this being the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) associated with the performed sacrifice—he should set forth and depart, regardless of knowledge or other requirements. The meaning is: "Having declared, 'Fearlessness toward all beings from me,' one should go forth into the wandering life. Furthermore, they cite this: [text follows].

"The sage who wanders about after having granted fearlessness to all beings, for him too there is never any fear from any being. For one who gives the gift of fearlessness with all beings as the recipients, from that very act fearlessness—liberation—comes to pass. By this, it is stated that the fruit of renunciation is liberation. He now speaks of the fault in falling away from the life of a wandering mendicant: [955]

"But he who, having granted safety to all beings, turns back from his vow, destroys those already born and those yet to be born in his own lineage, as well as those whom he accepts [as dependents]; the meaning is that he consigns them to hell.

Thus, one who turns back from the life of renunciation—which is characterized by the gift of fearlessness—destroys those born in his own family and those yet to be born, as well as those belonging to whom he accepts [as his followers]; the sense is that he causes them to go to hell.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the highest austerity;
begging is superior to fasting; and compassion excels giving.

That which is the single syllable called *praṇava*, the supreme and most excellent Brahman of the Vedic corpus; that which is superior to breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and austerity such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*; that which is better than fasting (*anaśana*) and the collection of alms (*bhikṣā*); and because compassion (*dayā*) excels giving (*dāna*) in its quality—therefore, one should constantly practice the *praṇava*, breath-control, the conduct of begging, and compassion. This is the essential meaning. Likewise, in that same text: "Shaven-headed (*muṇḍa*), free from the sense of 'mine' (*amama*), and without possessions (*aparigraha*). Shaven-headed means without a top-knot (*śikhā*). This is optional, according to the statement of Gautama: "Either shaven-headed or with a top-knot. Free from the sense of 'mine' means devoid of attachment to sons and the like. Without possessions means he should be devoid of items such as umbrellas, other than those implements like the staff and water-pot prescribed by the scriptures. "He should wander for alms at seven houses not previously intended [for him]. When the smoke has ceased and the pestle is at rest, wearing a single garment or an antelope skin. Having put on either a single garment or an antelope skin, he should wander for alms at seven houses during the afternoon time, characterized by the absence of smoke and the cessation of pestle-work, thinking: "Alms are to be sought here. He should wander for alms at houses not previously intended out of greed for food. "With his body covered by grass cropped by cows, sleeping on the bare ground (*sthaṇḍila*). The word "should be" is understood. "Cropped by cows" means cut for the sake of the cattle. "With his body covered" means his body is clothed. "Sleeping on the bare ground" means sleeping on the floor. "He should dwell in an unstable residence. In another village, in an empty house, in a temple, or at the root of a tree, studying the knowledge through the mind. Studying through the mind alone the *Upaniṣads*, which are the means to the knowledge of Brahman, he should dwell—that is, establish his residence—in villages and so forth, in an unstable location. "He should not wander where domestic animals are visible. The essential meaning is that he should wander in the forest. Now they also cite:
For one who dwells constantly in the forest, whose senses are conquered, who has turned away from the gratification of all the senses,
whose mind is absorbed in reflection on the inner self, and who is equanimous— certain indeed is his non-returning.

For one who dwells eternally in the forest, having mastered the senses, who avoids even that which brings pleasure to the senses when it arises from desire out of fear of the emergence of passion; for one whose mind is inclined toward reflecting on the meaning of the scripture intended for the self, who is indifferent toward all things, and who is devoid of the notion of anything to be rejected or accepted—his non-return, his liberation, is certain and fixed. "He whose signs are unmanifest, whose conduct is manifest, who is not mad, yet endowed with the appearance of a madman. He is so described because his signs of yoga-perfection are unmanifest or hidden. His conduct is manifest, consisting of the performance of prescribed purity and other such practices. Though not mad, he may be endowed with the appearance of a madman out of fear of being honored and the like. Furthermore, they cite this example:
"There is no liberation for one who delights in the science of grammar, nor for one who delights in grasping at the world;

nor for one proud of food and clothing, nor for one who is fond of a very beautiful dwelling. Liberation is not attained by one who is dogmatically attached to the view that knowledge of grammatical science alone is the supreme goal, nor by one who delights in the company of worldly people, nor by one who praises food and such things, nor by one who desires a pleasant residence. To whom, then, does it belong? To this he says:

"He who has no attachment to a hut, nor to water, nor to clothing, nor to the three hollows [of the body], nor to a house, nor to a seat, nor to food—he is indeed a knower of liberation. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that he who has no attachment to huts and other such things used for ascetic practice, nor is devoted to them, becomes a knower of liberation (*mokṣavin*) and a partaker in the attainment of liberation. He states an exception for one who is unable to wander for alms: "Or whatever he may obtain in the house of a Brāhmaṇa, let him eat that in the evening and in the morning, excluding honey and meat. One who is unable to beg for alms due to illness or other causes should eat, either in the evening or in the morning, whatever he obtains in the house of a Brāhmaṇa, provided it is free from honey and meat. This applies when he is incapable in both cases; however, for one who is incapable [of begging], there is the favor of eating in the evening alone. He should also avoid honey and meat even at a *śrāddha* ceremony. To prevent excessive indulgence even in this concession, he says: "And he should not eat to satiety. The meaning is that he should eat only what is necessary for the maintenance of life. He mentions another concession: "Or he may live in a village. Furthermore: "He should be straightforward, honest, and not fickle. The word "should be" is understood. "Crooked" (*jihma*) means deceitful. "Honest" (*aśaṭha*) means free from guile. "Fickle" (*saṃkusuka*) means one who hoards. The sense is that he should not be of such a nature. "And he should not engage in sexual union with anyone. [957] "Sexual organ" (*indriya*) refers here to the generative organ; he should not engage in its union with anyone. Moreover: "He should be indifferent toward all beings. The meaning is that he should be free from passion, hatred, and the like toward all living creatures. "The avoidance of backbiting, envy, pride, bowing, egoism, lack of faith, dishonesty, self-praise, censuring others, hypocrisy, and greed is the most righteous duty for all stages of life (*āśrama*). Backbiting (*paiśuna*) is the act of pointing out faults. Envy (*matsara*) is intolerance of another's prosperity. Pride (*abhimāna*) is arrogance. Bowing (*namasyā*) means prostration. Egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) is conceit regarding one's lineage, wisdom, and so forth. Lack of faith (*aśraddhā*) is atheism regarding the next world and such matters. Dishonesty (*anārjava*) is guile. Self-praise (*ātmasaṃstava*) is the glorification of one's own virtues. Censuring others (*paragarhā*) is slandering others. Hypocrisy (*dambha*) is practicing dharma with a fraudulent motive. Greed (*lobha*) is the taking or withholding of property by transgressing the rules. The avoidance and abandonment of these is superior to the duties prescribed for all other stages of life. "Wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavītin*), with a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his hand, pure, and avoiding the food of a *vṛṣala*, the Brāhmaṇa [should be thus]. The renunciant (*parivrājaka*) should wear the sacred thread. However, it is not appropriate to connect the phrase "wearing the sacred thread" with "all stages of life. Nor should the word "all stages of life" be modified to the nominative case and connected [to the subject]; for the word "renunciant" is directly the subject of the context without modification. Thus, the wearing of the sacred thread is not enjoined for the other stages of life by this [text], since it is already established by the words "wearing the sacred thread" and so on. Likewise, by enjoining the sacred thread for all stages of life, the status of wearing the sacred thread is obtained for the renunciant as well. Therefore, the view is that the general injunction of the sacred thread is set aside by the specific injunction of discarding it, as ordained by the Jābāla Śruti: "Having cut off his nails, he should discard the sacred thread. True, if there were not another statement: "Having cut his nails, having discarded old clothes, the sacred thread, and the water-pot, and having taken new ones, he should enter the village. Furthermore, the word "all stages of life," being in the genitive plural, would remain plural even if modified to the nominative; thus it cannot be in grammatical apposition with the singular word "renunciant. Therefore, it is connected with the word "renunciant" which is the subject in the singular nominative. "With a water-pot" means with a water-pot full of water in his hand. "Pure" means possessing the specific purity required for his own stage. "Avoiding the food of a *vṛṣala*" is intended as a concession for the food of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas when the food of a Brāhmaṇa is unavailable. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is for the purpose of indicating the twice-born (*dvija*). [958] He states the fruit of the life of renunciation: "He is not fallen from the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*). The world of Brahman is Brahman itself. Āpastamba says: "Now, the renunciant departs from that very state, having been a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*). He who departs after abandoning the three desires is a renunciant. His duties will be stated: "From that very state of dwelling in the teacher's family, he departs as one whose student-life is unbroken. For him they prescribe: 'He should be without fire, without a fixed dwelling, without comfort, without shelter, a silent sage (*muni*), relinquishing speech except for Vedic study. He is 'without fire' (*anagni*) because fire does not exist for him. By this, worldly and Vedic fire-rites, such as cooking and oblations, are prohibited. 'Without a fixed dwelling' (*aniketana*) means without a permanent place. 'Without comfort' (*aśarmā*) means devoid of effort for the sake of pleasure. 'Without shelter' (*aśaraṇa*) means homeless. 'A silent sage' (*muni*) means one who restrains his speech. 'Relinquishing speech except for Vedic study' means he should speak only during the recitation of mantras not intended for ritual action. But for the ascetic, there is no study of the *brahmayajña*. 'Having touched water, he goes to houses. Whatever he gives there is his sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). The meaning is: 'In the village, having obtained food merely for the maintenance of life, he should wander the earth without longing, free from actions that bear fruit in the next world. 'Clothing that has been discarded is prescribed for him. 'Discarded' (*mukta*) means abandoned by the owner of the garment because it is unfit for wearing. Here he introduces the opinion of some: 'Some hold that there is complete liberation from everything. Some teachers believe there is total abandonment of everything. He explains that: 'Having abandoned truth and falsehood, pleasure and pain, the Vedas, this world, and the next, one should realize the Self alone; in the realized Self is the attainment of security. Truth is that which one might say in some cases, and falsehood is that which one might say in certain circumstances—truth and falsehood as enjoined by rules. Having abandoned pleasure and pain, as well as all objects prescribed by the Vedas, one should realize the Self alone. Because when that Self is realized, there is the attainment of security, which consists in the cessation of ignorance. To refute that, he says: 'This is contradicted by the scriptures. This position of the others is contradicted, opposed, and sublated by the scriptures, i.e., by the statements of the Śruti and Smṛti. For instance, the Mādhyandina Śruti says that the attainment of security is not the fruit of the realization of the Self—which is synonymous with knowledge—for one who is devoid of the obligatory castes and stages of life; rather, it is a transgression (*pratyavāya*)."
"They enter into blind darkness who worship knowledge;
those who delight in ignorance enter, as it were, into even greater darkness than that.

This is the meaning: those of deluded mind who, having disregarded *vidyā*—which is the knowledge of the Self—delight only in *avidyā*, which is ritual action (*karman*), they enter into blind darkness; and so too do those who delight in *vidyā*, which is the knowledge of the Self, while being devoid of obligatory and occasional rituals (*nitya-naimittika-karman*).
Having thus censured both knowledge alone and action alone, the Śruti prescribes their mutual combination as the means to liberation:
"He who knows both of these together—knowledge and ignorance—having crossed over death by means of ignorance, attains immortality through knowledge. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.4)

He who knows—that is, understands—this pair as the means to liberation, namely *vidyā* (knowledge), which is the meditation on the Self, and *avidyā* (non-knowledge), which consists of the collection of duties pertaining to caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*) mutually combined, does not enter the blinding darkness. Is this combination of knowledge and action like the performance of sacrifices subsequent to the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration)? Or is it like the *Āgneya*, *Āgnīṣomīya*, and other rites? Or is it like the relationship between a subordinate part (*aṅga*) and a primary act (*pradhāna*)? Upon such deliberation, for the sake of a definitive conclusion, it is said: "Having crossed over death by means of *avidyā*, he enjoys immortality through *vidyā*" (*avidyayā mṛtyuṃ tīrtvā vidyayāmṛtam aśnute*). Through *vidyā* he directly enjoys—that is, attains—immortality, which is liberation. However, having crossed over death—that is, that which is equivalent to death and constitutes an obstacle to liberation—he attains immortality through *vidyā*, which is the knowledge of the Self. It is not the case that anyone attains liberation through *vidyā* alone, without the subsiding of obstacles brought about by good actions. Therefore, it is established that the combination of *vidyā* with actions—which produce the service of crossing over obstacles for *vidyā*, the cause of attaining immortality—is distinct from the relationship of subordinate part (*aṅga*) and primary act. Nor should it be argued that actions serve as the cause only for crossing over death and not for liberation itself, and therefore they are merely subordinate parts of *vidyā*. For if that were so, there would be a split in the sentence into two separate meanings—one for "crossing over death by *avidyā*" and another for "enjoying immortality by *vidyā*"—yet this is a single sentence, as is understood from the force of the suffix *-ktvā*. Indeed, that suffix expresses a common agent for both the crossing over death and the attainment of immortality. And that [common agency] is not possible between those two without a relationship of cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*). Therefore, it is here ordained that actions, by virtue of being subordinate parts of *vidyā*, possess the status of being a cause toward liberation. As for those passages that negate the status of actions as causes toward liberation, such as: "Not by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth; by renunciation alone some have attained immortality" (*na karmaṇā na prajayā dhanena tyāgenaike amṛtatvam ānaśuḥ*), these refer to mere action [without the support of knowledge], and thus there is no contradiction. Precisely because actions possess the status of being a cause toward liberation, the statement—"For one who meditates on the Self alone as his world, his action is not exhausted"—which establishes the non-exhaustion of action, leads us to understand its status as a means to liberation. For the non-exhaustibility of action is due to its having inexhaustible results, not due to its inherent nature, since by its very nature it is perishable. For this very reason, the scriptural use of the instrumental case in "They desire to know [Brahman] by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting" (*vividiṣanti yajñena dānena tapasānāśakena*) establishes that [these acts] are subordinate parts of *vidyā*, which is the means to liberation. Nor should it be argued that the instrumental case assigns the actions as subordinate parts to the "desire" denoted by the desiderative suffix (*san*), because in desiderative forms, the root meaning is perceived as the desired object (*īpsita-karman*) in relation to the desire which is the meaning of the suffix; thus, that [root meaning] is the primary element. Therefore, it is that [primary element] which is connected with other word-meanings. Just as in the phrase "he wishes to go by horse," the horse is perceived as an instrument (*karaṇa*) for the act of going, and not for the desire itself. And clearly, regarding the combination of knowledge and action concerning liberation, the text says: "By that [path] goes the knower of Brahman, the radiant, and the doer of meritorious deeds" (*tenaiti brahmavit taijasaḥ puṇyakṛc ca*).
Thus have been cited the scriptural passages that refute the position that mere intellectual knowledge brings about liberation. Now, the Smṛti passages are cited; therein Manu says:
"Austerity and knowledge are the supreme means for a Brahmin to attain the highest good.
Through austerity he destroys impurity; through knowledge he attains immortality."
By means of non-violence, detachment from the senses, Vedic rituals,
and the practice of severe austerities, they attain that Supreme here in this world.
Yogayājñavalkya states:
"By the performance of one's own duties, by the perfect realization of the Self,
and by the thorough knowledge of the Vedāntas, even a householder is liberated."

The word "api" (also/even) implies that other members of the [four] stages of life (*āśramin*) are likewise liberated. As stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "The restraint which is excessively practiced by men through delusion due to the non-performance of prescribed duties, instead of granting liberation, actually results in a downward state of existence."
"You think to yourself, 'I am washing [myself],' O child."
You are not consumed by the sins arising from the non-performance of prescribed duties;
even ignorance, like poison, serves for the benefit of men.
Even when performed with skillful means, or even unjustly, it leads to bondage. Pulastya said:
Through the union of knowledge and action, a person attains the Supreme.
Because they do not succeed when separate, one should therefore rely upon both.
Knowledge is primary, but not devoid of action; action is primary, but not devoid of wisdom.
Therefore, success comes from both together, for a bird does not fly on one wing alone.
Vyāsa said: O Dharmaja, actions do not bind one who has renounced actions through yoga, whose doubts have been severed by knowledge,
and who possesses self-mastery.

He who performs actions, having offered them to Brahman and abandoned attachment, is not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. One who is disciplined, having renounced the fruit of action, attains the peace of final liberation.
One who acts impelled by desire, being attached to the fruit, is bound;
but he who performs the necessary action without depending on the fruit of action is not so bound.
He is both a renunciant and a yogi, not one who maintains no sacred fires nor one who performs no action;
for whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, and whatever you give—
Whatever austerity you perform, O son of Kuntī, do that as an offering unto Me. Brahman is the instrument of offering, Brahman is the oblation, and it is offered by Brahman into the fire of Brahman.

By means of which one must go to Brahman through the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) on the action of Brahman—that by which the oblation is offered or cast forth with the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) and other implements is "offering" (*arpaṇa*). By this [verse], the practice of perceiving Brahman within the factors of action (*kāraka*) and the action itself is enjoined. He who meditates upon—that is, perceives—the action as having Brahman as its essence is one whose meditative absorption is on the action of Brahman (*brahmakarmasamādhi*). In the *Viṣṇudharma*, the two Aśvins say:
"O best of men, two types of actions have been proclaimed by Brahmā."
For those two indeed have the fruits of heaven and liberation as their respective results—namely, the path of worldly engagement and the path of cessation.
O King, even action that is undertaken for the sake of liberation arises;
it is traditionally held to be action fallen from its own nature when it is devoid of desire for results.
Viṣṇu said:
"O best of the twice-born, even for those possessed of such knowledge who perform actions such as procreation, liberation occurs, according to the words of Rauma."
Just as a fire that is not fanned by the wind is extinguished when it is blown upon,
so too the fire of knowledge of one who is devoid of action is utterly extinguished.

Therefore, all those belonging to the stages of life (āśramins), always wearing the sacrificial thread (yajñopavītin), should perform their obligatory and occasional rites (nityanaimittika-karma) at the proper time without indolence. —
Hārīta.
Just as horses without a chariot, or a chariot without horses,
so too is austerity for one lacking knowledge, or knowledge for one who lacks austerity.
Just as food combined with honey, or honey combined with food,
so too are austerity and knowledge together a great medicine.

Thus, the refutation of the scriptures has been stated regarding the position that the mere knowledge of the Self leads to the attainment of security (*kṣema*). Now, he states the refutation of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): "If liberation were attained through knowledge, one would not experience suffering even here. If liberation occurs at the very moment the Self is known, then while still in this body, as it is dying, one would not experience any suffering whatsoever. However, according to the view of cumulative practice (*samuccaya*), liberation occurs when actions have been performed throughout one's life; thus, while living, there is no connection with that [liberation]. Thus says Baudhāyana: "A wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), having abandoned his kin and being without possessions, should go forth; having gone to the forest, he may wear a topknot or be shaven-headed, clothed in a loincloth and dyed garments. *Kāṣāya* refers to that which is dyed with *kaṣāya*, the resin of a tree. "By the restraints of speech, mind, and action, he should be non-injurious toward living beings and a bearer of purifiers, performing his duties with water drawn up for the sake of purification. "Duty" (*kārya*) refers to the washing away of impurities. As for sipping water (*ācamana*), however, it should be done with water that has not been drawn up. (3.57)
It has been stated that one should resort to a village for the sake of alms; regarding that, he explains how the acquisition of alms should be performed:

Free from negligence, one should go about for alms in the evening, unobserved, in a village devoid of other mendicants, seeking only as much as is necessary for subsistence and free from greed. (3.58)

He should be vigilant and respectful. He should remain unobserved by those who give alms, not being recognized for his virtues. Free from greed, he should be devoid of longing for delicious food. He should wander for alms at eventide—the final three *muhūrta*s of the day—in a village where other mendicants, such as celibate students (*brahmacārin*s) and others, have already finished their begging. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha says: "Clad in a single garment or an antelope skin, he should go for alms to seven houses that have not been pre-selected, when the smoke has ceased and the pestle has been laid down. The phrase "when the smoke has ceased and the pestle has been laid down" is an indicator of the evening time. That time at which the pestle is laid down—that is, motionless—is what is meant. Manu says:
One should go for alms at a single time and should not be attached to abundance;
for an ascetic who is excessively attached to alms sinks even into the objects of the senses.
One should not be despondent in the absence of gain, nor should gain delight one;
one should possess only what is necessary for the maintenance of life, having emerged from attachment to material requisites.
The quantity of requisites is the measure.
One should avoid gains obtained through honor in every way;
for even a liberated ascetic is bound by gains obtained through honor.
Gains preceded by honor are highly esteemed; likewise:
"A monk should never seek alms through portents or omens, nor through the science of astrology and bodily marks, nor through instructions or discourses."

A portent (*utpāta*) is the sight of something extraordinary; a sign (*nimitta*) refers to omens such as those of birds; a limb (*aṅga*) refers to grammar and so forth, or alternatively, to physiognomy such as the marks on the hands; and *sāmudra* refers to [the science of] prognostication. Regarding the dissolution (*saṃvarta*):
having collected eight, seven, or five alms, that sage, having washed all of it with water, should eat it with a well-composed mind.
Having eaten, the brahmin should again dwell alone in a solitary forest;
joined in mind, speech, and body, he should constantly engage in reflection.
Yama says:
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should subsist on alms; he should never eat the food of a single person.

And this applies when there is the capacity [to obtain food from the prescribed sources]. However, in the case of incapacity, one should observe what was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "Or whatever he may obtain in a Brāhmaṇa family," and so forth. If a Brāhmaṇa family is not available, he may eat the food of other castes, with the exception of the food of a Śūdra. To that effect, he (Vasiṣṭha) himself says: "Avoiding the food of a *vṛṣala*. Hārīta states: "The teachers say that when the food is pure, the inner being (*sattva*) becomes pure"; here, *sattva* refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Baudhāyana says: "Now, regarding the practice of begging for alms: he should seek alms from Brāhmaṇas who are *śālīna* or *yāyāvara*, before the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice has been concluded. He should prompt them, beginning with the word *bhavat*. Having returned from the practice of begging, he should wait for the duration of milking a cow. Having placed [the food] in a clean place, washed his hands and feet, and sipped water (*ācamya*), he makes an offering before the Sun with the verses *ud u tyaṃ citram*. It is known from scripture that he makes an offering to Brahman with the verse *brahma jajñānam*. From the time of the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*) onwards, the fires belong to the sacrificer himself: the *gārhapatya* fire is his out-breath (*prāṇa*), the *anvāhāryapacana* fire is his down-breath (*apāna*), the *āhavanīya* fire is his diffused breath (*vyāna*), and the *sabhya* and *āvasathya* fires are his upward-breath (*udāna*) and equalizing-breath (*samāna*). Or rather, these five fires reside in the self; he offers into the self itself. It is known from scripture that he is thus established in the sacrifice of the self, grounded in the self, and leads the self to security (*kṣema*). Before the rising of the stars, having divided the remainder and mixed it with water, he should consume it like medicinal herbs. Having consumed it and sipped water, he worships the Sun with the verse *ud vayaṃ tamasas pari*. Having muttered the mantra *vāṅma āsann o prāṇaḥ*..."
One should eat only such food as is necessary for the maintenance of life— food that is unasked for, not prepared with intention, and obtained by chance.

Devala says: "When the sun has turned back [at midday] and has set, at a time when the smoke has subsided, one should enter the village for the sake of alms. Wandering everywhere for alms while looking only a yoke’s length ahead, one should enter the houses of others that were previously designated and whose doors are closed, provided one is unable to do so without speaking. Having entered, one should avoid idle chatter, intimacy, deceit, wonder, mockery, laughter, begging, and glancing about. Having stayed for only as long as it takes to milk a cow, one should depart. One should not be angry if alms are not obtained; one should accept alms from those who are outcasts, from enemies, from kinsmen, from lords, or from those in a state of impurity due to a death, but one should reject alms that have been specially prepared for oneself or that cause distress to others. Having taken alms free from honey, meat, and raw grain, one should eat them in a secluded place, using either that same bowl or another, silently and in moderation. (3.58)
The vessels of ascetics are made of clay, bamboo, wood, or gourd;
their purification is by water and scrubbing with cow-hair.

The alms-bowls of ascetics, made of clay or other materials, are intended for the purpose of eating alms. For these, when soiled with food remnants, immersion in water and scrubbing with a cow-hair brush (*govāla*) are the means of purification. Manu says: "His vessels shall be non-metallic and free from cracks;
their purification by water is prescribed, just as that of the *camasa* cups at a sacrifice."

Hārīta says: "One who uses a bowl made of clay, wood, split bamboo, gourd, or withered leaves, or one who uses his hand as a bowl, may enter a village for the sake of alms; he should not give away leftovers, nor discard them, nor revile them; he should not eat to excess. [965] Śaṅkha and Likhita say: "The alms-vessel may be made of wood, gourd, split bamboo, or earth. Its individual purification consists of scrubbing it with water using a rope of cow-hair. One should not rinse one's mouth there, nor throw [the vessel] on the ground, nor touch it while impure. Having spoken [impure words], one should rinse one's mouth again, sprinkle the objects [with water], and [cleanse] the rope and whatever else is not prohibited. In the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*:
For the sake of his own sustenance, he should constantly practice wandering for alms;
at the time of evening, the ascetic should go from house to house among the brahmins.
One should indeed uncover the armor with the right hand;
having placed the vessel in the left hand, one should leave the remainder with the right.
One should practice begging for as much food as is required for subsistence;
then, having finished that meal, the self-controlled one should set aside the bowl, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and remain composed.
Having washed [the hands] with four fingers' breadth of water, being composed,
one should offer a mouthful of food, combined with all its condiments, into a separate vessel.
Having offered food to the deities such as the Sun and to the living beings, and having sprinkled it with water, the ascetic,
maintaining silence, should eat from a leaf-cup or a vessel.
One should never eat from the leaves of the banyan, the arka, or the aśvattha, nor from the leaves of the kumbhī, the tinduka, the kovidāra, or the karañja.
All ascetics who eat from bell-metal vessels are said to be defiled;
this applies equally to the bell-metal vessel of a householder as well.
A mendicant who eats from bell-metal incurs all the sin of those two;
having eaten from a vessel, the mendicant must always wash it with the accompaniment of mantras.
His sacrificial vessel would not be defiled, like the chalices in sacrifices;
then, having sipped water and restrained his breath, he should worship the Sun.
A wise man should spend the remainder of the day in recitation, meditation, and the study of ancient histories;
having performed the twilight rites, he should then spend the night in temples and similar sacred places.
Having meditated upon the stainless Self within the abode of the heart-lotus,
the ascetic— devoted to dharma, tranquil, equanimous toward all beings, and self-controlled— [attains liberation].
He attains the supreme state, reaching which he does not return. || 3.59 ||
Having fully restrained the collection of the senses, having abandoned passion and hatred,
and having cast off fear toward living beings, the twice-born becomes immortal. [3.60]

Having fully restrained the group of sense-faculties and made them inclined toward meditative absorption (*niṣadyā*), one should act thus; for even though the engagement of the senses with their objects is harmful, immortality cannot be attained as long as passion and aversion toward those objective domains persist. With this in mind, it was said: "and having abandoned passion and aversion. And so says the Śruti:
"When all the desires that dwell in his heart are cast away, then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains Brahman."

Likewise: "Having removed the fear of beings caused by their own [past] causes, and having brought about non-arising, the twice-born becomes immortal and is liberated. And here, the mention of the "twice-born" (dvija) is intended to convey its literal meaning; it is not merely an indicative term for a Brāhmaṇa. Thus, another Smṛti states:
"Having discharged the three debts, free from the notion of 'mine' and free from egoism, a Brāhmaṇa, or even a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, may renounce his home and go forth [into the forest]. (3.60)
Moreover: A mendicant, in particular, must cultivate purity of intention regarding his duties, because it is the cause for the arising of knowledge and for the attainment of independence. (3.61)

The purification of the inner organ—that is, the state of being free from defects—must be practiced by all those in the stages of life (*āśrama*) for the sake of generating knowledge of the Supreme Self and for the soul’s attainment of independence, consisting in the removal of subjection to passion, hatred, and delusion; this is especially so for the mendicant ascetic (*yati*). Atri says:
"For the highest attainment of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is not obtained here by those who are impure;
therefore, for the sake of purification, a state of being must be cultivated by those desiring to know Brahman."
One should first accomplish this through recitation and, according to one's capacity, through breath-control;
thereafter, for the purified self, Brahman becomes manifest.
Purified by breath-control (prāṇāyāma), one should recite the Brahman with diligence;
for the study of the Vedas is said to be the supreme austerity for a Brahmin in this world.
For one who likewise recites the Gāyatrī together with the Praṇava and the Vyāhṛtis, there is no further task remaining here; everything is completed within that.
Having practiced the recitation for three years with a pure disposition, that best of the twice-born,
having restrained the collection of his senses, should thereafter practice the *praṇava*.
The twice-born [realizes] Brahman as blissful, all-pervading, immutable, and absolute; there is no Brahman higher than this, nor is it attained here by those who are impure.
Having practiced the recitation of even a single year [of other mantras], one should thereafter practice the *praṇava*.
There is no doubt that an impure soul, by reciting this, is freed from sin.
This is the direct name of Brahman, more powerful than all else;
by its being uttered, one shall attain the presence of Brahman.
Just as a teacher, when treated with contempt, may destroy even a devoted disciple, so too does the Supreme Person, though served with unwavering devotion, [destroy one who treats him with disdain].
Therefore, an impure twice-born man who lacks faith should not practice the *praṇava*;
practicing while lacking faith and being impure, he goes to a downward state.
Chastity, purity through austerity, constant habituation to solitude,
lack of longing for sense objects, steadfastness, and compassion toward all beings.
Endowed with these means— patience, fortitude, purity, and the restraint of the mind— one should then practice the Praṇava.
Yama said: Just as the dust of mountain ores is consumed when they are being smelted, so too should one completely burn away the defects of the senses by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma). 3.61.

In the Yoga treatises, liberation is said to result from detachment from cyclic existence (saṃsāra) and from the realization of the true nature of the self. Regarding this, he first states the means for achieving detachment:

"One should contemplate dwelling in the womb, as well as the various states of existence born of karma, mental anxieties, physical ailments, afflictions, old age, and the transformation of form. (3.62)
Throughout thousands of births, there is the reversal of the pleasant and the unpleasant.

These matters should be examined and contemplated according to their true nature (*tattvataḥ*). First, regarding dwelling in the womb: for ten months one remains in the mother’s belly, which is extremely cramped and filled with urine and feces; there, bound tightly by all its limbs in a mass within the *ulba* (inner membrane) and *jarāyu* (outer membrane), one experiences unbearable pain even for a moment. Thus, one should infer that a multitude of intolerable sufferings is produced for the embryo by the specific foods and movements undertaken at the mother’s will. Furthermore, the suffering occurring at the time of birth is no different from the suffering of death. Likewise, the falls into hells resulting from sinful actions (*pāpakarma*) are to be known from the scriptures. Mental afflictions (*ādhayaḥ*) are mental activities that produce suffering. Diseases (*vyādhayaḥ*) are fevers and the like. Defilements (*kleśāḥ*) are ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the clinging to existence. Old age (*jarā*) is the decay of the body due to the power of time. The transformation of form (*rūpaviparyaya*) is the turning of a beautiful appearance into ugliness. Birth (*janma*) is existence among thousands of contemptible species, such as dogs, pigs, and so forth. The non-attainment of what is dear, the loss of what has been attained, the acquisition of what is unpleasant, and the persistence of that which is unpleasant—these and other such matters should be examined and contemplated according to their true nature. Manu says:
One should contemplate the destinies of men arising from the fault of desire,
as well as their falling into hell and the torments in the abode of Yama.
Separation from those who are dear, as well as union with those who are not dear,
being overcome by old age, and being tormented by diseases.
The departure from this body, the rebirth in a womb again,
and the paths of this inner self through thousands of millions of wombs— [all these he perceives].
He understands the connection with suffering for embodied beings arising from unrighteousness,
as well as the imperishable union with happiness arising from righteousness and purpose.
And the arising within bodies— whether among the highest or the lowest,
or among beings of high and low status— is difficult to understand for those who have not disciplined themselves.

In the abode of Yama, in the house of Yama—Śaṅkha says: "By perceiving the impurity within purity, the reversal of the pleasant and the unpleasant, and the dwelling in the womb, one shall be liberated; not otherwise."

In continuation of the phrase "one should see," Viṣṇu states: "At the time of birth, one experiences great suffering from the passage through the narrowness of the womb; in childhood, delusion and subjection to the teacher, along with the hardship of learning and receiving instruction; and in youth, the failure to obtain sense-objects, or, if obtained by improper means, the falling into hell due to the indulgence in those objects. In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, the son said: "[One should observe] the impregnation of women during their fertile period, the entry of the seed, and its abiding in the blood."
As soon as one is liberated from hell or even from heaven, one attains [the state beyond].
O Father, thereafter the two seeds, being unoverpowered, attain stability;
then they become the *kalala*, then the *budbuda*, and then the *peśī*.
Just as the sprout and other parts arise from the seed through the medium of the embryo,
so too do the five limbs arise from the body in an undivided manner.
The secondary limbs—the fingers, eyes, nose, mouth, and ears—emerge from the [primary] limbs;
likewise, the nails and hair emerge from them.
It grows simultaneously with that very source of its emergence,
just as the coconut fruit increases together with its husk.
In the same way, that downward-facing treasury increases;
likewise, the living being situated within the womb of a woman undergoes growth in due succession.
In this posture, however, one grows by placing both hands on the sides of the knees;
likewise, one places the two thumbs above the knees and the fingers at the tips of the knees.
Likewise, [the two hands] are placed on the back of the knees, the eyes, and the middle of the knees;
the nose is [aligned], and the two buttocks are situated on both sides, positioned between the knees.
In this way, the living being situated within the womb of a woman undergoes gradual growth; having entered the interior of the waters, the being develops according to its form and its state.
Hardness is overcome by fire; it lives by what is eaten and drunk.
So too, the state of a living being within the womb consists of its store of merit and demerit.
A channel named Āpyayanī is attached to his navel;
likewise, in women, it is produced when it is attached to the aperture of the mouth.
In that same way, what has been eaten and drunk by women enters into the womb;
thus nourished in body, that living being indeed attains growth.
There, many realms of cyclic existence come to his memory;
then, being tormented here and there, he arrives at a state of world-weariness.
Once I have been released from this womb, I shall never act in such a way again;
I will conduct myself in such a manner that I shall not conceive a fetus once more.
Thus he reflected, recollecting indeed hundreds of sufferings of birth,
which were previously experienced by him while he was a god and a son of a deity.
Then, in the course of time, the creature turns head-downwards;
in the ninth or even the tenth month, it is born again.
As he is being expelled, he is tormented by the wind belonging to Prajāpati;
and as he is being expelled, he cries out, afflicted at that time by suffering.
Having emerged from the belly, he falls into an unbearable faint;
then, accompanied by the pleasure of the touch of wind, he regains consciousness.
Then that deluding Māyā of Viṣṇu seizes him;
his mind being utterly deluded by her, he suffers a fall from knowledge.
Having stated the means for detachment, he now states the means for self-knowledge:
"The subtle Self, abiding within the self, is to be perceived through the yoga of meditation. (3.63)

*Dhyāna* (meditation) and *yoga* (union) constitute *dhyānayoga*. By means of this, the self—the subtle *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field), difficult to know—is to be "beheld" (*saṃdṛśya*), that is, correctly perceived, as being established in identity with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). One must realize directly: "I am indeed the Supreme Self. *Dhyāna* is the continuous flow of thought, "I am indeed the Supreme Self. *Yoga* is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind from other objects. The skillful one, having made the mind free of fluctuations and having unified the *kṣetrajña* with the Supreme Self, is liberated; this is called the primary *yoga*.
One should dissolve the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), which is liberated from all existents, into Brahman;
this is both meditation and yoga, while all other extensive treatises are merely superfluous.
Pulastya said: Where does Govinda abide for those whose minds are captivated by external objects?
Therefore, Hari can be meditated upon only by one whose mind is free from attachment.
Dakṣa says:
For one who is occupied with the affairs of the world, yoga does not come about through silence, mantras, various deceptions, or even through extensive learning.
Through application, as well as through practice, by means of firm conviction in that very [object], and through repeated disillusionment, yoga is accomplished; not otherwise.
Śaṅkha says:
During the first and last watches of the night, the yogi, always untiring,
should meditate upon the Supreme Person, Viṣṇu, who is beyond the qualities (nirguṇa) and the twenty-fifth principle.

Likewise: "With a tranquil self, one should constantly contemplate that which transcends the twenty-four principles, which is eternal, beyond the senses, devoid of qualities, and beyond sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; which abides in all, yet is exceedingly vast, all-pervading, and exceedingly subtle; whose hands and feet extend everywhere, whose eyes, heads, and faces are on every side, and which possesses the power of all the senses in every direction—one should meditate thus. Within a year, the manifestation of yoga occurs; reflection, discernment, and deliberation arise for the sage who is composing himself in the first stage of meditation from the beginning."
One should consume, in rotation, broken grains, boiled sour gruel, oil-cake, leafy vegetables,
barley-meal, as well as roots, fruits, and alms-food.
Standing in the midst of great austerity, blazing like fire,
he was a practitioner of penance who lived in solitude, ate sparingly, and had his senses fully restrained.
One whose afflictions have been burnt away by knowledge, who delights in practice, and who possesses self-mastery,
attains that supreme state with a mind free from mental activity.
Dattātreya said: In a windless,
secluded place that is auspicious, delightful, free from insects,
undisturbed, and devoid of gravel, sand, and the like.
Having prepared a clean seat in a place free from noise and other distractions,
one should assume a comfortable posture there, facing either east or north.
Having made his body perfectly straight with three points elevated, the best of those who know yoga paid homage to Mahādeva Hari, the great lord of yogins.
Having first purified the channels, one should then practice breath control (prāṇāyāma);
one should practice breath control until the mind becomes serene. (3.63)
Moreover:
"Lifestyle stage (āśrama) is not the cause of dharma; for dharma exists when it is being practiced.
Therefore, one should not do to others that which is unwholesome for oneself. (3.64)

In the context of the wandering mendicant’s stage of life (*parivrājaka-āśrama*), it has been stated that the Dharma—consisting of the conquest of the senses, the abandonment of passion and hatred, the granting of fearlessness to living beings, detachment from worldly existence, meditation, and so forth—is the cause for attaining immortality through the realization of the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Soul (*para*). In this Dharma, the fourth stage of life alone is not the sole cause; for even when performed by those residing in other stages of life, that Dharma certainly exists. Therefore, anyone engaged in this Dharma must not practice toward other living beings that which is unwholesome or a cause of suffering for oneself. By this, the quality of being a source of fearlessness toward all beings is expressed, and this is intended as an illustration. Consequently, the very means for attaining immortality, such as the restraint of the senses and so forth, must be practiced by one who has entered upon that Dharma. (Manu)
One may practice the Dharma according to one's stage of life, dwelling in whichever āśrama one resides;
being equal toward all beings, the external mark is not the cause of Dharma.
Atri says:
Thus, one who knows the twenty principles, regardless of which stage of life he may dwell in, is liberated when he is equal toward all beings; of this there is no doubt.
And he himself stated those principles:
"A wise person should recognize these five as the great elements (mahābhūta): earth, water, fire, air, and space."
One should know that the ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth—
these five are the organs of perception within this body.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—
the wise person should always understand these five as the objects of the senses.
The two hands, the two feet, the generative organ, the tongue, and likewise the anus—
these are the five organs of action that are always present in this body.
The mind, the intellect, as well as the self and the unmanifest—
these four are indeed said here to be superior to the senses.
These twenty-four principles have indeed been described;
likewise, the self is the non-dual Puruṣa, the twenty-fifth.
Likewise: "Those who contemplate the senses remain here for ten Manvantaras;
those who contemplate the elements remain for a full hundred, and those who contemplate through inference for a thousand."
Ten thousand high-souled ones remain free from fever;
however, those who contemplate the Unmanifest remain for a full hundred thousand years.
Having attained the Person who is devoid of qualities, no further enumeration exists.
He states the completeness of that dharma which has been declared as the means to liberation across all stages of life:
"Truthfulness, non-stealing, freedom from anger, modesty, purity, wisdom, fortitude, self-restraint, control of the senses, and knowledge—this is proclaimed as the universal dharma. (3.65)

Truthfulness is speaking according to the facts. Non-stealing is the absence of theft. Absence of anger is the avoidance of anger even when there is a cause for it. Modesty is shame regarding engagement in what is unjust. Purity is the purification of one's disposition, body, and wealth. Intelligence is the discrimination between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. Fortitude is the steadying of the mind—which might otherwise waver toward what should not be done—by means of directing it toward purity. Self-restraint is the taming of the mind through austerities (*kṛcchra*) and other such means. Control of the senses is the subjugation of the sense organs. Knowledge is self-realization. This entire collection of categories beginning with truthfulness is declared to be *dharma* in its entirety. Furthermore, this is stated as a duty common to all stages of life (*āśrama*), beginning with that of the student (*brahmacārin*), for those desiring liberation; it is not intended to subvert the specific duties of particular castes and stages of life, as there is no contradiction between them. (Manu).
Contentment, forgiveness, self-restraint, non-stealing, purity, control of the senses, wisdom, learning, truthfulness, and freedom from anger— this tenfold set is the characteristic of dharma.
Those twice-born who study the Dharma consisting of ten characteristics, and having studied it, live according to it, they go to the supreme goal. [3.65]

The claim that the individual soul (*jīva*), established in identity with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), is an object of perception (*dṛśya*) is untenable. To explain: if there is non-difference (*abheda*) between the individual soul and the Supreme, how can that very same entity be both the perceived and the perceiver? It is not possible for a single thing to stand in the relationship of agent and object within a single action. If, on the other hand, there is difference (*bheda*), how can it be seen through non-difference? To this, he says:
"Just as sparks fly out from a heated mass of iron, even so do individual selves indeed emerge from the Self. (3.66)

Just as sparks—tiny particles of fire—issue forth from a heated iron ball that is glowing red, and are perceived as distinct both from that mass of iron and from one another, even so do the individual selves (jīvas) emanate from the Supreme Self (paramātman). In the word *ātmanaḥ*, the ablative case is prescribed by the grammatical rule *bhuvaḥ prabhavaḥ* ("the fifth [case ending is used for the source of origin of a thing]"), as in the expression "the Gaṅgā originates from the Himālayas. Thus, the meaning is this: the individual selves emanate—that is, they manifest—from the Supreme Self; and because the Supreme Self is the cause of their manifestation, it is established by scripture (*śruti*) that "by His light all this shines. The particle *hi* indicates what is well-known. Indeed, this is well-established through scripture, and the scripture is this: "As tiny sparks fly out from a fire, even so from this Self all vital breaths (*prāṇas*), all worlds, all gods, and all beings fly out. The meaning of this is as follows: although there is no difference between the fire existing as a spark and the fire existing in the iron ball insofar as they are both fire, yet due to the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the iron ball and its parts, there arise the cognition and the conventional usage of difference. Similarly, the distinction among the individual selves arises from the difference in the limiting adjuncts consisting of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), while from the perspective of their own nature, there is indeed non-difference, just like fire. Therefore, the relationship of meditator and object of meditation is based on the difference caused by limiting adjuncts, whereas the vision of unity refers to the natural non-difference; thus, there is no contradiction. (3.66)

Now, if the individual soul (*jīva*) is non-different from the Supreme, then how is it that he performs desirable and prohibited actions, as well as actions that bind him and serve as causes for his bondage? To this, the author replies:
"In that regard, the self indeed performs some action by itself, some through its own nature, and some through habituation—[all] resting upon both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). (3.67)

In this regard, since the Supreme Self itself, when conditioned, exists in the state of the individual soul (*jīva*), that Self having attained the state of a *jīva* effects, by its own nature, certain acts of indifference consisting of withdrawal, while performing others, such as sacrifice and the like. Its "own nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to the state of possessing a body acquired through its own past actions; for specific acts such as sacrifice, which reside in the mind, have the Self as their agent. Nor should it be asked: "How can one be the agent of an action belonging to another? For we observe and understand from common usage and cognition that "one goes by chariot" or "one goes by horse. Even though the act of going inheres in the chariot and the horse, the owner of the chariot and the rider of the horse are considered the agents. In that case, the chariot and the horse possess only the status of instruments (*karaṇa*), as indicated by the use of the instrumental case, not the status of agents. By this, it is said that the chariot and so forth possess only the status of an instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*), not independent agency (*svatantra-kartṛtva*). Therefore, it is logical that the Self possesses independent agency over actions residing in the intellect, the body, and the senses. If the agency of selves is thus established, how is it that some among them perform virtuous deeds (*dharma*) while others perform non-virtuous deeds (*adharma*)? He provides the answer: "Some [acts arise] from habituation" (*kiṃcid abhyāsāt*). Indeed, he who has practiced certain actions in previous births performs those same virtuous deeds in subsequent existences. Likewise, some perform non-virtue. Consequently, by the force of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), one performs only a particular kind of action—just as someone is inclined toward giving, someone toward study, and someone toward austerity; similarly, someone toward slander, someone toward violence, and someone toward harshness. Thus, even for the omniscient Self, agency with respect to optional or prohibited actions is possible due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*) caused by connection with beginningless limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). (3.67)

If the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para) is innate, then the attributes of the Supreme Self—such as being the cause of the world, immutability, and omniscience—must also exist in the individual soul. If so, how can it be said that "this one was born"? To this he says: "The Imperishable (akṣara), the agent, the knower, Brahman, the possessor of qualities, the controller, the unborn—because of the assumption of a body, He is proclaimed as 'born'. (3.68)

Although he is unborn (*aja*) by nature, being devoid of birth, nevertheless, because he assumes a body that possesses birth—accepting it as an adjunct (*upādhi*)—he is said to be "born" in the form conditioned by that adjunct. Since his state of being unborn is the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the fact that he is the cause is presented as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). He is fixed as the cause, the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), because there is no distinction; he is the cause of the entire range of effects, therefore he is unborn. Nor should it be said that, like *tattva* and other such things, he is the cause of the world merely because the world is an effect. For he is imperishable (*akṣara*), meaning he does not undergo the dissolution of parts due to his partlessness. Now, one might object: even for a cause that is partless, destruction is observed in the case of action (*karman*) and qualities (*guṇa*); so how can he be called imperishable? To this it is said: "He is the agent" (*kartā*). An agent is independent (*svatantra*). Thus, he is distinct from qualities and actions, which are dependent on something else. And the independence of the agent implies his partlessness and eternity. To refute the Sāṃkhya position that the unmanifest (*avyakta*) alone is the creator of the world and not the Self (*ātman*), it is said: "He is the Knower" (*boddhā*). The world, endowed with the arrangement of various enjoyers, the bodies of enjoyment, and the instruments of enjoyment, could not have been created by the unmanifest had it first deliberated upon it, because the unmanifest is insentient. The Supreme Self, however, can bring the entire range of effects into play like a pure myrobalan fruit held in the palm of a clean hand; thus his agency is logical. Nor should it be asked: "How can the Self be the creator of the world, which is so vastly extended? For he is Brahman, meaning he is great (*bṛhat*) to the end. Nor should it be argued: "How can the solitary Supreme Self, who is distinct in both essence and assistance, produce an effect that is so different? Because he is possessed of qualities (*guṇin*); here "quality" (*guṇa*) refers to power (*śakti*). And since this is understood in every way without distinction, his skill in fashioning diverse effects is appropriate due to his possession of all kinds of powers. Now, one might say: even if he possesses all powers, when performing an action, he would be an agent only by depending on a collection of auxiliary causes such as tools and materials, like a potter; he cannot be non-dual. Furthermore, prior to the creation of the world, he was not accompanied by anything else; therefore, his agency is untenable. The answer to this is: "The Master" (*vaśī*).
