"Master" means self-willed, that is to say, not dependent on others. The intention is this: his status as the creator of the world is not accessible through inference, as it is sublated by reasoning. Rather, it is known solely through scripture (*śāstra*), and scripture—such as "From this very Self, space was produced"—declares that the solitary Supreme Self alone brings about all effects. And the contradiction of such a scriptural statement with reasoning is simply not to be resolved by those who possess the practice of the *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā* (Vedānta). 3.68.

Along with an illustration, he also explains the manner in which the body is assumed: "Just as at the beginning of creation He creates space, air, fire, water, and earth, each possessing one additional quality, so too does He assume [them] when coming into existence. (3.69)

Just as at the beginning of the creation of the world, the Supreme Self creates objects such as space and the rest, each possessing one more quality than the preceding; wherein space has sound as its single quality, and that [sound] along with touch belong to air, those two along with form belong to fire, those three along with taste belong to water, and smell is the fifth belonging to earth—thus there is an increase of one quality for each starting from space; in the same manner that He produces them, so you, being born, take up those very elements, space and the rest, as the constituent causes of the body. (3.69)
He states the manner of accepting [the elements] such as space:
"The sun is nourished by the oblation; from that comes rain, then the plants;
that food, in the form of sap, attains the state of semen. (3.70)
When there is union between a woman and a man and the semen and blood are pure, the Lord, himself the sixth, simultaneously takes up the five elements. (3.71)

[976] The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a heap of filth; the person who is like a jewel casket; the person who is like a blue lotus; and the person who is like a white lotus. And how, monks, is one a person like a heap of filth? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a noble family, a family of high birth, with great wealth, abundant grain, many possessions, and vast property. Yet he is ugly, unsightly, and ill-favored; he has a foul complexion, is deformed, and is afflicted by disease. He is short-lived, often ill, and weak. He is dull-witted, slow in understanding, and lacks intelligence. Such a person, monks, is called ‘one like a heap of filth. And how, monks, is one a person like a jewel casket? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a noble family, a family of high birth, with great wealth, abundant grain, many possessions, and vast property. He is handsome, beautiful, and well-favored; he has a fair complexion, is well-formed, and is free from disease. He is long-lived, rarely ill, and strong. He is wise, quick in understanding, and possesses intelligence. Such a person, monks, is called ‘one like a jewel casket. And how, monks, is one a person like a blue lotus? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a noble family, a family of high birth, with great wealth, abundant grain, many possessions, and vast property. He is handsome, beautiful, and well-favored; he has a fair complexion, is well-formed, and is free from disease. He is long-lived, rarely ill, and strong. He is wise, quick in understanding, and possesses intelligence. Yet he dwells secluded, aloof from the crowd, delighting in solitude, finding joy in seclusion, and taking pleasure in seclusion. Such a person, monks, is called ‘one like a blue lotus. And how, monks, is one a person like a white lotus? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a noble family, a family of high birth, with great wealth, abundant grain, many possessions, and vast property. He is handsome, beautiful, and well-favored; he has a fair complexion, is well-formed, and is free from disease. He is long-lived, rarely ill, and strong. He is wise, quick in understanding, and possesses intelligence. He dwells secluded, aloof from the crowd, delighting in solitude, finding joy in seclusion, and taking pleasure in seclusion. Furthermore, he attains the four meditative absorptions (dhyāna), which belong to the realm of form and are produced by detachment, being peaceful and sublime. Such a person, monks, is called ‘one like a white lotus. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [976] The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Well-Gone One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: “Friends, the Blessed One has just risen from his seat and entered his dwelling after speaking these words: ‘Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world…’” [The monks asked: “What, friend Ānanda, is the purpose, what is the benefit of the Blessed One’s having spoken thus? [Ānanda replied: “Friends, the Blessed One, knowing the purpose, knowing the benefit, spoke thus: ‘Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a heap of filth; the person who is like a jewel casket; the person who is like a blue lotus; and the person who is like a white lotus. And how, monks, is one a person like a heap of filth? … [as above] … ‘These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The monks asked: “But what, friend Ānanda, is the purpose, what is the benefit of the Blessed One’s having spoken thus? By means of the oblation consisting of food, dung, and so forth, when performed according to the prescribed rule, the Sun is nourished and made full with essence (*rasa*). From that solar orb comes rain; from rain, the plants such as rice and other grains—here the singular number is used in the sense of the genus. The food related to those plants, such as cooked rice, when consumed by a man and a woman, undergoes a series of transformations into essence, blood, and so on, until it attains the state of semen and ovum within the bodies of the man and woman. Then, at the time of their union during the fertile period, that pure semen and blood—which are unimpaired by wind, bile, and other humors—are brought together and attain unity. Within that [mixture], the Self (*ātman*), being the sixth, spontaneously takes up for the sake of the body those five elements beginning with ether simultaneously and at one and the same time. The mention of "the sixth" is intended to indicate that the Self is also denoted by the word "element" (*dhātu*); it is the Lord, the Master of the world. And its lordship over that [body] is due to its being a portion of the Supreme Self. This has been stated by the Blessed Lord in the *Gītā*:
"A portion of My very self, eternal, becomes a living soul in the world of the living. (3.70, 71)
Moreover: "The sense organs, mind, vital breath, knowledge, lifespan, happiness, fortitude, retention, impulse, suffering, desire, and even egoism [are the effects of the unmanifest]. (3.72)
Effort, form, color, likes and dislikes, existence and non-existence—all this is born of the Self for him who desires a beginning for that which is beginningless. (3.73)

For that *jīva*, who is the *anādi* (beginningless) [self] desiring a body and so forth, there arise the sense organs and other faculties born of the self, because they are produced by the *dharma* and *adharma* acquired by the self. The "sense organs" (*indriya*) are the external instruments to be described hereafter. The "mind" (*manas*) is the internal instrument. "Vital breath" (*prāṇa*) is the bodily wind characterized by five functions. "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) is cognition. "Life-span" (*āyus*) is the maintenance of the vital breaths. "Happiness" (*sukha*) is joy. "Fortitude" (*dhṛti*) is the steadiness of the body and senses. "Retention" (*dhāraṇā*) is the power of memory. "Impulsion" (*preraṇa*) is the instigation of the sense organs. "Suffering" (*duḥkha*) is pain. "Desire" (*icchā*) is passion. "Egoism" (*ahaṃkāra*) is self-conceit. "Effort" (*prayatna*) is exertion. "Form" (*ākṛti*) is genus, or rather, the specific configuration of the limbs of the body, such as being an elephant, a human, or an animal. "Color" (*varṇa*) is caste, such as Brahminhood, or physical complexion, such as fairness. "Voice" (*svara*) is sound. "Hatred" (*dveṣa*) is aversion. "Existence and non-existence" (*bhavābhāvau*) refer to prosperity and its opposite. (3.72, 73)
He describes the process by which even a very small amount of semen and blood initiates a great effect:
"In the first month, the element becomes moistened and coagulated;
in the second month, it becomes an *arbuda*; but in the third month, it is endowed with limbs and sense organs. (3.74)

[977] The Blessed One said this: “Ānanda, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who is a victim of both cold and heat; the person who is a victim of cold but not of heat; the person who is a victim of heat but not of cold; and the person who is a victim of neither cold nor heat. Ānanda, what kind of person is a victim of both cold and heat? Here, Ānanda, a certain person is one who has committed many evil deeds and performed many unwholesome actions. Having died and passed away from that state, he is reborn among humans. There, he experiences the ripening of those very same deeds as a result of his own misconduct. He is afflicted by both cold and heat, and he undergoes intense, sharp, and piercing suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the person who is a victim of both cold and heat. “Ānanda, what kind of person is a victim of cold but not of heat? Here, Ānanda, a certain person is one who has committed few evil deeds and performed few unwholesome actions. Having died and passed away from that state, he is reborn among humans. There, he experiences the ripening of those very same deeds as a result of his own misconduct. He is afflicted by cold, but he does not experience heat. This, Ānanda, is called the person who is a victim of cold but not of heat. “Ānanda, what kind of person is a victim of heat but not of cold? Here, Ānanda, a certain person is one who has committed many evil deeds and performed many unwholesome actions. Having died and passed away from that state, he is reborn among humans. There, he experiences the ripening of those very same deeds as a result of his own misconduct. He is afflicted by heat, but he does not experience cold. This, Ānanda, is called the person who is a victim of heat but not of cold. “Ānanda, what kind of person is a victim of neither cold nor heat? Here, Ānanda, a certain person is one who has committed few evil deeds and performed few unwholesome actions. Having died and passed away from that state, he is reborn among humans. There, he experiences the ripening of those very same deeds as a result of his own misconduct. He is afflicted by neither cold nor heat, and he does not undergo intense, sharp, or piercing suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the person who is a victim of neither cold nor heat. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Gone One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: “Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling after saying: ‘Ānanda, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world…’” When this was said, the Venerable Udāyin asked the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, when the Blessed One said, ‘There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world,’ what did he mean? “Friend Udāyin, the Blessed One said this with reference to the four stages of meditation (dhyāna). Friend, the first stage of meditation is like the person who is a victim of both cold and heat. Why is that? Because, friend, in the first stage of meditation, there is the application of thought and sustained thought, which are like heat; and there is the arising of the five hindrances, which are like cold. Therefore, friend, the first stage of meditation is like the person who is a victim of both cold and heat. “The second stage of meditation is like the person who is a victim of cold but not of heat. Why is that? Because, friend, in the second stage of meditation, there is no application of thought or sustained thought, which are like heat; but there is still the arising of the five hindrances, which are like cold. Therefore, friend, the second stage of meditation is like the person who is a victim of cold but not of heat. “The third stage of meditation is like the person who is a victim of heat but not of cold. Why is that? Because, friend, in the third stage of meditation, there is the arising of the joy and bliss born of concentration, which are like heat; but there is no longer the arising of the five hindrances, which are like cold. Therefore, friend, the third stage of meditation is like the person who is a victim of heat but not of cold. “The fourth stage of meditation is like the person who is a victim of neither cold nor heat. Why is that? Because, friend, in the fourth stage of meditation, there is neither the application of thought nor sustained thought, which are like heat; nor is there the arising of the five hindrances, which are like cold. Therefore, friend, the fourth stage of meditation is like the person who is a victim of neither cold nor heat. It was with reference to these four stages of meditation that the Blessed One said: ‘There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. When this was said, the Venerable Udāyin asked the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, how many kinds of persons are there who, having been reborn here, go to heaven? “Friend Udāyin, there are four kinds of persons who, having been reborn here, go to heaven. What four? They are: the person who is a victim of both cold and heat; the person who is a victim of cold but not of heat; the person who is a victim of heat but not of cold; and the person who is a victim of neither cold nor heat. Friend, how is it that a person who is a victim of both cold and heat goes to heaven? Here, friend, a certain person is one who has committed many evil deeds and performed many unwholesome actions. Having died and passed away from that state, he is reborn among humans. There, he experiences the ripening of those very same deeds as a result of his own misconduct. Having exhausted that karma, he passes away from the human state and is reborn in a heavenly realm. There, he experiences the ripening of those very same deeds as a result of his own wholesome conduct. This, friend, is called the person who is a victim of both cold and heat who goes to heaven. “Friend, how is it that a person who is a victim of cold but not of heat goes to heaven? Here, friend, a certain person is one who has committed few evil deeds and performed few unwholesome actions. Having died and passed away from that state, he is reborn among humans. There, he experiences the ripening of those very same deeds as a result of his own misconduct. Having exhausted that karma, he passes away from the human state and is reborn in a heavenly realm. There, he experiences the ripening of those very same deeds as a result of his own wholesome conduct. This, friend, is called the person who is a victim of cold but not of heat who goes to heaven. “Friend, how is it that a person who is a victim of heat but not of cold goes to heaven? Here, friend, a certain person is one who has committed many evil deeds and performed many unwholesome actions. Having died and passed away from that state, he is reborn among humans. There, he experiences the ripening of those very same deeds as a result of his own misconduct. Having exhausted that karma, he passes away from the human state and is reborn in a heavenly realm. There, he experiences the ripening of those very same deeds as a result of his own wholesome conduct. This, friend, is called the person who is a victim of heat but not of cold who goes to heaven. “Friend, how is it that a person who is a victim of neither cold nor heat goes to heaven? Here, friend, a certain person is one who has committed few evil deeds and performed few unwholesome actions. Having died and passed away from that state, he is reborn among humans. There, he experiences the ripening of those very same deeds as a result of his own misconduct. Having exhausted that karma, he passes away from the human state and is reborn in a heavenly realm. There, he experiences the ripening of those very same deeds as a result of his own wholesome conduct. This, friend, is called the person who is a victim of neither cold nor heat who goes to heaven. These, friend, are the four kinds of persons who, having been reborn here, go to heaven. When this was said, the Venerable Udāyin asked the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, how many kinds of persons are there who, having been reborn here, fall into hell? “Friend Udāyin, there are four kinds of persons who, having been reborn here, fall into hell. What four? They are: the person who is a victim of both cold and heat; the person who is a victim of cold but not of heat; the person who is a victim of heat but not of cold; and the person who is a victim of neither cold nor heat. The aforementioned element, consisting of the five gross elements (*pañcabhūtātmaka*), in the first month of gestation, having become a state of moisture, abandons its extreme fluidity and becomes intent on reaching a solid state, like milk mixed with an acidic substance. In the second month, however, that semen and blood (*śukra-śoṇita*) becomes an *arbuda*; the meaning is that it increases. An *arbuda* is a specific type of disease characterized by increased flesh; the meaning here is that [the embryo] becomes similar to that. In the third month, it becomes endowed with limbs beginning with the head, with sense organs—the seats of the senses such as the ears, eyes, and nose—and with the tongue, hands, and so forth. The meaning is that the process begins for the arrangement of even more subtle constituent parts conducive to the production of the limbs and sense organs. (3.74)
In the third [chapter], he states another internal function pertaining to the month:
"From space [come] lightness, subtlety, sound, the power of hearing, and so forth;
from wind, however, touch, movement, expansion, and even roughness. (3.75)
From bile (pitta), however, come vision, digestion, heat, color, and clarity;
from the tastes (rasas) come tasting, coolness, unctuousness, moisture, and softness. (3.76)
Then, during the third pulsation, the unborn Self perceives the smell of the earth, as well as the sense of smell, heaviness, and form. (3.77)

Lightness is the absence of heaviness. Subtlety is the non-obstruction of the outward exit of sweat and other secretions from within the body. The capacity for the production of sound when there is articulation and so forth. The ear is the sense organ of hearing. Strength is capability. By the word "etcetera," the inclusion of the cavities of the intestines (*antra*) and so forth is intended. All of this the Self (*ātman*) acquires in the third month while the unborn one is being born in the body. Likewise, from air (*vāyu*), it acquires touch, the sense organ of the skin, movement, pulsation, expansion, the separation of limbs, dryness, and roughness of touch. From bile (*pitta*), which is fire (*tejas*), it acquires sight, the sense organ of the eye, digestion—the transformation of what has been eaten—heat, the color of the constituent elements such as fairness and so forth, luminosity, and brilliance. From the fluids (*rasa*), which are water, it acquires the tongue, the sense organ that perceives taste, coolness in the limbs, unctuousness (*sneha*), the absence of dryness, and moisture (*kleda*). From earth, however, it acquires smell, the sense organ of the nose which grasps odor, heaviness—the state of having weight—and solidity (*mūrti*). Having acquired all this in the third month, the Self vibrates in the fourth month; the meaning is that it causes the limbs to tremble. On this point, the *Garbhopaniṣad* states: "From space [come] sound, the ear, distinctness, and the collection of all apertures. Likewise, heroism, indignation, sharpness, digestion, heat, brilliance, burning, color, form, and the sense organs are products of fire (*taijasa*). (3.75, 76, 77)
[978] He states what must be done for the protection of the fetus during the fourth month:
"By not granting the longings of pregnancy (dohada), the fetus may incur harm."
Or even deformity or death; therefore, one should do what is pleasing to a woman. (3.78)

A "dohada" is an object desired by a pregnant woman; by not granting it, defects may arise for the fetus, such as disease, deformity, physical disability, or even death. For this reason, what is dear to the woman must be done; that is to say, her pregnancy-longing (dohada) must be fulfilled. || 3.78 ||
Moreover:
In the fourth month there is the stabilization of the limbs; in the fifth, the production of blood; and in the sixth, the emergence of strength, complexion, nails, and body hair. (3.79)

In the fourth month of gestation, the firmness of the fetal limbs, beginning with the head, occurs. In the fifth, however, there is the emergence of blood—that is, the production of the blood. It should be understood that in the sixth month, the development of strength, complexion, nails, and body hair takes place. (3.79)
Moreover:
Endowed with mind and consciousness, joined with channels, sinews, and veins, in the seventh or even the eighth month, he also possesses skin, flesh, and memory. (3.80)

In the seventh month, this embryo becomes endowed with the mind (*manas*), the internal organ which is consciousness that illumines objects; with the channels (*nāḍīs*), such as the arteries (*dhamanīs*) and so forth; with the sinews (*snāyus*), which bind the bones; and with the vessels (*śirās*), which are like ropes and serve as the binding supports for the entire body. It should be understood that in the eighth month, it becomes possessed of skin, flesh, and memory (*smṛti*). (3.80)
Moreover:
his vital energy (ojas) flows away again toward the womb and again toward the nurse;
therefore, the fetus born in the eighth month is deprived of life. || 3.81 ||

In the eighth month of gestation, the vital energy (*ojas*), which is the cause of life, flows toward the mother, the umbilical cord, the nourishing sustenance, and the embryo. For this very reason, a living being born in the eighth month does not live for long. (3.81)
In the ninth or tenth month, by powerful birth-pangs,
he is expelled like an arrow through the opening of a machine, accompanied by feverish distress.

[979] In the ninth or tenth month, by means of powerful and even more potent winds that cause birth, the being is expelled and impelled through the vaginal opening as if through the aperture of a machine, like an arrow, lacking autonomy. At that stage, the creature born becomes feverish due to the intensity of unsurpassed suffering. 3.82.
Now he defines the body:
its sixfold bodies maintain the six layers of skin; likewise, there are six limbs and three hundred and sixty bones. (3.83)

The bodies of that living being (*jīva*) are of six kinds: viviparous, oviparous, sweat-born, soil-born, daily-renewed, and pertaining to hellish torment. All six of these possess skin. The mention of "six" again is to indicate that while skin alone is constant across all six, other features such as the "six-limbedness" (*ṣaḍaṅgatva*) and so forth, which will be described later, are not constant; for egg-born, sweat-born, and soil-born beings lack the state of having six limbs and the rest. By the phrase "having six limbs" and so on, he specifically defines the human body. Therefore, he will say: [as follows].

"Thus, this body is unstable; he who acts for the sake of liberation [from it]," so it is said. The six limbs are the head, the two hands, the two feet, and the middle trunk. Furthermore, the human body maintains three hundred and sixty bones; although the word for "bones" (*asthīni*) is plural, it should be understood here in the singular by virtue of its connection with the word *varṣma* (body). 3.83.
In order to establish the aforementioned number of bones, he says:
"Together with the sockets, there are sixty-four teeth; the nails are twenty;
and the digits of the hands and feet—these constitute four locations for them. (3.84)

There are thirty-two teeth. There are exactly thirty-two bones for them called *sthāla*. Thus, the teeth together with the *sthālas* amount to sixty-four. The reading *sthālaiḥ* is for the sake of clarity, meaning "together with the *sthāla*-bones. There are twenty nails. And there are four bones that serve as the location for those [nail] pegs. Thus, there are one hundred and eight bones. (3.84)
There are sixty bones in the fingers; two in the heels and four in the ankles; four bones in the forearms, and exactly as many in the shanks. (3.85)

In each finger there are three bones; thus, all the fingers together have sixty bones. The two rear parts of the feet are the heels (*pārṣṇī*); they have two bones. The joint regions of the shanks and heels are situated internally and externally. In one foot there are two ankles; thus, for both feet, there are four bones in the ankles. [980] *Aratnika* means the same as *aratni*. Although the word *aratni* refers specifically to the end of the forearm, it is used here to denote the entire hand in order to complete the count of four bones. Thus, there are four bones of the *aratnika*. The word *jaṅghā* here also denotes the whole foot. Consequently, there are likewise four bones in the two shanks. These seventy-four, together with the previous eight hundred, total one hundred and eighty-two. (3.85)
Furthermore:
One should designate two each arising from the knees, the cheeks, the thighs, and the shoulder-blades, as well as the two eye-sockets, the two palate-bones, and the two hip-bones. (3.86)

The knees are the joints of the shanks and thighs. The cheeks are the *gallau*. The thighs are the *sakthinī*, and they are shaped like planks. The shoulders are the roots of the arms. Likewise—the *akṣatālūṣake* are the bones at the corners of the eyes; the *śroṇīphalake* are the two distinct middle regions of the shanks. For each of these locations, there are two bones respectively. With this enumeration, the total is one hundred and ninety-four. 3.86.
Furthermore: there is one bone in the pelvis, likewise forty-five in the back;
the neck has fifteen bones, and likewise the collarbone is one, as is the jaw. (3.87)

The hip bone and the bone of the generative organ are one. There are forty-five in the back. There are fifteen in the neck. There is one at the joint of the collarbones and the shoulders. The chin is also a single bone. Thus, these sixty-three, together with the previous count, amount to two hundred and fifty-seven. 3.87.
Furthermore:
At its base are two [bones], the forehead, the eyes, and the cheeks; the nose consists of solid bone; and there are seventy-two ribs together with their sockets and tubercles. (3.88)

At its base are two bones at the jaw-root; likewise, there is one bone of the forehead, two of the eye-sockets, and two of the cheeks—the cheeks being the regions between the temples and the eyes. The nose is to be understood as consisting of the bone known as the *ghoṇa*. Thus, this [nasal] bone is one; the ribs (*pārśvakā*) are seventy-two, together with the *sthālaka* and *arbuda*-named bones. Together with the previous eight, they total eighty. Together with the previous count, they amount to three hundred and thirty-seven. (3.88)
Furthermore:
"There are two temples, four skull-bones, and likewise seventeen bones of the chest; such is the collection of bones in a person. (3.89)

The two bones named *śaṅkhaka*, located in the region between the eyebrows and the ears, are related to the head and are shaped like skull-bones; there are four of them. As for the Vedic statement, "The head indeed consists of nine skull-bones," there the word "head" (*śiras*) refers to the head including the face; here, however, it refers to the head excluding the face, and thus there is no contradiction. The chest (*uras*) or breast has seventeen; likewise, the [bones] of the back are twenty-three, which, when added to the previous count, makes three hundred and sixty. Such is the summary of the number of bones in the body of a human being, the body of a man. [3.89]

Having examined the body, the sense organs must be examined, because they are dependent upon the body. Since these organs are beyond the reach of the senses themselves, they are to be postulated on the strength of the experience of smell and so forth, which follows the presence and absence of the nose and other parts. Therefore, by way of defining their respective objects, he mentions the organs of knowledge—smell and the rest—as being indicated by the terms "nose" and so forth:
Smell, form, taste, touch, and sound are known as the objects;
the nose, eyes, tongue, skin, and ear are the sense organs. (3.90)

The essential meaning is that the objects—smell and so forth—and the sense organs which apprehend them, having their respective bases in the nose and so on, are to be understood as five. Furthermore, by the use of the term "object" (*viṣaya*), it is implied that smell and the others possess a fixed status as things to be grasped. For the word "object" is employed in the sense of being exclusive to something else; therefore, that base of the nose which brings about the direct perception of smell alone is one sense organ. Thus, the word *ghrāṇa* (nose) is etymologically meaningful according to the derivation: "that by which one smells. Similarly, among the qualities (*guṇas*), the locus of the eye is another sense organ, the cause for the direct perception of form (*rūpa*) alone. The word *cakṣus* (eye) is used there according to the derivation: "that by which one sees. Likewise, the tongue-base, which is the specific cause for each [perception] of taste, is the gustatory sense organ (*rasanendriya*), distinct from the other organs. In the same way, the skin-base, which is the cause for the apprehension of touch alone, is the tactile sense organ (*sparśana*). And similarly, the ear is that which apprehends sound alone. (3.90)

In an embodied being who has been born, the organs of knowledge function first, and thereafter the organs of action; thus he speaks of the organs of action after the organs of knowledge: "Know that the two hands, the anus, the generative organ, the tongue, and the two feet are the five organs of action, and the mind is of the nature of both. (3.91)

The five organs of action (*karmendriya*) are so designated because they are conceived as the means for the accomplishment of action, having the hands as their primary locus. Among these, the single organ denoted by the word "hand" is the hand-locus itself, which is the cause of the specific action characterized by grasping. Another, however, is to be inferred from its function of discharging urine and feces; it is the anus-locus, characterized by that term. The third is the organ denoted by the word "organ of generation" (*upastha*), which refers to the generative seat; it is characterized by the word *upastha* itself as the instrument for producing a particular kind of bliss, indicated by the discharge of semen and blood. Furthermore, the two feet are characterized as the organ whose function is the action of locomotion. The organ characterized by the word "tongue" is the instrument of speech, because its locus is the tongue. The action consisting of opening and closing the eyes does not establish a distinct organ, as it is accomplished by the vital air (*vāyu*) alone; for such an action is observed in trees and leaves to be produced by the wind. And the mind (*manas*) is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which partakes of the nature of both the organs of cognition and the organs of action. O sages, know this: when the mind is directed toward another object, neither the sense of smell and the rest, nor the hands and the rest, are capable of performing their own respective functions. Thus says Manu: [Manu 2.90–91] "The ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth—these are the organs of perception (*buddhīndriya*). The hands, the feet, the anus, the organ of generation, and the tongue as the fifth—these are the organs of action (*karmendriya*). That which is called the 'mind' (*manas*) is said to be the eleventh; it is the ruler over all of them, and it is both a sense of perception and an organ of action. [Manu 2.97] "When the mind is elsewhere, these senses do not perceive their respective objects; therefore, the mind is the eleventh, and it is called the 'inner sense' (*antahkaraṇa*). [Manu 2.98] "The ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth—these are the organs of perception; the hands, the feet, the anus, the organ of generation, and the tongue as the fifth—these are the organs of action. [Manu 2.99] "That which is called the 'mind' (*manas*) is said to be the eleventh; it is the ruler over all of them, and it is both a sense of perception and an organ of action. [Manu 2.100] "When the mind is elsewhere, these senses do not perceive their respective objects; therefore, the mind is the eleventh, and it is called the 'inner sense' (*antahkaraṇa*). [Manu 2.101] "The ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth—these are the organs of perception; the hands, the feet, the anus, the organ of generation, and the tongue as the fifth—these are the organs of action. [Manu 2.102] "That which is called the 'mind' (*manas*) is said to be the eleventh; it is the ruler over all of them, and it is both a sense of perception and an organ of action. [Manu 2.103] "When the mind is elsewhere, these senses do not perceive their respective objects; therefore, the mind is the eleventh, and it is called the 'inner sense' (*antahkaraṇa*). [Manu 2.104] "The ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth—these are the organs of perception; the hands, the feet, the anus, the organ of generation, and the tongue as the fifth—these are the organs of action. [Manu 2.105] "That which is called the 'mind' (*manas*) is said to be the eleventh; it is the ruler over all of them, and it is both a sense of perception and an organ of action. [Manu 2.106] "When the mind is elsewhere, these senses do not perceive their respective objects; therefore, the mind is the eleventh, and it is called the 'inner sense' (*antahkaraṇa*). [Manu 2.107] "The ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth—these are the organs of perception; the hands, the feet, the anus, the organ of generation, and the tongue as the fifth—these are the organs of action. [Manu 2.123] "That which is called the 'mind' (*manas*) is said to be the eleventh; it is the ruler over all of them, and it is both a sense
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth;
the anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and speech is recorded as the tenth.
The five organs of knowledge are the ear and so forth in their proper order;
the five organs of action are said to be the anus and so forth.
The eleventh, the mind, should be known as being of a dual nature by virtue of its own quality;
when it is conquered, these two groups of five [the senses] become conquered. (3.91)
The seats of the sense organs have been described; now, for the sake of explaining the origin of the fivefold vital air (prāṇa) within the body, he says:
"The navel, the ojas, the anus, the semen, the blood, the two temples, as well as the head, the throat, and the heart—these are indeed the seats of the prāṇa. (3.92)

The navel and other such locations are the abodes or seats of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); expanding within these, the *prāṇa* performs its own functions. Therefore, in order to bring it under control, one should fix [the mind] upon these places. That which is called "vigor" (*ojas*) is a certain substance residing within the heart-lotus; the rest is well known. (3.92)
By means of detailed elaboration, he states the internal organs of the belly:
the omentum, the pericardium, the navel, the lungs, the liver, the spleen, the small intestine, the kidneys, the bladder, and the receptacle of feces. (3.93)
The stomach, the heart, the large intestine, the anus, and the two upper anal folds—this is described as the detailed enumeration of the visceral cavities (koṣṭha). || 3.94 ||

The group beginning with *vapā* (omentum) is cited as the group of organs (*arthagaṇa*) by way of the expansion of the seats of the vital breaths (*prāṇāyatana*). *Vapā* and *vasā* (fat) are well known. *Avahanana* is what is called *puppha-sa* by the common people. *Kloman* is the spleen, as is well known among those versed in sacrifice. *Yakṛt*, *plīhan*, and *vasti* are well known in Āyurveda. *Purīṣādhāna* is the large intestine (*pakvāśaya*). *Apakvasthāna* is the stomach (*āmāśaya*). The two circles situated internally beyond the external anal circle are the "upper anus" (*uttarau gudau*). This has been stated as the internal abdominal expansion. (3.93, 94)
Now he describes the entire body in detail:
the two pupils, the two eye-sockets, the two temples, the two earlobes, the two ears, the two temporal bones, the two eyebrows, the two gums, the two lips, and the two hollows of the loins. (3.95)
The groins, the testicles, the kidneys, the two masses of phlegm, the breasts, the uvula, the buttocks, the arms, and the calves, thighs, and shanks. (3.96)
The palm of the abdomen, the top of the bladder, the chin, the two tonsils, and the nape of the neck—these are the locations here in this body. (3.97)

The *kanīnike* are the pupils of the eyes; the *akṣikūṭe* are the eyelashes; the *śaṣkulī* is the outer ear; the *karṇaputrakau* are the earlobes; the *dantāveṣṭau* are the gums; the *kukundare* are the hollows of the buttocks; the *vaṅkṣaṇau* are the joints between the thighs and the groin; the *vṛkkau* are two masses of flesh that are accumulations of phlegm; the *upajihvā* is the uvula; the *sphijau* (dual) are the hips; the *piṇḍākārā māṃsapiṇḍikāḥ* are the fleshy protuberances situated on the shanks and the thighs; the *udara* is the hollow of the belly; the *cibuka* is the chin; the *galaśuṇḍike* are specific parts of the throat; the *avaṭu* is the cavity at the nape of the neck; the rest are well known. The body itself is called the *śarīraka*. Thus, these are the locations that serve as the bases for its existence. 3.95, 96, 97.
The four eyelids, the two feet, the two hands, and the heart—these nine apertures are indeed the abodes of the vital breath (prāṇa). 3.98.

The four paths of the eyes, the two white circles and the two black circles—thus [there are] four; the feet, the hands, and the heart; and those which are the nine apertures—the anus, the generative organ, the mouth, the two nostrils, the two eyes, and the two ears—these are the abodes of the vital breaths (prāṇa). 3.98.
Likewise: there are exactly seven hundred channels, nine hundred sinews, two hundred vessels, and five hundred muscles. (3.99)

The *sirās* are the channels that carry *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman*. Of those which originate from the navel and pervade the entire body in every direction, there are seven hundred principal ones. Furthermore, the other *sirās* that branch out from these—resembling the fibers of a *palāśa* leaf—are infinite. Likewise, there are nine hundred *snāyus*, which serve as the cause for binding the connections between the bones. As for the *dhamanīs*, the channels that conduct the *vāyu*, there are two hundred. And there are five hundred *peśīs*, which are small masses of flesh. (3.99)
The number of the large vessels has been stated; now he speaks of the small vessels:
"Know that there are twenty-nine lakhs, as well as nine hundred and fifty-six vessels designated as *dhamanīs*. (3.100)
The vessels designated as *dhamanis* are nine hundred and fifty-six; that is, twenty-nine lakhs, nine hundred, and fifty-six *dhamanis*. (3.100)
Furthermore: Three hundred thousand hairs of the head and beard are to be known for embodied beings;
likewise, there are one hundred and seven vital points (marmas) and two hundred joints.
There are fifty-four crores, sixty-seven hundred thousand, and half a [thousand] more pores of the body, together with the openings for sweat. (3.102)
The atoms are enumerated and distinguished by those who possess the power of wind; even if one were to know them individually, such is the established nature of these entities. (3.103)

The hair of the head and the beard—these together are known to number three hundred thousand (*lakṣa*). The word "of him" (*tasya*) is to be supplied. Likewise, one should know that there are one hundred and seven vital points (*marman*); a region of the body where one dies when struck is a *marman*. Two hundred bone-joints (*asthisaṃdhi*) are to be known. Of the hairs and the pores (*svedāyana*), combined, fifty-four crores (*koṭi*), sixty-seven lakhs, and half a lakh are to be known. A "pore" (*svedāyana*) is a door for sweat. These pores are to be understood individually by their measure as being composed of corporeal atoms (*śarīraparamāṇu*) divided by aerial atoms (*vāyavīya-paramāṇu*) which are one-sixtieth part of a mote (*trasareṇu*). The meaning is that each pore is measured by a single atom. Consequently, because they are beyond the range of our perception, they are not observed by us; however, this is not because they do not exist. Even if only a single lord of yogis (*yogīśvara*), through the power of yoga, were to perceive—that is, know—the established numerical configuration of these entities such as the vessels (*sirā*) and so forth, and not the entire world, nevertheless, he is to be honored because his perception is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). By speaking in this way, I have indicated to the ignorant that "this has been known by me through the power of yoga," thereby providing proof. (3.101, 102, 103)
Furthermore:
Nine *añjali*s of rasa are to be known, ten of water, seven of feces, and eight of blood are proclaimed. (3.104)
Phlegm is six [palas], bile five, and urine four; muscle fat three, while fat is two, marrow one, and half a [pala] in the head. (3.105)
Of phlegm-ojas there is that much, and of semen there is that much as well.

The transformation of consumed food into its essence is *rasa* (nutritive fluid); nine *añjali*s of this are to be known. Of the water that supports the bodily fluids and the earthy elements, there are ten *añjali*s. Of feces, seven; of blood, eight; of phlegm (*śleṣman*), six; of bile (*pitta*), five; of urine, four; of muscle fat (*vasā*), which is the body's oil, three; of marrow (*medas*)—that specific constituent located within the flesh—two; of the specific constituent called marrow (*majjā*) situated within the bones, one; and half an *añjali* in the head. Of the phlegm-essence (*ojas*), there is likewise half an *añjali*. *Ojas* is a specific substance residing in the heart that is the cause of life. Of semen (*retas*) also, there is half an *añjali*. (3.104, 105)
He states the purpose of the analysis of the body thus: "He for whose sake this unstable body exists is the one who acts for the sake of liberation. (3.106)

Thus, this body is unstable; yet for that distinguished person for whom it serves as the means to liberation, he is successful and wise. The essential meaning is that liberation is accomplished even by means of an unstable body. (3.106)

Thus, the impermanence of the body has been stated for the sake of distinguishing it from the eternal Self. Now, for one who is unable to practice the meditation on the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) as non-different from the Supreme Self, he describes a different mode of self-meditation:
"Seventy-two thousand channels named Hitā issue forth from the heart; in their midst is that which has the luster of the moon. (3.107)
The mandala is his center, the self, immovable like a lamp;
that is what is to be known, and having known it here, one is not born again.

[986] Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”—“Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is bound by both ends; the person who is bound at one end and free at the other; the person who is free at one end and bound at the other; and the person who is free from both ends. And how, bhikkhus, is a person bound by both ends? Here, someone is addicted to sensual pleasures and is also held back by views. This is called a person bound by both ends. And how, bhikkhus, is a person bound at one end and free at the other? Here, someone is addicted to sensual pleasures but is not held back by views. This is called a person bound at one end and free at the other. And how, bhikkhus, is a person free at one end and bound at the other? Here, someone is not addicted to sensual pleasures but is held back by views. This is called a person free at one end and bound at the other. And how, bhikkhus, is a person free from both ends? Here, someone is neither addicted to sensual pleasures nor is he held back by views. This is called a person free from both ends. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [986]

Those channels which have issued forth from the region of the heart-lotus, extending upwards, downwards, and across, are known as the *hitā* and number seventy-two thousand; for the word "hi" indicates a well-known fact. In the midst of those channels, within the space of the heart, there is a lunar orb resembling the moon in its radiance. In the center of that is the Self (*ātman*), situated motionless like a lamp; that is what is to be known—that which is to be directly realized. By saying "like a lamp," the intention is this: just as a lamp shines by itself and illuminates the range of the eye without requiring another lamp, so too the Self is the illuminator of all, shining by itself and illuminating the entire multitude of things without requiring another illuminator. Having thus known and directly realized the Self, one is not born again in this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). The meaning is that the absolute severance of the body occurs. (3.107, 108)

He states the means for attaining knowledge of the Supreme Self, which has been declared as the cause of liberation: "The *Āraṇyaka* which I received from the Sun, and the Yoga-śāstra proclaimed by me—this must be known by one who desires Yoga. (3.109)

That which one has studied from the *Āditya* [Upaniṣad] as the *Āraṇyaka*, and that Yoga-śāstra which has been composed by me—both of these should be understood in their essential meaning by one desiring to attain yoga. This is mentioned merely for the sake of illustration; therefore, other Upaniṣads and Yoga-śāstras must also certainly be studied. That which is to be studied in the forest (*araṇya*) is the *Āraṇyaka*; and yoga is the knowledge of the non-difference between the individual self (*jīva*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*), unmixed with other objects. Thus says the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*: "The union of the mind with Brahman, through a specific movement of the mind dependent upon personal effort—that is designated as yoga."
Devala says: "Yoga is the withdrawal of the mind from sense objects and its stabilization upon the intended object. Dakṣa says:
"Having rendered the mind free of fluctuations and having unified it with the Supreme Self, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) shall be liberated; this is called the primary yoga."

It has been stated that the *Yogaśāstra* was proclaimed by me; this serves as an indicator for what follows. Among those things to be indicated therein, some will now be pointed out briefly. On this point, Devala says: "Now, therefore, because they are devoid of *dharma*, there is no instruction on the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*) regarding the animal realm. For gods and humans, the goals of human life are twofold: worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Of these two, worldly prosperity has been described previously. The supreme good is twofold: Sāṃkhya and Yoga. Knowledge of the twenty-five principles is Sāṃkhya. Yoga is the withdrawal of the mind from sense objects and its stabilization upon the intended object. In both cases, liberation (*apavarga*) is the fruit. Liberation is the absolute cessation of the suffering of birth and death. With reference to these two—Sāṃkhya and Yoga—I shall here state, in brief and by way of enumeration, those extensive and profound treatises composed by various authors through reasoning and tradition. In that regard, for the Sāṃkhyas: there is one root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*); seven which are both natures and transformations (*prakṛtivikṛti*); five subtle elements (*tanmātra*); sixteen modifications (*vikāra*); the five organs of perception; and the five specific objects, namely the particularities of the five gross elements. There are thirteen instruments (*karaṇa*): three internal instruments (*antaḥkaraṇa*), four sheaths (*kośa*) derived from the mother and the father, and five specific vital airs (*vāyu*). There are three qualities (*guṇa*). There is threefold bondage, three causes of bondage, and two types of attachment to bondage. Likewise, creation (*sarga*) is twofold. Likewise, error (*viparyaya*) is fivefold. Disability (*aśakti*) is twenty-eightfold. Contentment (*tuṣṭi*) is ninefold. Perfection (*siddhi*) is eightfold. Thus, there are fifty varieties of cognitive states (*pratyayabheda*).”
Existence, oneness, and purposefulness; otherness for the sake of another, as well as cessation;
conjunction, disjunction, the plurality of spirits, the persistence of the body, and the remaining state of existence.

Thus, there are ten *tanmātras*; these are the *prakṛtis* and *vikṛtis*. The *tanmātras* are: the *tanmātra* of sound, the *tanmātra* of touch, the *tanmātra* of taste, the *tanmātra* of form, and the *tanmātra* of smell. The sense organs (*indriyas*) are of two kinds. The specific elements (*bhūtaviśeṣas*) are the *vikāras*. The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and skin are the organs of cognition (*buddhīndriyas*). Form, sound, smell, taste, and touch are their respective objects. Speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ are the organs of action (*karmendriyas*). Speaking, grasping, movement, excretion, and sexual pleasure are their functions. Air, fire, water, ether, and earth are the specific elements. The ten organs, along with the intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and mind (*manas*), are the instruments (*karaṇas*). Among these, the mind, intellect, and ego are the internal instruments (*antaḥkaraṇas*). The ten external instruments are the organs. The Unmanifest (*avyakta*), characterized by the equilibrium of the *guṇas*, is synonymous with *pradhāna*, *prakṛti*, and *vidhāna*. That which is characterized by determination (*adhyavasāya*) is the Great One (*mahat*), synonymous with *buddhi*, *mati*, and *upalabdhi*. That which is characterized by self-conceit (*abhimāna*) is the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), synonymous with the transformative (*vaikārika*) and self-conceit. There is no further *prakṛti* preceding this. From *prakṛti* the Great One arises; from that, the ego; from the ego, the *tanmātras* and the organs; and from the *tanmātras*, the specific elements (*viśeṣas*); such is the order of evolution. Furthermore, the order of dissolution is that whatever arises from something else dissolves back into it. Thus says Yama.
Mind, intellect, ego, space, air, fire, water, and earth—
these are the eight primary natures (prakṛtis), while the other sixteen are the transformations (vikāras).
The ear, eye, tongue, nose, and skin; as well as volition;
and sound, form, taste, touch, smell, speech, hands, and the anus.
The feet and the generative organ—these are recorded as the sixteen modifications.
The wise declare this [totality] to be the twenty-fourfold knowledge.
The twenty-fifth is the unmanifest; the twenty-sixth is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Having known this, ascetics with tranquil intellects are liberated.
"One who knows the twenty-five principles, regardless of which stage of life he is devoted to, knowing both primordial nature and its transformations, goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (3.109)
To explain the practice of that which was mentioned as the object of meditation, he says:
"Having made the mind, intellect, memory, and senses have no other object, one should meditate upon the Self who resides here in the heart like a lamp, the Lord. (3.110)

The totality of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇasāmagrī*) is made manifest in one place because volition and other functions are observed there, even though they are all-pervasive. Just as fire, although pervading all wood, is clearly perceived only where the conditions for friction and so forth exist, so too is this Self to be meditated upon for the sake of attaining the previously mentioned results. How? By making it the exclusive object. What is this? It is the mind, intellect, memory, and the senses. The term "exclusive object" is used to ensure that these are understood to have the Self as their object by way of negating other objects; otherwise, if the object-status of the Self were merely negated, meditation upon it would be impossible. For the mind does not function without an object, nor do the intellect and memory—since memory has as its object what has been previously experienced—and there can be no perception if the senses lack an object. Therefore, it is not that the status of the Self as an object is denied. Thus, even that which was stated by Patañjali—"Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind"—is intended with this very meaning; otherwise, the absence of mental fluctuations would result in the failure to achieve the desired goal, because the forms [of experience] would be utterly severed. For this very reason, he himself stated: "Then the Seer abides in his own nature."
"One should gradually come to rest through the intellect held with firmness;
having made the mind established in the Self, one should not think of anything at all. Thus [it is said].

When these senses are made to withdraw from the manifestation of external objects so that they have no other object [of perception], at that very moment there occurs an inclination toward internal objects. Just as when the rays of a lamp are directed outward, they illuminate objects such as a jar; but when their expansion is obstructed by a pair of bowls, they remain established within themselves—exactly so, for one who is alone and situated in darkness, there is an abiding in one's own pure consciousness through the cessation of outward-directed manifestations. For this very reason, in the *Āraṇyaka*, when the question was asked, "When speech has become silent, what is the light? the answer given was, "The light of the Self (*ātmajyotiḥ*). Thus, this knowledge of the Self consists in the establishment of the consciousness of the Self by setting aside all objects, because its ultimate nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Therefore, it is stated in the *Āraṇyaka*: "This is neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, without taste, without smell, without form, without touch," and so forth. [Objection: But surely everyone experiences their own consciousness in the form "I see"; therefore, [this] instruction is useless. [Reply: True, if the knowable were merely this much. However, the state of one's own consciousness devoid of other objects must be achieved as something unshakable, free from the desire to act, and devoid of the causal factors of agent and instrument, according to one's will. For this very reason:
"As a lamp standing in a windless place does not flicker, such is the simile remembered.

And for this reason, it is accomplished through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), meditation (*dhyāna*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), deliberation (*tarka*), and absorption (*samādhi*). Among these, by means of breath controls characterized as previously described, the defects of the sense organs are dispelled.
Just as: "The impurities of ores being smelted are indeed burnt away."
"Likewise, the defects of the senses are burnt away through the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Then comes meditation (*dhyāna*), which is the recollection of the Self (*ātman*). Following that is *pratyāhāra*, the withdrawal [of the mind] from each respective object, because the mind is by nature restless and tends toward objects. As it is said in the *Gītā*:
"From whatever cause the restless and unsteady mind wanders away..."
"Then, withdrawing it from here and there, one should gradually bring it under control.
This is said because the mind is difficult to grasp and because it is rooted in the senses;
for the mind, O Kṛṣṇa, is restless, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate.
"I consider its restraint to be more difficult even than that of the wind. Thus [he said].

Retention (*dhāraṇā*) is so called because, having been drawn back again and again, it is held within oneself. These [practices] have distinct fruits, as it is said: "One should burn away defects by means of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and sins by means of retention; one should burn away attachments by means of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), and non-divine qualities by means of meditation (*dhyāna*). [990]

The qualities such as passion, hatred, and so forth, are not the sovereign master. Therefore, through the abandonment of the mind and the intellect, there is inquiry into the Self; that is reasoning (*tarka*).
When one does not perceive a second thing whatsoever apart from the Self, having become Brahman, then, being tranquil, one enjoys absolute bliss. Thus it is said.

Therefore, the perfect placement of the self, which has known all that is to be known, is called *samādhi* because of its unshakability. For this very reason it is said: "Breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), as well as meditation (*dhyāna*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), deliberation (*tarka*), and *samādhi*—this is called the six-limbed yoga (*ṣāḍaṅga-yoga*)."
Thus it is recorded in the Smṛti. 3.110.

Furthermore, for one whose mental activity does not find delight in this savitarka samādhi because it lacks an objective support and thus rejects outward-directed appearances, he states the means for attaining the supreme Brahman through the practice of the knowledge of Brahman by means of the worship of Śabdabrahman: "One who sings the Sāman chant with proper attention, without a discordant note, likewise attains the supreme Brahman through such attentive practice. (3.111)

Reciting the *sāman* with attentiveness and one-pointedness of mind, studying it without discordant or conflicting tones—just as one sings so that he is fully attentive while practicing the knowledge of Brahman—he attains, that is, knows, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self. || 3.111 ||

He states the specific means for practicing the knowledge of Brahman: "The Aparāntika, the Ullopya, the Madraka, the Prakarī, as well as the Traiveṇuka, the Surābinda, and the Uttara—these are the songs. (3.112)
Singing these *ṛk*-verses, hand-clapping songs, compositions of skillful poets, and hymns of Brahmā, he did so for the sake of practicing that which is designated as liberation. (3.113)

The *aparāntikā* and other such specific types of song mentioned in the *Bhārata-śāstra* are to be sung for the purpose of practicing the knowledge of Brahman. While these are being sung, one must understand that from which the sound arises and wherein it dissolves; that alone is Brahman. Therefore, it is appropriate to say that they are to be sung for the sake of practicing the knowledge thereof. (3.112, 113)
Moreover:

"One who knows the true principles of playing the lute, who is proficient in the musical scales (*śruti*) and modes (*jāti*), and who understands rhythm (*tāla*), attains the path of liberation without effort. (3.114)

The *vīṇā* is a particular musical instrument. He who knows the true principles of playing it according to the method taught in the *Bhārata-śāstra*, and likewise understands *tāla* (rhythm) in its true essence through the *śrutis*—which are the melodic scales defined by the science of music—and is proficient (*viśārada*) in the *jātis* as prescribed by that same science; and he who, according to the path taught in the *Gandharva-veda*, understands *tāla* in its true essence—he effortlessly attains the path to liberation, namely one-pointedness of mind (*manasa aikāgrya*), which is the means to liberation and the cause of the knowledge of Brahman. (3.114)

But for one who does not correctly understand that from which the sounds of the lute and other instruments arise and in which they dissolve—distinguishing them from their constituent parts—the author says in response:
"If a knower of song does not attain the supreme state through singing, he becomes an attendant of Rudra and rejoices together with him. (3.115)

If, due to the influence of mental distraction brought about by fate, one who knows song does not attain the supreme state even while singing, then, having become an attendant and follower of Rudra, the Supreme Lord, he rejoices and exults together with that very Rudra. || 3.115 ||
He states the question of the sages: "The self is said to be beginningless, yet its beginning is the body; the entire world arises from the self, and the self originates from the world. (3.116)
"How is it that we, along with the worlds of gods, asuras, and humans, are thus deluded?
Tell us how the world has arisen and what the self is within it. (3.117)

"O Blessed Yājñavalkya, you have stated that the Self is beginningless and devoid of prior non-existence. Yet, it was also said that its conventional designation as having a beginning occurs through the possession of a body: 'The unborn is proclaimed to be born because of the assumption of a body.'"

Thus [it is said] here. Furthermore, you yourself have stated that the entire world arises from the Self in the passage: "At the beginning of creation, He, according to His will... Likewise, you assert that the birth or origin of the embodied Self occurs from the world. We are bewildered by these mutually contradictory words of the Blessed One. Since the Blessed One is the most authoritative person, your word ought not to be contradictory; yet we perceive a contradiction, and therefore we are bewildered. He clarifies this very contradiction: If the world, including gods, asuras, and humans, has emerged from the Self, and if the Self performs its own work entirely independent of assuming a body, then how can there be the birth or origin of the Self when space and the other elements have already become the causes? Since the Self would perform the work of creating the world and so forth independently of a body, the assumption of a body would be purposeless. Alternatively, if the Self acts only while possessing a body so that such an assumption is meaningful, then how is it that at the beginning of creation the bodiless Self creates space and the rest? Speak to us for the sake of dispelling this confusion. (3.116, 117)
To this he replies:
"For that person who is seen here after casting off the net of delusion—he has a thousand arms, feet, and eyes, possesses the radiance of the sun, and is the Thousandfold One. (3.118)
He is indeed the Self, the sacrifice, the multiform Prajāpati.

That Person who, having cast off and discarded the manifold web of delusion—that is, false knowledge—by virtue of performing righteous deeds and plunging into the meaning of the Vedānta, is seen by the wise as having a thousand hands (indeed, immeasurable hands), a thousand feet, a thousand eyes, and a thousandfold solar radiance like the sun, possessing a thousand lights, and a thousand heads; He alone is the Self, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), the individual soul (*jīva*), that is to say, the conscious self (*vijñānātman*). He alone is the sacrifice and righteousness; He is the Supreme Person known solely through the Vedānta, the Universal Form (*viśvarūpa*), meaning He is the enjoyer, the enjoyed, the body of enjoyment, the means of enjoyment, and the act of enjoyment itself. That a single entity can possess multiple forms is observed, just as a tree has the form of a trunk, branches, and twigs; therefore, its universal form is not illogical. He alone is the Lord and Master of all creatures, even those whose forms are beginningless. Here, the connection of the formless and partless Supreme Self with countless hands and so forth is stated figuratively, because He possesses the power to produce effects such as hands everywhere and at all times. Thus it is said that the creation of the universe, including space and the rest, by the bodiless Supreme Self—who possesses inconceivable power over all objects—is not illogical. Furthermore, by the mention of His being the Universal Form, He teaches that the Supreme Self alone is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of the world. Just as clay, which takes the form of jars, pots, bowls, and water-jars, is their material cause, so the Self, which takes the form of the world, is its material cause. Although the term "Universal" (*viśva*) already includes the sacrifice, its separate mention is for the purpose of declaring its preeminence. In this way, it is stated that the Supreme Self performs His own work independently of a body; consequently, it follows by implication that the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) depends upon a body. And thus, there arises a contradiction between dependence and independence. (3.118)

It has already been stated that there exists for that Supreme Self a distinction based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*). Having established that the Supreme Self is the cause of the great creation by virtue of its omnipotence, [the author] now speaks, demonstrating that it is also the cause of the intermediate creation:
"And that Virāj, in the form of food, attains the state of sacrifice" (3.119).
That supreme essence which is produced from the relinquishing of the substance and the deity,
having fully satisfied the gods, [satisfies] the sacrificer with its fruit.
Having been joined with the wind, the Soma is then led by the rays;
it is brought to the solar abode ordained by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
That sun creates that maṇḍala, the supreme nectar;
from that is the birth of all beings, whether they are of the nature of eaters or non-eaters.
From that food, again comes sacrifice; from sacrifice, again food; and from food, again ritual action.
Thus does this wheel revolve, without beginning or end. (3.123)

It shines variously or completely, thus it is *virāṭ*, the Sun; that very one previously mentioned as the Supreme Self is that Āditya, who becomes the sacrifice in the form of food. To elaborate on that, it is said: "He who [consists of] substance and deity," and so forth. From that sacrifice—which is the renunciation consisting of the connection between the substance (such as the sacrificial cake or other oblation to be offered) and the deity (such as Agni, who is the factor effecting the designation)—there arises the supreme essence (*rasa*), which is synonymous with merit, dharma, and so on. Having gratified the gods with nectar and having joined the sacrificer with fruits such as heaven, that dharma-essence becomes nectar. That nectar, whose nature is immortal, is led by the wind to the lunar orb. From that lunar orb, it is brought by the rays to the solar abode, the station of the Sun, which is ordained by the Vedas as consisting of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman*—as indicated by passages such as "This very triple knowledge indeed shines. That which is ordained as consisting of the triple Veda should be understood as the orb of the Sun. For all beings, whether mobile or immobile, stable or otherwise, whose nature is both eating and not eating, the Person residing within the solar orb emits the essence in the form of food. And from that food, in the form of the sacrificial cake and so forth, when it is being sacrificed, there is again the arising of sacrifice. And from that sacrifice, by the aforementioned sequence, there is again the production of food. And from that, the ritual act (*kratu*) comes into being. Thus, this collection of entities, devoid of beginning or end, established through the mutual relationship of cause and effect, revolves like a wheel; it rotates and persists—this is the meaning. From food all beings come into existence; from rain comes the production of food;
from sacrifice rain comes into being; and sacrifice originates from action.
Know that action originates from Brahman, and Brahman originates from the Imperishable (Akṣara).
Therefore, the all-pervading Brahman is eternally established in sacrifice.
He who does not follow this wheel thus set in motion here, O Pārtha, lives in vain— he whose life is sinful and who delights in the objects of the senses.
Sacrifice is the *apūrva*; Brahman is the Veda; the Imperishable is the Supreme Self. Manu [says]:
"An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain food, and from that, living beings. (3.119, 120, 121, 122, 123)
If the wheel of saṃsāra were established as a relationship of cause and effect, then liberation in the form of the soul's isolation (kaivalya) would not be possible; to this, he says:
"The self is beginningless; no origination exists for the inner self.
But the person (puruṣa) is a composite [entity], born from delusion, desire, aversion, and karma. (3.124)

If the Self were indeed something that had a beginning, it would then be subject to destruction; and consequently, upon its destruction, the attribute characterized as liberation would not belong to it. Rather, the Self is beginningless and unproduced, for there is no cause for the origination of this inner Self. Nor should it be argued that even though it is eternal, there can be no liberation because it is connected by way of natural inherence (*samavāya*) with the previously mentioned wheel [of the body]; for this person, the inner Self, is the inherent constituent and relative of the wheel of sacrifice and so forth, and is born from action due to the arising of delusion, desire, and aversion, but not of itself. And those factors such as delusion—which serve as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) through their inherence in the wheel—cease through the excellence of knowledge, austerity, and practice, as well as through dispassion (*vairāgya*), and along with them, the actions based upon them cease as well. (3.124)
He describes a specific aspect of the Supreme Self’s role as the great creator of the universe:
"The primordial deity who has been described by me as having a thousandfold nature—his social classes arise from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet, respectively. (3.125)
From his feet the earth was born, and from his head the sky;
from his nose the vital breaths, from his ears the directions, from his touch the wind, and from his mouth the fire.
From his mind the moon was born, and from his eye the sun; from his loins came the intermediate space and the world with all its moving and unmoving beings. (2.127)

Regarding the verse beginning, “He who has a thousand arms and a thousand eyes, who is sun-bright and possesses a thousand [rays]”: the primordial god (*ādideva*), the cause of the universe, whom I have thus described to you— from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet, the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras were born respectively. Likewise, from his feet the earth was born, and from his head the sky. From his nose the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) were born; from his ear the directions; from his skin the wind; from his mouth the fire; from his mind the moon; and from his eye the sun was born. From his loins and from his navel the moving and stationary world was born. (3.125, 126, 127)
Regarding this, the sages raise an objection:
"If it is so, O Brahmin, how is he born in sinful wombs?
How can he, who is the Lord, be joined with undesirable states? (3.128)

And why does one who is endowed with the sense organs not know his previous cognition? Furthermore, why does the all-pervading self, though itself omnipresent, not experience [the sensations of] others? (3.129)

If the Self is, as stated, the cause of the creation of the universe, and for that reason omniscient, omnipotent, and the Lord of all, then how is it, O Brahmin Yājñavalkya, that the Supreme Self is born in sinful wombs such as those of dogs and pigs—that is to say, how does It assume a contemptible body? Furthermore, even though the Lord is independent, why is He connected with undesirable conditions such as being mute, blind, or deaf? Likewise, although He is endowed with the six instruments—the sense organs which are the causes of knowledge—why is there no recognition by the eyes and other senses of objects experienced in previous births, nor remembrance by the mind? And why, even though He is the Self of all knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) and is omnipresent, does He not perceive the sensations and suffering belonging to all persons? The mention of "sensation" (vedanā) is intended as an illustration; thus the meaning of the objection is: why does He not perceive the states such as pleasure and so forth inherent in all persons? (3.128, 129)
To this,
he says the following reply:
"By means of actions born of mind, speech, and body, one attains the state of the lowest animals or of stationary beings."
Through the afflictions, this living being wanders among hundreds of wombs of existence.

The Lord, being devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*), does not assume the body of an outcaste or other contemptible beings by His own individual nature; rather, being a *jīva* conditioned by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), He undergoes birth as an outcaste, a bird, or an immobile being—corresponding respectively to the defects and prior sins produced by prohibited mental, vocal, and physical actions throughout hundreds of births and hundreds of contemptible wombs. And here, the mention of "birds" is intended to indicate all animals in general. Thus says Manu:
Through the defects of actions born of the body, a man goes to the state of an immobile being;
through those of speech, he becomes a bird or a beast; and through those of the mind, he attains birth among the lowest castes.

Furthermore, the property that belongs to the conditioned [space] cannot belong to that same [space] when it is unconditioned; just as dust, smoke, and so forth may attach to the space conditioned by a jar, yet they do not attach to the great space, so too the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) is beginningless, and because it is beginningless, there can be no connection with limiting conditions (*upādhi*). (3.130)
Moreover: "Just as the states of embodied beings within their bodies are infinite, so too are the forms of those possessed of bodies here in all wombs. (3.131)

Just as there are infinite and innumerable mental states (*bhāva*)—the fluctuations of the mind (*cittavṛtti*)—of living beings (*jīva*) who inhabit bodies, which serve as the causes for engaging in wholesome or unwholesome actions, so too do there exist inauspicious forms such as being one-eyed, hunchbacked, blind, or deaf among embodied beings existing in all wombs (*yoni*). By this, the objection—"How can that Lord (*īśvara*) be joined with such undesirable states?"—is refuted. Furthermore, by these two verses of lamentation, the resolution is stated that the attainment of a contemptible womb and a contemptible form occurs due to the power of sin for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) when it has become a living being (*jīva*) endowed with a subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*), but not for the Supreme Self itself. For this very reason, the non-recognition of states experienced in other births should be understood; therefore, the authors of the scriptures state that yogis whose defects (*doṣa*) have been exhausted possess the memory of their past births (*jātismaratva*) and so forth. (3.131)

The diversity of existence is not caused solely by the diversity of form; rather, even though the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome actions pertain to both this world and the next, that very [action] is the cause. Thus he says:
"The ripening of actions for some occurs after death, while for others it arises in this life."
For some, there is an interest in that [state] both here and in the hereafter. (3.132)

The ripening (*vipāka*) or fruit of certain actions is auspicious, such as longevity and so forth, while for others it is the opposite, such as their exhaustion and so forth. For some actions performed with intense obsession (*marmāgraha*), the result occurs after death in another birth; for others, however, performed again and again due to extreme attachment, the ripening occurs in this very life. But for those other actions performed with even greater intensity of obsession, the fruit manifests both in this life and in the next. In that regard, regarding the diversity of all fruits, "state" (*bhāva*)—meaning the specific mode of mental activity—is the motive, that is to say, the causal agent (*prayojaka-kāraṇa*). (3.132)
Expanding upon what was stated—that one reaches the state of the lowest animals or stationary beings through defects born of the actions of mind, speech, and body—it is said:
Coveting the property of others, likewise brooding over what is undesirable, and being intent on what is false, one is born into the lowest wombs. (3.133)

The meaning is: "coveting the wealth of others," that is, thinking, "How might these things not belong to another, but rather become mine? Likewise, one who thinks of what is undesirable and adverse for another—thinking, "If only this person were childless, without cattle, or without wealth; if that were the case, it would be right"—likewise, one who is intent on falsehood, being attached to false doctrines such as those of the Buddhists and Cārvākas which lack valid authority, and being an extremist grasping at extremes—one incurs sin through such acts and is born in the lowest wombs, such as those of the Caṇḍālas. This is the threefold mental sin. Regarding this, Manu says:
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind, and adherence to falsehoods—this is the threefold mental action. (3.133)
He speaks of verbal [karma]: "A man who speaks falsely, who is slanderous, harsh, and a speaker of idle chatter is born among beasts and birds. (3.134)

A person who speaks untruth or what has not been seen, who is of such a character, and who is slanderous—meaning one who points out the faults of others—or who is habitually causing distress to others, or who is a babble-er, propounding contradictions well-known in fields of learning such as the *purāṇas* and so forth, is born among the wombs of beasts or birds according to the degree of his addiction to these faults and takes on that particular body.
