Having attained these ten dhāraṇās, one attains identity with the Imperishable;
provided one is neither bloated, nor hungry, nor fatigued, nor of distracted mind.
O Indra among kings, a yogi, being diligent for the sake of perfection,
should practice yoga at a time that is neither too cold nor too hot, and free from the dualities caused by wind and water.
One intent on meditation should practice yoga during these times,
and not in a place with noise, near fire or water, in a dilapidated cow-pen, or at a crossroads.
On a heap of dry leaves, by a river, in a cemetery filled with reptiles,
on the bank of a dangerous well, or on a mound of a shrine or an anthill.
In these places, one who knows the truth should avoid the practice of yoga,
as well as when the internal state of being (sattva) is unattainable and when deprived of the proper place and time.
The vision of the existent is not sacrifice; therefore, one should avoid it.
He who, disregarding these faults, engages in it out of delusion, indeed commits an error.
Learn from me those defects that arise as obstacles for him:
deafness, dullness, loss of memory, muteness, and blindness.
Just as fever arises immediately [from a wound], so too do defects arise for a practitioner of ignorance through negligence; if these defects should occur in a yogin, this is the treatment.
Listen to me as I explain what the yogin must do for their destruction:
having eaten very hot, unctuous gruel, he should retain it right there.
For the purpose of pacifying vātagulma, one should administer curd, or even gruel, in cases of gulmāvarta;
likewise, one should apply [medicines] against vāyu for vāyugranthi.

In the same way, one should hold a great mountain steady in the mind during trembling; or, when there is an obstruction of speech, one should do so regarding the vocal organ, and when there is deafness, regarding the faculty of hearing.

In the same way, one who suffers from thirst should meditate on a sour fruit when the sense of taste is afflicted; and in whichever part of the body there is pain, one should meditate on that which is beneficial for it.
One should maintain the dhāraṇā, using a cooling [substance] in heat and a heating one in cold;
having placed a peg upon the head, one should strike wood with wood.
By that means, memory immediately arises for the yogin whose memory has been lost,
as long as he maintains the pervasive winds and fire within the earth element.
If there should be affliction from a non-human class of beings, one should treat it;
if a non-human being enters the interior of the yogin, the ascetic [should perform the following].
By means of the concentration on air and fire, one should completely burn away that which resides within the body;
thus, O King, protection must be performed by the knower of yoga with his whole being.
Since the body is the means for attaining virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation,
ten and two breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) are said to constitute one concentration (dhāraṇā).
Two types of concentration (dhāraṇā) are taught in yoga by the seers of reality, the practitioners of yoga;
such indeed is the case for the yogi who is disciplined in yoga and self-controlled.
All defects perish and one becomes established in well-being;
one beholds the supreme Brahman and perceives the primal qualities as distinct from it.
And likewise [he perceives] the atoms of space and so forth, as well as the stainless self.
Likewise:
"When the senses, withdrawn from sound and the other objects,
are drawn back by means of yoga by those of self-restraint, that is therefore known as pratyāhāra (withdrawal)."

Hārīta states: "Withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is the drawing back of the mind—which, due to its subtlety, lightness, and fickleness, has fallen away from yoga—and the application of it to the [meditative] object. In the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"The knower of yoga should make the senses, which are attached to sound and other objects, conform to the mind; that is called withdrawal (pratyāhāra)."
Supreme mastery over those senses of exceedingly powerful nature arises [only when they are subdued]; for one who has not brought them under control, the yogi cannot achieve yoga.

Devala says: "It is called *dhāraṇā* because of the sustaining (*dhāraṇa*) of the body, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and the self (*ātman*); here, 'self' refers to the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). Śaṅkha says:
"The knowers of that [reality] declare it to be *dhāraṇā* because of the restraint of the mind.
[This is stated] in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
A yogi who is constantly engaged in yoga, moderate in diet, and has conquered the senses,
should maintain the seven subtle concentrations (dhāraṇās) beginning with earth and ending at the crown of the head.
The yogi, supporting the earth, attains subtlety of smell;
he regards himself as the earth and abandons that [external] smell.
In the same way, one who maintains the meditation on that [Self] which sustains the subtle taste in water, likewise form in fire,
and likewise touch in air;
Just as sound is abandoned by the ether when it has become subtle, so too does he [the yogi] abandon it;
and when he enters the mind of all beings with his own mind, he likewise abandons that.
Maintaining mental concentration (*dhāraṇā*), he abandons even the subtlety of the mind;
likewise, the knower of yoga, having reached the intellect, transcends all sentient beings.
Having attained unsurpassed subtlety of intellect,
he abandons these seven dhāraṇās once he has reached that subtlety.
Having repeatedly perceived success, one should abandon it again and again and resort to the Supreme.
And by concentrating upon these very seven subtle elements, O King—
For one who knows the true nature of these things, detachment from the realms beginning with Bhūḥ leads here to liberation.

In the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "Having brought the vital breaths under control through prāṇāyāma and the senses through pratyāhāra, one should then cause the mind, once stabilized, to rest upon a virtuous object."
O King, that single continuity of consciousness which has that form as its object and is free from desire for anything else—that is dhyāna; it is accomplished through the first six factors.

This is the meaning: the stream, which consists of a continuous succession of cognitions whose nature is Brahman, when it remains untouched by other objects, is called meditation (*dhyāna*). Likewise:
"That grasping of its own true nature, free from conceptual construction, which is produced by the mind through meditation—that is designated as absorption (*samādhi*)."

The meditation upon that Brahman—free from conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), devoid of the distinctions of the object of meditation, the act of meditating, and the meditator—and which is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) through a mind accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by meditation, is the direct realization (*pratyakṣa-samādhi*) that "I am Brahman. Although the direct perception of Brahman occurs while the body still persists, the word "by the mind" is used with the intention that this realization is mental in nature. Liberation itself is the self-luminous state of becoming Brahman; and it is understood from this very statement that liberation occurs only after the fall of the body. Viṣṇu says: "With the feet placed upward upon the thighs, having placed the hand upon the left hand, with the tongue motionless against the palate, not touching the teeth with the teeth, looking at the tip of one's own nose and not looking toward the directions, fearless and with a tranquil mind, one should constantly contemplate that which transcends the twenty-four principles of the self, which is eternal, beyond the senses, and devoid of qualities (*aguṇa*), transcending sound, touch, taste, form, and smell, which dwells in all, is exceedingly gross, yet all-pervading and exceedingly subtle, with hands and feet on all sides, eyes, heads, and faces on all sides, and possessing power everywhere—one should meditate thus. For one intent on meditation, the manifestation of Yoga occurs within a year. Now, if one is unable to fix the mind upon the formless, then having meditated first on earth, then water, fire, air, ether, and so forth, up to the mind, intellect, the self, the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the person (*puruṣa*), and having found the mark (*lakṣya*) therein, one should abandon that and meditate on the next. In this way, the person ascends through meditation. If one is incapable even of that, one should meditate on the Person like a lamp in the center of the heart-lotus. Thus one should set aside the meditation on the Person. If one is incapable even of that, one should meditate on the Lord Vāsudeva, coiled (*kuṇḍalina*), adorned with armlets, his chest decorated with a forest garland, his true form four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, with the earth situated between his feet. Whatever one meditates upon, that one attains—this is the secret of meditation. Therefore, having abandoned everything perishable, one should meditate only on the imperishable (*akṣara*). There is nothing imperishable other than the Person; having attained Him, one becomes liberated. Manu says:
Because the Great Lord, having pervaded the entire city, lies within it,
he is therefore called "Puruṣa" by those who contemplate reality.
In the first, middle, and last watches of the night, the yogi, ever vigilant,
constantly meditates upon the eternal, attributeless Twenty-fifth Principle.
All this has been declared to you, which brings about the supreme good;
a Brahmin who does not fall away from this attains the highest goal.
Thus that Blessed Lord, for the welfare of the worlds,
has told me all this, the supreme secret of Dharma.
One who is composed should perceive everything—both the existent and the non-existent—within the self;
perceiving everything within the self, one does not direct the mind toward unrighteousness.
The self alone is all the deities; everything is established within the self.
For the self indeed produces the connection with karma for these embodied beings.
One should place space within space; wind within movement and touch;
the supreme fire within the row [of teeth] and sight; water within moisture; and earth within the solid forms.
One should meditate upon Indra in the mind, the quarters in the ears, Viṣṇu in the stride,
Hara in strength, Agni in speech, Mitra in excretion, and Prajāpati in procreation.
One should know that supreme Puruṣa as the ruler of these, subtler even than the subtle, lustrous like gold, and attainable through the intellect in deep sleep.
Some call him Agni, others Manu, others Prajāpati;
some Indra, others Prāṇa, and still others the eternal Brahman.
Pervading all beings with its five forms,
this [Self] perpetually causes them to revolve like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay.
He who thus perceives the Self within all beings by means of his own self, having attained equanimity toward all, reaches Brahman, the supreme state. (3.198–201)

He states the characteristics of the accomplishment of yoga: "Invisibility, memory, radiance, vision, as well as knowledge through hearing, and the ability to enter another's body after casting off one's own. (3.202)
The creation of objects at will is the characteristic mark of perfection in yoga;
when yoga is perfected, one who casts off the body is fit for immortality. (3.203)

Invisibility (*antardhāna*) is the state of having an invisible body; this occurs when one possesses an atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇatva*). This [atomicity] results from attaining the quality known as *aṇimā*. Memory (*smṛti*) is the recollection of objects experienced in previous births. Radiance (*kānti*) is loveliness. Vision (*dṛṣṭi*) has as its object things that are past, future, concealed, or distant. Knowledge of hearing (*śrotrajñatā*) is the direct perception by the faculty of hearing. By this, one’s capacity for the direct perception of everything other than the Self—namely, the unmanifest (*avyakta*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the eleven organs, and the five gross elements—is indicated. Abandoning one’s own natural body, which was commenced by prior karma, and entering the body of another to experience its objects while remaining within it. The creation of objects such as earth and so forth, which are to be produced, according to one’s own will and with complete independence—this is the definition and mark (*liṅga*) of yogic perfection (*yoga-siddhi*). Moreover, this is merely the definition of yogic perfection, not its purpose. The purpose, however, is indeed the state of immortality (*amṛtībhāva*); thus he says: "When yoga is perfected, abandoning the body, one is fit for immortality. By the force of the expression "abandoning the body," he shows that there is no liberation while in the body. And this is logical: for liberation is the absence of bondage. Bondage, moreover, is the connection with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which serves as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). It is contradictory to say that the body is bound by the internal organ, while the embodied soul is limited by that very body. The destruction of passion, hatred, delusion, and so forth, along with the arising of qualities such as invisibility, is not liberation; on the contrary, it is an obstacle to liberation. For this very reason, the authors of the scriptures state that the yogi must strive to avoid attachment to these [powers]. (3.202, 203)
All of this has been stated with reference to the ascetic (yati). Now, he speaks concerning the forest-dweller (vānaprastha):

"Furthermore, even by practicing the Veda while living in the forest, having renounced ritual actions, eating only what is unasked for and being moderate in diet, one shall attain supreme perfection. (3.204)

Having mastered one Veda out of the four Vedas and one branch of it in a solitary forest, eating only what is unasked for or spontaneously offered, eating sparingly solely for the maintenance of life, having laid aside ritual actions—that is, having abandoned both optional and prohibited rites—or else having entrusted all necessary duties to Brahman, he shall attain the supreme perfection of liberation. (3.204)
Now he speaks concerning the householder:

"One who has acquired wealth by righteous means, who is devoted to the knowledge of reality, who is fond of guests, who performs ancestral rites, and who speaks the truth—even such a householder is liberated. (3.205)

One by whom wealth has been earned and accepted through occupation not forbidden by law is "one who has acquired wealth by righteous means" (*nyāyārjitadhana*). Likewise, one whose devotion—that is, whose intent—is fixed upon the knowledge of reality is "one steadfast in the knowledge of reality" (*tattvajñānaniṣṭha*). One for whom guests are dear is "one who loves guests" (*atithipriya*); by his love for them, his status as a host who honors them is indicated. One who performs the obligatory *śrāddha* rites, such as the *pārvaṇa* and others, is "one who performs the *śrāddha*" (*śrāddhakṛt*). One whose character is such that he speaks words of truth for the welfare of living beings is "one who speaks the truth" (*satyavādī*). Such a householder, even though a householder, is liberated—that is, he is released. By the word "even" (*api*), other members of the [other] stages of life (*āśrama*) are also included. In this context, the duties of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramadharma*), as well as the obligatory and occasional rites (*nityanaimittika*), characterized by the aforementioned qualities such as acquiring wealth by righteous means and accompanied by knowledge, are prescribed for liberation; however, some do not accept this interpretation, because it would result in a contradiction with the Veda regarding this Smṛti text which has this meaning. For instance: [The following verse from the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* (4.4.23) follows: "One who eats alone eats sin alone; alone he goes to the world of darkness. But he who eats together, with him the ancestors eat; together they go to the world of heaven. This [Smṛti] contradicts the sense of such Vedic passages. Furthermore: [The following verse from the *Manusmṛti* (6.87) follows: "The wise man should always avoid untruth; untruth leads away from the heavenly world. Truth is the path leading to immortality; therefore, one should speak the truth at all times. And likewise: [The following verse from the *Manusmṛti* (10.63) follows: "Even a learned man, if he is devoid of good conduct, is despised in this world and the next, like a sacrificial offering poured into ashes. And: [The following verse from the *Manusmṛti* (10.64) follows: "But even one who knows little, if he is well-conducted and free from malice, is honored in this world and the next, like a fire well-tended with oblations. In these cases, the Veda clearly teaches that liberation is attained through the practice of the duties of caste and stage of life, accompanied by knowledge, rather than through mere renunciation. Therefore, the view that liberation is achieved solely through the abandonment of all action is untenable. Thus, it is established that the householder, endowed with the aforementioned virtues, is indeed liberated. This is the conclusion.
Neither by ritual action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality—
[that state] which shines forth, placed beyond the heavens in the secret cave, which the ascetics enter.

By this [statement], having negated that the duties of a householder—such as sacrifices, procreation, and so forth—are causes for attaining immortality (*amṛtatva*), it is ordained that only ascetics (*yatis*) attain it. Therefore, by the word "renunciation" (*tyāga*) here, it is established that one becomes immortal through the renunciation of the duties belonging to the three stages of life beginning with studentship (*brahmacarya*). Likewise, the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* states: "All these [others] attain worlds of merit; he who is established in Brahman attains immortality. Here, "established in Brahman" refers to the mendicant (*bhikṣu*). Furthermore, obligatory rites such as the *agnihotra* are prescribed by Śruti for the destruction of evil (*durita*). A Smṛti that prescribes these for liberation (*mukti*) is indeed in contradiction with Śruti. As for the claim that Śruti itself—in passages such as "They desire to know [Brahman] by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting"—assigns the duties of the castes and stages of life to liberation, that is not so; for this Śruti assigns the duties only toward the desire for knowledge of Brahman, not toward liberation, nor toward the knowledge that effects it. Moreover, a desire is the counter-correlative of that which is to be enjoined, just as hunger is the counter-correlative of a specific medicine. Now, it is said: "One thing is enjoined toward the principal, not toward a subordinate. In the phrase "they desire to know," the act of knowing (*vedana*) is the principal relative to the desire; therefore, the injunction of duties applies to knowledge—which is the object of such desires as these—and not to the desire itself. It is argued: "Just as in the expression 'one wishes to go by horse,' the horse is connected to the act of going, not to the desire for it. True, another thing is enjoined toward the principal. However, the principal is of two kinds: verbal (*śābda*) and real (*ārtha*). Of these, the verbal principal is what is relevant for syntactical connection (*anvaya*), not the real one. For this reason, in the command "Bring the king's man," the man is connected with the act of bringing, but not the king, even though the king is the real principal. For the king is brought into the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) for the man, who is the principal qualified (*viśeṣya*) by the word. In words ending in desiderative suffixes (*sannanta*), the desire alone is the principal because it is the meaning of the suffix; therefore, the application of sacrifice and other duties is to that [desire] alone. In the case of the horse, however, its connection to the act of going is due to other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), not from the word. Furthermore, in the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), which has well-known causes, Vedic sacrifice and the like are the means, just as the *Citrā* sacrifice is the means for obtaining cattle in the passage "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā. Moreover, while performing rituals, one must maintain the firm conviction: "I am the agent of these actions and the enjoyer of their fruits. One established in the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), however, must bring about the falsity of this very conviction. Consequently, because there is a contradiction between the instrument of knowledge and [the performance of] action, there can be no combination (*samuccaya*), just as there is none between the taking and not taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup. Moreover, when the ultimate effect is non-different but the intermediate operations are different, one causal factor may be combined with another. As in "He buys Soma with a red, one-year-old, yellow-eyed cow," the redness is combined with the one-year-old cow, but not with the intermediate operation. Indeed, rice is not combined with barley. And the destruction of evil is equally the intermediate effect of both knowledge and action. Nor should it be said that the effect of knowledge is only the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*) and not the destruction of karma; for it is impossible for knowledge to effect the cessation of that ignorance which is produced by karma without first destroying the karma itself. Therefore, the Smṛti tradition regarding combination is contrary to logic and contradicts other Smṛtis. Regarding this, [it is stated] in the *Mahābhārata*: [The text continues with verses from the Mahābhārata.]
Śuka said:
Regarding this Vedic injunction that one should "perform action" and also "renounce action"—
to what state does one go by means of knowledge, and to what does one go by means of action?
"These two exist in mutual opposition, being contrary to one another.
Having been addressed thus, the son of Parāśara replied this to his son:
I shall explain these two, consisting of action and knowledge, as the perishable and the imperishable;
the direction one goes by means of knowledge, and that which one attains through action.
Listen with a one-pointed mind, my son, for this interval is indeed profound:
a living being is bound by action and is liberated by knowledge.
Therefore, ascetics who see the further shore do not perform ritual action;
for through action, one is born after death as a corporeal being composed of sixteen elements.
Through knowledge one is born eternally as the imperishable, for one's nature is indeed imperishable;
yet some men of very little intelligence praise ritual action alone.
Therefore, those who delight in the pleasures born of the body attend upon them;
but those who have entered the path of wisdom perceive the subtleties of Dharma.
They do not praise one's past actions, just as one drinking from a river does not praise a well;
through action one obtains the fruit—happiness and suffering, existence and non-existence.
Through knowledge one attains that state, having gone to which one does not grieve;
having gone to which one does not die; having gone to which one is not born again.
"Wherever one goes, one does not diminish; wherever one goes, one does not increase. Thus it is said in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between father and son.
"O dear one, while wandering in this manner within this perilous world, he reflected thus."
This knowledge, which is the cause for attaining liberation, has been proclaimed by me.
Since this entire collection of rituals known as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas appears defective and does not manifest correctly to me once [Reality] is realized,
what purpose do the Vedas have for me who has attained awakening?
Bṛhaspati says: "Truth, knowledge, austerity, and charity—these are the means for accomplishing Dharma.
From Dharma, happiness and knowledge are obtained; from knowledge, liberation is attained. Thus it is said.

Therefore, in order to avoid the aforementioned contradiction, this Smṛti must be explained as follows: "Even a householder who performs the duties prescribed by injunction, though not entitled to liberation [by that alone], is liberated because he is devoted to the knowledge of reality; how much more so the mendicant who has renounced action and is solely devoted to the knowledge of reality? Others do not accept this, for there is no lack of authority in the Smṛti that enjoins the combination [of action and knowledge] due to its contradiction with Śruti, since it has a direct Śruti statement enjoining the combination as its very source. For example:
He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together—
having crossed over death by means of ignorance, he enjoys immortality through knowledge.

*Vidyā* is the knowledge of Brahman; *avidyā* is ritual action (*karman*). He who knows both of these together—as being culminating in the performance of Vedic rites—crosses over death, that is, transcends the evil that yields the fruit of death, and through *vidyā* attains immortality (*amṛta*); this is the well-known meaning. Here, some explain the word *vidyā* as referring to the knowledge of the deities (*devatā-jñāna*), but that is incorrect, because it would entail abandoning the subject under discussion (*prakṛtahāni*) and introducing something not under discussion (*aprakṛtaprakriyā*). This is because, by the verse beginning with "The Lord is to be enveloped" (*īśā vāsyam*), the Supreme Lord alone is the subject under discussion. Thus, in this mantra, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of *vidyā* and *karman* for the sake of becoming immortal. And as a means of establishing that, the distinction in their intermediate functions is stated in the phrase "having crossed over death through *vidyā*" (*vidyayā mṛtyuṃ tīrtvā*). Furthermore, by the suffix *-ktvā*, the status of *karman* as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to *vidyā* is indicated. This very point is clarified by the scriptural text: "They desire to know [Brahman] through sacrifice" (*vividiṣanti yajñena*), and so forth. Although here, because it is the meaning of the suffix, the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) is primary according to the will of the speaker, nevertheless, the connection of sacrifice with that [desire] is not the meaning established by the sentence, because it is already established by implication. To explain: the sacrifices and other rites do not have the purpose of producing knowledge (*vidyā*) without a connection to the desire to know. Indeed, that which is not desired cannot be primary. Therefore, since knowledge is primary with respect to the sacrifices, their connection to the desire to know—which is understood—is not what is enjoined, but rather their connection to knowledge, because that is not otherwise established. Just as in the text "One desiring food should cause [him] to sacrifice with this [offering]," having restated the connection with the act of sacrificing, the connection with the sacrifice itself is enjoined for one desiring food. For this very reason, in the expression "he wishes to go by horse," the connection of the horse with the act of going is indeed verbal (*śābda*). Or, let it be that the desire to know itself is primary with respect to the sacrifices; however, the term "desire to know" (*vividiṣā*) refers to a desire qualified by knowledge, which is the instrumental cause (*prayojanībhūta*) of that desire. And whatever is an auxiliary to that which possesses a purpose is also an auxiliary to that purpose itself. For example: "Having piled the fire-altar (*agni*), one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī. Here, the Sautrāmaṇī is an auxiliary to the fire-altar, and by being so, it becomes an auxiliary to the sacrifice, which is its purpose. Knowledge (*vidyā*) also, being powerful through its fruit which is liberation (*apavarga*), becomes the purpose of the desire, but not in its isolated state. Consequently, even though ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest become auxiliaries to knowledge, they attain the status of auxiliaries to liberation. And liberation is the fruit of knowledge, as is well known from such texts as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (*brahmavid āpnoti param*) and "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman" (*brahma veda brahma bhavati*). Nor should it be argued: "Just as the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is an auxiliary to the production of the nature of the *āhavanīya* fire and the like, but not to their subsequent function in the rituals (*kratu*), so too sacrifices and the like produce the nature of knowledge but do not effect its result, which is liberation. It is correct that the establishment of the fires has as its sole remainder the production of the nature of the *āhavanīya* and other fires. For at the stage of the application (*viniyoga*) of the establishment, there is no comprehension of the *āhavanīya* and others as having a purpose through such texts as "What they offer in the *āhavanīya*. Indeed, the comprehension of their purpose occurs once the *āhavanīya* is already established. And that establishment depends upon the application of the rite of establishment. Therefore, first the establishment is applied to the fires, and afterwards the fires are applied to the rituals. Thus, in the absence of any other way, the status of being an auxiliary to the nature of the *āhavanīya*—which is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*)—is accepted for the establishment, but not when another way is possible. And such a way is possible here, because even before the application of the sacrifices and the like, knowledge is known to have liberation as its goal, and because the nature of knowledge is perceptible (*aindriyaka*). Nor should it be argued: "Just as for animals and the like, whose status as human goals is known through other means of knowledge, the scripture prescribes the *Citrā* sacrifice and others as the means, so too sacrifices and the like are prescribed for knowledge. That is not so, because in that case, their status as human goals is not known from any other source of knowledge. Therefore, it is established that sacrifices and the like are applied to knowledge—which is understood from scripture to be the cause of liberation—either directly or through the medium of desire. Consequently, all the obligatory duties (*karma*) of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*) are conjoined with the knowledge of Brahman for the sake of achieving liberation. As for texts such as "Not by action... (*na karmaṇā...*), they refer to actions devoid of knowledge, because they prohibit action as a means to liberation. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the injunction regarding conjunction (*samuccaya*). For this very reason, after censuring action—which is denoted by the word *avidyā*—in the mantra, knowledge (*vidyā*) alone is also censured: [Mantra 9: "The ignorant perish; the wise ones transcend death through action; and those who have realized the Self through knowledge, having transcended death, enjoy immortality. (Katha Upanishad 2.5) [Mantra 10: "Some enter the womb for the embodiment of a mortal body; others, purified of sin, enter into immutable things. (Katha Upanishad 2.6) [Mantra 11: "Those who worship ignorance (*avidyā*) enter into blind darkness; those who delight in knowledge (*vidyā*) enter into even greater darkness. (Isa Upanishad 9) [Mantra 12: "From ignorance (*avidyā*) one goes to death; from knowledge (*vidyā*) one goes to deathlessness. (Isa Upanishad 11) [Mantra 13: "The ignorant, deluded by the illusion of wealth, perform various sacrifices, desiring heaven, and rejoice in the cycle of rebirth. (Isa Upanishad 3) [Mantra 14: "But those who practice austerity (*tapas*) and faith (*śraddhā*) in the forest, and dwell in truth, eat the nourishment of bliss through the subtle essence (*rasa*) of the Supreme Being. (Isa Upanishad 15) [Mantra 15: "The ignorant, deluded by the illusion of wealth, perform various sacrifices, desiring heaven, and rejoice in the cycle of rebirth. (Isa Upanishad 3) [Mantra 16: "But those who practice austerity (*tapas*) and faith (*śraddhā*) in the forest, and dwell in truth, eat the nourishment of bliss through the subtle essence (*rasa*) of the Supreme Being. (Isa Upanishad 15) [Mantra 17: "The ignorant, deluded by the illusion of wealth, perform various sacrifices, desiring heaven, and rejoice in the cycle of rebirth. (Isa Upanishad 3) [Mantra 18: "But those who practice austerity (*tapas*) and faith (*śraddhā*) in the forest, and dwell in truth, eat the nourishment of bliss through the subtle essence (*rasa*) of the Supreme Being. (Isa Upanishad 15) [Mantra 19: "The ignorant, deluded by the illusion of wealth, perform various sacrifices, desiring heaven, and rejoice in the cycle of rebirth. (Isa Upanishad 3) [Mantra 20: "But those who practice austerity (*tapas*) and faith (*śraddhā*) in the forest, and dwell in truth,
"Into blind darkness enter those who worship knowledge; into even greater darkness, as it were, enter those who delight in ignorance. Thus [it is said].

Furthermore, even the statement, “All these [ascetics] attain worlds of merit,” refers exclusively to the domain of mere ritual action (*karma*). The meaning of the passage, “One who is established in Brahman attains immortality” (*brahmasaṃstho ’mṛtatvam eti*), is this: among the stages of life (*āśrama*) under discussion, he who is “established in Brahman”—meaning one who is inclined toward Brahman and performs actions that serve as auxiliaries to the knowledge of Brahman—attains immortality. However, the term *brahmasaṃstha* does not designate the mendicant (*bhikṣu*); for there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) for such a designation. As for the contradiction between knowledge (*vidyā*) and action that was mentioned, that too applies not to knowledge consisting of meditative worship (*upāsanā*), but rather to knowledge consisting of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). And so it has been said:
"The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are cut asunder, and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen. Thus [it is said].

Therefore, the Smṛti statement that "even a householder is liberated" is not to be explained as a contradiction [of scriptural injunctions]. Indeed, the liberation of the householder is stated in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "A householder, studying the Veda in a pure place, performing righteous deeds, establishing all his senses in the Self, and practicing non-violence toward all beings except at the sacred fords (tīrtha)—he, conducting himself thus throughout his life, attains the world of Brahman and does not return. For violence is prescribed [only] at the sacred fords. The "world of Brahman" (brahmaloka) means Brahman itself is the world. Furthermore, the authors of the Smṛtis have declared the combination of knowledge and action (jñāna-karma-samuccaya) regarding liberation. On this point, Manu says:
This Vedic action is twofold: that which leads to worldly prosperity and that which leads to the supreme good;
it is both active and withdrawn.
Action performed with a desire for results, whether in this world or the next, is called "pravṛtta" (active); however, action preceded by knowledge is taught by the wise as "nivṛtta" (disengaged).
By practicing active (*pravṛtta*) karma, one attains the state of identity with the gods; but by practicing renunciate (*nivṛtta*) karma, one indeed perceives the five elements. Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as food combined with honey, or honey combined with food,
so too are austerity and knowledge together a great medicine.
The *Yogayājñavalkya* states:
"Liberation arises from thorough knowledge; this is the mark of indolence.
And out of fear of physical hardship, the wise do not desire [worldly] action."
Through the union of knowledge and action, a person attains the Supreme;
separate existence cannot be established, therefore one should rely upon both.

And so forth. Furthermore, that Smṛti text beginning with "wealth acquired by righteous means" (nyāyārjitadhana) must be explained in its primary sense. Therefore, whichever of these two views is more reasonable should be accepted. 3.205.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, on Liberation (and Renunciation), in the Aparārka— a commentary on the Yājñavalkya-smṛti composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born of the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the noble Vidyādhara clan.
Now begins the section on expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* with its commentary.

(5) Expiations will be prescribed for the destruction of sin; and since sin has suffering as its fruit, the performance of expiation is undertaken for the purpose of destroying that [sin]. Therefore, he first states that sin has such a result:
Having reached the terrible and censured hells born of great sins (mahāpātaka), those who committed such great sins are reborn here upon the exhaustion of their karma. (3.206)

Having reached and experienced the terrible, most unbearable, censured, and utterly despicable hells—such as Tāmisra and others—which result from sins such as the great crimes (mahāpātaka) beginning with the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, those who possess remnants of great crimes are born in this world in the contemptible wombs to be described hereafter, due to the exhaustion of that karma whose specific fruit is the particular suffering to be experienced in a region of hell. The exhaustion of karma consists in the cessation of its form as a giver of extremely intense suffering experienced in hell, while its persistence takes the form of bestowing slight suffering; thus, there is no contradiction between the exhaustion of karma and the state of being a perpetrator of a great crime. 3.206.
He states the meaning that was mentioned in general terms in detail:

"The killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a deer, a horse, a pig, or a camel; the drinker of spirituous liquor likewise enters the womb of a donkey, a Pukkasa, or a Venā—of this there is no doubt. (3.207)

The slayer of a Brāhmaṇa attains a body of the species of deer and so forth; the drinker of spirituous liquor attains a body of the species of donkey and so forth. The Pukkasa and the Veṇa are specific types of those born in the inverse order (pratiloma). (3.207)
Moreover: "A stealer of gold shall become a worm, an insect, or a moth;
and one who violates the Guru's bed shall gradually become a grass, a shrub, or a creeper. (3.208)
One who steals gold from a Brahmin becomes a worm or an insect; one who violates the Guru’s bed shall become grass, shrubs, and the like, respectively. (3.208)
Having stated that sin leads to a miserable birth, he now declares that it leads to an inferior body:

"The killer of a Brahmin shall be afflicted with consumption; the drinker of spirituous liquor, with black teeth; the stealer of gold, with deformed nails; and the violator of the Guru’s bed, with a skin disease. (3.209)

Whatever [sin] they have committed in this world, he is born with the corresponding mark: one who has killed a Brahmin or associated with such a person becomes afflicted with consumption (kṣayarogin), pulmonary tuberculosis (rājayakṣman), or leprosy (kuṣṭhin); one who has stolen gold becomes black-toothed by nature; one who has drunk liquor becomes black-nailed; one who has had sexual intercourse with the wife of a guru becomes afflicted with a skin disease (duścarman)—that is, a loathsome skin condition—or is impotent; and one who associates with those who have killed a Brahmin or the like becomes marked by sinful diseases and other such signs. (3.209)
Furthermore:
"The stealer of food shall suffer from chronic illness; the stealer of speech shall be a fool. (3.210)
One who steals grain shall have an extra limb; a slanderer, a putrid nose; one who steals sesame shall drink oil; and a backbiter shall have a foul-smelling mouth. (3.211)

One who steals food and so forth becomes afflicted with disease; here, "afflicted with disease" refers to having weak digestion (*mandāgni*). A mute is one deficient in speech. "Stealing speech" means studying without permission, stealing books, or claiming as one's own a work composed by another. One who mixes grain is one who adulterates rice and other crops with *kodrava* and the like. One with an extra limb is one with six fingers, or one whose single foot is thick, and so on. A slanderer is one who exposes the faults of others. [1036] One with a putrid nose has a foul-smelling nostril. A "tail-drinker" (*tailapāyī*) is a specific kind of animal. A "whisperer" (*sūcaka*) is one who speaks of the faults of others. However, a slanderer (*piśuna*) is one who makes known the faults of others through gestures of the eyes, face, and so forth; thus there is no tautology. (3.210, 211)
Moreover: Having gone to another's wife and having stolen the property of a Brahmin, one becomes a Brahma-rākṣasa in a desolate place in the forest. (3.212)
This has been explained by the very words [of the verse]. 3.212.
Those who steal jewels are born into low castes; having stolen leaf-vegetables, one becomes a peacock, and having stolen auspicious fragrances, one becomes a muskrat. (3.213)
A mouse indicates the theft of grain; a camel, a vehicle; a monkey, fruit; a water-fowl, water; a crow, milk; and a house-builder ant, household utensils. (3.214)

A stealer of honey becomes a gadfly; a stealer of meat, a vulture; a stealer of a cow, a monitor lizard; likewise, a stealer of fire, a crane; a stealer of clothing, one with white leprosy; a stealer of liquids, a dog; and a stealer of salt, a cricket.

One born of a low caste, such as from the womb of a *śūdra* and so forth, becomes there a thief of gems—gems being rubies and the like. One who steals leafy vegetables and such becomes a peacock and the like. A *chucchundari* is a musk-rat. A vehicle is a horse and so forth. A *plava* is a specific kind of bird. A *gṛhakārī* is a specific kind of creature. Household utensils are domestic implements. Flesh is meat; a *godhā* is a hole-dweller, a specific kind of creature resembling a porpoise. A *śvitrin* is one with white skin; "juice" refers to milk and the like. A *cīrī* is a specific kind of creature. The rest is well known. (3.213, 214, 215)
He himself states the intended meaning of what has been said:

"I have stated this, however, merely for the sake of illustration regarding the act of theft; for just as there are various kinds of objects, so too are there various classes of living beings. (3.216)

As for what was said—that such a person becomes a thief of this kind—that is not for the sake of a restrictive rule, but rather for the sake of illustration. For just as the objects to be stolen are infinite, so too are the specific types of rebirth to be attained by the thief of those objects infinite. Therefore, it is impossible to describe these exhaustively. (3.216)
[1037] It has been stated that the fruit of evil is the attainment of hell, an inferior womb, and a wretched body; now he speaks of the fruit of that accumulated [evil]:
"Having obtained the fruit according to their karma, they attain the state of an animal after the lapse of time."
They are born devoid of auspicious marks, impoverished, and the lowest of men. || 3.217 ||

Having experienced the fruit of their actions according to their karma and without deviation—first attaining hell and thereafter the state of animals such as deer and so forth through the passage of time and the sequence of time—those inferior men are born with auspicious marks lost and possessed of defects such as poverty. (3.217)
Then, having become free from conceptual construction, they are born into a great family as enjoyers of wealth, endowed with knowledge and possessed of riches and grain. (3.218)

Then, having exhausted their sins through the enjoyment of the aforementioned fruits, they are born by virtue of the remainder of their merit (*dharma-śeṣa*) into a virtuous family, endowed with knowledge such as the Purāṇas, Nyāya, and Mīmāṃsā, as well as with enjoyments of sense objects that do not contradict Dharma, and with the means for those [enjoyments], such as wealth and grain. (3.218)
The effect of evil has been stated; now he describes its cause:
"By the non-performance of what is enjoined, by the performance of what is censured, and by the lack of restraint over the senses, a man undergoes downfall. (3.219)

From the non-performance of what is enjoined and obligatory, from the performance of what is other than that; from the indulgence in what is censurable and prohibited; and even regarding the enjoyment of sense-objects that are not prohibited, from the failure to restrain the attachment of the senses—a man, whether initiated (*upanīta*) or uninitiated (*anupanīta*), incurs or attains *patana*, which is sin. From this very statement, it is understood that a transgression (*pratyavāya*) arises from the non-performance of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*). Or rather, men engage in obligatory acts for the sake of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of that transgression. Although the prior non-existence of a transgression is not something to be produced, it serves to remove what is suspected [of occurring]. The purpose is the removal of what was suspected, just as the prior non-existence of disease is the purpose of medical treatment. Alternatively, let the destruction of accumulated demerit (*durita*) alone be both the result and the purpose of obligatory acts. And on this view, in the sentence "A man incurs downfall from the non-performance of what is enjoined," the non-destruction of unaccumulated demerit is somehow indicated by implication (*lakṣyate*) as the cause for the arising of sin. This being so, it is established that the purpose of occasional rites (*naimittikakarman*) is either the avoidance of the transgression caused by their non-performance or the destruction of accumulated demerit. Thus it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*: [1038]
The performance of obligatory rites is clearly intended even without a fruit;
however, that of optional rites is for the sake of their own specific fruits, while [the performance of obligatory rites] is solely for the sake of destroying defects.
The performance of omens is the threefold fruit of actions;
some declare that it is the field for the misfortune already acquired.
Likewise, others consider it to be the non-arising of transgression;
and others consider it to be the performance of obligatory rites, based on the scriptural mention of incidental results.

The meaning of this is as follows: ritual acts (*karman*) are of three kinds—obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*). Among these, at times the performance of optional acts is undertaken with a view toward a fruit that has become an object of attachment, but this is not the case for the obligatory acts. As for the occasional acts, which are prescribed on specific occasions such as the killing of a Brahmin, their fruit is the destruction of the resulting fault (*doṣa*). When it is asked what, then, is the fruit of the obligatory acts, it is stated that their fruit is either the destruction of accumulated sins (*upāttaduritakṣaya*) or the non-arising of transgression (*pratyavāyānudaya*). As for the claim that heaven is an incidental fruit of the obligatory acts, it is merely an incidental benefit and thus not the primary purpose. (3.219)
Therefore, he must perform an expiation here for the sake of purification;
thus his inner self and the world itself become gracious toward him. (3.220)

Since sin has suffering as its fruit, therefore, for the sake of its purification, a person who is free from disease and possesses the resolve not to commit [further sins] and so forth must perform the expiation (prāyaścitta) that will be described. When that has been performed, the inner self (*antarātman*) of the wrongdoer and the world become gracious toward him; the meaning is that he no longer feels loathing, the fear of experiencing suffering ceases, and his exclusion from social intercourse (*lokāsaṃvyavahāra*) comes to an end. For the sake of the purification of the aforementioned expiation: "purification" means the destruction of sin and fitness for social intercourse. (3.220)
He states the established rule:
"A penance must always be performed for the sake of purification;
in this way, both his inner self and the world become pleased."
Sin committed through ignorance is removed by penances;
however, one who acts out of desire becomes fit for social intercourse here only according to the sacred word. (2.221)

Whatever sin has been committed unknowingly—such as when someone is killed by one falling from a bed while asleep, or when liquor is drunk under the mistaken belief that it is water—that departs and is destroyed through penances (*prāyaścitta*). However, for one who intentionally harms mortals out of passion, there is no destruction of sin through penances; rather, by virtue of the scriptural injunction regarding penance, he becomes fit for social interaction (*saṃvyavahāryatā*) among people. And this applies only to the great sins (*mahāpātaka*). But sins such as minor offenses (*upapātaka*), even if committed intentionally, are destroyed by penances. As Chāgaleya says:
Expiation exists for those who act unintentionally; it does not exist when there is the attainment of one's desire.
Likewise, it applies only to minor offenses (upapātaka) and to one who has committed self-destruction.

The meaning is this: regarding the attainment of desires, there is no expiation for a sin preceded by intentional desire that extends to the total destruction of that sin. However, in the case of minor offenses (*upapātaka*) and self-killing, such expiation does exist when preceded by intentional desire. Furthermore, as for those expiations ending in death (*maraṇāntika-prāyaścitta*), the destruction of the sin certainly occurs through them. Thus says Āpastamba: "Having killed a Guru or a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), one should perform the *ucchvāsa* penances according to this very rule until the completion of the rite; though there is no restoration to his status in this world, his defilement is indeed destroyed. Yama also says:
"Even all four who have committed great sins (mahāpātaka) without distinction are purified by entering the fire or by bathing at a great sacrifice."

And this is logical; otherwise, the injunction for a penance ending in death (*prāṇāntika*) would be purposeless. Gautama says: "Now, indeed, that man becomes tainted by performing a sacrifice for one for whom one should not sacrifice. As follows: sacrificing for one for whom one should not sacrifice, eating what should not be eaten, speaking what should not be spoken, failing to perform the duties of the learned, and practicing what is forbidden—regarding these, it is deliberated whether one should perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) or not. Some say: 'One should not perform it, for an action is not destroyed. Others say: 'One should perform it,' for it is known from scripture: 'Having sacrificed with the *Punaḥstoma*, they re-enter [the community]; and having sacrificed with the *Vrātyastomas*, he overcomes all evil, he overcomes it, he overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin who performs the *Aśvamedha* sacrifice. And: 'Having sacrificed with the *Agniṣṭut*, one should sacrifice for one who has been falsely accused. [The view that] 'an action is not destroyed' means that its fruit remains until it has been experienced. The other opinion—that one should perform it—is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Regarding the fact that the fruits of expiation are social reintegration and the destruction of sin, he cites scripture as authority: 'Having sacrificed with the *Punaḥstoma*' and so forth. By this, he shows that they attain social reintegration, characterized by being no longer excluded. By stating that through the *Vrātyastomas*—expiatory sacrifices prescribed for those who have not been initiated at the proper time—one overcomes all evil characterized by the status of a *vrātya*, he demonstrates that the fruit of expiations for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) is the destruction of sin. Not only are minor offenses such as the status of a *vrātya* destroyed by expiations, but great sins (*mahāpātaka*) as well; to state this, he gives another example: 'He overcomes the murder of a Brahmin who performs the *Aśvamedha*. And here, according to the principle of the *Rātrisattra*, the two results mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—social reintegration and the destruction of sin—are accepted. Here, the sentence beginning with 'by expiations he is freed from [sin]' should be concluded with 'but he is fit for social intercourse if [it was done] intentionally. Considering that 'intentionally' (*jñānataḥ*) follows from the context of that opening, he said 'deliberately' (*kāmataḥ*). Thus the meaning becomes: one who commits a sin intentionally and deliberately is made fit for social intercourse by expiations. But he who commits a sin intentionally yet not deliberately (unwittingly) certainly becomes free from sin through expiations, such as when one is forcibly made to drink liquor by barbarians. What occurs through desire occurs both preceded by delusion and preceded by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In this regard, by the phrase 'fit for social intercourse if [done] deliberately,' it should be understood that this refers specifically to deliberate action preceded by valid cognition. Sin committed deliberately but preceded by delusion is indeed removable by expiations, as in the case of killing a Brahmin while mistaking him for a tree stump. Precisely because sin committed through passion preceded by delusion is to be removed by expiations, Manu says: [Manu 11.89–90] "But he who, out of passion, slays a Brahmin unintentionally, shall perform the penance for killing a Brahmin for twelve years. "Sin committed unintentionally is destroyed by the study of the Vedas;
but sin committed intentionally is destroyed by various kinds of expiatory rites.
Thus [it is said]. Ignorance, doubt, and error constitute delusion (moha). (3.221)

In the verse beginning "the terrible [sins] born of the great transgressions" (*mahāpātakaja*), the experience of suffering in hell is stated to be the fruit of sin. Having referred to that, he names the twenty-one hells known as Tāmisra and so forth:
"Men who do not perform penance, who are devoted to sins, and who feel no remorse, go to most dreadful hells. (3.222)
Tāmisra, Lohaśaṅku, Mahāraurava, Śālmalī, Raurava, Kuḍmala, Pūtimṛttika, and Kālasūtraka. || 3.223 ||
Saṃghāta, Lohatoda, Ṛbīsa, Saṃpratāpana,
the great Naraka Kākola, Saṃjīvana, and the Path of the River.
Avīci, Andhatāmisra, and likewise Kumbhīpāka; Asipatravana and Tāpana—these twenty-one [hells]. (3.225)
These verses have been explained by the prose commentary. 3.222, 223, 224, 225.
It is not only those who have committed great sins (*mahāpātakin*) who go to hell; rather, even those who have committed minor offenses (*upapātakin*) do so. Thus it is said:
"Those lowest of men, who have not performed expiation, go [to hell] accompanied by the terrible consequences born of great sins as well as those born of minor offenses. (3.226)

Just as base men who have committed great sins (mahāpātaka) and have not performed expiation go to hell, so too do the lowest of men who possess the unprecedented sins of the minor offenses (upapātaka) about to be described go to hell. (3.226)
Now he states the designation of those who commit great sins (mahāpātakin):

"The slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of intoxicants, a thief, and likewise one who violates the teacher’s bed—these are the perpetrators of great sins, as is he who drinks with them for a year. (3.227)

The killer of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahā*), the drinker of spirituous liquor (*surāpaḥ*), the thief of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold (*brāhmaṇasuvarṇasteyī*), and the violator of his father’s wife (*pitṛdāragāmī*): each of these is to be known as a perpetrator of a mortal sin (*mahāpātakī*). Furthermore, he who drinks together with, or engages in social intercourse with, any one of these for a full year, he too is a perpetrator of a mortal sin. He who performs an action resulting in the loss of a Brāhmaṇa’s life is a *brahmahā*. And the agent (*kartā*) is either the independent doer (*svatantra*) or the instigator (*prayojaka*). In this context, the "independent" is defined as one who initiates the action without depending on another intermediary agent. The "instigator," however, is one who, by acting in a manner favorable to the independent agent, brings about the action accomplished by him. Regarding this, it should not be argued that the term *brahmahā* denotes only the independent killer of a Brāhmaṇa because of its direct connection (*antaraṅgatva*), and not the instigator because of his indirect connection (*bahiraṅgatva*). As Āpastamba says: "The instigator, the consenter (*anumantā*), and the doer are sharers in the fruit of actions that result in heaven or hell; among them, the distinction in the fruit belongs to whoever exerts the greater effort. Nor should it be asked how a consenter can be a "doer," or how one who is not the actual doer can be connected to the fruits of heaven or hell. For through the role of an instigator, he too possesses the status of a doer. Indeed, when the king or another wielder of punishment is powerful, even if a person has the intent to kill a Brāhmaṇa, no one would be able to carry it out without his consent. Conversely, according to the maxim of the "cow and the ox" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), one who has the consent of the instigator-doer would indeed be able to do so. Thus, in acts such as killing, the consenter possesses the status of an instigator-doer. By the "cow and the ox" maxim, the consenter is mentioned separately from the instigator-doer. This is for the sake of illustration. Consequently, anyone without whom the killer could not even perform his own act—even if that person is engaged in other activities—is considered a slayer (*ghātaka*) for the accomplishment of the killing. Therefore, Paiṭhīnasi says: [The text continues with further definitions and citations.]
The killer, the one who consents, the instructor, the encourager, the facilitator,
the one who initiates the act, the assistant, and likewise the one who points out the way.
The one who provides shelter, the giver of weapons, the giver of food to those engaged in wrongful acts,
the instructor of war, and the one who demonstrates the means of their destruction.
One who remains indifferent, one who voices a fault, one who approves,
one who does not forbid, and one who is patient— all these are participants in that deed.
One should indeed inflict punishment upon them in accordance with their capacity and the nature of the offense.

If those who provide food and the like offer such things with the intention (*abhisaṃdhāya*) of causing another's death, then they are causes for killing, not merely by the act of giving food and so forth. If mere [giving] were to constitute causality, then even parents who beget a son would be the causes for the virtuous or non-virtuous actions performed by that son. Furthermore, the maker of a well or similar structure intended for religious purposes would incur the status of being a cause for the death of a Brahmin who falls into it through negligence. But this is not the case, because being a cause of a cause does not constitute being a [direct] cause. If an action performed by another—even without aiming at killing—is regarded as qualified by the specific agent who carries out the killing, then it indeed becomes a cause for that [death]. For example, if one intends, "I shall kill myself because I have been reviled, beaten, or made destitute by him," and then kills himself, the perpetrator of the reviling and so forth becomes a cause for that death. However, it is not so in the case of a well or similar structures; for there is no such intention on the part of the person [who falls], namely: "Because this well was constructed by Devadatta, I shall fall into it. Nor is there such an intention on the part of a son: "Because I was begotten by these two parents, I shall perform this action [of killing them]. Viṣṇu states that the perpetrator of the reviling and so forth is the cause for the killing of a Brahmin.
Whether reviled, beaten, or even deprived of his wealth,
he who gives up his life on account of such [an offense] is called a slayer of a Brahmin.

But where a Brāhmaṇa, by means of delusion or the like, kills himself while intending another—without any prior connection such as verbal abuse or physical assault—the fault belongs to the killer alone and not to the intended victim; thus says Sumantu:
"If any twice-born man should give up his life without [prior] connection [to the victim], that sin shall belong to him alone, and not to the one he might have named."

Vyāsa has said that even for one who kills a Brāhmaṇa who is an *ātatāyin* (an aggressor), there is no sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā*). "Even if he is a master of the Vedānta, if an *ātatāyin* approaches with intent to kill, one may kill him; by doing so, one does not become a killer of a Brāhmaṇa."
*bhrūṇahā* is also a reading; in that case, it means "a killer of a learned Brahmin" (*brahmahā*). Manu says:
"One may indeed kill, without hesitation, an assailant (*ātatāyin*) approaching, even if he be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a Brahmin deeply learned in the Vedas."
Vasiṣṭha says: He who slays an assailant born of noble family and devoted to his sacred studies does not thereby become a slayer of a Brahmin; it is fury that encounters fury.
Bṛhaspati: One who returns an insult for an insult, or strikes back when struck,
commits no offense by killing one who approaches seeking his destruction.
Viṣṇu: Those who are addicted to the wives of others, thieves, or twice-born men who have incurred guilt,
or those killed by one another in battle— one does not become a slayer of a Brahmin on that account.
Manu says:
"Weapons may be taken up by the twice-born when their duty is obstructed,
for their own protection, and in battle for the sake of sacrificial fees."

Baudhāyana says: "One falls [from his status] by killing six who are not practicing sorcery. That is, against six types of assassins (*ātatāyin*). Vasiṣṭha speaks of them: "The arsonist, the poisoner, one with a weapon in hand, the robber of wealth, and the seizer of land or wife—these six are indeed assassins."
*Garada* means one who administers poison. *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"One who seizes houses, fields, and so forth; likewise one who approaches another's wife;
one who sets fire [to a dwelling]; one who administers poison; and likewise one who has raised a weapon."
One who practices malevolent magic and one who slanders others to the king—
these indeed are declared in the world by those who know the Dharma to be *ātatāyin*s (assassins).
Vyāsa says: [One should avoid] one who has raised a poison or fire like the sun, likewise one who has raised his hand to cast a curse,
one who kills by means of Atharvan rites, and a slanderer of the king.
And one who abducts one's wife—they say there are indeed six such assailants (ātatāyin).

And here, those who are currently engaged in acts such as arson are called *ātatāyin*s (aggressors). The permission for their killing applies only in cases where the prevention of such an act is not possible without taking their life. However, where it is possible to prevent it merely by the striking of a staff, a weapon, or the like, their killing is indeed a cause of sin. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati stated: "One who is reviled should revile in return; one who is struck should strike back."

And so forth. Having considered this very point, Sumantu also stated: "There is no fault in killing an *ātatāyin* (an aggressor), except in the case of cows and Brahmins. This being so, where it is possible to save oneself from the death of a cow or a Brahmin by merely striking them and without killing them, one who kills them in such a situation certainly incurs the sin of *brahmahatyā* (killing a Brahmin) and other such crimes. Consequently, all those traditional rules (*smṛtis*) regarding the fault in killing an *ātatāyin* and those regarding penance (*prāyaścitta*) should be understood as referring to the cases previously mentioned. Therefore, such a person is a killer of a Brahmin. In this context, the word *madya* (intoxicant) is to be taken as signifying *surā* (liquor). And thus says Manu:
They declare that the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, violating the teacher’s wife,
and association with those who commit such acts, are the great sins (mahāpātaka).
And *surā* is indeed that made from flour (*paiṣṭī*). As Manu says:
"The three kinds of *surā* are to be known as that made from molasses (*gauḍī*), that made from flour (*paiṣṭī*), and that made from honey (*mādhvī*).
Just as one is [forbidden], so are all; they must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born."

By taking one type of *paiṣṭī* liquor as the illustrative example, [the text] establishes a prohibition against all [liquors] for a Brāhmaṇa, thereby showing that one is primary (*mukhyā*) while the others are secondary (*gauṇī*). Thus, all three types of liquor are forbidden for a Brāhmaṇa, whereas for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, only the *paiṣṭī* is forbidden. As he himself says:
"Liquor is indeed the impurity of foods, and sin is called impurity;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink liquor."

Furthermore, the quality of being "food" (*anna*) belongs to that which consists of the flour of rice and other grains; this, however, is not possible in the case of liquor made from molasses (*gauḍī*) or honey (*mādhvī*), for molasses and honey are not food, whereas food consists only of rice and the like. Consequently, the drinking of flour-based liquor (*paiṣṭī*) is prohibited for the twice-born. It should be understood that the prohibition of *paiṣṭī* applies to all twice-born, while the prohibition of the other two types applies specifically to the Brāhmaṇa. For this very reason, Viśvāmitra says: "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed, nor should liquor be drunk by the twice-born;
the stealing of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold must never be committed."
One should not approach the wife of a guru, nor should one associate with such persons;
this is designated by the wise as being known as a "great sin" (mahāpātaka).

In this context, the word *stena* should be understood as denoting the theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold. They declare the five great sins (*mahāpātakas*) to be: “violating the Guru’s bed, drinking liquor, killing a Brāhmaṇa, stealing a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, and associating with those who have fallen” (*patitasamyoga*). He will later state both of these in the verse: “But the stealer of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold... Here, the *Guru* is the father; his *talpa* is the wife; one who goes to her is a *gurutalpaga*. Because of the use of the plural marker *taiḥ* in the rule, one who associates with any one of these four is a perpetrator of a great sin, but not one who associates even with such a person. Furthermore, the qualification by the term “greatness” is for the purpose of making known that these possess a greater degree of fault than other types of fallen persons (*patitas*). Therefore, it is understood that the rule “water-libations must be performed for a fallen person” and so forth applies specifically to these [four], and not to other types of fallen persons. For this very reason, Devala says: “Having committed these five great sins, a Brāhmaṇa is not to be spoken to by the virtuous, nor is he to be favored; being accused, he is excluded from all rites and becomes equal to one who has fallen. The mention of the “Brāhmaṇa” is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*), for there are other fallen persons as well. As Gautama says: “The killer of a Brāhmaṇa, the drinker of liquor, the violator of the Guru’s bed, and one related to the mother or father through the womb... [and so on].

"A thief, an atheist, one who habitually performs censurable acts, one who abandons those who have not fallen from their status, and one who does not abandon those who have fallen—these are fallen (*patita*). Likewise, those who instigate others to commit mortal sins (*pātaka*) are also fallen; and by associating with them for a year, one becomes fallen. The meaning of this is as follows: *One who approaches a woman related through the mother* refers to the mother’s sister, her daughter, and so forth. *One who approaches a woman related through the father* refers to the father’s sister, her daughter, and so forth. *One who approaches a woman related by birth* refers to the sister, her daughter, and so forth. *A thief* is one who steals the gold of a Brāhmaṇa. *An atheist* is one who, by relying on Buddhist or other doctrines, transgresses the injunctions of the Śrutis and Smṛtis. *One who habitually performs censurable acts* is one who repeatedly engages in prohibited actions over a long period. *One who abandons those who have not fallen* refers to one who casts out sons and others who have not incurred a fall. *One who does not abandon those who have fallen* refers to one who fails to cast out those very same sons and others who have incurred a fall. These are the fallen. Furthermore, those who incite others to mortal sins are also fallen. The separate mention of "those who instigate others to mortal sins"—who could otherwise be included under terms such as "brahmin-killer" (*brahmahā*)—is intended to demonstrate that their expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is distinct. One should not suspect here that, like those who instigate others to mortal sins, officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who instigate others to perform religious rites (*dharma*) would also obtain the fruit of the sacrifice. For he who, being the subject of an injunction, instigates another toward the object of that injunction, is indeed a partaker of the fruit of that merit. However, officiating priests are not the subjects of the injunction for the sacrifice itself; therefore, they do not partake of its fruit. But as for the fruit in the form of a transgression (*pratyavāya*), since agency in the performance of an act arises from passion (*rāga*), the scripture makes it known; thus, the statement "those who instigate others to mortal sins are fallen" is logical. What, then, is "falling"? To this, he says: "Falling is the loss of the duties of the twice-born (*dvijāti*); it is non-attainment in the next world. Falling is the disqualification of the twice-born from their own duties, such as Vedic study and the like. Here, the mention of "twice-born" is for the sake of illustration. Therefore, the meaning of the Sūtra is: falling is the disqualification of anyone from whatever duty is prescribed for them. Otherwise, women would not be said to fall, because they are not twice-born. Nor should it be argued that marriage, which stands in place of the initiation (*upanayana*), effects their status as twice-born; for if that were so, they too would perform Vedic study. Since this is not the case, even non-twice-born people such as Śūdras can incur a fall. Furthermore, before the occurrence of a fall, there is the non-attainment of the enjoyment of the fruits of previously performed auspicious deeds in the next world—that is falling. Moreover: "Some call that [non-attainment] hell. Some teachers say that hell is a specific experience of suffering in the next world consisting of non-attainment. Gautama, however, does not think so; his intention is that while a fallen person experiences hell, that experience itself is not what constitutes the fall. A fall has been described regarding offenses against women related through the mother and others. Regarding that, he states an optional exception: "Some say there is no fall for women in cases other than violating the teacher's bed (*agurutalpa*). This view of others concerns an unintentional single instance. The term "other than violating the teacher's bed" excludes the wife of one's father. It should be understood that women of the Caṇḍāla caste and others are also excluded here. For this very reason, Manu says: [1046] Manu: "One who has had sexual intercourse with the wife of a paternal uncle, a maternal uncle, a sister, a sister-in-law, a daughter-in-law, a female friend, a king’s wife, a woman initiated for a sacrifice, a woman belonging to the same lineage (*gotra*), a woman of the same family (*kula*), a woman who has approached for protection, a woman entrusted to one’s care, a woman who seeks refuge, a cowherd’s daughter, a low-caste woman, a woman who has violated her vow, a woman of the lowest caste (*antyajā*), or a woman of the highest caste (*uttamā*)—he is called a violator of the teacher’s bed (*gurutalpaga*). Having approached women of the Caṇḍāla or lowest castes, having eaten [with them], or having accepted gifts from them, a Brahmin falls [from his caste] through ignorance; but through knowledge, he becomes equal [to them].

Furthermore, one who approaches women other than his father’s wives and so forth does not fall [from caste], nor does he become disqualified from the performance of *śrauta* and *smārta* rites. [Regarding the rule: “The officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the teacher (*ācārya*) are to be abandoned for failing to officiate or teach, respectively, and for serving those who cause loss of caste; otherwise, by abandoning them, one falls [from caste]. [This means: the priest for not officiating; the teacher for not teaching; likewise, both are to be abandoned if they perform acts that cause loss of caste; otherwise, by abandoning them, one falls. And regarding this, some say: “And of him who abandons [them]”—meaning, of one who abandons the priest or the teacher without a scriptural reason. It has been stated that “one who does not abandon those who have fallen [from caste] falls [himself]”; now he states an exception to that: “Never [is there] non-provision for mother and father. “Never” means at no time, even when they have fallen from caste, is there non-provision—meaning a lack of service or lack of nourishment. However, Vasiṣṭha speaks of the abandonment of a father who has fallen from caste: “A fallen father is to be abandoned, but a mother does not fall [by causing loss of caste] with respect to her son. In that case, there is no contradiction, as the abandonment of the father applies when he is a perpetrator of a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*), and not when he has fallen from caste in any other way. Here too, he states another exception: “But he shall not share in the inheritance. That is, the wealth of the parents.
Having intentionally eaten onions, village pigs, mushrooms, village cocks,
garlic, or leeks, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste].

Vasiṣṭha says: "They declare that one born of an outcast becomes an outcast, except in the case of a woman; for she belongs to another [man]. Likewise: 'One falls immediately by selling meat, lac, or salt; a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra in three days by selling milk.'"

Baudhāyana says: "Seafaring, stealing the deposit of a Brāhmaṇa—these are causes for falling (patanīya). Āpastamba says: "Even after having recognized a fault, one should not proclaim it to others; for by proclaiming it, one becomes fallen. Devala says: "One who kills a cow, a master, one who trusts him, a provider of food, a renunciant, or a kinsman or friend; one who abandons his mother, father, son, or wife; a destroyer of sacrifices; the husband of a *vṛṣalī*; a seller of Soma; a *vrātya*; and one who has been bought out of slavery—these are the fallen (*patita*). [1047] Regarding those among these which are listed under minor offenses (*upapātaka*), their status as causes for falling is not contradictory, depending on the gravity of the circumstances, the intention, and the repetition. 3.227.
Excessive reviling of gurus, disparaging the Vedas, killing a friend, and the wasting away of what has been studied should be known as equal to the murder of a Brahmin. (3.228)

To falsely accuse or slander with untruth one's preceptors, whether principal or secondary; to revile the Vedas by declaring them to be non-authoritative; to kill a friend—a well-wisher other than a Brāhmaṇa; and to destroy or abandon the Veda that has been studied by relying on the doctrines of Baudhāyana and others through lack of practice: each of these should be understood as equal to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. As stated by Manu: "Neglecting the Veda, reviling the Veda, giving false testimony, killing a friend, eating forbidden food, and consuming what should not be eaten—these six are equal to the drinking of liquor."

Thus, the abandonment and reviling of the Veda are specified as being equal to the drinking of liquor, and the killing of a friend is also mentioned. It should be understood that because they are stated to be equal for the purpose of providing options for expiation (*prāyaścitta*), there is no deficiency [in the gravity of the offense]; this refers to a Brāhmaṇa who is equal to a seer (*ṛṣi*). "Prohibited" is well known; "not to be eaten" means unfit for consumption due to foul odor and other such qualities. Manu says: "Falsehood regarding one's excellence, slander directed at the king, and persistent lying to a teacher—these are equal to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa."

In the context of excellence or the possession of virtues, "rivalry" refers either to competition for superiority or to the examination of one's virtues. In both these cases, a false statement by the examiner is equal to the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). "False persistence" refers to making a false accusation. Thus says Gautama: "Giving false testimony, malicious tale-bearing that reaches the king, and making a false accusation against one's teacher are equal to mortal sins (*pātaka*). Pracetas states: "The killing of a cow, a pregnant woman, or a child is also equal to the killing of a Brahmin. (3.228)
Eating what is forbidden, dishonesty, speaking falsehood for the sake of self-exaltation, and tasting the mouth of a woman in her menses are equal to the drinking of liquor. (3.229)

The eating of prohibited items such as garlic and the like, deceit—which is the lack of uprightness in the actions of speech, mind, and body—and speaking falsehoods for the sake of one's own excellence have already been explained. Kissing the mouth of a woman in her menses—each of these acts is equal to the drinking of *surā* liquor. In the reading *abhakṣyabhakṣaṇam*, the word *abhakṣya* (that which should not be eaten) here refers to such things as onions and other substances that are utterly contemptible. (2.229)
The seizure of a horse-jewel, a human being, a woman, land, or a cow, as well as the misappropriation of a deposit, is indeed equal to the theft of gold. (3.230)

The theft of each of the items belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, such as horses and so forth, is equal to the theft of gold. "Man" refers to a male; "woman" refers to a female, following the association with the term "man," and the repetition is avoided according to the maxim of the "cow and the bull. A "dhenu" is a cow that has recently calved. "Deposit" (nikṣepa) refers to something other than gold.
