Viṣṇu states: "The seizure of land and the seizure of a deposit by a Brāhmaṇa are equal to the theft of gold. Manu states: "The theft of a deposit, and of men, horses, and silver..."
And for gems from the earth or diamonds, it is considered equal to stealing gold. || 3.230 ||

Sexual intercourse with the wives of friends, virgins, women of one's own uterine kin, women of the lowest castes, women of the same lineage (sagotra), or the wives of sons is declared to be equal to violating the Guru’s bed. (3.231)

The emission of semen upon the wife of a friend and others is declared by the sages to be equal to violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*). Although the prohibition against approaching the wives of one’s sons is already established by the fact of their belonging to the same lineage (*sagotra*), their separate mention here is for the purpose of proclaiming the gravity of the offense committed by one who approaches them. Thus says Hārīta: "Approaching a mother, a daughter, or a daughter-in-law—these are crimes of extreme transgression (*atipātaka*).
Those who commit such extreme transgressions must enter the fire;
indeed, no other expiation for them exists at any time."

"One's own kin" refers to a sister; "born of the lowest castes" refers to those born from inverse unions (*pratiloma*). Manu says: "Emission of semen upon one’s own kin, upon virgins, or upon women of the lowest castes, as well as upon the wives of a friend or a son—they know these acts to be equal to violating the Guru’s bed."

Because the act ceases before the emission of semen, it is not equal to violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*). Gautama states: "Some say that in the case of a female friend, a uterine sister, a woman of the same lineage, a pupil’s wife, a daughter-in-law, or a cow, the emission of semen (*avakāra*) is equivalent to violating the Guru’s bed (*talpasama*). Here, *talpa* means the Guru’s bed; *avakāra* means the emission of semen. (3.231)
He states the definition of violating the Guru’s bed:
"The father's sister, the mother's sister, the maternal uncle's wife, the daughter-in-law as well, the mother's co-wife, the sister, and likewise the teacher's daughter. (3.232)
One who approaches the wife of his teacher or his own daughter is a violator of the guru’s bed; having had his penis cut off, he shall be executed, as shall the woman if she was willing. (3.233)

One who approaches any one of the father’s sisters or others becomes a violator of the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpagah*); the meaning is that he becomes subject to the expiation for violating the Guru’s bed. Furthermore, in the case of anyone other than a Brāhmaṇa, the king shall inflict the death penalty after cutting off his organ and his generative organ. Among the aforementioned women, if a woman, being of intense passion, incites a man, her punishment is likewise the cutting off of her organ and the previously mentioned death penalty. For one thus punished, there is the destruction of sin. As Vasiṣṭha says:
And men who have committed sins, once they have been punished by kings,
go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds.

Nārada says: One’s mother, maternal aunt, mother-in-law, maternal uncle’s wife, paternal aunt, the wife of a paternal uncle or a friend, a female disciple, sister, her female friend, and daughter-in-law.
A daughter, a teacher’s wife, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge,
a queen, a female renunciant, a nurse, a virtuous woman, and even one of the highest caste.
One who approaches any one of these women is said to have violated the teacher's bed;
for that offense, no punishment other than the excision of the penis is ordained.

In this context, the mention of the mother is for the purpose of declaring the gravity of the offense in approaching other women who are like a mother, and not to establish that the degree of the offense is equal [to that of incest with one's own mother]. For this very reason, Saṃvarta says:
"That lowest of men who approaches his mother, his sister, or likewise his own daughter—for him no atonement is known."
Likewise:
"Having approached his mother, the wife of his guru, a sister, or a daughter, he shall enter the fire; no other purification is prescribed."

The wife of a guru is the wife of one’s father, or the wife of one’s teacher (*ācārya*). Marīci states: “If these [others]—the paternal uncle, the brother, and the maternal uncle—are not the ones who performed the initiation (*upanayana*), one should perform the penance for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa-vrata*). From this statement of Marīci, it is understood that the violation of the Guru’s bed does not apply to one who has sexual intercourse with the wives of paternal uncles and others who did not perform the initiation. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha said: “It should be understood that in times of distress, the husband of the Guru’s bed is indeed the brother-in-law (*devara*). “Having approached a mother’s sister, a mother’s female friend, a daughter, a father’s sister, a maternal aunt, a sister, or a mother-in-law, a twice-born man falls immediately. (3.232–233)
He states the minor offenses (upapātaka):
killing a cow, being a Vratya, theft, non-payment of debts, not maintaining the sacred fires, selling forbidden goods, and superseding a younger brother in marriage. (3.234)
[1050] Receiving instruction for a fee, likewise teaching for a fee, adultery, abandoning a younger brother who has married before the elder, usury, and the manufacture of salt. (3.235)
Killing a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; living by means of censured wealth; atheism; the abandonment of religious vows; and the sale of one's own sons. (3.236)
Stealing grain, base metals, or livestock; officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice; abandoning one's father, mother, or son; and the sale of a tank or a grove. (3.237)
Defiling a maiden, officiating at the sacrifice for one who has married before his elder brother, giving a daughter in marriage to such a man, crookedness, and the breaking of a vow. (3.238)

Engaging in purposeful activity for one's own sake, consorting with women who drink intoxicants, abandoning one's Vedic study, the sacred fire, and one's children, as well as the abandonment of one's kinsmen; 2.239.

Cutting down trees for the sake of fuel, living by the killing of women or the sale of medicinal herbs, the construction of lethal machines, vices, and the selling of oneself—these are [prohibited]. (3.240)
Service to a Śūdra, friendship with the low-born, consorting with those of base birth, likewise dwelling outside the stages of life (āśramas), and being nourished by the food of others. (3.241)
Studying false scriptures, engaging in mining operations, and the sale of one's wife—each of these is a minor offense (upapātaka). (3.242)

Each one of these acts, beginning with cow-slaughter, should be understood as designated an *upapātaka* (minor sin). *Vrātyatā* is the state of having fallen away from the *Sāvitrī*. *Steya* is theft; and that refers to the theft of gold or anything other than its equivalent. *Ṛṇānām anapākriyā* is the non-payment of debts, the failure to perform sacrifices, the failure to procreate offspring, and the failure to study the Veda. Alternatively, it is the non-return of wealth borrowed from a member of a superior caste. *Anāhitāgnitā* is the failure to maintain the sacred fires when one has the requisite qualification. The sale of forbidden goods—articles that ought not to be sold—is [the act of] selling prohibited substances. *Parivedana* is the marriage of a younger brother while an elder brother remains unmarried, despite being fit for the marriage rites involving a wife and the sacred fires. The acquisition of the Veda by paying a fee (*bhṛta*) and the teaching of it for a fee are [also minor sins]. *Pāradārya* is adultery with another man’s wife, or with the wife of a teacher, or with women who are their equivalents. *Pārivittya* is the state of being an elder brother whose younger brother marries before him. Regarding the elder brother who so marries, Manu says: [Manu 3.172] "The elder brother who marries before his younger brother is called a *parivitti*; the younger brother who so marries is a *parivettṛ*."
"He who enters into the union of marriage and the agnihotra while his elder brother remains [unmarried] is to be known as a *parivettṛ*; the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti*. [1051]

Usury (*vārdhuṣya*) is living by means of prohibited interest. The manufacture of salt (*lavaṇakriyā*) is the production of salt; this refers to anyone other than a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), for whom Manu has prescribed the manufacture of salt provided it is done solely by himself. The killing of a woman other than an *Ātreyī*, as well as the killing of a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice, and the killing of a Śūdra. Living by means of forbidden goods, even if they are otherwise permitted for sale. An atheist (*nāstika*) is one who holds the view that there is no divine power; his state of mind is atheism (*nāstikya*). A vow (*vrata*) is celibacy (*brahmacarya*), or the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa and so forth; its interruption or abandonment is what is meant here. The sale of children—that is, offspring. Grain (*dhānya*) refers to rice and the like. Base metals (*kupya*) refer to tin, lead, and so forth; cattle (*paśu*) refer to cows and the like. Since theft is already established as a minor offense (*upapātaka*) by the term "theft" itself, the specific mention of the theft of grain and other items is intended to indicate that the theft of superior property is optionally a minor offense. Alternatively, it is for the purpose of proclaiming the gravity of stealing grain and such; from which follows the gravity of the required expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Abandoning one’s father and others without a valid reason for abandonment. The reasons for abandonment have been stated by Gautama: "One should abandon a father who is a regicide, a priest for a Śūdra, a priest who officiates for the sake of a Śūdra, a corrupter of the Vedas, or a killer of an embryo; and likewise one who lives with those of the lowest castes. The sale of tanks and the like is the sale of the religious merit associated with tanks and such. Defiling a maiden (*kanyādūṣaṇa*) is making her a deflowered virgin by means of a finger or similar object, or publicly proclaiming her faults. Officiating at a marriage for a "marrying-before-the-elder-brother" (*parivindaka*) means acting as the *Brahman* priest in a marriage caused by the elder brother's failure to marry first, or giving a daughter in marriage to such a person. Crookedness (*kauṭilya*) is dishonesty. The violation or falsification of a vow—that is, a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) such as the vows of a *Snātaka*. The commencement of an action is the commencement of the act of cooking.
He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin.

This is because such things are heard as censures in passages beginning with these words. "Service" (*niṣevaṇa*) refers to consorting with one's own wife who drinks liquor. "Abandonment of Vedic study" (*svādhyāya-tyāga*) means neglecting it due to being distracted by other activities, but not through the conviction that it is invalid; for that [latter] is said to be equal to the killing of a Brahmin. "Abandonment of the fire" refers to the abandonment of either the *śrauta* (Vedic) or *smārta* (traditional) fire. Here, "abandonment" regarding a son means failing to protect him, because it occurs in conjunction with the abandonment of Vedic study and the fire. However, in the phrase "abandonment of father, mother, and son," the "abandonment of a son" means the failure to perform his sacraments (*saṃskāra*), such as the birth rite (*jātakarma*). Regarding "relatives" (*bāndhava*), such as paternal uncles and maternal uncles, it means abandoning social interactions like eating together or conversing when there is no scriptural reason for doing so. "Cutting trees" (*drumaccheda*) is the breaking of green trees for the purpose of kindling fire for cooking and other needs. "Living off a woman" (*strījīvana*) is making a living by turning one's wife into a prostitute. "Living by violence" (*hiṃsājīvana*) is making a living by the slaughter of living beings. "Effort at violence" (*hiṃsrayatna*) is the effort of pressing sesame, sugarcane, and so forth. "Vices" (*vyasana*) are the eighteen [types], such as hunting and the rest. "Selling oneself" (*ātmavikraya*) is making oneself a slave after receiving wealth. "Service to a Śūdra" (*śūdrapreṣya*) is an expression where the abstract state is emphasized; thus, the meaning is making oneself a servant toward a Śūdra. "Friendship with the base" (*hīnasakhya*) is friendship with those inferior in birth or qualities. "Base womb" (*hīnayoni*) refers to a Śūdra woman; "consorting with her" (*tanniṣevaṇa*) means having her as one's sole wife. "Dwelling without an order of life" (*anāśrama-vāsa*) is the absence of the stages of life (*āśrama*), such as studentship (*brahmacarya*) and the others. "Being nourished by the food of others" (*parānna-paripuṣṭatā*) is living predominantly on the food of others. "Studying false scriptures" (*asacchāstra-adhigamana*) refers to hearing and reflecting upon texts that contradict the Vedas; the origin of such false scriptures is well-known in the treatises themselves as having been spoken by the Lord (*Īśvara*) precisely with the desire to manifest the decline of the duties of the non-supreme ages. Thus, in the Varāha Purāṇa, in a former history, Rudra says to Agastya: [The passage continues...]
In the Kṛta age, the pure Nārāyaṇa, whose form is subtle, is worshipped;
in the Tretā age, in the form of sacrifice; and in the Dvāpara age, by means of the Pañcarātras.
In the Kali age, that Supreme Self, Janārdana, is worshipped by those dominated by darkness (tamas) through various forms of the honored path with a mind of hatred.
Therefore, there shall be no god superior to him, nor will there ever be.
Furthermore, in that very place:
Having been addressed thus, the Lord Janārdana then said to me,
"Many living beings will approach me throughout three ages."
In the final age, those who take refuge in me will become rare.
I shall quickly create this delusion which will bewilder the people.
And you, O mighty-armed Rudra, compose scriptures of delusion;
having shown them to involve little effort, display their fruits as being far-reaching.
O Maheśvara, quickly delude all people by displaying deceptions, magical illusions, and contradictory behaviors.
Thus addressed then by that god, the Supreme Lord,
I, being impelled by my own self, immediately manifested as the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra).
"From that time forward, O best of beings, the world, though largely devoted to the scriptures composed by me, does not know me. Thus [it is said].

In this manner, one should connect [the prohibitions] with the sacred traditions (*āmnāya*) and so forth established by Tāyi and others. In all authoritative sources (*ākara*), such as the mines where gold, gems, and other treasures originate, "sovereignty" (*ādhipatya*) consists of exercising authority through royal appointment. "Sale of a wife"—by the word "and" (*ca*), there is the inclusion of those things not explicitly mentioned: violence, medicinal herbs, living off women, malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), and root-rites (*mūlakarman*), as well as acts such as subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) and so forth, according to the treatises of Manu and others. 3.234, 235, 236, 237, 238, 239, 240, 241, 242.
[1053] Following the sequence of regions, he first states the penances for the murder of a Brahmin:
"Bearing a skull as a banner, subsisting on alms, and proclaiming his deed..."
A killer of a Brahmin shall attain purification by eating sparingly for twelve years.

A slayer of a Brahmin—one who has committed the killing of a Brahmin—shall carry a human skull and a portion of a human bone for twelve years; he shall bear a banner and a *khaṭvāṅga* staff, subsisting on alms by observing the rule of eating only begged food. By proclaiming and declaring his own committed deed called "Brahmin-slaughter," he becomes purified and is released from the sin of Brahmin-slaughter. Furthermore, the skull must be taken from a Brāhmaṇa whom he himself killed. As Śātātapa says: "A Brāhmaṇa, having caused a Brāhmaṇa to be slain, shall take his skull and wander to sacred fords (*tīrthas*). And the skull must be held in the hand, as Gautama says: "With a *khaṭvāṅga* and a skull in his hand. Here, the *khaṭvā* is for the purpose of carrying away a corpse; it is specifically a part of that [corpse] which is intended by the word "banner. He must have the skull fixed to the top of the banner, for so Manu says.

"A killer of a Brahmin shall dwell in the forest for twelve years, having constructed a hut, subsisting on alms for the sake of self-purification, and carrying a human skull as his banner. Regarding the specific rules for subsisting on alms, Saṃvarta says:
But the slayer of a Brahmin, having gone to the forest, wearing hair-cloth, with matted locks and carrying a staff,
subsisting only on wild fruits and renouncing all desires;

Subsisting on alms, he should indeed wander; if he cannot live on forest produce, the man, disciplined and carrying a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), may seek food from the four castes. Having thus collected alms, he should then go to the forest once again.

*Vālāḥ* refers to the hairs found on a cow’s tail. Regarding this very point, Vasiṣṭha states a specific rule: “He should seek alms at seven houses without prior intention. Another specific rule here from Āpastamba is: “If he does not obtain [food], he shall fast” (ĀpDhS 1.24.17). Furthermore, the wearing of matted hair (*jaṭā*) should be performed after the shaving of the head. As it is said: “Having completed his residence, he should dwell in a cow-pen, at the edge of a village, in a cattle-stall, in a hermitage, or at the foot of a tree, devoted to the welfare of all beings.”

Thus, according to the statement of Manu. In this context, it should be understood that the injunction for other types of dwellings applies when a leaf-hut (*araṇyakuṭī*) is unavailable. "The edge of the village" (*grāmānta*) refers to the boundary between the village and the forest. An "hermitage" (*āśrama*) is the dwelling place of great sages. Furthermore, in accordance with the principle that "a single ritual act is recognized across all Vedic branches," those duties mentioned in other Smṛtis that are not contradictory should be performed in combination; however, those that are contradictory may be performed as alternatives. Regarding this, Śaṅkha says:
"Constantly bathing at the three periods of the day, having constructed a leaf-hut in the forest, sleeping on the ground, wearing matted hair, and subsisting on leaves, roots, and fruits."
Seeking alms, he should enter a village while proclaiming his own deed;
eating but once a day, this continues until the twelfth year has passed.
The stealer of gold, the drinker of spirituous liquor, the slayer of a Brahmin, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—
these perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin) are purified by this vow.

Gautama states: "Carrying a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) and a begging bowl in his hand, practicing celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for twelve years, he should enter the village for alms while proclaiming his deed; he should step aside from the path upon seeing a noble person (*ārya*), remaining in a state of standing or sitting; by bathing in water at the [three] libations (*savanas*), he shall be purified. The inclusion of the term *brahmacārin* (celibate student) here is intended to include those practices not incompatible with the duties of a student, such as abstaining from honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, sleeping during the day, collyrium, ointments, shoes, umbrellas, lust, anger, greed, delusion, joy, dancing, singing, calumny, and fear. Regarding the phrase "he should step aside from the path upon seeing a noble person": the meaning is that he should withdraw from the path of a noble person—that is, a member of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*)—who is on the way of right vision (*samyagdarśana*). Vasiṣṭha states: "For twelve years, having resolved upon [the penance] for himself, he should dwell neither in a village nor in a forest. Carrying a skull-topped staff, with a skull-bowl in his hand, he should wander for food among seven houses where no prior intention was made [to give him alms], announcing his own deed: 'O giver, give alms to a killer of an embryo. Thus, the sin, once declared, becomes diminished. "Having resolved upon [the penance] for himself" means having determined the purpose of the scripture for himself, having intended and resolved upon the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). He should dwell neither in a village nor in a forest, but rather in the junction between the two. "Where no prior intention was made" refers to houses where, out of greed for alms, it has not been predetermined whether he should enter or not. "The sin, once declared, becomes diminished" means that the proclaimed evil is exhausted. Yama [states]: ...
Alternatively, having worn the skin of a donkey for the duration of the penance for killing a Brahmin,
he shall wander about proclaiming his own deed with a potsherd in his hand.
Endowed with austerity, he should dwell in a cow-pen, at the edge of a village, or even on a bare patch of ground;
or at the foot of a tree or in a cremation ground, with his beard, body hair, and nails grown long, wearing matted locks.
Having constructed a hut, he should dwell there, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins,
[fearing] falling into water, fire, or danger from thieves, disease, and the like.
Having rescued a cow or a Brahmin, one removes the sin of killing a Brahmin;
one should avoid all dwellings of Brahmins and sacred fire-chambers.
Grieving and censuring himself as he wandered,
he remained thus— a Brāhmaṇa of firm vows, ever truthful, and one who had conquered his senses.

He should slowly recall seven houses that are new and where no one has been invited; when the smoke has ceased and the people have finished eating, he should approach them. Having announced his transgression, he should wander for alms, saying: "O slayer of a learned Brahmin, give me alms."
He should go for alms only once a day; if he receives nothing, he should drink water.
Moving about in this manner while constantly confessing his brahmin-murder,
he removes that sin of killing a brahmin once twelve years are complete.
He should avoid the dwellings of Brahmins and not enter them; standing at a distance, he should beg for alms, and standing at a distance from their houses, he should pay homage to the gods.
He should be a celibate student, gentle, self-controlled, delighting in the Dharma, pure, and patient;
he should be constantly devoted to ritual bathing and vows, wearing clothes of bark, an antelope skin, or matted hair.
Clad in garments of bark, flax, hemp, or the inner bark of trees, covered with dirt,
his body emaciated and hairy, he is peaceful and free from both pleasure and pain.
Abandoning intoxicants, oils, sugarcane juice, and pleasant attachments, with senses conquered,
he should then [resort to] temples, caves, groves, sacred trees, and the like.
The slayer of a Brahmin shall perform the entire twelve-year vow;
upon its completion, he should give a hundred cows in this auspicious rite.
One should offer food and clothing to Brahmins according to one's ability— whether fifty, half of that, or ten— prepared from alms.

"Gentle" (*mṛdu*) means not harsh. "Tamed" (*dānta*) means enduring cold and other such hardships. "Delighting in Dharma" (*dharmārāma*) means being devoted to one's own penance (*prāyaścitta*). "Rags" (*cīra*) refers to pieces of cloth; "woolen blanket" (*kutapa*) refers to a woolen rug; "hemp" (*kṣumā*) is *atasī*, and "flax" (*śāṇa*) is well known. The "fibers" (*valka*) of these two mean their bark or rind. Garments made from these, such as rags and so forth, are prescribed as options. A "thicket" (*kuñja*) is a dense grove; a "caitya tree" is a tree in a cremation ground. "Cows maintained by alms" (*bhaikṣasaṃbhṛtā gāḥ*) are those obtained through begging for food. Such contradictory rules (*viruddhadharma*) are to be understood from other *Smṛtis*. However, the conflicting ones are to be practiced according to the specific jurisdiction of the subject matter. In that regard, the twelve-year vow is to be understood as applying to the unintentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa. This very subject matter is covered by the codes of Manu and Vasiṣṭha. For this reason, it was said by the Lord to Guha in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
O hero Guha, the sages have declared that among great sins, the killing of a Brahmin is considered the foremost; it is that which has been designated as the first among them.
In that regard also, O observer of noble vows, thirteen penances for the killing of a Brahmin have been proclaimed here by Manu in their proper sequence.
All those [teachings] must indeed be established according to their subject matter;
otherwise, O Greatly Powerful One, the instructions for those of lesser capacity would not be suitable here for those of greater capacity. [1056]
Then, having thoroughly sifted through other Smṛtis and the Purāṇas in their entirety.
In this manner, the object [of the transgression] is to be determined in comparison with such acts as the killing of a guru.
In that regard:
O best of gods, when one has killed a Brāhmaṇa in general,
having performed the penance according to the rules for twelve years;
"At the end of his life, he attains purity and, together with his kinsmen, the state of heaven. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Āpastamba: "Having built a hut in the forest, restrained in speech, bearing a human skull as his banner, wearing a garment made of half-śāṇī cloth below the navel and above the knees, he should see two paths and, upon seeing them, step aside onto another. He should enter a village with a broken, red earthenware bowl. Saying, 'Who gives alms to one who is cursed?', he should wander among seven houses; this is his livelihood. If nothing is obtained, he should perform the penance according to the rule until the final breath. For him, there is no restoration to his former status in this world, but his stain is destroyed. This should be understood to apply to the killing of a mother, father, guru, or similar persons. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
Having killed his mother, his father, and likewise his uterine brother,
or having killed his teacher, or even a learned Vedic scholar who maintains the sacred fires;
By this method, the sinner, confessing his own sin, wanders over the entire earth; hear now the rule as I describe it.
Having said this, [the rule] beginning with "having built a hut in the forest" is stated by Āpastamba himself. Aṅgiras says:
"Eating only once a day, he should subsist on his own prescribed food;
carrying a skull in his hand and bearing a staff (khaṭvāṅga), he should remain celibate and always alert."
Free from malice, sleeping on the ground, and making his deed known to the world,
the man who has killed a Brahmin is purified when the twelfth year has passed.
A distinction regarding the killing of multiple Brahmins simultaneously, whether intentionally or unintentionally, is stated in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*:
"O son of the gods, O Lord, when one should kill many at once at the same time, either by relying on a single cause or by means of many [causes]. [1057]
O hero, having slain a single Brāhmaṇa, two Brāhmaṇas, or even very many Brāhmaṇas all at once, O hero, one may choose a single [expiation] that ends with death.
But listen, O tiger among gods, as I explain the distinction here;
listen to the distinction between that which is intentional and that which is unintentional, my son.
O Guha, when a man should kill Brāhmaṇas unintentionally,
he must then wander in a terrible forest until the exhaustion of his life-force.
And when one should kill Brāhmaṇas out of desire, O best of gods, then one should burn oneself in fire according to the rite; listen to that.
Having become naked, O hero, and having wrapped himself in a garment smeared with ghee,
O mighty-armed one, he indeed gave away all his possessions.
O best of gods, having cast off your feet, you should diligently burn yourself in a fire of dried cow-dung according to the prescribed rite, without flinching, up to the very crown of your head.
"O mighty-armed one, here the entire instruction has been proclaimed.

From this, the following meaning is established: if one kills several Brahmins simultaneously unintentionally, then the twelve-year penance that was prescribed for that case must be performed for the rest of one's life; however, if it is done intentionally, then one must enter the fire according to the method previously described. (3.243)
Furthermore:
By rescuing a Brāhmaṇa, or by saving twelve cows, or likewise by bathing at the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of a horse sacrifice, one may attain purification. (3.244)

By protecting a Brāhmaṇa who is being killed by a serpent, a tiger, or the like, one attains purification from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā*). If the vow has already been commenced, it should be abandoned because there is no longer a purpose for its performance. Alternatively, one is purified by saving twelve cows from slaughter; or else, by the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. Regarding the specific details of the Aśvamedha avabhṛtha, Manu says: "Or, having informed the gods on earth (the Brāhmaṇas) at an assembly of kings, one is released from one's own sin after bathing at the avabhṛtha of the horse-sacrifice."

The *bhūmidevas* are the Brahmins; the consecrated Kṣatriya is the *naradeva*. When these two meet one another, having confessed their own sin—the killing of a Brahmin—and having performed the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), he becomes pure; this is the meaning. And this applies only to one who has already commenced the twelve-year penance. As Śaṅkha says: "Or, by intervening to save a Brahmin from death, or by rescuing twelve cows, one becomes purified immediately by the purificatory bath. "Intervening" means in the midst of the twelve-year vow. In this context, the rescue of cows and Brahmins and the purificatory bath of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) are prescribed as causes for the destruction of sin; however, the death of the performer of the vow is not intended, as it is not mentioned. If death should occur during the performance of the undertaken vow, then the destruction of the sin is accomplished by that alone. As Yama says:
"If the performer dies once the penance has been resolved upon,
he becomes pure on that very day, both in this world and in the next. Thus says Aṅgiras.
If one who practices dharma for a certain purpose should die before attaining it,
Manu has declared that he shall obtain the fruit of that merit after death.
And this pertains to the domain of all dharmas. As for that which was stated by Manu:
"One should completely renounce one's life for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of a cow;
the protector of a cow or a Brāhmaṇa is liberated from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa."

Thus, this should be understood as referring to the twelve-year penance that has already been introduced. Even in the case of failing to protect cows or Brahmins, one is purified by the sacrifice of one's life for their protection. As for the meaning of the statement, "He who exerts effort unto the sacrifice of his life is a protector of cows and Brahmins, even while living," it refers to that very person. (3.244)
Explaining further that which was stated regarding "by saving a Brāhmaṇa," he says:
"Having seen on the road a Brāhmaṇa or even a cow afflicted by a long-standing or severe illness, the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure by making them free from danger. (3.245)

Having seen on the road or path a Brāhmaṇa—or a cow—seized by a long-lasting, intensely painful illness or disease and utterly tormented, and having rendered him free from fear and healthy, the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa shall become pure and sinless. The phrase "having seen on the road" is intended to indicate that [the victim] is helpless. Since it has been stated that [this applies to] "a group of twelve cows," the singular number in the word *gām* ("a cow") is not intended to be restrictive. Furthermore, the mention of "illness" (*āmaya*) here is for the sake of illustration; therefore, Yama says:
"From falling into water, from fire, or from fear of thieves, tigers, and the like..."
Having rescued a cow or a Brāhmaṇa from danger, one removes the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.

He states the means for the destruction of evil even for one who has committed a mortal sin (ānantarya): "Having been brought before [the king], or having had all his property seized, or having been killed, or having been wounded by weapons on that account—even while living—he is purified. (3.246)

He who brings back all the property of a Brahmin stolen by thieves in order to give it to the owner, or he who is killed or slain by thieves for that purpose, or he who, on account of that, is wounded by the thieves with weapons or abandoned as one nearly dead—he is entirely released from the sin of killing a Brahmin. And this should be understood to apply to a virtuous Kṣatriya who has unintentionally and without premeditation killed a Brahmin devoid of virtues. (3.246)
[1059] The penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa unintentionally has been stated. Now he speaks regarding intentional [killing]: "To the body-hairs, svāhā!"—for [the sacrifice] begins with the body hair.
Or one may offer oblations ending with the marrow, using these mantras in their proper sequence.

"Oblation to the body hairs, oblation to the skin, oblation to the blood, oblation to the flesh, oblation to the sinews, oblation to the fat, oblation to the bones, oblation to the marrow. With these mantras, one should offer that body part by part, starting from the hair and ending with the marrow, in due order and without deviating from the sequence of the Vājasaneyi recension. Here, by the power of the mantras, the body hairs and the other parts possess the status of deities; furthermore, by the force of the statement "one should offer their very body, beginning with the hair," they also possess the status of sacrificial offerings (*havis*). The first word "vā" (or) here serves to indicate an option for these mantras according to the teaching of the Vāsiṣṭhas. The second "vā," however, refers to the alternative of performing the oblation there during the twelve-year penance. In this regard, there is a specific rule from the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra].
"Or he should throw himself three times head-first into a kindled fire," so it is said.

This must be performed by one who has observed a fast. As Gautama says: "The expiation for a slayer of a Brahmin is immersion in fire while fasting three times. *Avacchāta* means hungry. And likewise the Kāṭhaka Śruti states: "Emaciated by fasting, he should ascend the fire. And this refers to a case of intentional action (*kāmakāra*), because it culminates in death. Thus Aṅgiras says: "That expiation which has been declared by the wise as ending in the loss of life..."
This concerns the scope of acting according to one's own will; there is no doubt about this.
Likewise:
"If a man should ever commit a great sin intentionally, no purification for him is prescribed except by falling from a precipice or into fire. Thus it is said.
And for a Kṣatriya, the penance ends only with death. Thus says the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
"Having intentionally killed a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with excellent qualities, a resolute Kṣatriya should perform the penance according to the rules for the sake of his own purification."
Or he may become a target for weapon-wielders at his own will,
or he may throw himself headlong three times into a well-known fire.
"Or a Kṣatriya who has killed a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha;
for these three penances have been proclaimed for a Kṣatriya.
However, for a Brāhmaṇa who kills a Brāhmaṇa intentionally, the vow is double.
"For that which is prescribed for those who act unintentionally, it shall be double when done intentionally," according to the traditional teaching of Devala (3.247).
He further states another penance that ends with death:
"Or, being slain in battle as a target, one may attain purification."
One who is nearly dead and afflicted by blows is purified even while still living. || 3.248 ||

Alternatively, in the event of a mutual battle between kings, one who becomes a target in the zone where arrows discharged by both armies fall—whether he is killed and has gone to the other world, or is merely struck by a blow and remains alive yet as good as dead—is purified. Manu says: "Or he may become a target for those bearing weapons, according to the wish of the learned. This means that in the absence of [other] learned persons, he may become a target for those fighting according to their own will, provided they are learned in the sense of being instructors of penance (*prāyaścitta*). The scope of this rule has already been established previously. (3.248)
Having recited the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times in the forest with self-restraint, one becomes pure; or else, eating sparingly, one may follow the Sarasvatī river against its current.

Restrained in the forest or the woods, with his food regulated; for this very reason Manu says: "Or, with his food regulated, he should recite the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times. The regulation of food consists in its being sacrificial (haviṣya) or in its being limited in quantity. By reciting the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times, he becomes purified. Alternatively, as before, having become one who eats measured food, he becomes purified by going against the current of the Sarasvatī river, starting from its mouth up to its source. Manu [says]:
Or, eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya), he may follow the Sarasvatī river against its current;
or else, learn from me the expiation (prāyaścitta) declared by Sumantu.
On this point, the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa states:
"O Guha, when a slayer is devoid of Vedic knowledge and possesses wealth, one should prescribe this expiation for him; learn it from me."

A killer of a Brahmin shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for one year, sleeping on the ground, bathing three times a day, subsisting on alms, and frequenting the sandy banks of celestial rivers, confluences, hermitages, cow-pens, mountains, springs, groves, and places of asceticism. Remaining standing or sitting in the *vīrāsana* posture, when the year is complete, he shall give gold, gems, a cow, a bull, food, sesame seeds, land, and clarified butter to Brahmins; thus he becomes purified. Or, he may be purified by bathing at the concluding ritual (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice.
Moreover:
By giving sufficient wealth to a worthy recipient, one may attain purification;
and for the sake of the purifier of the receiver, the Vaiśvānara sacrifice is prescribed by tradition. (3.250)

[1061] Alternatively, one attains purification by giving wealth sufficient to sustain for life a person of noble birth who possesses knowledge, austerity, and vows. He who accepts this wealth must perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice for his own purification. Manu says:
"Or he should bestow his entire property upon a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas."
Either wealth sufficient for livelihood, or a house together with its furnishings.

One who is unable to give wealth sufficient for a lifetime should give his house along with its furnishings; one unable even to do that should give everything. "Furnishings" refers to the collection of household implements. Regarding this, Aṅgiras says:
"That which exceeds eighty thousand *paṇas* is called 'all one's property.
O Lord of Men, a Brahmin-killer who is destitute shall be released [from the sin] due to the abundance of his [remaining] happiness."
In the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*, it is stated that this same [penalty] applies even to a Brāhmaṇa:
"O Guha, when a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of Vedic study, wealthy, and destitute of the sacred fires, should kill another Brāhmaṇa who is merely by birth."
Then one should perform this expiation for the purification of that sin:
[giving] wealth sufficient for a livelihood, or a house together with its furnishings.
Or else, one becomes purified by the expiatory rite (prāyaścitta) declared by Parāśara.
For example:
In the case of one who has committed the murder of a Brahmin but possesses the fourfold knowledge,
one should prescribe the journey to the bridge over the ocean as the penance.
He beheld the Setubandha, the bridge across the great ocean on the path to Laṅkā,
ten yojanas wide and a hundred yojanas long.
On the path of Setubandha, he should collect alms from the four castes,
avoiding those engaged in improper occupations, and he should remain without an umbrella or sandals.
I am a doer of evil deeds, a perpetrator of great sins;
as a slayer of a Brahmin, I stand at the doors of houses seeking alms.
In cow-pens and cattle-sheds, in villages and cities,
in penance groves and sacred fords, and at rivers and waterfalls.
Proclaiming his sin at these places and proceeding to the ocean,
a killer of a Brahmin is liberated after bathing there in that great sea.
Then, having become purified, having returned home, having fed the Brahmins,
and having recited the most sacred prayers, he, with his soul purified, should enter his house.
Or one should give a hundred cows as a sacrificial fee to a master of the four Vedas;
thus, with the approval of the master of the four Vedas, he attains purification.
It is proclaimed that his residence is to the north of the Vindhya mountains.
The view of Parāśara regarding that Setubandha.

"By the command of Rāmabhadra, even one who has committed the murder of a Brahmin is completely liberated upon seeing the Setu, which is not accumulated by means of hoarding, but is of great merit. Thus it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*.
When a Brahmin is killed merely by birth, the expiation prescribed for the killer— provided he is destitute—
is said to be the three-year penance of Aṅgiras.
It is as follows:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the Kṛcchra penance, honored by Śakra and others;
if it is studied or even heard, it liberates a person from sins.
Disciplined and observing the vow of silence, one who bathes at the three sessions of the day should bathe;
having bathed in the morning, one should diligently undertake the recitation of prayers.
One should recite the Sāvitrī and the three Vyāhṛtis eight thousand times,
placing the syllable Oṃ at the beginning and likewise at the end of each form.
Sitting like one pierced by an arrow, he should drink cow's milk or cow dung;
if cow's milk is unavailable, he should likewise consume cow's curd.
In the absence of that, one should drink buttermilk; in the absence of buttermilk, however, barley-gruel. Whichever of these is available, that shall be used.
One should also employ barley-gruel mixed with cow urine;
this is seen as a definitive *kṛcchra* penance by Aṅgiras himself.
"The divine remover of all sins is known by the name Vajra;
indeed, the Brāhmaṇa alone is the cause of the aforementioned Time. (3.250)

He states the instruction for the vow for killing a Brahmin: "One who kills a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya while they are engaged in a sacrifice shall perform the vow for a killer of a Brahmin; likewise, one who destroys a fetus and one who slays an Ātreyī woman [shall do so] according to their respective castes. (3.251)

The killer of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who are situated in a sacrifice—that is, who stand as performers of the sacrifice by virtue of their entitlement (*adhikāra*)—must perform that various kinds of vow (*vrata*) prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa. Here, "sacrifice" is intended to mean the Soma-sacrifice, because of the Vedic statement: "Having laid aside his own weapons and become a Brāhmaṇa through [Brāhmaṇical] weapons and form, he approaches the sacrifice as a Brāhmaṇa"; this declares that the Kṣatriya sacrificer attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa with respect to the Soma-sacrifice. Thus, it should be understood that this vow is extended to the killer of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who are engaged in the sacrifice after the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering and prior to the conclusion of the *avabhṛtha*. Furthermore, regarding what was stated by Vasiṣṭha—"Having killed a Brāhmaṇa woman who is an *Ātreyī*, one performs the penance for killing an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*); likewise for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who have gone to the *savana*"—there too, the phrase "who have gone to the *savana*" is intended to mean those who have indeed performed the *dīkṣaṇīyā*. And whichever person carries the embryo of a particular caste, he shall perform the penance for the killing of that caste. Manu, however, states the extension of the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa even in other circumstances.
Having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown, one should observe this very same vow; as also for killing a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice, or a woman who is an Ātreyī.
"Having given false testimony, having reviled a guru, having misappropriated a deposit, and having committed the murder of a woman or a friend. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that the fetus is not yet distinguished as being male or female. Furthermore, this fetus belongs only to a Brāhmaṇa; thus Āpastamba says: “And his [the Brāhmaṇa’s] fetus when undistinguished. This means “of that Brāhmaṇa. But when the fetus is distinguished, the penance is according to its gender: if the fetus is female, the penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) applies; in the other case (if male), the vow of a Brāhmaṇa-slayer applies. By the phrase “this very vow,” he refers back to the various types of vows for killing a Brāhmaṇa mentioned immediately prior, and not specifically to the twelve-year penance alone, because there is no specific reason [to limit it to that]. As for the twelve-year penance stated by Āpastamba for one who kills a Brāhmaṇa fetus or an *Ātreyī*, that is for the sake of illustration and not as a restrictive rule. For if that were the case, it would lead to the unjust consequence of treating unequal cases as equal—namely, that the twelve-year vow must be performed in every instance of killing, regardless of whether it was intentional or unintentional, or whether it was a single act or a repeated practice, and so forth. Moreover, by the mention of the “vow” (*vrata*), there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the penance. Thus, one who has been assigned a penance is indeed eligible for the duties of the twice-born (*dvijāti*), since he has not fallen from caste (*apatita*). “Obstruction” (*pratirambhaḥ*) means hostility. Regarding the phrase “having committed the murder of a woman or a friend,” it is not merely any woman that is intended, because otherwise the mention of the *Ātreyī* would be rendered meaningless. For this very reason, Aṅgiras states the specific distinction regarding her.

Having killed the blameless wife of a foremost twice-born man who has maintained the sacred fires, one should perform the penance for killing a Brahmin; the same applies to the slayer of an Ātreyī woman.
Parāśara, however, states another distinction:
"Having killed a woman in her menses, one should perform the vow prescribed for a killer of a Brahmin."

Viṣṇu states: "Having killed a Brāhmaṇa who has undertaken this great vow (*mahāvrata*), one should perform [the penance] for twelve years; or [having killed] a woman of the Atri lineage (*ātreyī*), or a female friend. By this, it is implied that she belongs to the lineage of Atri. Vasiṣṭha, however, says something else (to the same effect): "They call a woman who has bathed after her menses an *ātreyī*," thereby indicating that she remains an *ātreyī* from the onset of menstruation for sixteen days and nights. Here, the etymological demonstration—"for her offspring (*apatya*) arises [from such a union]"—is intended to exclude a barren woman; otherwise, [the definition] would be meaningless, according to some. Others hold that this is merely for the sake of etymology. He (Vasiṣṭha) himself prescribes the extension of another vow for killing a non-*ātreyī*: "Having killed a Brāhmaṇa woman who is not an *ātreyī*, [one should observe the vow] for one year; having killed a Kṣatriya woman, as in the case of killing a Kṣatriya; having killed a Vaiśya woman, as in the case of killing a Vaiśya; having killed a Śūdra woman, as in the case of killing a Śūdra. The meaning is this: having killed a Brāhmaṇa woman who is not an *ātreyī*, one should perform whatever vow has been prescribed for killing a Kṣatriya for one year. The same applies to the subsequent cases. Having killed a Śūdra woman, a year-long expiation must be performed. As for the statement that the killing of a woman's fetus is a minor offense (*upapātaka*), that should be understood to refer to the killing of a fetus whose female nature is already manifested. Viṣṇu states: "In the case of a lie regarding one's own excellence, or in the case of persistent false accusation against a teacher, or in the case of slandering him, one subsists on milk for a month. This refers to cases of minor offenses. In the case of a major offense, the very expiation for killing a Brāhmaṇa applies. For this very reason, the venerable Yājñavalkya did not prescribe a separate expiation for reviling a teacher and so forth, as they are declared to be equal to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa and other such crimes. (YDh 3.251)
Moreover:
"Even if one does not actually kill, one should observe the vow [of penance] if one has come together with the intent to kill."

If one has set out to kill a Brāhmaṇa but does not kill him due to the force of an obstacle—and not by virtue of scriptural authority—nevertheless, he must perform the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa. It is not proper that the same vow should apply equally to one who has committed the killing and one who has not; therefore, for one who does not kill, a three-quarter (pādona) penance should be prescribed. The same applies to the killing of a Kṣatriya and others. As for what was stated by Gautama: “If he has touched [the intent] regarding the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, even if he does not kill,” there the mention of the Brāhmaṇa is for the sake of illustration. Āpastamba says: “In a conflict between dharma and artha, this very penance applies to one who chooses the artha”; the meaning is that it is the vow of a Brāhmaṇa-slayer itself.
Moreover: "And if a Brahmin is situated at a Soma-sacrifice, one should observe double the penance. (3.252)

Upon the killing of a Brāhmaṇa who has undergone initiation (*dīkṣā*) for a *Soma* sacrifice, one should perform the vow for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā-vrata*) twice over. Likewise, for one who has set out to kill him but does not actually kill him, the penance is likewise double, though reduced by one-quarter. Thus far, certain vows for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa have been stated by the venerable Yājñavalkya; other sages also mention some others. Among them, Jamadagni says:
"Or else, one should go to Vārāṇasī, or to the Setu, Śrīparvata, and so forth; one should also visit other sacred fords (*tīrtha*s) and likewise mutter the *Gāyatrī*. [1065]
Atri:
A Brahmin who has killed a Brahmin shall then practice the Gāyatrī for three years;
being self-controlled and pure, he should perform one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) every day.
A thief shall perform this very same vow for a period reduced by one quarter;
having approached the bed of his teacher unintentionally, he shall perform this very same [vow].
In the case of those who instigate others to commit acts equal to the killing of a Brahmin, a man who performs the *kṛcchra* penance for six years is purified;
by performing the *parāka* penance month after month, he removes the sin in three years.
One who eats [only] once a month is purified within a year; of this there is no doubt.
One should duly bestow a thousand cows upon worthy recipients.
Even a slayer of a Brahmin shall be liberated from all sins indeed.

"One who eats after a month has passed is called a *māsāśī*. Devala says: "By properly renouncing the body at most meritorious sacred sites (*tīrtha*), a Brāhmaṇa is liberated from great sins (*mahāpātaka*). By giving up one's life in a righteous war, or in the seizing of cattle, the destruction of a village, and so forth, a Kṣatriya is purified. Viṣṇu says:
"Those who have committed great sins may be purified here by means of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), or by visiting all the sacred sites on earth."
Regarding the persistence of a major sin (mahāpātaka), Kaśyapa states:
"For the sake of purification, a man should perform the Kṛcchra penance for three years,
or he should give gold equal to his own weight, which brings satisfaction to a Brahmin."
From the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
If one should intentionally kill a Brāhmaṇa who is a Brāhmaṇa by birth alone,
he should then give a thousand cows or perform the Svarjit sacrifice.
Aṅgiras:
That which is the assembly for Brāhmaṇas shall be double for kings, and triple for Vaiśyas; such is the assembly and the vow that is prescribed.
On this point, the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa* states:
"A Kṣatriya, having killed a Brāhmaṇa, shall perform two penances; or he may sacrifice with the Aśvamedha. In the case of a Vaiśya, it is recorded that [the penance] is double that."

The meaning is that there are two types of penance, namely the twelve-year penance (*dvādaśavārṣika*). It is understood from the injunctions for sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha that there is no abandonment of the *vaitāna* (sacrificial) fires for one who has fallen (*patita*). For this very reason, Kātyāyana states:

"If one possessed of the sacred fires should, by fate, become joined with a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), a son or other relative shall maintain those fires, being diligent, until the destruction of the fault."
If one does not perform the expiation, or if one dies while performing it,
one should extinguish the entire household fire and cast away everything along with its implements.
One should pacify both with water, since fire arose from the waters;
one should give the vessels to a Brahmin, or burn them, or cast them into the water.

The meaning is: "until the exhaustion of faults" (doṣasaṃkṣaya) and "until the completion of the expiation" (prāyaścittāpavarga). This being the case, statements such as "one should cast the sacrificial fires into the water and burn the sacrificial vessels" are to be understood as applying to one who does not perform expiation. (From the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.)
O Lord of the Gods, having killed a Brahmin, a Vaiśya must perform three penances for twelve years,
subsisting on alms and dwelling in the forest.
Reciting any one of the Vedas, eating sparingly and with his senses controlled, he should walk a hundred yojanas in order to remove the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having shaved his head, he should dwell at the edge of a village, or in a cow-pen, or in a hermitage,
or at the foot of a tree, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
Or a Śūdra, having killed a Brāhmaṇa, shall perform fourfold penance for the sake of self-purification; listen duly, O observer of noble vows.
O Guha, having first given his entire possession to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas,
he should thereafter subsist on sacrificial food and proceed upstream along the Sarasvatī.
Then, having shaved his head and subsisting on alms, he should go to Setubandha;
there, for the sake of cows or for the sake of Brahmins, he should properly sacrifice his life.

Śaṅkha says: "A killer of a Brāhmaṇa who acted unintentionally, with the consent of the assembly, shall wander about proclaiming his own deed, carrying a skull-topped staff, wearing the skin of a donkey, eating the remains of food fallen into an earthen vessel, bearing a banner marked by a skull, subsisting on a single meal a day, and making his dwelling in deserted houses, mountain caves, riverbanks, or at the roots of trees. Having given a thousand cows in this manner after twelve years, he attains purification. Or, having in the interim saved a Brāhmaṇa from death or protected twelve cows, he becomes pure immediately upon bathing in the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. [1067] Furthermore, the subject is stated in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa as follows:
"But that expiation which was declared by the high-souled Śaṅkha, O hero, is proclaimed for the destruction of a Brahmin present at a sacrifice. Thus [says Śaṅkha].

Vasiṣṭha states: "Now, furthermore, for the killing of a learned Brahmin (bhrūṇahatyā), one should subsist on water for twelve nights and likewise fast for twelve nights. The scope of this rule is also stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*.
When one is utterly devoid of virtues, excluded even from the Gāyatrī, and likewise slain by his own actions— then hear from me what shall become of him.
If a killer who is unable to give [the prescribed gift] should at that time reflect thus:
"Vasiṣṭha has declared this as the means for removing the sin of killing a Brahmin."

"One should subsist on water for twelve nights and fast for twelve nights. Thus say Śaṅkha and Likhita: "One who eats the food left over by an outcast (patita) attains purification after twelve years by giving a thousand cows at the end of the twelfth year. Here, "left over by an outcast" means other than [food left over by] an outcast. This also refers to the case of killing a Brāhmaṇa engaged in a Soma sacrifice. Bṛhaspati says: "Or else, at the world-renowned confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā..."
A twice-born man shall become purified by bathing at the three sessions of the day and fasting for three nights.

There exist such expiations, both heavy and light; their application to specific cases must be determined by taking into account the place, time, capacity, age, caste, qualities, and so forth. Otherwise, the instruction regarding heavy penances would be purposeless. In the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*, Guha said:
"If a Brāhmaṇa himself should indeed kill a twice-born man for a certain purpose..."
O Lord, what indeed might happen to him if he were to suddenly strike himself out of anger?
Īśvara said: O Guha, having indeed shaved the hair, beard, nails, and so forth,
O hero, one who is devoted to that vow should practice celibacy for one year.
O Guha, O Lord, when a Brahmin, having lost his wealth such as house and field, suddenly kills himself out of anger due to some grievance, the king becomes devoid of merit.
One who has committed the murder of a Brahmin should perform the three-year vow in the forest;
thus he attains purification, provided that he dies by taking his own life.
O sinless son, when a Brahmin devoid of virtues dies after having been insulted, that very act serves as the cause for his complete purification.
A Brahmin shall become pure by practicing celibacy for three years;
or, subsisting on restricted food, he may travel against the current of the Sarasvatī.
O son, a brahmin who is utterly devoid of qualities, yet stands far above those possessed of qualities, dies while being reviled, even without [close] kinship.
One should perform this expiation for the purification of that sin;
for three years, a man should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for the sake of complete purification.
One should indeed give gold equal to one's own weight to satisfy a Brahmin;
however, having spoken such words, if a weapon were offered and a Brahmin were killed, he would go to destruction.
I shall now declare the atonement for one who thus neglects a dying Brahmin, especially for such a person who is devoid of virtue.
Having shaved his head, including the top-knot, O Guha, being purified and likewise anointed,
he should burn himself in the fire from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head.
"Chāta" means fasting.
O Guha, listen with a focused mind as I declare the atonement for those many Brahmins who kill a single innocent Brahmin.
Among them, he by whose blow that Brahmin met his death shall perform penance upstream along the Sarasvatī for the purification of his sin.
"O son Guha, lord of the fourfold knowledge, others may perform this expiation for the sake of purification; they should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for two six-month periods."
Lions and the like, as well as serpents, and the king and the assembly of Brahmins—
these are not tainted by fault even while destroying the entire world.
When personal satisfaction regarding the relative weight [of the mantra] does not arise,
it is taught that its fulfillment should indeed be achieved through recitation and other such means.
And for all [offenses], including recitations and so forth, this is declared in all the Dharmaśāstras as a specific expiation for every case.
O tiger among gods, the great purification consists of recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth;
namely, recitation, austerity, fire-offerings, fasting, and the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite.
This is the supreme purification for sins committed both knowingly and unknowingly.
And regarding the expiations taught in other scriptures, O Lord of the Gods.
For in this way, the object must always be considered in terms of its relative gravity or lightness.
Thus ends the section on the expiation for the killing of a Brahmin.
He now states the penances for drinking intoxicating liquor, which follow in the order of the enumeration:
"A drinker of *surā* who has drunk any one of water, clarified butter, cow’s urine, or milk that has been made to resemble fire by [boiling] shall attain purification through death. (3.253)

Any one of the [forbidden] liquors such as *surā* becomes like fire through its heat due to being heated; when it is drunk, death occurs for the drinker. Having drunk such a substance, the liquor-drinker becomes purified by death. This refers to the case of intentional drinking of *surā*. And so says Manu:
"For intentional [drinking], there is no other prescription; the established rule is that it ends with life."

"Intentionally" means preceded by desire. By stating that it is "inexplicable," he indicates that one should perform the penance resulting in death even without it being declared by an assembly, having understood it for oneself from the scriptures. On this point, the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa* states:
"Gauḍī, Paiṣṭī, and Mādhvī—these three types of liquor are to be known.
Just as one is so are all; they must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born."
For the liquor made from flour is declared to be the primary [type]; the others are not equal to it.

The meaning is that the word *surā* refers primarily to [the third type of liquor] among the two others. And here, the mention of "the best of the twice-born" (*dvijottama*) is intended to be significant; by this, only the *paiṣṭī* (grain-based) liquor is prohibited for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, not the other two. Furthermore, even the intermediate types of intoxicants are prohibited only for the Brāhmaṇa, not for the other two. As Manu says: "Liquor, meat, and spirituous extracts of *surā* are the food of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas.
That must not be consumed by a Brāhmaṇa who eats the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) of the gods."

Consequently, even prior to initiation (*upanayana*), wine must be avoided by the twice-born (*dvijāti*); however, for a Brāhmaṇa, even liquor derived from molasses (*gauḍī*) or honey (*mādhvī*) and the like [is forbidden]. For the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya, however, [the prohibition applies] only while they are students (*brahmacārin*). As for that which was stated by Gautama: "Prior to initiation, there is freedom of action, speech, and consumption," that is intended to signify the cessation of restrictive rules such as "one must eat only what has been offered" or "one must rinse the mouth after eating," and not to grant permission for the consumption of things that are otherwise unfit to be eaten. For this very reason, Jātūkarṇya says: "If a boy who has not been initiated should drink liquor out of delusion..."
"His mother, brother, and likewise his father shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances. Thus it is said.

Regarding the drinking of *surā*, however, six *kṛcchras* are to be prescribed; for it is observed that the penance for drinking *surā* is doubled compared to the drinking of other intoxicants (*madya*). And this applies after the fifth year; prior to that, there is no fault. As Kumāra says:
"In the case of consuming liquor, urine, or excrement, there is no [penalty] whatsoever."
"But the fault [of drinking] lasts until the fifth year; after that, [the responsibility for] parents, friends, and teachers [is incurred].

Thus, it should be understood that the prohibition against the twice-born drinking liquor applies from the fifth year onwards. Furthermore, even for a child, there is no penance ending in death (*maraṇāntika*), because a penance ending in death is not to be prescribed by an assembly (*parṣad*); rather, it must be performed by the individual himself once he has understood it. In that regard, if even a child is of mature intellect, then the penance ending in death is indeed required. And the statements regarding leniency refer to such cases. As Viṣṇu says:
"One who is eighty years of age, or even a child under sixteen,
as well as women and the sick, deserve only half of the penance. Thus says Pulastya.
Half [of the fine] should be given to women, as well as to the elderly and the sick;
a quarter should be given to children—this is the rule regarding all offenses.
Likewise:
"One who is unconditioned, one who lacks enthusiasm, one who is ill, and one who is ninety years old—one should practice the vow according to one's ability; for among these, the vow is not violated."
Aṅgiras: For one who is less than eleven years old but more than five years old,
the teacher or even a friend should perform the penance for the sake of purification.

Furthermore, it is not logical to conceive of the penance for one who dies [from drinking] as being half of a quarter-penance. Moreover, there is liquor other than that made from molasses (*gauḍī*) and honey (*mādhvī*); because of these varieties, Bṛhad-Viṣṇu says:

"Liquor made from honey (*mādhvīka*), sugarcane juice (*aikṣava*), *maira*, *tāla*, dates (*khārjūra*), *pānasa*, that produced from honey (*madhūttha*), *mārdvīka*, *maireya*, and that produced from coconut."
These ten types of intoxicants are impure for a Brāhmaṇa.
Agastya, moreover, stated that it is of eleven kinds:

the juice of the jackfruit tree (*pānasa*), grape wine (*drākṣa*), honey-wine (*mādhūka*), date-palm wine (*khārjūra*), palmyra-fruit wine (*tāla*), sugarcane juice (*aikṣava*), liquor from honey (*madhūttha*), *maireya* wine, *āriṣṭa* liquor, *maireya* [from other sources], and coconut wine (*nārikelaja*).
One should know that there are exactly eleven types of intoxicants that are equal;
however, the twelfth is the liquor made from grain (surā), which is declared to be the lowest of all.

[Since liquor is of many kinds distinct [from *surā*,] but that which consists of *surā* is the last and most base,] for this very reason Vasiṣṭha says: [1071] "In the case of drinking liquor other than *asurā* or *surā* when done unknowingly, there shall be the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances, followed by the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśa*) and re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*). This should be understood as referring to one who is utterly incapable, a mere child, or one who lacks parents and such, and who does not know that this drinking is forbidden, having been forced to drink against his will. In the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*: "But regarding the drinking of *paiṣṭī* (liquor made from flour), listen to me concerning the expiation for these [other types]: there is no expiation for them."
O mighty-armed one, that which was spoken by Manu has been presented both in brief and in detail.
"Of these" means "of the gods. Yama says:
"Having drunk liquor through delusion, a twice-born man shall drink liquor that is fire-colored;
when his body has been thus consumed by fire, he is then released from the sin."
One should drink either cow’s urine that is fire-colored, or water,
or milk, or ghee, or gold, or the liquid from cow dung.
Having repeatedly drunk the liquor of Varuṇa through ignorance, the twice-born man falls;
death, as previously specified, is ordained as the expiation.
A Brahmin should drink the heated Vāruṇī liquor from an iron vessel;
it is fire-colored and removes sin, and by drinking it, he is liberated from that evil.
But at the time of the end of life, the rite prescribed for the cremation ground is ordained.

This refers to the *gauḍī* (molasses-based) and *mādhvī* (honey-based) types of liquor. Uśanas states: "One who drinks *surā*, dressed in cow-hair cloth, becomes purified after drinking *surā* that is the color of fire. Bṛhaspati says:
"In the case of intentional drinking of *surā*, having cast it, as if blazing, into his mouth, he shall attain purification when he dies, consumed by it."
Or one should practice fasting until one is separated from the vital breaths.

Devala states: "A Brāhmaṇa who has drunk liquor is purified by casting off his body after drinking one of these—silver, copper, tin, or lead—when they have been heated until they are like fire. Hārīta says: "A drinker of liquor becomes pure through death after having drunk liquor that is the color of fire, or after having melted gold, clarified butter, water, or milk. Regarding the phrase "having committed the drinking of liquor once," Aṅgiras continues:
"He may throw himself down from a precipice, enter a blazing fire, or set out on the Great Journey; thus he is released from all sins. (3.253)
He states another penance:
[1072] "Or else, clad in hair-cloth or even in bark, he should perform the vow for a killer of a Brāhmaṇa;
or he should eat oil-cake or even grain-husks at night for a year. (3.254)

Wearing hair supported by a tail, clothing made of that [hair], and matted locks, he should perform the twelve-year vow prescribed for the slayer of a Brahmin. Furthermore, the inclusion of the phrase "wearing hair" (*vālavāsā*) and so forth here is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) to ensure the application of the twelve-year vow for killing a Brahmin; otherwise, it might refer to some other vow of his. If, however, this were intended as a restriction regarding only two attributes—namely, wearing hair-cloth and having matted locks—then Manu would not have included the mention of "carrying a flag" (*dhvajitva*) here; yet he did include it.
"Or he may eat grains for a year, or oil-cake once at night;
wearing hair-cloth, with matted locks and carrying the [skull] banner, for the purpose of removing the sin of drinking liquor. Thus it is said.

One should eat oil-cake from which the oil has been extracted, sesame paste, or grains (kaṇāḥ) or rice, once a night for as long as a year. Regarding this, some explain the word *samāḥ* as being in the plural to mean three years; however, that contradicts the statement of Manu: "Or he should eat grains for a year. Precisely because of the expression "for the purpose of removing the sin of drinking liquor," it is understood that this vow applies to one who has already consumed liquor, and not to one who has merely touched the liquor with the palate. This is because the word "drinking" (*pāna*) is not applied to an action whose result is merely such contact. Even though the twelve-year vow prescribed for the killing of a Brahmin is extended here by analogy, the drinker of liquor should perform that very same twelve-year penance. As Vṛddha-Hārīta says: "Those who have committed mortal sins (*mahāpātakin*) are purified in twelve years. Furthermore, since the eating of oil-cake and the rest constitutes an ascetic practice (*tapas*), it excludes all other food. And the instruction regarding the vow for killing a Brahmin is to be understood as applying when liquor is drunk unintentionally and only once, provided it is immediately confessed. For this very reason, Vyāsa [states] in the section following the discussion on the killing of a Brahmin:
"One should perform this very same vow when vomiting liquor has occurred;
however, the consumption of *pañcagavya* is prescribed for him every day as a purification of the body. Thus it is said.

By consuming oil-cake and the like, one merely becomes fit for social intercourse, but there is no destruction of sin. For this very reason, Hārīta states: "Or, with the permission of Brāhmaṇas, by subsisting on cow-urine and dung for a year while following cows, and having undergone purification again, one becomes fit for social intercourse. Alternatively, it may be inferred from the general statement that even the consumption of oil-cake and such acts serves to destroy sin for one who is incapable of performing the twelve-year penance, as it is intended for the removal of the sin of drinking liquor (*surāpāna*). Regarding the phrase "having drunk liquor once," Aṅgiras says, continuing [the discussion]: [1073]
"Having performed the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice, a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk liquor shall again attain equality with Brahman"— this is the Vedic revelation.
If the best of the twice-born, having drunk liquor, should make a gift of land and never drink it again, he becomes purified once he has been consecrated.
He was brought before the court by a refined gentleman. Viṣṇu says:
"Indeed, for the drinking of liquor, whether done intentionally, through negligence, or even in association with others, two *kṛcchra* penances should be performed for a duration of one year."
In the first case, there shall be the *taptakṛcchra* penance and the rite of re-consecration;
thereafter, his second birth occurs, which is considered equal to that [first].
Then a Prājāpatya penance must be performed, and at its conclusion a Parāka;
by practicing the Cāndrāyaṇa three times, one is thereafter released from sin.
According to his ability, he should cause gold, silver, cows, and land to be given.

Sumantu states: "For a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk *surā*, there shall be bathing for six months in water drawn from the ocean; he should offer eight thousand oblations of the *Sāvitrī* mantra every day, observe fasts for three nights, and by means of the *taptakṛcchra* penance, he becomes purified—or else by bathing at the final purificatory rite (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice. Bṛhaspati says:
"Having drunk *gauḍī*, *paiṣṭī*, or *mādhvī* liquor, a Brāhmaṇa should perform the *taptakṛcchra*, the *parāka*, and the *cāndrāyaṇa* in that order."

This applies to one who has drunk [liquor] once, unintentionally and without desire, and has vomited it out, provided he is incapable of undertaking other penances. Penances such as these—whether heavy or light—should be determined by the assembly (*pariṣad*) according to the gravity of the circumstances, whether the act was habitual or not, and in accordance with the degree of its consequences, as well as the place, time, qualities, caste, and capacity [of the offender]. 3.254.
Furthermore: "If one has drunk *vāruṇī* out of ignorance, or has discharged semen, feces, or urine, the three twice-born castes must undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) again. (3.255)

If a twice-born person—whether a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya—should out of ignorance and unintentionally drink *surā* even once, or consume semen, feces, or urine, they ought to undergo the purificatory rite of initiation (*upanayana*). By performing the penance prescribed for the drinking of *surā* and then undergoing initiation again, purification is attained; however, purification resulting from the cause of the penance is not intended to occur through the mere performance of the purificatory rite alone. With this very intention, Manu also stated:
"Having unintentionally drunk *vāruṇī*, one deserves to undergo initiation again."
It is the established rule that [an offense] committed intentionally, which cannot be remedied by confession, results in the loss of life.

The drinking of *surā* intentionally is a penance that cannot be prescribed [by others]; even if it has been pointed out by an assembly, he who possesses the cause [of the offense] must perform it himself. Otherwise, the instruction [regarding it] would be useless. Likewise:
"Having unintentionally consumed feces, urine, or even that which has come into contact with *surā*, the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) again."

That which has been touched by *surā* should be understood as water whose *surā*-flavor has disappeared, such as water remaining in an empty *surā* vessel; however, drinking anything else [containing the flavor] constitutes the actual drinking of *surā*. Even in that case, purification must be preceded by penance. Regarding that penance, Śātātapa says: "Upon drinking water from a *surā* vessel, there shall be vomiting, the consumption of ghee, and a fast for a day and night. Baudhāyana speaks concerning the drinking of water that has stood overnight in a *surā* vessel: "He who drinks water that has remained overnight in the vessels used for drinking *surā*..."
He should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for three days.

And because of his asceticism, he should drink only a small amount of milk. Regarding the habitual drinking of water from a vessel that once held liquor, whether intentional or unintentional, Manu says: "Having drunk water that stood in a vessel for *surā* or likewise in a vessel that held intoxicants, one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights."

In this context, *payas* means milk. Regarding the unintentional drinking of water from a vessel that held *surā*, Viṣṇu states: "Having drunk water situated in a *surā* vessel, one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for seven nights. With respect to this same subject, Bṛhad-Yama says regarding habitual practice:
"If a twice-born man should drink water contained in a *surā* vessel, he should drink *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā* with milk for twelve days."

*Brāhmī* is *suvarcalā*; *lavaṇikā* is *brāhmī*. As for that which was stated by Gautama regarding the persistence of drinking liquor—"If one drinks unintentionally, milk, ghee, water, or air, heated, for three days each, followed by the *taptakṛcchra* penance; thereafter his purification [is required], as is the case with the consumption of urine, feces, or semen"—wherein the purification preceded by the *taptakṛcchra* is prescribed, even there the *taptakṛcchra* applies only to cases of minor offense; in other instances, however, another expiation (*prāyaścitta*) should be observed. For this very reason, Baudhāyana says: "For unintentional drinking of liquor, a quarter of a year-long *kṛcchra*. This means a quarter of a year-long *kṛcchra*, i.e., for three months. Vasiṣṭha says: "If any twice-born man should drink water situated in a vessel for intoxicants, he becomes pure in just three nights by drinking water from the *padma*, *udumbara*, *bilva*, *palāśa*, and *kuśa* plants; thereafter, there is a re-initiation (*punar-upanayana*), and there is an exemption from shaving and the like. And they cite here a verse from Manu:
"Shaving, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—all these are dispensed with for the twice-born upon the performance of the rite of re-consecration.
