And "liquor" (*madya*) refers to something other than *surā*. Regarding this, Pulastya says:
The juice of the jackfruit, grape wine, honey-wine, date-wine, palm-wine, sugarcane wine, wine from honey, wine from the *aira* plant, *ariṣṭa*, *aireya*, and coconut-wine.
One should know that there are exactly eleven types of intoxicants that are equal;
however, the twelfth, the liquor of fermented rice (surā), is recorded as the lowest of them all.
But regarding the juice of grapes, sugarcane, *taṅka*, dates, jackfruit, and so forth—
if a twice-born man drinks that which has been freshly expressed, he shall become pure after three days.
The Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa states:
"O Lord of the Gods, in almost all the treatises on Dharma, it is declared that for intentional drinking of liquor, the penalty is the loss of life."
"O Lord of the Suras, regarding the drinking of liquor distilled from flour, the sages have prescribed expiation for that alone and never for any other;
thus indeed was it stated by Vasiṣṭha."

But regarding the drinking of intoxicants out of desire, one must never drink *surā*. However, for the drinking of an intoxicant that is not *surā*, or for drinking *surā* unintentionally, there is the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penance, followed by the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśa*) and a formal re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*). But in the case of repeated practice, one should drink *surā* that is red-hot like fire. This [penance] applies to the intentional drinking of *gauḍī* or *mādhvī* liquor. O Lord of the Asuras, having intentionally drunk an intoxicant even once—
Having performed the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances, he becomes pure again through the rite of re-consecration.
"Intoxicant liquor" (*madya*) refers to that which is distinct from *surā*.
O delighter of a noble family, having unintentionally drunk *surā* made from flour,
one becomes pure by performing the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances and undergoing the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*).
This applies to the case of a very young person who is utterly incapable.
O Guha, a Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor, if he eats only at the fourth mealtime, shall remain for three years according to the rule for the sake of self-purification. [1076]
This [penance] applies to drinking *paiṣṭī* liquor once, whether unintentionally or intentionally, as well as to the repeated drinking of *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* liquors.
Having drunk *asura* liquor even once through negligence, the best of the twice-born becomes pure after ten nights of subsisting on cow’s urine and barley-gruel (*yāvaka*).
If a preeminent twice-born man drinks liquor even once through ignorance, he should perform the Taptakṛcchra penance; thereafter, by consuming clarified butter, he becomes pure.

Here too, only that intoxicant other than *surā* is intended. O Lord of the Suras, the prohibition regarding the drinking of *surā* and [other] intoxicants has been stated by Gautama and others as applying exclusively to the best of the twice-born.
That which is called the *taptakṛcchra* penance, as described by Gautama and others,
is prescribed for the unintentional drinking of liquor made from molasses (*gauḍī*) or honey-sugar (*mādhvī*).
O Guha, when the drinking of Gauḍī and Mādhvī wines is performed intentionally,
the auspicious Vāsiṣṭha rite should be understood as the means for removing all sins in that case.
The Vāsiṣṭha [Smṛti] states: "But regarding the drinking of *asurā* liquor," and so forth:
"If a Brāhmaṇa intentionally drinks *asurā* liquor, he who desires purification should practice the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for the sake of complete purity."
Or, regarding this very subject, one might prescribe a human ordinance such as:
"One should eat grains for a year," and so forth.
Likewise, for the habitual consumption of liquor made from molasses or honey, the penalty is declared to be the end of life.
O Lord of the Gods, if a Brahmin drinks the honey-wine even once through negligence, he incurs sin.
O best of gods, having drunk even once liquor made from molasses out of ignorance, one is purified by subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel for ten nights.
O beloved of the Brahmins, if a Brahmin has unknowingly drunk liquor made from molasses, the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances as well as the drinking of clarified butter are prescribed for him.
Having performed the *taptakṛcchra* penance and being purified through the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*), O Lord of the Gods, if a Brahmin intentionally drinks *gauḍī* liquor,
he should then perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance and give a cow to an excellent twice-born man.
In the continuation of the discussion on penances for acts ending in death, the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa* states:
"These penances are prescribed for the intentional drinking of *paiṣṭī* liquor;
now learn from me the penances for the drinking of *gauḍī*. [1077]
"Having performed the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice, a Brāhmaṇa who drinks intoxicants shall again attain equality with Brāhmaṇas; such is the Vedic revelation. (3.255)
Furthermore: "That Brahmin woman who drinks liquor does not go to the world of her husband; even in this very life, she is reborn as a female dog, a vulture, and a sow. (3.256)

A Brāhmaṇī who drinks liquor does not go to the world of her husband, nor to heaven and other such realms, even if those have been earned through virtuous deeds. Since husband and wife possess joint entitlement [to religious rites], the intention is that whatever world belongs to the husband—who is entitled to perform sacrifices—belongs equally to the wife; thus it is said, "she does not go to the world of her husband. Not only does she fail to reach worlds such as heaven, but she also attains a contemptible birth among dogs and other such creatures. Therefore, the meaning is that liquor must not be drunk by a Brāhmaṇī either, and if it has been drunk, an expiation must be performed.
Consequently, a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink liquor.

Considering that the gender mentioned in the phrase is intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*), [the author] states separately the prohibition against women drinking liquor. The authors of the *Smṛtis* also consider a qualification, even if it is not something to be adopted as a predicate, to be intended. For this very reason, the prohibition "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed" does not have the killing of a Brāhmaṇa woman as its object. Precisely for this reason, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa to one who commits the murder of an *Atreyī* woman and others. This being the case, when it is stated that "stealing the gold of a Brāhmaṇa is a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*)," it follows that stealing the gold of a Brāhmaṇa woman is not a mortal sin. Here, the mention of "Brāhmaṇa woman" is for the purpose of excluding women of the Kṣatriya and other castes. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha said: "The gods do not lead that Brāhmaṇa woman who drinks liquor to the world of her husband; she wanders right here with her merit exhausted, becoming a water-snake, or a pearl-oyster, or a female shell. Śaṅkha also said: "Liquor, garlic, onions, leeks, and meat are not to be eaten; for the body consists of essence (*rasamaya*). Because it is composed of that [essence], the Brāhmaṇa is so designated, since the embryo arises from what the mother has eaten and drunk. (3.256)
Thus ends the section on the expiation for drinking liquor.
Now, following the order of enumeration, he states the penances for stealing gold:
"But one who steals the gold of a Brāhmaṇa shall hand over a wooden pestle to the king;
declaring his own deed, whether killed by it or released, he becomes pure. (3.257)

Having stolen gold belonging to a Brāhmaṇa by any means whatsoever, one should offer a club to an anointed Kṣatriya king, proclaiming his own deed known as the theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold. Struck by that king with that club, he becomes pure; if the king does not strike him but releases him, then even without being struck, he becomes pure. Although the word *suvarṇa* here refers specifically to the species of gold, nevertheless, this expiation is to be understood as applying only to the theft of gold characterized by a specific weight, because it results in death. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
In the theft of gold, there is sin even by the taking of a single *māṣaka*;
we do not know what will happen by the theft of a full *niṣka*.
If even as much as the tip of a hair is stolen, one should perform *prāṇāyāma*;
likewise, for stealing even as much as a nit, a wise person should perform three *prāṇāyāmas*.
If [the sin] is the size of a black mustard seed, one should perform four breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and recite the Gāyatrī mantra eight thousand times for the purification of sin.
If [the theft] is the size of a white mustard seed, one should indeed recite the Gāyatrī for one day;
if it is the size of a barley grain of gold, the expiation lasts for two days.
Having stolen even a single *suvarṇa-kṛṣṇala* of gold, the best of the twice-born should perform the *sāṃtapana* penance for the removal of that sin.
Having stolen even a single *māṣa* of gold, the lowest of the twice-born is purified after three months by subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel (*yāvaka*).
"By stealing gold, one must subsist on barley-gruel for a year; beyond that, it should be known as a penance ending in death, or else the vow prescribed for a slayer of a Brahmin. Thus says Manu.
The thief must go before the king with disheveled hair,
running while carrying a pestle or a club made of khadira wood upon his shoulder.
By carrying an iron spade or a staff with a sharp point at both ends,
or even by undergoing punishment or release, a thief is freed from the guilt of theft.
"But if the king does not punish him, he incurs the guilt of the thief.
And that same [author] has stated: "Even a Brāhmaṇa deserves death;
a thief is purified by execution, or else by ascetic penance alone. [1079]

The interpretation that this statement is a restrictive rule (*vyavasthā*) is not tenable, because it would result in the word "or" (*vā*) being rendered meaningless. As for what was stated by Manu himself:

"One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is guilty of every possible crime," that refers to the subject of punishment (*daṇḍa*). This present passage, however, refers to the subject of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). For this very reason, he (Manu) speaks in the section on expiation: [as follows].
A Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king and taken up a club, should say: "May Your Majesty punish me."
Taking up a mace, the king himself should strike him once.

And here, the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is not for the purpose of excluding other castes; rather, it is for the purpose of setting aside the prohibition [stated elsewhere], namely, "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed. The prohibition "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed" refers to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa prompted by passion (rāga). However, in the case of a Brāhmaṇa who has stolen gold and returned to the king seeking his own death, there is indeed execution. As it is said: "Having seized a club, the king himself shall strike him once."

Thus, because it has been so ordained, this is indeed the duty (*dharma*) of the king; and by failing to perform it, he incurs sin. For this very reason, Gautama says: "A king who does not kill [the thief] becomes a sinner. But when even one who has been struck survives, he is purified by that alone. As Saṃvarta says: "Then, taking up a club, he himself should strike him once;
if that thief lives, he is then released from the theft."

Vasiṣṭha states otherwise: "In the case of stealing gold from a Brāhmaṇa, one with disheveled hair should run to the king, saying: 'O sir, I am a thief; may your majesty instruct me. The king should give him a weapon made of *uḍumbara* wood; with that he should take his own life, for by death he becomes purified. This applies when the king is incapable of dealing a fatal blow. "*Auḍumbara*" means made of copper. "Or, having shaved off all his hair (*niṣkālaka*), anointed with ghee, he should burn himself starting from the feet in a fire of cow-dung; by death he becomes purified—so it is known. One who has removed (*niṣkālaka*) the black parts such as hair is called *niṣkālaka*. Such penances ending in death are to be understood as applicable to theft committed intentionally. Thus says Aṅgiras:
"For that expiation has been declared by the wise to end only with death;
and that should be understood to apply to a sin committed intentionally—of this there is no doubt. (3.257)
He states another expiation:
[1080] Without having informed the king, one may become pure by performing the vow for a liquor-drinker;
or one should give gold equal to one's own weight, which brings satisfaction to a Brahmin. (3.258)

Even without reporting his theft to the king, one who performs the vow for drinking liquor shall be purified. If the thief possesses much wealth, he should give to a Brahmin gold whose weight is equal to the heaviness of his own body. If he possesses little wealth, he should give to a Brahmin gold that is sufficient to satisfy him by providing for his family's livelihood for as long as he lives. Manu says:
"One who desires to remove the impurity born of stealing gold through austerity should, dressed in bark garments, perform in the forest the vow prescribed for the slayer of a Brahmin."

In this context, the wearing of a skull and similar practices are excluded. With this very intention, the venerable Yājñavalkya stated: "While performing the vow for a liquor-drinker. This [penance] is to be understood as applying to the theft of gold belonging to a *brāhmaṇa* devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), committed during a time of distress for the sake of a family by one who possesses qualities (*guṇavat*). However, for one who steals a much greater amount belonging to a qualified person for the purpose of gambling and the like, the penance is indeed that which ends only with death. Regarding the word "thief" (*stena*), Āpastamba continues: "He may enter fire, or undergo severe austerity, or bring about his end by diminishing his food, or he may perform the *kṛcchra* penance for a year. "Diminishing food" means fasting. Sumantu says: "A thief of gold should offer eight hundred oblations of clarified butter with the *gāyatrī* mantra every day for a month; there is a fast for three nights. He becomes purified by the *taptakṛcchra* penance, or by bathing at the final purificatory rite (*avabhṛtha*) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. Thus says Laghu-Viṣṇu.
But when theft of gold belonging to a Brahmin has been committed,
he must restore it to that person with an additional eleventh part.
Then, for the sake of purifying the debt,
one who desires thorough purification should perform three *cāndrāyaṇa* penances over the course of a year.
In the absence of gold, this vow shall be fourfold;
one who has restrained the self and is free from attachment should perform it for a full four years.
Upon its completion, gold, cows, horses, and silver should be given according to one's ability;
furthermore, auspicious food should be offered to the foremost of the twice-born for the removal of sins.

"Elevenfold" means eleven times more than the original amount. Since that gift is prescribed for the purification of the debt [of the sin], one should practice for one year that triad of *cāndrāyaṇa* penances consisting of the *yavamadhya*, *pipīlikāmadhya*, and *yati-cāndrāyaṇa*, which constitute a supplementary part of the extraordinary (*apūrva*) expiation. However, if one is unable to give the elevenfold gift due to poverty, one should practice that same [penance] for four years. Regarding the continuation of the expiation for killing a Brahmin, Vyāsa states: "A thief should perform this very vow, reduced by one quarter.
Atri says:
Or a twice-born man may perform the *kṛcchra* penance for six years, or he may sacrifice with a *kratu*;
by wandering to sacred fords (*tīrtha*), the learned man is thereby liberated from theft.

The specific penance (*ṛtu*) for the theft of gold should be understood from the section on expiations for killing a Brahmin. The singular number is used with reference to the class [of the offense]. Sumantu states: "A thief of gold shall subsist on air for twelve nights. Thus, both heavy and light expiations are prescribed in the scriptures. For women, children, the elderly, and the infirm, as well as for these [other categories], half the penance is ordained. According to the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "Having stolen [gold], one should perform the penance after giving ten times [the value]; having stolen silver through delusion, a twice-born man should observe the *Cāndrāyaṇa* vow."
Beyond ten *vaṭaka* coins and up to a hundred, one should perform a double penance;
up to a thousand, however, it is triple; beyond that, the procedure for gold is prescribed.
For all other metals and alloys, one should perform the *parāka* penance.
From the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"But those lowest of men who seize [property] by force through their own will—
for those snatchers by force, the penalty ending in death is declared here."
In the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*,
within the enumeration of the great sins (*mahāpātaka*), theft is stated to be the third.
Furthermore, it is never committed by anyone anywhere without prior intention.
O Guha, the sages declare that the state of being a grave offender is no different [in either case],
whether the one who seizes [the property] is a Kṣatriya or another, provided there is a purpose such as gambling.
And one should perform this offering, along with its subsequent rites, for the sake of purification at that very time.

It is known from tradition that one who has stolen gold becomes purified by burning himself with a fire of cow-dung, starting from the feet, while hairless and smeared with clarified butter, until death.
Having stolen gold from a Brāhmaṇa Agnihotrī, a Kṣatriya,
being hairless and smeared with clarified butter, should burn himself in a fire.
O Lord of Armies, the fault is indeed far greater when the theft involves the property of a distinguished Brāhmaṇa, even if the thieves are Kṣatriyas and others;
likewise, in this very matter of theft, if it is committed by the best of the twice-born, [the fault is even greater].
For when a minor offense has been committed by a Kṣatriya or anyone else, [the punishment should be light].
A consecrated king, as well as a virtuous Kṣatriya who has stolen the gold of a Brahmin,
shall perform this expiation.

In the case of stealing gold from a Brāhmaṇa, one should go to the king with disheveled hair and say: "I am a thief, O sir; may you punish me. The king should give him a weapon made of Udumbara wood, with which he should take his own life. It is known from tradition that by dying thus, he becomes purified.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "tathāsminn eva viṣaye" (likewise, in this very case) is as follows: In the case of stealing gold from a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the *agnihotra* sacrifice, the thief may be a Brāhmaṇa with extremely heavy consequences (*atyanta-sānubandha*) due to gambling and other such acts, or he may be a Kṣatriya or another caste with light consequences (*alpa-anubandha*). In that situation, if there is a consecrated Kṣatriya king possessing the requisite qualities, then the thief should perform what was stated by Vasiṣṭha regarding the theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold: "Having disheveled his hair, he should approach the king," and so forth.
"O King, having stolen gold from a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya should thereafter go before the king, carrying a piece of gold weighing one *niṣka*."
Therefore, O Guha, having obtained an axe made of udumbara wood, you should take your own life;
there is no doubt that you will avoid transgression if you live on, O observer of noble vows.
O Hero, O Lord of the Gods, it is for this very reason that the wise Brāhmaṇa, through his ascetic power alone, utters these words.

By the very word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "by penance alone," the death penalty is prohibited for a learned Brāhmaṇa; however, in this matter, for one who is unlearned, the death penalty indeed applies. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the statement of Manu beginning with, "A Brāhmaṇa who has committed the theft of gold... (MDh 11.100). || 3.258 ||
Thus ends the section on the expiation for the theft of gold.
Now he states the penances for violating the Guru’s bed:
"He should lie upon a heated iron bed with an iron woman; or, having cut off his testicles and grasped them, he should cast off his body in the southwest direction. (3.259)
One who has violated the teacher’s bed shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year,
or he shall practice the Vedic Saṃhitā for three months according to the Cāndrāyaṇa rite.

One who has violated the teacher’s bed (*gurutalpagas*), as defined by the aforementioned characteristics, shall lie down for the sake of death upon a heated iron bed glowing like fire; he shall not do so alone, but together with an iron woman (*āyasyā yoṣitā*). Alternatively, having himself cut off his own testicles and holding them in his joined palms (*añjali*), he shall go toward the southwest direction and there cast off his body. The meaning is that he should proceed until his body collapses. These and similar penances are to be understood as applying to one who unintentionally approaches his mother, a woman of a higher caste, or her co-wife; however, they apply to one who intentionally approaches any other such woman. And it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"But he who, having recognized his father's wife as being of the same caste, approaches her,
or who does so with his own mother without recognizing her, shall not attain purification unless he dies."

For approaching a woman of the same caste who is unchaste, or the wife of a teacher, unintentionally, one should—provided there has been no emission of semen and one has desisted—perform the *prājāpatya* penance for one year or for three months; or one should practice the *cāndrāyaṇa*, which will be defined below, while reciting the *svādhyāya-saṃhitā*. Furthermore, the penance ending in death (*maraṇāntika*) must be performed there, after confessing the act of violating the teacher’s bed (*gurutalpa*). As Manu says:
"Having confessed his sin of violating the teacher’s bed, he should lie down upon a heated iron bed."
Or he shall embrace a glowing iron image; by death, he is purified.
Or, having himself cut off his penis and testicles and holding them in his cupped hands,
he should walk straight toward the direction of Nirṛti until he collapses.

"Gurustrīgamanaṃ" means having spoken of or declared [the act] as a rule; "sūrmi" refers to a female effigy made of iron or other metals. Hārīta says: "One who has violated the Guru’s bed becomes purified by making a female effigy out of clay or iron, heating it until it is fire-colored, and embracing it. Vasiṣṭha states: "It is known that one who is clean-shaven and anointed with ghee becomes purified by embracing a heated *sūrmi* until death. "Niṣkālaka" means one who has not yet shaved his body hair, beard, or head hair. He also mentions a specific rule regarding the repeated performance of the *Prājāpatya-kṛcchra* penance.
Carrying a skull-topped staff or clad in rags, with a beard grown,
he should perform the Kṛcchra penance for one year with a concentrated mind in a solitary forest.
Restrained by his vows, he should practice the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months,
subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) or barley-gruel (yavāgū), in order to expiate the sin of violating the Guru’s bed.
— Yama.
Alternatively, having cut off his penis and testicles and holding them in his hands,
he becomes purified from his sin by standing facing his teacher.

Eating only at the proper time or at the eighth meal-time, always remaining celibate and observant of his vow, he should pass his time by alternating between standing and sitting, and approaching water for ablutions three times a day.
Sleeping on the ground, he dispelled that sin within three years.
Aṅgiras says: One who has violated the teacher's bed should quickly lie down upon a heated iron slab,
or else, having cut off his testicles, he should hold them himself in his cupped hands.
Or else, he may walk toward the northern direction on foot until his death;
by the liberation of the body, he is released from unwholesome karma.
Or he may observe the great vow (mahāvrata), or give away his entire possessions, or if he is killed in battle for the sake of his guru; thus one who has violated the teacher's bed is liberated.
The *mahāvrata* lasting twelve years is the vow for the slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmahavratam*). It has also been stated by Śaṅkha:
"Sleeping on the ground, wearing matted hair, subsisting on leaves, roots, and fruits, and eating only once a day—when twelve years have passed..."
The stealer of gold, the drinker of liquor, the slayer of a Brahmin, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—
these perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin) are purified by this vow.

Thus, that [penance] refers to the case of approaching a heavy (senior) wife who is of the same caste (*savarṇā*) and not approached intentionally (*amatipūrva*). As for what was stated regarding the extension (*atideśa*) of the *gurutalpa* vow by the passage beginning with "the mother’s co-wife, a sister," etc., which prescribes a penance reduced by one-quarter (*pādonam*), that refers to the case of approaching a senior wife (*gurutalpa*) of a different caste (*asavarṇā*). Even in that case, some hold the view that for a son of a Brāhmaṇa who approaches a Kṣatriya wife of his father, the *gurutalpa* vow lasts nine years; for a Vaiśya wife, six years; and for a Śūdra wife, three years. Others, however, say that everything prescribed by extension must be performed in its entirety, because the extension applies the rule without fragmentation, and there is no evidence for assuming a reduction such as "one-quarter less. Consequently, the statements of Yājñavalkya and Aṅgiras have exactly the same scope. And the very use of the word "equal" (*sama*) is the proof that the penances prescribed therein are not inferior [to the standard]; for we see the use of the word "equal" in cases where the scope is not inferior, such as in the expression "the minister is equal to the king. Vyāsa, in the section on the murder of a Brāhmaṇa, says:
Having gone there, one should perform this very same penance for approaching the bed of a guru unintentionally;
however, it is declared that for intentional acts, the penance prescribed for the previous cases is doubled.

Regarding the aforementioned acts such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā*), a twelve-year vow of penance is prescribed; the meaning is that even for such a sin, if committed intentionally, the penance becomes double. Sumantu states: "One who has approached the wife of his guru shall embrace the branch of a thorny tree for one year, sleeping on the ground, bathing three times a day, proclaiming his deed, and subsisting on alms; he becomes purified, or else by bathing at the final purificatory rite (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). This applies to the son of a Brāhmaṇa woman in the case of wives of non-gurus belonging to the Vaiśya class. Āpastamba says: "One who violates the wife of his guru shall put on the skin of a donkey with the hair outside, and wander for seven houses, saying, 'Give alms to me, a violator of my guru's wife'; this is his mode of livelihood for six months. This applies to the son of a Brāhmaṇa woman in the case of wives of gurus belonging to the Śūdra class. Viṣṇu states: "Approaching one’s mother, approaching one’s daughter, and approaching one’s daughter-in-law are *atipātaka* (most grievous sins)."
But those who have committed heinous crimes should enter the fire;
for indeed, no other expiation for them exists at any time."
Saṃvarta says: If that lowest of men should approach his mother or his daughter-in-law,
as well as his own daughter, there shall be no atonement found for him.

The meaning is that there is no atonement for one who lives [after such an act]. Uśanas states: "One who approaches the bed of his guru shall perform the vow of a Brahmin-killer for one year, or for six months he shall perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance. This refers to the son of a Kṣatriya who approaches the wife of his guru who is of Śūdra origin. Vṛddha-Manu says: "In the case of approaching the wife of a guru, or likewise in approaching the wife of a guru, one should constantly perform the *kṛcchra* penance for three years if it was unintentional."
Saṃvarta:
But a Śūdra, upon approaching a Brahmin woman, shall perform the penance for violating the Guru’s bed;
having approached her either unknowingly or knowingly, the settled rule is that it ends only with his life.

Vasiṣṭha: "If a Śūdra should approach a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should encircle the Śūdra with creepers and cast him into the fire; having caused the shaving of the Brāhmaṇī’s head and having anointed her with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a black donkey and cause her to be driven along the high road. It is known from tradition that she becomes purified. The word "on the head" (*śirasi*) is used to indicate that the shaving of multiple tufts of hair is required. "If a Vaiśya should approach a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should encircle the Vaiśya with red *darbha* grass and cast him into the fire; having caused the shaving of the Brāhmaṇī’s head and having anointed her with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a white donkey and cause her to be driven along the high road. It is known from tradition that she becomes purified. "If a Kṣatriya should approach a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should encircle the Kṣatriya with reed-shards (*śara-patra*) and cast him into the fire; having caused the shaving of the Brāhmaṇī’s head and having anointed her with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a white donkey and cause her to be driven along the high road. It is known from tradition that she becomes purified. The "high road" (*mahāpatha*) refers to the royal highway. "She becomes purified" means she becomes fit for religious rites (*prāyaścitta*). Yama:
Emission of semen into virgins, Cāṇḍāla women, or women of the lowest castes,
as well as into the wives of one's sapinda relatives or offspring, is ordained to be expiated by the forfeiture of life.

This [penance] applies to repeated intentional intercourse with maidens and others, and to a single instance of unintentional intercourse with the wives of one's offspring. Regarding the application of the penance for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*), Hārīta states: "In the same way, for intercourse with the wife of a paternal uncle, a daughter, a woman of the same lineage (*sagotra*), or a sister, there is a *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance; however, if it is repeated and done intentionally, the penance for violating the Guru’s bed applies to intercourse with the wife of a paternal uncle and others. Otherwise, however, it is a *Cāndrāyaṇa*. After describing the penance for violating the Guru’s bed, Vasiṣṭha says: "And likewise in the case of the wives of the teacher’s son and pupil. Thus says Kratu.
One who emits semen into women of his own lineage, into cows, into the wives of disciples, or into the wives of friends or noble sons, is a violator of the Guru's bed (gurutalpagah). (3.259, 260)
Thus ends the penance for violating the Guru’s bed.
Now, following the order of enumeration, he states the rule for the penance of one who associates with the four types of outcasts, beginning with the slayer of a Brahmin:
"He who indeed associates with these for a year becomes equal to them."

Among these [offenders], such as the slayer of a Brahmin and others, he who lives together with them and engages in social interaction for the duration of a year—even he becomes equal to them through the performance of penance; whatever specific penance is prescribed for that [original offender], that very same one applies to the associate as well. Their equality in terms of loss of caste (*pātitya*) has already been stated previously. Furthermore, regarding birth-status, the attainment of that [original] penance occurs due to extreme association for a period of up to one year. As Devala says: "A man who, knowing it, lives for a year in the company of an outcast and mixes with him, shall himself become an outcast at the end of that year."

Bṛhaspati states the causes of contamination: "Sharing a bed or a seat, sitting in the same row, mixing of vessels or cooked food, officiating at sacrifices for one another, teaching one another, traveling together, and likewise eating together. [1087]
Ninefold confusion has been declared; one should not engage in it with the base.
Devala says: Through conversation, touch, breathing together, sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food,
as well as through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and marriage, the sin of men is transmitted.

By performing a sacrifice for one who is fallen, forming a matrimonial alliance with one, studying the Veda together with one, or eating together with one, one falls immediately; of this there is no doubt.

In this context, each act beginning with officiating at a sacrifice (*yājana*) is a cause for loss of caste (*pātitya-hetu*) because they are mentioned separately and not in a compound. However, conversation (*saṃlāpa*) and the rest are causes when combined. For this very reason, there is a mention of them as a copulative compound (*dvandva*): "conversation, touching, breathing together, traveling in the same vehicle, sitting together, and eating together. Here, "officiating at a sacrifice" refers specifically to the *Soma* sacrifice. "Giving a daughter to an outcaste," "taking a daughter from him," and "blood-relationship" (*yonisaṃbandha*) are also included. By the mention of "Vedic study" (*svādhyāya*), both the study of an outcaste and teaching one are intended here. Likewise, "eating together" means eating simultaneously from a single vessel. Each of these is a cause for the immediate loss of caste for one who associates with such persons. — Manu.
One becomes an outcast by associating with an outcast for a year through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or marriage; but not by sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food.

The meaning of this is as follows: by performing religious acts together with a known outcast for the duration of a year, one falls; that is to say, one becomes equal to him. In this regard, when the question arises as to which acts constitute the cause of outcasting independently of other acts, and which depend upon them, it is stated: "By officiating at sacrifices, by teaching, and by matrimonial alliance. Officiating at sacrifices and the others are each individually causes of outcasting without mutual dependence; however, this does not apply to traveling, sitting, or eating. Traveling and the others do not become causes of outcasting independently of one another, but rather only when they are dependent [upon the others]. Furthermore, in the case of matrimonial alliance, the act performed for a year consists of such things as eating in association with that person. With this very intention, Bṛhaspati says:
But in the case of association for six months through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and so forth,
or by sharing a seat and bed in one place, one should perform half of the prescribed penance.

Vasiṣṭha states that in the case of contact with an outcaste (patita) that is very slight and occurs unintentionally: "One must abandon whatever property (*mātrā*) has been acquired from them—whether through Vedic study (*brāhma*), officiating at sacrifices (*srauva*), or marriage (*yauna*). One should not live with them; it is known from tradition that by going toward the north, fasting, and studying the *Saṃhitā*, one becomes purified. Here, "Vedic study" refers to teaching, "officiating at sacrifices" refers to performing sacrifices for others, and "property" refers to wealth. Parāśara speaks regarding contact that is likewise unintentional.
If a Brahmin unintentionally associates with those who have fallen from their caste (patita) and others,
he should observe penance for five days, ten days, or even twelve days.
For one year, or for a single year, he should observe [the penance]; beyond that, it is equal to that [offense].
In the first case, [he should fast] for three nights; in the second, he should perform the Kṛcchra penance.
In the third fortnight, however, one should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra;
in the fourth, it should be a Daśarātra; and in the fifth, the Parāka is prescribed.
In the sixth [period], one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa; in the seventh, two Cāndrāyaṇas;
and likewise in the eighth fortnight, one should practice the Kṛcchra for six months.
Regarding the case of intentional association, however, another Smṛti states:
"In the case of five days, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; in ten days, the Taptakṛcchra;
in half a month, the Parāka; and in a full month, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa."
But for a three-year association, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa;
however, for a six-month association, one should practice the Kṛcchra for half a year.
But if the contact lasts for a full year, a man should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one year.
Saṃvarta:
Whatever sinful person enters into association with these [sinners],
he shall perform the previously mentioned vow for six months or for one year.

The meaning is this: whoever associates for six months with these people, beginning with the slayer of a Brahmin and ending with one who violates the Guru’s bed, intentionally, or whoever associates unintentionally for one year, must perform the same penance as those very individuals. As for that which was stated by Vyāsa:
"Whosoever drinks [with] another for a year, he too shall attain equality with him;
that twice-born man should perform a penance for each of them that is one quarter less."

Thus, this refers to one who has been touched by someone other than those guilty of a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*). Bṛhaspati says: "Likewise, in the case of association for a year, and especially in the case of a blood relation, one should perform the penance for an outcast (*patita*) according to the rule previously stated."

*Yoni* means the female organ; the meaning is that one who has engaged in sexual intercourse with a woman who is either fallen due to such a connection or is herself fallen. As for what was stated by Sumantu—"In the case of association, one should perform the *Prājāpatya* penance for a year"—that should be understood to apply to one who has been touched by someone equal to a *mahāpātakin* (a great sinner). *Sāhacarya* means social contact. Viṣṇu states: "In cases of slight contact, excluding the sharing of food, drink, and so forth, purification is attained by performing the *Taptakṛcchra* and then the purifying *Cāndrāyaṇa*. Śātātapa says: "Having lived together with a fallen person, one is purified by the *Taptakṛcchra*."

This refers to contact with a small amount [of an outcast] that was unintentional. Regarding contact with a large amount, Śaṅkha says: "One who, having been touched by an outcast, seeks to purify himself, shall perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance for one year. Likewise, one who transacts business with an outcast, a betrayer of friends, a killer of those seeking refuge, one who lives by forgery, and one who subsists on water, lying in the water, the five-fire austerity (*pañcatapa*), or eating only *yāvaka*, shall remain [in these states] during the winter, summer, and rainy seasons. Here, the four months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa constitute winter; the four months beginning with Caitra constitute summer; and the four months beginning with Śrāvaṇa constitute the rainy season. One who "lives by forgery" is one who, while not belonging to any stage of life (*anāśramin*), wears the insignia of a stage of life. Likewise, he should drink cow's urine mixed with *yāvaka* for one month. In this way, he becomes purified.
Furthermore: "One should marry a maiden from among these who is fasting and possesses nothing. (3.261)

One should marry—that is, wed—a maiden related to these outcasts, such as those who have killed a Brahmin, provided she has been deprived of their property, has observed a fast, and has declared: "I am not theirs; they are not mine. Although born of an outcast, she herself is not an outcast, as Vasiṣṭha states: "They say that one born of an outcast is an outcast, except in the case of a woman; for she belongs to another. One may take her, though she be without inheritance (*arikthām*)," thereby implying that one should marry her when she is given by others or comes of her own accord. Likewise, Hārīta says: "One should marry the maiden of an outcast, after she has fasted for a day and night naked, and in the morning has been clothed in a fresh white garment, while she loudly declares three times: 'I am not theirs; they are not mine,' for the sake of a sacred ford or a difficult situation. Regarding the penance for a maiden born of an outcast, Baudhāyana states: "For those born from impure semen who desire it, the penances for acts causing loss of caste are reduced by one-third; for women, it is a third of that [male] portion. The meaning is this: the penance for men born of an outcast father is one-third of the penances prescribed for the acts that caused that father’s loss of caste; and for women born of an outcast, it is one-third of that [one-third] portion. (3.261)
Furthermore:

"One should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance after killing all those who are degraded. Having killed all those excluded from the castes—outcastes and persons of the lowest birth—one should perform a Cāndrāyaṇa for each individual. As for that which was stated by Aṅgiras: [1090]
"For abandoning, traveling with, eating with, or causing the death of all those who have renounced the world, purification is achieved through the Parāka penance; so it was declared by Aṅgiras."

Thus, that [penance] refers to the case of killing a low-caste person unintentionally; whereas the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance refers to the case of intentionally killing a low-caste person—there is therefore no contradiction.

Now, one might ask: since penances such as the *cāndrāyaṇa* and *parāka* are joined with the recitation of mantras like the *gāyatrī*, how can there be eligibility for them in the case of a *śūdra* or others who have not studied the Veda? To this he says:
"Even though a *śūdra* lacks eligibility [for Vedic study], he becomes purified by this [prescribed] time. (3.262)

Even a Śūdra who is devoid of the qualification for recitation (*japa*), burnt offerings (*homa*), and so forth, becomes purified—becomes free from sin—by performing the bodily rites as prescribed over this aforementioned period of time, such as months or years. Now, if this were the case, would it not follow that a cripple would have the qualification for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other rites even when they lack the *viṣṇukrama* steps, and a Śūdra would have the qualification even when they lack the mantras and other requirements? Do not speak thus. For in those [primary rites], a Śūdra is nowhere directly designated by a scriptural statement as the agent, such that one could postulate his qualification for rites like the *darśa* when they are devoid of mantras and the like. Furthermore, since there are twice-born (*dvija*) persons qualified for the performance of rites complete with all their auxiliary parts, including the mantras, the scriptural injunctions regarding the desire for heaven and so forth are restricted to them alone. However, in the case of penance (*prāyaścitta*), just as the Niṣāda is directly taken by scripture as the agent in the *sthapati-iṣṭi* despite being devoid of mantras and the like, so too is the Śūdra in the case of penances. And thus says Aṅgiras:
Therefore, having approached a Śūdra who always stands upon the path of dharma,
penance should be prescribed that is devoid of japa and homa.
Likewise: "A Śūdra shall become pure in time, provided he is devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins,
through gifts, or fasts, or likewise by service to the twice-born."
Jābāla also said:
"Brāhmaṇas prescribe a penance for those who drink [liquor] unintentionally;
some, however, prescribe it even for the intentional act of twice-born men and for Śūdras."
Having encountered a Śūdra who has committed an offense, one should always, while keeping dharma foremost,
prescribe a penance that is devoid of Vedic mantras.
As it was stated by Mārkaṇḍeya:
"These penances (kṛcchra) must always be performed by the three [upper] castes;
however, no entitlement to these penances is prescribed for a Śūdra."
Thus, that [text] prohibits the specific *kṛcchra* penance; however, one should indeed perform the *kṛcchra* excluding the mantras. As for that which was stated by Manu:
"One should not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor his leavings, nor what has been prepared as an oblation (*haviṣkṛta*).
One should not teach him the Dharma, nor should one prescribe a vow (*vrata*) for him. [10.91]

Thus, that [statement] is intended to prohibit the extension of vows that constitute penance for those who do not perform the *antarā-brāhmaṇa* rite. For this very reason, Śaṅkha says: "Having performed the *antarā-brāhmaṇa*, the instruction of the vow must be carried out.
According to logic and the path of tradition, for a Kṣatriya or others who have quickly committed a sin, one should perform the *antarā-brāhmaṇa* and then prescribe the entire vow.
"He who provides the livelihood for Brahmins, and he who is devoted to the Brahmins—he is to be rescued by every possible effort. Thus it is said.
Thus end the penances for the great sins (*mahāpātaka*).
Now, the penances for all great sins are stated; regarding this, Viṣṇu says:
"These perpetrators of great sins may be purified by means of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*)."
Or likewise, by following all the sacred fords on earth.

An expiation in the form of the Aśvamedha and other sacrifices is prescribed for one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and has performed his first sacrifice (*iṣṭaprathamayajña*), because the rites beginning with the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) must be performed by members of the twice-born classes. Similarly, the recitation of the *Saṃhitā* and other such acts are prescribed only for one who has studied the Veda. Furthermore, the Aśvamedha is a royal sacrifice. Therefore, if a king unintentionally kills a virtuous Brāhmaṇa, drinks *paiṣṭī* liquor, steals gold from a virtuous Brāhmaṇa, or intentionally approaches the wife of his guru, he should perform that sacrifice as an expiation for each of those great sins (*mahāpātaka*). Āpastamba states: "Having committed theft, having drunk *surā*, or having approached the wife of a guru—provided it is not the killing of a Brāhmaṇa—they should eat at every fourth mealtime and subsist on water. Performing the ritual substitutes for the Soma-pressings (*savanānukalpa*) by alternating between standing and sitting, they dispel the sin in three years. The phrase "provided it is not the killing of a Brāhmaṇa" is stated to indicate that this expiation does not apply to the murder of a Brāhmaṇa among the five great sins. Those whose eating occurs at the fourth mealtime are called *caturthakālāḥ*. "Eating sparingly" (*mitabhojinaḥ*) means those for whom the vow is non-satiety regarding food; likewise, "they should subsist on water" means they should perform their bath in water found on the ground. "Performing the ritual substitutes for the Soma-pressings" refers to [the three times]: morning, midday, and evening. "By standing and sitting" means they should remain standing during the day and sitting at night. "Wandering" (*viharaṇa*) means they should travel from place to place daily according to their ability. This should be understood to apply to a virtuous person in cases of stealing gold from a Brāhmaṇa lacking in merit, drinking *gauḍī* or *mādhvī* liquor once unintentionally, or approaching the wife of a guru once without conviction. And as for the vow called the *Vajra* which was declared by Aṅgiras:

Disciplined, bathing at the three sessions of the day, self-controlled, and established in silence, he should bathe in the morning and, remaining steady, undertake the recitation. He should recite the Sāvitrī and the Vyāhṛtis eight thousand times.
Having placed the syllable Oṃ at the beginning, and likewise at the end of each form.
Seated on the ground in the *vīrāsana* posture, well-restrained, he should perform his recitation (*japya*).
Sitting there, he should drink cow’s milk once from a bronze vessel.
In the absence of cow's milk, one should drink cow's curd;
in the absence of curd, one should drink buttermilk; and in the absence of buttermilk, one should drink barley gruel.
Whichever one among these may be appropriate, that he should drink;
or he should consume barley-gruel mixed with cow urine.
This Kṛcchra penance, which destroys all sins and is divine, was taught by Aṅgiras himself to be completed in a single day; it is traditionally known by the name Vajra.
One should prescribe this expiation for those who have committed mortal sins (pātaka), as well as for those who have committed minor offenses (upapātaka),
and for those accused of great crimes.
Those joined with great sins (mahāpātaka) are indeed purified in three years.

This also applies to the great sins (*mahāpātaka*). It covers the same scope as the rule of Āpastamba because the suffering involved is of a similar nature. For one guilty of a *pātaka*, the practice lasts for one month; however, for one guilty of a minor sin (*upapātaka*), it lasts for three months. Jābāla states: "One is purified by a year of *kṛcchra* penance for the theft of gold, and likewise for approaching the wife of a guru and for the drinking of liquor."

This [penance applies] to one who steals a small amount of gold belonging to a person of high quality who is destitute of much wealth and of low caste; and to one who, unintentionally, approaches once the wife of a Guru of low caste against her will; and to one who, having drunk spirituous liquor that is not the primary kind once unintentionally, has vomited it. 3.262.
Thus end the general penances.
Furthermore:
"The guilt of one who makes a false accusation is double that of one who speaks the truth."
And by speaking falsely, one incurs the guilt of a false accusation. (3.263)

For one who brings a false accusation—that is, one who represents a faultless person as being guilty—there is a twofold fault: both from the employment of a false statement and from the act of accusation itself. But for one who speaks of a fault that truly exists, his fault is equal, meaning it is commensurate with the fault being proclaimed. Furthermore, whatever fault belongs to the person falsely accused, the false accuser takes upon himself; the intended meaning is that he incurs a fault equivalent to the fault inherent in the accused person. However, there is no evidence for the transference of a fault belonging to one person to another person. Moreover, human testimony must be corroborated by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); in such a matter, the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) is not the authority, but rather the practical application (*kārya*). — Manu.
Having called one who has fallen a "fallen one," or likewise a thief a "thief," one incurs an equal fault through that speech; if it is false, one incurs double the fault.

Āpastamba states: "Having recognized a fault, one should not be the first to proclaim it to another; rather, one should remove it through righteous conduct. The meaning is that even if one has personally discovered a fault, one should not disclose it to others if they are unaware of it. (3.263)

Now, having reached the appropriate occasion, I shall declare the penances for minor offenses (*upapātaka*). Following the order of their enumeration, he first states the penances for the killing of a cow: "Drinking the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the killer of a cow should remain self-restrained for one month;
sleeping in a cow-pen and following the cows, he becomes purified by the gift of a cow. (3.264)
Or, being composed, he should perform the Prājāpatya or the Atikṛcchra penance;
or, having fasted for three nights, he should give ten cows and one bull as a gift.

A cow-killer—one who has committed the slaughter of a cow—shall subsist for a month on the *pañcagavya* (the five products of the cow: milk, curd, clarified butter, dung, and urine), avoiding all other food; sleeping at night in a cow-pen or cow-stable, and during the day following the cows, he must follow them with self-restraint while they move about, remaining indifferent to all other affairs. At the conclusion of the vow, he is purified by giving a cow as a gift. Alternatively, he may perform a *prājāpatya* penance. In response to the inquiry regarding the duration and the specific actions to be performed, the terms mentioned in the preceding verse are applied here. The phrase "drinking *pañcagavya*" is excluded because it contradicts the rules for the *kṛcchra* penance. Consequently, the meaning of the sentence is established as follows: "Sleeping in a cow-pen, following the cows, he shall perform the *prājāpatya* penance for a month; at the end of the vow, he is purified by the gift of a cow. Alternatively, he may perform an *atikṛcchra* penance for a month as previously described. Or else, having fasted for three nights, he shall give cows with a bull as the eleventh, or cows numbering eleven including a bull. On this point, Jābāla says: [text follows].
If one has killed a cow unintentionally, he shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for a month;
by acting for the benefit of cows and following after them, he is purified by the gift of a cow.

By association with this, the penances prescribed by Yājñavalkya, such as "drinking the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for a month," also refer to cases of unintentional killing. The relative gravity or lightness of these [penances] must be determined in relation to the place, time, age, and physical capacity [of the offender]. In all cases, the owner of the cow must be satisfied with compensation for the property. As Manu says:
"Whoever destroys the goods of another, whether intentionally or unintentionally, shall provide satisfaction to that person and pay an equivalent amount to the king."
Regarding these, Śātātapa has stated another method of penance that covers the same scope as the first method of penance:
"A killer of a cow is purified in one month by means of *pañcagavya*;
he should recite the *Gomatī* mantra and lie down in a cow-pen."

Some read it otherwise: "The cow-killer shall perform three *prājāpatya* penances; he shall also recite the *gamatī* mantra. Regarding this very subject, if the killer is virtuous, then that which was stated by Saṃvarta applies: "The cow-killer shall construct a dwelling in a cow-pen in the presence of cows;
there he shall sleep for half a month, lying upon the bare ground."
Barley meal, barley gruel, milk, curd, *śara*, and *śakṛt*—
the latter being the uppermost layer of boiled milk and so forth—
a man who eats these in succession shall be liberated from that sin.
He shall become pure within half a month, provided he is devoid of nails and hair;
his bathing shall be three times a day, and he must remain ever self-controlled in his senses.
A man, composed and free from envy, should perform this;
he should also constantly recite the Gāyatrī and other purificatory prayers according to his ability.
When the half-month is complete, that twice-born man should feed the Brahmins;
and when the Brahmins have finished eating, the wise man should give cows as gifts.
"If cows cannot be obtained, the price of a cow must be given; of this there is no doubt.
By this procedure, the killer of a cow is released from his sin. Thus it is said.

On this very subject, Śaṅkha also says: "A cow-killer, subsisting on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), shall fast for twenty-five nights; having shaved his head including the top-knot (śikhā), he shall follow the cows while covered with a cow-hide, dwell in a cow-pen, and give a cow as a gift. Paiṭīnasi states: "A cow-killer is purified by eating a handful (prasṛti) of gruel mixed with rice for one month, doing what is pleasing to the cows. This refers to the same subject as the rule: "He shall drink the five products of the cow for a month. Regarding one who unintentionally causes the death of a cow that was already near death due to illness, Sumantu says: "For a cow-killer, there is the gift of a cow, the consumption of the five products of the cow for twelve nights, libations of water, ritual rinsing, and following the cows. Alternatively, the rule of Sumantu should be understood to apply to one who causes the death of a cow through the force of fear or the force of an illness that has arisen. Parāśara says:
Death may occur unintentionally through the tethering ropes of cattle;
one should confess an unintentionally committed sin to the Brāhmaṇas.
A learned Brahmin who knows the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and is well-versed in the treatises on Dharma,
shall prescribe an expiation for a sin committed unintentionally.
When draft animals are being driven and struck with a staff,
or even when they are beaten with a piece of wood, a clod of earth, or a stone;
Whether they faint, fall down, or even die instantly—
regarding draft animals that have met such ends, I shall explain the procedure according to the rule.
Having risen, he should take five, seven, or even ten steps;
or if he himself takes a morsel of food or drinks water.
For those whose every ailment has been destroyed, no expiation exists;
however, in other cases, there certainly is expiation.
In the case of confinement, it shall be one quarter, but in the case of binding, it shall be exactly half.
For a distance of one yojana it shall be reduced by a quarter; and for causing death, the Prājāpatya penance applies.
If one neglects a woman who has been struck by cold or fire, or even one who has died by hanging,
in an empty house or similar location, one should prescribe the Prājāpatya penance.
Likewise:
"A cow grazing somehow might perish due to lack of protection—
whether by falling into a pool of water or being struck by lightning from a cloud."
If a cow falls unexpectedly into a pit, or even if it is devoured by wild beasts,
the owner of the cow shall perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra, the highest vow.
One should perform a tonsure including the top-knot and bathe at the three junctions of the day;
[the image should be] endowed with horns, hooves, a tail, ears, and so forth.
Indeed, having donned that very moist hide, he should walk evenly;
he should dwell among them at night and walk with them during the day.
This applies especially to a Brāhmaṇa, as well as to a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya.
Then, once the penance has been performed, one should provide a feast for Brahmins.
"And one should give a cow together with a bull as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin.
From this very [text], the scope of this [rite] is understood. On this point, Aṅgiras states that it pertains to the same subject:
"In thickness it is the size of a thumb; in height it is the size of an arm."
That which is moist and possessed of leaves is designated as the staff (daṇḍa).
If one should cause a cow to fall by means of a measuring instrument beyond this [height],
the established rule is that one must perform double the penance in that case.
Whether by obstructing, binding, or yoking cattle, or by causing them pain,
or even by bringing about their death, one who is the instrumental cause therein is defiled by that act.
One should perform one quarter of the penance for confining [an animal], two quarters for binding it;
for yoking it, one should perform three-quarters, and for killing it, one should perform the whole.
In the event of a broken horn, a broken bone, or even the shedding of its hide,
one should drink the *vajra* for ten nights, provided that the cow remains healthy.
"Except for branding or marking, or when released outside, or for the sake of concealment in the evening, there is no offense in confining or binding [the animal]. Thus it is said.

When destruction occurs unintentionally due to causes such as tethering and so forth, it should be understood that the penance prescribed by Parāśara applies. Regarding this very subject, when there is the capacity for giving, that which was spoken by Kāśyapa is as follows: "In the case of the intentional killing of a cow or a bull, there is a penance. Some say there is one even for what is done intentionally. There is a penance in the event of death resulting from milking, taming, tethering, carrying loads, using a rope or noose, jostling, attaching bells or ornaments, yoking, feeding, giving oil to drink, or administering medicine. Having informed the Brāhmaṇas and shaved his head including the top-knot, he should perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance. At the conclusion of its performance, he should give a cow as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brāhmaṇa, and also a sesame-cow. This is to be understood as applying when death results from acts such as administering medicine out of negligence. For Saṃvarta says:
"In the case of confinement, for the purpose of treating a cow, or in the effort to release a dead fetus, if a misfortune should occur despite the effort being made, no expiation is required.
[1097] A *mūḍhagarbha* is a fetus that has died inside; or alternatively, it is a *gūḍhagarbha*. As for that which was stated by him [the author]:
But if many [cows] have perished due to confinement or even bondage,
or if a physician has administered improper treatment, one should perform the cow-vow (govrata) twice over.

Thus, that [rule] is for the purpose of preventing the recurrence of the occasional rite for every single occasion. And here, the deficiency of whatever has been performed according to the degree of intention (*matis*) or lack of intention (*amati*) is prescribed. Furthermore, as he himself stated:
"If some woman is killed by several people somewhere by chance, they shall each perform one quarter of the penance for killing separately."

Thus, even that [rule] which prescribes the infliction of injury is intended, according to reason, to establish the partial observance of the vow when the completeness of the vow has been attained. This applies to killing unintentionally, because of the expression "by chance" (*daivāt*). However, in the case of intentional killing, there is the application of the complete vow for each individual, because each person is a killer, and because there is no contradictory statement [to the contrary]. For this very reason, the doubling of the punishment in the rule—"For many who kill one [woman], the fine is double that which has been stated"—is logically justified. Thus says Āpastamba.

Cows should not be tied with coconut fibers, nor with hair-ropes, nor even with ropes made of muñja grass, nor with body-fetters; having tied them, however, one should remain standing while holding an axe.
One should bind [the fire] with kuśa and kāśa grass in a place free from danger;
in the event of a house fire that has taken hold, no penance is prescribed.
If one falls into a ravine, one should perform a *kṛcchra* penance; if onto a stone, one should perform two *kṛcchras*;
if into a large pond, it shall be half a *kṛcchra*; and if into a well, it shall be less by a quarter.
Kāśyapa says: One should perform the Sāṃtapana penance with wooden sticks, the Prājāpatya with clods of earth,
the Taptakṛcchra with stones, and likewise the Atikṛcchra with iron pieces.

The meaning is that after striking with wood or similar materials, one must perform the *sāṃtapanakṛcchra* penance; this applies only to the act of striking, not to killing. When those confined in a stable meet with disaster from fire or are killed by the onset of rain and wind, it constitutes the sin of cow-slaughter.
Furthermore, in wildernesses, or in difficult terrains, during a house fire, or among wicked people—
if misfortune should occur there, one quarter [of the penance] is prescribed.
A "quarter" (pāda) means one-fourth part. And here, that refers to the penance, not to the *prājāpatya* [penance], because the latter has not been introduced as the subject matter.

One who strikes with a weapon should perform three *kṛcchra*s; one who strikes with a staff should perform two. For striking with a clod of earth, one should perform an *atikṛcchra*; for striking with cow dung, a *prājāpatya*.
If the distance is one *yojana*, the penance is reduced by a quarter; likewise for bathing with muddy water.
One who steals a cow is purified by the *taptakṛcchra* penance, and one who crosses a river [for this purpose] by the *parāka* penance.
By stealing [grain] with one's own hands, one incurs an Ardhakṛcchra penance; by touching it, a Pādakṛcchra;
by means of a cart, a Kṛcchra; and by means of water, an Ardhakṛcchra.
If a miscarriage occurs due to the killing of cows,
one shall perform a Kṛcchra penance for each individual cow, just as prescribed previously.
If one foot has merely been raised, but both feet have become firmly planted,
it is declared that the vow is deficient by one quarter for having killed an insentient embryo.
When a fetus has developed all its major and minor limbs and is endowed with consciousness, one should perform a double cow-vow; this is the expiation for a killer of a cow.
The elder Prekṣitā says:
"When a one-year-old calf is killed unintentionally, a quarter-kṛcchra penance is prescribed for a man; however, it shall be a half-kṛcchra for a two-year-old."
In the third year, it should have three legs; beyond that, it should belong to Prajāpati.
Bṛhaspati says:
Having killed a woman who is excessively old, excessively emaciated, very young, or diseased,
a twice-born man shall perform the year-long vow according to the previously prescribed rule.
By the gift of gold, food, and sesame seeds, a person is liberated from sin.
Parāśara says: He who causes a wound must provide for its healing;
if death occurs because of that, his sin is equal to the killing of a cow.
If a horn is broken, one must fast for three nights; if a hoof is broken, the penance is double.
If blood is drawn from cows, one should eat only at the fourth mealtime.
Having struck with his foot and given the cow its daily fodder, he may eat at night.
Cyavana says:
A killer of a cow should perform the three Saumya penances or the nine-month Kṛcchra;
or, subsisting on cow's urine and barley-gruel, he is purified in three months.

For one who unintentionally kills a virtuous cow belonging to a virtuous owner, this is the mild specific penance: Saṃvarta says, "Having caused a pregnant cow, a tawny cow, a milch-cow, or a well-behaved golden cow to be killed by means of confinement or other such methods, one should perform double the vow."
As for that which was stated by Bṛhaspati:
"A killer of a cow is released from that sin after twelve days,
or else he should recite the Gāyatrī one hundred thousand times while subsisting on barley-gruel."
Having shaved his head until it is bald and wearing a girdle of muñja grass, a loincloth, and garments,
he shall dwell in a cow-pen in the midst of cows and follow them during the day. Having performed this vow, he should give cows and gold to the foremost of the twice-born.

Thus, this should be understood as applying to those who cause the loss of life, produce disease, or commit terrifying acts. For one capable of reciting the Gāyatrī, a recitation of one hundred thousand times is to be observed when there is an excessive transgression. Regarding this very subject, it has been said: "In this case, he may subsist on milk alone, or even consume milk and curd."

Thus, that [rule] refers to one who is incapable of eating for twelve days. Furthermore, some recite the opinion of Bṛhaspati: "For twelve nights one should subsist on *pañcagavya*, for six nights on *yāvaka*; one should dwell in a cow-pen according to the requirements of place, time, and physical condition; having shaved the hair of the head, beard, nails, and so forth, and having prostrated before the Brāhmaṇas, being permitted by them, at the conclusion of the penance one should give a cow and feed the Brāhmaṇas—this, says Bṛhaspati, is purification. That too refers to the same subject matter as the preceding rule. Āpastamba: "In wildernesses, in difficult terrains, in house-fires, and in pits..."
If there should be a failure in that regard, one quarter [of the penance] is prescribed.
If a cow dies there due to the fault of a bell or an ornament, one must indeed perform a vow; for that [ornament] was intended solely for the purpose of decoration.

In the case of treading upon [a cow] while it is being subdued, or when it is extremely crowded, or if it has perished due to dust, one should perform three-quarters of the penance. If the cow has actually died, one should perform the full penance.
In cases of excessive milking or excessive carrying, or by piercing the nose,
or when there is obstruction by a river or mountain, one should perform three-quarters of the penance if the animal dies.
If one yokes a weak animal to either a cart or a plow,
when an accident occurs, he incurs the sin of killing a cow.
Having caused a fracture of the bones of cows, or having cut off their tails,
or even having broken their horns, one should drink barley-gruel (*yāvaka*) for half a month;
fodder should be given to them until that wound has healed.
Having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of that same color, one is then liberated from that sin.

Thus, the penances prescribed in other Smṛtis that share the same subject matter with the Yājñavalkya-smṛti, along with their incidental details, have been shown in their entirety. However, where a person devoid of merit (*nirguṇa*) intentionally and deliberately kills a cow possessed of merit belonging to a Brāhmaṇa of merit by means of a sword or similar weapon, Gautama says: "And [for killing] a cow, as in the case of a Vaiśya. This means that one should perform the penance after giving away a cow, just like the penance for killing a Vaiśya. Regarding the killing of a Vaiśya, three vows (*vrata*) have been taught by him himself: first, having killed a Vaiśya, one should observe for three years the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) consisting of the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa; second, "one should give eleven bulls and cows"; and third, the three-year vow accompanied by the gift of a hundred cows. In this very context, by the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and a cow," another triad of penances is extended by analogy (*atideśa*). For if only the extension of the Vaiśya-vow were intended, there would have been only a single Sūtra stating, "having killed a Vaiśya or a cow. By beginning a separate Sūtra, he makes it known that another set of vows is also extended here. That extension is to be explained as follows: the word "and" (*ca*) should be construed by changing the order to "and a cow, as in the case of a Vaiśya. From that, by the word "and," the rule "as in the case of a Śūdra" is obtained. Immediately following that, in the case of killing a Śūdra, the previously mentioned one-year vow of celibacy and the gift of eleven bulls and cows are established; and as before, that too has a threefold nature. Thus, six vows are extended by this [rule]. In that regard, if the cow of a Brāhmaṇa householder who maintains the sacred fires—being an auxiliary to the Agnihotra and other rites, sustaining the family during famine, yielding much milk, having young calves, tawny-colored (*kapilā*), and well-behaved—is killed, and the killer is wealthy, devoid of merit, and a transgressor of many prohibitions, his penance consists of austerity accompanied by gifts. But for one who is destitute, there is austerity alone. For a wealthy man unable to perform austerity, there is only the gift. In this very same situation, if the killer possesses qualities such as Vedic study and the like, and this is the first transgression, then for him there is the vow for killing a Śūdra accompanied by gifts; for one unable to perform austerity, there is only the gift.

But when one kills, out of ignorance and unintentionally, the cow belonging to an owner possessing the aforementioned characteristics, Vasiṣṭha says: "If he should kill a cow, he shall remain for six months clothed in her moist hide, performing the *kṛcchra* and *taptakṛcchra* penances; he shall give a bull and a *vehat* cow. From the use of the dual number, it is understood that this instruction regarding expiation applies to two killers. In that case, for the killer of a bull, the performance of the *prājāpatya-kṛcchra* for six months along with the gift of a bull is prescribed. For the killer of a female cow, however, there is likewise the performance of the *taptakṛcchra* and the gift of a *vehat*; a *vehat* is a cow that miscarries, specifically a cow that has been impregnated by a bull. But when one intentionally kills a cow lacking the aforementioned qualities belonging to an owner who lacks those same qualities, Manu says:
One who has committed the minor offense of killing a cow shall drink barley gruel for one month;
having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with the hide of that very cow.
For two months, with his senses restrained, he should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent salt, at every fourth mealtime, and perform his bath with cow urine.
He should follow those cows during the day, and while standing, he should inhale the dust rising from them;
having served and paid homage to them, he should remain in the vīrāsana posture at night.
When they stand, he should stand; when they walk, he should follow;
likewise, when they sit, he should sit, self-controlled and free from envy.
One should liberate with all one's strength a woman who is afflicted by illness, or threatened by dangers such as thieves and tigers, or one who has fallen or is stuck in the mud.
Likewise, whether it rains, or when there is cold, or when a fierce wind blows,
one should not seek protection for oneself without first having done so for the cow to the best of one's ability.
Whether it be one's own or another's, one should not speak of a cow eating in a house, a field, or a threshing floor; nor should one speak of a calf drinking.
But he who, following this rule, attends upon cows as one who has killed a cow, removes the sin committed by that cow-slaughter within three months.
"One who has successfully observed the vow should give ten cows and a bull;
if these are not available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas. Thus it is said.

One should drink barley that has been turned into gruel (*yavāgū*). "One should eat at every fourth meal-time" means that, having fasted, one should break the fast (*pāraṇa*) at night. "Measured" means not to the point of full satisfaction. This practice of drinking barley-gruel daily should be performed for two months during the first month. However, all other rules apply for three months. *Vīrāsana* (the hero’s posture) is sitting without leaning against a pillar, a wall, or the like. One should perform whatever among standing, walking, or sitting is most frequently practiced by others. *Matsara* is the inability to endure the prosperity of others. *Ātura* means afflicted by disease. *Abhiṣiktā* means bound, as by dangers such as thieves and the like. One should liberate such a cow with all of one's vital breaths; the meaning is that one should do so regardless of one's own life. Regarding this very matter, Yama has stated a specific rule: eating at the sixth meal-time daily, the recitation of the *Gāyatrī* mantra ten thousand times plus one thousand, the recitation of the Vedas, the recitation of the *Praṇava*, and the recitation of the *Gomatī*. The *Gomatī* is described by him in the verse beginning, "Cows are always fragrant," and so forth. Thus it is said: [1102] Cows are always fragrant, cows are the source of all fortune, Cows are the supreme purifiers, cows are the highest heaven. Cows are the path to heaven, cows are the supreme austerity, Cows are the highest Brahman; there is nothing higher than cows. Cows support the world, cows sustain the universe, Cows are the mothers of the three worlds; there is no wealth equal to cows. Cows are the past, cows are the future, cows are the present, Cows are the eternal truth; there is no wealth equal to cows. Cows are the gods, cows are the ancestors, cows are the guests, Cows are the refuge of all beings; there is no wealth equal to cows. Cows are the sacrificial fires, cows are the offerings, cows are the priests, Cows are the fruit of all rites; there is no wealth equal to cows. Cows are the earth, cows are the sky, cows are the waters, Cows are the light of the sun; there is no wealth equal to cows. Cows are the protectors, cows are the saviors, cows are the physicians, Cows are the destroyers of sin; there is no wealth equal to cows. He who gives a single cow to a virtuous man, Shall dwell in the world of the Sun for sixty thousand years. He who gives ten cows, along with a bull, Shall dwell in the world of Indra for a hundred thousand years. He who gives a hundred cows, along with a bull, Shall dwell in the world of Brahmā for a million years. He who gives a thousand cows, along with a bull, Shall attain the state of Viṣṇu, which is difficult to reach. He who gives ten thousand cows, along with a bull, Shall become a *Brahmā* himself, O King, and dwell in the world of Brahmā. Thus ends the section on the gift of cows. One should also observe the following: one should not look at the rising or setting sun, nor at the moon, nor at a naked woman, nor at a woman in her courses, nor at an outcaste, nor at a corpse, nor at a person who has committed a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*), nor at a person who has undergone a ritual bath after a funeral (*sūtikā*), nor at a person who has just eaten, nor at a person who is vomiting, nor at a person who is defiled by impurity (*ucchista*). One should not step over a rope to which a calf is tied, nor over a water-pot, nor over a broom, nor over a stone, nor over a clod of earth, nor over a fire, nor over a weapon, nor over a person who is superior in status. One should not sit upon a bed, a seat, or a stone without first sprinkling them with water. One should not eat food that has been touched by a dog, nor food that has been looked at by a dog, nor food that has been smelled by a crow, nor food that has been tasted by a cock, nor food that has been touched by a menstruating woman, nor food that has been touched by a corpse, nor food that has been touched by an outcaste, nor food that has been touched by a person who has committed a mortal sin, nor food that has been touched by a person who has undergone a ritual bath after a funeral, nor food that has been touched by a person who is impure.
