One should not eat food that has been prepared for oneself alone, nor food that has been prepared for a group of people, nor food that has been prepared for a festival, nor food that has been prepared for a sacrifice, nor food that has been prepared for a guest, nor food that has been prepared for a deity, nor food that has been prepared for a funeral, nor food that has been prepared for a person who is ill, nor food that has been prepared for a person who is bound, nor food that has been prepared for a person who is terrified. One should not eat food that has been served with the left hand, nor food that has been served with the right hand while one is seated on a high seat, nor food that has been served while one is lying down, nor food that has been served while one is reclining, nor food that has been served while one is wearing shoes, nor food that has been served while one is wearing sandals, nor food that has been served while one is wearing a turban, nor food that has been served while one is wearing a head-dress, nor food that has been served while one is wearing a garland, nor food that has been served while one is wearing perfumes, nor food that has been served while one is wearing ornaments. One should not eat food that has been served in a vessel made of iron, nor in a vessel made of wood, nor in a vessel made of clay, nor in a vessel made of stone, nor in a vessel made of glass, nor in a vessel made of lead, nor in a vessel made of tin, nor in a vessel made of brass, nor in a vessel made of copper, nor in a vessel made of bell-metal, nor in a vessel made of silver, nor in a vessel made of gold. One should not eat food that has been served in a vessel that has been used for storing oil, nor in a vessel that has been used for storing honey, nor in a vessel that has been used for storing salt, nor in a vessel that has been used for storing spices, nor in a vessel that has been used for storing sour gruel, nor in a vessel that has been used for storing wine, nor in a vessel that has been used for storing meat, nor in a vessel that has been used for storing fish, nor in a vessel that has been used for storing vegetables. One should not eat food that has been served in a vessel that has been licked by a dog, nor in a vessel that has been gnawed by a rat, nor in a vessel that has been scratched by a crow, nor in a vessel that has been broken, nor in a vessel that has been cracked, nor in a vessel that has been chipped, nor in a vessel that has been stained, nor in a vessel that has been defiled. One should not eat food that has been served in a vessel that has been used for a previous meal, nor in a vessel that has been used for a previous drink, nor in a vessel that has been used for a previous bath, nor in a vessel that has been used for a previous purification, nor in a vessel that has been used for a previous sacrifice, nor in a vessel that has been used for a previous funeral, nor in a vessel that has been used for a previous festival, nor in a vessel that has been used for a previous wedding. One should not eat food that has been served in a vessel that has been touched by a woman in her courses, nor in a vessel that has been touched by a woman who has recently given birth, nor in a vessel that has been touched by a woman who is impure, nor in a vessel that has been touched by a woman who is angry, nor in a vessel that has been touched by a woman who is grieving, nor in a vessel that has been touched by a woman who is intoxicated, nor in a vessel that has been touched by a woman who is insane, nor in a vessel that has been touched by a woman who is possessed. One should not eat food that has been served in a vessel that has been touched by a person who is blind, nor in a vessel that has been touched by a person who is deaf, nor in a vessel that has been touched by a person who is mute, nor in a vessel that has been touched by a person who is lame, nor in a vessel that has been touched by a person who is leprous, nor in a vessel that has been touched by a person who is afflicted with a skin disease, nor in a vessel that has been touched by a person who is suffering from consumption, nor in a vessel that has been touched by a person who is
Cows are eternally fragrant; cows possess the scent of guggulu resin.
Cows are the foundation of all beings; cows are a great means of securing well-being.
Cows are indeed the supreme food; they are the highest oblation for the gods, the purifier of all beings, and they both protect and carry [the world].
With oblations purified by mantras, they gratify the immortals in heaven;
in the fire-sacrifices of the seers, cows are the initiators of the oblation.
For all living beings, cows are the supreme refuge;
cows are the highest purifier; cows are the ultimate auspiciousness.
Cows are the ladder to heaven; cows are auspicious and eternal.
Homage to the cows, the glorious ones, and to the daughters of Surabhi.
Salutation to the daughters of Brahmā, who are pure; salutation, salutation! Thus.

And this specific rule must also be observed in the *Mānava* vow according to the principle of "reliance on all Vedic branches" (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*). In this manner, other specific rules mentioned in different Smṛtis that are not contradictory should also be adopted. However, those that are contradictory should be applied as heavy penances when the connection with sin is more serious, and as light penances when it is less so. Moreover, Aṅgiras has stated that the acts of bathing, sipping water (*ācamana*), and so forth, must be performed with water alone. [The mention of "washing the feet" there is intended to indicate all ritual acts accomplished with water. Likewise, a specific rule has been stated that one should carry a staff like a student (*brahmacārin*). As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha:
One should perform three-quarters [of the penance] for killing a Śūdra, as well as for approaching a woman in her courses;
likewise for killing a cow, and likewise for sexual intercourse with another's wife.

Thus, this should be understood to apply to both the instigator and the one who consents. Baudhāyana states: "The killing of a woman and the killing of a cow are explained by [the rules for] the killing of a Śūdra. This is with the exception of an Ātreyī woman, and also of a milch-cow and a bull. For a milch-cow or a bull, one should perform a Cāndrāyaṇa penance at the end [of the period]. Others say it is at the end of the penance itself. A *dhenu* is a cow that has recently calved. Viśvāmitra says: "In the case of intentional cow-killing, one should perform four Kṛcchra penances; if unintentional, two should be performed, and half of that for the elderly and children."
In the case of killing a woman or a Śūdra, it is exactly the same; there is no doubt regarding this.
Alternatively, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed for all these occasions.

The *kṛcchra* penances, such as the *prājāpatya* and others whose characteristics will be described below, are intended; it is not the case that only the *prājāpatya* is to be observed. This is because they differ in their scope according to their number. Furthermore, this refers to cases where one is unable to perform the vows prescribed by Manu. Cyavana states: "Two *prājāpatyas* constitute the expiation for killing a cow. For [the offenses of] confining, binding, or killing with a tether, there is an increase of one quarter [of the penance] for each. One should shave the nails and hair, except for the tuft (*śikhā*); or, including the tuft, one should shave them. One should bathe at the three periods of the day, follow behind cows, sleep together with them, and graze them on very large amounts of grass in the streets. At the conclusion of the vow, one should feed Brāhmaṇas and give ten cows and one bull as the eleventh. In the case of confinement, there is cutting [of the hair]; in the case of binding, shaving the hair; and in the case of killing, shaving including the tuft. Yama says:
If one should cause cows to fall by striking them upward with a staff,
the established rule is that one must perform double the penance in that case.
Parāśara says: There is no vow without a sacrificial fee, especially not in the case of violence;
likewise, there is no shaving of the hair for women, nor sleeping on the bare ground.
He should not stay in a cow-pen at night, nor should he follow after them by day;
this applies especially to rivers, confluences, and mountains.
One should prescribe this very vow for women: they must not dwell in a secluded place;
having plucked out all their hair, they should cut off two finger-breadths.
In the same way, however, the shaving of the head is prescribed for women.
Saṃvarta states: "In the case of a one-fourth offense, there is the shaving of the hair on the limbs; in the case of a one-half offense, the cutting of the beard;
in the case of a three-fourths offense, the top-knot must be worn; but in the case of a complete fall [from caste], even the top-knot is removed."
One should give two garments for a foot [of the fine], a bronze vessel for two feet;
but for less than a foot, one cow, and for causing a miscarriage, a pair [of cattle].
When the Brahmins have finished eating, the wise man should present a cow;
but in the absence of a cow, the price of a cow must be given—of this there is no doubt.
Having given a bull to the officiating priests, the king should request them for the sake of his hair;
likewise, in the event of a siege he should give a pair of cattle, and in the event of captivity, a bull.
One should give garments at the distance of a yojana [from the village] upon killing [a cow]; eleven bulls upon the Vadha penance;
five cows upon the Sāṃtapana; and three cows upon the Prājāpatya.
Likewise, there are eight [days] for the *taptakṛcchra* and thirteen for the *atikṛcchra*.
Śaṅkha says: "One should provide medicine, oil, and food to cows and Brāhmaṇas."
For the purpose of sustaining the life of living beings, no expiation is prescribed.
Sumantu says: "In cases of affection, food, medical treatment, and emergencies, taking from all living beings is always considered a fault. Vyāsa says:
"Medicine, salt, oil, oil-cake, and likewise food—these should not be given in excess; one should cause them to be given in amounts equal to one's own hair [on the head]."
For those whose [portions] are excessive or spoiled, a *kṛcchrapāda* penance is prescribed;
one should give eight *palas* of oil and sixteen *palas* of milk.
And thirty-two mouthfuls of water—this is prescribed as the proper measure. One should give exactly this amount, never more than that.
An expiation is prescribed for the offering of what is excessive.
Yama says: For those who die at night while imprisoned, those killed by tigers or snakes,
and those perished by fire or lightning, no expiation is required.
And this should be understood as applying to cases such as binding according to the scriptures;
however, if there should be doubt in that regard, or if [the person] dies after being confined in the evening,
one should drink barley-gruel mixed with cow urine for three nights.
If, after causing the breaking of the bones of cows as well as the breaking of their hips,
one survives for six months, no expiation is required.

[The meaning is that there is indeed an expiation for such causes as the breaking of bones and so forth, but not the expiation for killing a cow. When an effort is made for the purpose of restraining [an animal], for the sake of treating a cow, or for releasing a hidden fetus, if death should occur, no expiation is prescribed.
For Brahmins who provide assistance through efforts such as cauterizing, cutting, or opening veins for the sake of the welfare of cows, no expiation is required.
One who dies while wandering in a pit for digging a well perishes during a house fire;
likewise, one who dies in a village pit due to thieves—there is no atonement prescribed for such cases.
There is no fault regarding medicine if one drinks it by one's own will;
however, if it is administered otherwise [by force], an expiation is prescribed.
The meaning is "an unqualified physician. Parāśara states: "There is no sin if a twice-born man dies from drinking medicinal oil, from eating food, or from the extraction of a fetus's placenta."
Bṛhaspati says:
Having killed a cow with a weapon or the like, one should perform the penance prescribed by Manu;
or, if it was by means of confinement and so forth, one should perform the penance prescribed by Aṅgiras or that stated by Āpastamba.
One should perform one quarter of a Kṛcchra penance for confining and killing [an animal], and half a Kṛcchra for binding and beating it;
one should perform one quarter of a Kṛcchra for confining and killing, and half a Kṛcchra for binding and beating.
In the case of those who must be carried across [a river], if one strikes them out of ignorance, the penance is three-quarters of a *kṛcchra*.
Regarding other minor offenses (upapātaka), he states the penances through both direct instruction and extension:
"The purification for a minor offense may be achieved in this manner, or by the Cāndrāyaṇa, or by subsisting on milk for a month, or again by the Parāka penance. (3.266)

For minor offenses (*upapātaka*) such as being a *vrātya* and so forth, purification may occur in the same manner as the method for purifying the killing of a cow; or else by means of a *cāndrāyaṇa* lasting one month, or by a milk-vow (*payovrata*), or by a *parāka* penance. The nature of the *cāndrāyaṇa* and the *parāka* will be explained later. Regarding the fourfold set of expiations beginning with the drinking of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), their instruction is intended specifically for the purification after killing a cow, not for the purification of other minor offenses; rather, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of these rules to those cases. For if they were directly prescribed (*upadeśa*) for all instances, then the specific duties such as covering oneself with a cow-hide, sleeping in a cow-pen, and following behind cows would not be set aside [in other contexts]. Indeed, that which is directly prescribed is not set aside. However, when there is an extension, there is a setting aside of those elements associated with the specific nature of the purification for killing a cow in other instances. This is just as the *pārvaṇa-homas*, which are associated with the nature of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, are set aside in their modified forms (*vikṛtis*). Furthermore, this extension of expiation for minor offenses should be understood to apply to unintentional acts; however, for intentional acts, the rule of Manu applies.

"Twice-born men who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) shall perform this very vow for the sake of purification, with the exception of the *avakīrṇin* [one who has violated his vow of celibacy], or else they may perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*.

Thus, the three-month penance is extended here by analogy (*atideśa*). Furthermore, even in those cases among the minor offenses where a specific expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is taught, [this same rule applies].
"Purification from minor offenses (upapātaka) may be achieved by this [general penance] or by the Cāndrāyaṇa," and so forth;

by such a statement, though it is generally applicable, the entire group of vows including the expiation for cow-slaughter is obtained. In that case, the relationship between the sublated and the sublater must be understood through the principle of the general and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣanyāya*). If that were so, their inclusion in the list of minor offenses would be purposeless. Therefore, both those prescribed generally and those prescribed specifically are to be considered. These ritual options for expiation, beginning with the consumption of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), are to be determined according to the commonality of the agent. (3.266)

The general expiation for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) has been stated. Now, he declares the specific expiations for particular minor offenses consisting of the killing of a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or a woman:
"For the killing of a Kṣatriya, a man should give one thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh, or else he should observe the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa for three years. (3.267)
A killer of a Vaiśya shall perform this for one year or give one hundred cows;
a killer of a Śūdra shall perform this for six months, or else give ten cows.

That which has one more than a thousand is "one-thousand-plus" (*ekasahasra*). That which completes a thousand is "the thousandth" (*ekasahasra*). Those cows of whom there is a bull as the thousandth are "cows with a bull as the thousandth. For the killing of a Kṣatriya, a man should give those [cows]. Or, he should perform the vow for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa for three years. Furthermore, a slayer of a Vaiśya should observe the vow for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa for one year, or he should give one hundred cows. But the killer of a Śūdra should observe the vow for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa for six months, or he should give ten milch-cows. This should be understood to apply to a Brāhmaṇa who unintentionally kills a Kṣatriya who merely follows his own livelihood. And so says Manu:
The fourth part of the penance for killing a Brahmin is prescribed for the murder of a Kṣatriya;
for a Vaiśya who is established in his duty, it is the eighth part, while for a Śūdra, it should be known as the sixteenth part.
But having unintentionally caused the death of a Kṣatriya, or having killed a Vaiśya who is established in his proper conduct, the best of the twice-born should give one hundred cows.

"A killer of a Śūdra shall perform this entire vow for six months, or he shall give ten white cows and a bull to a Brāhmaṇa. Here, "fourth" means the fourth part. The term "established in conduct" (*vṛttastha*) is connected with every [caste], beginning with the Kṣatriya; and "conduct" (*vṛtta*) is described in other Smṛtis.
Veneration of the guru, compassion, purity, truthfulness, and restraint of the senses,
as well as engagement in beneficial acts— all that is called *vratam* (right conduct).

Regarding the case of intentionally killing a Kṣatriya or others, Gautama says: "For killing a Rājanya, one should observe the standard vow of celibacy for six years and give a thousand cows with one bull. As for what Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Having unintentionally killed someone among the four castes, one should prescribe vows for twelve years, six, three, and one year respectively; at the end of these, one should give a thousand cows, half of that, half of that, and half of that again, in order for all of them"—this should be understood as referring to the killing of members of higher castes who possess superior qualities. As for what Vṛddha-Hārīta has said: [1107]
For killing a Kṣatriya, one should perform the vow for a Brahmin-slayer minus one-third;
for killing a Vaiśya, one should perform half; but for a Śūdra, one-fourth.

Thus, this [penance] refers to a Brāhmaṇa who has killed a Kṣatriya or others possessing similar qualities. Regarding this very subject, Vasiṣṭha also says: "In the same way, having killed a Rājanya, one performs it for eight years; six years for a Vaiśya, and three for a Śūdra. The word "in the same way" (evam) serves to extend the application of the vow prescribed for killing a Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, the quality of the killer must be considered here in relation to the Kṣatriya caste. Alternatively, these two vows mentioned by Hārīta and Vasiṣṭha—which are independent of the giving of gifts—refer specifically to those who are Kṣatriyas and so forth by birth alone. Viṣṇu states: "For the killing of a king, this Mahāvrata should be performed for double the duration. For killing a Kṣatriya, it is reduced by one-quarter; for killing a Vaiśya, by half. In all cases, the perpetrator shall have the head of a corpse as his banner. A "king" (nṛpati) is a Kṣatriya who protects the realm. The "Mahāvrata" is the twelve-year vow of penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa. Saṃvarta says:
But having killed a Kṣatriya, one is purified by three Kṛcchra penances;
and with a concentrated mind, one should perform three Kṛcchras in their regular order.
But if a man, deluded by passion, somehow commits the murder of a Vaiśya,
that slayer of a Vaiśya should perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances.
Having committed the killing of a Śūdra, one should, with a concentrated mind, perform the Taptakṛcchra penance.

The sequence, however, is the *kṛcchra*, the *atikṛcchra*, and the *taptakṛcchra*. This should be understood to apply when the killer is more virtuous and the killing was unintentional. But in the case of killing a Kṣatriya or others who possess only their caste status, the general penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) must be performed. Regarding other minor offenses as well, specific penances mentioned in other Smṛtis are now shown. In this regard, Manu says:
"Those twice-born men for whom the *Sāvitrī* has not been recited according to the rule..."
Having made them perform three *kṛcchra* penances according to the rule, one should initiate them.

"Three *kṛcchras*" means three *prājāpatya*, *kṛcchra*, and *atikṛcchra* penances. One should prescribe this very same [penance] even for those twice-born men who perform forbidden acts, those who desire to perform expiation, and those who have been abandoned by the Veda.
Yama says: He whose Sāvitrī has fallen for fifteen years shall,
having shaved his head including the top-knot, perform the vow with a concentrated mind.
For twenty-one nights, he should drink a handful of barley gruel and feed five or seven Brahmins with sacrificial food (havis). Then,
for one who has been purified by that barley gruel, the initiation (upanayana) is prescribed.

Both of these [rules] refer to the same subject matter. As for that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "One whose *sāvitrī* has lapsed (*patitasāvitrīka*) shall perform the *Uddālakavrata*: he should subsist on *yāvaka* for two months; on milk for one month; on *āmikṣā* for half a month; on clarified butter for eight nights; on unsolicited food for six nights; he should subsist on water for three nights and fast for a day and night, or go to the final bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an *Aśvamedha*, or perform the *Vrātyastoma* sacrifice"—this is to be understood as referring to one who, in the absence of a calamity (*anāpadi*), intentionally remains a *vrātya* for a long period. For one who, in the absence of a calamity, has not been initiated after the sixteenth year but has not remained so for a long time, the penance is the three-month vow prescribed by Manu for general minor offenses (*upapātaka*). For one incapable of that, there is the *yāmya* penance of eating *yāvaka*. For one incapable even of that, there is the threefold *kṛcchra* beginning with the *Prājāpatya*, which is the rule of Manu. For one incapable even of that, the *Cāndrāyaṇa* is common to all minor offenses. However, in the case of a lapse of the *Sāvitrī* committed unintentionally due to the absence of an instructor such as a father, the penance is a *Parāka* or a month-long vow of subsisting on milk. Āpastamba says: "When the time for the *Sāvitrī* has passed, one should observe the student-life (*brahmacarya*) pertaining to the three Vedas for one season (*ṛtu*), that is, for two months, until the initiation (*upanayana*). Then, after that, there is bathing in water for one year, after which he may be taught. Now, if the father and grandfather of a person have remained uninitiated, they are designated as 'slayers of Brahman' (*brahmaha*); one should avoid visiting them, eating with them, or marrying them. For those who desire purification, there is the following penance: for the lapse of one season, there is bathing; for a year, the initiation. In that case, the bathing in water is calculated per person for as many years as they have remained uninitiated, using the seven *Pāvamānī* verses, the verse 'yac ca dūrake,' the *Yajuṣpavitra*, the *Sāmapavitra*, the *Āṅgirasa*, and also the *Vyāhṛtis*; after this, he may be taught. If the initiation of one's great-grandfather and so forth is not remembered, they are considered 'born from the cremation ground' (*śmaśānasambhūta*); one should avoid their arrival, eating with them, or marrying them. For those who desire purification, the penance is to observe the student-life for twelve years. Then follows the initiation. Therein, the bathing in water is performed with the *Pāvamānī* verses and others. Then follows instruction in the duties of a householder (*gṛhamedha*). Therefore, for one who is born from a person who has turned away from those duties, the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) is as in the first case of the lapse of the *Sāvitrī* time. After that, his eligibility for social intercourse is like that of one who has not exceeded the *Sāvitrī* time. The meaning of this is as follows: when the time for the *Sāvitrī*—the time for initiation, which consists of sixteen or twenty-two years for Brāhmaṇas and others—has passed, one should observe for one season (two months) the student-life related to the three Vedas, consisting of living on alms, serving the teacher, and so forth. Alternatively, one should observe the student-life for three seasons (six months) for the sake of the three Vedas. Then, after the three-season student-life, the initiation takes place. Following that, there is bathing in water for one year, meaning a daily bath. After that, he may be taught. However, in the case of a *vrātya* whose father and grandfather are also *vrātyas*, all three are designated by the term 'slayer of Brahman. One should avoid visiting them—that is, visiting them for the purpose of accomplishing family rites—as well as eating with them or marrying them. For those desiring their purification, the penance is to be taught as follows: for the lapse of one season, there is bathing; for a year, the initiation. Thus, the student-life must be observed for three years per person. Then follows the initiation, followed by bathing in water for one year. The mantras used therein are the seven beginning with "yac ca dūrake," the *Yajuṣpavitra* beginning with "yena devāḥ pavitreṇa," the *Sāmapavitra* beginning with "kayā naś citra ābhuvat," and the *Āṅgirasa* beginning with "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat"; with these, or with the *Vyāhṛtis*, there is bathing in water for one year. These mantras are to be studied for the sake of the penance. Once the penance is completed, he may be taught. But in the case of one whose initiation is not remembered starting from the great-grandfather, it follows by implication that these persons also remain uninitiated; they are all impure, like a cremation ground. When they arrive, one should avoid rising to greet them or eating with them, even in times of distress—the meaning is that one should not do so. For those who themselves desire purification, the penance to be taught is the twelve-year student-life pertaining to the three Vedas. After the penance, the initiation occurs; after that, bathing in water for one year with the aforementioned mantras. After that, there is no teaching, but rather instruction in the duties of a householder. From that point, for a person born from one who has been instructed in the householder's life, the sacramental rite is as in the first case of the lapse of the *Sāvitrī* time. After that, his status for social interaction is like that of one who has not exceeded the *Sāvitrī* time. Aṅgiras says: [text follows].
Having caused all twice-born men to perform the Vrātyastoma sacrifices for the sake of expiation, he should initiate them again according to the prescribed rule.

Now, regarding specific penances for minor offenses against women, Manu says: "Having intentionally committed thefts of grain, cooked food, or wealth from the house of one of his own caste, the best of the twice-born is purified by performing the *kṛcchra* penance for one year."

The "best of the twice-born" (*dvijottama*) is a Brahmin; thus, for a Brahmin who steals grain or other property belonging to another of his own caste, the penance is a *kṛcchra* lasting one year. In this context, by the word "wealth" (*dhana*), solid goods other than gold are meant, and "grain" (*dhānya*) should be understood as measured by ten *kumbhas*, because of the gravity of the expiation. A *kumbha* is a measure of five thousand *palas*. For a Kṣatriya or others as well, when stealing grain or other property belonging to their own caste, a practice of *kṛcchra* lasting nine, six, or three months respectively must be prescribed. However, for one who is incapable, considering factors such as the circumstances of the offense, a three-month penance common to minor sins (*upapātaka*) and the like may also be assigned. Likewise:
For the abduction of human beings, women, fields, or houses,
and for [the theft of] water from wells or tanks, purification is achieved through the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

Although the term "of men" (*manuṣyāṇām*) is already included, the separate mention of "of women" (*strīṇām*) is for the purpose of making known that the abduction of a woman is equal in fault to the abduction of a man; otherwise, there would be a disparity even regarding abduction, as there is in the case of violence (*hiṃsā*). The qualification of the water by "wells and ponds" (*kūpavāpībhyām*) is for the purpose of excluding water from jars and the like; therefore, this expiation applies to the theft of an entire pond or well. This should be understood to apply to the abduction of humans and others belonging to Kṣatriyas and other castes. Furthermore, the abduction of humans and others belonging to Brāhmaṇas is stated to be equal to the theft of gold.
The misappropriation of a deposit, as well as the theft of men, horses, silver, land, diamonds, and gems, is recorded in tradition as equal to the theft of gold.

Thus it is said here. Likewise: "For stealing five kinds of food, as well as vehicles, beds, and seats, and for taking flowers, roots, and fruits, the purification is the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)."

[The consumption of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) is the purification for one who does not take other food. Paiṭhīnasi states: "If one takes only as much of edible food as fills the stomach, the rule is to subsist on *pañcagavya* for three nights or one night. The application of this rule of subsisting on *pañcagavya* for either one night or three nights should be understood according to the smallness or greatness of the quantity of the stolen substance. Furthermore, the word "night" (*rātri*) is intended to indicate a full day and night (*ahorātra*). In the phrase "theft of grain, food, or wealth," the word "food" (*anna*) refers to a larger quantity of food, because the penance is more extensive. — Manu.
For grass, wood, trees, dried food, molasses,
oil, leather, and meat, there shall be a fast of three nights.
This refers to the theft of grass and other such items that can be obtained for a quantity of food sufficient for three men. Likewise:
"For stealing gems, pearls, coral, copper, silver, iron, bronze, or stones, one must subsist on grain-particles for twelve days. [11.11]
In the case of stealing gems and other articles belonging to a Brāhmaṇa that are of little value, the rule is to subsist on rice for twelve days. Likewise:
"For cotton, silk, worn-out cloth, animals with two or one hoof, birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, and rope, one must drink milk for three days."
Viṣṇu: "Upon stealing birds, fragrant substances, medicinal herbs, ropes, or bamboo mats, one should fast for a day. Jābāla:
"Having stolen horses, cows, land, or maidens, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
as well as for cooked food, medicine, oil, a bed, clothing, or sandals."
For stealing bell-metal, iron, copper, lead, or tin, one should perform half a *kṛcchra* penance;
for water, fruits, roots, flowers, leaves, fragrant substances,
earthenware, honey, or meat, a quarter *kṛcchra* is prescribed.
The "lotus-born" refers to the conch, oyster shell, and so forth; [specifically] the conch.
For whichever species one should cause the destruction of its livelihood, for the killing of that very species, one should perform the prescribed penance.
If a Brahmin, through negligence, should seize the land of the other castes, the prescribed expiation is death; he should perform this according to the consensus of the Brahmins.
For the theft of an elephant or a horse, of jewels or silver,
and likewise for the theft of wealth, one shall observe the vow for one year.
With a concentrated mind, one should observe this vow for half a year regarding sesame, grain, food, clothing, beds, and meat.
Having stolen small animals, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
as well as for stealing molasses, cotton, grain, clarified butter, and salt.

In all cases, by the statement of Śaṅkha, the word *vrata* refers to subsisting on cow-urine and barley-gruel. Hārīta states: "For stealing silver, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa or the Atikṛcchra; for copper or iron, the Prājāpatya. Viṣṇu declares that every expiation for theft must be performed only after returning the stolen property to its owner:
"Having returned the stolen object to the owner by some means, one should then perform the expiation for the removal of the taint."
Having given lead twice the amount [stolen], or even four times the amount according to his capacity,
the thief shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for purification.

The mention of the *prājāpatya* penance is intended to indicate the previously mentioned expiations. Alternatively: "Having stolen any property whatsoever belonging to another, the sinner shall attain purification by giving up twice as much [as was stolen] and performing half a *kṛcchra*."
Having given four times the value of goats, sheep, sacrificial grass, cotton, copper, grain, sesame seeds, and so forth, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
For one who steals a cow, there shall be the Taptakṛcchra penance; for one who steals an elephant or a horse, half [of that].
For one who steals gold or silver, the capable person must perform an elevenfold gift-offering.
For the sake of purification, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance and give gifts according to one's ability;
for stealing bell-metal, brass, iron, or copper, the expiation for release from the theft is twofold.
And half a *prājāpatya* is the purifying expiation.
Thus end the expiations for theft.

Now follow the penances for the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇānapākriyā-prāyaścittāni*). In that regard, regarding the non-performance of the three debts—namely, sacrifice (*yajña*), progeny (*prajā*), and Vedic study (*adhyayana*)—as well as the discharge of debt prescribed by the *Dharmaśāstra* in such passages as "the debt must be paid by sons and grandsons," if one fails to discharge that debt, one should perform one of the general penances for minor offenses (*upapātaka*), such as the *cāndrāyaṇa* or the penance for killing a cow, according to one's capacity. In this matter, the specific application should be determined with due regard to factors such as the gravity of the transgression and the duration of its omission. Similarly, when one possesses the qualification for the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) but fails to perform it, the general penance for a minor offense must be performed. Regarding one who has the qualification but does not establish the fires, the penance for a minor offense applies after a year has passed; however, before the year is complete, Kārṣṇājini states a specific rule: [The text continues with the specific rule.]
A Brahmin, having established the sacred fires at the proper time, should perform the ritual according to the prescribed rules;
if he fails to do so, he is purified by a three-night fast month after month.
If a son intends to perform a sacrifice while his father or other ancestors have not maintained the sacred fires,
he should indeed perform that sacrifice according to the *vrātya* rite for the purpose of redeeming them.
Regarding the non-establishment of the domestic fire (āvasathya), that same author says:
"The eldest brother who, having married, does not establish the sacrificial fire in his house, shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for a year, or even for a single day every month. [1113]

Upon the lapse of a year [of such forbidden trade], one must perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance; upon the lapse of a month, a day’s fast (*upavāsa*). Now follow the penances for selling non-marketable goods (*apaṇya-vikraya*). Regarding this, Hārīta states: "In the sale of jaggery, sesame, roots, fruits, or cooked food, one must perform the *Somāyana*. In the sale of any one of the following—lac, salt, honey, meat, oil, milk, curd, clarified butter, buttermilk, perfumes, sandalwood, or inferior clothing—one must perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. Likewise for the sale of wool, hair, lions, earth, cows, oxen, houses, or weapons. In the sale of edible meat, sinews, bones, horns, nails, or pearls, one must perform the *Taptakṛcchra*. The same applies to the sale of asafoetida, bdellium, resin, yellow orpiment, realgar, collyrium, red ochre, alkali, salt, gems, pearls, coral, ivory, shells, bamboo, cane, or earthenware. For the sale of gardens, tanks, wells, lotus-pools, or embankments that one has constructed, one becomes purified after a year by bathing at the three periods of the day, sleeping on the ground, and eating only at every fourth mealtime. This also applies to the use of deficient weights and measures, and to the sale of mixed goods. The nature of the *Somāyana* will be explained later. *Ūrṇinaḥ* refers to sheep and the like; *keśinaḥ* refers to yaks and the like; *kesariṇaḥ* refers to horses and the like. *Māna* refers to measures such as the *prastha*; *unmāna* refers to scales such as the balance. By these, grain and other goods are "mixed" or adulterated. In the context of the rule "one should perform the *Prājāpatya*," Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "This very same [penance applies] to the sale of weapons, bonds, land, or single-hoofed animals. Having sold a house, a shelter, a garden, a grove, an assembly hall, a water-station (*prapā*), a tank, an object of worship, or a bridge, one should perform the *Taptakṛcchra*. *Bandhana* refers to fetters and the like. In the reading *udyānāgama*, *āgama* refers to the Vedas and so forth. Likewise: "One should not sell items that ought not to be sold. By selling sesame, oil, curd, honey, salt, grapes, liquor, meat, prepared food, women, men, elephants, horses, cattle, bulls, perfumes, liquids, linen, black antelope skins, Soma, water, or indigo, a Brāhmaṇa falls immediately from his caste. In that case, the penance is for unintentional acquisition. Some say it applies even to intentional acts: 'Having fallen, he should rescue himself; he should perform the *Taptakṛcchra* for a year. Having shaved his head and become pure, he should enter the water three times. Wearing a single wet garment, observing silence like wood, he should sit in the *vīrāsana* posture at night. During the day he should stand, intent on the fire-ritual, and mutter the *Sāvitrī* mantra following the *savana* periods. Having undertaken the vow himself, wearing grass or bark garments, with a girdle of muñja grass, a staff, and holding purifiers in his hands, he should cook sacrificial food or a *caru* offering, or eat blameless alms sufficient for his journey. There should be a fast for twelve nights. After satisfying the Brāhmaṇas and providing daily gifts of cows, he may be treated as fit for social intercourse. Otherwise, he is fallen and should not converse with the learned; he follows the dharma of a Śūdra, observing silence like wood, and should not engage in speech or bodily action even through hand gestures. Likewise: "Fresh herbs, flowers, roots, fruits, vegetables, leather, cane, split bamboo, husks, potsherds, hair, ashes, bones, inspissated milk, brushes, and specific preparations of milk. [From the Caturviṃśatimata.]
Having sold liquor, one should perform four Saumya penances;
for selling lac, salt, or meat, one should perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
One should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow for selling milk, milk-rice, cakes, curd,
sugarcane juice, molasses, buttermilk, and similar items.
For all items cooked in oil, one should prescribe the Parāka penance;
this applies to plantains, coconuts, ginger, and citrons.
For the sale of these, as well as for jambīra and similar fruits, there shall be a quarter-pādakṛcchra; likewise, for the sale of perfumes such as musk, one should perform a kṛcchra penance.

For the sale of camphor and similar items, the penance shall be half of that; for the sale of asafoetida and similar items, it is one day. Having sold sesame seeds, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
For the sake of dharma, one should abandon the sale of creatures born from worms, as well as for the sake of sacrifice;
likewise, one should avoid garments that are red, yellow, and so forth, as well as those that are black and the like.
Regarding the sale of these, the rule is three days, according to the statement of Garga:
"A man, deluded by wealth, having sold a cow for the sake of profit..."
One should perform a *prājāpatya* penance for the sale of elephants; for the sale of donkeys, mules, and young camels, an *aindava* (cāndrāyaṇa) is prescribed.
In that case, one should perform the Parāka penance; for sons, one should perform double that. Having sold women, one should observe the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
The wise have declared that for a man who sells the Vedas, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance must be performed for twice as long as for a single day.
For the Vedāṅgas, however, there shall be a Parāka penance; for the Smṛtis, one should perform a Kṛcchra;
and for the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, a twice-born man should perform a Sāṃtapana.
For the secret Pāñcarātra texts, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance in this manner;
likewise for the Gāthās, the Nītiśāstras, and those in Prākṛta.
For all branches of knowledge whatsoever, one should perform the Parṇakṛcchra.

Viṣṇu states: "One who sells living beings, land, merit, or Soma shall perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance. One who sells fresh herbs, roots, fruits, leather, cane, bamboo-splits, chaff, skull-cups, hair, ashes, bones, milk-products, oil-cakes, sesame oil, or resin shall perform the *prājāpatya*. For selling phlegm (mucus), lac, beeswax, conch-shells, mother-of-pearl, tin, lead, black iron, *udumbara*, swords, or vessels, one shall perform the *mahāsāṃtapana*. Phlegm refers to a product of the skin, well known in the world as *dṛḍhaka*. For selling meat, salt, lac, or milk, one shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* and undergo initiation (*upanayana*) once again. Thus says Śaṅkha.
A merchant who, having used a crooked scale, practices deception,
and who sells milk while dealing in liquor, salt, and wine;
One who sells lac or meat should perform the Mahāvrata penance for half a year;
likewise, a seller of living beings or sesame seeds should perform it for one year.

This refers to the subject of repeated practice. The *mahāvrata* lasts for twelve years. These specific penances (*viśeṣa-prāyaścitta*), being presented as alternatives to the general penances for minor offenses (*upapātaka*), are to be determined according to considerations such as caste (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), and attendant circumstances (*anubandha*).

Now, regarding the penances for supersession (*parivedana*), Vasiṣṭha states: "The superseded elder brother (*parivitti*), having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, may enter [the household life] and marry her. One who has not yet married, while his younger brother marries before him, is superseded; he, having performed the *prājāpatya* *kṛcchra* for twelve nights, may enter [the state of a householder] and marry her—that is, he should take as his wife that very girl previously married by his younger brother and given by him—meaning he should accept her. She is his wife alone, not that of the younger brother, because their marriage is contrary to the scriptures, and the status of being a wife is produced only by a scripturally sanctioned marriage. Furthermore: "The one who causes supersession (*parividāna*), having performed the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances and having given [the bride] back to him [the elder], should marry again. The meaning is this: the younger brother who performs a marriage out of order is called the *parividāna*; he, having performed the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* (whose characteristics will be described), having given the girl married out of order to that elder brother, should marry again—that is, he should marry another. And this should be understood to apply when the elder brother is residing in another country, because the penance is relatively light. Regarding a case where the elder brother is virtuous and the younger brother marries despite being forbidden by him, Hārīta says: "[1116] When the elder brother has not entered [the household state], the younger brother who enters it is the *parivettā*; the elder brother is the *parivitti*; the girl is the *parivedanī*; the giver is the *paridāyī*; the officiating priest is the *parikartā*; all of them are fallen and should complete their purification by the *prājāpatya* *kṛcchra* for one year. At the end of the year, they should hand over that girl to the elder brother. If the younger brother marries without handing her over, he would otherwise enter [the state of a householder]; thus the Dharma is not violated. Śaṅkha speaks regarding intentional supersession when the elder brother lacks virtues.
"The elder brother who has been superseded, the younger brother who supersedes him,
the woman by whom he is superseded, the giver of her hand, and the officiating priest— these shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow," so says Yama.
For one who has superseded his elder brother in marriage, two *kṛcchra* penances are prescribed; for the girl herself, it is indeed a single *kṛcchra*.
The giver of the bride should perform an *atikṛcchra*, and the officiating priest (*hotṛ*) should perform a *cāndrāyaṇa*.

As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha—"The elder brother whose younger brother marries before him (parivitti) and the younger brother who so marries (parivettṛ) shall subsist on alms at the houses of Brāhmaṇas for one year"—that should be understood to apply when there is the supersession of a wife (*dāraparivedana*) or the supersession of the sacred fires (*agniparivedana*). Furthermore, the eating of alms should not be done to the point of full satiation, because it constitutes an austerity (*tapas*). As for that which was stated by Sumantu—"For the elder brother whose younger brother marries before him, the younger brother who so marries, the giver of the girl, and the officiating priest, there is the drinking of barley meal (*saktu*) for twelve nights and the gratification of Brāhmaṇas; they call her a *punarbhū* (remarried woman), and he may go to her again"—that refers to the case of Kṣatriyas and others, or those who are extremely ignorant. Pracetas says: "For the parivitti, the parivettṛ, the paryāhita (one whose younger brother has established the fires before him), the paryādhātṛ (the younger brother who establishes the fires first), and the husband of an *agredidhiṣū* (a woman whose younger sister is married before her), there is the standard year-long celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and the vow of a Brāhmaṇa. Vasiṣṭha says: "The husband of an *agredidhiṣū*, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, may enter [her] and marry her. When it is asked how this is to be done, he says: "And he should marry her alone. This means he should marry—that is, wed—that younger sister known as the *agredidhiṣū* who has been given by her [former] husband. The meaning is: the husband of the *agredidhiṣū*, having performed the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances and having returned her to him, may then enter [another woman] and marry another. This applies to one who is utterly incapable [of performing the rites], or when the offense is caused by ignorance and the like.
Now, the penance for teaching for wages and so forth. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states, following the rule "one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā*":
"Having taught for wages, as well as one who has been taught for wages, shall drink [the decoction] while self-restrained for three fortnights by means of the 'anuyoga' (instruction)."
"Anuyoga" refers to the reproach that one who studies correctly for the sake of fame or wealth is not studying correctly; likewise, another Smṛti states:
"Manu declared that those who study after having engaged in such [improper] inquiries have fallen."

Śātātapa states: "In cases of selling the Veda, questioning [the Veda], or engaging in [its] application, one should give twenty-four 'Brahma-forms' (*brahmarūpa*). A "Brahma-form" refers to the complete recitation of the Veda. Regarding this, there is an option based on one's capacity and other factors, similar to general penances. In this context, another point is mentioned incidentally. On this matter, Vasiṣṭha says: "Upon hearing of an outcaste (*patita*), a Caṇḍāla, or a corpse, they should remain for three nights silent and fasting; it is known that by practicing [the Veda] up to a maximum of a thousand [times], they become purified. Hearing of a corpse means studying while in the vicinity of a corpse. The meaning is that they are purified by practicing the Veda—up to a maximum of a thousand, meaning with a limit of the number one thousand—in such a way that the Veda which was studied in the presence of an outcaste or the like reaches that count.

Now, the penances for approaching the wives of others—excluding major sins (*mahāpātaka*), their analogues (*atideśaka*), and those equal to them—are being stated. Regarding this, Śaṅkha says: "One who has spilled his seed upon a Vaiśya woman shall observe celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for one year, performing the three daily ablutions; for two years if it is a Kṣatriya woman; for three years if a Brāhmaṇa woman; and for a Śūdra woman, as prescribed for a Vaiśya. Here, "celibacy" refers to the vow consisting of the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyāvrata*). Thus Āpastamba states: "They declare that in the case of a single act of intercourse with a woman of the same caste who has not belonged to another, one quarter of the sin falls away; likewise in each repetition, and at the fourth [repetition], everything [falls away]. And here, the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa is the subject under discussion. Since the performance of three daily ablutions is already established by extension (*atideśa*), the explicit prescription of "three daily ablutions" is intended to exclude other duties such as dwelling in the forest and so forth. Furthermore, the three-year penance should be understood to apply to approaching the wife of a learned (*śrotriya*) Brāhmaṇa. As Gautama says: "Two years for the wife of another; three years for the wife of a *śrotriya*; and upon receiving wealth [from her husband], one must relinquish it and cause her to be restored to her proper place. Likewise: "The wealth given must be relinquished; she should be returned to him to whom she belongs. In the same manner, for a Kṣatriya approaching a Kṣatriya woman, three years; for a Brāhmaṇa, two; for a Vaiśya approaching a Vaiśya woman, three; for a Kṣatriya, two; but for a Brāhmaṇa, one year should be assigned. Saṃvarta says:
Having approached a maternal aunt, a sister, a paternal niece,
or the daughter of a maternal uncle, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
This refers to intentional repetition. However, regarding unintentional intercourse once, Manu states:
"Having approached the daughter of his father’s sister, his own sister, the daughter of his mother’s sister, or the daughter of his mother’s brother, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
The word *bhaginī* (sister) is used here in apposition with *paitṛṣvasreyī* (daughter of the father’s sister) and the others; for immediately thereafter [the author] says:
"A wise man should not take these three as wives; they are not to be approached because of kinship, for by marrying them he falls low."
Kinship (*jñātitva*) consists of *sāpiṇḍya*, and how this applies to the daughter of one's father’s sister (*paitṛṣvaseyī*) and others has been explained in the section on marriage. Saṃvarta says:
"Having approached out of delusion these women—the mother’s sister, a woman of the same lineage (*sanābhi*), a daughter-in-law, or the mother’s own sister—one is purified by a *parāka* penance."

This should be understood as referring to a case where one unintentionally abandons his vigor while approaching someone of extremely virtuous character, and then desists before completion. "Sanābhī" means a sister. However, regarding women of other regions, Manu has declared the vow for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa-vrata*):
"One should perform the vow for violating the Guru’s bed after discharging semen upon one's own female kin, upon the wives of a friend or a son, upon virgins, and upon women of the lowest castes."
Yama also says: "Having approached a paternal aunt, a daughter-in-law, a mother, a female friend, a maternal aunt, a daughter,
a maternal uncle's daughter, or a mother-in-law, a twice-born man falls immediately."
A self-controlled twice-born man should constantly avoid these and other such women; by approaching those who should not be approached through these acts, a twice-born man indeed falls immediately.
Likewise, he who out of delusion spills [semen] is joined with the sin of violating the Guru's bed;
having had his penis cut off, he is purified by the relinquishment of life.

[In the section concerning the violation of the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*), Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “By approaching the wife of a maternal uncle, a mother’s sister, a father’s sister, a daughter-in-law, or a daughter; and by approaching the wife or daughter of a teacher. [In the section concerning the violation of the Guru’s bed,] Vasiṣṭha states: “Having approached a female friend of the Guru, a female friend of the Guru’s wife, a newly married girl (*navapātrā*), or an outcaste woman, one should perform a quarter of the *Kṛcchra* penance for one year (*kṛcchrābdapāda*). [1119] The rule for the quarter-year *Kṛcchra* should be understood to apply to unintentional intercourse with women of lower caste, prostitutes, or other such corrupt women. "Gurvī" means the wife of the Guru. "Navapātrā" means a maiden. Baudhāyana states: "A mother’s sister, a father’s sister, a sister, a sister’s daughter, a daughter-in-law, a maternal uncle’s wife, and a female friend are women who should not be approached (*agamyā*). For approaching those who should not be approached, the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitti*) consists of the *Kṛcchra*, the *Atikṛcchra*, and the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. For approaching those who should not be approached, one should perform the *Mahāvrata* rite for a year, wearing bark garments in the forest, or perform the *Prājāpatya*. The universal expiation applies to a single instance of unintentional intercourse; however, for a single instance of intentional intercourse, one must perform a *Kṛcchra* for one year. In the case of repeated practice of that same act, the *Mahāvrata*—which is the vow for killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyāvratam*)—prescribed by another text, ending in death, must be performed. Saṃvarta states:
Having approached the daughter of his guru, or his father’s sister,
or even the daughter of his maternal uncle, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.

In this context, "guru" refers to the officiating teacher (*upādhyāya*) and others. "Father’s sister" refers to one of a lower caste. This should be understood to apply when the paternal uncle or brother acts as the initiator (*upanetṛ*), based on another *smṛti* text stating, "if these [others] are the initiators. Vasiṣṭha says: "If a Brāhmaṇa intentionally approaches the wife of a Brāhmaṇa who has ceased his religious duties, he must perform the *kṛcchra* penance; if she has not ceased her religious duties, he must perform the *atikṛcchra*. The term "nivṛttadharmakarmā" means one from whom the religious duty of the *agnihotra* has ceased; the meaning is "his wife. Saṃvarta says:
Having had sexual intercourse with the wife of a friend, or likewise with one's mother-in-law or sister-in-law,
one should fast for a day and night and perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.

This refers to approaching [a woman] once unintentionally. Having ascended to the wife of his father— excluding his own mother— the lowest of the twice-born [incurs sin by approaching] his mother’s sister,
his own sister, or a sister born of another mother.
Having approached these three women, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance;
for approaching a young girl as well, this very vow is prescribed.

This refers to approaching [a woman] once unintentionally. It should be understood as approaching a father’s wife who is of a lower caste than one's mother and has been violated; likewise, it includes approaching a sister born of another mother who is of a lower caste, because of the word "having approached" (*āruhya*). This applies when one desists before the emission of semen. Sumantu says: "Upon approaching a woman of the same *ṛṣi*-lineage (*sagotra*), there shall be an oblation with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras and a fast for three nights. Baudhāyana says:
"Having approached the wives of a paternal uncle or a brother, a maternal aunt, a mother-in-law, or a nurse, one should perform two *taptakṛcchra* penances."
This applies to one who has no subsequent connection [to the act]. Likewise:
"But having intentionally approached the wife of his own younger brother, he should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra or even the Cāndrāyaṇa."
This refers to the case of a *vṛṣalī*. Likewise:
"But having approached his mother's sister, his father's sister's daughter, or likewise the daughters of those two, he shall perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance for six nights."
Having approached the daughter of his guru, one should perform the Parāka penance;
having approached his sister's daughter, a twice-born man should perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances.

In this context, "guru" refers to the preceptor. Hārīta states: [One should avoid] a Caṇḍālī, a Pukkasī, a woman afflicted by disease, a daughter-in-law, her sister, a female friend, a mother’s or father’s sister, one who has been entrusted to another’s care, and one who has come for refuge.
Having approached a maternal aunt, a sister, a woman of the same lineage even if she is unwilling,
the wife of a disciple, or the wife of a teacher, one shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

This [penance] applies when an act is committed once, unintentionally, without subsequent persistence, and before it has been completed. Śātātapa states: "One who defiles a maiden shall perform the Prājāpatya penance. A "defiler of a maiden" (kanyādūṣin) is one who causes injury to the maiden’s vulva with a finger or similar object. Saṃvarta says:
"A Brāhmaṇa who has approached a Śūdra woman shall subsist on cow-urine and barley-gruel for either a month or half a month, remaining thus to be liberated from that sin."

If one engages in sexual intercourse intentionally, he should subsist on cow’s urine and barley gruel for one month; if unintentionally, for half a month. Furthermore, if one who is deluded by lust should approach a Kṣatriya woman or a Vaiśya woman, the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance shall be his means of liberation from that sin.
Having approached a Brahmin woman who is not a relative, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance.

"Not a relative" means she is not connected by marriage to either the maternal or paternal side. This should be understood to apply to a single act of intercourse with the wife of a non-Vedic scholar (*aśrotriya*), provided no child is conceived.
Furthermore, for approaching a cow, a man should perform either the Kṛcchra or the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

Viṣṇu states: "If a Brāhmaṇa approaches a Kṣatriya woman against her will and the act is persistent, the penance is that for killing a cow. For approaching a Vaiśya woman, it is a Cāndrāyaṇa; for approaching a Śūdra woman, it is a Sāṃtapanaka; however, the penance for killing a cow is three-monthly. Yama states:
"A Brāhmaṇa who has approached a Brāhmaṇa woman shall give a deer-skin to a twice-born man;
if he has approached a Kṣatriya woman, he shall give a bow; if a Vaiśya woman, an iron slab."
If a Brahmin has approached a Śūdra woman, he should give a water-pot;
having fasted for three nights and bathed, he should likewise give a broom.

This [penance] applies to approaching women of the Brāhmaṇa caste and others who are absolutely unrestricted. Śaṅkha states: "In the case of approaching female animals, with the exception of cows, one should bathe with one's clothes on and give a load of herbs to the cows. This refers to a situation where one is incapable of performing other penances. Hārīta says: "Having approached the wives of others who have been violated (abhipluta) or are of lower caste, one should mutter the mantra 'O waters, carry away my sin' (*vedam āpaḥ pravahata*) one hundred and eight times while submerged in water and give an *āḍhaka* measure of sesame seeds to a Brāhmaṇa. "Violated" (*abhipluta*) means those who have committed adultery. Āpastamba says: "In the case of transgression regarding a wife, having put on a donkey-skin with the hair outside, and subsisting on alms for the duration of the transgression, one should wander for seven houses saying, 'Give alms'; that shall be his mode of life for six months. For a woman, however, in the case of transgression against her husband, there is the practice of the twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance for that same period if the connection [with the sin] persists; in the case of a prior repetition, these two penances [are prescribed]. From the Caturviṃśatimata: "One born of a *vṛṣalī* should, during the fourth period [of the day], perform the *nakta* rite for three years. "Born of a *vṛṣalī*" means one who has begotten offspring upon a *vṛṣalī*. And here, a *vṛṣalī* is a married Śūdra woman. Manu [says]:

Having approached women of the Caṇḍāla or lowest castes, having eaten [with them], or having accepted gifts from them, a Brahmin falls [from his caste] through ignorance; but through knowledge, he becomes their equal.
And when such equality exists, the penance must indeed be one that ends with death. And Uśanas says:
"But upon contact with an outcaste, whether through eating together or sexual intercourse, he shall enter a blazing fire; by death he is purified. Thus it is said.
As for that which was stated by him:
"Whatever a twice-born man commits by serving a *vṛṣalī* for a single night,
he removes that by subsisting on alms and constantly reciting [sacred texts] for three years."

The statement, "From that knowledge, through practice limited to a single night, and from that knowledge thereafter, he attains equality," refers to practice delimited by multiple nights. Here, *vṛṣalī* means a *caṇḍālī*. Regarding this very subject, Gautama also says: "For approaching a woman of the lowest caste (*antyāvasāyinī*), there is a year-long *kṛcchra* penance. As for what was stated by that same author—"Twelve nights [of fasting] if it is unintentional"—that should be understood to apply when the fruit of the act has not yet ceased. However, regarding a single instance of unintentional cessation, Vasiṣṭha says: "He should subsist on water for twelve nights, fast for twelve nights, or go to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. By this, marriage with a *caṇḍālī* is also explained. Viṣṇu says: "Upon approaching a *caṇḍālī*, one attains equality with her; if it is unintentional, one should perform a *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance. This covers the same subject matter as the preceding [text]. On this very point, Saṃvarta says:
If a twice-born man, somehow deluded by lust, should have sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍālī woman,
he shall be purified by three Kṛcchra penances performed in the sequence beginning with the Prājāpatya.
Whether intentionally or unintentionally, one who has sexual intercourse with a Pukkasi woman should perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances to be liberated from that sin.

If done unintentionally, the *kṛcchra* penance is prescribed; if intentional, the *cāndrāyaṇa*. Regarding the application of the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*, Baudhāyana states: "By this, sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍālī woman is explained. This refers to cases of repeated practice when not preceded by conscious intent. Saṃvarta says: "Having approached an actress, a female hunter, a washerwoman, a basket-weaver, or one who lives by leather, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance."

This refers to the case of repeated practice when done unintentionally. But when one intentionally approaches a woman who subsists by washing clothes, hunting, acting, or working with bamboo and leather, he shall perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances.

Atri: Having eaten the food of, or having accepted gifts from, those who are unfit to dine with or receive gifts from—such as actors, dancers, musicians, singers, perfumers, potters, *macūcupas*, *madguvas*, *kuśīlavas*, *andhras*, *draviḍas*, Śakas, Kāmbhojas, Tukhāras, Vāhīkas, Khaśas, Utrayas, Gotrakas, and others—one should perform a secret penance for a secret act of sexual intercourse with a woman, and a public penance for a public act.
For a secret act, however, a Brahmin, being composed, should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
And in the case of daytime, the best of the twice-born, having gone there once, should perform the Aindava rite.
If a secret sin has been committed unknowingly, a man should perform the *sāṃtapana* penance;
if it was known, he should perform the *taptakṛcchra*. This is always the prescribed rule.
Having caused conception among those born of the lowest castes, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow;
having caused conception in a Caṇḍālī woman, one should perform the vow prescribed for violating the Guru’s bed.
This subject has not been previously understood:
"The washerman, the leather-worker, the actor, the basket-maker,
as well as the fisherman, the Meda, and the Abhiga (or Ābhīra)— these seven are recorded as the Antyajas."
Having eaten the food of these [outcastes], having had sexual intercourse with their women, having drunk their water, and having accepted gifts from them,
one-half of a *kṛcchra* penance is prescribed if done intentionally, and two *aindava* penances if done unintentionally.
This applies to excessive practice prior to one year. Āpastamba states:
"Having had sexual intercourse with a Mlecchī woman, a female dancer, a leather-worker’s wife, a washerwoman, or a *varuḍī*, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow."
This refers to habitual practice out of desire. Hārīta says:
"A fisherwoman, a woman of the *dhvajinī* caste, and others born of the lowest castes—if a Brahmin dwells with these out of desire, he should perform these very same penances."
For two months he subsisted on alms-food, for two months on barley-gruel, for two months on the five products of the cow; having thus performed his vow for six months, he was purified.
In this way, one attains purity in accordance with the prescribed expiation.
This applies when there has been excessive practice prior to a year; however, after that, it is penance ending only with death. Āpastamba says:
"Having unintentionally approached the women of Caṇḍālas, Medas, Śvapacas, or those who observe the Kapāla-vow, one should perform the Parāka vow."

But if [a child] is born from intentional [intercourse], there is no doubt that he is equal to him; through unintentional procreation or intentional intercourse with repetition, he is equal to him. He who intentionally approaches a Brāhmaṇa woman who is considered a Śūdra [by marriage] is equal to him.
What is the expiation for that? A three-year *kṛcchra* penance is prescribed.
This applies to repeated practice and to approaching a Brāhmaṇa woman who has gone to a man of a lower caste.
That twice-born man, however, should perform the Kṛcchra penance for one year for the sake of purification.
This refers to repeated practice out of desire. Uśanas says:
"But upon having sexual intercourse, one should perform the vow; if a fetus is conceived, one should perform it twice as much.
Now, regarding the penances for the transgression of women: on this point, Manu says:
A husband shall confine a wife who has become corrupted in a single room;
he shall make her perform that same penance which is prescribed for a man regarding the wives of others.

And in this regard, the general rule—"Women and the sick deserve only half of the expiation"—is not to be respected here, because that rule concerns the instruction of vows common to both men and women. This, however, is an exceptional extension (atideśa) of the rule. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:

"The vow that a man should observe regarding the wives of others who are of equal [caste], a woman should observe that in its entirety in the event of infidelity toward her husband. Here, "equal" means those of the same caste (*savarṇa*). This refers to infidelity committed intentionally. However, regarding unintentional infidelity, the same author says:
But if a husband keeps his protected wife in the house against her will,
she shall have her limbs soiled, sleep on the ground, and subsist on nothing more than a single morsel of food.

She should perform an expiation consisting of either the *kṛcchra* or the *parāka* penance; the choice between them depends on her capacity. "Approached by an equal" means approached by one of the same caste (*savarṇa*).
She who has been enjoyed by one of a lower caste should either be abandoned or else slain.

However, in the case of intentional intercourse with a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, she should be abandoned up until the point of conception. Likewise, in the case of intercourse with a Śūdra, she is to be executed; here, "execution" refers to the cutting off of her nose and other such parts. Viṣṇu states: "A woman who has once committed adultery shall perform the same penance as the man for adultery with another's wife. Manu says:
"If she should commit adultery again, having been enticed by a man of equal status, the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances are prescribed as her means of purification."

Āpastamba states regarding a six-month-long transgression: "But for a woman who has committed a transgression against her husband, there is a twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance to be repeated for that same duration. This refers to the case of intentional and extreme habitual practice. Uśanas says: "One should cause an unfaithful wife—who wears dirty clothes, follows a low livelihood, and has been deprived of her rights—to perform either a *cāndrāyaṇa* or a *prājāpatya* penance. If she is unable to perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* along with the *kṛcchra* prescribed by Manu, she may perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* alone. The *prājāpatya* penance applies to the case of one who was enjoyed through force. And so says Saṃvarta:
If she has been enjoyed by force, while her mind is burning with anguish, purification may be achieved through the Prājāpatya penance; there is no other means for her purification.
Regarding the lack of capacity in this matter, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
"If a woman is approached by force by a man of her own caste,
one should prescribe a three-night penance for her as the means of purification."

Regarding the rule that one should observe the ordinary vow of celibacy for one year, Gautama states: "A woman who has committed adultery, even if she is protected [by her kin], shall receive a portion of food. This refers to the same subject matter as the following statement of Manu: "If she should again become corrupt... Saṃvarta says:
"If a Brāhmaṇa woman should have intercourse with a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, she is purified after one month by consuming cow-urine and barley-gruel, or after half that time."

For approaching a Vaiśya woman, purification occurs after one month; for approaching a Kṣatriya woman, after half a month. If contact with a Śūdra woman should somehow occur for a Brāhmaṇī woman, purification shall be through the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; that is her supreme means of purification.

This refers to the case of forceful violation. Bṛhat-Pracetas states: "If a Brāhmaṇa woman has sexual intercourse with a Śūdra and dwells with him until she gives birth, the expiation prescribed for her is a Kṛcchra penance followed by three Cāndrāyaṇas."
For a Brahmin woman’s sexual union with a Vaiśya, two Cāndrāyaṇas and two Kṛcchras [are prescribed];
for a Brahmin woman’s sexual union with a Kṣatriya, one Kṛcchra and one Cāndrāyaṇa [are prescribed].
A Kṣatriya woman, having approached a Śūdra, shall perform a Kṛcchra penance and two Cāndrāyaṇas;
in the case of union with a Vaiśya, she shall perform a Cāndrāyaṇa and a Kṛcchra.
A Vaiśya woman, having approached a Śūdra, shall perform a Kṛcchra followed by a Cāndrāyaṇa.
The Kṛcchra penance prescribed in its regular order is reduced by one quarter.

"Reduction of a quarter" means a reduction by one-fourth. Consequently, for approaching a Kṣatriya woman, the penance for a Brāhmaṇa is a *kṛcchra*; for a Vaiśya woman, two quarters; and for a Śūdra woman, one quarter. For a Vaiśya approaching a Kṣatriya woman, the penance is a *kṛcchra*. In the same way, this should be calculated for a Śūdra approaching a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya woman.
A *cāndrāyaṇa* is prescribed for repeated acts with a woman of the same caste, while a single *kṛcchra* is for a single act.
This same principle should be applied to cases of intercourse with the thumb or in cases of unintentional union.

Repetition is practice (*abhyāsa*). In that regard, for an intentional act, there is a single *kṛcchra* penance; for an unintentional approach to a woman of low caste (*abhicāriṇī*) by means of the thumb, the meaning is that the assembly (*pariṣad*) should determine the expiation. Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says:
"If a woman of the lowest castes should be desired, she should perform a *kṛcchra* for one year;
likewise for a pregnant woman or a young girl who has been desired by one of the lowest castes."
One should not perform any expiation until the fetus has been delivered;
nor should one move about within the house, nor engage in the decoration of the limbs and so forth.
She should not sleep with her husband nor eat with her relatives;
when the fetus has perished, she should perform the expiation consisting of a year-long *kṛcchra* penance according to the prescribed rule.
Then one should give gold or a cow as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin.

Vasiṣṭha: "If a Śūdra should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, one should wrap the Śūdra in *vīraṇa* grass and cast him into the fire. Having caused the Brāhmaṇa woman’s head to be shaved and having anointed her with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a donkey and cause her to be paraded along the high road. It is declared that she becomes purified. If a Vaiśya should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, one should wrap the Vaiśya in red *darbha* grass and cast him into the fire. Having caused the Brāhmaṇa woman’s head to be shaved and having anointed her with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a white donkey and cause her to be paraded along the high road. It is declared that she becomes purified. If a Rājanya should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, one should wrap the Rājanya in reed leaves (*śara*) and cast him into the fire. Having caused the Brāhmaṇa woman’s head to be shaved and having anointed her with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a black donkey and cause her to be paraded along the high road. It is declared that she becomes purified."
In this way, a Vaiśya with a Kṣatriya woman, and a Śūdra with a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya woman, becomes purified; the meaning is that she becomes fit for the performance of penance. [1127]

"If she performs an act of sorcery against her husband through the mind (*manas*), she shall eat barley-gruel or rice with milk for three nights and sleep on the ground. After the three nights, while submerged in water, she should offer oblations with her head [immersed] one hundred and eight times while reciting the *Sāvitrī* mantra; it is known that she thus becomes purified. In the case of verbal connection [with another man], having performed this same penance for one month, after the month she should, while submerged in water, offer oblations with her head [immersed] one thousand and eight times while reciting the *Sāvitrī*; it is known that she thus becomes purified. But in the case of sexual intercourse, she should wear a cloth soaked in ghee for one year. She shall eat while sitting on a bed of *kuśa* grass in a pit filled with cow-dung and sleep on the ground. After the year, while submerged in water, she should offer oblations with her head [immersed] one thousand and eight times while reciting the *Sāvitrī*; it is known that she thus becomes purified. However, in the case of sexual intercourse, she is excluded from visiting sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*) and from religious duties (*dharma*). By "religious duties," it means she is excluded from the entitlements to perform rites; because of the word "and" (*ca*), she is also excluded from [the performance of] expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). — Thus says Saṃvarta.
Excellent women who have approached a Caṇḍāla, a Pukkasa, a Mleccha, a Śvapāka, or likewise one who has fallen from his caste, shall perform three Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
Women of the higher castes are the best [to be protected]. According to the Caturviṃśatimata:
"Upon having sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa, a Brāhmaṇa woman shall perform half a Kṛcchra penance;
for a Kṣatriya man, she shall perform a full Kṛcchra; for a Vaiśya, it is recorded that she shall perform a Sāṃtapana."
And upon having sexual intercourse with a Śūdra woman, one should perform the Parāka penance;
when these aforementioned sins have been committed, the wise have declared that half [of the prescribed penance] shall suffice.

The meaning is that when there has been a prior cessation due to the failure of virility, for Brāhmaṇa women and others who have had intercourse with Śūdras and so forth, the penance is half of the fourfold penances beginning with the *kṛcchrārdha*. Likewise:
"In the case of a Brāhmaṇa's womb, the *parāka* penance shall be performed; for a Kṣatriya, likewise the *aindava*;
for a Vaiśya, that same [penance] should be performed, combined with a *parāka*."
There may be abandonment [of the child] if it is born from a Śūdra womb, and [abandonment] occurs there upon seeing a Caṇḍāla.
However, regarding usury and the manufacture of salt, there are only the penances for general minor sins (upapātaka), because no specific [penances] have been prescribed. (3.267, 268)
Now he states the specific penance for killing a woman:

"Having killed women of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes who have behaved wickedly, one should give, respectively, a water-skin, a bow, a goat, or a sheep for the sake of purification. (3.269)

Having killed women of the Brāhmaṇa and other castes who are of bad conduct and wanton, one should give a water-skin (*dṛti*) and so forth to a Brāhmaṇa according to the sequence of their respective castes. A *dṛti* is a water-vessel made of leather and such materials; a bow (*dhanus*) is well known; and a *basta* is a goat.
