Along with the gift of the water-skin and the rest, gold should also be given as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Its quantity should be determined in consideration of the circumstances, such as the gravity of the offense. Manu also says: "For purification, one should separately give a worn-out bow, a goat, and a sheep."
Having killed women of even all four castes, they remain unsettled.
"Unstable" means unstable toward their husband; that is to say, those who are unfaithful to their husbands. Aṅgiras states:
"One should cause a Brahmin woman to be placed in a pit or before a Brahmin;
for the killing of a Kṣatriya woman, a bow is prescribed, and for the killing of a Vaiśya woman, a goat is traditionally ordained."

"And for killing a Śūdra woman, one should touch wool; for killing a Vaiśya woman, one should touch water. The meaning of this is: upon the killing of a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should give a leather water-vessel (*kośa*) to a Brāhmaṇa for the sake of helping others at a well. But when a Vaiśya woman—or indeed a Brāhmaṇī and so forth—is killed, one should give nothing; rather, one should merely touch water. (3.269)

Having killed a woman who is not corrupt, one should perform the vow for killing a Śūdra. One who is "not corrupt" (*apraduṣṭā*) is so called because she is not excessively corrupt (*praduṣṭā*); that is to say, she is slightly corrupt. Having killed such a woman belonging to the Brāhmaṇa or other castes, one should perform the six-month vow for killing a Śūdra, or give ten cows as a gift. Regarding the killing of a non-corrupt woman, Śātātapa says: "For the killing of a woman, one should perform the *Prājāpatya* penance for six months; however, if it was unintentional, one should perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. Vyāsa states: "Having unintentionally killed a Brāhmaṇa woman, one should perform the penance prescribed for a Vaiśya."
It is declared that for an offense committed out of lust, the fine is double; however, in the case of a corrupt woman, there is no penalty at all.
He who causes a Śūdra woman to drink [the water of penance] attains meritorious worlds;
for those women who kill their husbands or destroy their fetuses are indeed creators of social confusion.

As for the statement of Parāśara: "Having killed a Brāhmaṇa woman who has not reached puberty, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for one year or six months; having killed a Kṣatriya woman, for six months or three months; having killed a Vaiśya woman, for three months or a month and a half; and having killed a Śūdra woman, for a month and a half or twenty-two days"—this refers to a killer who lacks virtuous qualities (*nirguṇa*). In this context, among all the optional alternatives (*vikalpa*), the former option applies to intentional acts (*kāmakāra*), while the latter applies to the opposite case. As for what was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "In the case of killing a non-Ātreyī Kṣatriya woman, [the penance is that for killing a Kṣatriya]; in the case of killing a Kṣatriya woman, [that for killing] a Vaiśya; in the case of killing a Vaiśya woman, [that for killing] a Śūdra; and in the case of killing a Śūdra woman, [one should observe the vow] for one year"—this refers specifically to the wife (*sahadharmacāriṇī*). Here, the specific distinction is that the rule "having killed a Śūdra woman, for one year" constitutes the penance for killing an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā-prāyaścitta*). On this very subject, Hārīta also says: "For a Kṣatriya woman, the standard student-vow (*brahmacarya*) for six years; for a Vaiśya, three years; for a Śūdra, a year and a half; and for Brāhmaṇa women, as for a Kṣatriya. For a Kṣatriya woman, as for a Vaiśya; for a Vaiśya woman, as for a Śūdra; and having killed a Śūdra woman, for nine months. Aṅgiras, however, prescribes an extension of the vow in specific cases.
Having killed the blameless wife of a foremost twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires, one should perform the penance for killing a Brahmin; the same applies to one who kills an Ātreyī woman.
This concerns the subject of penance for minor offenses (*upapātaka*). Regarding a specific type of killing a woman, that same author says:

"For the wives of those who have not maintained the sacred fires, as well as for the women of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, and likewise always for a Śūdra woman, one should perform the vow prescribed for a cow-killer."
Paiṭhīnasi states: "A cow-killer is purified by standing and sitting for three years and eating only at night, or by performing the Prājāpatya penance for one year.
He now mentions the penance applicable by extension even to other acts of violence:
"Or [he is purified] by [killing] a thousand vertebrate animals, or likewise by [killing] a cartload of invertebrate animals. (3.270)

"Having killed [these], one should perform the vow for killing a Śūdra"—this phrase is understood to carry over. Having killed a thousand vertebrate animals or a cart (*anaḥ*, i.e., a wagon) of invertebrates, one should perform the vow for killing a Śūdra. Here, the "cart" is intended as a measure of quantity; therefore, this refers to the slaughter of as many animals as would fill a cart. For a slaughter exceeding the stated quantity, an increase in penance should be prescribed. However, regarding a small slaughter, he will state later: "But as for what was said by Manu: 'The killing of worms, insects, and birds, eating food mixed with liquor, stealing fruit, firewood, or flowers, and lack of fortitude—these bring about impurity.'"* *Manusmṛti 11.149. (Note: The provided text contains a slight variation from the standard reading of the verse, specifically "adhairyaṃ ca" instead of "adharmaśca".)*
For acts that cause defilement, one should undergo the *yāvaka* penance for three days.

This should be understood to apply to boneless creatures such as worms and the like, which possess a smaller size relative to those previously mentioned. Furthermore, those with bones who are not subject to specific penances prescribed for them should be included here. The vow for killing a Śūdra is a six-month penance equivalent to that for killing a Brāhmaṇa, or alternatively, the gift of ten cows. Regarding the killing of certain boneless creatures numbering one thousand, Yama states: [1130] "Beyond this, having killed a thousand of worms, insects, moths, ants, bees, gadflies, mosquitoes, and flies, it is the same as killing a Śūdra. Having killed a male load of cuckoos, parrots, pigeons, grey partridges, cocks, lapwings, dates, and wagtails, it is the same as killing a Śūdra. Following the phrase "as in the case of a Vaiśya," Gautama says: "Having killed a thousand of those with bones, or a load of oxen of those without bones. This refers to cases where there is certainty and a continuous connection [to the act]. Vasiṣṭha says: "Having killed a herd or a heap of boneless beings, one should perform a *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights and give some small gift. [And for each single one with bones. (3.270)"
He will state that something should be given for the killing of each individual creature possessing bones; he now states an exception to that rule:
"Having killed a cat, an iguana, a mongoose, a frog, or birds, one should drink milk for three days or perform a quarter *kṛcchra* penance. (3.271)

Upon killing any one of the animals beginning with the cat, one should drink milk for three nights, or perform the *pādakṛcchra* penance to be described below. Here, the term "birds" refers specifically to crows, owls, and so forth, because of the subsequent explanatory statement (*anuvākyavaśāt*). This [penance] applies to a single killing committed unintentionally. As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu: "Having killed a dog, one should fast for three nights; having killed any one of a cat, mongoose, frog, *ḍuṇḍubha*, or python, one should fast, feed those who eat *kṛsara*, and give an iron staff as a sacrificial fee; upon killing a monitor lizard, an owl, a crow, or a blue jay, one should fast for three nights"—that refers to a person of meager means who has committed a minor offense. As for the rule of Manu:
Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay,
a frog, a dog, an iguana, an owl, or a crow, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra.

Thus, that refers to the case of intentional and repeated practice. Yama states: "Having killed a dog, a mongoose, a snake, a cat, a frog, a *bimbika*, a woodpecker, a lizard, a vulture, an owl, a crow, a peacock, a village-rat, a squint-eyed bird, or a jackal—upon the killing of each one of these, the penance is the same as for killing a Śūdra. Paiṭhīnasi states: "The killing of a crow, an owl, a chameleon, a heron, a wolf, a donkey, a jackal, a hare, a peacock, a mouse, a ruddy goose, a swan, a *praveṇī*, a mongoose, a frog, a cat, or a dog—in the case of each of these, the rule prescribed is the same as for killing a Śūdra. Both of these [texts] have the same scope as the text of Manu. As for the Vasiṣṭha text: "Having killed a dog, a cat, a frog, a blue snake, a *dahara*, or a mouse, one should perform a twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance and give some small gift," that refers to the case of unintentional repetition. *Dahara* means small. As for what was stated by Manu regarding the killing of a cat specifically, [it follows the same principle].
One should drink milk for three nights, or travel a distance of one yojana,
or bathe in a flowing river, or mutter the hymn dedicated to the waters (the Āpohiṣṭhīya Sūkta).

Thus, this is on the same subject as the rule of Yājñavalkya. The term "for three nights" (*trirātram*) is to be connected with every case. Laghu-Viṣṇu states: "In the event of killing a cat, a snake, a mongoose, a dog, a jackal, or a deer through negligence, a quarter *kṛcchra* penance must be performed for purification."

Kaśyapa states: "In the case of killing a donkey, a camel, a horse, or a woman who belongs to the same species as a dog or a cat, one should inform the Brahmins and, having fasted for six nights, give sesame seeds at the conclusion of the penance. Hārīta says: "Upon killing any one of a monkey, a hyena, a cat, a web-footed bird, or a peacock, one should give a cow to a Brahmin. Aṅgiras says: "The venerable Manu declared that the killing of a crow, a vulture, a hawk, a lapwing, or a wagtail is equivalent to the killing of a cow."
This applies when the killing occurs once, unintentionally. || 3.271 ||
For an elephant, five blue bulls; for a parrot, a two-year-old calf; for donkeys, goats, and rams, a bull should be given; and for a crane, a three-year-old [bull]. (3.272)

Having killed an elephant, five dark-colored, spirited bulls must be given to Brahmins; for killing a parrot—a specific type of bird—a two-year-old calf must be given. For the killing of any one of a donkey, a goat, or a sheep, a mature ox must be given. But for killing a crane, a three-year-old bull must be given. An *anaḍvān* is a bull that draws a cart. (3.272)
Having killed a swan, a hawk, a monkey, a carnivorous beast, a water-fowl, a land-fowl, or a peacock, one should give a goat; but for killing a village-predator, one should give a heifer. [3.273]

Having killed swans and other such birds, one should give a cow to a Brahmin. *Kravya* is raw meat; he who eats that is a *kravyād*, such as a tiger, a jackal, or the like. By the words "water" and "land," birds that frequent those environments are indicated. *Śikhaṇḍin* is a peacock. Manu says:
"Having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, and likewise a peacock..."
One should touch a monkey, a hawk, and a vulture, and [one should offer] a cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed carnivorous wild animals, one should give a milch cow;
for non-carnivorous animals, a heifer; but having killed a camel, a *kṣṇalā* coin.
According to the Caturviṃśatimata:
"Having killed wicked lions, tigers, wolves, and other fanged beasts,
or having killed reptiles and the like, one must fast for one day."
Having killed a fish, a lizard, and even a frog,
one becomes pure by fasting for seven nights and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, a myna bird, a parrot, a partridge, a crane, a blue jay, a vulture, or similar birds, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance.
Upon killing a pigeon, a crane, a kāka, or a vulture, as well as for the killing of all other birds, a twice-born man shall observe a fast for one day. (3.273)
For [killing] snakes, an iron rod; for a eunuch, tin and lead; for a ruddy goose, a jar of ghee; for a camel, a guñjā seed; for a horse, a piece of fine cloth. (3.274)

When snakes or reptiles have been killed, an iron rod capable of digging must be given as compensation. In the case of a *paṇḍaka* (a eunuch), one *māṣa* each of tin and lead must be given. For a boar (*kola*), a jar filled with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) must be given. For a camel (*uṣṭraka*), gold weighing one *guñjā* must be given. For a horse, a cloth of the *bandhūka* color [must be given]. Manu says:
"An excellent twice-born man, having killed a snake, shall give an adze made of black iron;
for killing a eunuch, a load of straw and a *māṣaka* of lead."
Palāla means straw; aghṛtadhāna means grass. || 3.274 ||
If one is unable to give a gift of a partridge, a drona of sesame, or an elephant and so forth, one should perform a Kṛcchra penance for the purification of each such failure. (3.275)
[1133] When a *tittiri* (partridge), a specific kind of bird, has been killed, one should give a *droṇa* of sesame seeds. Eight handfuls (*muṣṭi*) make a *kiṃcit*; four *kiṃcit*s make a *puṣkala*.
And four *puṣkala*s are proclaimed to be one *āḍhaka*.
Four āḍhakas make one droṇa, and sixteen droṇas make one khārī.

It has been stated that "the expiation for killing an elephant is a *droṇa* of salt. However, one who, due to poverty, is unable to perform the gift (*dāna*) for the sake of purification from the slaughter of an elephant or similar creatures, should instead perform a *kṛcchra* penance as a substitute cause (*pratinimitta*) for the destruction of the sin of killing an elephant and so forth. The term *kṛcchra* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) to refer to a specific type of austerity known as the *prājāpatya*. In this context, since the destruction of the sin of killing elephants and the like is accomplished through a more extensive gift, a repetition of the *prājāpatya* penance is to be inferred. It is not, however, a single *prājāpatya* alone, because that would result in an unequal balancing of the offense. Alternatively, the word *kṛcchra* refers to austerity (*tapas*) in general; and that [penance] should be determined as either heavy or light according to the gravity or lightness of the occasion (*nimitta*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
Having killed an elephant, a horse, a rhinoceros, a buffalo, a camel, a donkey, a deer, a rohita deer, or a śambara deer, a twice-born man shall perform the Sāṃtapana penance.
Saṃvarta says:
Having killed an elephant, a horse, a buffalo, a camel, or likewise a monkey,
one should perform a fast for seven nights in each of these cases.
Having killed a tiger, a dog, a donkey, a lion, a rhinoceros, or even a boar, a twice-born man should provide a feast for Brāhmaṇas.
Having stayed for a day and night, one should remain reciting the Jātavedas mantra for the sake of all species of wild animals that roam the forest.
Having killed a swan, a crane, a dog, a cat, a *kaṇḍu* bird, a peacock,
a monkey, a hawk, or a vulture, a twice-born man shall remain [in penance] for three days.
Having killed a *ṭiṭṭibha*, a web-footed bird, a cormorant, or a cock,
a twice-born man should observe a fast for seven nights.
Jābāla says:
Having killed an elephant, a horse, a buffalo, a camel, or likewise a monkey, one should perform the Mahāsāṃtapana penance; the same applies for lying regarding a cow, land, or a maiden.
"Gold and a cow"—the word "giving" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Parāśara states:
"Upon killing a curlew, a crane, a swan, a heron, a cock, a peacock, or a ram, one is purified by eating only one meal [per day]."
Upon killing water-fowls, lapwings, parrots, pigeons,
or cranes, one is indeed purified by eating only at night.
One who kills blue jays, crows, pigeons, sarīsṛpas,
or tittiris is purified by performing two breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) while submerged in water.
For killing vultures, hawks, other birds, or owls, [the same purification applies].
One who eats uncooked food should remain standing during the day and subsist on air alone at the two times of the day.

The two times are the evening and the mealtime. Hārīta states: "Upon killing a horse or a donkey, one should perform a *kṛcchra* and a *cāndrāyaṇa*. For killing an animal in vain, one should perform a *prājāpatya* and fast for three nights. Upon killing any one of a monkey, a cat, a web-footed bird, or a peacock, one should give a cow to a Brāhmaṇa. Viṣṇu says: "For killing an unspecified wild animal, one should fast for three nights. Śaṅkha says: "Having killed domestic animals, a wise man should perform [the penance] for a month;
likewise, for giving away what has not been given, half of that is prescribed."
The grammatical connection is as follows: "Having killed a twice-born man, or likewise a snake, or one that dwells in water or a hole, a Brāhmaṇa shall perform the vow for a month. (3.275)
Moreover:
"In the case of killing something with bones, some [gift] must be given; for that which has no bone, a breath-control exercise (prāṇāyāma) is required.
For cutting trees, shrubs, or creepers, one hundred Ṛg-verses are to be recited. (3.276)

In the case of killing a creature possessing bones for which no specific expiation has been prescribed, some amount such as a *kārṣāpaṇa* or more should be given. However, in the case of killing a creature without bones, one should perform *prāṇāyāma*. On this point, Sumantu says: "For the killing of lice, nits, flies, bedbugs, stinking insects, leeches, earthworms, and other boneless creatures, *prāṇāyāma* is required; for the killing of those with bones, a *paṇa* should be given; and for cutting [plants], a hundred *ṛc*s should be recited. Shrubs refer to things like *kubja* (bushes), and creepers refer to things like *atimuktaka*. On this point, Manu says: "For cutting fruit-bearing trees, a hundred *ṛc*s should be recited."
And of shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and spreading herbs that are covered in flowers.
The phrase "of those in bloom" is connected with shrubs and so forth. This applies to trees and the like that have not been taken possession of:
"Whether it be grass or wood, or whether it be a flower or a fruit—one who takes them without asking deserves the amputation of a hand. [1135]

Thus, because a greater penalty is observed, an additional expiation is prescribed for [trees] that have been taken possession of. There is no fault in cutting trees for the purpose of cultivation. As Vasiṣṭha says: "One should not harm trees that bear flowers and fruit; however, one may cut them down for the sake of cultivation. Yama states: "For cutting trees, creepers, shrubs, or grass, the *Vṛddhakṛcchra* penance is required; for those bearing fruit, the *Prājāpatya*. Furthermore: "Having worn indigo-dyed clothing, having eaten, or even when merely fit for bathing, one should observe the vow for three nights after cutting a fruit-bearing tree."
Likewise for those who have fallen from their vows; and for a Kṣatriya who has fled from battle out of fear for his life, though he was mature and capable,
he must perform a vow for one year after cutting down a fruit-bearing tree.

"Lost" means having fled. In this context, the "vow" consists of subsisting on cow-urine and barley-gruel (*yāvaka*), because it is so stated in the *Śaṅkha-smṛti*. Regarding the phrase "having cut down a tree," this refers specifically to the cutting down of a tree that provides abundant enjoyment. (3.276)
One who has been bitten by an unchaste woman, a monkey, a donkey, a camel, or a crow,
becomes pure by performing breath control (prāṇāyāma) in water and consuming clarified butter.

One bitten by a harlot or similar creatures becomes pure by bathing, remaining in the water, performing breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*). The consumption of clarified butter serves as a substitute for other food, because it constitutes an austerity (*tapas*). By the use of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), jackals and other such animals are included. As Manu says:
"One bitten by dogs, jackals, donkeys, or by domestic carnivorous animals..."
And for killing a human, a horse, a camel, or a boar, one is purified by the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).

Regarding this, Sumantu states: "For those bitten by a dog, jackal, deer, buffalo, goat, sheep, crow, camel, mongoose, cat, rat, water-fowl, crane, or a human, there shall be bathing with the *Āpo hi ṣṭhā* verses and three suppressions of the breath (*prāṇāyāma*). This applies to one who is unable to perform a fast. Aṅgiras says: "A religious student (*brahmacārī*) bitten by a dog should drink milk for three days and a half."
If he is a householder, he should fast for two nights; if he maintains the *agnihotra* fire, for one day.
For one bitten above the navel, that same [penance] shall be doubled;
it shall be tripled for the mouth, but quadrupled for the head.

Vasiṣṭha: A Brāhmaṇa who has been bitten by a dog becomes pure by going to a river that flows into the ocean, performing one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and consuming clarified butter. [1136]
This applies to one bitten on the head. Parāśara says: A Brāhmaṇī woman who has been bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a wolf becomes pure immediately upon seeing the risen planets and stars.
A *jambuka* is a jackal. Regarding that same woman who has undertaken the vow (*savratā*), he says: "A woman who has undertaken the vow, if bitten by a dog, should fast for three nights;
having eaten barley-gruel with ghee, she should complete the remainder of her vow."
Pulastya: When a woman in her menses is bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a donkey,
she becomes pure after fasting for five nights and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Regarding one who is incapable of performing breath control (prāṇāyāma), Marīci says:
"When one has been bitten by a hyena, or by a donkey, a camel, a human, or a monkey,
one becomes pure immediately upon seeing the sacred fires being offered oblations."

*Tarakṣu* is a species of tiger. Thus, for one bitten during the day, there is fasting from the evening until the time of the morning *homa*; it is understood that for one bitten at night, this applies until the morning *homa*. Śaṅkha says:
"One who has been bitten by a promiscuous woman (*puṃścalī*) should observe a vow for three nights. Pulastya says:
One who is engaged in a vow and has been bitten by a dog should fast for three nights;
having consumed barley-gruel with ghee, he should complete the remainder of his vow.
Whether he be without vows or even with vows, the best of the twice-born who has been bitten by a dog should bathe in the water from a cow's horn at the confluence of a great river.
Or even by touching the ocean, one bitten by a dog becomes pure;
likewise, a Brāhmaṇa bitten by a dog in a village devoid of other Brāhmaṇas [becomes pure].
Having circumambulated a bull, one is purified by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma),
even if bitten by dogs, jackals, donkeys, or likewise by village pigs, cows, or crows.
If one drinks from the currents of a great river, one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) shall suffice;
or one may become purified by consuming clarified butter or by fasting for three nights.
Having bathed with gold and silver, or with water from the horns of cows, or with new jars, one becomes purified by means of four [of these].
A Brahmin woman bitten by a dog should cast her gaze upon the Soma plant;
likewise, a Brahmin who has completed his Vedic studies and the ritual bath (snātaka) but has been bitten by a dog [should perform the following].
By reciting the *gāyatrī* one hundred times, one attains purification;
or, by consuming ghee mixed with gold and water, one becomes pure.
— Śaṅkha.
A Brahmin wounded by the wood of the indigo plant, as well as one bitten by a dog,
and one struck by the teeth of an unchaste woman, shall observe a vow for three nights.
Yama says: A Brahmin who has been bitten by a jackal, a pig, a donkey, a dog, a man, or an elephant should perform ritual ablutions three times during the day.
One should feed five or seven Brahmins with sacrificial food (haviṣya).

Regarding the topic of the religious student (*brahmacārin*), Hārīta states: "One bitten by a dog shall eat only one meal a day for three days, go to a river flowing to the ocean, perform one hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), and consume clarified butter; thereafter he becomes pure. The same applies to those bitten by a jackal, a cat, a snake, a mongoose, or a rat. Devala says: "A Brāhmaṇa bitten by a dog becomes pure after bathing at a sacred ford with water from nine or four jars over which the *Gāyatrī* has been recited eight thousand times. Or, at the confluence of rivers, the father—meditating mentally on the boy who is ignorant or incapable—shall perform all his duties; in the absence of the father, the teacher (*ācārya*) shall do so. The phrase "having consecrated [the water]" implies that it is the site of the bite that is to be consecrated. "Meditating" means reflecting upon the removal of the fault. Paiṭhīnasi says: "For one bitten by a dog, there is a fast of three nights, as well as staying in the house of a Brāhmaṇa. Bhānu [says the same].
O gentle one, if a worm should arise from the opening of a wound in a Brahmin where pus and blood have gathered, I shall declare the expiation for that.
One should perform ablutions three times a day with the urine and dung of cows;
having drunk curd, milk, and ghee, one bitten by worms is purified.
O son of Vinatā, lord of birds, one should generally prescribe this atonement for one bitten below the navel down to the feet.
O Hero, when a worm is produced within the space between the navel and the throat,
the wise have declared that the penance lasts for six nights.
O son of Vinatā, when worms bite one's head,
a wise person should then perform a difficult penance for the sake of purification, O son of Vinatā.
Parāśara states:
Having bathed and drunk cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass for three days, one bitten by a worm is purified.
Some read the text as "having bathed, having drunk, and having offered oblations.
[1138] If a limb becomes like a wound due to worms or is struck by flies,
one should perform half a *kṛcchra* penance and give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability.

Aṅgiras: "Upon seeing a wound containing worms, one must perform the Sāṃtapana penance; a bull is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). For Śūdras, purification is indeed achieved through fasting and giving gifts;
one should give a cow and a single bull as a fee to Brahmins. (3.277)
If one kills a living being produced from fruit, flowers, food, or sap, one should subsist on ghee;
if one cuts medicinal herbs in vain, one should subsist on milk for a day while following behind cows.

Regarding those beings that are born within fruits such as the *udumbara*, flowers such as the *madhuka*, and others such as cooked rice (*odana*), one should consume only ghee for one day upon killing or harming them. This consumption of ghee serves as a substitute for a meal because it constitutes an ascetic practice (*tapas*). Likewise, for the useless cutting of cultivated or wild plants—meaning without a scriptural purpose—one should follow behind cows for one day while observing a milk-vow (*payovrata*). Manu states: "For all beings born from food, born from sap, and those produced from fruits and flowers, one becomes pure by consuming ghee."

The term "killing" (ghāta) is understood to carry over. Likewise: for the purposeless destruction of cultivated plants or those grown spontaneously in the forest, one should follow a cow for one day while observing a milk-vow.
Vain undertaking is cutting that serves no purpose. || 3.278 ||
Furthermore:
"If my semen should be spilled today by these two [fingers], one should consecrate that semen with a mantra and touch the area between the breasts or the eyebrows with the ring finger. (3.279)

If semen is discharged without sexual intercourse with a woman, he should consecrate it with the two mantras beginning with "That semen of mine today... (*yan me 'dya retaḥ*). Then, using his ring finger and the finger next to the little finger, he should touch the area between his breasts or his eyebrows with that semen. Thereafter, he should perform bathing and other rites for the sake of purification; or, since this is prescribed, one may assume that there is no state of impurity. This rule pertains to householders (*gṛhastha*), because for those in other stages of life (*āśrama*), different penances are ordained. Regarding intentional emission of semen, Yama says: "If a householder should intentionally cause the emission of semen upon the ground..."
"One should recite the mantra of the Goddess one thousand times, together with three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). (3.279)
Furthermore:
"If one sees one's own reflection in water as 'that is me,' one should indeed mutter [the mantra]."
One should recite the Sāvitrī when seeing something impure, or when there is fickleness, or even when there is falsehood. (3.280)

Having seen one's own shadow or reflection in water, one should mutter the mantra beginning with "May splendor [be] in me," which is well-known in the *Vājasaneyi* [Saṃhitā]. However, if one sees something impure such as urine or feces, or if one has committed fidgeting with the hands or feet, or spoken a falsehood, one should mutter the *Sāvitrī*, the well-known verse whose deity is Savitṛ. Regarding false speech, Manu prescribes sipping water (*ācamana*): "After sleeping, eating, sneezing, spitting, speaking untruths, drinking water, and when about to study, one should sip water even if already purified."

This [touching of the ear] is to be performed in conjunction with the recitation of the *gāyatrī*, because their purposes differ: for the purpose of the sipping of water (*ācamana*) is purification, whereas the purpose of the *gāyatrī* recitation is the destruction of sin. As for that which was stated by Saṃvarta:
"Upon sneezing, upon spitting, likewise upon being defiled by food particles from the teeth, upon speaking untruths, and upon conversing with outcasts—one should touch the right ear."

Thus, this [penance] is to be understood as applicable when speech and mind are impossible due to incapacity or the absence of water. In this manner, the penances for specific minor offenses (*upapātaka*) characterized by women, *Śūdras*, Vaiśyas, and Kṣatriyas have been stated. In that context, by way of incidental discussion, other penances for other rules are also mentioned; furthermore, regarding the cutting down of trees and so forth, other penances have been stated because they fall under that same category. As for the minor offense characterized by subsisting on forbidden things and the like, the penance is simply that which has been taught in general. Although no specific penance has been stated for an atheist (*nāstika*), nevertheless, that which is declared in another scripture is now demonstrated. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha says: "An atheist, having performed the *Kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, shall desist from atheism; likewise, for one whose livelihood is based on atheism, the *Atikṛcchra* [is prescribed]. One whose livelihood or means of subsistence is through atheism is an "atheist-livelihood" person. "The ungrateful, the fraudulent dealer, and the false accuser—these five shall subsist on alms in the house of a Brāhmaṇa for one year. The meaning is that these five, beginning with the atheist, shall subsist on alms in the house of a Brāhmaṇa for the duration of one year. Hārīta, following the recurrence of the terms "atheist" and "atheist-livelihood," states: "They shall perform the five-fold heat (*pañcatapas*), staying in the open air during summer, in water during the rains, and lying on the ground during winter. This vow, intended for a year consisting of three seasons, is indeed an annual penance. (3.280)

[1140] Now, having first defined the state of being an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow) through the description of the transgression of the vow, he states the penance for it: "A religious student (*brahmacārī*), however, becomes an *avakīrṇin* by approaching a woman."
Having sacrificed an ass as an animal offering to Nirṛti, he becomes purified. || 3.281 ||

Whether he be a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika*) or another [type of student], one who approaches a woman—that is, a wife—becomes known as an *avakīrṇin*. In this context, because of the suffix *-ktvā* in the word "having approached" (*gatvā*), it is understood that the designation *avakīrṇin* applies only when the act has been completed. Such an *avakīrṇin* becomes pure and is released from sin by sacrificing a donkey (*gardabha*) dedicated to Nirṛti as a victim (*paśu*). The meaning is that he becomes pure by performing a sacrifice to Death with a donkey. The use of the word "victim" (*paśu*) is intended to include the ritual procedures for animal sacrifice as prescribed in the *Gṛhyasūtras*. On this point, Manu says: "But an *avakīrṇin* [should sacrifice] a one-eyed donkey at a crossroads..."
According to the procedure for the *pākayajña* sacrifices, he worships Nirṛti at night.
Having performed the oblations in the fire according to the rules,
and finally with the verse beginning "sam," one should offer oblations of clarified butter to Vāta, Indra, Guru, and Agni.
Those who know the Dharma and expound the Veda declare that for a twice-born man established in a vow, the emission of semen through lust constitutes a transgression of his vow.

In this context, the specific characteristic mentioned is that the animal is a one-eyed donkey (*gardabha*). Likewise, the procedure for the primary oblations consists of the performance of the ritual details as prescribed in the *Gṛhyasūtra* under the heading of the *pākayajña* rites. First, there is an offering of clarified butter (*ājyahoma*) with the four mantras beginning with "To Vāta, svāhā. The time is night, specifically on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). For it is stated in the *Taittirīyaka*: "If a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) should discharge semen, he should carry forward the fire on the night of the new moon and kindle it," and so forth. This should be explained as referring to the intentional emission of semen into a woman, based on the statement of Yājñavalkya. All of this rite is to be performed in the forest, at a crossroads, or in a common (*laukika*) fire. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha says: "If a student of sacred knowledge should approach a woman, he should sacrifice a donkey as an animal dedicated to the Rakṣases at a crossroads in the forest in a common fire; or he should offer a sacrificial pap (*caru*) to Nirṛti and sacrifice from it: 'To Kāma, svāhā! To Kāmakāma, svāhā! To Nirṛti, svāhā! To the deities who are Rakṣases, svāhā! In the absence of an animal, a sacrificial pap (*caru*) should be prepared. One should sacrifice portions of that pap individually with the four mantras beginning with "To Kāma, svāhā. He extends this rule by stating: "This very same [penance applies] to the intentional emission of semen during the day, in a dream, or in other instances, until the *samāvartana* ceremony. The word "this very same" (*etad eva*) is used with the particle *eva* to exclude the one-year penance that might otherwise be combined with the oblation. Consequently, for a student who emits semen into a woman, even the one-year austerity becomes a required expiation. Thus says Manu: [11.41]
When this offense has been committed, having worn the skin of a donkey,
he shall go for alms to seven houses, proclaiming his own deed.
He should subsist on alms obtained from them, not eating at a single mealtime;
by bathing three times a day for one year, he becomes purified.
Regarding those who emit semen in a dream, Manu himself has stated:
"A twice-born student who unintentionally emits semen in a dream shall bathe,
worship the sun, and then mutter three times the verse beginning with 'punar mām'."
Yama states: "But even a student who, though unintentionally, emits semen during sleep,
shall bathe, look at the sun, and, being self-restrained, mutter the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times."
Likewise:
"But a religious student who, oppressed by desire, should approach a woman,
shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year, remaining strictly self-controlled."
This concerns the subject of repeated practice. Vyāsa states:
"A celibate student who intentionally emits his own semen shall perform the vow of an *avakīrṇin*;
if he does so unintentionally, he becomes pure by bathing."

Gautama states: "In the event of seminal emission, fear, illness, or dreaming, one who has failed to perform the kindling of the fire, the begging for alms, or other duties for seven nights, shall offer oblations of clarified butter or fuel-sticks with the two *retasyā* verses. The two verses beginning with "bhavada-mīka" (or "punar mām ait") and "punar mana" are the *retasyā*s. (3.281)
In this context, he states another penance concerning the student (brahmacārin):

"But having neglected the begging for alms and the fire-ritual for seven nights while not being ill, one should offer two oblations of clarified butter with these two [verses] beginning with 'kāmāvakīrṇaḥ'. (3.282)
One should perform the two attendances, sprinkling [the disciple] with this [water].

If one who is not ill and free from disease, being a *brahmacārin*, eats anything other than alms-food for seven days and nights, or fails to perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), then he should offer two oblations with these two mantras: "I am defiled by lust, I am defiled; svāhā to lust! I have fallen into lust, I have fallen; svāhā to the desire for lust! Having offered these two oblations, he should worship the fire with the mantra, "May the Maruts sprinkle me. This should be understood to apply when he is preoccupied with other duties such as service to his teacher; however, in the absence of such circumstances, Manu has said: [1142]
"Having failed to go on alms-round and having failed to kindle the sacred fire,
one who is not ill shall perform the vow of an *avakīrṇin* for seven nights.
On this very point, Bṛhaspati says:
The performance of the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana) is prescribed first for the religious student (brahmacārin);
he should perform daily the kindling of the fire (agnīndhana) and the practice of begging for food (bhakṣacaryā).
By not performing these three, one who observes the vow becomes free from disease;
he should perform the *avakīrṇi* vow for seven nights, without a doubt.

Hārīta states: "A student (brahmacārī), having performed the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) and risen, should worship the sun with a thousand recitations of the Sāvitrī. Having stepped out and completed the fire-ritual (agnikārya), he should perform the worship after offering the Vratapati oblation. If the day has passed [without this being done], he should again perform the rite as appropriate with the Manas and Vratapati [mantras], and in the event of the loss of the girdle, staff, deerskin, sacred thread, or water-pot, he should proceed with the threefold oblation. The Praṇava, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Sāvitrī constitute the 'triple Veda' (trayī). In cases of eating improper alms-food, rising while still naked from sleep, vomiting, sleeping during the day, emitting semen, seeing a naked woman, stepping upon a cremation ground, riding horses and such animals, or neglecting those worthy of honor—he should offer clarified butter with these very [mantras]. For the sound of neighing or whinnying, he should offer clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍī verses. Upon receiving gifts such as jewels, garments, or cows, he should mutter the Sāvitrī eight thousand times. Paiṭhīnasi says: "If the wooden staff (daṇḍakāṣṭha) is lost, one should give food to a Brāhmaṇa and fast on that day. The same applies to the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). If the girdle (mekhalā) is lost, one should recite the two verses beginning with 'iyaṃ duruktāt'. Saṃvarta says: [The following rules apply:]... [text continues]... [text continues]... He who eats food alone while remaining at ease without having gone on a round for alms,
and he who eats without having bathed, should mutter the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times.
If he has not performed the fire-ritual at twilight,
he should bathe, worship the Sun, and become pure through breath control (prāṇāyāma).
If a student (brahmacārī) who is otherwise healthy should somehow sleep during the day, [he must likewise perform purification].
Having bathed and worshipped the Sun, one should recite the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times.
If one performs the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsti) without the sacred thread (brahmasūtra),
one should bathe with a concentrated mind and recite the Gāyatrī mantra eight thousand times.
If a twice-born man eats without his sacred thread (brahmasūtra),
he is purified by one hundred and eight repetitions of the Gāyatrī mantra and by breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Yama said: "He who sleeps at sunrise is called 'one awakened by the sun';
he who sleeps when the sun has set is indeed 'one released from the sun'."
Both of those who have stolen the Veda, having fasted for a full day and night and being purified,
should separately perform their daily rites with ten thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī.

One who is overtaken by the sun rising is one who has fasted for the day; one who is overtaken by the sun setting is one who has fasted for the night. Thus, both having fasted for a day and a night, they should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the *Gāyatrī* one thousand and ten times during the day. Vasiṣṭha says: "Being overtaken by the rising sun, he should remain standing during the day and recite the *Sāvitrī*; likewise, being overtaken by the setting sun, he should remain seated during the night. Viṣṇu says: "One overtaken by the rising or setting sun should bathe with his clothes on and repeat the *Sāvitrī* one hundred and eight times. Regarding the section on the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), Baudhāyana says: "In that case, if the evening prayer is omitted, there is a fast for the night; if the morning prayer is omitted, there is a fast for the day. Āpastamba says: "If he falls asleep after the sun has set, he should remain seated for the night without eating and restraining his speech; when dawn has broken, having touched water, he may release his speech. If he is overtaken by the sun while awake, he should remain standing during the day without eating and restraining his speech until sunset; some say he should restrain his vital breaths (*prāṇāyāma*) [until exhaustion]. "Without eating" means not consuming food. "Until exhausted" (*ātamita*) means until he is weary; or it refers to the intention of the sun's setting. (3.282)
Furthermore: "In the case of eating honey or meat, one must perform the Kṛcchra penance and the remaining vows. (3.283)

If a *brahmacārin* consumes honey or eats meat that is fit to be eaten by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), he must perform the *prājāpatya* penance. Alternatively, the remainder of the *brahmacarya* vow or of any one of the Vedic observances (*vedavrata*) that was commenced must be performed. This injunction regarding the performance of the remaining portion of the vow is intended to remove the suspicion that the *brahmacarya* must be undertaken anew. Such a suspicion arises because of the rule for re-initiation (*punar-upanayana*). Thus says Saṃvarta:
"If a *brahmacārin* should somehow consume honey or meat, he becomes pure by performing the ordinary *kṛcchra* penance and the *mauñjī-homa*."

And this refers to the eating of meat that is fit to be eaten by the *śiṣṭas* (cultured/learned). As Vasiṣṭha says: [1144] "If a student (*brahmacārī*) should eat meat that is fit to be eaten by the *śiṣṭas*, he should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights and complete the remainder of his vow. And this applies to one who is not ill. But for one who is ill, there is no fault even in eating honey and meat; thus he says: "If he should fall ill, he may at will eat all the remains of his teacher for the sake of medicine. Honey, meat, and so forth are not prohibited [in such cases]. Furthermore, there is no fault even in eating honey when it is obtained unintentionally; thus he says: "It is known from the *Vājasaneyaka* that honey obtained unintentionally does not cause defilement. The *Vājasaneyaka* is another branch of the Yajurveda. Regarding the subject of the student, Paiṭhīnasi states: "Upon eating honey or meat, there is a three-night fast and a re-initiation (*punar-upanayana*). This refers to a case where one is incapable of performing the *prājāpatya* penance. Manu says:
If a twice-born man who has not yet returned home from his teacher’s house should eat food given monthly (māsikānna),
he shall fast for three days and remain in water for one day.
In this context, "monthly" (māsika) refers to that which is prescribed for the anniversary of the day of death each month; it does not, however, refer to the new-moon śrāddha.
Regarding the food of a woman in childbirth, the *navaśrāddha*, and likewise the monthly śrāddha food:
if a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) should eat these, he becomes pure after three nights.

Thus, by the statement of Saṃvarta, [this applies] because of its association with the *navaśrāddha* (the first funeral rite). Baudhāyana says: "If he should fall ill, he may eat all the guru’s leavings for the sake of medicine. He may purify himself with whatever he desires. When he becomes free from disease, he should rise and worship the Sun with this verse: ‘The swan dwelling in purity... Here, *agada* means free from disease. Vṛddhayājñavalkya says: "A student (*brahmacārī*), one under a vow (*vratin*), and a Brāhmaṇa widow who, having eaten honey or meat, is purified in just three nights."
Yama states: "He who eats honey, meat, food offered at a śrāddha,
or food from a birth-impurity (sūtaka) shall perform the Prājāpatya penance and complete the remainder of his vow."
This refers to the absence of vomiting. Śātātapa says:
"If a Brahmin, especially a student (brahmacārī), should drink water, eat food, or touch [an impure person] out of ignorance during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka)... [1145]
If one drinks water [from such a vessel], one should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
for drinking [it] over three nights, it is prescribed; and having touched [it], bathing is ordained.

Viṣṇu: "A student (brahmacārī) who eats at an *āmaśrāddha* shall fast for three nights. Hārīta: "But a student who, weak in knowledge, eats the food of a Śūdra, shall be purified by the Parāka penance; there can be no other expiation."
If a religious student (brahmacārī) should eat the leavings of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, or even the leavings of a Śūdra,
how shall his purification be effected?
Having likewise performed the ritual bath, one should mutter the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times;
by fasting for twelve days, purification is achieved in each case individually.
In the same way, it is certain that for a householder, it is three-quarters [of the former].

This refers respectively to the eating of the remnants of food left by a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas. Furthermore, for a Brāhmaṇa who eats the remnants of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, and for a Kṣatriya who eats the remnants of a Śūdra, a somewhat greater penance should be prescribed. Devala states: "If one observing a vow should ever eat the food of a Sūta, honey, or meat, he shall fast for three nights and dwell for one night in water."

By this [verse], dwelling in water at night is prescribed; by Manu, however, during the day. Therefore, there is an option between them. But when the gravity of the offense is great, there is a combination of both. (3.283)

In connection with the topic of the religious student (*brahmacārin*), he says something regarding the teacher (*guru*): "If one sent by the teacher dies, the teacher shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances. If a religious student, having been sent—that is, dispatched—by his teacher into a situation where it is possible [to return] for the sake of food, should die, then the teacher must perform three *kṛcchra* penances, beginning with the *prājāpatya*. Here, the word "religious student" (*brahmacārī*) is understood from the preceding statement. Therefore, while the expiation for the religious student is the subject at hand, the expiation for the teacher is taught as a relevant digression.
Having acted in opposition to the guru, one becomes pure only after propitiating him. || 3.284 ||

Having committed an act contrary to the teacher that causes him pain, one becomes purified and free from sin by propitiating him so that his distress and anger have departed. On this point, Vasiṣṭha says: "In the case of false accusations against the teacher, one should bathe with one's clothes on and propitiate the teacher; thus he becomes pure—so it is known. [1146] This refers to a minor offense committed once unintentionally. However, regarding a major offense committed intentionally and with persistent intent, which constitutes hostility toward the teacher, Manu has prescribed the twelve-year vow of a student of Brahman (*brahmacarya*) for its expiation, stating: "Likewise, having embraced the teacher... Alternatively, the rule of Manu or Vasiṣṭha may refer to the father, while the rule of Yājñavalkya refers to a secondary teacher (*aupacārika-guru*). Viṣṇu states: "In the case of a lie concerning one's own excellence, false accusations against the teacher, or slandering him, one should subsist on milk for one month. This refers to cases of slight practice. 3.284.
Since the general grounds for expiation have been established, he states an exception to that rule in a specific case:
"But when a Brahmin who is providing assistance dies, there is no sin."

If, while performing medical treatment or similar acts for the sake of providing assistance, the living being who is to be helped—such as a Brahmin or another—should die, then no sin arises for the practitioner of the medicine or other means on account of that violence. Thus, for those who perform medical treatment and the like with proper knowledge and diligent effort, there is an absence of sin. However, if the death of a living being occurs due to such an act through ignorance or negligence, the perpetrator certainly incurs the connection with sin. For this very reason, Saṃvarta includes the word "diligently":
"And with diligence, for the sake of medical treatment, in the extraction of a dead fetus."
"If misfortune should occur despite an effort having been made, no expiation is required.
Here, the mention of a "Brahmin" is intended to indicate living beings in general.
He now states the expiation for one who utters a false accusation:
He who falsely accuses another of a great sin or a minor sin [commits a transgression]. (3.285)
Subsisting on water, he should remain for a month, reciting [the mantra] with his senses restrained.

If one falsely accuses another with a grave sin (*mahāpātaka*) such as the killing of a Brahmin, or a minor sin (*upapātaka*) such as the killing of a cow, saying to those engaged in legal dealings, "This person has committed this sin," he shall sit for a month subsisting on water alone, with his senses restrained, reciting [the *Śuddhavatī* verses]. This penance is to be understood as applying when the accusation of a grave sin is made once, or when the accusation of a minor sin is made repeatedly. The instrumental case in the phrase "by means of a grave sin or a minor sin" (*mahāpāpopapāpābhyām*) denotes the instrument. Regarding what is to be recited, Vasiṣṭha states: "Having falsely accused someone of the killing of a Brahmin—whether by a crime causing loss of caste (*patanīya*) or a minor crime (*upapatanīya*)—one becomes pure by subsisting on water for a month and repeating the *Śuddhavatī* verses, or by going to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse-sacrifice; by this, the case of one who is falsely accused is explained. The meaning is that even one who is falsely accused should perform the same penance. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "An atheist, a killer of a cow, a fraudulent dealer, one who destroys the livelihood of a Brahmin, and a false accuser—these six shall beg for alms in the houses of Brahmins for six years, or eat washed alms-food for one year, or follow cows for six months. This is to be understood as applying to cases of extreme repetition, where there is a continuous connection to the act, and when the accuser is a Brahmin who faces punishment such as branding or banishment. Regarding the penances prescribed for one who accuses a Brahmin, a reduction in the penance should be inferred for accusations involving the castes in the direct order of precedence (*ānulomya*), whereas an increase should be inferred for the reverse order (*prātilomya*). Therefore:
But for defamation in the reverse order of castes, the fines are double and triple;
for the castes in the direct order, they are reduced by half and half again from that amount.

Thus, the increase and decrease of punishment have been declared in cases of verbal abuse involving castes in the direct or inverse order. Yama says: "If a man, out of anger, ever declares his wife to be unapproachable, he shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for the purification of that sin."
A Brāhmaṇa should perform the Prājāpatya penance; a Kṣatriya for nine days;
a Vaiśya should perform it for six nights; and a Śūdra should perform it for three nights.
In the section concerning *suvarcalā*, Hārīta states:
"In cases of false accusation, verbal abuse, and backbiting against one's gurus,
one should diligently drink that very [juice] for twenty-one nights."

The meaning is that she is indeed *suvarcalā*. Śātātapa states: "In the case of transgressing against the gods, teachers, or Brahmins, there shall be three thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī. Āpastamba states: "Having reviled one who should not be reviled, or having spoken a falsehood, one must eat food free from pungent seasonings and salt for three nights; for a Śūdra, this lasts seven nights, and for women as well. Viṣṇu states: "But having made a false oath involving the killing of a Brahmin, a Brahmin should perform the severe Cāndrāyaṇa penance while subsisting on *yāvaka* (barley-gruel)."

For a Kṣatriya, there should be a Parāka penance; likewise for a Vaiśya, a Prājāpatya; but for a Śūdra, the vow should be observed for three nights as prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa. [1148] Śaṅkha states: "In cases of abusive speech and speaking falsehoods, there is a fast for one night. (3.285)
In connection with the penance for one who falsely accuses another, he states the penance for the one who is falsely accused:
"One who has been falsely accused shall perform the Kṛcchra penance and likewise the Āgneya penance. (3.286)
One should offer either a cake to Vāyu or a pap-oblation to Vāyu.

One who has been falsely accused should perform a penance. He should offer a *caru* or a *puroḍāśa* dedicated to Agni (the deity of fire), or he may offer a *caru* or a *puroḍāśa* dedicated to Vāyu. These alternatives are to be determined according to the gravity or lightness of the sin for which he was accused, or according to his capacity, circumstances, and so forth. As for what Vasiṣṭha stated—having prescribed subsisting on water for one month and the recitation of the *Śuddhavatī* verses for one falsely accused by a curse—"by this, the case of one accused [of a crime] is explained"—that should be understood as referring to one accused of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*). Furthermore, even for one who is innocent, a penance is required because of the scriptural injunction regarding the exclusion of one who has been falsely accused, just as there is for one who has performed a *parivitti* marriage. And as for what Paiṭhīnasi stated—"One being falsely accused of a minor sin (*pātaka*) should perform a *kṛcchra* penance; for two months if [accused] of mortal sins"—that is to be understood as referring to one accused of many mortal sins (i.e., *mahāpātakas*). Baudhāyana says: "For accusing someone of a mortal sin, a *kṛcchra* is prescribed; for one who is falsely accused, half of that. This refers to cases of accusation involving very minor faults. (3.286)
Furthermore:
"If one approaches his brother's wife without being appointed [for levirate], he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (3.287)

One who approaches the wife of an elder or younger brother without the scriptural authorization (*śāstrīyaviniyoga*) should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance to be described hereafter. This applies to a single instance of unintentional intercourse, or to intentional intercourse that ceases before the act is completed, or specifically to the case of approaching the wife of a brother who has already violated his own duty (*vipluta*). However, in the case of repeated unintentional intercourse, Śaṅkha says: "The one superseded (*parivitti*) and the one who supersedes (*parivettṛ*) shall subsist on alms at the houses of Brahmins for one year; the same applies to one who approaches the wife of an elder brother without being authorized, or the wife of a younger brother. But if the act is intentional and repeated, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the penance prescribed for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*). (3.287)
Furthermore:
at the end of three nights, having consumed clarified butter and approached a woman in her courses, one becomes pure.

Having approached one’s own wife who is *udakyā* (menstruating), one becomes pure by fasting for three nights and consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*) at the end of that period; one is thereby liberated from this sin. This applies to a single intentional act of approaching one’s own wife. However, regarding a single unintentional act of approaching her, Śātātapa says: “For voiding urine or feces without water, there shall be a bath with one’s clothes on and an oblation (*homa*) with the *mahāvyāhṛtis*; the same applies to approaching a menstruating woman. For non-human females, this is the rule, except in the case of a cow. Regarding a single intentional act of approaching another’s wife, Vasiṣṭha says: “In the event of sexual intercourse (*vyavāya*) with a menstruating woman, one should give a black bull with white marks. Here, *vyavāya* means sexual union, and *liṅga* means a mark or brand. As for that which was stated by Manu:

"Having discharged semen among non-human females, a woman in her courses, those who are not the [proper] womb, or in water, one should perform the *sāṃtapana* penance"— this refers to intentional and habitual sexual intercourse with another's wife. Regarding this very subject, Saṃvarta speaks concerning one who approaches a woman against her will:
If one should approach a woman who is menstruating, or one who is pregnant, or likewise one who is fallen (patita),
the atikṛcchra penance is the purification for the expiation of his sin.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Upon approaching a woman in her menses or an *avadhūtā*, there shall be a fast for three nights and the consumption of clarified butter. An *avadhūtā* is a harlot; and approaching her is a distinct cause [for penance]. Regarding intentional and excessive repetition—specifically regarding intercourse with the wife of a *śrotriya* until conception—Śaṅkha, having introduced the twelve-year penance, says: "But one quarter [of that] for killing a Śūdra, and likewise for approaching a woman in her menses (*udakyā*). The meaning is that, when the causes of killing a Śūdra or approaching a woman in her menses occur, one should perform the three-year vow, which constitutes one quarter of the twelve-year penance. Bṛhaspati speaks in this very context regarding cases where there is no conception or where the woman is not the wife of a *śrotriya*.
A man who has approached a Pukkasa woman unintentionally, one who is menstruating intentionally,
or the wife of his pupil, becomes pure by performing the Parāka penance.

Śātātapa states: "In the case of approaching a woman in her menses, [the penance lasts for] seven nights. This is of the same scope as the rule of Manu. Here, in all cases of approaching the wife of another who is in her menses, the penance for adultery (*pāradārya*) must be performed separately, because the causes [of the two offenses] are distinct and independent of one another. However, where [the offense] is inseparable from another cause, there is only a single occasional penance (*naimittika*). For example, in the case of violating the Guru's bed (*gurutalpaga*); for violating the Guru's bed is indeed inseparable from adultery. In that case, approaching a woman in her menses is a separate cause, because it lacks such inseparability. The same applies to approaching her by day or on a sacred festival day (*parvan*). Furthermore, for one committing the murder of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), the cause such as raising a weapon must be treated as a separate factor, since injury certainly occurs even without it—as in the case of covering the mouth and nose with a cloth and so forth, or by administering poison, or by throwing oneself from a precipice (*bhṛgu*).
[1150] He states the expiation for accepting gifts from the unworthy:
"Dwelling in a cow-pen for one month, observing the vow of milk, the student (brahmacārī) [should perform penance]. (3.288)
One who is devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī is liberated from the acquisition of what is unreal.

Dwelling in a cow-pen—that is, in the very place where the cows reside—the religious student (*brahmacārī*), following after a woman, shall subsist on milk alone as his vow and drink it while intent upon the recitation of the *Sāvitrī*. By proceeding in this manner continuously for one month, he is released from the acceptance of what is improper (*asat*). "Acceptance of what is improper" (*asat-pratigraha*) refers to the acceptance of that which is censurable (*nindita*); it does not, however, mean the acceptance of forbidden gifts (*pratiṣiddha-pratigraha*), for the latter is not enumerated among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*). Indeed, the taking of wealth from censurable persons was declared by Manu to be a minor offense; and he himself stated that dwelling in a cow-pen and so forth constitutes the penance for this.

"Having recited three thousand repetitions of the Sāvitrī with a concentrated mind, and having drunk milk for a month in a cow-pen, one is released from the sin of accepting improper gifts. Thus it is said.
The expiation must be performed only after having renounced the wealth that was accepted. Regarding this, Manu says:
"Whatever wealth Brāhmaṇas acquire through a censurable action,
they become purified by its renunciation, by silent recitation (japa), and indeed by austerity. Thus says Kaśyapa.
For accepting what is forbidden, one should live for a month in a cow-pen subsisting on milk;
or, for a killer of a cow, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance or the prescribed vow.
One should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; that is to say, the killer of a cow should observe the three-month vow. According to the Caturviṃśatimata:
"When even a mere morsel of alms is received, one should recite the meritorious mantra;
in all acts of acceptance [of gifts], one should assign a sixth part [to the deity]."
Having understood the nature of sacrifices and the acceptance of gifts, one should perform recitations, fire-offerings, and other rites;
through the Pavitreṣṭi sacrifice, all terrible consequences of accepting gifts are purified.
By means of the Aindava rite, the Mṛgāreṣṭi, or sometimes the Mitravindā,
as well as by the hundred-thousand-fold recitation of the Goddess’s mantra, people are liberated from the sin of accepting improper gifts.

"Should provide" means he should give to the Brahmins. "The Goddess Gāyatrī. Uśanas: "If a twice-born Brāhmaṇa accepts or consumes property from one who has fallen [from his caste], that twice-born man, having performed the renunciation of that [property], should perform the Atikṛcchra penance. [1151]

Hārīta states: "Upon accepting jewels, garments, cattle, and the like, one should mutter the Sāvitrī mantra a thousand times; five thousand times for a middling acceptance, ten thousand for a superior one, and observing a milk-vow for twelve nights; and for excessive acceptances, one hundred thousand times. For middling acceptances, one should mutter it five thousand times. The middling nature of the acceptance is determined by the middling nature of the object to be accepted. Likewise, for a superior acceptance, one should mutter it ten thousand times. On this point, Devala says: "Nine kinds are superior, four are middling according to their value; the remaining are inferior—thus they know this threefold classification."
Food, curd, honey, protection, cattle, land, gold, horses, and elephants—
these are the supreme gifts, owing to the excellence of the substances given.
One should know that gifts of clothing, dwellings, articles for use,
and medicines are "middling" because they consist of middling substances.
Sandals, swings, vehicles, umbrellas, vessels, and seats;
lamps, wood, fruits, and so forth—these last items may be kept for many years.
Because the varieties of objects are so numerous, a numerical limit is not prescribed for the remaining gifts;
therefore, the wise know all other gifts to be inferior.
Excessive giving (*atidāna*) is taught in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*:
"They say there are three excessive gifts: cows, land, and Sarasvatī.
Here, although the plural form "cows" (*gāvaḥ*) is used, it is intended as a singular; therefore, the acceptance of many of them constitutes the highest form of receiving a gift. Likewise:
Having accepted a gift from a king, one should always dwell in water for a month;
eating only milk at every sixth mealtime, he is liberated when the month is complete.
Having constantly gratified the twice-born with their desires while remaining firm in his vows,
a king is liberated from sin through austerity or even through sacrifice.

Sumantu: "One who performs sacrifices for Śūdras becomes purified by renouncing all his property. Baudhāyana: "Having accepted what should not be accepted, or having eaten the food of one whose food should not be eaten, or having performed a sacrifice for one for whom one should not sacrifice, or having accepted an excessive gift from one from whom gifts should not be accepted, one should mutter the *Taratsamandīya* [verse]. (3.288)
Moreover:
One who performs sacrifices for those excluded from the community (vrātya) should perform three kṛcchra penances, even if he does so for the purpose of malevolent magic.

One who has submerged the Vedas, one who eats barley for a year, one who has abandoned a person seeking refuge, and one who acts as a priest (*ṛtvij*) for *vrātyas* or those fallen from the *Sāvitrī*—these should perform the three types of *kṛcchra* penances beginning with the *Prājāpatya*, which will be described hereafter. One performing even an act of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) should perform this same penance. And malevolent magic is prescribed by Baudhāyana for six cases, beginning with arsonists and other assassins (*ātatāyin*), stating: "One falls [from his status] by practicing malevolent magic against these six. It is only when [the victim] is other than these that it becomes a cause for expiation. Manu says:
"Having performed the sacrifice for *vrātyas*, or having performed the funeral rites for others..."
One is purified from the practice of malevolent magic and the Ahīna sacrifice by three Kṛcchra penances.

The *antyakarma* (final rites) is the *antyeṣṭi* (funeral sacrifice). When one performs this for the sake of payment, it is not for the sake of dharma; however, when a Brāhmaṇa performs the final rites for Kṣatriyas and others, this [penance] applies specifically to him. An *ahargaṇa* consisting of a group of days beginning with two nights and ending with twelve nights is called an *ahīna*. Śātātapa says: "One should not initiate those whose *Sāvitrī* has been lost, nor should one teach them; he who initiates or teaches them must perform the *Uddālaka-vrata*. This refers to cases of intentional repetition. The *Uddālaka-vrata* has already been described. Regarding the service of a Śūdra priest, sacrificer, or teacher, Yama says:
And for all of them who request readmission,
the twice-born man, while subsisting on alms-food, shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One should cause the fruit to float unhesitatingly in the waters of the Nāga lake;
by the relinquishing of wealth at the conclusion of the effort, one is thereby liberated from that sin.
Having drunk the *brahmasuvarcalā* plant— which is dry and free from alkaline salt—
and having performed the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) for it, one then becomes eligible for social and religious intercourse.

The fruit [of this] is wealth obtained from a Śūdra; the effort [required] is penance. Regarding the continuation [of the rule], Vasiṣṭha states: "Or they should remain for three nights, restrained in speech and fasting; it is known that those who practice this for a maximum of a thousand [days] become purified. By this very [rule], those who teach what is censurable are explained; it is known that they become purified by the renunciation of their fees (*dakṣiṇā*). Likewise: a "corrupter of the Veda" (*vedaplāvī*) is one who causes the Veda to be corrupted. One who studies by himself in a forbidden place or time while being impure, or one who teaches what is forbidden, or one who studies from a forbidden source—such persons are "corrupters of the Veda. Furthermore, he who, though capable of protecting them, abandons one who has come for refuge after considering, "He shall save my life"—both of these should fast for a year. And so says Manu:

Having abandoned one who has sought refuge, or having caused the Veda to be lost, a twice-born man removes that sin by subsisting on barley for one year. A specific penance for one who abandons his father or mother has been stated by Manu due to their status as those excluded from the company at meals (*apāṅktya*).
Eating only at the sixth meal-time for a month, or the recitation of the Saṃhitā,
and daily Śākala oblations— these are the means of purification for those excluded from the company at meals.

And those unworthy of the company at a *śrāddha* have been shown by that very same author in the *Śrāddhakalpa*: "Those who are thieves, outcasts, eunuchs, and those who follow the lifestyle of nihilists."

By such statements as these, the general penances for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) are to be prescribed according to one's capacity, the nature of the connection [to the sin], and whether the act was preceded by habitual practice or not, taking all these factors into account. Regarding this, Hārīta says: "The defiler of a maiden, the seller of Soma, the husband of a *vṛṣalī*, the abandoner of a wife married in youth, the drinker of *surā* or other intoxicants, the officiant for a *śūdra*, the reviler of his guru, the atheist, one who lives like an atheist, the ungrateful, the fraudulent dealer, the destroyer of a Brāhmaṇa’s livelihood, the false accuser, the associate of outcasts, the betrayer of friends, the killer of those seeking refuge, and the one who lives by counterfeiting—these shall perform the penance of five fires, exposure to the sun, and sleeping in water. During the summer, the rainy season, and the winter, they shall eat barley-gruel mixed with cow-urine for one month. In this context, by the term "defiler of a maiden," it is not intended merely to denote the act of defiling a maiden; rather, it refers specifically to one who defiles her through *prātilomya* (intercourse with a woman of a higher caste), because the penance is more severe. In this very regard, the greater severity of punishment is recorded: "There is no fault in the case of willing women when approached in the direct order of castes (*ānulomya*), but otherwise there is death. According to this, in the case of defiling a maiden of the same caste, a three-month penance or a *Cāndrāyaṇa* should be prescribed according to the gravity of the offense. However, in the case of defiling her through *prātilomya*, a *Kṛcchra*, *Atikṛcchra*, or a month-long consumption of *pañcagavya* should be prescribed. As for what was stated by Śaṅkha—"The defiler of a maiden and the seller of Soma shall perform a *Kṛcchra* for a year"—that also refers to the defilement of a maiden through *prātilomya*. Even in the case of *prātilomya*, the punishment for a *śūdra* is death, but for defilement, it is the amputation of hands, as seen in the rule: "In the case of the highest [caste woman], there is death. Regarding the abandonment of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), Vasiṣṭha states: "One who has abandoned the Veda (*brahmojjha*) shall perform a *Kṛcchra* for twelve nights and then receive the Veda again from a teacher. Here, by virtue of the specific statement, all *Kṛcchras* that can be accomplished in twelve nights are prescribed. Among them, in the event of an extreme emergency or a very short period of abandonment, a *Prājāpatya* is required. For a longer period, an *Atikṛcchra*; and for a period even longer than that, a *Parāka*—the penance should be determined along these lines. But when one abandons Vedic study for a long time due to being preoccupied with the acquisition of wealth, then one of the general penances for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) should be prescribed. In that regard, for one who abandons the Veda during a mild emergency, a three-month penance equal to that of a cow-killer should be prescribed; in a moderate case, a *Cāndrāyaṇa*—this is the method of determination. If one abandons the Veda out of atheism (*nāstikya*), that should be known as equal to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, because of the rule of equality stating: "And the destruction of what has been studied. Regarding the abandonment of the sacred fires (*agni*), Vasiṣṭha also says: "He who casts away the fires shall perform a *Kṛcchra* for twelve nights and have the fires re-established. Here too, since multiple *Kṛcchras* achievable in twelve nights would otherwise apply, the specific *Kṛcchra*—whether light or heavy—and the duration of twelve nights should be determined by considering the cause of the abandonment of the fire and the brevity or length of that abandonment. Manu says:
If a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires should abandon those fires out of his own will, he must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one month; for that act is equal to the killing of a hero.

The syntactical connection is: "One should discard the fires for a month. The *vīra* is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). However, if they are abandoned after a longer period, the penance for killing a cow (*goghna-prāyaścitta*) lasting three months applies. As for that which was stated by Hārīta: "If the *Agnihotra* has been neglected for a year, one should perform a *Cāndrāyaṇa* and then re-establish them; if for two years, one should perform a *Somāyana* and a *Cāndrāyaṇa*; if for three years, one should practice the *Kṛcchra* for a year and then re-establish them"—this refers to unintentional abandonment of the fires. The *Somāyana* will be explained later. Śaṅkha says: "One who has let the fires go out (*agnyutsādī*) should perform a *Cāndrāyaṇa* for a year and give a cow"; this refers to the case where they have been neglected for three years. Gautama, under the rule "one should observe the standard student-discipline (*brahmacarya*) for a year," adds: "for those who have let the fires go out, those who are excluded (*nirākṛti*), and those who have committed minor offenses (*upapātaka*). This is equivalent to the year-long *Kṛcchra*. Paiṭhīnasi says: "One who has let the fires go out [purifies himself] with the *Taptakṛcchra*"; this applies before a month has passed since the re-establishment (*ādhāna*). Śaṅkha and Likhita say: "One who has let the fires go out and one who has studied falsely (*mithyādhītī*) should both live on alms in the houses of Brāhmaṇas for a year"; this is equivalent to the standard student-discipline. A "false student" (*mithyādhītī*) is one who corrupts the Veda. In this very context, Viṣṇu states a specific rule: "One who has let the Vedas or the fires go out should bathe at the three periods of the day, sleep on the ground, and subsist on alms for a year. As for what was said by Bharadvāja: "Twenty-four breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) for twenty-four nights, fasting for thirty nights, three nights for sixty nights, and from then on up to a year, a *Prājāpatya*; beyond that, as the time increases and the fault increases, so does the gravity of the fault"—this refers to the abandonment of the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*). "Upon the lapse of twelve [days], fasting for three days; upon the lapse of a month, fasting for twelve days; upon the lapse of a year, fasting for a month or subsisting on milk"—this also refers specifically to the intentional abandonment of the domestic fire. Regarding the sale of a son, if it consists of selling him, Pracetas states the penance: "A liar, a thief, a king's servant, one who lives by planting trees, a poisoner, an arsonist, one who lives by riding horses, elephants, or chariots, a stage-player, a dog-handler, a teacher of Śūdras, a maker of musical instruments (*bhāṇḍika*), one who lives by the stars, one who lives like a dog, one who lives by the Brahman, a physician, a temple-priest (*devalaka*), a domestic priest, a gambler, a drunkard, a forger, a seller of offspring, and a seller of humans or cattle—these Brāhmaṇas, having assembled, should righteously and according to rule redeem them. At the time of total renunciation, eating only at every fourth meal-time, they should bathe at the three periods of the day for a year. At its conclusion, there is the libation to gods and ancestors and the daily provision of a cow; thus they become fit for social intercourse. And this refers to intentional and excessive repetition. Here, those unfit for the funeral feast (*apāṅkta*) mentioned in the section on *Śrāddha* are referred to; for them, the penance stated by Manu beginning with "eating only at the sixth meal-time for a month" applies. As for those among these minor offenders (*upapātakin*) who have not been specifically mentioned, they incur whichever of the general minor-offense penances is prescribed. On this very subject, Baudhāyana also says: "Now, the causes of impurity: gambling, malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), living by gleaning for one who has not established the sacred fires, living by begging for one who has returned home from study, staying in the teacher's house beyond four months, and he who teaches him [beyond that], and one who points out the constellations. The expiation (*nirveśa*) for these is: twelve months, twelve half-months, twelve periods of twelve days, twelve periods of six days, twelve periods of three days, twelve days, six days, three days, one day.
