A "dog-handler" (*śvāgaṇika*) is one who lives by a pack of dogs. A "maker of musical instruments" (*bhāṇḍika*) is one whose speech is unfit for an assembly. *Nirveśa* means penance. Likewise: "Sea-voyage, misappropriation of a Brāhmaṇa’s deposit, trading in all kinds of merchandise, lying about land, service to a Śūdra, and he who is born even of a Śūdra woman, and his offspring—the expiation for these is: they should eat limited food at the fourth meal-time, bathe following the ritual of the *Savana*, and pass their time alternating between standing and sitting; in three years they destroy their own sin. And this refers to repeated practice. Regarding consorting with a woman of low birth (*hīnayoni*), Śātātapa states a specific penance: "A Brāhmaṇa who has previously married a Kṣatriya woman should perform a *Kṛcchra* for twelve nights, then dismiss her and marry her again. One who has previously married a Vaiśya woman should perform a *Taptakṛcchra*; one who has previously married a Śūdra woman should perform a *Kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. If a Kṣatriya has previously married a Vaiśya woman, he should perform a *Kṛcchra* for twelve nights, then dismiss her and marry her again. One who has a Kṣatriya woman as his first wife is "one who has previously married a Kṣatriya" (*rājanyāpūrvī*); he should marry a woman of his own caste. He should "marry her"—that is, take her as his wife—and so it is elsewhere too. This refers to one who is incapable [of the standard penance]. For one who is capable, the common three-month penance such as the *Cāndrāyaṇa* applies. By "consorting with a woman of low birth," intercourse with a woman of a lower caste is intended. And that, when she is married according to the order of castes, is neither a minor offense (*upapātaka*) nor can it be called adultery (*paradāra*), because that is already covered by the term "adultery" itself. Therefore, the term "consorting with a woman of low birth" should be explained as referring to intercourse with a woman married out of order or with a prostitute. Or else, it refers to intercourse with a woman of the lowest castes (*antyajāti*). In that regard, Saṃvarta states a specific penance for approaching a prostitute: "In the case of approaching a beast or a prostitute, a *Prājāpatya* should be prescribed. And this refers to a single instance of unintentional intercourse. As for that which was stated by Yama... [text continues].
The twice-born remove the sin arising from approaching a prostitute by drinking boiled water infused with *kuśa* grass once every day for seven nights.

Thus, this should be understood as applying to the case of approaching [a prostitute] twice or thrice unintentionally, or even once intentionally. As for that which was stated by Yama himself regarding approaching a prostitute—the vow of the *gurutalpa* penance and so forth—as in:
"Some prescribe the *gurutalpa* vow, some the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow; some desire it for the killer of a cow, and others for one who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*)."

Thus, this should be applied as referring to intentional repetition. Regarding living without belonging to an *āśrama*, Hārīta says: "One who lives without an *āśrama* should perform the *Prājāpatya* penance for one year and then enter an *āśrama*; for a second [year], the *Kṛcchra*; for a third, the *Kṛcchrātikṛcchra*; and beyond that, the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. This refers to cases of distress (*āpad*). In the absence of distress, the general penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) lasting three months applies. Eating forbidden food is declared by Manu to be a minor offense. And the forbidden nature of food is sixfold: by its own nature, by time, by contact, by the manner of preparation, by the intention [of the giver], and by the person from whom it is received. Among these, [forbiddenness] is due to its own nature in the case of garlic and the like; due to time in the case of fermented liquids and the like; due to contact in the case of what has been touched by a dog and the like; due to the manner of preparation in the case of side-dishes offered with the hand and the like; due to intention in the case of sugarcane juice and the like—for someone might have the intention that the sugarcane juice is wine; and due to the person from whom it is received in the case of the food of outcasts and the like.
Regarding the determination of expiation for eating what is forbidden to eat, Viṣṇu states:
"In the case of a Brāhmaṇa, the full amount should be given; for a Kṣatriya, it is considered one-quarter less;
for a Vaiśya, half or one-quarter; and for those of the Śūdra caste, one-quarter is prescribed."
On this point, Manu says:
"Having intentionally eaten mushrooms, a village pig, garlic, a village cock,
onion, or leek, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste]."
Having unknowingly eaten these six, one should perform the Sāṃtapanakṛcchra penance or the Yaticāndrāyaṇa; for the remaining [forbidden foods], one should fast for a day.

In the case of intentionally eating mushrooms and similar forbidden foods, there is a loss of status characterized by the forfeiture of the duties of the twice-born; the expiation for this is precisely the vow prescribed for a drinker of *surā*.
Abandoning the Veda, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, killing a friend, and eating forbidden food or drink—these six are equal to the drinking of *surā*.

Thus, Manu himself has declared that [eating certain forbidden things] is equal to drinking liquor. For consuming these unintentionally but habitually, one must perform the *yaticāndrāyaṇa*. For the remaining forbidden foods, when consumed, there is a fast for one day. According to the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"Having eaten garlic, leeks, the fruit of the *tṛṇarāja* (the date palm), or indigo, a twice-born man should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow."
This applies to eating once, whether unintentionally or intentionally, when it has been done habitually. The "king of grasses" is the palmyra palm (*tāla*).
Having eaten a gourd, a small eggplant, thornless safflower, a reed, hemp, or its flower, one must fast for a day.
One should not eat bulbs, roots, fruits, and the like that have been gathered in a state of confusion;
in such a case, there shall be a fast, according to the words of Śātātapa.
Those who are confused and doubtful regarding what is fit or unfit to be eaten—
having consumed hemp-flower, silk-cotton flower, curd churned with the hand,
or a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) outside the altar— shall not eat for a day and a night.

Those items such as garlic that are similar [to permitted foods] in smell, color, taste, and so forth, are not to be eaten by the twice-born; having consumed them, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

Śaṅkha states: "One should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for eating garlic, onions, leeks, mushrooms, Nāliṅga, the flesh of a village pig, a village cock, or the hair and nails [of such animals]. Gṛñjana is a plant that resembles garlic. A deer which is struck by a weapon smeared with poison—
That meat of his is unfit to be eaten, for it is considered to be the same as the gṛñjana plant.

Thus some read. Śātātapa states: "In the case of eating garlic, onion, or *gṛñjana*, there is a *taptakṛcchra* penance; as is also the case for intentional and habitual consumption of beef. Regarding the application of the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance, Viṣṇu says: "In the case of eating garlic, onion, *gṛñjana*, [the plant] *picchagandhi*, village-pig, village-cock, human flesh, or beef—and in all these cases for the twice-born—one should perform the consecration (*saṃskāra*) again at the conclusion of the penance. Sumantu states: "In the case of eating garlic, onion, *gṛñjanaka*, *kumbhīka*, food from a *śrāddha*, food from a woman who has recently given birth, food that is unfit to be eaten, honey, meat, urine, semen, or other forbidden substances, one should pour eight thousand recitations of the Sāvitrī over one's head with water-drops (*sampāta*), and observe a fast. These very things are not prohibited for one who is ill and undergoing medical treatment; and there is no fault in the case of other things of this same kind. The pouring of water-drops and the fast apply to children who have not yet been initiated (*anupnīta*). Pracetās.

If a twice-born man should unknowingly drink nectar, white garlic, eggplant, *gṛñjana*, onion, tree resin, the property of a deity, *kavuka* beans, camel’s milk, or sheep’s milk, [he must perform penance].
And by fasting for three nights and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one is purified.
Pīyūṣa is the milk of a cow that has recently calved. This refers to one who, being unable [to digest it], has immediately vomited it up. Yama says:
likewise, those produced from the cutting of *taṇḍulīyaka*, *kumbhīka*, and *vraścana* trees, as well as *nālikā*, *nālikerī*, and the fruits of the *śleṣmāntaka*.
Having eaten bhūstṛṇa, śigruka, khukhuḍa, and likewise kṣavaka, one should perform the Prājāpatya vow.

*Nālikera* is a specific type of vegetable. *Kṣavaka* is the black mustard (*rājasarṣapa*). Āpastamba says: "If a Brāhmaṇa should ever consume indigo through negligence, purification occurs by means of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; so the sage Āpastamba has declared."
Saṃvarta says:

Having consumed the milk of animals with undivided hooves, of those that have not yet had their first calf, or of a cow within ten days of calving, the best of the twice-born shall drink barley-gruel for three nights.
One should consume only a small measure of *yāvaka* (barley gruel) and not satisfy oneself with it. Likewise:

"Having consumed the milk of a woman, the milk of a sheep, and the milk of a cow that is both lactating and pregnant, as well as the meat of village-dwelling animals, one becomes pure after three nights."

This [penance] applies to consuming [the milk of these animals] once unintentionally. Viṣṇu states: "In the case of consuming the milk of a camel, a donkey, or a human female, one must perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance. This also applies to consuming them once unintentionally. Śaṅkha says:
"One should specify that the milk of a buffalo, a cow, and a goat is fit for consumption;
however, having consumed the milk of another [animal], a wise man should observe the vow for one month."
Cow’s milk within ten days [of calving], as well as that of buffaloes, goats, and of a cow whose calf has died, and likewise the milk of a cow in heat; these are forbidden.

Having eaten the milk of a cow that is in heat or one that eats impure food, one should observe a fast for a fortnight; likewise, a wise man who consumes the products of such forbidden milks must do the same.
One should observe the vow for seven nights as it has been thus proclaimed.

The vow consists of subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel (*yāvaka*). Even elsewhere, in the statement of Śaṅkha, this very thing is designated by the word "vow" (*vrata*). According to the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "If a twice-born man, somehow deluded by passion, drinks the milk of a woman, he must undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) again and then perform a *prājāpatya* penance."
Having drunk the milk of a camel, of a cow in heat, of wild animals that roam the forest,
or of a cow within ten days of calving, one must fast for a day.
This applies to the case of ministers when there is a single, immediate discharge; it concerns women, children, and the infirm. From another Smṛti:
"The three—skin, flesh, and wool—are pure together with sheep's wool;
however, the other three—feces, urine, and milk—are impure."
If he eats out of negligence, he should observe the vow for one day.
The vow for those three impure substances is fasting; this refers to the subjects previously mentioned. Śātātapa says:
"Having consumed camel's milk, ewe's milk, food during the period of death or birth-impurity, the food of a thief, or food from a *navashrāddha*, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance."

This refers to cases of intentional and repeated practice. Paiṭhīnasi states: "Upon consuming the milk of a she-ass, a camel, or a human female, there shall be a second initiation (punar-upanayana) and a Prājāpatya penance. Jābāla says:
"Having consumed the milk of a cow within ten days of calving, as well as that of a human or a camel, liquor, or food from a *navaśrāddha*, one should perform a Cāndrāyaṇa penance."

This applies to eating [forbidden substances] once out of ignorance. *Madirā* is wine; it is a distinct substance other than *surā*, whose form and taste are concealed by other ingredients. Aṅgiras states: "One should specify that buffalo milk, cow's milk, and goat's milk are among the permissible milks.
Having consumed milk from any other [animal], one should perform a quarter *kṛcchra* penance."

Hārīta states: "For drinking *asurā* liquor or wine, for minor theft, for eating the *śleṣmātaka* fruit, for vomiting *māsa*, *ṣaṣṭika*, or *masūraka* beans, for eating black pepper, and for drinking water contaminated with impurities, one should perform the *sāṃtapana* penance. Vasiṣṭha, following the context of the *kṛcchra*, *atikṛcchra*, the consumption of ghee, and the re-initiation (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*), says: "The same applies to the consumption of urine, feces, and semen. Bṛhaspati says:
"A twice-born man who has drunk liquor through negligence should perform the *atikṛcchra* penance;
he should undergo re-initiation and feed Brahmins according to his ability."
"Intoxicant liquor" (*madya*) refers to dates, *pānasa* fruit, and the like, but not *surā*. "Twice-born" (*dvija*) means a Brahmin. Manu says:
"Having drunk water that has stood in a vessel used for *surā* or likewise in a vessel used for intoxicants, one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights. [1161]

*Milk* means *kṣīra*. This applies when the liquid in a vessel for *surā* has not dried up—that is, when the liquor-vessel is still moist and the taste and smell of the liquor are no longer perceived—and when one has vomited after drinking another beverage, as in the case of women, children, and so forth. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "For intentionally drinking water from a *surā* vessel, there shall be six nights of fasting and the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. This refers to when the water from a moist *surā* vessel has been drunk and digested. Śaṅkha says:
"Having drunk water that stood in a *surā* vessel, one should observe a vow for a fortnight;
having drunk water situated in a liquor-vessel, one should observe a vow for seven nights."

In the context of the three-night fast followed by the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*), Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The same [penance applies] for drinking water from a vessel defiled by honey or liquor, or for eating together with a woman. Viṣṇu states: "But if one drinks water, milk, or other liquids from a vessel that has been touched by *surā* (liquor) or defiled by semen, urine, and so forth, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance."
If one drinks [liquor] once and vomits it, the *taptakṛcchra* penance lasting two nights is required; if there is no vomiting, it lasts seven nights. Kāśyapa says:
"An excellent twice-born man who, through negligence, has drunk *madya* or *asura* liquor even once, becomes pure after ten nights by subsisting on cow-urine and barley-gruel."

Lack of intelligence is negligence (*pramāda*). Amarasimha states: "Negligence is lack of attentiveness. *Asura* refers to that which is distinct from *surā* (liquor). Vasiṣṭha says: "If a twice-born man should drink water situated in a vessel for liquor, he becomes pure after three nights by drinking the water of the lotus, *udumbara*, *bilva*, *palāśa*, and *kuśa* grasses. This refers to the case of drinking water situated in a vessel for liquor other than *surā*. Jābāla says: "Having drunk water from a *surā* vessel, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights."

*Surā* is that made from flour (*paiṣṭī*). This [penance] applies to drinking it once unintentionally from a vessel that has been cleansed of all traces of it. Śātātapa states: "Upon drinking water from a vessel that held liquor, there shall be vomiting, the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and a fast for a day and night. From the consumption of clarified butter, other food is excluded; the fast for a day and night is another requirement. This refers to a case where one is physically capable [of performing the penance]. Yama says: "If any twice-born man should drink water remaining after being licked by a dog, he becomes pure in three days by consuming milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī*."
If any twice-born man should drink water contained in a vessel for liquor,
he must subsist on milk and Brahmasuvarcalā for twelve days.

One should perform the mental recitation (*mānasa-japa*) of the *gāyatrī* eight thousand times, or one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā* every day; the meaning is that one should perform that recitation every day. Hārīta says:
"If a twice-born man should drink water that remains after being tasted by a woman..."
One is purified by drinking milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for three days.
If any twice-born man should drink water that remains as the leavings of a Śūdra,
he must subsist for three days on milk boiled with the roots of Kuśa grass.
Parāśara says: If a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra consumes water, milk, or curd that has been kept in a vessel containing food unfit for consumption, he becomes tainted.
The Brahmakūrca penance and fasting should be applied as the expiation for this act;
however, for a Śūdra there is no fasting, and he is purified by a single gift.

*Upasajjati* means he comes for the purpose of performing penance (*prāyaścitta*). The nature of the *brahmakūrca* shall be described later. Vṛddha-Śātātapa says: "If one drinks water that has fallen from a vessel or has flowed out by its own force, that food becomes unfit to be eaten; having consumed it, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance."
Śaṅkha says:
Having drunk water that was left over after someone else has drunk, or having drunk water with his left hand, a Brāhmaṇa should perform a vow for three nights.
Parāśara says: Having seen a dog, a jackal, or a monkey fallen into a well,
and having drunk water that is impure due to the falling of bones, skin, and other such things, a twice-born man [must perform penance].
A human corpse, a crow, a village pig, a donkey, a camel,
a gavaya, a supratīka, a vāgguda, and likewise an ākhujanga;
If a bone of a tiger or a lion falls into a well,
or if one has drunk the water of a contaminated pond, [one must perform purification].
His expiation shall be performed entirely according to this sequence:
a Brahmin becomes pure in three nights, and a Kṣatriya in two days.
A Vaiśya is purified in one day, and a Śūdra is purified by eating only at night.

*Supratīka* is the name of an elephant; this [penance] belongs to one who has used its water. This refers to the use of water from a pond (*taḍāga*). However, for the use of water from a well (*kūpa*), a heavier penance should be prescribed. Viṣṇu states: "Having drunk water from a well containing a dead five-toed animal, or from one that is utterly defiled, a Brāhmaṇa shall fast for three nights; a Kṣatriya for two days; a Vaiśya for one day; and a Śūdra for a single night. At the conclusion of their respective vows, all shall drink the *pañcagavya*. Āpastamba says:
"[The same applies] when all five-toed animals have died or become wet within [the water]."
He who drinks water through ignorance becomes purified in six nights;
[if the water is] not moist, it shall be for three nights, but for Śūdras, it is for only one day. Thus says Aṅgiras.
If one should unknowingly drink water taken up by a Caṇḍāla,
one should know that his purification is always achieved through the Prājāpatya penance.
Those who are defiled by drinking from a single well may cause defilement through contact;
all such persons are purified by fasting and the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
But he who unintentionally drinks even a little [water] touched by a Caṇḍāla shall perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance for the sake of his own purification.
Laghuvishnu states:
If one should consume water that has been defiled by urine, feces, or similar substances,
then the Sāṃtapana vow is prescribed for the purification of the body.
Laghuhārīta:
A Brāhmaṇa who drinks water from a well defiled by a corpse becomes pure by performing three days of fasting and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If one should drink [water] located where a corpse is lying— whether it be moist, decomposed, or even a fresh corpse—
one should perform either the Cāndrāyaṇa or the Taptakṛcchra penance for purification.
The distinction [of the act] is determined by the agent's capacity, or whether it was done with knowledge or ignorance.
If a preeminent twice-born man should happen to bathe there through negligence,
he becomes pure by bathing at the three periods of the day and reciting prayers for a full day and night.
This refers to one who has performed a bath without drinking water. Devala says:
"If a corpse is seen in a well—whether wet, decomposed, or even partially decayed—one must fast for three nights while drinking only water; if this occurs among humans, the penance shall be double."

The meaning is that it is double the six-night penance. Uśanas says: "Having drunk water from a well where excrement and urine have been discharged, the best of the twice-born is purified by a three-night fast; this is recorded as the Sāṃtapana penance."
Āpastamba: If one should drink water from wells or tanks dug by Caṇḍālas out of ignorance,
he becomes pure by fasting for one night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If a twice-born man, being deluded, drinks water from a vessel belonging to a Caṇḍāla,
he is freed from that sin by performing three Kṛcchra penances.
If a twice-born man drinks water that has been touched by a Caṇḍāla,
he shall be purified by a quarter-kṛcchra penance, but he must undergo the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) once again.

In this regard, whatever purification (*saṃskāra*) is prescribed should also be understood to apply to the previous case as well. Atri states: "If Mlecchas and others drink water from a lotus pond or even a lake, it should be known that the portion reaching up to the knees is pure, while the part below is traditionally held to be impure."
Whatever Brahmin should drink that water, whether intentionally or even unintentionally—if unintentionally, he should eat only at night; but if intentionally, for a day and a night.
Śātātapa says:
If one who is thirsty drinks water from vessels belonging to a Caṇḍāla,
he is purified by a Prājāpatya penance provided he spits it out at that very moment.
If one does not throw water [into the fire], his food is digested only after a long time;
he must perform the Prājāpatya penance and observe the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra.
Manu says: Having touched liquor, having given it, or having accepted it according to rule,
or having drunk water that is the leavings of a Śūdra, one should drink water infused with Kuśa grass for three days.
Having unintentionally swallowed feces, urine, or anything touched by liquor,
the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the rite of re-initiation.
But a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk Soma, having smelled the breath of one who has drunk liquor,
becomes purified by suppressing his breath three times in water and consuming clarified butter.

Sumantu says: "A Soma-drinker who smells the odor of one who has drunk *surā* should submerge himself in water and, having recited the *aghamaṛṣaṇa* hymn three times, should perform the consumption of clarified butter. Bṛhaspati says: "If a twice-born man intentionally touches *surā*, garlic, or onion, he should drink water infused with *kuśa* grass for three days and likewise recite the *gāyatrī*."
Upon touching onions or garlic, one should bathe and observe a fast for the night;
having voided excrement, one should fast for a day and a night, and likewise for two days if one remains impure from food remnants.
This applies when it is done unintentionally. Manu says:
"Having consumed the urine or feces of a village pig, a donkey, a camel, a jackal, a monkey, or a crow, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
Aṅgiras says: A Vaiśya should perform the Prājāpatya penance, a Kṣatriya should perform the Atikṛcchra,
and a Brāhmaṇa should perform the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra for consuming feces or urine.
But how should one act regarding the consumption of the feces or urine of a Śūdra?
Having fasted for three nights and bathed, he should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods.
Bṛhaspati:
For consuming things that should not be licked, drunk, or eaten—namely semen, urine, and feces—the purification prescribed by tradition is the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. [1165]
This is at one's own discretion. Devala says: Having drunk *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, ghee, milk, a lotus stalk with its filaments, and a *puṣkara* leaf, one is released from the mixture of water.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In the case of swallowing hair, a fly, or blood; eating raw meat or earth; vomiting blood; or approaching a menstruating woman or one who has recently given birth, one should observe a fast for three nights and consume clarified butter. Sumantu states: "Upon swallowing nails, hair, or blood, one must bathe immediately and consume clarified butter, *kuśa* grass, gold, and water. Gautama states: "Regarding the consumption of forbidden food, one should remain free of excrement, fast for three nights or seven nights, or subsist on fruits that have fallen of their own accord, provided they do not exceed [the prescribed limit]. "Fruits that have fallen of their own accord" means those that have dropped naturally. "Provided they do not exceed" means not rejecting fruits that were obtained first, even if they lack desirable qualities. Saṃvarta states: [as follows].
Having consumed food that should not be eaten, a community of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas,
or Vaiśyas becomes purified in seven nights by subsisting on cow-urine and barley-gruel.
Bṛhaspati says:
Having drunk sour decoctions and having eaten food that is censured, a Brāhmaṇa becomes impure; he is unfit for ritual action and falls to a lower state.
The meaning is: when that food has gone downward and has become free of fecal matter (*niṣpurīṣatā*). Now follow the penances for eating meat. Regarding this, Saṃvarta says:
"Beef and human flesh, even if obtained from the hand of a butcher..."
All that would be unfit for consumption; having eaten it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Upon eating the crane (*baka*), the *balākā*, the *haṃsa*, the *splava*, the *khañjanaka*, the *kāraṇḍava*, the *cakravāka*, the *kaṭabhāra*, the domestic pigeon (*gṛhakapota*), the sparrow (*caṭaka*), the turtle-dove (*pārāvata*), the parrot (*śuka*), the *śārikā*, the *sārasa*, the *ṭiṭṭibha*, the owl (*ulūka*), the *kākola*, the red-footed bird (*raktapāda*), the web-footed bird (*jālapāda*), the *vāgguda*, the blue jay (*cāṣa*), the *bhāsa*, the crow (*vāyasa*), the cuckoo (*kokila*), the *śādvalika*, the cock (*kukkuṭa*), or the *hārīta*—one shall fast for ten nights, or drink barley-gruel mixed with cow’s urine. Here, *kākola* refers to the hawk (*śyena*). This [penance] applies to the habitual eating of any one of these, whether taken individually or as a collective group.
Śaṅkha states: "The water-fowl (*madgu*), the swan (*haṃsa*), the crane (*baka*), the crow (*kāka*), the cuckoo (*kokila*), and the wagtail (*khañjarīṭaka*)."

One should observe a vow for one month regarding those who eat fish, as well as fish themselves, cranes, parrots, mynas, ruddy geese, water-fowl, frogs, and serpents; furthermore, one must not eat them again.
The madgura is the water-crow.
For eating aquatic animals, water-born creatures, birds that peck with their beaks, birds that scratch with their claws,
those with red feet, or web-footed birds, one should observe the vow for seven nights.

Those that eat by pecking at living beings are called *pratudas*. Those that scatter [food] with their claws and eat are called *nakha-viṣkirās*. Those whose feet are webbed are *jālapādās*; those whose feet are red in color are *raktapādās*. Having eaten animals with teeth on both jaws, as well as single-hoofed animals, and likewise having eaten fanged animals, one should observe a vow for six months.
Having eaten meat from a slaughterhouse, dried meat, or meat prepared for one's own sake,
one should perform a vow for a month, being restrained and well-composed.
A *sūnā* is that wooden board upon which meat is cut;
one should carefully avoid all meat that has been roasted on a spit or cooked over a fire. However, if one consumes it unintentionally, one should observe a vow for one year.

*Ṛbhīka* is a specific place for cooking meat. Whatever remains cooked there, even if it is otherwise fit to be eaten, must not be consumed as meat. Manu states in his rule regarding the performance of the *taptakṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances: "Having eaten dried meats, mushrooms growing from the earth, or meat from a slaughterhouse that was unknown [to be such], one should observe this vow."
Regarding the consumption of mushroom-like fungi that have grown from the ground, this expiation applies; it does not apply to those growing on trees and the like.
For the consumption of carnivorous animals, dogs, pigs, camels, and chickens, as well as for humans, crows, and donkeys, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification.

This applies to eating once unintentionally. *Kravyādāḥ* are carnivorous animals such as tigers and others, so called because they eat raw flesh (*kravyam*), that is, uncooked meat. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Upon eating the flesh of a dog, jackal, crow, domestic cock, village pig, *kaṅka* vulture, *gṛdhra* vulture, *bhāsa*, crow, pigeon, human, *kāka*, owl, or crane, one must fast for seven nights, become free of feces, consume clarified butter (*ghṛta-prāśa*), and undergo the rite of re-initiation (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*). Viṣṇu states: "[The same applies to eating the flesh of] the *kalaviṅka*, swan, ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), *rajjudālaka*, crane (*sārasa*), *dātyūha*, parrot, and *śārikā*..."

One should fast for three nights for eating a crane, a cuckoo, or a wagtail; likewise for eating animals with a single hoof or those with teeth in both jaws. For eating the flesh of any bird—excluding the partridge, the grey partridge, the common quail, the *vartīra*, and the peacock—one should fast for a day and a night. For eating insects, one should drink *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā* for one day. This applies to eating the flesh of the back or the flesh from a slaughterhouse as well. A *kalaviṅka* is a domestic sparrow. All of this should be understood to apply to eating these once unintentionally. Chāgaleya says: "Meat should not be eaten in vain; it should be eaten during the performance of a *śrāddha* rite."
Otherwise, a Brahmin eating [forbidden food] should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
This refers to the rule regarding the meat of animals permitted by the learned. Śaṅkha says:
"The five-clawed animals that may be eaten are the monitor lizard, the tortoise, the porcupine, the rhinoceros, and the hare; having eaten these, one need not observe a vow of penance."
Likewise,
Yama has always declared that the partridge, the peacock, the quail, the francolin, the vādhrīṇasa, and the bustard are edible.
Likewise:
"The meat of the buffalo, goat, sheep, Ruru deer, and antelope,
as well as that of the spotted deer, is declared to be fit for consumption."

The *ruru* is a specific kind of deer with many-branched antlers. Viṣṇu states: "Upon eating the meat of five-toed animals, excluding the hare, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, and the tortoise, one should fast for seven nights. Parāśara says:
"For approaching women who should not be approached, and for consuming liquor or beef, one should go to a river that flows to the ocean and perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance for purification."
When the Cāndrāyaṇa penance has been performed, one should then provide a meal for Brahmins and give a cow together with a bull as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the learned.
Manu says: Having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten, or the leavings of women or Śūdras,
or having consumed forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights.
Having eaten the leavings of a cat, a crow, or a rat, or those of a dog or a mongoose, or food defiled by hair or insects, one should drink the Brahmasuvarcalā plant.

*Ākhu* means a mouse. Viṣṇu states: "Having fasted for one day after eating the leavings of a cow, one should drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). Saṃvarta states: "A Brahmin who has consumed feces or urine should perform the *Prājāpatya* penance;
however, for consuming the leavings left by dogs, crows, or cows, he should do so for three days."

Vasiṣṭha states: "For eating the remnants of food licked by dogs or crows, or the leavings of a Śūdra, one should perform an *atikṛcchra*; for other such cases, a *kṛcchra*. This applies except in the case of honey, meat, or preparations of fruit. This refers to habitual consumption done intentionally. Śaṅkha says: "Having eaten food that is the leavings of a Śūdra, one should observe the vow for one month;
having eaten what is left over by a crow or smelled by a cow, one should remain under the vow for a fortnight."
If food is defiled by hair or insects, or likewise by cats,
flies, or gnats, one should observe a vow for three nights.
Having consumed *kṛsara*, *saṃyāva*, *pāyasa*, *apūpa*, or *śaṣkulī* in vain, one should,
with a concentrated mind, perform this vow for three nights.

This should be understood to apply to cases where the practice was not preceded by intentional intent (*amatipūrvābhyāse*). When food has been smelled by a dog, a crow, or a cow, if this occurs intentionally and habitually (*kāmataḥ sābhyāse*), the vow (*vrata*) consists of subsisting on cow-urine and barley-gruel (*gomūtrayāvakāśana*). Regarding the case of eating once intentionally, however, Pracetas says: "The bird, the lizard, the glow-worm, that which is touched by a hundred [others], that which is made of clods of earth, the six-drops [insect], and the *durga*—these seven are evil insects."
If food has been defiled by these, such as crows and the like,
one who eats that food intentionally shall perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance.
Regarding unintentional consumption on a single occasion, Jābāla says: "If one eats stale food,
or garlic and the like that are unfit for consumption,
or the leavings of a Śūdra, a crow, or a cow, one should perform the penance for three days."
Food contaminated by hair or insects, as well as that which has been gnawed by women,
or touched by a dog, a menstruating woman, or a Śūdra, is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Having consumed *kṛsara*, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), cakes (*apūpa*), or meat in vain, one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) shall perform the *prājāpatya* penance. Yama states:
"Having eaten honey, molasses, vegetables, cow's milk products, salt, or ghee when they have been offered by hand, the eater shall perform the *sāṃtapana* penance."
This concerns the subject of repeated practice. *Phāṇita* is a specific derivative of sugarcane juice. Parāśara states:
"When Brahmins are seated in a single row for a communal meal, if even one should leave his vessel, one must not eat the remaining food."
A Brahmin who eats food from a row [of diners] after having already eaten at a fire sacrifice, or who eats the leavings of others,
shall perform the Kṛcchra and Sāṃtapana penances as expiation.
Sumantu: Upon eating the leavings of a Śūdra, one should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn for three nights. Yama: [Thus it is said.]
Having eaten food with a Brahmin, one is purified by a Prājāpatya penance;
having eaten food with a king, one is purified by a Taptakṛcchra penance.
Having eaten food together with a Śūdra, one should then perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
likewise for [administering] enemas, non-unctuous enemas, emetics, and purgatives.
They are purified from that sin by the Śiśukṛcchra penance; of this there is no doubt.

This refers to cases where the act was done intentionally. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Upon eating the leavings of a Brāhmaṇa, one should drink water consecrated with the Mahāvyāhṛtis. Upon eating the leavings of a Kṣatriya, one should subsist on milk for three days that has been boiled with the juice of the *brāhmī* plant. Upon eating the leavings of a Vaiśya, one should fast for three nights and then drink *brahmasuvarcalā*. Upon eating the leavings of a Śūdra, or drinking water from a vessel that once held *surā*, there shall be fasting for seven nights or the performance of a *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance. Viṣṇu states: "A Brāhmaṇa who eats at an *āma-śrāddha* (a funeral rite performed with raw food) should subsist on milk for three nights. After inducing vomiting, one should fast for seven nights upon eating the leavings of a Śūdra; for five nights upon eating the leavings of a Vaiśya; and for three nights upon eating the leavings of a Kṣatriya. A Kṣatriya who eats the leavings of a Śūdra should fast for five nights; a Vaiśya who eats the leavings of a Śūdra should fast for three nights."
For eating the leavings of a Śūdra, the penance lasts one month; likewise for a Vaiśya, one fortnight;
for a Kṣatriya, seven days; and for a Brāhmaṇa, one day.
A learned man who eats at a funeral rite (śrāddha) consisting of raw food (āma) should observe a vow for one month.

This refers to the subject of *navaśrāddha* (funeral rites for the newly deceased). Śātātapa states: "The food-remnants of one who is not one's guru are not to be eaten; likewise, one's own food-remnants and that which has been defiled by the remnants of another. For eating these, one must perform a *kṛcchra* penance. Śaṅkha says: "Having eaten food touched by an impure substance, an outcaste (*patita*), a Caṇḍāla, a Pukkasa, a woman in her menses, one with a withered arm (*kuṇi*), one suffering from leprosy (*kuṣṭhin*), or one with deformed nails (*kunakhi*), one should perform a *kṛcchra* penance. Here, *kuṇi* means one with a withered arm. Yama states:
"If a twice-born man eats lentils (*masūra*), black gram (*māṣa*), or meat, a three-night fast is prescribed as his expiation."
Having bathed with three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and consumed clarified butter, one becomes purified.
Viṣṇu:
Food enjoyed by a Śūdra, or even food touched by a dog,
is purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance or, alternatively, by the Prājāpatya.
"A Parāka penance should be given according to one's capacity; such is the certainty of Dharma.

[A penance] consisting of being trampled by donkeys and pigs, as practiced by Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and others, constitutes a Kṛcchra; a twice-born man should perform all this according to his ability."

"Juṣṭam" means eaten. Śaṅkha says: "Having eaten food that is defiled by speech or defiled in intention from a vessel defiled by intention, a Brāhmaṇa shall thereafter observe a vow for three nights."
Parāśara says: An excellent twice-born man who, through ignorance, eats from a broken vessel,
becomes pure by consuming ghee that has been touched by water containing gold.
Upon consuming clarified butter, there is a cessation of other food. Āpastamba:
"In the case of spitting by the twice-born, or eating from a broken vessel, purification occurs through the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); so said Śātātapa."
Saṃvarta:
Having eaten from the vessel of Śūdras, or having eaten repeatedly from a broken vessel,
one becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
The defect of a broken vessel applies specifically to bell-metal (*kāṃsya*), as Baudhāyana states:
"But the wise man who eats from a broken bell-metal vessel should go to a river and recite the *gāyatrī* eight thousand times while eating only one meal; thereafter he becomes pure."
Saṃvarta:
He who drinks or eats anything without having sipped water for purification becomes pure by performing eight thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī.
If a twice-born man eats without having performed the *āpośāna* rite when not in an emergency,
he should recite the *Gāyatrī* one hundred and eight times while eating.
[1171] Laghuhārīta:
If a Brāhmaṇa eats without his sacred thread,
he becomes pure by performing a bath, reciting prayers, and observing a fast.
Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
When a twice-born man becomes impure at the time of eating, he should place that morsel on the ground; having bathed, the Brahmin becomes purified.
Having consumed that morsel, one becomes pure after a day and night;
having eaten all food, however, one is purified after three nights.
If one should, out of delusion, eat or drink after voiding urine, defecating, or discharging feces,
Śātātapa declared that one should observe a fast for three nights in that case.
If one drinks while eating after voiding urine or excrement,
or if one drinks water while walking on a path after urinating due to a lapse of mindfulness,
one becomes pure by fasting for a day and night, bathing, and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If one urinates while swallowing, or eats after urinating has been performed,
one should fast for a day and night, bathe, and offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire.

The word "with the *vyāhṛtis*" is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. Bṛhatpracetā says: "If one has eaten out of negligence after performing purification with fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*), a composed Brāhmaṇa shall become pure by drinking barley-gruel (*yāvaka*) for six nights."
A twice-born man shall be purified in three nights after performing the ritual sipping of water (ācamana),
provided he has ensured the purity of the water and sips only *kāñjika* (fermented gruel).
Having fasted for one night, he is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Āranāla is sour gruel. When the need for bathing has arisen, the twice-born may then eat or drink.
Having bathed, one should, with a concentrated mind, recite the Gāyatrī mantra eight thousand times.
This [penance] applies after another bath following contact with those who have fallen from their caste (*patita*) and others. Regarding that specific cause, Paiṭhīnasi says:
"Upon contact with one who has committed a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*), bathing alone is prescribed;
but when one who has been so touched eats, he should then perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance."
Vṛddhayājñavalkya states:
"If a twice-born man eats without having bathed, or if he touches a Caṇḍāla, he shall fast for three days after bathing; if he has drunk [water under such circumstances], he shall fast for one day."
This refers to cases where one acts unintentionally:
"But if feces should fall upon the head of a Brahmin while he is eating, he shall discard the food, bathe in a river, and practice three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma). [1172]
He who, with his feet placed upon a seat, having made half of a garment into a funnel,
blows [the fire] with his mouth, shall perform the Sāṃtapanakṛcchra penance.

The meaning of *ardhapaṭīkṛtam* is that which has been made into a single portion of a garment. The phrase "having heated" implies "if one eats food and so forth. Having consumed hair, insects, or nails, as well as fish-bones, one becomes pure at that very moment by consuming ghee heated with gold.
Having swallowed bones, thorns, lotus roots, conch shells, pearl oysters,
cowrie shells, or even fresh water, one is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

*Śālūka* is a species of insect. *Kapardikā* is a cowrie shell. *Navodaka* (new water) refers to the floodwater found in small irrigation channels and the like within a village, or the water from newly constructed wells and such that has not yet undergone the prescribed purification. "If one should ever eat food or drink water with the hand of a Śūdra, having fasted for a day and night, he becomes pure by consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)."
Having eaten with one's wife or siblings, one should fast for a day;
with kinsmen, for a day and night; and with others, for three nights.
Likewise:
while drinking or swallowing urine, or during the act of vomiting,
if there are smears on the exterior or interior of the mouth, one should wash them off and perform a bath.

In the case of the emission of urine or vomiting, the abandonment of food must occur immediately; this is the rule. Now, if a healthy Brāhmaṇa who is eating should experience a discharge from the anus, how should the expiation be for that state of being defiled by impurity?
Having first performed purification, one should afterwards touch the heated [iron];
having remained fasting for a day and night, one becomes pure through the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
But that twice-born man who, having reached the sacrificial ground, eats out of negligence,
becomes pure by subsisting on cow’s urine and barley-gruel and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

If a man, having discharged urine or feces, drinks water out of delusion without first performing purification for himself, he must fast for three nights; by drinking barley-gruel, he becomes purified.
If any twice-born man who is worthy of bathing should drink or eat [forbidden things], he is purified by three thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī; of this there is no doubt.

This refers specifically to intentional acts. Hārīta states: "In the case of eating hair, eating food given by hand, eating without having washed one's hands and feet, eating more than is required, defiling a row of diners, eating at the head of a row, voiding urine or excrement without first discarding it, or eating the food of one who is impure due to death or birth, or the food of a Śūdra—[if these occur] in a dream—one must fast for three nights. For picking up a clod of earth or clay, purification comes from fasting for a day and a night. Saṃvarta says:
"If a twice-born man should drink or eat while still not having sipped water (anācānta), [he is purified by fasting]."
One should prescribe the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times as his atonement.

This refers to the occasion for bathing caused by touching a Śūdra or similar persons; however, if one neglects the bath required upon touching a Caṇḍāla or similar persons, there is an increase in the penance. If a Brāhmaṇa eats without his sacred thread (yajñopavīta), he becomes pure by performing a bath, reciting prayers, and observing a fast.
Hārīta: If a twice-born man sees a Caṇḍāla or similar person while eating, he should discard that morsel;
having washed the internal and external smears from his mouth, he should perform a bath.

Having eaten, one should not eat for three nights; having drunk water, one should fast for a day and night. Upon seeing a dog, one should likewise sip water (perform ācamana); after eating or drinking, the fast should be half that duration.

Upon seeing a dog, one should likewise perform *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water), but should not bathe. If, however, one has eaten [after seeing it], one should fast for a day and night and eat only at night; if one has drunk [water], one should eat only at night. According to the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "In the case of vomiting while fasting, or eating from a broken vessel, one becomes pure by bathing and consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) after having fasted for a day and night."
"Having stayed overnight" means having vomited the food eaten on the previous day.
However, that man who eats without ghee for five oblations,
and then eats with ghee afterwards, shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance after eating.
But while eating, if he should see a dog, an outcaste, or a donkey,
he should rinse his mouth, become pure, and perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).
But that best of the twice-born who eats after having seen [the food] out of greed,
becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If one eating in a single row should touch a Brāhmaṇa,
having eaten that remaining food, he should indeed mutter the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times. (From the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*).
But he who eats what has been left over, or eats with his mouth uncovered—
thus Vaivasvata has declared— that having so eaten, he should perform the Sāṃtapana penance.
This refers to the subject of repeated practice. Vyāsa states:

"If a twice-born man, through delusion, eats food contained in a vessel that has been touched by a woman who has recently given birth or the like, and was likewise touched by one who has touched her, he becomes pure after three nights."
When one who has voided urine or feces finds no water at all,
he becomes purified by bathing and performing ten breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).

In the phrase "bathing and purification," the word "having performed" is to be understood as the ellipsis. One who has been anointed with oil, as well as one who has vomited, after shaving, after sexual intercourse, or when one voids urine or excrement, becomes pure after three nights.
Parāśara:
Having consumed oil that is the residue of a lamp, or that which has been brought from a street at night,
or the residue remaining from anointing the body, one becomes pure by eating only at night.

Now, regarding the consumption of food defiled by its ownership, the venerable Yājñavalkya has set forth that food is defiled due to the fault of the owner in such passages as: "One should not eat the food of one who maintains no sacred fire, except in times of distress. On this point, Manu says: "A Brāhmaṇa should never eat at a sacrifice performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas, nor at one offered by a village priest, nor at one offered by a woman or a eunuch."
This is offensive to the virtuous wherein these people offer oblations;
this is contrary to the gods, therefore one should avoid it.

That which is indecorous causes shame; that which is perverse is contrary. One should never eat the food of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted by disease, nor food into which hair or insects have fallen, nor that which has been intentionally touched with the foot.
That which has been looked upon by a killer of an embryo, touched by a woman in her courses,
pecked by a bird, or even touched by a dog;

Food smelled by a cow, food proclaimed [for all], and specifically the food of a multitude, the food of a courtesan, and that which is despised by the learned; The food of a usurer, the food of a thief, the food of a physician, the food of a cruel person, the food of one who sells the Vedas, the food of a womanizer, and the food of a eunuch; The food of a liar, the food of a seller of soma, the food of one who has performed the Vājapeya sacrifice, the food of a harlot, the food of a woman who drinks liquor, and the food of one who lives off the interest of loans; The food of a public servant, the food of a messenger, the food of a goldsmith, the food of a dyer, the food of a person who eats the leavings of others, and the food of one who is hostile to his father-in-law; The food of a person who neglects the sacred fires, the food of a person who has abandoned his kin, the food of a person who sells sacrifices, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the unworthy, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for himself alone; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for women, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of cattle, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a village, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a town; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a kingdom, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a country, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a multitude, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a guild; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a corporation, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of artisans, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of merchants, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of actors; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of dancers, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of singers, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of musicians, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of bards; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of storytellers, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of jesters, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of gladiators, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of wrestlers; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of boxers, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of athletes, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of charioteers, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of elephant-riders; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of horsemen, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of foot-soldiers, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of scouts, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of spies; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of envoys, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of messengers, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of runners, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of porters; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of carriers, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of pack-animal drivers, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of boatmen, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of ferrymen; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of fishermen, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of hunters, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of fowlers, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of trappers; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of bird-catchers, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of snake-charmers, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of poisoners, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of assassins; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of thieves, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of robbers, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of burglars, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of highwaymen; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of cutthroats, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of murderers, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of executioners, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of torturers; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of impalers, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of flayers, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of castrators, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of mutilators; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of amputators, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of cauterizers, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of scarifiers, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of lancers; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of stabbers, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of hurlers, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of casters; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of stones, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of clubs, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of spears, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of javelins; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of arrows, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of darts, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of pikes, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of tridents; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of axes, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of hammers, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of mallets, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of maces; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of bludgeons, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of iron bars, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of firebrands, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of torches; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of lamps, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of smoke, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of dust, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of mud; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of water, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of wind, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of heat, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of cold; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of light, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of darkness, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of sound, and the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of silence; The food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of speech, the food of a person who performs sacrifices for the sake of a group of throwers of thought, the
And [the food] of a thief, a singer, a carpenter, a usurer,
one accused of a crime, a eunuch, an unchaste woman, and a hypocrite.
The fermented sour gruel, food that has stood overnight, and the leavings of a Śūdra;
the food of a physician, a hunter, a cruel person, and one who eats leavings;
the food of an Ugra, the food of a woman in childbirth, and food passed through several people before reaching oneself while she is still within ten days of delivery.
Meat that has not been honored, meat obtained in vain, and the food of a woman who has no male protector.
The food of an enemy, the food of a city official, the food of one who has fallen, that which is spat upon,
and likewise the food of a slanderer, a liar, or a seller of sacrifices.
The food of an actor, a weaver, an ungrateful person,
a blacksmith, a Niṣāda, and a stage-player;
[The food] of a goldsmith, of a Vena, of a seller of weapons,
of those who keep dogs, of liquor-sellers, and of a washerman [is forbidden].
[The food] of a cruel washerman, of one in whose house a paramour resides,
of those who tolerate a paramour, and of those who are entirely ruled by women— [these must not be eaten].
The food of one who has not passed ten days [of impurity] and the food of the deceased are indeed unsatisfying. The items belonging to the category of forbidden foods have been explained.
Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one must undergo a fast for three days.
Having intentionally consumed semen, feces, or urine, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance.
Having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten, or the leavings of women and Śūdras,
or having consumed forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights.

Paiṭhīnasi states: "One with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who quarrels with his father, one conquered by women, one afflicted with leprosy, a slanderer, a seller of Soma, a merchant, a priest for a village, one accused of a crime, one born of a Śūdra woman, a younger brother who marries before his elder, an elder brother whose younger brother marries first, the husband of a *didhiṣū* (a woman married while her elder sister remains unmarried), the son of a remarried woman, a thief, a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha* (one who lives off his teacher's wealth after completing his studies), and a servant—these are those whose food should not be eaten, who are unworthy of the row (*apāṅktya*), and unfit for the *śrāddha*. Having unknowingly eaten the food of these, or having given it, one must observe a fast for three nights. Śaṅkha states: "One accused of a crime, a dyer, an outcaste, a vintner, an oil-presser, a priest for a village..."

Śūdras who are annual tax-payers, family-heads, goldsmiths, blacksmiths, carpenters, painters by profession, bellows-blowers, weavers, dyers, those who use false measures, vintners, those who live by killing, the cruel, those who sell themselves, usurers, ferrymen, those who live by the vulva, outcasts, and thieves.

"In the case of eating food from a *gaṇa*, one should perform an *atikṛcchra* penance. [1176] A *kulika* is a temple-priest (*devalaka*). A *ghoṣaka* is a reciter for a fee. A *tārika* is one who lives by ferrying people across rivers and so forth. This refers to the subject of repeated practice. Viṣṇu states: "Having eaten the food of a *gaṇa*, a *gaṇastena*, a singer, or a musician, one should subsist on milk for seven nights. Sumantu states: "[One becomes an outcast by eating the food of] those accused of a crime, the fallen (*patita*), the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), a killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahan*), an unchaste woman (*puṃścalī*), the impure, a maker of weapons, an oil-miller, a wheelwright, a liquor-seller, a goldsmith, a painter, a eunuch (*paṇḍa*), a prostitute (*bandhakī*), a *gaṇa*..."

The food of courtesans is not to be eaten. Pigs-breeders, hunters, Niṣādas, basket-makers (Varuṭas), and leather-workers are those whose food is unfit to be eaten and from whom gifts are not to be accepted; for eating their food or accepting gifts from them, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. One who lives by or plays with pigs is to be called a *piṅgī* (or *piṇī*). A *varuṭa* is one who lives by bamboo. This [penance] refers to cases of intentional and repeated practice. Hārīta says: "Upon eating the food of a wheelwright or a blacksmith, one should fast for three nights and consume cow urine and cow dung. Upon eating the food of a twice-born trader, a merchant, or a usurer, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for five nights. This refers to cases of repeated practice. "Upon eating the food of an unchaste woman or a prostitute, [one should fast] for seven nights. Upon eating the food of one initiated for sacrifice (*dīkṣita*), a wandering mendicant (*pravrajita*), a member of a religious guild (*gaṇa*), a *uddhva*, or a *avaruddha*, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa. During a period of impurity due to death or birth (*mṛtake sūtake*), [the penance lasts] ten nights. Upon eating the remnants of a Brāhmaṇa's meal during a death or birth impurity, or at an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, [the penance is] three nights or one night. Upon eating the remnants of a Kṣatriya's meal during a death or birth impurity, or at an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, the Kṛcchra is required. Upon eating the remnants of a Vaiśya's meal during a birth or death impurity, or at an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra is required. Upon eating the remnants of a Śūdra's meal during a birth or death impurity, or at an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, the Cāndrāyaṇa is required. Upon eating the food of Mlecchas, or the food of those who work with copper, bronze, or lead, or of lepers, thieves, or criminals, the Taptakṛcchra is required. Upon eating the food of one who destroys the livelihood of a Brāhmaṇa, or of one who subsists by killing, binding, or harming others; and upon eating the food of a son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*) or of one born of a mixed union (*saṃkīrṇa*). An *ekoddiṣṭa* is other than the *navaśrāddha*. A *kirāṭī* is a specific type of merchant. Aṅgiras says:
Having eaten the prepared food of all those whose food is unfit to be eaten,
and having eaten the food of an Antyāvasāyin, one is purified by a quarter-kṛcchra penance.
This applies when there is a single instance of unintentional action and a lack of capacity. Śātātapa says:
"Where neither the gods, nor the ancestors, nor likewise the guest eat, that should be known as 'vain cooking' (vṛthāpāka); one should never eat there."
He who, having abandoned the sacred fire, considers himself a householder—
his food must not be eaten, for he is remembered as one who cooks in vain.
A twice-born man eating the food of one who cooks in vain should perform an expiation;
by practicing three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) and consuming clarified butter, he becomes purified.

Likewise: "A twice-born man who eats the food of one who abstains from cooking for others, of one who delights in cooking for others, or of one who does not cook at all, shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."

He has also desisted from even blameless cooking; such is the uncooked-food-eating (*apaca*) monk. Parāśara says: "If a Brahmin eats during a time of distress when food is provided by a Śūdra, he may be purified by mental remorse, provided he recites the *Drupada* verses one hundred times."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "And he who, as a performer of many sacrifices, performed the initiation for many people at a great sacrifice where Soma had been purchased for the sake of the ritual."
And where there is another who is not learned in the Vedas, or a village priest,
or a eunuch as the *hotṛ*, or a woman— there one should never eat.
He who is the buyer and he who is the seller of the fruits of asceticism and sacrifice,
having first addressed the time for the king's welfare, [acted] with the domestic priest at the forefront.

He who performs [these acts] is declared to be one whose food must not be eaten; so too are the royal priest, the deer-hunter, the snake-catcher, the liquor-drinker, the vintner, and the tavern-keeper.
The oil-presser, the wheel-turner, the washerman who cleans clothes, the dyer of garments,
and the one who prepares blue, red, and yellow dyes.
But he who brings praise among men while being a double-tongued person would be cruel;
indeed, he who is authorized for restraint should be known as a punisher.
He who is the protector of those who are bound becomes their captor;
furthermore, one whose family conduct is unknown should be understood as a stranger from a foreign land.
A gambler, a cheat at dice, a thief of gold, a goldsmith,
one for whom women are merchandise, and one who lives off his wife— these are the ones [excluded].
Furthermore, he may become a man born of illicit union who is devoted to his wife’s paramour;
or a maker of vessels, that is, a potter; or a painter, a performer of artistic works.
He who takes profit on commodities is a base usurer; a leather-worker is one who cuts hides; a butcher is a killer of animals. A man who lives off the sick is a quack physician.
A needle is *sūcī*; a tailor is *tunnavāya*, and a weaver is *tantuvāyaka*.
But the actor who enters the stage for the sake of livelihood, along with his assistants,
and seeks employment among actors, is known as a *śailūṣaka*.
Śaṇḍa was one whose vulva was on his face; Durloma was one with deformed hair;
Vaina was the maker of bow-staffs; and Karmāra was the fletcher.
The Niṣāda and the fisherman, as well as the other two, the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka—
whichever among these does not eat [meat] from childhood onwards is called Ajadaṃśa.
One who is thus wasted by disease upon his bed, utterly prostrate,
and fallen away from the dharma prescribed for his own caste, becomes an outcast.
He whose time for the initiation ceremony has passed is indeed a *vrātya*;
yet among many such, he alone was radiant, a king of great renown.
He who inflicts severe punishment is called "harsh and fierce";
he who abandons a friend for another is proclaimed a "gratefulless" person.
He who lives by killing others is proclaimed a "livelihood-by-slaughter" (vadhajīvī);
though his dharma is public, his sin is hidden—he is indeed merely a hypocrite.
He who practices righteousness in the form of unrighteousness is a wheelwright;
he who manufactures weapons for the sake of killing others is a seller of weapons.
And one must not eat from these: from one who is distressed, nor likewise from one who is weeping, nor from one who cries out piteously, nor from one who administers poison through deceit.
One should not eat the food of ascetics (yatins), those wearing sectarian marks (liṅgins), nor even of heretics (pāṣaṇḍins), nor of one who is ruled by his wife, nor of one who has no master.
The failure to honor a daughter who has not yet borne a child, or likewise a person of such a [low] nature;
the lack of respect for the virtuous, and the honoring of evildoers.
One should not eat food that is treated as equal [to what is forbidden],
nor food consecrated by a Śūdra, nor any food belonging to a Brāhmaṇa at any time.
A Brāhmaṇa should never eat the food of a Śūdra, even if it has been consecrated with mantras,
nor the food of those who are intoxicated, insane, or afflicted by disease, nor that of one who is about to die.
[The following are those whose food should not be eaten: a thief bound in shackles, a wicked man, one who is falsely accused, a carpenter, a miser, a rogue,
a physician, one who is imprisoned, a cruel person, and one who eats the leavings of others.
The same applies to a woman who opposes her son or husband, as well as to a courtesan.
Likewise, [one should avoid] a city governor who is an enemy, a slanderer, a liar, one who is contemptuous, a fool, one who offers no hospitality, or one who is evil-minded.
If one, with a mind full of anger, should give unconsecrated food that is unknown, accompanied by wrath and wonder, under the pretext that it is fit to be eaten when it is actually unfit to be eaten;
One must not eat even that which belongs to a guru if it is defiled by foul speech, for that is a great sin;
nor should one accept cooked food from an unworthy Śūdra, especially if offered without faith.

One should not eat food in the house of that person where the fire-ritual is not performed, nor where there is no Brāhmaṇa who eats the first portion, even if the owner of the sacred fires is away on a journey.
Who is afflicted by hunger, and who eats my very food? He who would speak for the sake of fame—that one is corrupt in speech and should not be consumed.
Having eaten in the house of these [persons], one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance in the forest; this refers to cases of intentional and repeated practice. Likewise:
"The conjunction of the Maghā constellation with the thirteenth lunar day is known as Kuñjaracchāyā (the Elephant's Shadow)."
It should take place when the moon is situated in Maghā, and the sun is stationed in Hasta.
Furthermore, having eaten during a death-impurity or a birth-impurity, or when the moon and sun are eclipsed,
or in the shadow of an elephant, one shall go to hell.
Having eaten [forbidden food] through negligence, a Brahmin should duly perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Baudhāyana says: "In the case of the Brahmaudana, the Soma sacrifice, and likewise the Sīmantonnayana ceremony..."
Having eaten at a birth-śrāddha or a new śrāddha, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Bharadvāja said:
Whether for a fortnight or for a month, if a twice-born man does not eat from the house of one from whom another twice-born man refuses to eat,
he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya states:
"Both the ascetic and the student are the masters of cooked food;
one must not eat the food of those two, and having eaten it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
According to the Caturviṃśatimata:
"Having eaten the food of a Brahmin who lacks proper conduct or who practices forbidden acts, a man should observe a fast for one day."
One who hates his teacher, the sacred fire, or a guru, as well as one who hates the treatises on Dharma,
and likewise one who hates cows or Brahmins, should perform that very same vow. This applies to one who has committed a minor offense (upapātaka) for a continuous period of one year.
Having eaten food, a man should perform the Parāka penance as a means of purification.
This applies to one who has eaten the food of someone guilty of a minor offense (upapātaka) repeatedly and intentionally over the course of an entire year. Hārīta says:
"When a Brahmin eats the food of an outcaste (patita) in the house of a Caṇḍāla, he should drink water for half a month; likewise, if it was done intentionally, for a full month."

The phrase "in the house of a Caṇḍāla" is an illustration [representing] food from a Caṇḍāla. Chāgaleya says: "If Brahmins eat out of ignorance during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtaka), they become pure by performing one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) in the case of a Śūdra's birth-impurity."
For a Vaiśya it shall be sixty days, for a Kṣatriya twenty days, and for a Brāhmaṇa ten days;
[or] fasting for one day, three days, five days, or seven nights.

Then the Brahmin shall become pure and drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). It should be understood that for the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, the penances last for one day and so forth, combined with breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). This applies when eating occurs once during a time of distress. Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"But having eaten during the period of impurity of a Kṣatriya, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is prescribed."
Likewise, having eaten during the period of impurity of a Vaiśya, one should perform the Mahāsāṃtapana penance.
Likewise, having eaten [the food] of a Śūdra, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
this refers to an instance where it was done intentionally once. Śaṅkha says:
"Having eaten during the period of impurity (sūtaka) of a Śūdra, one should observe a vow for six months."
Likewise, having eaten during the period of impurity of a Vaiśya, one should observe the vow for three months.

Likewise, during the impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, one should observe a vow for one month; this refers to cases of intentional and repeated practice. The vow consists of subsisting on cow’s urine and barley-gruel. Parāśara states:
"If Brāhmaṇas eat out of ignorance during the period of birth-impurity or death-impurity..."
How should one prescribe the expiation for each of them, according to their respective social class?
Purification from the birth-impurity of a Śūdra occurs through eight thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī;
for a Vaiśya, it is by five hundred, and for a Kṣatriya, by one hundred.
When one eats the food of a Brāhmaṇa, one is purified by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma);
or else, one is purified by a single recitation of the Vāmadevya Sāman.
This applies to one who is unable to perform the prescribed penances, or who eats once out of ignorance during a time of distress. Thus says Śātātapa.
There is no fault in consuming [food] from those of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya castes who maintain the *agnihotra* sacrifice,
even during the period of impurity following a birth (*sūtaka*) or a death (*śāva-śauca*), provided it is after the collection of the bones has taken place.

In times of distress, there is no fault for one who eats the food of Brāhmaṇas and others who maintain the *agnihotra* during birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*śāvaśauca*). Likewise, there is no fault after the collection of bones (*asthisaṃcayana*) has occurred following their death or birth-impurity. For those engaged in a continuous food-distribution (*annasatra*), raw food (*āmanna*) is not censured. However, having eaten cooked food (*pakvānna*) from these persons, one should drink only milk for three nights.

Viṣṇu states that those who eat the food of persons in a state of impurity (aśauca) must perform an expiation (prāyaścitta) once that impurity has passed: "If a Brāhmaṇa or others eats the food of another even once, his impurity lasts for as long as theirs; he should perform an expiation once their impurity has passed. If a twice-born man eats during the impurity of a person of his own caste (savarṇa), he should go to a flowing river, immerse himself therein, recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, and upon emerging, recite the Gāyatrī eight thousand times. During the impurity of a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure by fasting for three nights. During the impurity of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa likewise fasts for three nights; and during the impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or during the impurity of a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya should go to a flowing river and recite the Gāyatrī five hundred times. And during the impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, a Vaiśya should recite the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times. A twice-born man who eats during the impurity of a Śūdra should perform the Prājāpatya penance. And a Śūdra, having eaten during the impurity of a twice-born man, should perform a ritual bath. During the impurity of a Śūdra, a Śūdra, after bathing, should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). "Aṣṭasahasram" means one thousand plus eight. — Saṃvarta.
A Brahmin who has eaten the food of other Brahmins during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) shall not eat for three days;
if he drinks water unknowingly, he is purified by consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Vasiṣṭha says: "If a twice-born man eats at the command of another during the ten-day period of impurity following a death,
he becomes a worm after the end of that body and consumes its excrement."

"It is known from tradition that one who studies the *Saṃhitā* while fasting for twelve months, or for six months (twelve half-months), becomes purified. Twelve months apply when the act was intentional; half of that (six months) applies when it was unintentional. Both of these cases refer to extreme repetition of the act. "Fasting" means not eating prior to the mealtime.
