Śaṅkha states: "A *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance is prescribed for a *navāśrāddha*; a *Parāka* is remembered for a monthly (*māsika*) rite; an *Atikṛcchra* should be performed for three fortnights; but for a six-month rite, a *Kṛcchra* alone is required."
For an annual [śrāddha], there should be a quarter-pādakṛcchra; for a subsequent annual [śrāddha], a single day.
Beyond that, there shall be no fault, according to the statement of Śaṅkha.
This is according to one's desire, based on the Caturviṃśatimata:
"A Prājāpatya penance is prescribed for a Navaśrāddha; likewise, a quarter-less [penance] for a Māsika;
a quarter-less Kṛcchra is specified for a Ṣaṇmāsa, and likewise for an Ābdika."
In other months, it is prescribed for three nights; if it occurs every year, it is remembered as being for one day.
This applies when eating occurs once unintentionally, or even intentionally in times of distress. Likewise:
"But for a Śūdra at a *navaśrāddha*, one should perform three *cāndrāyaṇa* penances."
Two Cāndrāyaṇa penances are prescribed for a month, while for three fortnights, an Aindava is traditionally taught.
In the case of an *āmaśrāddha*, the penance shall always be half a *prājāpatya*; however, this applies when done once intentionally. According to the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"In a *navaśrāddha* it is a *prājāpatya*, but in a *misraka* it is less by a quarter."
In the case of a three-month period, half of that [penance] is prescribed; for a two-month period, one should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

This refers to one who, being incapable [of performing a formal Śrāddha], has once accepted an *āma-śrāddha* during a time of distress. The *miśraka* is a Śrāddha performed within the first year [of death]. Viṣṇu states: "Upon eating at an *āma-śrāddha*, one should subsist on milk for three nights. This applies to the case of a prohibited Śrāddha, or else to the case of a Śrāddha performed by a Śūdra. Bharadvāja says: "If a Brāhmaṇa eats food at a Śrāddha intended for those excluded from the company (*apāṅkteya*) on the eleventh day, he should perform the *śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa* penance."

Those excluded from the company at a *śrāddha* have been mentioned in the section on *śrāddhas*. The meaning is that one who eats at a *śrāddha* for those deities, as well as at the eleventh-day *śrāddha*, should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"Having eaten at a *śrāddha* with raw food (*āma-śrāddha*), one is purified by the *taptakṛcchra*;
likewise, having eaten at a *śrāddha* where the invitation has been formally resolved (*saṃkalpita*), there should be a fast for three nights."
This refers to the case of the food of a Śūdra. Aṅgiras says:
"One should drink water ten times consecutively, consecrated by the Gāyatrī; one should then perform the worship of the three junctions of the day, recite prayers, and offer oblations. [1183]

The phrase "ten times" (*daśakṛtvaḥ*) should be explained as referring to the practice of drinking water; for the suffix *kṛtvasuc* is prescribed for counting the repetition of an action mentioned in close conjunction with it. The *gāyatrī*, however, should be recited only once, because it is an auxiliary to the act of drinking performed repeatedly upon a single substance. As written [in the Smṛti]: "That food which has not been offered into the fire and that food to which [the guest] has not given [remnants] is not to be eaten by the twice-born; having eaten it, one should fast for a day."
Bharadvāja says:
Whatever food, such as roots, fruits, and so forth, that the learned do not eat,
having consumed that, a Brāhmaṇa should perform the penance of fasting.
Thus end the penances for minor offenses (*upapātaka*).
Now, the penances for acts causing loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*) and so forth will be described. Regarding this, Manu says:
"Causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa, smelling things that should not be smelled, or [smelling] intoxicants (*madya*),"
Deceit and sexual intercourse with men are recorded as causing loss of caste.

Causing pain means producing disease. That which is unfit to be smelled refers to foul-smelling substances such as garlic and the like. Having intentionally committed any one of these acts that cause loss of caste, one should perform the *sāṃtapana* penance; if done unintentionally, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance.
The killing of donkeys, camels, deer, and arrows, as well as goats,
sheep, fish, snakes, and buffaloes, should be known as acts that cause loss of caste (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*).
Likewise: "Accepting wealth from those who are censured, trade, serving Śūdras,
and speaking unrefined language should be known as acts that render one unworthy (apātrīkaraṇa)."
Improper speech for an assembly refers to talk concerning sexual intercourse, its practitioners, and so forth.
For acts causing mixture of castes (*saṃkara*) or those rendering one unworthy of receiving gifts (*apātra*), the purificatory penance is a month of the lunar fast (*aindava*).
Likewise:
Killing worms, insects, or birds; eating food during the Maghā asterism; stealing fruits, firewood, or flowers; and lack of fortitude—these bring about impurity.
For acts that cause defilement, one should undergo the *yāvaka* penance for three days;
or purification may be attained through the *śītakṛcchra*, or, if committed through delusion, by the *sāṃtapana*.
For acts that cause impurity, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification;
having committed an act that causes confusion of castes (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*), one should eat barley-gruel for one month.
Having rendered oneself unworthy [of receiving gifts], one is purified by the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra, or the Pārāka, or even the Pārajāpatya; indeed, one is purified by the Taptakṛcchra.

Depending on the degree of intensity and continuity of the practice, these [penances] apply when all acts among those that cause mixture of castes (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*), disqualification from receiving gifts (*apātrīkaraṇa*), or defilement (*malinīkaraṇa*) are performed intentionally. However, according to the *Mānava* [Smṛti], they apply when each act is committed once unintentionally. Regarding this, there is a specific rule by Bṛhaspati: "Having caused injury to a Brāhmaṇa, one should undergo the penance of half a *kṛcchra* after performing the expiation involving the slaughter of a donkey or similar animal, and after taking wealth from those who are censured."

Regarding those sins listed among the group beginning with "those causing loss of caste" for which Manu himself has prescribed other expiations, there is an option between them; and that [application] is determined according to one's capacity. 3.289.
Now he states other penances:
"Having performed breath-control (prāṇāyāma) in water, [one who has] ridden on a donkey-cart or a camel-cart [is purified]. (3.290)

"Naked" means being unclothed. "Having bathed, having eaten, and having gone to a woman by day"—the term *kharayānam* refers to a vehicle yoked with donkeys; likewise for a camel-vehicle (*uṣṭrayānam*). One who has mounted such [a vehicle], that is, one who has ascended it while naked or unclothed, or having bathed or eaten during the day, or having approached his own wife, or having bathed in water while standing on land—such a person should perform *prāṇāyāma*. This applies when done intentionally. As Manu says:
"Having intentionally mounted a camel-vehicle or a donkey-vehicle..."
Having emerged from the water naked, one becomes pure through breath control (prāṇāyāma).

Because of the mention of "intentionally," if it is unintentional, there is merely bathing. Viṣṇu states: "Having traveled by camel or donkey, or having bathed naked, slept, or eaten, one should perform three *prāṇāyāmas*. This refers to the case of habitual practice; however, for extreme habitual practice, Yama says:
"If a superior twice-born man should mount a donkey-cart or a camel-cart, or enter water naked, his penance shall be a fast for three nights."
Śaṅkha says: Having engaged in sexual intercourse during the day, or having bathed naked in water, or having seen another man’s wife naked, one should observe a vow for one day. (3.290)

Having addressed a guru with "thou," or having uttered "hum" to him, or having defeated a Brahmin in debate, or having bound him with a garment, one must quickly appease him and fast for a day. (3.291)

The meaning is that if one addresses a guru—who is most venerable—using the word "thou" (*tvam*) for the sake of reviling, or employs the sound "hum" (*huṃkāra*) which is used for reviling an inferior person, or having defeated a Brahmin in debate or the like, or having bound him even with a hempen rope, one should quickly and immediately appease him, making him free from anger, and then eat at night. Manu says:
"Having uttered 'hum' to a Brahmin, or having addressed a superior as 'thou,' one should bathe, fast for the remainder of the day, and having offered salutations, should appease him."
Having struck him even with a blade of grass, or having bound him by the neck with a garment,
or having defeated him in a dispute, one should propitiate him by prostrating.
Yama: Having touched a Brāhmaṇa with one's foot, an expiation is prescribed:
having fasted for a day and bathed, one should appease him by saluting him.
This is connected [to the previous]. Likewise: "Having spoken what should not be said to a Brāhmaṇa, an expiation is prescribed;
having performed the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance, one should propitiate him by prostrating."
If one embraces a Brahmin around the neck, an expiation is prescribed:
having fasted for three nights and bathed, one should propitiate him by prostrating.
This applies when the injury is extreme or the consequence is extreme:
"One should perform an insult, a falsehood, or violence corresponding [to the offense];
it is ordained for one night, three nights, or six nights. (3.291)
Furthermore:
"In raising a staff against a Brahmin, there is a *kṛcchra* penance; in striking him down, an *atikṛcchra*;
in drawing blood, a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*; and in shedding internal blood, a *kṛcchra*. (3.292)

If one raises a staff with the intent to strike a Brahmin, the penance is a *kṛcchra*; if the staff actually falls [and strikes him], it is an *atikṛcchra*; and if blood flows or is shed from the body of the Brahmin, it is a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. If blood is produced within the skin (without it being drawn out), the penance is a *prājāpatya-kṛcchra*. Bṛhaspati states: "Having struck [him] with wood or other objects, if the skin is pierced, one should perform a *kṛcchra*;
if a bone is broken, however, one should perform a *kṛcchra* and a *parāka*, and likewise for the amputation of a limb."
Yama says: Having threatened [another], one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; for striking [them], the Atikṛcchra;
and for actually hitting [them], one should perform either the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra or the Cāndrāyaṇa.
And one should give ten cows when there is the cutting off of a limb.
Viṣṇu: When causing a Brāhmaṇa to take an oath involving death under false pretenses...
A killer of a Brahmin shall perform the intense Cāndrāyaṇa penance while subsisting on barley-gruel.
For a Kṣatriya, there should be a Parāka penance; likewise for a Vaiśya, a Prājāpatya;
but for a Śūdra who has committed the act of killing, he should perform the vow of a three-night fast.
[1186] Some other rules prescribing miscellaneous expiations (*prakīrṇaprāyaścitta*) from other Smṛtis are also shown here. Among them, the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa* states:
If a Brahmin should ever enter into indigo by mistake,
he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
He who, through ignorance, uses a tooth-stick made of indigo must fast for one night and is purified by consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If the pollen of any kind of indigo should enter the hair-pores,
the common purification for the three castes is the *taptakṛcchra* penance.

Protecting [the property], as well as its expenditure and the livelihood derived from its increase—[if these are done improperly]—result in the loss of caste for a Brahmin; purification is achieved through three *kṛcchra* penances.
If blue indigo should pierce the body of a Brāhmaṇa and blood is seen there, the twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

The suffix *tasi* in the word *śarīrataḥ* is used in the sense of the accusative case. Śaṅkha says: "O best of the twice-born, having occupied a bed, a vehicle, a seat, or sandals made of *palāśa*, one who observes the vow must remain so for three nights."
A person who has thrown an impure substance into the fire or into water,
as well as one who has reviled his teacher, shall perform a vow for one month.

In the reading *upākrośet*, it means "having excessively transgressed. If one should pass between two Brahmins, or between a Brāhmaṇa and a sacred fire, or between a husband and wife— those being the most excellent of the twice-born— one should perform the *Sāntapana Kṛcchra* penance.

If a twice-born man should pass between [a cow and her calf] during the time of a fire sacrifice, at milking, while engaged in Vedic study, or when taking a wife, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having understood that obstacles arise regarding the acquisition of a wife, food, and wealth, one should practice them accordingly;
however, one should observe the vow of celibacy for each year.

In the event of lying regarding one's social rank or caste, one should consume cow’s urine and barley gruel. Upon seeing a bad dream or an ill omen, one should give clarified butter and gold. Atri says:

He who maintains the sacred fires but fails to perform the ritual worship on the festival days, and he who does not approach his wife during her season, shall likewise perform half a *kṛcchra* penance.
"Attendance" means standing near the fire. Manu says:
"Having discharged his bodily waste either without water or even within the water, he becomes pure by bathing outside with his clothes on and touching a cow."

The bodily [impurity] consists of the discharge of urine and so forth. Regarding this, Yama says: "How is purification prescribed for a Brahmin wandering in the forest, specifically in a place where water has disappeared?"
Upon seeing water, a Brahmin should perform purification with his clothes on;
he should mutter the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times, for this constitutes the supreme bath.
Having taken into account the place, the time, and likewise his own physical condition,
he should remain steadfast in the purity of dharma and must not suppress natural urges.

*Vega* refers to the force of impurity (*malavega*). Vasiṣṭha states: "Upon releasing one who deserves punishment, the king shall fast for one night; the domestic priest (*purohita*) for three nights. For punishing one who does not deserve punishment, the domestic priest shall perform a *kṛcchra* penance, and the king for three nights. Hārīta says: "For forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*) using village produce, there is a *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. For transgressing the rules of conduct prescribed by their own duty, there is a *phala-cāndrāyaṇa*. Vasiṣṭha states: "A forest-dweller, upon a breach of his initiation (*dīkṣā*), having performed a twelve-night *kṛcchra*, shall increase the great thicket (*mahākakṣa*). A breach of initiation is a transgression of one's own duty other than the observance of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). Regarding a transgression of celibacy, it will be stated that a mendicant (*bhikṣu*) must perform a six-month *kṛcchra*. That same rule applies to the forest-dweller as well, because he is equal to the mendicant. "Great thicket" means a large forest. Its "increase" is by means of watering and so forth. He (Hārīta) himself says: "A mendicant, like a forest-dweller, shall avoid the 'increase of soma' (*somavṛddhi*). A mendicant is an ascetic (*yati*). Upon transgressing his own duty, he should perform the vow like a forest-dweller. He should avoid the "increase of soma," which is the "increase of the thicket. Śaṅkha [says]: [End of excerpt]
Having performed the foot-warming rite and likewise having placed fire beneath [the feet], one should wipe the feet with *kuśa* grass; thus one becomes a practitioner of the vow for one day.

In the section on the observances of a *snātaka*, Kratu states: "If one deviates from even a single one of these practices, one becomes purified by reciting the *gāyatrī* one hundred and eight times. Manu says: "For the transgression of the obligatory rites prescribed in the Vedas, and for the neglect of the *snātaka* observances, the penance is fasting."

Fasting means abstaining from food. This applies when a specific expiation has not been prescribed for a transgression. Hārīta says: "In saluting those who have ascended a bed, those wearing sandals or shoes, those with feet placed upon [a seat], those who are impure, those standing in darkness, those who have received an impurity, those performing the *kṛcchra* penance, or those intent on the worship of a deity, and so forth, there shall be a fast for two nights. In the case of being invited elsewhere for a meal [after such an offense], it is three nights. Kratu says:
"One becomes pure by fasting for three nights when there is an interruption of the daily rites (*āhnika*).
If there is a lapse lasting many days, that same penance shall be doubled."

A lapse lasting many days is called *bahudaivasika*. Hārīta states: "Upon going out while impure from food remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*), there shall be a fast for one day; a householder must not eat when he has transgressed his observances. Aṅgiras says: "If a twice-born man living in a house should, in the absence of an emergency, go about seeking prepared alms, he should drink *vajra* [cow's urine] for ten nights; in times of distress, for three days."
This is declared to be non-edible every month out of apprehension;
and for a Vedic scholar (śrotriya), it is prescribed as such every year.
Carrying an empty water-pot, or eating food without having bathed,
one becomes pure after a day and night, or by becoming pure through recitation for that duration.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says:
If one should show the rainbow or the sacrificial fire to another,
the penance is a fast for a day and night, and the sacrificial fee is a bow and a staff.
Yama says:
"That twice-born man who, having caused a formal invitation to be made, subsequently causes it to be violated,
incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin and is born into the womb of a Śūdra."
When this sin has been incurred, a Brahmin who is firm in his vows is liberated from that evil by performing the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa penance.

*Ketana* means an invitation; *atipātana* means transgression—that is, the failure to provide food to one who has been invited. Likewise: "And for the one who diverts a river's confluence, for the one who creates obstacles for a maiden, and for the one who treats equals as unequals, no expiation is possible. [1189]
Furthermore, for all three of these, seeking restoration is prescribed:
a month-long vow of begging for alms, and for purification, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is traditionally taught.
Bṛhaspati: A householder who, while not being ill and possessing wealth, eats every day without having performed the great sacrifices, shall perform half a *kṛcchra* penance.
Śaṅkha says:

One who takes the wealth of a deceased person without having performed the funeral rites for that deceased shall perform half of the penance prescribed for the killing of those belonging to the [respective] castes.
Whether it be a woman or a man, out of excessive pride, excessive anger, fear, or even ignorance, one should bind that [debt], for they have no other course of action.
In a most dreadful hell, filled with pus and blood and shrouded in blinding darkness,
they dwell for sixty thousand years.
Those Brahmins who touch cattle that have been killed, as well as those that have been hanged or slain by a Brahmin, as well as those who set fires and those who administer poison;
Furthermore, those who follow after [the thieves], as well as others who cut their bonds—all these are joined with sin; I shall declare the expiation for them.
One shall be purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance; one should provide a meal for Brāhmaṇas and give a cow along with a bull as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brāhmaṇa.
Saṃvarta says: When a Brahmin has been killed by cows, or likewise when one has committed suicide,
those who desire their own welfare and are virtuous should not shed tears.
Whoever should carry or cremate any one of these deceased persons,
having performed the rites for the funeral bier and the water libation, shall perform the Taptakṛcchra penance.
If that corpse is merely touched, or if a tear falls [upon it],
and if one has failed to perform the previously mentioned rites, there shall be a fast for one night.
The man who performs the funeral rites for those who have committed suicide by fire should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow together with the Taptakṛcchra penance.
This is intentional. Yama says:
"There is no impurity, no water libation, no shedding of tears, no censure, and no compassion for those slain by the rod of Brahman; nor should the carrying of the funeral bier be performed."
But he who performs these acts out of affection, for the sake of his livelihood, or out of fear and so forth,
is purified by the Kṛcchra penance while subsisting on cow's urine and barley-gruel.
And this is the dissolution resulting from collective actions performed with prior intention:
for those who carry [the dead], those who provide the fire, and those who arrange the funeral rites.
Purification from two *taptakṛcchra* penances applies to those who follow [the deceased] only once.
This also applies when the act is committed collectively. Uśanas says:

"By means of fasting, starvation, weapons, fire, poison, hanging, falling from a cliff, water, wood, and the like, or by kings, Brahmins, or predatory beasts, one who kills himself [is subject to penance]."
For one struck by horns, fangs, claws, serpents, or lightning,
as well as for one born of a mixed caste (saṃkara), there is no impurity, nor water, nor fire [for the funeral rites].
If one touches that [impurity] or reviles it, there shall be fasting for one day;
however, if it occurs through ignorance during carriage and so forth, the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra is prescribed.
If that act is committed intentionally, however, the penance is the *kṛcchra* consisting of barley-gruel with cow's urine;
or, if one is incapable, it is the *taptakṛcchra*, or even subsisting on alms for a month.
For those who have constructed boats and such but do not perform expiation, purification is achieved through two *taptakṛcchra* penances; for their followers, it is through one alone.
But he who performs the remaining rites out of affection or for a fee must undergo the Taptakṛcchra followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa.
Bṛhaspati:
He who causes his own death by means of poison, hanging, or a weapon—once dead, he is to be smeared with the *medhya* [purificatory substance]; he does not deserve any other funeral rite.
He who cuts the noose, he who carries the body, and likewise he who provides the fire—
even he, the lowest of men, as well as the slayer, shall be purified through a *kṛcchra* penance.
Dakṣa says:
Having touched a Brahmin who has fallen from a high position, one who has emerged from the company of Caṇḍālas or dogs, or one who has died by hanging, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

Sumantu: "In cases of hanging, cutting the noose, or being carried [to the funeral pyre], one should subsist on alms for a month and perform the three daily ablutions (triṣavaṇa). Cyavana: "Upon touching, carrying, burning, or cremating a suicide, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance; twenty cows are the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to be given to the Brahmins. The Ādipurāṇa: "One who dies while playing with horned animals, fanged beasts, clawed creatures, serpents, poison, fire, or great waters must be avoided from afar."
Those who acted unfavorably toward the Nāgas were burned by lightning;
likewise, those who were apprehended by the king somewhere for the crime of theft,
as well as those who, out of anger, abducted the wives of others, were slain by their husbands.
But those killed by those of unequal status, by outcasts, or by Caṇḍālas and the like;
Thieves, those who administer poison or fire, heretics of cruel intellect,
and those driven by anger— these resort to fasting, poison, fire, weapons, hanging, or water.
Those lowest of men who cause mountains, trees, or precipices to collapse; those who live by ignoble crafts, and those who work in ornaments;
Those who have a mouth but no genitals, those who are mostly eunuchs, those who are neuter,
those struck by the rod of a Brahmin, and those killed by Brahmins;
Those who commit great sins (mahāpātakin) and those who have fallen from their caste (patita) are thus proclaimed.
For those who have fallen, there shall be no cremation, no funeral rite (antyeṣṭi), and no collection of bones (asthisaṃcaya).
Neither the shedding of tears, nor the offering of funeral cakes, nor any other rite such as the *śrāddha* should ever be performed for those who have fallen [from their caste].
Yet, some, being utterly deluded, perform these for the outcastes.
His purification occurs only through two *taptakṛcchra* penances, and not otherwise.
Parāśara says:
If a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires is killed by a Caṇḍāla, a Śvapāka, or by cattle,
or if he dies from poison, or even if he has committed suicide;
He who is devoid of the consecration of mantras should be cremated with the common funeral fire;
and the one who touches him, the one who carries him, and the sapinda relatives shall all be defiled in every respect.
Afterwards, following the instruction of the Brahmins, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
having gathered the bones again after cremation, the wise man should wash them in milk.
The cremation is performed again with one's own fire, using one's own mantra, separately for each.

Vasiṣṭha: "If one attempts suicide while still alive, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights and fast for three nights. Wearing a garment that is constantly wet, and having restrained the vital breaths within oneself, one should recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times. Alternatively, one may repeat the *gāyatrī* according to this same procedure.
Or else, having established the sacred fire, one should offer clarified butter with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras."

"Whatever else besides the great sins (mahāpātaka) there may be, all of it is purified by this. Now, one should sip water (ācamana): May Agni, and Manyu, and the lords of wrath protect me from the evils committed through wrath. Whatever sin I have committed during the day—with mind, speech, hands, feet, belly, or genitals—may the Day take that away, and whatever misfortune is in me; here I offer myself into the immortal source, into the light of Truth, Svāhā! May Sūrya, and Manyu, and the lords of wrath protect me from the evils committed through wrath. Whatever sin I have committed during the night—with mind, speech, hands, feet, belly, or genitals—may the Night take that away, and whatever misfortune is in me; here I offer myself into the immortal source, into the light of Sūrya, Svāhā. Viṣṇu says: "He who cuts the rope of one who has died by hanging is purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance. The one who performs the funeral rites for those who have abandoned their own lives, and the one who sheds tears for them, are both purified by bathing with their clothes on after the collection of the bones has been completed, provided they have shed tears for every deceased person along with the relatives. A twice-born man (dvija), having followed the corpse of a Śūdra, should go to a river and mutter the Gāyatrī eight thousand times; for the corpse of a twice-born man, he should mutter it one hundred and eight times. A Śūdra, having followed a corpse, should perform a bath. Now follow the penances for those who have fallen away from fasting unto death (anāśaka) and other such vows. Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
Those Brahmins who have fallen away from their vows due to renunciation, fire, water, and so forth;
or those who have desisted from fasting and desire the state of a householder.
Having caused them to perform three *kṛcchra* penances or three *cāndrāyaṇa* observances,
and having consecrated them with the sacraments beginning with the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), they become vessels worthy of purification.
Parāśara says:
But he who desists from fasting unto death while remaining established within the system of the four castes is to be known as a Caṇḍāla; he must be avoided with great effort.
Saṃvarta says:
"Any evil-minded person who, having renounced the world, should again resort to worldly life,
must perform the Kṛcchra penance without weariness for six months immediately thereafter."

Parāśara: What should be the expiation for those who have resolved upon and then desisted from throwing themselves into water or fire, as well as from wandering forth as ascetics or fasting unto death?
By the grace of Brahmins, by visiting sacred fords,
and by the gift of a hundred cows, the three social classes are indeed purified.

Yama said: Those who have perished by water or fire, by hanging, or by falling; those who have fallen from the mendicant life or from fasting unto death; and those who have perished through poison, leaping [from a precipice], or by the stroke of weapons—[1193]
All those who have fallen away and are censured by the whole world may be purified either by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance or by two Taptakṛcchra penances.
This refers to one who is incapable [of fulfilling his vows]. Aṅgiras says:
"The Brahmin who has fallen away from the life of a wandering mendicant due to fire, water, or other causes, and who, having desisted from fasting, desires to return to the state of a householder..."
One should cause him to perform three *kṛcchra* penances or three *cāndrāyaṇa* observances;
he deserves to undergo the purificatory rite (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) again, beginning with the birth ceremony (*jātakarman*).
This refers to the situation of one who has failed to perform penance for a long time. Āpastamba states:
"But a woman who has fallen from the funeral pyre, having strayed from it through delusion, shall be purified from that sinful act by means of the Prājāpatya penance."
From the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"O Lord of Birds, know that he who, having ascended to the perpetual dharma (naiṣṭhika-dharma), should fall back from it, must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one month."
This applies to a mental transgression.
Now follow the penances for contact: Dakṣa says, "In the case of drinking [forbidden liquids], sexual intercourse, and likewise contact with urine or feces..."
If one should come into contact with a corpse, a woman in her courses, or an outcaste;
One should observe [the penance] for one day in the case of urine, for two days in the case of feces,
for three days in the case of sexual intercourse, and for four days in the case of drinking [it].

Āpastamba: "If one who has eaten remains impure from food remnants and has not sipped water (anācānta), and should by negligence come into contact with a Caṇḍāla or a Śvapaca, he must perform a purification in that case."
By reciting the Gāyatrī eight thousand times and likewise one hundred Drupada verses,
and having fasted for three nights, one becomes purified by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Śātātapa says:
If a Brahmin who is impure from eating should somehow touch a Caṇḍāla,
that twice-born man, having been touched while still impure from food remnants, shall perform the Sāṃtapana penance.
One who has consumed leavings becomes pure by means of the five products of the cow at the end of three nights.

One who has eaten and left a remnant is *ūrdhvocchiṣṭa* (one defiled above). One who has discharged urine or feces is *adhaucchiṣṭa* (one defiled below). Uśanas says: "A twice-born man touched by a Caṇḍāla or a Śvapaca, or after having discharged urine or feces, shall be purified in three nights; however, if he has eaten and left a remnant, he must perform the penance for six nights. [1194]
A tiger [is purified] when touched by the water of a Caṇḍāla; he becomes pure through bathing.
One who is touched by him while he is impure from eating is purified after three nights.
Sumantu: A twice-born man who, while impure from eating, touches a Caṇḍāla, one who has fallen from his caste, or a woman in her menses, becomes pure by performing the Prājāpatya penance.
Kaśyapa states: If one who is impure from eating should touch a dog, a pig, an outcaste (caṇḍāla), a vessel for liquor, or a woman in her courses, he should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance.
Āpastamba states:
"If one who has eaten is touched by outcastes (antyaja), he should perform a Prājāpatya penance;
for being touched while half-eaten, a quarter-penance is prescribed, and likewise for a foot [of the meal] remaining, a quarter-penance applies to the act of sipping water."
If a Cāṇḍāla and a Brāhmaṇa have both climbed the same tree while one is still half-eaten from his current meal,
and they both eat fruit there, what should the expiation be?
Having obtained the permission of the Brahmins, he should perform a bath along with his clothes;
having fasted for a day and night, he becomes pure by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
When one has climbed onto a single branch and eats its fruits, the penance shall be three nights; he becomes pure by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If one should drink water unknowingly that has been taken up by a Caṇḍāla,
one should always understand that purification is achieved through the Prājāpatya penance.
If one who has eaten and left food remnants has not yet sipped water for purification and should touch something impure,
he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Bṛhaspati: A twice-born man who has been touched by one who is impure from food remnants, or by a dog, or by a Śūdra,
becomes pure by fasting, eating only at night, and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
This refers to cases where the act is intentional; however, regarding unintentional contact, that which was declared by Chāgaleya applies:
"If one is touched by those for whom bathing is prescribed when touched by the impure (ucchiṣṭa), then if touched by the impure by that very person, one should perform a Prājāpatya penance."
If one is touched by a blacksmith, a washerman, a Vena, a fisherman, or an actor, or likewise becomes impure through food remnants, one should drink milk for one night.
If a menstruating woman is touched by a Brahmin while he is eating, he shall remain impure for three nights; having consumed clarified butter, he becomes purified.
But one who has committed a minor offense (śiśukṛcchra) shall be purified by a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).
Āpastamba: But if a superior twice-born man is touched by the remnants of food (ucchiṣṭa), he becomes pure after fasting for one night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). [1195]
This refers to the case of Caṇḍālas and others. Hārīta states:
"Upon contact with one who has committed a mortal sin (mahāpātakin), bathing alone is prescribed;
but when one who has been touched is himself touched, he is purified by the Brahmakūrca penance."
Whether for three nights or one night, he who does not eat while consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and properly reciting the Praṇava shall thus attain purification.
If a twice-born man has voided urine or feces, or is defiled by food remnants,
or has been touched by a dog or similar impurity, he should perform a bath and then recite the thousand names of the Goddess.
Āpastamba:
"If a Brahmin is somehow touched by another Brahmin who is impure from food remnants, he becomes pure simply by sipping water; such is the statement of Āṅgirasa."
One who has been touched by a woman in her courses, one who is impure from eating, or one who has been touched by a village pig,
a cock, crows, cats, or carnivorous animals, becomes pure through fasting.
If one who is defiled by any kind of leavings should touch something impure,
he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Chāgaleya says: If a Brahmin should touch remnants of food, liquor, a Śūdra, a dog, or anything impure,
he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night, bathing, and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If one who is already impure by having food remnants is touched by another person of his own caste who is likewise impure, he should sip water (ācamana).
If he is touched by a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who is impure, he must perform a night-fast and a full-day fast respectively.
Śātātapa says:
"If even a Brāhmaṇa happens to enter the shadow of an outcaste (śvapāka),
bathing is prescribed for him there, and the consumption of clarified butter is the means of purification."
Likewise:
"If touched by outcastes with a wooden stick or a cloth, one should wash the limb and sip water; but if rendered impure by food remnants, one should throw away the night's [garment]."
Aupakāyana says:

One who crosses alone with an untouchable by means of a boat, a bridge, or the like, may place his shoes and other belongings in the water; he does not become defiled by that, provided he himself does not touch them.
Śātātapa says:
Upon touching Kāpālikas, one becomes pure by bathing according to the prescribed rule,
performing a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), and consuming clarified butter.
Vṛddha-Śātātapa says: A Caṇḍāla, an outcaste, one who is deformed, a madman, a corpse, an outcaste by birth,
a woman who has recently given birth, a woman in labor, and a woman overwhelmed by her menses.
Having touched domestic dogs, chickens, and pigs,
a person becomes pure immediately after bathing with their clothes on and including the head.
She who causes a birth is called a *sūyikā*.
If one who is himself impure should touch these [impure things],
he becomes pure by fasting for three nights and then another three nights.
"By the north" means by the remains of food [left] behind. Gārgya says:
"Upon touching carnivorous animals, horses, donkeys, or camels—even if the contact is mediated—twice-born man becomes pure by bathing either without clothes or with his clothes on."

In the case of intentional contact, one must bathe with one's clothes on; otherwise, it is without clothes. Having touched a Śūdra or a Niṣāda, a twice-born man becomes pure by sipping water (ācamana);
from touching those even lower than them, he is purified by bathing, breath-control (prāṇāyāma), and the power of austerity.

For one who is unable to bathe, there is the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) upon touching a *śūdra*; for one who is able, however, bathing itself is required. For this very reason, another *smṛti* states:
"Upon seeing a sheep, a cock, a crow, a dog, a *śūdra*, or an outcaste (*antyāvasāyin*), one should perform the [usual] rite; but upon touching them, one should perform a bath."

Alternatively, if one touches a *śūdra* who is pure, there is the requirement for sipping water (*ācamana*); if one touches a *śūdra* who is impure, there is bathing (*snāna*). Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya states:
"Having touched a Caṇḍāla, a Pukkasa, a Mleccha, a Bhilla, a Kāpālika, a child, or even one guilty of a minor offense (*upapātakin*), one should perform a bath."
Saṃvarta says:
Having touched even a fisherman, a hunter, a fowler, a soldier, a bird-catcher,
or a washerman, one should bathe and then take food.

The meaning is that one should eat only after having bathed. And thus, eating when there has been contact with a washerman or similar person should be understood as referring to cases involving those who are ill and so forth. From the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "Upon touching a Caṇḍāla or a corpse, one should perform a *kṛcchra* penance; regarding vehicles, beds, and seats, [the penance lasts] three nights. Regarding "touching a Caṇḍāla or a corpse": the meaning is touching a Caṇḍāla who has reached the state of being a corpse. Regarding "three nights on vehicles and so forth with a living Caṇḍāla," it is as follows: "In cases of bandaging a wound, anointing, bloodletting, or causing blood to flow, one should perform a *kṛcchra* for twelve nights. This refers to performing the acts of bandaging wounds and so forth toward a Caṇḍāla, or by a Caṇḍāla upon oneself. Thus says Āpastamba.
If one who has been anointed with any [unguent] should touch a Caṇḍāla,
he becomes pure by means of a single fast and the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

"One who has been anointed with oil, as well as one who has sipped water after shaving, sexual intercourse, or voiding urine or excrement, becomes pure after a day and night. Pracetās states: "If one touches one's own body after it has been touched by a Caṇḍāla or similar person, purification comes from not eating for two nights. This refers specifically to the case of embracing.
If a Caṇḍāla should cause blood to flow from the body anywhere,
purification would occur after three nights, or after one night in subsequent cases.

In the case of Kṣatriyas and others of higher castes, there is a reduction of one day and night for each successive stage beyond the three-night period. The *Kratu* states: "Upon giving the remnants of food to a Caṇḍāla, upon seeing a Caṇḍāla dance, upon hearing their singing or instrumental music, or upon performing medical treatment for them, purification is achieved by fasting for two nights. Having seen an impure person, one should gaze at the sun and perform fifteen *mātrās* of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). An "impure person" refers to a Caṇḍāla and the like. Parāśara says: "If one converses with a Śvapāka, a Ḍomba, or a Caṇḍāla among themselves, one should converse with a twice-born person or recite the *Sāvitrī* mantra once."
Having slept with a Caṇḍāla, one becomes pure after three nights;
having gone to a woman who is entirely a Caṇḍāla, one is purified by the recollection of the Sāvitrī mantra.

The meaning is that one should converse with Brāhmaṇas among themselves. Pracetās states: "Upon entering the house of a Caṇḍāla, or staying for a long time in the house of a Caṇḍāla or in the shade of a tree belonging to a Caṇḍāla, one becomes like a Caṇḍāla. For a Brāhmaṇa, the penance is a six-month Kṛcchra or a Kṛcchra lasting four, three, two, or one month; for the others [the remaining castes], it is as follows. The "others" are the Kṣatriya, the Śūdra, the Kaivarta, and so forth. For these, respectively, there are Kṛcchras lasting four, three, two, or one month. Uśanas states: "In the case of smelling, hearing, seeing, or uttering undesirable odors, sounds, forms, or words, purification occurs from beholding the sun. The meaning is that in cases of smelling, hearing, seeing, or uttering undesirable odors, sounds, forms, or words, purity is attained by looking at the sun.
In the event of contact with the dharma of a Caṇḍāla, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
and for using a well or bathing place belonging to a Caṇḍāla, one should observe a three-night fast.

The instruction on the conjunction with Dharma. Āpastamba: Having seen a Caṇḍāla or an outcaste when the time for the twilight prayers has arrived, one should look at the rising sun; likewise, upon seeing a woman in her courses or impure substances. [1198]
Manu says:
Having sipped water and being purified, one should always mutter, upon seeing something impure, solar mantras according to one's enthusiasm and *pāvamānī* verses according to one's ability.
Parāśara says: But if a Caṇḍāla lives in someone’s house unrecognized,
O twice-born ones, once he is discovered, the twice-born should show favor toward the food (of the one who has served it) [and toward the one who approached for it].
Reciting the teachings that have issued from the mouths of the sages,
the chanters of the Dharma should rescue him as he falls by means of a rite prescribed in the scriptures.
Accompanied by his dependents, he should subsist on curd, ghee, milk, and barley-gruel mixed with cow's urine as a penance, and perform immersion in water at the three junctions of the day.
One should eat with curd for three days, then with clarified butter for three days;
one should eat with milk for three days, and again with each of these individually for three days.
One should not eat food that is twice-defiled; rather, it should be eaten when saturated with cow's milk products.
For as many days as one has remained [in this state], for that many years one should continue to practice [this penance].
Three palas of curd, one pala of milk, and one pala of clarified butter constitute the purification for brass,
as well as for bronze.
A mine is a place of origin. Ārakūṭa is brass.
Clothes [are purified] by washing with water; earthenware by abandonment;
and safflower, molasses, cotton, salt, honey, and clarified butter [by sprinkling].
One should place grains at the door and maintain a fire within the house;
Manu has declared that which is touched by the flames of the sacrificial fire is pure.
Together with his sons and servants, he should provide a feast for Brahmins;
he should give twenty cows and one bull as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins.
Furthermore, by means of plastering, digging, fire-offerings, recitations,
and the authoritative testimony of Brahmins, no fault exists in that place.
This applies when the period of contact has been very short. Saṃvarta says:
"Where an outcaste or even one who has fallen from his caste remains in concealment, once he has been correctly identified after some time, one should then perform purification."
The Cāndrāyaṇa or the Parāka penance is the means of purification for the twice-born;
however, the Prājāpatya is prescribed for Śūdras, while for the remaining classes, this following rule is declared:
"For those who have eaten cooked food there, the sequence of rules has been stated. [1199]

The meaning is that it is a *prājāpatya* penance. However, for those among them by whom [the food] was eaten, a quarter of a *kṛcchra* is prescribed; as are those defiled by drinking from the same well or those defiled through association.
One should purify all of them through fasting and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
as well as those who have young children, the sick, pregnant women, or the elderly.
These should be administered at night for two watches to children,
or whenever pain is observed in those undergoing medical treatments.
One should complete the remainder [of the rite] so that no misfortune may befall them.
Here, "antyaja" refers to a *caṇḍāla*. Vasiṣṭha says: "If a *caṇḍāla* should dwell in one's house, even if unknown [to others]..."
But having eaten his food, a twice-born man should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
Having eaten [forbidden food] once unintentionally, the best of the twice-born should perform this;
if intentionally, purification is achieved by the Parāka or the Mahāsāṃtapana penance.
The Cāndrāyaṇa or the Parāka penance is the means of purification for the twice-born;
however, the Prājāpatya is for Śūdras, while this [following] is prescribed for the remaining classes.
If anyone else eats cooked food [received improperly], his purification shall be a *kṛcchra* penance;
for eating dry food, it is one-quarter [of that], so said the Blessed Manu.

Likewise: "If one who has been touched by them eats food without having bathed according to the rule in water, a *kṛcchra* penance is prescribed for eating; however, for drinking [the water], it is only a quarter of that."
If bell-metal or earthenware vessels are touched by a Caṇḍāla,
one who eats from a bell-metal vessel or drinks water from an earthenware vessel out of ignorance [must undergo penance].
Having eaten from a bell-metal vessel, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; however, for drinking water from such a vessel, one should perform the Kṛcchra.

*Kṛcchraka* is a quarter *kṛcchra*. Cyavana states: "In the case of commingling with a Caṇḍāla, one must burn one's own house; break all earthenware vessels; and plane down wooden objects. For bell-metal and copper, purification occurs at the mine. One must discard fermented gruel (*sauvīra*), milk, curd, and buttermilk. One should preserve fodder and other goods as if they were liquids. One should subsist on cow-urine and barley-gruel for a month. For children, the elderly, and women, the penance is half. [1200] A child is one up to sixteen years of age; an elder is one over seventy. When the penance has been performed, one should feed Brahmins and give a hundred cows; in their absence, one's entire property. Baudhāyana states: "Upon seeing a Caṇḍāla, one should look at the heavenly bodies (the sun). Upon conversing, one should converse with a Brahmin. Upon touching him, one should bathe. Upon seeing his leavings, one should fast for one night; upon conversing, for two nights; upon touching him, for three nights. When traveling on a road together with a Caṇḍāla, one should bathe with one's clothes on. Āpastamba says:
But those who have been forcibly enslaved by barbarians, Caṇḍālas, or bandits,
and compelled to perform inauspicious deeds such as the slaughter of living beings like cows and others—
The wiping away of leavings, as well as eating from such [leavings],
and the consumption of the flesh of donkeys, camels, dogs, and pigs.
Likewise, association with their women and eating together with them requires the Prājāpatya penance as a means of purification for a twice-born man who has resided [with them] for one month.
For one who has maintained the sacred fires, however, there shall be either the Cāndrāyaṇa or the Parāka penance;
having lived for a year [in such a state], he should perform both the Cāndrāyaṇa and the Parāka.
A Śūdra who has resided [as a guest] for one year should drink barley-gruel for half a month;
a Śūdra who has resided for a full month is purified by a quarter-kṛcchra penance.
After one year, an expiation should be prescribed by the best of the twice-born;
even after three years, he attains that same state [as the offender].

All these penances are to be determined according to one's capacity, the nature of the offense, and with regard to the intention and repetition. However, if someone of a lower caste should dwell together with outcastes (antyajas),
he shall shave his head, including the top-knot, and drink barley-gruel for one month.
If a washerwoman, a leather-worker, a hunter,
or a Pukkasi woman stays in the house of one of the four castes through ignorance, [the following applies].
Having understood this, one should perform the expiation, which is indeed half of what was previously stated;
one should not give a house as a gift, but should cause all the rest to be performed.
If a Caṇḍāla should enter the interior of anyone’s house,
that person must expel him from that house and discard the earthenware vessels;
however, one should never discard an earthenware vessel filled with liquids.
Likewise, one should sprinkle the house with water mixed with cow dung.
When a mixture with Caṇḍālas or Śvapacas occurs,
it is traditionally taught that the period of impurity shall be one day and night, two nights, three nights, or six days, respectively.
But if a Caṇḍāla has lived among them for seven days while remaining unrecognized,
O Brahmins, once he is known, they should grant favor to him as he approaches for refuge.
He should consume for one month continuously, together with his servants, the *kṛcchra* penance consisting of barley-gruel mixed with cow's urine, curd, milk, and ghee.
Now, the expiations for touching a woman in her menses. Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
"If one should touch a woman in her menses, a woman recently delivered, or even those who have touched a corpse or the remains of a funeral pyre..."
"But one shall indeed be purified in two nights," so said Śātātapa.
Śātātapa says: If an Ātreyī woman is touched by Caṇḍālas or even by Śvapacas,
she becomes pure by fasting for three nights and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Ātreyī is a woman in her menses. Kaśyapa says: "If a woman in her menses is ever touched by a Caṇḍāla, she should perform the penance after those days have passed."
There shall be a fast for three nights and purification by means of the five products of the cow;
having passed that night, however, one should cause [the cow] to be smelled by a goat.
Bṛhaspati:
If a woman in her menses is touched by an outcaste or a dog-eater, she should observe a fast for a day and night;
on the third day, and thereafter, she should observe only the night-fast.
Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:

If a woman in her menses is touched by a Caṇḍāla, an Antya, a dog, or a crow, she should remain without food for that duration; having bathed, she becomes pure after the lapse of the [prescribed] time.

This applies when there is a lack of capacity [to perform other rites]. Parāśara states: "If two people have climbed the same tree—one being a Caṇḍāla and the other a woman in her menses—they become pure by fasting for one day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)."
If a woman in her menses, while eating, should touch a Caṇḍāla or others of that sort,
she becomes pure after six nights by subsisting on cow’s urine and barley-gruel.
If she is unable [to give gold], she should give gold to Brahmins or even provide them with food.
Mārkaṇḍeya: But if a woman in her courses who belongs to the same caste should be touched by another woman in her courses, she attains purification without doubt by bathing on that very day. [1202]
This refers to the case of those belonging to the same *gotra*. Thus says Vṛddhavasiṣṭha:

"If two women who have become menstruating, or two who belong to the same *gotra* during a single period of birth-impurity, touch one another—whether intentionally or unintentionally—they both become pure immediately by bathing."
Kaśyapa: If a Brāhmaṇa woman who is menstruating is touched by another Brāhmaṇa woman,
she becomes pure after fasting for one night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
But if a woman of the Kṣatriya caste, while in her menses, is touched by one of the highest twice-born class, she becomes pure after three nights; such is the word of Vyāghra.
If a Brāhmaṇa woman who is menstruating is touched by a Vaiśya woman,
she becomes pure after fasting for five nights and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If a Brāhmaṇa woman who is menstruating is touched by a Śūdra woman,
she becomes purified after six nights if the contact was intentional.
A Brāhmaṇī woman should indeed observe this penance among all castes when she does so unintentionally.

Viṣṇu states: "If a menstruating woman touches another menstruating woman of a lower caste, she shall not eat food until she has become purified; having touched one of the same caste or of a higher caste, she may eat after bathing. Atri says:
"If two women who are menstruating touch each other..."

If [the contact] is with one of the same caste, there should be the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for three nights; if it is with one of a different caste, [the penance is] for three nights.
When a woman of a different caste— one of lower caste—
touches another who is menstruating, whether it be a Śūdra woman touching a Brāhmaṇa woman or vice versa,
the Brāhmaṇa woman is purified by the Kṛcchra penance, while the Śūdra woman is purified by giving gifts.
"By means of a gift" means by giving a fourth part of a *niṣka*. In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"If a woman in her courses should ever be touched by one who is impure from food remnants, she must not eat at all until she has attained purification."
Purity is the cessation of impurity caused by menstrual flow.
If a woman in her courses should touch twice-born men who are impure from eating, she must bathe;
if they are impure from eating, she must fast for one day and night, but if they are impure from vomiting, she should pass three days [in fasting].

*srāva* refers to the discharge of urine and so forth; *āśauca* (impurity) caused by that constitutes *taducchiṣṭa* (that which is defiled by it). Vyāghra states: "If a woman in her menses is ever touched by a dog, a donkey, or a camel, she shall remain without food until she becomes pure through bathing."
This refers to a case where one has the capacity [to perform the penance]. Regarding this also, Baudhāyana speaks of incapacity:
"But a menstruating woman who has been touched by domestic cocks or pigs, or by dogs, shall bathe and remain fasting until the appearance of the moon."
Pracetas says: If a woman in her menses should ever, through negligence, touch a dog,
she becomes pure by fasting for one night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Baudhāyana says: But if a woman in her courses is touched by a dog, a Caṇḍāla, or a donkey, she should observe a fast for one day and night;
on the third day thereafter, she should perform the ritual at night.

He states both that which should be devised when there is a conflict between two contradictory penances in order to avoid that contradiction, and that which is to be devised for sins for which no expiation has been mentioned:
"Having carefully considered the place, the time, the age, the capacity, and the nature of the sin, a penance should be prescribed where no expiation has been stated. (3.293)

When multiple optional penances of varying degrees of severity apply to a single offense, the assembly (*pariṣad*) must determine their application by taking into account factors such as place and other circumstances. A specific penance that might be feared to destroy the performer if applied in a particular place or time should not be prescribed there; for example, fasting in water is unsuitable in a snowy region or during the great winter season. Likewise, age (*vayas*) must also be considered; otherwise, if a penance that is too severe were imposed on children or the elderly, it would cause them to perish. Similarly, the physical capacity of the performer is a determining factor, since even a youth may suffer harm while performing a *parāka* or similar penance if his power for austerity is obstructed by an excess of bile (*pitta*) or other ailments. For this very reason, Hārīta says:
The Brahmins should prescribe an expiation according to age, according to time, and according to one's strength,
as well as for the elderly and the sick.
One does not attain purity by that through which one is deprived of life or undergoes great suffering; indeed, one should not prescribe such a vow.

Therefore, having ascertained the strength and weakness [of the offender] and the time, an expiation (prāyaścitta) is prescribed according to the rule, whether it be a full Kṛcchra, half a Kṛcchra, or even a quarter of one.
Viṣṇu:
"A child who is eighty years old, or one who is less than sixteen, women, and the sick, deserve half the expiation. [1204]
Aṅgiras states: "For one who is less than eleven years of age but more than five years old,
either the teacher or a friend should perform the penance for the sake of complete purification."

Having considered whether the sin for which an expiation is required is light or heavy, the expiation itself—whether light or heavy—should be prescribed accordingly. Thus it was stated by Gautama: "For a grave offense, the penances are grave; for a light one, they are light. And the gravity of a sin is known to be due to its being committed intentionally, with full awareness, and habitually; this is understood from the severity of the punishment, from the excessive nature of the condemnatory explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), and from the extreme degree of public reproach. This [gravity] should be determined with effort through established custom and by ascertaining the entirety of the Smṛti scriptures concerning that subject. In that regard, the general nature of the specific expiatory rites (*niṣkṛti*) to be prescribed in connection with the cause of the offense is shown. On this point, Gautama says: "The means of atonement for that are recitation (*japa*), austerity (*tapas*), burnt offerings (*homa*), fasting (*upavāsa*), and giving gifts (*dāna*). Regarding what is to be recited, he states: "The Upaniṣads, the beginnings of the Vedas, the Vedāntas, the *Saṃhitās* in all meters, the *Madhus*, the *Aghamarṣaṇa*, the *Atharvaśiras*, the *Rudras*, the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Rājanarauhiṇa*, the *Samanī*, the *Bṛhadrathantara*, the *Puruṣagati*, the *Mahānāmnīs*, the *Mahāvairāja*, the *Mahādivākīrtya*, any one of the *Jyeṣṭhasāmans*, the *Bahiṣpavamāna*, the *Kūṣmāṇḍas*, the *Pāvamānīs*, and the *Sāvitrī*—these are the purifiers. Likewise: "Subsisting on milk, eating only *śaṅkha*-grass seeds, eating only fruits, the *prasṛti-yāvaka* (barley-gruel), consuming gold-dust, and drinking *soma*—these are the pure and sanctifying practices. Likewise: "All mountains, all rivers, holy lakes, sacred bathing places (*tīrthas*), the dwellings of seers, and the paths around cow-pens (*goṣṭha-pariskandha*)—these are the appropriate locations. A cow-pen is a place where cattle stand; the path leading there is the *pariskandha*. Likewise: "Speaking the truth, celibacy, touching water at the three daily libations (*savanas*), wearing wet clothes, and fasting—these are the austerities. Gold, a cow, clothing, land, horses, sesame seeds, clarified butter, and food—these are the things to be given. Likewise: "One year, six months, four, three, two, or one month; twenty-four days, twelve days, six days, three days, or a day and night—these are the durations. When no specific rule is given, these should be performed as alternatives according to the gravity of the sin: for a grave sin, grave penances; for a light sin, light ones. The *Kṛcchra*, *Atikṛcchra*, and *Cāndrāyaṇa* are the standard expiations. (3.293)

The penances for those who have fallen (patita) have been stated; now he declares what must be done by their relatives toward them: "Their own kinsmen should carry a water-jar outside the village; they should exclude the fallen man from all social functions. (3.294)

The slave-girl and the kinsmen (*bāndhava*) of the outcast (*patita*) shall carry a jar full of water outside the village. From that time forward, they shall exclude him from all affairs, whether worldly or Vedic; they shall not have any dealings with him. The mention of "kinsmen" is intended to include all relatives by marriage. Therefore, all those related through learning (*vidyā*) or birth (*yoni*) shall also carry [the jar]. And thus says Gautama: "His teachers of learning (*vidyā-guru*) and those related by birth (*yoni-sambandha*), having assembled, shall perform all the funeral rites (*pretakārya*), beginning with the water-libations. They shall overturn his vessel. A male slave or a laborer, having brought a vessel from the refuse-heap and filled it from the jar of a female slave, shall, facing south, overturn it with his foot, saying, 'I make so-and-so waterless,' while mentioning the name. All of them, wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*) and with hair-locks unbound, shall touch it. The teachers of learning and the blood-relatives shall look upon it. Having touched water, they enter the village. After this, having conversed with him, one should remain standing for one night and mutter the *Sāvitrī*; if [the conversation was] intentional, for three nights. The meaning of this is as follows: For one who is declared "to be abandoned" due to such causes as being a regicide, his sons and other *sapindas* shall perform all the funeral rites—such as the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), water, and *śrāddha*—for that very person while he is still alive, for the sake of the one to be abandoned. They shall overturn the vessel for that person to be abandoned, i.e., cast it down. To the question "How? he says: "A male slave or a laborer," etc. A "slave" is defined as above. A "laborer" is a servant. Whichever of these two is available, he brings a vessel from the refuse-heap—that is, a place of excrement—and fills that vessel with water from the jar of a female slave. Then the other [the relative], facing south, overturns it with his foot, saying, "I make Devadatta waterless. As he overturns it, the *sapindas*, such as the sons, shall touch it, wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder and with hair-locks unbound. The teachers of learning and the blood-relatives shall look upon it. Then, having bathed, he enters the village. After this, if one converses with him unintentionally, one should stand for a day and night muttering the *Sāvitrī*; but if intentionally, for three nights. Vasiṣṭha says: "Those who corrupt the Vedas, those who sacrifice for Śūdras, and those fallen from the class of the highest caste (*uttamavarṇa*)—for them the overturning of the vessel is performed. Because of the mixing of unworthy vessels (*apātra-saṃkara*), having taken a broken piece of a vessel from a collection of contemptible vessels, a slave, or the son of a woman of a different caste, or a kinsman who is dissimilar, or one devoid of merit, shall spread out Darbha grass with red tips (or red-colored) with their left foot, and pour the water-filled vessel for that outcast with his left foot. And the kinsmen of the outcast, having placed their sacred threads over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), shall touch the one pouring at the time of pouring; then, staying in their own houses, they may engage in their duties as they please. The meaning of this is: He who studies or teaches the Veda contrary to the rules is a "corrupter of the Vedas. A "sacrificer for Śūdras" is well known. The "highest caste" refers to Brāhmaṇas; those fallen from that group are the killers of Brāhmaṇas (*brahmahā*) and others. For them, the overturning of the vessel must be done for their sake. Because of the mixing of unworthy vessels, having taken a broken piece of a vessel from a heap of contemptible vessels, a slave, or the son of a woman of a different caste—meaning a Śūdra woman—or another kinsman who is dissimilar, of a different caste, or devoid of merit, shall spread out Darbha grass with cut-off tips or red-colored [grass] dyed with minerals and the like, and pour the water-filled vessel for that outcast with his left foot. And the kinsmen of the outcast, having placed their sacred threads over the right shoulder, shall touch the one pouring at the time of pouring. Then, staying in their own houses, they may engage in their duties as they please. By the force of the statement "they may engage as they please in their houses," it is understood that prior to the overturning of the vessel, there is no freedom of action regarding religious duties for the kinsmen of the outcast. Manu says: [text follows]
The sapinda relatives and kinsmen shall perform the water-libation for one who has fallen from his caste outside the village on an inauspicious day,
in the evening, in the presence of agnates, officiating priests, and teachers.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Having proclaimed the fault of that teacher—who is fallen, accused, evil-minded, or a destroyer of his family—in the presence of his kinsmen and the king, and having addressed him, one should say, 'May you regain your composure. If, even so, he remains of unsteady mind, then taking a broken vessel, filling it with water and earth, and placing it on the left foot while facing the southern direction, one should overturn the vessel. Having performed the *apasavya* rite, they should sit for purification with *pavitra* grass and water. For one who has been excluded from the community (*apapātrita*), inheritance, the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*), and the water libations cease. One should not engage in conversation, sitting together, or legal transactions with him. Having performed this, one should mutter the Gāyatrī mantra while wearing the garment over the right shoulder (*vasanānugā*). (3.294)
Furthermore:
When one who has completed his vows arrives, they should offer him a new water-jar.
They would neither despise him nor drink from him in any way.

When he has completed his observances and performed the penance, and has returned, all the *sapiṇḍas* should pour out a new jar filled with water into a pure body of water; they should cast it away. From that time forward, they should neither despise nor revile him. On the contrary, in all matters and in all activities, they should drink together and conduct business together. Vasiṣṭha says: "Regarding those who have fallen but have performed their vows, there is a restoration; as they say: 'The one restoring [the fire] should go forth as if playing, as if laughing;
the one who caused the fall should follow behind as if grieving, as if weeping.'"

"Those who have killed their teacher or mother become free from their sin through his favor. Their restoration is performed by filling a golden vessel or one made of *māheya* (copper) with water and sprinkling [the person] with the verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*. The restoration of one thus consecrated is explained by the rules for the birth of a son. The meaning is this: the "restoration" (*pratyuddhāra*) and "acceptance" (*parigraha*) of those who have fallen refers to both those who have fallen and those who have not, provided they have performed penance. In that regard, the leader among those who restore him should be joyful, while the one who caused the fall should be inferior and dejected. Those who kill or cause pain to the teacher and others become free from their sin (*yāvyam*, i.e., evil) solely through his favor. Therefore, their restoration should not be performed as if they were outcasts (*patita*). However, in the absence of the teacher's favor and so forth, the restoration of one who has completed his vows must certainly be performed. For these outcasts and others, "restoration" means bringing them back; having filled a golden vessel or a copper one with water from a full pond or from a flowing stream, they should sprinkle the person being restored with the verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā. The restoration of one thus consecrated is explained by the rules for the birth of a son: just as the *jātakarma* and other sacraments are performed for a son, so should they be performed for him by his relatives; and since they are seen to occur at the same place and time, they should be done collectively (*tantra*). Gautama says: "But he who is purified by penance—once he is pure—they should fill a vessel made of gold with water from a most holy pond or from flowing springs, and then bathe him. Then they should give that vessel to him; having received it, he should recite: 'May the sky be peaceful, may the earth be peaceful, may the atmosphere be peaceful, may the atmosphere be auspicious; I would indeed take that seed here. With these *yajus* formulas, with the *taratsamandī* verses, the *pāvamānī* verses, and the *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras, he should offer clarified butter into the fire. He should give gold to a Brāhmaṇa and a cow to the teacher. But he for whom the penance ends in death shall be purified upon dying. They should perform all the funeral rites for him, beginning with the water libations. This very same *śāntyudaka* (water of peace) applies to all minor offenses (*upapātaka*). (GDh 3.295)
Extending the aforementioned rule for men to women, he says:
"This very same rule for those who have fallen from their caste is proclaimed for women as well; they should be given a dwelling near the house, food, clothing, and protection. (3.296)

For women who have become outcasts as well, this very same procedure for abandonment and readmission previously mentioned is prescribed. "Procedure" (*vidhi*) refers to the collection of actions that must be performed. However, there is this distinction: even for women who have been abandoned, a residence—a dwelling—must be provided in the vicinity of the house. Likewise, food and clothing must be given to them for their livelihood, along with protection. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha states an exception: "But four [wives] are to be abandoned: one who has gone to a disciple, one who has gone to a teacher, one who specifically kills her husband, and one who has approached a man of low caste."* (*juṅgita* = a man of low or degraded caste).
One who goes to her husband’s teacher, her own teacher, her father, or her father-in-law; one who is abandoned; and one born of an inverse (pratiloma) union. 2.296.
The acts such as killing a Brāhmaṇa that cause loss of caste for men and women have been mentioned. Now, he states those which are specifically causes of loss of caste for women alone:
"Approaching a low-caste man, causing an abortion, and harming the husband—these also are certainly specific acts leading to loss of caste for women. (3.297)

A "low-born" person (*nīca*) is one of inferior caste, a *śūdra*. Approaching women such as Brahmin women and others intentionally against their will is "approaching the low-born" (*nīcābhigamana*). Likewise, causing the abortion of one's own fetus—even if it is a Brahmin—and the killing of one's own husband—even if he is a Brahmin—these are specifically causes of loss of caste (*patanīya*) for women; the meaning is that these alone are the grounds for the loss of caste for women. The word "also" (*api*) is used to indicate that these are not the only ones, but that acts such as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) and so forth are also included. The sense is that this is certainly authoritative (*dhruvam prāmāṇikam*). As for that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha:
Those who know the Dharma recognize three sins for a woman in this world:
the murder of her husband, the killing of an embryo, and the causing of an abortion of her own fetus.
Thus, in this context, the term "killing of a fetus" (bhrūṇahatyā) is intended as an indicative mark for all causes of loss of caste. || 3.297 ||

He states an exception to the rule that "they should despise him and not drink from him at all": "One should drink from those who harm those who have sought refuge, children, and women, even if they have completed their vows; one should always avoid these along with the ungrateful. (3.298)

One should not associate with or conduct business with those who kill or slay those who have sought refuge, nor with ungrateful persons—even if they have performed penance—for such association is not permitted. Nor does this non-association render the penance useless; for the penance remains purposeful as it effects the destruction of sin. As for the statement that "one who intentionally steals [gold] is born here [in this world] as a worm," that refers to cases other than these. Manu says:

"One should not dwell with those who kill children, those who are ungrateful, those who have killed those who sought refuge, or those who kill women—even if they have been purified according to the law."
By the statement, "even those who are pure according to the nature of reality," he shows that the purpose of penance for killing a woman and so forth is the destruction of evil. || 3.298 ||
Having thus stated this incidental matter, he states the remainder of the meaning of the passage beginning with "and they should not despise him," which pertains to the subject at hand:

"When the water-jar has been set down, he who stands in the midst of his kinsmen should first offer grass to the cows; for one who is honored by the cows, there shall be participation in ritual acts. (3.299)

In the verse beginning with "caritavrata āyāte," the removal of the water-pot (ghaṭāpavarjana) has been mentioned. When that removal has been performed, one who has completed his vow, while staying among his kinsmen, should offer fodder for the cows to eat. If the cows eat that fodder given by him who has completed his vow, then he is honored by the cows and declared to have his sins destroyed. For one thus honored by the cows, it is proper to engage in ritual acts and social dealings with his relatives; otherwise, however, the performance of the penance must be undertaken again. Therefore Hārīta says: "Taking fodder upon his own head, he should give it to the cows; if they accept it, then they shall admit him [to the community]. By implication, it is understood that this does not apply to others. (3.299)
He states that those penances prescribed for killing a Brahmin and other such offenses must be performed with the approval of the assembly, and not otherwise:
"One whose fault is publicly known shall perform the vow approved by the assembly.

One whose fault is well-known—that is, one whose transgression has been established by many—is called *vikhyātadoṣaḥ*. He should perform that vow or penance (*prāyaścitta*) which is approved and agreed upon by the assembly (*pariṣad*) characterized as previously described; he should not act independently based on his own proficiency in determining the meaning of the scriptures. In this context, even a fault that is not personally known to someone is said to be "known" or "explained" by him if it is established [by others]. Consequently, even a learned person whose fault is widely known must present himself before the assembly. However, regarding a specific penance that has been prohibited by the assembly—such as the rule, "The first three [offenses] are not to be specified"—it is the same according to Manu as well.
"The established rule is that [an offense] committed intentionally is inexpiable and ends only with death.

In this regard, even a learned man whose fault is well known may, by his own authority, perform the vow after having transcended [the state of being bound]. As Śaṅkha says, beginning with "one who, though fallen, seeks to uplift himself": "Having personally undertaken the vow, he shall wear rags and bark garments, sleep on the ground," and so forth. Where the instruction for the vow is not prohibited, there the learned man must indeed present himself before the assembly (pariṣad). On this point, Aṅgiras states: "When a sin has been committed beyond doubt, one should not eat without having presented oneself [before the assembly]."
One who eats increases their evil as long as they do not confess it before an assembly.
Having bathed with his clothes on, restrained in speech, wearing wet garments, and composed in mind, a man,
with the approval of the assembly, shall proclaim the entire truth.
Then, having approached quickly, one who is afflicted should fall upon the earth on his limbs and his head, and should not utter anything at all.
Then, seeing him standing before them after he had approached with prostrations, the Brahmins asked what his business was as he sat down.
"What is your business, or for what purpose do you search so intently, O twice-born one?
Tell me all that in truth; for truth is the ultimate refuge within oneself."
If you speak the truth, you will certainly attain what is auspicious;
but if you have come here with falsehood, there shall never be any purification for you.
Therefore, falsehood must not be spoken by the virtuous who are discerning in matters of dharma;
for when that [falsehood] has been reported regarding a matter, the one who brought the matter forward will surely suffer for it.
When that brahmin had been removed, those who were the reciters of the Dharma there likewise spoke in that manner, deliberating with one another.
