Having deliberated upon everything that is stated in the treatises and whatever may be compassionate, the entire assembly should prescribe the penance according to the time,
the place, and the nature of other duties. [1211]
And one must consider the consensus of the assembly as well as the strength and weakness of the litigant.
Having encountered some misfortune through fate or due to past actions,
one should approach a master of the three Vedas or even one of the four Vedas.
As long as the vow is not fulfilled through deed, mind, and speech,
one who is intent on the welfare of cows and Brahmins should always maintain that vow.
Having committed a sin, one should not eat for three nights or even for a single day;
rather, one should perform service to a Brāhmaṇa until the completion of the vow.
Having arisen, one person should proclaim it to the assembly according to the rule:
that which is certain for all, and that which one must not cause to be lost.

Other duties include the service of aged parents and so forth. Devala states: "A wrongdoer, having fully confessed his own committed sin in an assembly, should then bathe and beg for expiation from that act."

And that vow, approved by the assembly, shall be explained further below as it is to be undertaken. Yama says: "The daily provision of fodder for a cow, worship of the gods, the study of the Vedas, and bathing in a river quickly destroy even those sins born of the great transgressions."
One should never engage in conversation with Śūdras or sinners;
nor should one ever hold conversation with women or with them.
When a doubt has arisen, it must be resolved by a Brahmin alone.
"Conversation" means talking together. *Marīci* says:
"Sleeping on ashes, cow-dung, in a cow-pen, or on sand;
and not conversing with those who have fallen from their caste, with *vrātyas*, with *caṇḍālas*, with women, or with *śūdras*."
One should always perform the threefold bath, meditation, recitation, and worship of the gods;
one should worship whichever deity is most favored by a person in this world.
He states the secret vow:
"But one whose fault is not publicly known should perform the secret vow. (3.300)

One whose own fault has not been made public—that is, one who has not revealed it—is called "one of undisclosed fault" (*avikhyāpitadoṣa*). Such a person, by his own learnedness, should deliberate upon and perform some vow prescribed for the jurisdiction of secret penance (*rahasyaprāyaścitta*). In this case, appearing before an assembly (*pariṣad*) is not required, because that is ordained specifically for cases where the fault is publicly known. "Non-publicity" (*avikhyātatva*) means being unknown because it falls outside the collection of factors that cause the fault to become manifest; it is in such a case that the rule for secret penance applies. And in that regard, only the learned (*vidvat*) have the authority. As it is said in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"For one who has maintained the sacred fires, who is disciplined, aged, or learned, the expiation is that which is declared in secret; but for another, it is as previously stated. (3.300)

Now he declares the specific secret penances for expiation: "A slayer of a Brahmin, having fasted for three nights and recited the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn while submerged in water, shall be purified by giving a milch cow. (3.301)

Having observed a fast for three nights, on the fourth day, one who has committed the murder of a Brahmin shall be purified by reciting three times while submerged in water with his entire body immersed the triplet of *Ṛgveda* verses beginning with "Ṛtaṃ ca" and "Satyaṃ ca," which belongs to the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn, is composed in the *Anuṣṭubh* meter, and has Bhāvavṛtta as its deity; thereafter, by giving a milch cow yielding much milk to a Brahmin, he is cleansed. 3.301.
Furthermore, it is said: "Saying 'Svāhā to the body hairs,' one who subsists on air during the day, standing in water, should offer forty oblations of clarified butter. (3.302)

Alternatively, having fasted for an entire day by subsisting only on air, and having remained standing in water for the whole night, one who desires purification from the murder of a Brahmin should, upon the rising of the sun, emerge from the water and offer five oblations with each of the eight mantras beginning with "Svāhā to the body hairs," desiring purification from the killing of a Brahmin. This [is the penance] for the specific cause of Brahman-murder. 3.302.
Having fasted for three nights and offered clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍī verses, one becomes pure;
likewise, a drinker of spirits or a stealer of gold is purified by reciting the Rudra-hymns while standing in water.
One who recites the *Sahasraśīrṣa* [hymn] is liberated from the sin of violating the Guru’s bed;
at the conclusion of this rite, a milch cow must be given separately by each of these [offenders].

He who drinks spirituous liquor made from flour in secret, having fasted for three nights and bathed, shall offer clarified butter into a common fire while reciting the *Kūṣmāṇḍī* verses beginning with "Whatever offense against the gods, O gods... (*yad devā devaheḍanam*); thus he becomes pure and free from sin. Furthermore, a stealer of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, having fasted for three nights and remained within the water, shall become pure by muttering the eleven Rudra sections beginning with "Obeisance to your wrath, O Rudra" (*namas te rudra manyave*). Likewise, one who has violated the Guru’s bed, having fasted for three nights and bathed at its conclusion, shall be released from the sin of violating the Guru’s bed by being habitually devoted to the muttering of the hymn "A thousand heads" (*sahasraśīrṣā*). The suffix of habit (*tācchīlya*) in the word "jāpī" indicates that the muttering of the Rudras and the *Puruṣasūkta* must be practiced until the mind is fully satisfied. At the conclusion of these rites, such as the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* oblation, a milch cow must be given by the drinker of spirits and the others. (3.303, 304)
Now he states those secret penance-vows which concern minor offenses (upapātaka) as opposed to the great sins (mahāpataka):
"A hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) should be performed for the removal of all sins, indeed for those belonging to the class of minor offenses and for those not specifically prescribed. (3.305)

A hundred of the breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) characterized as previously described should be performed for the removal—that is, the destruction—of all sins, including those categorized as minor offenses (upapātaka), those designated as minor offenses, and those sins not specifically mentioned whose penance is not prescribed in one's own scripture. Furthermore, for each individual sin, a repetition of the hundred breath-restraints must be performed. (3.305)
Furthermore:
Having consumed semen, feces, or urine, the best of the twice-born should drink the purifying Soma-water consecrated with the syllable *oṃ*. (3.306)

Having consumed any one of semen, feces, or urine, one should drink Soma-water or Soma-juice—which is purifying and cleansing—after it has been consecrated by being recited over a hundred times with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om). This applies to a single unintentional consumption; however, in the case of intentional repetition, that which is declared in other Smṛtis should be observed. That will be explained further below. || 3.306 ||
Furthermore, it is said:
"Whatever has been done through ignorance, whether by night or by day, all that is completely destroyed by performing the twilight devotions at the three times of day. (3.307)

Whatever slight evil may have been committed unintentionally by day or night, all of that perishes through the performance of the *saṃdhyā* rites prescribed for the three periods of the day, such as midday and so forth. In this context, the word *saṃdhyā* refers back to the *saṃdhyā-karma* (the ritual act of twilight) enjoined in another section, and its power to destroy sin is thereby enjoined; it does not, however, refer to some other ritual act distinct from the *saṃdhyā-karma*. If it were otherwise, there would be a loss of the word’s own primary meaning (*svārtha-hāni*). Nor should it be suspected that the obligatory nature (*nityatva*) of the *saṃdhyā-karma* is lost in this case, because the desire for the destruction of sin is possible for everyone at all times. Alternatively, both its obligatory and optional character are possible through the principle of "separation of connection" (*saṃyoga-pṛthaktva*). (3.307)
Thus, the specific expiations for individual sins have been stated. Now, he describes the general means for the destruction of sin:
"The recitation of the Śukriya and the Āraṇyaka, and especially that of the Gāyatrī—these, as well as the Rudraikādaśinī, remove all sins. (3.308)

The verses beginning with “viśvāni deva savitaḥ” are known as the *Śukriyas* in the *Vājasaneyaka*. The *Āraṇyaka* is that which is to be studied in the forest; the recitation (*japa*) of these two, as well as the recitation of the *Gāyatrī*, are each capable of destroying all sins when performed with a specific number—either small or large—depending on the particularity of the sin. Likewise, the *Rudraikādaśinī*—the collection of the eleven sections known as the *Rudras*—should be understood to cause the destruction of all sins when recited. Furthermore, the recitation of the *Śukriyas* and the rest must be performed separately for each individual sin, and not just once. (3.308)
Moreover:
"In whatever place a twice-born man considers himself defiled, in that very place there shall be an oblation with sesame seeds as well as the recitation of the Gāyatrī. (3.309)

In whatever matter a twice-born person considers himself to be tainted by the mixture of castes—such as being born of a mixed marriage or having fallen from his status—in each such case, an oblation of sesame seeds (*tila*) must be performed. Furthermore, there should be the repetition and practice of the *gāyatrī*. Regarding the sesame oblation, the *vyāhṛtis* are the mantras;

for it is seen in another scripture that "what is recited together with the *gāyatrī* is not equal [in merit], nor is what is offered in sacrifice together with the *vyāhṛtis* equal [to other offerings]. And so says Saṃvarta:
A twice-born man should perform an oblation with sesame seeds accompanied by the Mahāvyāhṛtis,
numbering one thousand, for the sake of purification from minor offenses (upapātaka).
And for this reason, it is understood that its scope concerns the mixture of minor offenses (upapātaka). || 3.309 ||

Moreover: "Neither do sins, even those born of the great transgressions (mahāpātaka), touch one who is devoted to the study of the Vedas, who is patient, and intent upon the performance of the great sacrifices. (3.310)

The essential meaning is as follows: one who is constantly engaged in the practice of the Veda—consisting of its reception, study, reflection on its meaning, recitation, chanting, and exposition; who is patient, not retaliating even against one who has committed an offense against him; and for whom the supreme purpose is the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*)—such a person, being intent on these great sacrificial rites, is not touched by even those sins born of the "great transgressions" (*mahāpātaka*), nor do they abide in him, let alone other [lesser] sins. Therefore, having resolved upon the destruction of sins other than the great transgressions, one must become devoted to the practice of the Veda. (3.310)
Furthermore:
Subsisting on air, he should stand during the day and spend the night in water while gazing at the sun;
by reciting the Gāyatrī a thousand times, there is purification—except in the case of killing a Brāhmaṇa. (3.311)

Subsisting on air, eating nothing other than air, he should remain standing during the day and not sit down. Having spent the night in water, looking at the sun, whoever performs the recitation (*japa*) of the *Gāyatrī* one thousand times when the sun has risen—for him there shall be purification from sin, with the exception of the killing of a Brahmin. Now, the secret penances (*rahasya-prāyaścitta*) mentioned in the Smṛtis will be enumerated in order. Regarding this, Yama says: "For a secret offense, a secret [penance] alone must be performed. Viśvāmitra states:
"Whatever has been declared for public [offenses], a twentieth part [of that] applies to secret ones."
A thirtieth part or a sixtieth part should be assigned according to the caste and other factors.
I shall now describe, in their entirety, the purification for all great sins whose faults have not been publicly proclaimed, as well as for all minor offenses (upapāpa).

By means of purifying breath-control (prāṇāyāma), as well as gifts, burnt offerings (homa), and recitations (japa) performed with dedication, they are liberated from their sins; of this there is no doubt.
The purifying hymns (*sūkta*s),
breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), the sacred utterances (*vyāhṛti*s), and likewise the *praṇava*—
with the sacred thread held in hand and seated, one should indeed practice the daily Veda (*brahma*).
Always disciplined, he should repeatedly practice breath control again and again;
from the tips of his hair to the tips of his nails, he performs supreme austerity.
Baudhāyana says: One should perform breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) according to the rule prescribed in the scriptures;
whatever sin has been committed by the organ of generation or whatever has been done by the feet [is thereby purified].
With the two arms, with the mind, with speech, and with the ears, skin, nose, and eyes.

The ellipsis is to be supplied as "that shall destroy all [of that]. Likewise: "In cases of transgressions involving the ear, skin, nose, or mind, one is purified by three *prāṇāyāmas*. In the case of eating the food of a *śūdra*, sexual intercourse with a woman, or consuming [forbidden food], when these occur individually and separately, one should maintain seven *prāṇāyāmas* for each for a period of seven days. The same applies to eating what is unfit to be eaten (*abhakṣya*), what is unfit to be consumed (*abhojya*), drinking what is unfit to be drunk (*apeya*), or tasting what is unfit to be tasted (*anādyaprāśana*). Likewise in the sale of goods unfit for sale (*apaṇyavikraya*), excluding honey, meat, clarified butter, the twelve types of oils, lac, salt, liquids, and cooked rice; and whatever else may be similarly categorized, one should maintain twelve *prāṇāyāmas* for half a month. Furthermore, regarding mortal sins (*pātaka*) other than those that cause loss of caste (*patanīya*), and whatever else may be similarly categorized, one should maintain twelve *prāṇāyāmas* for twelve half-months. — Manu.
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the vyāhṛtis and the praṇava,
performed day after day, purify even the killer of a learned Brahmin within a month.

This [penance] removes all great sins (*mahāpātaka*). And here, by the principle that "by performing the function of one thing, the properties of that thing are acquired," the duties of public penance—such as celibacy, speaking the truth, sleeping on the ground, eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), and so forth—are obtained. By reciting the *Kautsa* hymn and the three verses of the *Vasiṣṭha* hymn, even a drinker of liquor (*surāpa*) is purified through their conjunction with the *Śuddhavatī* verses.

Having muttered the eight-verse hymn beginning with "apa naḥ śośucad agham," which was seen by Kutsa, addressed to Agni, in the Gāyatrī meter; and likewise the triplet beginning with "prati stomebhir uṣasam," seen by Vasiṣṭha, addressed to Uṣas, in the Triṣṭubh meter; as well as the triplet "mahitrīṇām," seen by Satyadhṛti Vāruṇi, addressed to Āditya, in the Gāyatrī meter; and the three Śuddhavatī verses beginning with "eto nv indram," addressed to Indra, in the Anuṣṭubh meter, seen by Aṅgiras Tiraścī—having muttered these, a drinker of spirituous liquor is purified. Furthermore, the muttering here should be performed sixteen times.
By reciting the Āsyavāmīya and the Śivasankalpa even once,
one who has stolen gold becomes stainless in an instant.

The hymn beginning with “*asya vāmasya palitasya hotuḥ*” belongs to the Dawn (*auṣasya*), was seen by Dīrghatamas, consists of fifty-two verses, and is composed in the *triṣṭubh* meter. The verses “*pañcapādaṃ pitaram*,” “*sākaṃjānāṃ saptatham*,” “*yad gāyatre adhi*,” “*saptārdhagarbhāḥ*,” and “*gaurīr mimāya*” are in the *jagatī* meter. The verse “*tasyāḥ samudrāḥ*” is a *viṣṭārapaṅkti* addressed to the Viśvedevas. The six-verse section beginning with “*yaj jāgrataḥ*” has the mind as its deity and is in the *triṣṭubh* meter. Likewise, one should recite the *Haviṣpāntīya* and the verse “*na tamaṃhaḥ*.”
And by reciting the Puruṣasūkta, one who has violated the Guru’s bed is liberated from that sin.

The hymn beginning with “*haviṣpāntam ajaraṃ svarvidi*,” consisting of nineteen *triṣṭubh* verses, was seen by Vāmadeva Mūrdhanvat; it has Sūrya-Vaiśvānara as its deity. The hymn consisting of eight verses beginning with “*na tamaṃho na duritam*” was seen by Vāmadeva Āhomuc; it has the Viśvedevas as its deity, and of this, the first seven are *upariṣṭād-bṛhatī* meters while the final one is *triṣṭubh*. The hymn consisting of thirteen verses beginning with “*iti vā iti me manaḥ*” was seen by Lava; it has Indra as its deity, is in the *gāyatrī* meter, and is dedicated to him. The *Puruṣasūkta* beginning with “*sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ*,” consisting of sixteen verses, was seen by Sādhya Nārāyaṇa; it has Puruṣa as its deity, and of this, the final verse is *triṣṭubh* while the others are *anuṣṭubh*. The recitation (*japa*) of the hymns beginning with “*haviṣpāṅktīya*” should be performed sixteen times. Likewise:
Desiring to remove gross and subtle sins,
one should recite for a year the verse beginning with "Having known" (avet) and that which begins with "Whatever this" (yat kiṃcedam).

The verse beginning with “*ava te heḍo varuṇa namobhiḥ*” is dedicated to Varuṇa; it was seen by Śunaḥśepa, the son of Ajīgarta, and is in the *triṣṭubh* meter. The verse beginning with “*yat kiṃcedaṃ varuṇa*” is also dedicated to Varuṇa, seen by Vasiṣṭha, and is in the *triṣṭubh* meter. For the verse beginning with “*iti vā iti me manaḥ*,” the seer and other details are as previously stated. Likewise:
“Having accepted what should not be accepted, or having eaten food that is censured, a man is released from [the sin] after three days by reciting the *Taratsamandīya* hymn.”

That which is not to be accepted includes forbidden gifts, as well as even things like cows that belong to outcasts such as those who drink *surā* liquor; it also includes censured food, such as garlic and the like. There is the fourteen-verse hymn beginning with "The *taratsamandī* runs," seen by Avatsāra, addressed to the deity Pavamāna-Soma, and composed in the *gāyatrī* meter. Likewise:
"By practicing the *saumāraudra* rite for a month, one is purified;
or by performing a bath in a flowing river, or even by reciting the *aryamya* verse."

"Somarudrā dhārayethām"—this fourteenth [verse] belongs to the lineage of Aṅgiras, was seen by Bhāradvāja, has Soma and Rudra as its deities, and is in the Triṣṭubh meter. "Aryamyaṃ varuṇaṃ mitryaṃ vā"—this Triṣṭubh verse was seen by Arjanyātṛ and has Varuṇa as its deity. Likewise, one who has committed an offense should mutter this seven-verse hymn beginning with "abdārdhm indram.
However, having performed an act that is not praiseworthy, he should subsist on alms for a month while remaining in water.

The hymn consisting of seven verses, beginning with “Indraṃ mitraṃ varuṇam agnim ūtaye,” was seen by the seer Kutsa; it is addressed to the Viśvedevas, composed in the Jagatī metre, and concludes with a Triṣṭubh verse. Having performed the discharge of urine, feces, or semen into water—an act that is not praised—one should subsist on alms for a month. The meaning is that one should conduct oneself by abandoning all other activities.
By offering oblations with the Śakala-homa mantras for a year, a twice-born man destroys even a very heavy sin; or he may do so by reciting the Ṛgvedic verse beginning with “Namaḥ.”

The six mantras beginning with "devakṛtasyainasaḥ" are those used for the Śākala-homas. "Nama id ugraṃ nama āvivāsa" is a Triṣṭubh verse addressed to the Viśvedevas, seen by the sages Aṅgiras and Bhāradvāja. That penance which ends only with death is extremely heavy.
One who is joined with a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) shall follow cows with a concentrated mind;
by reciting the Pāvamānī verses for a year while subsisting on alms, he becomes purified.

The *pāvamānī* verses beginning with "svādiṣṭhayā" and ending with "yat te rājañ chṛtaṃ haviḥ" apply to the case of extremely grave and great sins (*mahāpātaka*). Likewise: "Or, having recited the Vedic *saṃhitā* in the forest, one who is purified by three *parāka* penances is released from all sins."
This also has the same scope as the preceding [rule]:
"Restrained, one should fast for three days, approaching water three times a day;
by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, one is released from all sins."
In this case, for every bath, one should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times;
or, being composed, by reciting the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā three times, or the Yajus formulas,
or the Sāmans together with their secret portions (rahasya), one is liberated from all sins.
Just as a clod of earth quickly perishes upon reaching a great lake,
so does every evil deed sink away when one has mastered the threefold Veda.
The Ṛg verses, the foremost Yajus formulas, and the various Sāman chants—this is to be known as the threefold Veda; he who knows this is a knower of the Veda.

The first [term], consisting of three syllables, refers to the *praṇava* as Brahman. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "A killer of a Brāhmaṇa, having fasted for three nights, shall recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* mantra three times while submerged in water. One who has violated the Guru’s bed [shall recite] the *pavitra* and the *ṛṣabha*; a thief of gold [shall recite] the *rudrādhyāya*; and a drinker of liquor [shall perform] a *ghṛta-homa* with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras at midday. A thief of gold, having sprinkled himself with the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarā*, shall place gold into the water. Yama states: "Now, a drinker of liquor, having descended into water reaching up to his neck and taking a handful (*prasṛti*) of soma-juice, shall consecrate it with the syllable *oṃ* and drink it. Then, having immersed himself in the water, he shall recite the *mānastokyā*. Thereby he becomes purified."
"mā nas toke tanaye mā na āyau"—this *jagatī* verse concerning offspring, seen by the seer Kutsa, is dedicated to Rudra.

"Having committed the theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, one should throw the gold into a hall, descend into water up to the neck, submerge oneself in the water, sprinkle oneself with the four *hiraṇyavarṇā* verses, perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *mānastokīya* hymn, and thereby becomes purified from that sin. Now, having committed sexual intercourse with the Guru’s wife, one should recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* three times while submerged in water and thereby becomes purified from that sin. Now, having committed the murder of a Brāhmaṇa, one should go out toward the east or the north, kindle a fire with abundant fuel, and offer eight thousand oblations with the *aghamarṣaṇa*; thereby he becomes purified from that sin. In this case, clarified butter (*ājya*) is the sacrificial offering. "In the event of encountering any of the sins of transgression (*pātaka*), minor transgression (*upapātaka*), great transgression (*mahāpātaka*), or extreme transgression (*abhitipātaka*), one should simply mutter the *aghamarṣaṇa*. Baudhāyana says: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the *aghamarṣaṇa*, which is the purifier of purifiers—one who has gone out from the village toward the east or the north, bathed, pure, wearing clean clothes, having smeared a sacrificial mound at the water's edge, should study the *aghamarṣaṇa* as his private recitation (*svādhyāya*) with a hand once moistened and once purified by water. One hundred times in the morning, one hundred times at midday, and an unlimited number when the stars have risen; he should consume a handful of barley-gruel. From minor transgressions, whether committed unknowingly or knowingly, he is released after seven nights. After twelve nights, even the killing of an embryo (*bhrūṇahanana*). Excluding sexual intercourse with the Guru’s wife, the theft of gold, and the drinking of liquor, after twenty-one nights he overcomes even those, conquers all, obtains the fruit of all sacrifices, has fulfilled his vows in all the Vedas, has bathed in all sacred fords (*tīrtha*), is known among all gods, purifies the assembly line (*paṅkti*) as far as the eye can see, and his undertakings succeed. Baudhāyana further states: "Those [sins] which are greater than the minor transgressions (*upapātaka*) but less than the great transgressions (*mahāpātaka*), all of them he removes after twelve nights; after twenty-one nights, even the great transgressions. Aṅgiras says: [The same].
Or by repeating the eleven Rudra hymns, one who knows the Dharma is released even when touched by great sins; there is no doubt about this.
Whether one is a drinker of liquor, a thief, a killer of an embryo, or a violator of the Guru’s bed,
one is liberated from all sins by constantly reciting the Rudra-mantras.
Śātātapa says:
Having drunk liquor, having approached the wife of a guru, having committed theft, or having perpetrated the murder of a Brahmin—
one who recites the Rudrādhyāya while covered in ashes and lying on a bed of ashes is liberated from all sins.
Yama says:
By reciting the *Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa* and the *Pāvamānī* hymns while fasting for a fortnight,
one may destroy even the sin of killing a Brahmin, according to the word of Vasiṣṭha.
By reciting this *Indra-mantra*, this hymn (*sūkta*) of Mādhucchandasa which is beneficial to friends,
or by the recitation of the *Pāvamāna* verses, one shall be liberated from the sin of drinking liquor.
One should recite the seven-verse hymn beginning with "I praise Agni, the domestic priest" (*agnim īḷe purohitam*) and ending with "Indra, all have magnified," which belongs to Mādhucchandasa;
or the *Śaunaka*, the *Nāsadiya*, the *Kautsa* hymn for the destruction of theft;
or else one may recite the *Asyavāmīya* or the *Pāvamāna*.
Having recited the Kuntāpa, the Vālakhilyas, the Nivids, the Praiṣas, the Vṛṣākapis, the Hotṛ-formulas, and the Rudras, one is liberated from all sins.

By three hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) performed with the Gāyatrī mantra preceded by ten *praṇavas*, one is liberated even from the murder of a Brahmin; how much more so from other minor sins?

Having offered oblations of clarified butter or sesame seeds as fuel-sticks with the mantras beginning with "devakṛtāt," or having recited them while restrained in water, one becomes pure on that very day.
By muttering the *vāruṇī* verse beginning with "yat kiṃca" while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sins. Vasiṣṭha says:
When a mixture of all kinds of sins has occurred...
Ten thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī constitute the supreme purification through practice.
In the continuation of the *Gāyatrī* [section], Śaṅkha states:
"A Brahmin who has stolen gold, a killer of a Brahmin, one who has violated the Guru’s bed, and a drinker of liquor—these are purified by a hundred thousand recitations; of this there is no doubt."
The Goddess, when offered oblations, especially destroys all impurities;
she is the bestower of all desires, the giver of boons, and affectionate toward her devotees.
Having offered oblations into the fire with sesame seeds mixed with ghee while being well-composed,
even a sinful person is liberated from transgressions by means of a hundred-thousand-fold homa.
Thus, being freed from evil, he attains his desired world.
Manu says:
By reciting this triad a thousand times outside [the village],
a twice-born man is freed from even great sin within a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.

Outside the village. The *trika* consists of the *vyāhṛtis* and the *sāvitrī*. Hārīta says: "The *paṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī* constitute the *sāvitra* purifier, by which one is liberated from all sins. Having recited it a hundred times, one becomes pure within a month; having recited it ten thousand times, they say one becomes a soul purified of everything. Likewise: "'Haṃsaḥ śuciṣat' is the stainless purifier, by which one is released from all sins. One should recite it while in water, or offer oblations of ghee, sesame seeds, or fuel-sticks; or one should worship the Sun, and thus one becomes pure. Likewise: "By worshipping the Sun with 'Ā kṛṣṇena,' one becomes a soul purified of everything. Yama says:
By practicing the syllable Oṃ ten thousand times, one becomes purified on that very day.

Likewise: "Now, having accepted alms from a family of Caṇḍālas, actors, boxers, hypocrites, those accused of crimes, outcasts, or any other family of sinful deeds whose food is unfit to be eaten, or having eaten while hungry, one should depart from the village toward the east or north. Standing in pure ground on the earth, floating in water, one should mutter the *Taratsamandī* hymn, or the *Vyāhṛtis* preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*; thereby one becomes purified from that sin. Having approached a mother, a sister, a maternal aunt, a daughter-in-law, a female friend, or committed any other forbidden sexual act, one becomes purified from this sin by reciting the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times while submerged in water. Having committed the killing of a cow, the killing of a woman, the killing of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, the misappropriation of a deposit, or the defilement of a maiden, one should depart from the village toward the east or north, kindle a fire with abundant fuel, and offer a thousand oblations of cow’s ghee with the *Vyāhṛtis*. Or, having recited the *Gāyatrī* eight thousand times while looking at the sun, sprinkling oneself with water while reciting the four *Hiraṇyavarṇā* verses, and reciting the *Vāmadevya* three times, one becomes purified from this sin. Having approached a Caṇḍāla woman, a Pukkasa woman, or the wife of a friend, or having touched them, one becomes purified from this sin by performing three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while reciting the *Vāmadevya*. Having consumed semen, urine, or feces; having eaten garlic, onions, leeks, mushrooms, and other such forbidden foods; or having eaten the flesh of swans, village cocks, dogs, pigs, or jackals—one should descend into water up to the neck, perform breath-restraint while reciting the *Śuddhavatī* verses, and drink water reaching the chest while reciting the *Vyāhṛtis*; thereby one becomes purified from this sin. Atri says: "One should practice meditation for a quarter of the night. That which precedes it and that which follows it is the Brahman of Savitṛ. One is completely released from eating what should not be eaten, drinking what should not be drunk, and performing what should not be done. By reciting the *Vāmadevya* three times, one is released from the murder of a Brāhmaṇa. By muttering *ayaṃ ta indra somo*, the defiler of a maiden is purified. By muttering *somaṃ rājānaṃ varuṇam*, those who administer poison, those who give poison, and arsonists are released from their sins. By worshipping the sun seven times with *ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam*, one is released from sins committed here and in previous lives. Yama says: "Having drunk what should not be drunk or eaten what should not be eaten, one should bathe, perform ritual sipping (*upaspṛśya*), perform three breath-restraints while reciting the *Ṛṣabha* Sāman, and recite the *Gāyatrī* one hundred and eight times; thereby one becomes purified from this. The *Ṛṣabha* is a specific Sāman. (Cited from the *Caturviṃśatimata*).
A twice-born man should perform a fire-oblation with sesame seeds using the Mahāvyāhṛtis one thousand times for the sake of purification from minor offenses (upapātaka).
One does not dispel all sins— every sin pertaining to this world and the next— without remainder in the same way that one does through the recitation of the Veda.
By reciting the Gāyatrī for five nights, one removes [sin]. Vasiṣṭha says:
"Henceforth, I shall declare all the purifiers of the gods."
Those who are purified by means of recitations and burnt offerings—of this there is no doubt.
The Aghamarṣaṇa, Devakṛta, Śuddhavatīs,
Taratsamās, Kūṣmāṇḍas, Pāvamānīs, Virāj, and Mṛtyulāṅgala.
The auspicious Vyāhṛtis are Durgā, the destroyer of great faults;
I shall now describe the well-known expiations in detail.
How could negligence arise in those who are composed and disciplined?

"By reciting the *aghamaṛṣaṇa* verse, 'ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca,' three times while submerged in water, one is released from all sin. By reciting the verse, 'āyaṃ gauḥ pṛśnir akramīt,' three times while submerged in water, one is released from all sin. By reciting the verse, 'haṃsaḥ śuciṣat,' three times while submerged in water, one is released from all sin. Or alternatively, by reciting the *gāyatrī* verse—foot by foot, half-verse by half-verse, and the whole verse—three times while submerged in water, one is released from all sin."

Viṣṇu: "Now, therefore, follow the purifiers for all the gods, by the recitation (*japa*) and oblations (*homa*) of which the twice-born are purified from sins. These are: the *aghamarṣaṇa*, the *devakṛta*, the *śuddhavatīs*, the *taratsamandī dhāvati*, the *kūṣmāṇḍyas*, the *pāvamānyas*, the *durgāsāvitrī*, the *abhiṣaṅgas*, the *padastomas*, the *vyāhṛtis*, the *bhāruṇḍas*, the *aindrasāman*, the *puruṣavrata*, the *bhāsam*, the *abliṅga*, the *bārhaspatya*, the *vāksūkta*, the *gosūkta*, the *aśvasūkta*, the *madhvṛcas*, the two *sāmans* of Candraśuddhi, the *śatarudriya*, the *atharvaśiras*, the *trisuparṇa*, the *mahāvrata*, the *nārāyaṇīya*, the *puruṣasūkta*, the three *ājyadohas*, the *rathaṃtara*, the *agnivrata*, the *vāmadevya*, and the *bṛhat*. When these are sung, they purify a person; he who so desires attains the memory of his past lives."—Hārīta.
"Even after killing these three worlds, one should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times;
Maitri has declared that it is equivalent to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of a horse sacrifice."
Having recited the Rudraikādaśinī, one becomes purified on that very day;
or one should offer oblations of clarified butter, sesame seeds, or fuel-sticks for the sake of [the sin] committed against the gods.
Or, being restrained, having recited [the following] while standing in water, one is purified on that very day:
the Viraja, the Vimala, the Śuddha, the Trimadhu, and the Jyeṣṭhasāman.
The Apratiratha, the Aśvastomīya, the Kayāśubhīya, the Manobhāsūkta,
as well as the Trisuparṇa, the Suparṇa, the Pratyaṅga, and the Mṛtyulāṅgala.
Either the Atharvaśiras, or the Bhauma, or the Vāmadevya,
or else the Ādityasūkta, the Vāksūkta, or the Śrīsūkta— all these are equally meritorious.
And the various Vāksūktas, which destroy all sins. Thus [it is said].

Now follows the bodily purifier (*śārīra-pavitra*). Whatever sin I have committed by day or by night, with my feet—may Viṣṇu release me from that evil, from all distress. Whatever sin I have committed by day or by night, with my private parts—may Prajāpati release me from that evil, from all distress. Whatever sin I have committed by day or by night, with my anus—may Mitra release me from that evil, from all distress. Whatever sin I have committed by day or by night, with my hands—may Indra release me from that evil, from all distress. Whatever sin I have committed by day or by night, with my speech—may Agni release me from that evil, from all distress. Whatever sin I have committed by day or by night, with my tongue—may the Waters release me from that evil, from all distress. Whatever sin I have committed by day or by night, with my breath—may the Earth release me from that evil, from all distress. Whatever sin I have committed by day or by night, with my eye—may Sūrya release me from that evil, from all distress. Whatever sin I have committed by day or by night, with my two ears—may Parjanya release me from that evil, from all distress. Whatever sin I have committed by day or by night, with my skin—may Vāyu release me from that evil, from all distress. Whatever sin I have committed by day or by night, with my mind—may Candra release me from that evil, from all distress. Whatever sin I have committed by day or by night, with my intellect—may Brahmā release me from that evil, from all distress. Whatever sin I have committed by day or by night, with my ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*)—may Rudra release me from that evil, from all distress.
Whatever misfortune is in my hair, at my parting, or on my head; whatever is in my forehead, my ears, or my eyes—may Agni drive that away from me.
He who has emerged from the great ocean, shining forth from the midst of the waters—
may that bull, the red-eyed sun, the wise one, purify me with his mind.

Or, having been struck down or stepped over [by a cow], one becomes purified by reciting [the mantra] while standing in water. Taking pure *arghya* water for one who has just risen, one should say: "Homage be to you, the one with eighty rays, the dispeller of darkness; destroy my misfortune and rise for my good fortune. With the two verses, "Upwards that [sun]" and "The bright face of the gods," he should pour [the water] with his hands and worship the sun with joined palms (*añjali*) while reciting, "The swan dwelling in purity. This vow fulfills all desires. One who has not yet performed his daily rites should give fodder to a cow, saying: "Homage to the auspicious ones, homage to the abundant ones, homage to the milch-cows, homage to the mothers of the gods of all worlds. If he does not find a cow, he should neither criticize nor revile her; this vow is to be observed at all times. He should give food that has been set aside to a Brāhmaṇa who arrives unexpectedly, saying: "Homage to the Brahmas, to those who know the Brahman, to the Brāhmaṇas, homage. If he does not find a Brāhmaṇa, he should neither criticize nor revile him; this vow is to be observed at all times.
Atri:
One should not take delight in evil deeds by relying on the power of the Veda;
for it is through ignorance and negligence that one is consumed by karma, and not otherwise.
Hari:
By bestowing the gift of gold, the gift of a cow, and likewise the gift of the earth,
one is indeed liberated from all sins.

From the Purāṇa: "Having committed minor sins, great sins, secondary sins, and so forth, without exception, out of delusion, one who has desisted from them [should perform penance] according to that [offense], as prescribed for gold. [1225]
Having first requested a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas and has mastered them,
and having honored him with flowers, garments, and other offerings, one should cause [the gift] to be given with this mantra:
The deerskin belongs to all the gods, gold to Agni,
the bark garment to the Pitṛs, and clarified butter is the splendor of the dwellers of heaven.
O observer of noble vows, one should offer sesame seeds according to the rule with this mantra:
"Sesame seeds are known to have been created from the body of the great seer Kaśyapa."
Therefore, by their grace, may this entire cage of my accumulated sins dissolve like an unbaked clay vessel in water.
Likewise, O lord of men, one should give honey and clarified butter to a twice-born man according to the prescribed rite;
he thereby delivers all his ancestors as well as himself.
Yoked with four cows and likewise provided with a piece of land,
it should be given to a learned man who maintains the sacred fires and is capable of receiving such a gift.
Having given a deerskin on the full moon day of Kārttika or especially on that of Vaiśākha, as well as at the equinoxes,
the solstices, and during lunar or solar eclipses.
With difficulty, he is released from terrible darkness and from fear on all sides;
having uplifted seven generations of ancestors as well as others yet to come,
that man goes to the eternal world of Brahmā.
Vasiṣṭha and Bṛhaspati declare:
whatever sin a person, deluded by greed, commits,
he may quickly destroy it all through the gift of land.
In the Ādipurāṇa:
"He who bestows even land the size of a cow-hide,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Viṣṇu."
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
Where a hundred cows and one bull may stand without being crowded,
those who know the Dharma call this the measure of a *gocarma*.
Bṛhaspati says: A staff ten cubits long, with ten such staves on each side and likewise five more added— this is the definition of a *gocarma* (cow-hide area).
In the *Mātsya*: "Thirty staffs (*daṇḍa*) of seven cubits each constitute a *nivartana*;
Prajāpati has declared that three-tenths less than this is the measure of a *gocarma*."

Vasiṣṭha: "Now, if one should consider oneself heavy due to actions performed by oneself, one should cook a handful of barley-gruel for one's own sake; one should not offer it into the fire. Nor is there a *bali* offering in this case. One should consecrate it—whether uncooked, while being cooked, or already cooked—with the mantra:
'You are barley, the king of grains, belonging to Varuṇa and mixed with honey;
you are the cleanser of all sins, purified as declared by the seers.'"
Barley is ghee, barley is honey, and barley is indeed the nectar of immortality;
may they purify all my evil, whatever misdeed I have committed.
O barley grains, destroy the evil deed committed by speech, the evil dream, and the evil thought; destroy misfortune and purify everything for me, O barley grains!

May the barley grains purify for me all this: food from a group, food from a courtesan, food from a Śūdra, officiating at a sacrifice for a Śūdra, food from a thief, and food from a recent funeral rite (navashrāddha).
The conduct of a fool, that which is unrighteous, and whatever is done at the royal gate;
the theft of gold, the neglect of vows, and officiating at a sacrifice for one unworthy to sacrifice.
May the barley grains purify for me all slander against the brahmins.

While it is being cooked, one should perform a protective rite (*rakṣā*). Once cooked, one should eat it quickly, reciting: "Brahmā is the path of the gods, the leader of the poets... Having poured it into a vessel while remaining pure (*prayata*), one should offer it into oneself (*ātmani juhvīt*) with the mantra: "Those gods who are born of the mind, yoked by the mind, highly skillful, whose father is Dakṣa—may they protect us, may they favor us; obeisance to them, Svāhā! Then one should touch the navel, reciting: "O Waters, become peaceful and drunk within our bellies, you who are auspicious gods. May you be free from consumption, free from disease, and free from decay for us. May the divine, immortal ones, who increase the Truth (*ṛta*), relish this. One seeking wisdom (*medhā*) should drink this for three nights; a doer of evil for six nights; and having drunk it for seven nights, one purifies even the murder of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, the theft of gold, and violation of the Guru’s bed. Having drunk it for eleven nights, one casts out even the sins committed by one's ancestors. Having drunk it for twelve nights, one performs the acts of striking, opening, anointing, and subjugation. Having drunk it for twenty-one nights as a "remover of what has been said," one perceives the sciences (*vidyā*); one perceives the lords of the sciences; one perceives the hosts (*gaṇa*); one perceives the lords of the hosts—thus spoke the blessed Vasiṣṭha. Regarding this very matter, the specific details stated by Vṛddhavasiṣṭha are as follows: "One should consecrate a handful (*prasṛti*) or a double-handful (*añjali*) of barley, whether while it is being cooked or once it is cooked, with this mantra: 'You are barley, you are the king of grains, belonging to Varuṇa and mixed with honey; you are the remover of all sins, a purifier praised by the seers. Or alternatively, with this: 'Barley is ghee, barley is honey, barley is a purifier, barley is nectar; may all of these cleanse my sin arising from speech, mind, and body.'"
One should not perform the fire-ritual (agnikārya), nor likewise the offering to the spirits (bhūtabali);
one should not discard the first portion of food, nor alms, nor hospitality, nor the remnants of a meal.

"Those gods who are born of the mind, yoked by the mind, highly skillful, and possessing the wisdom of Dakṣa—may they protect us, may they guard us; to them, svāhā!"—with these words, one should offer the oblation into oneself.

"For three nights for the increase of intelligence; for a sinner [of other types], six nights; for those who have committed the murder of a Brahmin and so forth, twelve nights; and for one born of an outcast, likewise. One should eat boiled barley-gruel along with cow's urine and the liquid from cow dung, together with milk, curd, and ghee; thus one is instantly liberated from sin.

Laukāxi: "One who considers himself as if impure should offer oblations with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* verses; he shall be released from whatever sin has been committed since his last conception, including the murder of a learned Brahmin (*bhrūṇahatyā*), or from the emission of semen in a non-vaginal place—except in a dream—and from other such acts. This is the means for one desiring purification. On the full moon or the new moon day, or under the asterism Rohiṇī during the bright fortnight, having bathed, being pure, wearing clean clothes or a black antelope skin, he undertakes the vow according to the rule for a student (*brahmacārin*) for a year, a month, twelve nights, or six nights. He must not eat meat, nor approach a woman, nor sit with her; he should loathe falsehood. His primary rule is subsisting on milk. Alternatively, while consuming barley-gruel (*yāvaka*), he may perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, or subsist on alms in such circumstances. Milk is the vow for a Brāhmaṇa, barley-gruel for a Kṣatriya, and curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) for a Vaiśya. Having kindled the fire in the forenoon and cooked the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), he should offer clarified butter (*ājya*) verse by verse with these hymns: "Whatever offense against the gods," "Whatever debt I incurred while gambling," and "Bestowing long life upon you from all sides. He should also offer with the three verses beginning "O gods, whatever offense against the gods," with the four verses beginning "May we hear what is auspicious with our ears," with the nine verses beginning "May the fathers purify me," with the three verses beginning "May power return to me," with the four verses beginning "In the chariot, in the axles," and with the three verses beginning "Golden-colored. The *vrata-homa* (vow-oblation) is offered to Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, Brahmā, Prajāpati, and the Kūṣma seers. With the verse "O Agni, do thou ferry us across," he should worship the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering. Facing east with palms joined, he should worship with the *Vaiśvānara* hymn. He should mutter the five hymns addressed to the Aśvins and the *Vaiśvānara* hymn. Thus says Vasiṣṭha.
"Having bathed, one should recite the Gāyatrī a hundred times; having remained under water, one should mutter it a hundred times;

and indeed, by drinking water a hundred times, one is released from all sins. Thus [it is said]. Even the secret expiations (rahasya-prāyaścitta) must be applied as heavy for heavy sins and light for light sins, in order to avoid the futility of prescribing such weighty methods.
Thus end the secret penances. 3.311.

With two verses, he states the common auxiliary limbs known as *yamas* and *niyamas*, which apply both to the *prakāśa-vratas* already mentioned and to the austerities such as the *kṛcchra* that will be described hereafter—even those not constituting formal expiations (*prāyaścitta*).
"Celibacy, compassion, patience, charity, truthfulness, sincerity, non-violence, non-stealing, gentleness, and self-control—these are recorded as the *yamas*. (3.312)
Bathing, silence, fasting, sacrifice, study of the Vedas, restraint of the generative organ, service to the teacher, purity, freedom from anger, and vigilance are the observances (niyamas). (3.313)

Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and the other qualities designated as *yama* are to be practiced as ancillaries (*aṅga*) to penances such as the *kṛcchra*. Although these are prescribed for the sake of human goals (*puruṣārtha*), their prescription here serves to establish them as ancillaries to the vows (*vrata*). In this context, by the term "celibacy," the duties of a student (*brahmacārin*), such as the avoidance of honey and meat, are understood. *Ekabhakta* is eating one meal during the day within the course of a day and night (*ahorātra*). Thus, the *pādakṛcchra* penance is accomplished in four days. The instrumental case in "by *ekabhakta*" and so forth denotes a specific qualification. Three days in the evening, and likewise one quarter for three days; three days in the morning, and likewise one quarter for three days. Thus.
These four parts have been established for each caste by that very same [authority]:

but for a Rājanya it is unasked, and for a Brāhmaṇa it is prescribed as being for three nights. Thus it is said.

One quarter consists of eating once in the morning; three quarters consist of eating only at night for three days; one quarter consists of eating only what is unasked for (uninvited) for three days; and three quarters consist of three days of fasting—this is the meaning. Because of this mention of a "single location," it is understood that this very [Kṛcchra] is to be accomplished in twenty-four nights. (3.320)
He says it is *saumya*:
"The daily consumption of oil-cake, water from boiled rice, buttermilk, water, and barley-meal, followed by a fast for one night—this is called the *saumya* *kṛcchra*. (3.321)

Passing each of the five substances—oil-cake and the rest—one by one for each day, with a fast observed on the sixth day; this is the *kṛcchra* known as the *saumya*. The term "purifying" (*pāvana*) carries over [from the previous rule]. Therefore, it should be understood that the nature of the *kṛcchra* is prescribed in this very sentence, and its application is directed toward the destruction of sin. *Piṇyāka* is oil-cake; *ācāma* is the rinsings of boiled rice; the others are well known. Jābāla, however, states it otherwise:
"Oil-cake, barley-meal, buttermilk, and fasting on the fourth day."
"One should give a garment as the sacrificial fee; this is called the Saumya Kṛcchra. (3.321)
Regarding the tulāpuruṣa:
"Through the practice of each of these for three nights in succession, this is to be known as the 'tulāpuruṣa' lasting fifteen days. (3.322)

By practicing the consumption of each of these—oil-cake and so forth—for three nights, there occurs the fifteen-day *kṛcchra* penance known as the *tulāpuruṣa*. Yama, however, describes a *tulāpuruṣa* that is to be accomplished over twenty-one nights: "One should consume gruel, oil-cake, buttermilk, water, and barley-meal for three days each, and for the final three days, subsist on air alone."
"The Tulāpuruṣa is said to consist of twenty-one nights.

Thus, by practicing each of the five [penances] beginning with the *ācāma* for three nights, there are fifteen days; and by practicing the air-consumption (*vāyubhakṣa*) for three nights twice, there are [another] six days—thus the Tulāpuruṣa consists of twenty-one nights. It is also seen as being performed in six nights: "On the first day, one should never eat during the various *kṛcchra* penances."
Therefore, one should eat four palas of oil-cake.
On the third day, one should drink a decoction of wild rice grains (nīvāra-taṇḍula) equal in quantity to that [of the previous day];
on the fourth day, buttermilk; and on the fifth day, water, in due order.

"Having consumed barley-meal produced from cow-urine and barley-gruel, one should eat an equal amount of that [meal]," according to another Smṛti text. Regarding this, there is a specific detail stated by Hārīta: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the Tulāpuruṣa as taught by the Three-eyed One (Śiva). Furthermore:
'For those born of improper wombs due to obstacles and other such factors...'"
Having performed sacrifices for those unworthy of sacrificing, or having consumed urine or feces;
Having accepted gifts from those who should not be accepted, or having performed sacrifices for those who are censurable,
or for one afflicted by Vināyaka or struck down by a great disease—
one should perform the Tulāpuruṣa Kṛcchra, which destroys even the most heinous sins (mahāpātaka).
This meritorious gateway to heaven was created by Mahādeva.
Consuming gruel, oil-cake, buttermilk,
and water-mixed barley-meal for three days each, and subsisting on air alone for the final three days.
Improper speech, foot-dust, and particles of dust destroy the benefits of meritorious acts once they have been performed;
likewise, the *ācamana* rite destroys the impurity of a recent funeral (*navaśrāddha*) and birth-impurity (*sūtaka*).
Having consumed even a small amount of oil that has been defiled by hair or insects,
or having consumed urine, feces, or that which has been touched by a killer of a Brahmin;
Oil-cake destroys those [impurities], as well as whatever remains after breaking through the bone; it also removes the defects found in mines and any defects present in oils.

That which has been touched by the mouth of a donkey or a camel, or even that which has been touched by liquor—one removes those impurities with buttermilk; and so too does one who eats what has been looked upon by a dog.
Gold, sesame seeds, cows, land, clothing, and women—
a righteous soul purifies all these, even when they are hidden, by means of water and barley-meal.

One who subsists on air purifies the sin of killing a Brahmin, the sin of killing an embryo, stealing gold, drinking liquor, violating the teacher’s wife, defiling a maiden, or even approaching a eunuch.
Having fashioned two male figures the size of an *uśīra* stalk and equal in measure to a *parṇa* leaf,
or alternatively, one should have two male figures made from river mud.

Having had an iron spear made, firm and a span long, with both its ends sharpened, he caused it to be fashioned from that very arrow by which the great beast was pierced and from that weapon which had achieved its mark upon both.
One should have the goddess Tulā fashioned from gold or silver;
one may even have her made from sandalwood or even from the jujube tree.
In its absence, a balance should be used, or whatever else is appropriate.

"I shall invoke that tawny, brown man who holds a plow, a mace, a trident, and a thunderbolt in his hands—that tawny, brown man with the plow, mace, thunderbolt, and trident in his hands. Come of your own accord, come indeed by your own truth to your own abode! O Kṛṣṇājina, come! Welcome, most welcome to you, O Tulāpuruṣa, O Mahādeva! Here is the *arghya*, here is the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), and here is the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*). Be gracious! Accept this perfume, garland, incense, lamp, and recitation of prayers. Be well-disposed toward me instead of being angry on account of my sins. Then one should consecrate the balance with a mantra: "The truth of the seers, the truth of the gods, the truth of Brahman—whatever truth exists, by that truth, O speaker of truth, declare the prosperity of the lands: what seed will you cause to grow?"
Tell us of the prosperity of kings—whom will you cause to prosper? Tell us of our own prosperity—whom will you cause to prosper?
And when one repeatedly weighs oneself against the guru on a scale and considers oneself to be lighter than the other, then one may undertake the ritual action.

“Svāhā to Agni, lord of the earth! Svāhā to Vāyu, lord of the atmosphere! Svāhā to Sūrya, lord of heaven! Svāhā to Soma, lord of the stars! Svāhā to Vāsuki, lord of the *nāgas*! Svāhā to Takṣaka, lord of the serpents! Svāhā to Kubera, lord of the *yakṣas*! Svāhā to Indra, lord of the gods! Svāhā to Skanda, lord of the armies! Svāhā to Brahmā, lord of the three worlds! Svāhā to Devī, mistress of fortune! Svāhā to Sālakaṭaṅkaṭa, son of the king of the *kūṣmāṇḍas*! Svāhā to Mahāvināyaka Vakratuṇḍa, lord of the *gaṇas*! Svāhā to Dharma! Svāhā to Tulāpuruṣa! This is the god of progeny; together with the Maruts, may he always return—svāhā! By performing this once, one becomes pure and fit for ritual action. By performing it twice, one attains the status of a leader of the *gaṇas*. By performing it thrice, one attains the abode of Mahādeva. This dharma is prescribed for the full moon of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, or Phālguna, or under an auspicious lunar mansion.”
Other difficult penances are also written down. Regarding this, Jābāli says:
"A wise man, remaining in the midst of water while fasting, should pass a day and night;
the *jalakṛcchra* removes the sin committed during a year."
Viṣṇu states: "The *udakakṛcchra* consists of subsisting for a month on water and barley-meal; the *śītakṛcchra* consists of subsisting on lotus stalks (*bisā*). Śaṅkha says:
"Restrained, one should eat water-born plants such as *śaṅgāṭa* and lotus stalks prepared with water for a month;
drinking water only once a day for a month is called the *vāruṇakṛcchra*. [1242]
With bilva fruits, or even with āmalaka, or else with auspicious padmākṣa seeds—for a month, this is called the *śrīkṛcchra* by the best of the twice-born. (3.322)
The *kṛcchra* penances have been described. Now he speaks of the *cāndrāyaṇa* and others:

"One performing the *cāndrāyaṇa* should eat morsels of food the size of a peacock’s egg, increasing them by one each day during the bright fortnight; during the dark fortnight, he should decrease the morsel by one each day. (3.323)

Performing the austerity known as *cāndrāyaṇa*, one should consume morsels (*piṇḍa*) the size of a peacock’s egg, increasing them according to the lunar days (*tithi*) during the bright fortnight. By the term "increase of lunar days" (*tithivṛddhi*), what is intended is the increase in the number of lunar digits (*kalā*) on the first, second, and subsequent days. Since the number of morsels is made to correspond to that [increase], the fact that this serves as the basis for the practice of eating the morsels is not subject to objection—even though human-authored statements have their meanings determined by other means of knowledge (*māna*). For in the case of words, such things as dependent compounds (*sāpekṣasamāsa*) or non-appositional compounds (*asamarthasamāsa*) are not to be challenged. Likewise, having consumed fifteen morsels on the full moon day, one should decrease the morsels one by one starting from the first day of the dark fortnight. Having consumed one morsel on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should fast on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). This is the *yavamadhya* (barley-middled) *cāndrāyaṇa*. Vasiṣṭha says:
At the beginning of the dark fortnight of the month, one should eat fourteen morsels;
consuming with a gradual reduction of morsels, one should complete the entire fortnight.
In the same way, at the beginning of the bright fortnight, he should consume another morsel;
eating while increasing the number of morsels, he should complete the remainder of the fortnight.

Gautama, however, describes the *yavamadhyama* (barley-shaped) *cāndrāyaṇa* differently: "Now, therefore, the *cāndrāyaṇa*. Its procedure has been stated in the section on *kṛcchra*. One should perform the shaving of the head and observe the vow. On the day following the full moon, one should fast. With the verses, "May you swell," "May your milks gather," and "New, new," one performs the satiation (*tarpaṇa*). There is an oblation of clarified butter (*ājya-homa*) and the consecration (*anumantraṇa*) of the sacrificial food (*havis*), as well as the worship (*upasthāna*) of the Moon. With the four verses beginning with "Whatever offense against the gods" (*yad devā devaheḍanam*), one should offer clarified butter; and at the end, with the verse "Of that which was done by the gods" (*devakṛtasya*) and with fuel-sticks (*samidh*). "Oṃ bhūḥ, Oṃ bhuvaḥ, Oṃ svaḥ, Oṃ mahaḥ, Oṃ janaḥ, Oṃ tapaḥ, Oṃ satyam; Oṃ yaśaḥ, Oṃ śrīḥ, Oṃ ūrk, Oṃ iḍā, Oṃ ojaḥ, Oṃ tajaḥ, Oṃ puruṣaḥ, Oṃ dharmaḥ, Oṃ śiva"—with these, there is the consecration of each morsel (*grāsa*). Or, for all of them together, one may mentally recite "namas" and "svāhā" after each mantra. The size of a morsel is such that it does not distort the mouth. The sacrificial foods (*havīṃṣi*) are: cooked rice (*caru*), alms-food (*bhikṣā*), barley-meal (*saktu*), grain-particles (*kaṇa*), barley-gruel (*yāvaka*), vegetables (*śāka*), milk, curd, clarified butter, roots, fruits, and water; each subsequent one is more highly praised. Having eaten fifteen morsels on the full moon, one should eat during the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) by decreasing the number by one each day. Having fasted on the new moon, one should eat during the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*) by increasing the number by one each day. According to some, this is the *cāndrāyaṇa* month performed in reverse order. By performing this once, one destroys all sin and becomes free from impurity. By performing it a second time, one purifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, oneself as the twenty-first, and one's entire lineage. By performing it a third time, one attains the same world (*salokatā*) as the Moon."

The meaning of this is as follows: the rule—that is, the procedure—of this Cāndrāyaṇa has been stated: "One should perform the shaving and the vow; one should perform the penance. It is said that one should fast on the coming full moon; thus, fasting on the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight] is implied. On the full moon, the consumption of fifteen morsels (*grāsa*) is the standard practice, for otherwise the term *Cāndrāyaṇa* would not apply. A morsel is to be consumed at the rising of the moon. As Hārīta says: "Having cooked the *caru* offering to the Moon during the third pressing (*savana*), and having offered it with the mantra 'new, new,' one should eat the remaining balls of *caru*, consecrated by the *Sāvitrī* mantra, in the moonlight. The number of morsels to be taken should correspond to the lunar day (*tithi*) at the time of consuming the morsels. By the word "moonlight" (*jyotsnā*), the rising of the moon is indicated. Therefore, the morsels are to be consumed specifically at moonrise, whether by night or by day. On the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), there is no eating because of the absence of moonrise. Thus says Yama.
"Just as when the moon is waxing, the mouthfuls [of its digits] increase proportionally,
but when it is waning they decrease, and upon its total disappearance, none are consumed"—
thus say Śaṅkha and Likhita.
One should observe the initiation wearing a single garment; having bathed, one should not wear clothes that have been washed with soap.
One should always perform the daily rite (*āhnika*) ten thousand times with the *gāyatrī* mantra.
It has been described as "barley-shaped" (*yavamadhya*), but it may also be "ant-shaped" (*pipīlikāmadhya*) if the commencement is on the first day of the dark fortnight. Regarding this, Manu says:
"One should decrease the morsel by one each day during the bright fortnight and increase it during the dark fortnight;
touching water at the three sessions of the day, this is remembered as the *cāndrāyaṇa*."
Likewise:
"With self-restraint, eating eight morsels of sacrificial food at midday while performing the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa."
A Brahmin, with a concentrated mind, should eat four morsels in the morning;
having eaten four when the sun has set, this is remembered as the Śuci-candrāyaṇa.
Bṛhadviṣṇu:
"One who is self-restrained and firm in his vow should eat three balls of food at each meal for half a month; this is remembered as the Ṛṣicāndrāyaṇa penance, consisting of sacrificial food."
Śaṅkha says:
"In the moon-vow (induvrata), the morsels are the size of a fresh myrobalan fruit;
likewise, there are oblations (āhuti) there, and earth for the purpose of the morsels. (3.323)
He states another form of the Cāndrāyaṇa: "Alternatively, one may consume two hundred and forty morsels in a single month; this is another Cāndrāyaṇa. (3.324)

In whatever manner, by not being restricted to a specific number of morsels each day, one should consume two hundred and forty morsels in a month—that is, over exactly thirty lunar days (tithis). This is another form of *cāndrāyaṇa* than the previously mentioned one. And in this *cāndrāyaṇa*, the previously undertaken vow of fasting on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) and so forth is not annulled; for here, a specific number is prescribed to be accomplished within a month, rather than being accomplished on each individual day as in other types of *cāndrāyaṇa*. Even while fasting on the eleventh day, one is able to accomplish the total number of two hundred and forty morsels to be completed in a month; however, if one were to fast on the eleventh day at the end of the *cāndrāyaṇa*, one would certainly fail to accomplish the number eleven based on the morsels required for that occasion, and would instead ruin the count. Although the act of eating morsels is not something to be enjoined because it is already prompted by natural desire (*rāga*), nevertheless, the injunction for *cāndrāyaṇa* does indeed take as its object the specific number dependent upon those morsels. Just as the performance of the *godohana* vessel is obtained through the operation of the injunction for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), yet the injunction for one desiring cattle (*paśukāma-vidhi*) prescribes: "One desiring cattle should fetch water with the *godohana*"; in that case, if there were no fetching of water performed in connection with the New and Full Moon sacrifices, then the scriptural meaning of "one desiring cattle should fetch water with the *godohana*" would not be established. Likewise, if one does not eat morsels on the eleventh day and so forth, the *cāndrāyaṇa* injunction—whose object is the specific number dependent on them—is simply not fulfilled. Here too, a secondary quality (*guṇa*) characterized by a specific number of morsels based on eating already prompted by desire is enjoined for the sake of results such as the destruction of sin. Therefore, in the phrase "this is another *cāndrāyaṇa*," when other forms of *cāndrāyaṇa* are observed where fasting on the eleventh day and so forth is respected, the *cāndrāyaṇa* injunction is not fulfilled. When five morsels are consumed, then the five mantras beginning with "To Prāṇa, Svāhā! To Apāna, Svāhā! are employed as obligatory rites with distinct objects. When the number of morsels is fewer than five, Baudhāyana says in response to the question of how to proceed: "One should eat with 'To Prāṇa' first; with 'To Apāna' second; with 'To Vyāna' third; with 'To Udāna' fourth; with 'To Samāna' fifth. When there are four, then [use] two for the first; when three, then two for the first; when two, then two for the first; when one remains, then all together for the one. The meaning of this is: when the option of four morsels is taken, one should swallow the first morsel with the first two mantras. In the case of three morsels, the first with the first two, the second with the third and fourth, and the third with the fifth. But when there are only two morsels, the first is done with the first three mantras and the second with the final two. When only one morsel is reached, all mantras are used for that single one. (3.324)
He states the procedure common to both the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances:
"One who bathes at the three sessions of the day should likewise perform the *kṛcchra* and the *cāndrāyaṇa*;
he should mutter purificatory prayers (*pavitra*) and consecrate the morsels of food (*piṇḍa*) with the *gāyatrī* mantra. (3.325)

Bathing at the three *savanas*—performing ablutions in the morning, at midday, and in the afternoon—one should perform the *kṛcchra* penances such as the *sāṃtapana*, as well as the *cāndrāyaṇa*. One should mutter the purificatory mantras (*pavitrāṇi*), such as the *gāyatrī* and others, as established in the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas according to one’s own *śākhā*. And with the *gāyatrī*, one should consecrate the morsels (*piṇḍas*) or mouthfuls (*grāsas*). The *gāyatrī* is also differentiated by the mantras for consecrating the morsels mentioned by Gautama. Alternatively, the triad of mantras beginning with "āpyāyasva," "same tu te," and so forth, along with the *gāyatrī*, have the consecration of the morsels as their object; therefore, because they share a common objective, their combination is appropriate. Furthermore, a specific rule regarding the consecration of the morsels has been stated by Yama:
"One should consume a morsel placed on the tip of a finger, consecrated with the Gāyatrī;
having rinsed the mouth, one should again perform the consecration for another [morsel].

By the statement of Manu, "One who bathes once daily and has conquered his senses," the requirement of bathing three times a day (*triṣavaṇa*) during the *taptakṛcchra* penance is set aside. As for that which [is prescribed] in other *kṛcchra* penances...

"One should enter the water three times during the day and three times at night, wearing one's clothes"—this [rule] is an alternative to bathing at the three *savanas* (the three periods of the day). Among these, the injunction for six baths applies to one who is capable or who desires an abundance of merit; however, for others, the injunction is for bathing at the three *savanas*. Vaiśampāyana states that even for one unable to perform the three *savana* baths, there should be two baths: "The twice-born should bathe twice a day, or three times."

Regarding the bath, however, there is a specific rule stated by Hārīta: "Having bathed at least three times with the *Śuddhavatī* verses, having muttered the *Aghamarṣaṇa* in the water, and having put on a washed or new garment, one should worship the Sun with the *Saumya Sāman*. As for that which was stated by Gautama—"One should constantly recite and employ the *Raurava* and *Yaudhājaya*"—that refers specifically to the Sāmavedins; for there is no study of these for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Nor should it be said that only those belonging to the Sāmaveda are entitled to the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance, since we see that the muttering of purificatory texts found in the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda is also prescribed as an ancillary part of the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. Furthermore, those mantras such as "namo 'hamāya" and so forth, which were enjoined by Gautama for the fire-oblation (*homa*), are not obligatory but rather optional, because Manu says: [Manu 11.257] "Or, having fasted for three days and bathing at the three times of the day, he should offer oblations of sesame seeds with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras.
