[Manu 11.294] "Or, subsisting on water for a month, while muttering the *Sāvitrī*, he is released from every sin, even if he has stolen gold. [Manu 11.295] "Or, subsisting on water for a month
"One should personally perform the fire-oblation daily with the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
Thus he mentions other mantras. And the Mahāvyāhṛtis are the three beginning with *bhūḥ*; regarding this, Manu himself has said:
"The three imperishable Mahāvyāhṛtis are preceded by the syllable *oṃ*."

Regarding the *mahāvyāhṛtis*, there is a triad; they are to be recited (*japa*) alone, but in the case of a fire-oblation (*homa*), they should be employed either separately or collectively, as seen in other scriptures. Furthermore, in the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance, the entire procedure (*itikartavyatā*) prescribed for the *Kṛcchra* is to be adopted. Regarding this, Gautama says: "Now follows the *Cāndrāyaṇa*; its rule has been stated. Vaiśampāyana states the number [of recitations] for the *Kṛcchra* and the *Atijapa*: "One should recite the *Ṛṣabha*, the *Virāj*, and likewise the *Aghamarṣaṇa*, or one should recite the divine Gāyatrī, the purifier, the mother of the Vedas."
"One hundred, or even one hundred and eight, or even a thousand at most.
And at the conclusion of the Cāndrāyaṇa, a cow should be given as an ancillary part of that rite, and Brahmins should be fed; as Yama says:
"When the Cāndrāyaṇa has been performed in this manner, one should give a milch-cow."
One should feed the Brahmins according to one's ability and give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 3.325 ||
He states the application of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance:
"In the case of unspecified sins, purification is indeed by means of the Cāndrāyaṇa."

In the case of sins for which no specific penance has been prescribed or taught, purification is achieved through the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. It is not only by two *Cāndrāyaṇas* that this occurs, but also by the *Kṛcchra* and *Atikṛcchra* penances; as Vasiṣṭha says: "The *Kṛcchra*, the *Atikṛcchra*, and the *Cāndrāyaṇa* constitute the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitti*). When the gravity of the sin is great, the *Cāndrāyaṇa* is performed together with the *Kṛcchra* and *Atikṛcchra*; otherwise, it is performed alone. Even though they constitute a universal expiation, the *Kṛcchra* and other penances are to be applied individually for each specific sin, because the difference in the occasion (*nimitta*) necessitates a difference in the application of the occasional rite (*naimittika*). Furthermore, regarding the *Kṛcchra* and other penances that are to be performed as occasional rites, the authors of the *Smṛtis* have declared certain concessions when the performer encounters incapacity once the rites have already commenced.
Now, therefore, I shall describe the favors for one who is weak but possesses self-discipline;
by performing which, he is released from evil just as a snake is freed from its slough.
Having fasted and observed silence, one should recite the Goddess twelve thousand times according to the rules at the edge of water; this is called the Prājāpatya rite.

Having offered twelve thousand oblations of sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, grain, or sesame seeds while subsisting on air, one shall accomplish the *kṛcchra* penance through the recitation of the *gāyatrī*.

A "twelve-thousand" is a thousand increased by twelve. A "thousand" is simply a thousand. One who subsists on air should satisfy twelve pure Brāhmaṇas with gifts of food and gold; this is called the Śrotriya-kṛcchra.
Having fasted with faith and according to the law, one who gives vessels of sesame seeds to twelve teachers of the Veda attains a merit equal to that of the Prājāpatya penance.
He who, having fasted, personally carries loads of grass upon his head and gives them to a herd of cows, performs twelve *kṛcchra* penances; of this there is no doubt.

Having performed one hundred and thirty-two breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) during times of distress, one should remain standing facing the east for a day and night; this is called the Kṛcchra penance.
One who is firm in his vows should perform twelve thousand prostrations before cows, Brahmins, ancestors, and deities; this shall constitute three *kṛcchra* penances.
Vasiṣṭha said:

Now, if the one who subsists on air (the wind-eater) hastens to perform [the rite] during the day, he should remain standing at night and recite [the mantra]; when dawn has broken, that is equal to the Prājāpatya penance.
One should consume barley gruel combined with cow urine;
this is declared by Aṅgiras himself as the one-day penance (aikāhika-kṛcchra).
Sitting at night and standing during the day for three nights while subsisting on air—this one should know as the Prājāpatya penance; one should offer clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras.
He who performs these supreme acts of grace every year in the spring goes to the abode of Brahmā, a person of vast stature and radiant form.
In the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, there are three Kṛcchras and thirty thousand recitations.
Parāśara says: An *ayuta* recitation of the Gāyatrī, a fast, and likewise the gift of a cow to a Brahmin—these four are equal in merit. [1248]

The meaning is that these four [penances] are equal to the *prājāpatya*. Pracetā states: "One should mutter the *gāyatrī* for as long as it takes to study the *saṃhitā*. From the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "Twelve Brahmins should indeed be fed, and likewise the *pāvakeṣṭi* sacrifice;
or some other expiatory rite (*pātanī*); the wise say they are all equal."
Likewise: the Cāndrāyaṇa, the Mṛgārī sacrifice, the Pavitreṣṭi, as well as the Mitravindā, the animal sacrifice, and the two-month Kṛcchra penance.
For obligatory, occasional, and optional rites,
as well as for *iṣṭi* sacrifices and animal sacrifices, when the [standard] materials are unavailable, *caru* offerings are prescribed.
The Cāndrāyaṇa penance is equal to three Kṛcchras, while the Parāka is equal to two;
this is the measure of the Kṛcchra as proclaimed by the learned.
Those who do not perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance should perform four Kṛcchra penances.
Likewise:
"He who is unable to perform expiation by means of the Cāndrāyaṇa or the Parāka penances should perform the Prājāpatya for the sake of self-purification as the fifth [alternative]."

Mārkaṇḍeya says: A cow equal in value to a *prājāpatya* penance is required for that; two such cows for a *taptakṛcchra*; for a *parāka*, a *suvarṇa* of gold; and likewise, a cow with golden horns for an *aindava*.

The *taptakṛcchra* and the *mahātaptakṛcchra* [are defined as above]. For a *parāka*, the price of gold is equal to the price of two cows. By the mention of "gold-horned," one indicates a cow equipped with all accessories such as bronze milking vessels and the like.
In the procedure for the *pratyāmnāya* (substitution), eight cows are always to be given in the *cāndrāyaṇa*;
"cows" is the word to be supplied. This refers to the *cāndrāyaṇa* which is accomplished by eight *kṛcchras*, according to the *Caturviṃśatimata*.
In the Prājāpatya penance, one should give one cow; in the Sāṃtapana, two;
and likewise in the Parāka and the Taptakṛcchra, three cows each.

From the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "In place of the *parāka*, the *taptakṛcchra*, and the *atikṛcchra*, one should perform three *kṛcchras*; and for the *sāṃtapana*, one and a half. One should observe this vow in case of incapacity. [1249]
A single fast, a thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī, feeding a Brahmin,
and twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas)— these four are equal in merit.
One should perform the Kṛcchra penance, ten thousand recitations for the Goddess, two hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas),
feed twelve Brahmins, and likewise perform the Mṛgāreṣṭi sacrifice.
The wise say that any other purifying rite is equal to ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds and two *parāka* penances.
Bṛhaspati has declared that one hundred thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī are equal [in merit] to the Atikṛcchra,
the Parāka, and likewise the Taptakṛcchra penances.
One should perform three Prājāpatya penances; for a Kṛcchra, there should be a pair of cows.
He states another fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa: "He who performs this for the sake of dharma attains the same world as the Moon. (3.326)
He who performs and practices this Cāndrāyaṇa for the sake of dharma, for the sake of wealth, or for the sake of worldly prosperity, attains the same world and the same realm as the Moon. (3.326)
One who performs the *kṛcchra* penance while desiring the Dharma shall attain great prosperity;
and being composed, he obtains the fruit of a sacrifice according to its weight. (3.327)

He who, desiring "May I possess dharma," performs difficult penances such as the *kṛcchra* and *sāntapana*, shall attain great prosperity and wealth (*śrī*) that is coveted by all the world. But he who performs a "heavy" *kṛcchra*—that is, one who, being composed and intent, should perform with reverence each such *kṛcchra* that is very difficult to accomplish according to the scriptures—he attains and gains the fruit of sacrifices such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, namely heaven and so forth. Viśvāmitra says:
"The *kṛcchra*, *Cāndrāyaṇa*, and other [penances] purify those who commit both [types of offenses]."
Whether it be manifest or secret, spoken or unspoken, or when there is clear doubt.
The Prājāpatya, the Sāṃtapana, the Śuśuc-kṛcchra,
the Parāka, the Atikṛcchra, the Parṇakṛcchra, the Saumya, and the Kṛcchrātikṛcchraka.
The Mahāsāntapana is for purification; the Taptakṛcchra is purifying;
the Jalopavāsakṛcchra and the Brahmakṛcchra are both cleansers.
The *phalakṛcchra* and the *mūlakṛcchra* may also be performed individually for each;
they are to be diligently applied for all major sins (*pātaka*) and minor offenses (*upapātaka*).
These rites, when joined with *cāndrāyaṇas* or performed alone, lead to purification.
The *śuci-cāndrāyaṇa* has been proclaimed, as well as the *yati-cāndrāyaṇa*, the *yava-madhya*,
and likewise the *pipīlikā-ākṛti*.
A fast for one day, or half of that, or for a month, or for a fortnight, or half of that.
For those seeking the fruit of accomplishing their tasks, a six-day period, a twelve-day period, and so forth,
are prescribed for those who have committed minor offenses (upapātaka) as well as for those regarding whom no specific penance has been ordained.
In both public and private matters, depending on the intention and so forth,
one should act after considering the person's power, caste, and qualities, as well as what has been done once by the intellect.
Having observed the consequences and so forth, everything should be postulated in accordance with the scriptures.
Now, the nature of the Brahmakūrca is described. Regarding this, Parāśara says:
"One should prescribe a fast for a day and night as the Brahmakūrca;
and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) were ordained for the castes by the divine eye."
It is pure throughout the three worlds and presided over by the deities:
Varuṇa is present in the cow’s urine, and the Fire-god (Havyavāhana) is in the cow dung.
Vāyu is prescribed for curd, Soma for milk, and Ravi for ghee;
the milk of a golden-colored cow and the dung of a white cow [are likewise used].
Cow’s urine from a copper-colored cow, ghee from a blue cow,
and curd from a black cow— this constitutes the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
There are eight māṣakas of cow urine, but ten of cow dung;
twelve are prescribed for milk, while ten are declared for curd.
It is said that the cow-urine [to be used] with the ghee is equal in measure, while the kuśa-water is half of that;
this is the quantity of liquids for purification, which effects the cleansing of the body.
Taking cow's urine with the Gāyatrī mantra, cow dung with "Gandhadvārā," milk with "Āpyāyasva," and curd with the verse "Dadhikrāvṇo."
Reciting "Tejo 'si śukram" [he takes] the clarified butter; "Devasya tvā" [for] the water with *kuśa* grass;
and having looked at [the water] with "Āpo hi ṣṭhā," he should then drink from it while reciting the *praṇava*.
One should drink from a vessel made of Madhūka wood, or from a lotus leaf, or indeed from a copper leaf; these are the vessels for Brahman.

"Whatever sin resides in a human body, reaching even to the skin and bones, the *brahmakūrca* shall burn it all away, just as fire consumes dry fuel. Now follows the *somāyana*. Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
One should drink cow’s milk for seven nights from four teats,
for seven nights from three teats, and for seven nights from two teats.
Likewise, one should subsist on milk for six nights or three nights, and then live on air;
this is the vow called Somāyana, which destroys all impurities.
Vyāsa says: One who desires prosperity, one who desires nourishment, likewise one who desires heaven,
and one devoted to the propitiation of the deities, should perform the *kṛcchra* penance.
All elixirs, mantras, and likewise medicinal herbs succeed for that man who performs the Kṛcchra penance.
And all Vedic rites whatsoever that are performed for specific desires always attain success for one who performs the Kṛcchra penance; of this there is no doubt.
But those evil-minded men who have been tormented by hardships for their sins go to heaven once they are cleansed of sin; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Whether it be unknown or known, a difficult penance (kṛcchra) purifies sin. For those whose sins have been purified by such penance, hell is not ordained. (3.327)

Having heard the duties pertaining to the castes, stages of life, and so forth—which constitute the entire meaning of the scriptures previously mentioned—the great sages now spoke as follows regarding that high-souled lord of yogis of immeasurable splendor:
"Having heard these duties spoken by Yājñavalkya, the ṛṣis said this to the high-souled lord of yogis of immeasurable power. (3.328)
Those who, unwearied, shall uphold this treatise on Dharma will attain fame in this world and go to the third heaven.
A seeker of knowledge shall obtain knowledge, and likewise one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth;
similarly, one desiring long life shall obtain long life, and one desiring prosperity shall obtain great prosperity. (3.330)

Having heard the various duties (*dharma*) spoken by Yājñavalkya—who was endowed with the power of perfected yoga (*saṃsiddhayogabala*), who knew the true meaning of all branches of knowledge such as the Vedas (*śruti*), and whose pure intention was inclined toward the welfare of all the world—and having mastered them both in text and in meaning, the sages addressed these words to the Great-Souled One, the Lord of Yogins (*yogīndra*), who was liberated from all defects such as the sword of passion and hatred and possessed a capacity equal to that of the Sovereign of Yogins (*yogeśvara*). They said: "May you grant your approval for this: those twice-born (*dvija*) who, unwearied and diligent, shall uphold this treatise on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*) composed by you through the activity of reciting and so forth, they shall obtain great and priceless fame in this very world, and after casting off the body, they shall go to heaven (*triviṣṭapa*). Likewise, one studying this scripture, when desiring knowledge and the like, shall then obtain knowledge and the rest; wealth (*dhana*) consisting of gold and so forth; and prosperity (*śrī*), which is of many kinds: that consisting of Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*) is Brāhmaṇic; that characterized by invincibility and skill is Kṣatriya; and that characterized by material wealth is Vaiśya-prosperity. Therefore, because the word 'wealth' has already been mentioned, the word 'prosperity' is used separately. [3. 328, 329, 330]
He explains this very point:
"For whoever shall cause even these three verses to be heard during a *śrāddha* ceremony, his ancestors will attain inexhaustible satisfaction; there is no doubt about this. (3.331)
A Brāhmaṇa attains the state of being a worthy recipient, a Kṣatriya becomes victorious, and a Vaiśya becomes possessed of grain and wealth through the retention of this scripture. (3.332)
Whoever should cause all these twice-born ones to hear this on every festival day,
may you grant your approval for him to obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice.
The fifteenth lunar day is the [auspicious] *parvan*. The rest is well known. 3.331, 332, 333.
Having heard this speech of the sages, Yājñavalkya, his soul filled with joy, said,
"So be it," after having paid homage to the Self-Existent One (Brahmā).
To the self-existent Brahmā; the rest is not obscure. 3.334.
Having dispelled the turbid darkness that clings to the entire circle of the earth and obstructs the path of the virtuous,
he leads the world— which had fallen into a state of extreme disorder due to the arising of faults— to illumination, just as the sun does.
Though he is the sole lord of the universe, his kingdom is unrestrained by limits, his treasury is overflowing, his capable ally is at hand,
his army is invincible in its approach to fortresses, his ministers are devoted,
and his mind is dedicated to chewing upon the nectar of the meaning of the scriptures.
Aparāditya, whose wealth was valor, magnanimity, and fame, composed this treatise. || 2 ||

Thus ends the fifth chapter, on Expiation (*prāyaścitta*), in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkyadharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, who was born in the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the noble Vidyādhara race.
This third chapter on expiations is completed. || 3 ||
This Yājñavalkyasmṛti, together with its commentary, is completed.
